To do the same for \mathbf F(u, v) we need the “derivative” of a function of two variables that returns two numbers.

One-slide recap only; the previous unit has the details (derivation, failure modes, the secant method). The key idea to carry over: approximate the nonlinear function by a linear one, solve the linear problem exactly, repeat. Digits roughly double each step: quadratic convergence. For a system, “linear function” will mean a matrix times a vector, and “solve the linear problem” will mean solving a linear system. The missing piece is the derivative.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Partial derivatives: hold the others fixed
text:
Partial derivatives: hold the others fixed
F_1(u, v) = \dfrac{3}{1+v^2} - u depends on two numbers. Ask one question at a time:

How fast does F_1 change when only u moves? Treat v as a constant and differentiate in u as usual: \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial u} = -1
How fast does F_1 change when only v moves? Treat u as a constant (it drops out) and use the chain rule on 3(1+v^2)^{-1}: \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial v} = -\frac{3 \cdot 2v}{(1+v^2)^2} = -\frac{6v}{(1+v^2)^2}
At the point (u, v) = (3, 0.5): \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial v} = -\dfrac{6 \cdot 0.5}{1.25^2} = -\dfrac{3}{1.5625} = -1.92.

The curly \partial (“partial”) just means: other variables held fixed.

Go slowly; this is the first time many students see this. A partial derivative is nothing new: it is the ordinary derivative of a one-variable function, obtained by freezing all the other variables at numbers. Freeze v at 0.5 and F1 is 2.4 - u, a straight line with slope -1. Freeze u at 3 and F1 is 3/(1+v^2) - 3, a curve in v whose slope at v = 0.5 is -1.92. Read the units: dF1/dv = -1.92 means that raising the repressor V by 0.01 lowers F1 (the net rate of change of U) by about 0.0192. Work the chain rule on the board: d/dv (1+v2)-1 = -(1+v2)-2 * 2v.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Partial derivatives are slopes of slices
text:
Partial derivatives are slopes of slices

f1 <- function(u, v) alpha / (1 + v^2) - u
h <- 1e-6
(f1(3 + h, 0.5) - f1(3, 0.5)) / h      # move u only
# [1] -1
(f1(3, 0.5 + h) - f1(3, 0.5)) / h      # move v only
# [1] -1.92

Left: freeze v = 0.5 and plot F1 against u: a straight line, slope -1 everywhere. Right: freeze u = 3 and plot F1 against v: a curve, and the dashed tangent at v = 0.5 has slope -1.92. The code checks both numbers with a forward difference, exactly as in Convergence and cost: nudge one input, keep the other fixed, divide the change by the nudge. This is also the recipe for the finite-difference Jacobian later in the lecture. If a hand-derived partial derivative disagrees with this check in the first few digits, the hand derivation is wrong.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: The Jacobian: all partial derivatives in one matrix
text:
The Jacobian: all partial derivatives in one matrix
Row i = equation F_i, column j = variable x_j:


J = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial v} \\[8pt] \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial v}\end{pmatrix}
\phantom{J} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -\dfrac{6v}{(1+v^2)^2} \\[8pt] -\dfrac{6u}{(1+u^2)^2} & -1\end{pmatrix}
At (3, 0.5): \dfrac{6\cdot 3}{(1+9)^2} = 0.18 and \dfrac{6\cdot0.5}{1.25^2} = 1.92.

J <- function(x) {
  u <- x[1]; v <- x[2]
  matrix(c(-1, -alpha * n * v^(n - 1) / (1 + v^n)^2,
           -alpha * n * u^(n - 1) / (1 + u^n)^2, -1),
         nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
}
J(c(3, 0.5))
#       [,1]  [,2]
# [1,] -1.00 -1.92
# [2,] -0.18 -1.00


The Jacobian (after Carl Jacobi) is the multivariable version of f’(x). For n equations in n unknowns it is an n by n matrix. Check the bottom-left entry by hand: 6 * 3 / (1 + 9)^2 = 18/100 = 0.18. Read the matrix as biology: the diagonal -1 is degradation (each protein reduces its own rate of change); the off-diagonal entries are the repression strengths, how much each protein lowers the production of the other. At (3, 0.5), V at 0.5 is right on the steep part of its Hill curve, so it acts strongly on U (-1.92); U at 3 is far above threshold, the Hill curve is flat there, so a small change in U hardly matters to V (-0.18). byrow = TRUE lets us type the matrix row by row as it is printed.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
The linear approximation, with numbers
One variable: f(x + \delta) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\,\delta. Two variables, one line per equation:
\begin{aligned}
F_1(u + \delta_u, v + \delta_v) &\approx F_1 + \tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial u}\delta_u + \tfrac{\partial F_1}{\partial v}\delta_v\\
F_2(u + \delta_u, v + \delta_v) &\approx F_2 + \tfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial u}\delta_u + \tfrac{\partial F_2}{\partial v}\delta_v
\end{aligned}
In matrix form: \mathbf F(\mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \mathbf F(\mathbf x) + J\,\boldsymbol\delta (matrix J times vector \boldsymbol\delta).
x <- c(3, 0.5); d <- c(-0.1, 0.05)
F(x + d)                       # the true value
# [1] -0.5967370 -0.2311902
F(x) + J(x) %*% d              # the linear prediction
#        [,1]
# [1,] -0.596
# [2,] -0.232

Each change adds up: moving u changes F1 by (dF1/du) times the move, moving v changes it by (dF1/dv) times its move, and for small moves the two effects simply add. Written as a matrix-vector product that is J times delta. Check one entry by hand: F1 = -0.6, plus (-1)(-0.1) = +0.1, plus (-1.92)(0.05) = -0.096, total -0.596. True value -0.5967: agreement to 3 digits for a step of size 0.1; the mismatch is second order in delta, just as for the tangent line. %*% is R’s matrix product (Python: @).

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: The Newton step: one linear solve
text:
The Newton step: one linear solve
Ask for \mathbf F(\mathbf x_k + \boldsymbol\delta) = \mathbf 0 in the linear approximation:
\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k) + J(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = \mathbf 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{J(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k)}, \qquad \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k + \boldsymbol\delta







one variable
system




f(x_k), a number
\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k), a vector


f'(x_k), a number
J(\mathbf x_k), a matrix


\delta = -f/f' (divide)
solve J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F (linear system)


fails if f' = 0
fails if J is singular (\det J = 0)




Each step is a linear system, which we know how to solve (Gaussian elimination). In R: solve(J, -F).


This slide is the whole method. Division by the derivative becomes solving a linear system with the Jacobian. Write the analogy table on the board. “Singular” is the matrix version of “derivative zero”: the linear approximation then has no unique solution, and near-singular Jacobians give huge steps, just as a nearly flat tangent does in one dimension. We will see that failure later in the lecture.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
One step by hand
Start \mathbf x_0 = (3, 0.5). We have \mathbf F(\mathbf x_0) = (-0.6, -0.2) and J from before. Solve
\begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1.92 \\ -0.18 & -1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta_u\\ \delta_v\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.2 \end{pmatrix}

Row 2 minus 0.18\times row 1: (-1 + 0.3456)\,\delta_v = 0.2 - 0.108, so \delta_v = 0.092 / (-0.6544) = -0.1406.
Row 1: -\delta_u = 0.6 + 1.92\,\delta_v = 0.3301, so \delta_u = -0.3301.
\mathbf x_1 = (3 - 0.3301,\; 0.5 - 0.1406) = (2.6699,\; 0.3594).

delta <- solve(J(c(3, 0.5)), -F(c(3, 0.5)))
delta
# [1] -0.3300733 -0.1405868
F(c(3, 0.5) + delta)              # residual: was (-0.6, -0.2)
# [1] -0.013126396  0.009658204

Gaussian elimination on a 2 by 2 system, as in a first linear algebra course. The residual went from size 0.6 to size 0.013 in one step. The exact steady state is (2.6180, 0.3820), so the error went from 0.4 to 0.05. Students repeat this by hand in the exercise and do a second step. Note: never compute the inverse matrix; solve(J, b) solves the system directly. Why that matters is a topic of Gaussian elimination as LU.

title: Newton for systems of equations
Newton for systems of equations
Newton for systems of equations
section: Three steady states: which one do we get?
text:
Three steady states: which one do we get?
starts <- rbind(c(3, 0.5), c(0.5, 3), c(1, 1), c(1, 0.2), c(4, 4))
t(apply(starts, 1, function(s) newton_sys(F, J, s)))   # (printing switched off)
#          [,1]     [,2]
# [1,] 2.618034 0.381966       U on, V off
# [2,] 0.381966 2.618034       V on, U off
# [3,] 1.213412 1.213412       middle
# [4,] 0.381966 2.618034       V on: although U > V at the start!
# [5,] 1.213412 1.213412       middle

Bistable: two “decided” states, plus the middle one. Newton finds one root per start.
To find them all: run from many starts and collect the distinct answers.
The start (1, 0.2) has more U than V, yet Newton lands on “V on”. Newton’s choice is not the cell’s choice.


The apply line runs Newton from each row of starts (the cat line is switched off for this slide). The first two answers are mirror images: the model is symmetric under swapping u and v. The middle state has u = v = 1.2134, the real root of u^3 + u - 3 = 0. A start on the diagonal u = v stays on the diagonal for ever (by symmetry), so (1,1) and (4,4) can only find the middle state. The fourth start is the interesting one: biologically a cell with U = 1 and V = 0.2 will switch U on, but Newton jumps to the other state. Next slide shows why.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Where Newton goes vs where the cell goes
text:
Where Newton goes vs where the cell goes


Left: colour = the steady state Newton converges to from that start. Right: where the ODE (the cell) ends up.
Newton’s regions (basins) are curved, with thin bands of all colours; the middle, unstable state takes 57 % of this square.


Each pixel is a start (u0, v0); colour = the root reached. Right panel: simulate the ODE from the same start; the line u = v separates the two fates (by symmetry), and nobody ever ends in the middle state because it is unstable: the slightest push sends the cell to one side. Left panel: Newton’s basins have nothing to do with that. Newton is a root finder: it finds points where F = 0, stable or unstable, and the middle state, with 57 percent of the square, is the most common answer. Near the boundaries, thin interleaved bands appear, where tiny changes of the start change the answer. Lesson: Newton tells you where the steady states are, not which one the cell goes to, nor whether a steady state is stable. Stability needs the eigenvalues of the Jacobian: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Bistability needs a strong promoter




Run Newton from a 7 × 7 grid of starts for each promoter strength \alpha, keep the distinct roots.

\alpha < 2: one steady state; the circuit is not a switch.
\alpha > 2: three; the circuit is bistable.
Designing the switch (Gardner et al.) meant tuning promoters until the circuit was in the bistable range.



This is the biological payoff: the number of steady states is a property you can compute, and it decides whether the circuit works as a memory. Gardner and colleagues showed exactly this kind of diagram for their toggle and picked promoters and ribosome binding sites to sit inside the bistable region. For this symmetric model with n = 2 the threshold is exactly alpha = 2 (the exercise shows why: the outer states satisfy u + v = alpha, uv = 1, which has real solutions only for alpha >= 2). With n = 1 (no cooperativity) there is never bistability. The multi-start loop is the honest way to count roots when you do not have a formula, and it can miss roots whose basins your starts do not touch.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: No formula for J? Finite differences
text:
No formula for J? Finite differences
Often \mathbf F is a long function (a 20-gene network, a model with many terms) and deriving J by hand is tedious and error-prone. Approximate column j by nudging only x_j:
J_{:,j} \approx \frac{\mathbf F(\mathbf x + h_j\,\mathbf e_j) - \mathbf F(\mathbf x)}{h_j}, \qquad h_j = \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\max(|x_j|, 1) \approx 1.5\times10^{-8}\max(|x_j|, 1)
(\mathbf e_j = 1 in place j, 0 elsewhere.)

One nudge gives a whole column: how every equation responds to x_j.
Cost: n + 1 evaluations of \mathbf F per Jacobian.
h = \sqrt\varepsilon balances truncation and rounding error (Convergence and cost): about 8 correct digits.


This is the forward difference from Convergence and cost, applied one variable at a time. Column j, not row: moving one input changes all outputs at once. Scaling h with the size of x_j keeps the nudge relative: a concentration of 1000 needs a bigger absolute nudge than one of 0.001. For n genes the Jacobian costs n + 1 function evaluations; for big models (or expensive F, like an ODE solve) this dominates, which is why library codes reuse a Jacobian over several steps (Broyden’s method, quasi-Newton in Part 9). Central differences give more digits for twice the cost; see Numerical differentiation.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Finite-difference Jacobian in R


fd_jacobian <- function(F, x,
                        h = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)) {
  Fx <- F(x)
  Jm <- matrix(0, length(Fx), length(x))
  for (j in seq_along(x)) {
    hj <- h * max(abs(x[j]), 1)
    xh <- x; xh[j] <- x[j] + hj
    Jm[, j] <- (F(xh) - Fx) / hj     # column j
  }
  Jm
}
max(abs(fd_jacobian(F, c(3, 0.5)) - J(c(3, 0.5))))
# [1] 1.311302e-08




Use it also to check a hand-derived J: a wrong entry shows up as an error much larger than 10^{-7}.


Twelve lines, and it works for any F of any size. The error 1.3e-8 is what sqrt(eps) predicts. The figure shows the same V as in Convergence and cost: truncation error on the right (slope 1), rounding error on the left (slope -1), best near h = 1.5e-8. Comparing a hand-written Jacobian with the finite-difference one is the standard bug check before trusting a Newton code: a sign error or a missing factor gives a difference of order 1, not 1e-8. numDeriv::jacobian in R does this with a more accurate (Richardson) scheme.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: The cost of a step: one linear solve
text:
The cost of a step: one linear solve
Per Newton step for n genes:







part
cost




evaluate \mathbf F
depends on the model, often \sim n


Jacobian by finite differences
n + 1 evaluations of \mathbf F


solve J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F (Gaussian elimination)
\approx \tfrac23 n^3 operations




n = 2: nothing. n = 1000: \approx 7\times10^8 per step, still under a second. n = 20\,000: hours, unless J is sparse (most genes do not regulate most others).
Never form solve(J) (the inverse) and multiply: solve(J, -F) is cheaper and more accurate.


For small networks the cost is irrelevant. For genome-scale models the linear solve dominates, and the structure of J matters: a gene regulatory network has few edges, so J is mostly zeros, and sparse solvers are vastly faster. The why and how of these costs (LU factorisation, why not the inverse, sparsity) is Part 3: Gaussian elimination as LU and Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse. Today: one step = one linear solve.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
The library routine: rootSolve::multiroot
library(rootSolve)
sol <- multiroot(f = F, start = c(3, 0.5))      # Jacobian by finite differences
sol$root;  sol$f.root;  sol$iter
# [1] 2.618034 0.381966
# [1] -1.471712e-12  8.891221e-13
# [1] 5
sol2 <- multiroot(f = F, start = c(3, 0.5), jacfunc = J)  # supply your own J

multiroot is Newton–Raphson with a finite-difference Jacobian (unless you pass jacfunc), plus tolerances (rtol, atol, ctol), an iteration limit and sparse-Jacobian options for large models.
It stops at its own tolerance: here \|\mathbf F\| \approx 10^{-12}, not 10^{-16}. Check f.root, and set atol tighter if you need it.
It finds one root, from your start. Multiple starts are still your job.


rootSolve was written for steady states of ODE models (it has runsteady and stode for that purpose too). The output list has root, f.root (the residual at the root), iter and estim.precis. Default tolerances are about 1e-8 absolute, so the answer is correct to about 12 digits here, which is plenty for biology but worth knowing. Python users: scipy.optimize.root (default method hybr, Powell’s hybrid method from MINPACK, which adds a trust region so that it cannot take arbitrarily large steps) or the older fsolve. Neither knows about multiple steady states.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Failure 1: a nearly singular Jacobian
x0 <- c(1.9, 0.5)
det(J(x0))                          # close to 0
# [1] -0.02992175
x0 + solve(J(x0), -F(x0))           # the first step
# [1] -5.136430  4.425224           # negative concentration!
newton_sys(F, J, c(1.9, 0.5))       # ends in the middle state
newton_sys(F, J, c(2.0, 0.55))      # a nearby start: "U on"

\det J \approx 0: the linear model is nearly flat in some direction, so the step is huge. It lands at u < 0, which is not a concentration.
With a non-integer Hill coefficient (n = 2.5) the same kind of jump gives (-3.2)^{2.5} = NaN, and Newton returns NaN.
Check: watch \|\boldsymbol\delta\| and \det J (or the condition number); check all(is.finite(x)) and all(x >= 0).


The analogue of a flat tangent in 1-D. Near the curve where det J = 0 (here det J = 1 - (dF1/dv)(dF2/du)), the Newton step blows up. This is where the thin coloured bands of the basin picture come from: start near det J = 0 and you are thrown far away, and from there you can end anywhere. Two starts 0.1 apart end in different steady states. Negative concentrations are a sign the iteration has left the biologically meaningful region; with v^2 it happens to recover, but with x^2.5 negative numbers give NaN. Remedies used by library codes: damping (take only part of the step if the residual does not decrease), trust regions (scipy’s hybr), or working with log-concentrations so that they stay positive. In rootSolve: multiroot(F, c(2, 0.5)) with n = 2.5 warns “steady-state not reached”; multiroot(F, c(2, 0.5), positive = TRUE) keeps the iterates non-negative and converges to (2.955, 0.187).

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Failure 2: a root, but not the one you wanted
text:
Failure 2: a root, but not the one you wanted

Newton from (1, 1), (2, 2) or (4, 4) converges, quickly and correctly, to the middle state (1.2134, 1.2134): a start with u = v stays on the diagonal by symmetry.
The residual is 10^{-16}: nothing in the output warns you that this state is unstable, i.e. that no real cell sits there.
A single run hides the other two states completely: you would conclude the switch is not bistable.

Checks

Run from many starts (a grid, or random) and list the distinct roots.
Check each root for stability: eigenvalues of J at the root (Equilibria, stability and the phase plane), or a short ODE simulation from a nearby point.


This failure is the worse one, because everything looks fine: quadratic convergence, residual at machine precision. In practice people start from a symmetric guess (all genes equal, all at 1) more often than you would think. The cure is not a better root finder but a better procedure: many starts, deduplicate, then classify each root. Here the middle state is a saddle: J there has eigenvalues 0.19 and -2.19, one positive. That calculation is the topic of the phase-plane unit.

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Checklist for Newton on a system
text:
Checklist for Newton on a system

Check J against a finite-difference Jacobian before anything else (difference \sim 10^{-8}, not \sim 1).
Watch the iteration: \|\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k)\| should fall fast (digits double). If it grows or stalls, the start is too far or J is wrong.
Look at the root: finite, non-negative, residual small (f.root in multiroot).
Large steps / tiny \det J → the start is near a singular Jacobian; try another start or a damped/trust-region solver.
Many starts → collect distinct roots; one run finds one root.
Stability is a separate question: a root of \mathbf F is not necessarily where the cell goes.


A practical list to go through whenever a steady-state computation is part of an analysis. The first item catches most bugs in hand-written Newton codes. The last two items are about the biology: counting and classifying steady states.

title: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Summary

A partial derivative \partial F_i/\partial x_j is an ordinary derivative with all other variables held fixed. The Jacobian J collects them: row = equation, column = variable.
Linearise: \mathbf F(\mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \mathbf F(\mathbf x) + J\boldsymbol\delta. Newton step: solve J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F, set \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta. One linear solve per step: solve(J(x), -F(x)).
Convergence is quadratic near a root, as in one variable.
Finite-difference Jacobian: one column per nudge, h = \sqrt\varepsilon\max(|x_j|, 1), about 8 correct digits, n + 1 evaluations of \mathbf F.
Library: rootSolve::multiroot (R), scipy.optimize.root (Python).
The toggle switch has three steady states when \alpha > 2 (bistable). Which one Newton finds depends on the start, in complicated ways, and it finds unstable states as happily as stable ones.
Failures: nearly singular J (huge steps, negative concentrations, NaN), and converging to a root you did not want. Checks: step size, positivity, many starts.

Next: Part 3, Gaussian elimination as LU: what solve does inside, and what it costs.

Recap the three new objects: partial derivative, Jacobian, Newton step as a linear solve. The toggle switch comes back in Equilibria, stability and the phase plane, where the Jacobian at each steady state decides its stability, and the Jacobian comes back in Part 9 as the derivative of a gradient (the Hessian) in Newton’s method for optimisation. Part 3 opens the black box solve.

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

explain why Gaussian elimination without pivoting fails on a tiny pivot, and show it with 3-digit arithmetic,
carry out partial pivoting by hand and write \(PA = LU\) for a \(3\times 3\) matrix,
compute the 1-, 2- and \(\infty\)-norms of a vector and the 1- and \(\infty\)-norms of a matrix,
compute the condition number \(\kappa(A)\) of a \(2\times2\) matrix by hand and with kappa() / np.linalg.cond / nalgebra’s singular_values(),
use the rule “lose about \(\log_{10}\kappa\) digits” for rounding errors and for measurement noise,
tell the residual from the error, and say what each one checks,
predict how much detector noise is amplified when unmixing dyes with overlapping spectra.

The by-hand part uses pen and paper (and a calculator for B1, where you must round to 3 digits on purpose). The code part checks the hand answers and then works at sizes where only code works.

text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

tell the residual from the error, and say what each one checks,

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
By hand
B1. A tiny pivot in 3-digit arithmetic. Solve \[\begin{pmatrix}0.0001 & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\] on a “computer” that rounds every intermediate result to 3 significant digits. (a) Without pivoting: compute the multiplier, the new row 2, then \(x_2\) and \(x_1\). (b) With partial pivoting: swap the rows first and repeat. (c) The exact solution is \(x_1 = 1/0.9999 = 1.0001\ldots\), \(x_2 = 0.9998/0.9999 = 0.9999\ldots\). Which answer is right to 3 digits? Where exactly was the information lost in (a)?
B2. \(PA = LU\) by hand. Use partial pivoting on \[A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 & 1\\ 4 & 3 & 3\\ 8 & 7 & 9\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf b = \begin{pmatrix}4\\10\\24\end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Which row becomes the first pivot row? Eliminate column 1 and write down the multipliers. (b) Which row becomes the second pivot row? Eliminate column 2. (c) Write \(P\), \(L\) (unit lower triangular, holding the multipliers) and \(U\). Check that \(PA = LU\) in at least one row. (d) Solve \(A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\) using \(L\mathbf y = P\mathbf b\) and \(U\mathbf x = \mathbf y\).
B3. Vector norms. (a) Compute \(\|\mathbf v\|_1\), \(\|\mathbf v\|_2\) and \(\|\mathbf v\|_\infty\) for \(\mathbf v = (3, -4, 12)\) and for \(\mathbf w = (1, 1, 1, 1)\). (b) Two dyes, true amounts \(\mathbf x = (1, 1)\), unmixed \(\hat{\mathbf x} = (1.2, 0.8)\). Compute the relative error in all three norms. (c) Sketch the sets \(\|\mathbf v\| = 1\) in 2D for the three norms. For which vectors is \(\|\mathbf v\|_1 = \|\mathbf v\|_\infty\)?
B4. The condition number of the two-dye matrix. \(A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.95\\ 0.95 & 1\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Compute \(\|A\|_1\) and \(\|A\|_\infty\). (b) Compute \(A^{-1}\) (fact 7), then \(\|A^{-1}\|_\infty\) and \(\kappa_\infty(A)\). (c) The eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(1 + 0.95\) and \(1 - 0.95\), with eigenvectors \((1, 1)\) and \((1, -1)\). What are \(\sigma_{\max}\), \(\sigma_{\min}\) and \(\kappa_2(A)\)? (d) For general overlap \(0 \le c < 1\), show that \(\kappa_2 = (1 + c)/(1 - c)\). Evaluate it for \(c = 0.5, 0.9, 0.99\). (e) The detector readings have 3 significant digits. About how many digits of the dye amounts can you trust for \(c = 0.5\), \(0.95\) and \(0.99\)?
B5. Worst and best directions. Keep \(A\) from B4 and \(\mathbf b = (1.95, 1.95)\), so \(\mathbf x = (1, 1)\). Use the 2-norm. (a) For \(\Delta\mathbf b = (0.01, -0.01)\), find \(\Delta\mathbf x = A^{-1}\Delta\mathbf b\) and the amplification \(\dfrac{\|\Delta\mathbf x\|/\|\mathbf x\|}{\|\Delta\mathbf b\|/\|\mathbf b\|}\). (b) Same for \(\Delta\mathbf b = (0.01, 0.01)\). (c) Explain the two answers with the eigenvectors from B4(c). What kind of detector error is dangerous?
B6. Residual vs error. Still \(A\) from B4, \(\mathbf b = (1.95, 1.95)\), true \(\mathbf x = (1, 1)\). Two programs return \(\hat{\mathbf x}_a = (1.2, 0.8)\) and \(\hat{\mathbf x}_b = (1.01, 1.01)\). (a) Compute both residuals \(\mathbf r = \mathbf b - A\hat{\mathbf x}\) and the relative residuals \(\|\mathbf r\|_\infty/\|\mathbf b\|_\infty\). (b) Compute both relative errors \(\|\hat{\mathbf x} - \mathbf x\|_\infty/\|\mathbf x\|_\infty\). (c) Which answer would you pick by looking at the residual? Check the bound \(\text{error} \le \kappa_\infty \times \text{residual}\) for \(\hat{\mathbf x}_a\).
B7. A zero pivot in a well-conditioned matrix. Detector 1 sees no dye 1: \[A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0.3\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf b = \begin{pmatrix}1\\1.3\end{pmatrix}.\] (a) What happens if you eliminate without pivoting? (b) Solve with partial pivoting. (c) Compute \(\kappa_\infty(A)\). Is the problem hard? Whose fault was the failure in (a)?

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
In code
C1. Elimination without pivoting. Write solve_nopivot(A, b) (elimination, then back substitution). For \(A = \begin{pmatrix}\delta & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\mathbf b = (1, 2)\) and \(\delta = 10^{-2}, 10^{-5}, \ldots, 10^{-20}\), compute the relative error (2-norm) against the exact solution \(x_1 = 1/(1-\delta)\), \(x_2 = (1-2\delta)/(1-\delta)\), and compare it with \(\varepsilon/\delta\).
C2. Partial pivoting. (a) Add partial pivoting to your function (solve_pivot) and repeat C1. (b) Solve B2 with solve_pivot and compare \(P\), \(L\) and \(U\) with a library: Matrix::lu with expand() in R, scipy.linalg.lu in Python, nalgebra’s lu() with .l(), .u(), .p() in Rust. Careful: R and scipy return \(A = PLU\), so their \(P\) is the transpose of ours.
C3. Norms. (a) Check B3(a)–(b) in code. (b) Compute \(\|A\|_1\), \(\|A\|_\infty\) and \(\|A\|_2\) of the two-dye matrix from the formulas (column sums, row sums, largest singular value) and with norm() / np.linalg.norm. (c) The 2-norm as the largest stretch. Compute \(\|A\mathbf v\|_2\) for 1001 unit vectors \(\mathbf v = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\), \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi]\). Compare the largest and smallest values with \(\sigma_{\max}\) and \(\sigma_{\min}\).
C4. Condition number and overlap. For \(c = 0.5, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99, 0.999\), compute \(\kappa_2\) of \(\begin{pmatrix}1 & c\\ c & 1\end{pmatrix}\) with kappa(A, exact = TRUE) (Python: np.linalg.cond(A); Rust: largest over smallest of singular_values()) and compare with \((1+c)/(1-c)\) from B4(d). In R, also print the default estimate kappa(A) and 1 / rcond(A); in Python, np.linalg.cond(A, 1).
C5. Lose \(\log_{10}\kappa\) digits. A panel of 6 dyes with Gaussian emission spectra (width 30 nm), detectors at the peaks, peaks spacing nm apart:
\[A_{ij} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(p_i - p_j)^2}{2\cdot 30^2}\right), \qquad p_i = 500 + \text{spacing}\cdot(i - 1).\]
For spacing \(= 60, 30, 20, 10, 5\) nm, take the true amounts \(\mathbf x = (5, 1, 3, 2, 4, 1)\), compute \(\mathbf b = A\mathbf x\), solve, and print \(\kappa\), the relative error, the number of correct digits \(-\log_{10}(\text{error})\) and the prediction \(16 - \log_{10}\kappa\).
C6. Residual vs error. For the panel with spacing 6 nm, solve as in C5 and print \(\kappa\), the relative residual \(\|\mathbf b - A\hat{\mathbf x}\|/\|\mathbf b\|\), the relative error, and the bound \(\kappa\times\) residual. What does the residual tell you about solve()? What does it tell you about the answer?
C7. Detector noise in unmixed cells. Simulate 1000 cells that all carry 1 unit of each of two dyes. Add independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.01 to both detector readings of every cell, and unmix all cells with \(c = 0.5\) and with \(c = 0.95\). Compare the standard deviation of the unmixed dye 1 with the prediction \(0.01 \times \|\text{row 1 of } A^{-1}\|_2\) and with \(\kappa\).

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — 3-digit arithmetic (B1)





Round after every operation: \(1 - 10000 = -9999\) becomes \(-1.00\times10^4\) with 3 significant digits. Keep the exact numbers next to the rounded ones so you see which digits disappear.









Hint 2 — partial pivoting by hand (B2, B7)





At step \(k\), look only at column \(k\) from the diagonal down. Swap the row with the largest \(|a_{ik}|\) into position \(k\) (swap the whole row, including \(b_i\), and the multipliers already stored in that row of \(L\)). \(P\) is the identity with its rows in the final pivot order; \(P\mathbf b\) is \(\mathbf b\) in that order.









Hint 3 — norms of a 2 × 2 matrix (B4, C3)





1-norm: add the absolute values in each column, take the largest. \(\infty\)-norm: same with rows. For a symmetric matrix, the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues. In code: R norm(A, "1"), norm(A, "I"), norm(A, "2") and svd(A)$d; Python np.linalg.norm(A, 1), np.linalg.norm(A, np.inf), np.linalg.norm(A, 2) and np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False); Rust nalgebra v.lp_norm(1), v.norm(), v.amax(), a.singular_values() (docs).









Hint 4 — κ for overlap c (B4(d))





The eigenvalues of \(\begin{pmatrix}1 & c\\ c & 1\end{pmatrix}\) are \(1 + c\) (eigenvector \((1, 1)\)) and \(1 - c\) (eigenvector \((1, -1)\)). Check by multiplying.









Hint 5 — writing the elimination (C1, C2)





Loop over \(k = 1, \ldots, n-1\) and \(i = k+1, \ldots, n\). Back substitution runs \(i = n, \ldots, 1\): \(x_i = (b_i - \sum_{j>i} a_{ij}x_j)/a_{ii}\). R has backsolve() for the last step, Python scipy.linalg.solve_triangular. To find the pivot row: which.max(abs(A[k:n, k])) + k - 1 in R, k + np.argmax(np.abs(A[k:, k])) in Python. Swap rows with A[c(k, p), ] <- A[c(p, k), ] (R) or A[[k, p], :] = A[[p, k], :] (Python). In Python, copy the inputs first (A = A.astype(float).copy()), or you will overwrite the caller’s matrix.









Hint 6 — building the spectra matrix (C5, C6)





R: outer(p, p, function(d, q) exp(-(d - q)^2 / (2 * 30^2))). Python: broadcasting, np.exp(-(p[:, None] - p[None, :])**2 / (2 * 30**2)). Rust: DMatrix::from_fn(n, n, |i, j| ...). The relative error is sqrt(sum((xh - x)^2)) / sqrt(sum(x^2)) in R and np.linalg.norm(xh - x) / np.linalg.norm(x) in Python.









Hint 7 — many cells at once (C7)





Put the readings of all cells in a \(2\times 1000\) matrix \(B\) (one column per cell); solve(A, B) (R) or np.linalg.solve(A, B) (Python) solves all 1000 systems with one LU factorisation. Generate the noise with rnorm(2 * 1000, sd = 0.01) (R) or rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=(2, 1000)) (Python).

title: Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
Exercise: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
Where this leads

Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse (next unit): the same LU machinery, made faster when \(A\) is symmetric positive definite (Cholesky needs no pivoting) or banded or sparse.
Least squares: normal equations vs QR (Part 4): spectral cytometers have more detectors than dyes, so unmixing becomes least squares (that unit teaches the method on calibration curves rather than spectra). Forming the normal equations \(A^\top A\) squares the condition number; QR avoids that.
The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation (Part 4): the singular values used here as numbers get their full meaning, and regularisation trades a little bias for much less noise when \(\kappa\) is large.
Every Newton step in Newton for systems of equations (Part 2) solves a linear system with the Jacobian; a large \(\kappa\) there means an inaccurate step. In Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (Part 9), a nearly singular matrix means parameters the data cannot pin down.

title: Quiz: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of partial derivatives, the Jacobian and Newton’s method for systems. The toggle switch is \(F_1 = \dfrac{3}{1+v^2} - u\), \(F_2 = \dfrac{3}{1+u^2} - v\). Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is \(\dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}\big(u^2 v^3\big)\), and what is its value at \((u, v) = (2, 1)\)?






Hint





Treat \(v\) as a fixed number.









Answer





\(2u v^3\); at \((2, 1)\) it is \(4\). (\(v^3\) is a constant factor, like the 5 in \(5u^2\).)




Q2. In the toggle switch, \(\partial F_1/\partial u = -1\) everywhere. What biological process does this entry describe, and why is it constant?






Hint





Which term of \(du/dt\) contains \(u\)?









Answer





Degradation and dilution of protein U: the term \(-u\) in \(du/dt\). It is linear in \(u\) (first-order decay, rate 1 in the chosen time units), so its derivative is the constant \(-1\). Production of U depends only on \(v\), so it does not contribute to \(\partial F_1/\partial u\).




Q3. For a model of 50 genes (50 equations in 50 unknowns), what is the size of the Jacobian? What does entry \((7, 12)\) tell you?






Hint





Row = equation, column = variable.









Answer





\(50 \times 50\). Entry \((7, 12)\) is \(\partial F_7/\partial x_{12}\): how fast the net rate of change of gene 7 responds to a change in the level of gene 12. If gene 12 does not regulate gene 7, it is 0, so for a sparse network most entries are 0.




Q4. In one-variable Newton we divide by \(f'(x_k)\). What replaces the division in Newton for systems, and when does it fail?






Hint





What is the “derivative” of \(\mathbf F\), and how do you “divide” by a matrix?









Answer





Solving the linear system \(J(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k)\): in R, solve(J(x), -F(x)). It fails when \(J\) is singular (\(\det J = 0\), the analogue of \(f' = 0\)), and behaves badly when \(J\) is nearly singular: the step becomes huge.




Q5. Newton for the toggle switch gives these errors: \(4\times10^{-1}\), \(6\times10^{-2}\), \(2\times10^{-3}\), \(3\times10^{-6}\), \(6\times10^{-12}\). What kind of convergence is this, and roughly what will the next error be?






Hint





Look at the exponents.









Answer





Quadratic: the exponent roughly doubles each step (\(-3 \to -6 \to -12\)), \(e_{k+1} \approx C e_k^2\) with \(C \approx 0.66\). The next would be about \(0.66 \cdot (6\times10^{-12})^2 \approx 2\times10^{-23}\), but rounding stops it at about \(10^{-16}\).




Q6. You approximate the Jacobian of a 10-gene model by forward differences. How many evaluations of \(\mathbf F\) does one Jacobian cost, which step \(h\) do you use, and about how many correct digits do you get?






Hint





One nudge per variable, plus the unshifted point. The step balances truncation and rounding error.









Answer





11 evaluations (\(n + 1\)). \(h_j = \sqrt\varepsilon\,\max(|x_j|, 1) \approx 1.5\times10^{-8}\max(|x_j|, 1)\). About 8 correct digits (half of the 16), which is enough for Newton to converge practically as fast as with the exact Jacobian.




Q7. A Newton run for the toggle switch from \((u_0, v_0) = (2, 2)\) converges to \((1.2134, 1.2134)\) with residual \(10^{-16}\). A colleague concludes that the switch has one steady state. What is wrong with that conclusion?






Hint





What happens to a Newton iterate that starts with \(u = v\)?









Answer





One Newton run finds one root. From a start with \(u = v\) every iterate stays on the diagonal (by symmetry), so it can only find the symmetric middle state. The switch also has \((2.618, 0.382)\) and \((0.382, 2.618)\), the two stable states. Run from many starts and collect the distinct roots. Also, the middle state is unstable: no real cell sits there.




Q8. True or false: “Newton converges to the steady state that the cell would reach from the same starting concentrations.”






Hint





Recall the two basin pictures in the lecture.









Answer





False. Newton follows tangent-plane jumps, not the dynamics. From \((1, 0.2)\) the cell switches U on, but Newton lands on “V on”; and more than half of the starts in \([0, 4]^2\) go to the unstable middle state, which the cell never reaches. Newton locates steady states; stability is a separate question (eigenvalues of \(J\), Equilibria, stability and the phase plane).




Q9. A Newton step takes \((u, v)\) from \((1.9, 0.5)\) to \((-5.14, 4.43)\). What went wrong, and what two checks would have flagged it?






Hint





What is \(\det J\) at the start? What do you know about concentrations?









Answer





The Jacobian at the start is nearly singular (\(\det J \approx -0.03\)), so the linear model is almost flat in one direction and the step is huge. Checks: the step length \(\|\boldsymbol\delta\| \approx 8\) is far larger than the scale of the problem; and \(u < 0\) is not a concentration (check all(x >= 0) and all(is.finite(x))). A damped step or a trust-region solver avoids this.




Q10. multiroot returns root = 2.61803398875534 0.38196601124783 with f.root about \(10^{-12}\). The exact root is \((2.618033988749895, 0.381966011250105)\). Is multiroot broken?






Hint





Look up its default tolerances.









Answer





No. It stopped when its tolerances (atol \(= 10^{-8}\), rtol \(= 10^{-6}\) by default) were met, which here left an error of about \(5\times10^{-12}\): 11–12 correct digits. That is plenty for biology; if you need more, pass tighter atol/rtol and the exact jacfunc. Always look at f.root.




Q11. For the symmetric toggle switch with \(n = 2\), the two “decided” steady states satisfy \(u + v = \alpha\) and \(uv = 1\). For which promoter strengths \(\alpha\) is the switch bistable, and why does Newton struggle exactly at the boundary?






Hint





When does \(t^2 - \alpha t + 1 = 0\) have real roots? What is \(\det J\) at \(u = v = 1\) for \(\alpha = 2\)?









Answer





Bistable for \(\alpha > 2\) (real roots need \(\alpha^2 \ge 4\)). At \(\alpha = 2\) the three states merge at \((1, 1)\), where the off-diagonal entries of \(J\) are \(-2\cdot2\cdot1/(1+1)^2 = -1\), so \(\det J = 1 - 1 = 0\): the Jacobian is singular at the root. Like a double root in one variable, Newton then converges only linearly.

title: Quiz: pivoting, norms and conditioning
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of pivoting, norms and condition numbers. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Gaussian elimination without pivoting on \(\begin{pmatrix}10^{-20} & 1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\mathbf x = \begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) returns \(\mathbf x = (0, 1)\) instead of about \((1, 1)\). Is this matrix ill-conditioned?






Hint





What happens to the same system if you just swap the two equations?









Answer





No. Its condition number is about 2.6; with the rows swapped, elimination gives \((1, 1)\) to full precision. The failure is the algorithm’s: the multiplier \(10^{20}\) swamps row 2, so \(1 - 10^{20}\) and \(2 - 10^{20}\) both round to \(-10^{20}\) and the information in row 2 is lost. Elimination without pivoting is unstable.




Q2. State the rule of partial pivoting in one sentence. What does it guarantee about the multipliers?






Hint





Which entry of column \(k\) becomes the pivot?









Answer





Before eliminating column \(k\), swap rows so that the entry of largest absolute value in column \(k\), on or below the diagonal, becomes the pivot. Then every multiplier \(m = a_{ik}/a_{kk}\) has \(|m| \le 1\), so no row is scaled up and added to another, and rounding errors stay small. The swaps give \(PA = LU\).




Q3. For \(\mathbf v = (2, -6, 3)\), compute \(\|\mathbf v\|_1\), \(\|\mathbf v\|_2\) and \(\|\mathbf v\|_\infty\).






Hint





Sum of absolute values; square root of the sum of squares; largest absolute value.









Answer





\(\|\mathbf v\|_1 = 2 + 6 + 3 = 11\), \(\|\mathbf v\|_2 = \sqrt{4 + 36 + 9} = 7\), \(\|\mathbf v\|_\infty = 6\). As always, \(\|\mathbf v\|_\infty \le \|\mathbf v\|_2 \le \|\mathbf v\|_1\).




Q4. Compute \(\|A\|_1\) and \(\|A\|_\infty\) for \(A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -3\\ 2 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}\).






Hint





1-norm: columns. \(\infty\)-norm: rows. Use absolute values.









Answer





Column sums \(|1| + |2| = 3\) and \(|-3| + |0.5| = 3.5\), so \(\|A\|_1 = 3.5\). Row sums \(1 + 3 = 4\) and \(2 + 0.5 = 2.5\), so \(\|A\|_\infty = 4\).




Q5. Two dyes with overlap \(c\) give \(A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & c\\ c & 1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\kappa_2 = (1 + c)/(1 - c)\). What is \(\kappa\) for \(c = 0.8\)? With detector readings good to 3 significant digits, roughly how many digits of the unmixed abundances can you trust?






Hint





Digits left \(\approx\) digits in the data \(- \log_{10}\kappa\).









Answer





\(\kappa = 1.8/0.2 = 9\), \(\log_{10} 9 \approx 0.95\), so about \(3 - 1 = 2\) digits. With \(c = 0.95\) (\(\kappa = 39\)) it would be about 1.4 digits, and with \(c = 0.99\) (\(\kappa = 199\)) less than one.




Q6. True or false: “If my solver uses partial pivoting, the computed solution is accurate to about 16 digits.”






Hint





Pivoting makes the algorithm stable. Does it change the problem?









Answer





False. Partial pivoting makes the algorithm backward stable: the answer is the exact solution of a system within rounding distance of yours. The forward error can still be about \(\kappa\,\varepsilon\), so with \(\kappa = 10^{10}\) you have about 6 correct digits. And if \(\mathbf b\) comes from measurements, the error is about \(\kappa\) times the measurement error, however the system is solved.




Q7. You solve \(A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\) and find a relative residual \(\|\mathbf b - A\hat{\mathbf x}\|/\|\mathbf b\| = 10^{-16}\). kappa(A) is \(10^{12}\). How large can the relative error of \(\hat{\mathbf x}\) be? What does the small residual tell you?






Hint





Error \(\le \kappa \times\) residual.









Answer





Up to about \(10^{12} \times 10^{-16} = 10^{-4}\): only about 4 correct digits. The tiny residual says the solver worked (it is backward stable, as LU with partial pivoting should be); it does not say the answer is accurate. A small residual certifies a small error only when \(\kappa\) is small.




Q8. For the two-dye matrix with overlap 0.95, a perturbation \(\Delta\mathbf b = (0.01, -0.01)\) of \(\mathbf b = (1.95, 1.95)\) is amplified 39 times, but \(\Delta\mathbf b = (0.01, 0.01)\) is not amplified at all. Explain.






Hint





The eigenvectors of \(A\) are \((1, 1)\) (eigenvalue 1.95) and \((1, -1)\) (eigenvalue 0.05). Solving divides by the eigenvalue.









Answer





Solving \(A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\) divides each eigen-component of \(\mathbf b\) by its eigenvalue. \(\mathbf b\) and the second \(\Delta\mathbf b\) both lie along \((1, 1)\), so both are divided by 1.95 and their ratio is unchanged (factor 1). The first \(\Delta\mathbf b\) lies along \((1, -1)\) and is divided by 0.05, so it grows 1.95/0.05 = 39 times more than \(\mathbf b\) does. Anti-correlated detector errors are the dangerous ones: the detectors see the sum of the two dyes well, but their difference badly.




Q9. R gives kappa(A) \(= 39.95\) but kappa(A, exact = TRUE) \(= 39\). Which should you report, and does the difference matter?






Hint





What do you use \(\kappa\) for?









Answer





kappa(A) without exact = TRUE is a cheap estimate; exact = TRUE computes \(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}\) from the singular values. For the digits rule (\(\log_{10} 39 = 1.59\) vs \(\log_{10} 39.95 = 1.60\)) the difference is irrelevant; the estimate is usually within a small factor. Use the exact value for small matrices if you want to quote it, the estimate (or 1/rcond(A)) for large ones. In Python, np.linalg.cond(A) is exact (2-norm).




Q10. A spectral panel has \(\kappa = 500\). The cytometer’s detectors have about 1 % noise. A colleague suggests solving the unmixing in quadruple precision to get more accurate abundances. Will it help? What would?






Hint





Where does the error in \(\hat{\mathbf x}\) come from: rounding, or the data?









Answer





No. In double precision the rounding error is at most about \(500 \times 10^{-16}\), already negligible. The error comes from the 1 % detector noise amplified by up to \(\kappa\): up to about \(500 \times 1\,\% = 500\,\%\) in the worst direction. That is the conditioning of the problem, and no arithmetic can fix it. What helps is changing the problem: dyes with more distinct spectra (smaller overlap, smaller \(\kappa\)), more detectors than dyes (least squares, Part 4), less noisy measurements, or regularisation (The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation).




Q11. Why do spectral flow cytometry plots of unmixed data often show populations smeared out along a diagonal, including negative values, for dyes with similar spectra?






Hint





Look at the inverse of \(\begin{pmatrix}1 & 0.95\\ 0.95 & 1\end{pmatrix}\).









Answer





\(A^{-1} \approx \begin{pmatrix}10.3 & -9.7\\ -9.7 & 10.3\end{pmatrix}\): each unmixed abundance is a difference of two large multiples of the detector readings, so independent detector noise is amplified (about 14 times for 1 % noise here) and the errors of the two dyes are strongly anti-correlated, i.e. along \((1, -1)\). Cells with little of a dye then scatter to both sides of zero, including negative values. This is the noise amplification that \(\kappa\) predicts, called spillover spreading in cytometry; it is not a software bug.

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
About this lecture
In Least squares: normal equations vs QR we solved \min_x \|Ax - b\| with QR and assumed the columns of A were clearly different. This lecture is about what happens when they are not.

The singular value decomposition A = U\Sigma V^T: every matrix is a rotation, a stretch along the axes, and another rotation.
The singular values \sigma_i give the condition number and the numerical rank. Small \sigma_i mark combinations of parameters the data cannot pin down.
Least squares through the SVD shows where noise is amplified: by 1/\sigma_i.
Three remedies: the pseudoinverse, the truncated SVD, and Tikhonov (ridge) regularisation, and how to choose \lambda (the L-curve).
Non-negative least squares for quantities that cannot be negative.
Biology: estimating cell-type proportions from bulk RNA-seq, when two cell types (CD4 and CD8 T cells) have almost the same expression profile.


This is the second least-squares unit. The previous one gave the machinery (QR, what lm does) for well-posed problems. Here the problem itself is the trouble: two columns that are nearly the same. The SVD is the tool that shows exactly which combination of parameters is badly determined, and every remedy (truncation, ridge, the pseudoinverse) is easiest to understand as “do something to the small singular values”. NNLS comes at the end because it is what deconvolution tools actually use, and because it fails in an instructive way on the same data.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: A biology problem: what is in this tissue?
text:
A biology problem: what is in this tissue?


A signature matrix S (genes × cell types) holds the expression of each gene in each pure cell type.
A bulk sample is a mixture: b \approx S p, with p the proportions of the cell types. Given S and b, find p.
40 genes, 5 cell types: an overdetermined least-squares problem. But the CD4T and CD8T columns differ by 2 % on 2 genes.


This is “deconvolution” of bulk RNA-seq (or microarray) data: tools such as CIBERSORT, EPIC, quanTIseq and MuSiC all solve some version of b = S p, with signature matrices built from sorted cells or single-cell data. Our signature is simulated so that we know the truth, but the structure is realistic: blocks of marker genes, and two T-cell subsets that share almost all of them. In real signatures CD4 and CD8 T cells, or naive and memory B cells, are the classic near-duplicates. The colour scale is logarithmic.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: The simulated signature and bulk sample
text:
The simulated signature and bulk sample
g <- 1:40                                  # 40 genes
S <- matrix(10, nrow = 40, ncol = 5,
            dimnames = list(NULL, c("CD4T", "CD8T", "B", "NK", "Mono")))
S[1:16, 1:2] <- 100                        # T-cell genes, high in both T types
S[cbind(17:40, rep(3:5, each = 8))] <- 100 # 8 marker genes each for B, NK, Mono
S <- S * (1 + 0.5 * sin(outer(g, 1:5)))    # gene-to-gene variation
S[, "CD8T"] <- S[, "CD4T"]                 # CD8 = CD4 ...
S[1, "CD8T"] <- 0.98 * S[1, "CD4T"]        # ... except 2% lower on gene 1
S[2, "CD8T"] <- 1.02 * S[2, "CD4T"]        #     and 2% higher on gene 2
p_true <- c(0.30, 0.15, 0.15, 0.10, 0.30)
b <- drop(S %*% p_true) * (1 + 0.05 * sin(37 * g))   # 5% "noise"

The “noise” is a fixed pattern of size 5 %, so the numbers on the slides are reproducible. Random noise comes later.


Walk through the construction. Every cell type has a block of high genes; the sin factor makes genes differ from each other without a random number generator, so R, Python and Rust in the exercise get the same matrix. The last two S lines are the whole point: the CD8 column is a copy of the CD4 column with two genes nudged by 2 percent. The bulk sample is the true mixture times a multiplicative error of up to 5 percent, a realistic size for bulk RNA-seq of a well-measured gene.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: Least squares gives a negative cell type
text:
Least squares gives a negative cell type
x <- qr.solve(S, b)                # least squares by QR (previous unit)
round(x, 3)
#   CD4T   CD8T      B     NK   Mono
#  0.543 -0.092  0.149  0.099  0.299
sqrt(sum((b - S %*% x)^2))         # residual of the least-squares fit
# [1] 9.621707
sqrt(sum((b - S %*% p_true)^2))    # residual of the TRUE proportions
# [1] 9.707244

B, NK and monocytes are within 0.001 of the truth. CD4 is 0.54 (truth 0.30) and CD8 is −0.09 (truth 0.15).
The wrong answer fits the data better than the truth. No amount of iterating or pivoting fixes this: the data do not contain the information.
QR did its job. The problem is ill-conditioned; we need a tool that shows which part of p is undetermined.


qr.solve with a rectangular matrix returns the least-squares solution, as in the previous unit. Point out the two residuals: the least-squares answer is by definition the best fit, so it beats the truth, which also has to fit the noise. A negative proportion is the visible symptom; the invisible one is that CD4 is off by 80 percent. Note that CD4 + CD8 = 0.451, almost exactly the true 0.45. Keep that in mind; it comes back.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Recap: conditioning of least squares
From Pivoting, norms and conditioning and Least squares: normal equations vs QR:

The condition number \kappa(A) bounds how much a relative error in b is magnified in x: \;\dfrac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|} \lesssim \kappa(A)\,\dfrac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}.
Rule of thumb: lose about \log_{10}\kappa digits. That counts rounding errors and measurement errors.
The normal equations A^TA x = A^Tb square \kappa; QR does not. So we used QR.

kappa(S, exact = TRUE)
# [1] 223.6613

With 5 % noise and \kappa \approx 224, the bound allows a relative error in x of up to 224 \times 0.05 \approx 11. QR cannot help: the trouble is in the problem, not the algorithm.


One slide of recap only. For a rectangular matrix, kappa is sigma_max / sigma_min, which we define properly in a few slides. A condition number of 224 would be harmless for rounding errors (we lose 2 to 3 of 16 digits), but measurement noise is not 1e-16, it is 5 percent. That is the general lesson: the condition number multiplies whatever error is in the data. The bound is a worst case; here the actual damage is a relative error of about 1 in the CD4/CD8 entries and almost none elsewhere. The SVD explains why.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
The singular value decomposition
Every m \times n matrix A (here m \ge n) can be written
A = U \Sigma V^T = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i\, u_i v_i^T

V (n\times n): orthonormal columns v_i, directions in parameter space (here: combinations of cell types).
\Sigma = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma_1 \ge \sigma_2 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_n \ge 0): the singular values.
U (m\times n): orthonormal columns u_i, directions in data space (combinations of genes).
Key relation: A v_i = \sigma_i u_i. Input direction v_i comes out as u_i, multiplied by \sigma_i.

Example: A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix} has \sigma_1 = \sqrt{45} = 6.708, \sigma_2 = \sqrt{5} = 2.236, v_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1), u_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}(1, 3), and A v_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(3, 9) = 6.708\, u_1.

Orthonormal means V^T V = I and U^T U = I: the columns are unit vectors at right angles. This is the “thin” or “economy” SVD that R returns; the full SVD pads U to m x m, which we never need. Unlike eigenvalues, singular values exist for every matrix, rectangular or not, and they are always real and non-negative. Check the example on the board: A times (1,1)/sqrt2 is (3,9)/sqrt2, whose length is sqrt(90)/sqrt2 = sqrt(45). The by-hand exercise derives this SVD from A^T A.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Rotate – stretch – rotate

A x = U\,\Sigma\,V^T x: (1) V^T rotates v_1, v_2 onto the axes; (2) \Sigma stretches axis i by \sigma_i; (3) U rotates the axes onto u_1, u_2.

The unit circle becomes an ellipse with half-axes \sigma_1 u_1 and \sigma_2 u_2 (in n dimensions: an ellipsoid).
\sigma_1 is the largest stretch, \|A\|_2 = \sigma_1; \sigma_n is the smallest. A direction with \sigma_i \approx 0 is squashed flat.


Same matrix as the last slide, A = [[3,0],[4,5]]. Point at the orange vector: v1 goes to the horizontal axis, gets stretched to length 6.7, then rotated to sigma1 u1. The blue one is stretched only by 2.24. (Strictly, U and V may include a reflection; for this picture we chose signs so both are rotations.) The ellipse picture is the whole story of conditioning: if the ellipse is very thin, two quite different inputs give almost the same output, and going backwards from output to input is unstable.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
svd() in R
A <- matrix(c(3, 4, 0, 5), 2, 2)
s <- svd(A)
s$d                                          # singular values, largest first
# [1] 6.708204 2.236068
s$v                                          # right singular vectors (columns)
#            [,1]       [,2]
# [1,] -0.7071068 -0.7071068
# [2,] -0.7071068  0.7071068
max(abs(s$u %*% diag(s$d) %*% t(s$v) - A))   # reconstruct A
# [1] 1.33808e-15

svd returns d, u, v (LAPACK underneath, cost O(mn^2), a few times a QR).
Signs are arbitrary: (-u_i, -v_i) is just as valid. Never compare singular vectors across programs without fixing a sign.


R uses LAPACK’s dgesdd. Here both v columns came out with the opposite sign of the slide before; that is fine because u flips too and u_i v_i^T is unchanged. Students comparing R with numpy or Rust will see different signs, so in the exercise we fix a sign convention. The reconstruction error 1e-15 is a few machine epsilons times the size of A: the SVD is computed by a backward-stable algorithm.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: Why not take eigenvalues of A^TA?
text:
Why not take eigenvalues of A^TA?
A^TA = V\Sigma^2V^T, so \sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^TA)}. Correct on paper, but:
B <- rbind(c(1, 1), c(1, 1 + 1e-9), c(1, 1 - 1e-9))   # nearly equal columns
svd(B)$d
# [1] 2.449489743 0.000000001
sqrt(eigen(crossprod(B))$values)
# [1] 2.449490e+00 2.107342e-08

Forming A^TA squares the condition number: \sigma_2^2 = 10^{-18} is below the rounding error of the entries (\approx 10^{-16}) and is lost. The small singular value comes out 20 times too large.
Same lesson as the normal equations: work with A, not A^TA. LAPACK’s SVD does that (it first reduces A by orthogonal transformations, like QR).


crossprod(B) is t(B) %*% B. The two columns differ by (0, 1e-9, -1e-9), and the small singular value is 1.000e-9, as svd prints. By hand the A^T A route is fine (and the exercise uses it for a 2x2), but in floating point it throws away half the digits. The squared small singular value 1e-18 sits next to entries of size 3, whose rounding error is about 7e-16: the eigenvalue that comes out is mostly rounding error. The full algorithm (Golub-Kahan bidiagonalisation then an implicit QR iteration) is in Trefethen and Bau; we do not need its details.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: The singular values of our signature
text:
The singular values of our signature
sv <- svd(S)
sv$d
# [1] 642.934939 340.639955 278.842837 269.081951   2.874591
sv$d[1] / sv$d[5]                 # = kappa(S, exact = TRUE)
# [1] 223.6613
round(sv$v[, 5], 3)               # the direction that is squashed
# [1]  0.707 -0.707  0.000  0.000  0.000

Four singular values of a few hundred, then a gap to 2.87. \kappa = \sigma_1/\sigma_n.
v_5 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0, 0, 0): “more CD4, less CD8”. Changing p by t\,v_5 changes Sp by only 2.87\,t.
The singular vectors name the problem: the data barely see the CD4 − CD8 difference. They see CD4 + CD8 fine.


This is the diagnostic slide. The small singular value says something is badly determined; its right singular vector says what. Moving 0.1 of the population from CD8 to CD4 (t = 0.14) changes the predicted bulk profile by 0.4 in norm, while the noise has norm about 10. So that move is invisible. Moving 0.1 into B cells instead changes the profile by tens. In real deconvolution work, looking at the smallest singular vectors of the signature matrix tells you which cell types you cannot separate before you ever see a bulk sample.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Numerical rank


Make CD8 identical to CD4: exact rank 4, but \sigma_5 = 6.6\times10^{-14}, not 0. Rounding makes every matrix full rank on paper.
Numerical rank = number of \sigma_i above a tolerance. Default: \max(m,n)\,\varepsilon\,\sigma_1 = 5.7\times10^{-12} → rank 4.
For measured data the useful tolerance is the noise level, not \varepsilon: by that standard \sigma_5 = 2.87 is also “zero”.


The red curve is the same signature with the two T-cell columns exactly equal. The fifth singular value is about 1e-13, i.e. epsilon times sigma_1 times a small factor: it is pure rounding. The tolerance max(m,n) eps sigma_1 is what numpy’s matrix_rank uses by default. R’s qr() uses a pivoted QR with tol = 1e-7 to decide rank; it gives the same answer here. The important third point: for real data the question is not “is sigma exactly zero” but “is sigma times the size of a plausible change in p bigger than the noise”. 2.87 is far above epsilon but far below what we can resolve with 5 percent noise.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: Exact rank deficiency: what R does
text:
Exact rank deficiency: what R does
S0 <- S;  S0[, "CD8T"] <- S0[, "CD4T"]     # CD8 identical to CD4
qr(S0)$rank
# [1] 4
coef(lm(b ~ S0 - 1))
#     S0CD4T     S0CD8T        S0B       S0NK     S0Mono
# 0.45135405         NA 0.14888175 0.09887964 0.29860311
qr.solve(S0, b)
# Error in qr.solve(S0, b) : singular matrix 'a' in solve

lm detects the rank deficiency (pivoted QR), drops CD8 and gives all of the T cells to CD4: one of infinitely many solutions.
qr.solve refuses. numpy.linalg.lstsq instead silently returns the minimum-norm solution (next slides).
Check: an NA coefficient in lm means collinear predictors. Look at the SVD.


lm’s NA is a feature: it is telling you that a predictor is a linear combination of the others. Many people delete the NA and move on, but the remaining coefficient (CD4 = 0.451) is not the CD4 proportion; it is CD4 + CD8. The same happens with collinear predictors in any regression: two drug doses always given together, or two genotype columns in perfect linkage. Different software chooses different members of the infinite solution set; the SVD gives a principled choice.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Least squares through the SVD
With A = U\Sigma V^T, the least-squares solution is
x = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{u_i^T b}{\sigma_i}\, v_i
beta <- drop(crossprod(sv$u, b))       # u_i^T b: the data in the u-basis
round(cbind(sigma = sv$d, beta = beta, ratio = beta / sv$d), 3)
#        sigma     beta  ratio
# [1,] 642.935 -246.178 -0.383
# [2,] 340.640   83.736  0.246
# [3,] 278.843   34.739  0.125
# [4,] 269.082    5.328  0.020
# [5,]   2.875    1.290  0.449

Noise \delta b adds u_i^T\delta b/\sigma_i to coefficient i: divided by \sigma_i. Small \sigma_i, large amplification.
Coefficient 5 is 0.449. Without noise it would be 0.106; noise of size 1 in u_5^Tb became 0.34 in x.


Derivation in one line: ||Ax - b|| is unchanged by rotating with U^T, and U^T A x = Sigma V^T x, so with y = V^T x the problem becomes sigma_i y_i ≈ u_i^T b, one equation per i. Solving each gives y_i = u_i^T b / sigma_i. crossprod(U, b) is t(U) %*% b. The ratio column is y: the coordinates of x in the v-basis. Since v_5 is the CD4-minus-CD8 direction, the 0.449 is exactly the CD4/CD8 split, now dominated by noise. Coefficients 1 to 4 have the noise divided by about 300 and are fine.

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: The Picard plot: where noise takes over
text:
The Picard plot: where noise takes over


For a good problem, |u_i^Tb| (orange) falls faster than \sigma_i (blue), so the ratios (green) stay small.
Noise gives every u_i^Tb a floor of about the noise level. Where \sigma_i drops below that floor, the ratio is noise / small number.
Check: plot \sigma_i and |u_i^Tb| on a log scale. Components where they meet carry no information.


This is called a Picard plot after the discrete Picard condition (Hansen). With only 5 components it is a small picture, but in inverse problems with hundreds of singular values (image deblurring, spectral unmixing, inverse heat problems) it is the standard first plot. The open green squares are the noise-free coefficients: they agree with the noisy ones for i = 1..4 and disagree at i = 5. In practice you do not have the noise-free version, but you can see where |u_i^T b| stops falling and levels out.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
The pseudoinverse
A^+ = V\,\Sigma^+\,U^T, \qquad \Sigma^+ = \mathrm{diag}(1/\sigma_i \text{ if } \sigma_i > \text{tol, else } 0)
pinv <- function(A, tol = max(dim(A)) * .Machine$double.eps) {
  s <- svd(A)
  keep <- s$d > tol * s$d[1]               # drop (numerically) zero sigmas
  s$v[, keep] %*% (t(s$u[, keep]) / s$d[keep])
}
round(drop(pinv(S0) %*% b), 3)              # CD8 identical to CD4
# [1] 0.226 0.226 0.149 0.099 0.299

A^+b is the least-squares solution with the smallest \|x\|. With identical columns, that splits CD4 + CD8 = 0.451 equally.
Full rank: A^+b is the ordinary least-squares solution. Library: MASS::ginv.
Never compute A^+ and multiply when you only need x; but the formula shows what is done.


The pseudoinverse (Moore-Penrose inverse) is the formula from the last slide with the terms for zero singular values left out. Leaving out the v_5 term means the solution has no component along CD4 minus CD8, so CD4 = CD8. That is the minimum-norm choice: among all p with the same fit, the one with the smallest sum of squares, which for two identical columns is an equal split. It is a convention, not information from the data. MASS ships with R. The tolerance matters: the default here keeps everything above 1e-14 relative, so on the near-duplicate S (sigma_5 = 2.87) pinv would keep sigma_5 and reproduce the bad least-squares answer. That leads to truncation.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: Truncated SVD: drop what the noise owns
text:
Truncated SVD: drop what the noise owns
Keep only the k largest singular values: \;x_k = \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}\, v_i
tsvd <- function(A, b, k) {
  s <- svd(A)
  drop(s$v[, 1:k] %*% (crossprod(s$u[, 1:k], b) / s$d[1:k]))
}
round(tsvd(S, b, 4), 3)
# [1] 0.226 0.226 0.149 0.099 0.299

Same as the pseudoinverse with a tolerance at the noise level. The CD4 − CD8 component is set to 0, so the split is equal.
CD4 + CD8 = 0.451 (true 0.45); B, NK and Mono unchanged. We report what the data determine and say so for the rest.


The truncated SVD (TSVD) is the simplest regulariser: decide that components with sigma below some threshold are noise, and drop them. Here k = 4 gives CD4 = CD8 = 0.226. Compared with the truth (0.30, 0.15) that is still wrong, but it is honestly wrong: it is the answer “the T-cell total is 0.45 and we cannot tell you the split”. Least squares gave 0.54 and -0.09, which looks like information but is noise. The right way to report the result is the sum, plus a statement that the split is not identifiable from this signature.
