k too small: real signal is thrown away (bias), and the residual is large. k too large: noise is amplified.
Check: the residual drops steeply until k = 4, then barely moves (9.71 → 9.62). Stop where it levels off at the noise level.
No k recovers the true split. Regularisation cannot create information.


The error column uses the truth, which we only know because we simulated. The residual column is available in real life and tells the same story: by k = 4 the fit is as good as the noise allows (the true p has residual 9.71, the same number). Adding component 5 lowers the residual by only 0.09 and moves the solution by 0.34: a sure sign that the component is fitting noise. This is the “discrepancy principle”: choose the least regularisation for which the residual is about as large as the expected noise.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Tikhonov (ridge) regularisation
Penalise large solutions: \;\min_x \|Ax - b\|^2 + \lambda^2\|x\|^2. In SVD form:
x_\lambda = \sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i\,\frac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}\,v_i, \qquad f_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\sigma_i^2 + \lambda^2}





Filter factors f_i: \approx 1 for \sigma_i \gg \lambda (keep), \approx 0 for \sigma_i \ll \lambda (damp).
TSVD is the step function; ridge is a smooth step at \sigma = \lambda.
Our \sigma’s (ticks): any \lambda between about 5 and 100 damps \sigma_5 and keeps the rest.



Ridge regression in statistics is the same thing (the statistics literature writes lambda for what we call lambda squared). To derive the filter factors: the normal equations of the penalised problem are (A^T A + lambda^2 I) x = A^T b; substituting the SVD gives (sigma_i^2 + lambda^2) y_i = sigma_i u_i^T b. Numbers: with lambda = 10, f_5 = 8.26 / 108.26 = 0.076, and f_4 = 72405 / 72505 = 0.9986. Ridge never sets a component exactly to zero, which is usually gentler than truncation.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Ridge in code: two routes
ridge <- function(A, b, lambda) {
  s <- svd(A)
  f <- s$d^2 / (s$d^2 + lambda^2)          # filter factors
  drop(s$v %*% (f * crossprod(s$u, b) / s$d))
}
round(ridge(S, b, lambda = 10), 3)
# [1] 0.250 0.201 0.149 0.099 0.298
lambda <- 10                               # same thing as a stacked least squares
x_aug <- qr.solve(rbind(S, lambda * diag(5)), c(b, rep(0, 5)))
round(x_aug, 3)
#  CD4T  CD8T     B    NK  Mono
# 0.250 0.201 0.149 0.099 0.298

Ridge is ordinary least squares on the stacked system \begin{pmatrix}A\\ \lambda I\end{pmatrix}x \approx \begin{pmatrix}b\\0\end{pmatrix}, so QR works too, without the SVD.
Do not solve (A^TA + \lambda^2 I)x = A^Tb for small \lambda: that is the normal equations again.


The stacked form is how ridge is computed when the SVD is too expensive: add n rows that say “x should be close to 0, with weight lambda”. Both give 0.250 and 0.201: closer to the truth than TSVD, but by luck; the noise pattern happened to push in the right direction. Python: scipy and sklearn have ridge solvers, but the two routes above are all one needs. Note ridge depends on the scaling of the columns: if one cell type’s signature is in different units, it is penalised differently. Scale the columns comparably first.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Choosing \lambda: the L-curve


L-curve (left): residual norm against solution norm for many \lambda, log–log. Small \lambda: \|x\| grows, fit barely improves. Large \lambda: fit gets worse fast. Pick the corner (\lambda \approx 10).
Failure (right): too large a \lambda shrinks everything towards 0. At \lambda = 100 the proportions sum to 0.96, at 300 to 0.74.
Alternatives: the discrepancy principle (residual ≈ noise), generalised cross-validation, cross-validation.


The right panel uses the truth and is not available in practice. Its sharp minimum near lambda = 5 is luck of this noise pattern; with other noise it moves. That is why we choose by a criterion that uses only the data. The L-curve corner is a heuristic; it works when the noise is roughly white and the singular values decay. Shrinkage towards zero is a real bias for proportions: ridge does not know they should sum to 1. An alternative is to penalise the distance from a prior guess instead of from 0, which the same formulas handle by a change of variables.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Proportions cannot be negative: NNLS
\min_x \|Ax - b\| \quad \text{subject to} \quad x_j \ge 0 \text{ for all } j
Active-set idea (Lawson–Hanson, 1974):

Start with every x_j = 0 (all “held at the bound”).
Free the variable whose increase would reduce the residual fastest (largest a_j^T(b - Ax)).
Solve ordinary least squares on the free variables. If some go negative, step back until the first one hits 0, and hold it at 0.
Repeat until no held variable wants to increase.


Each step is a small least-squares problem (QR, as in the previous unit). It ends after finitely many steps.
Used, with variations, by deconvolution tools (EPIC and quanTIseq use constrained least squares; MuSiC uses weighted NNLS).


The optimality condition: for every held variable, the gradient of the residual says increasing it would not help, and every free variable is positive. That is the KKT condition for this problem, the topic of Constraints and linear programming in Part 9. We do not need the full theory; the algorithm is easy to follow on a 2-variable example, and the exercise does one step by hand and writes it in Rust. Note what NNLS does not do: it does not regularise. It only rules out the negative half of the bad directions.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
NNLS in R
library(nnls)
fit <- nnls(S, b)
round(fit$x, 3)
# [1] 0.451 0.000 0.149 0.099 0.299
sum(fit$x)
# [1] 0.9977186

nnls::nnls (Python: scipy.optimize.nnls): no negative proportions, sum close to 1, B, NK and Mono right.
But it puts all T cells in CD4 and none in CD8. A clean-looking answer, confidently wrong.
Least squares wanted CD8 = −0.09; NNLS moved to the nearest feasible point along v_5: CD8 at the bound, CD4 + CD8 kept.


This is the instructive failure. The constraint removed the obvious symptom (negative proportion), so the result looks trustworthy, but the split along the badly determined direction is still decided by noise: here the noise pushed towards CD4, so CD8 sits at 0. With a different noise pattern it would be CD4 that sits at 0. A zero from NNLS is therefore not evidence that the cell type is absent. The sum 0.998 comes for free here because the true proportions sum to 1 and the fit is good; some tools also enforce sum = 1 or rescale.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: The check: refit with new noise
text:
The check: refit with new noise

500 bulk samples from the same p, each with fresh 5 % random noise. Standard deviations: least squares 0.86 (CD4), ridge 0.065, NNLS 0.21, TSVD 0.004. CD4 + CD8: 0.007 for all four.

NNLS sets CD8 = 0 in 38 % of the replicates and CD4 = 0 in 37 %. TSVD is stable but biased (0.225 each).
Check: perturb the data (bootstrap genes, or add noise of the measured size) and refit. Quantities that jump are not determined.


This is the general-purpose check for any fit and it needs no theory: if a small, realistic change in the data moves an estimate a lot, do not report that estimate. All four methods agree perfectly on the T-cell total, which is the well-determined quantity. They disagree on the split, and each disagrees in its own characteristic way: least squares wildly, NNLS by flipping between the two bounds, ridge with moderate spread, TSVD by always returning the equal split. The way out is biological, not numerical: add genes that separate CD4 from CD8 (CD4, CD8A, CD8B and their co-expressed modules) to the signature, which raises sigma_5.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
section: Checklist: rank trouble in a least-squares fit
text:
Checklist: rank trouble in a least-squares fit

Look at svd(A)$d before trusting coefficients. A gap, or a \sigma_n near the noise level, means some combination is not determined.
Read the smallest right singular vectors v_n, v_{n-1}: they name the confounded parameters (here CD4 − CD8).
NA coefficients in lm, or a “singular matrix” error → exact collinearity.
Negative or huge estimates that should be positive and moderate → ill-conditioning, not biology.
Refit with perturbed data: estimates that jump are not identifiable; report the combinations that are stable (sums, differences along large \sigma).
Regularise knowingly: TSVD or ridge trade noise for bias. Pick k or \lambda from the residual (L-curve, discrepancy principle), and say that you did.
Constraints are not regularisation: NNLS hides the symptom but not the cause.


Each line maps to a slide. The common thread: the numerics can tell you that something is not determined and which combination it is, but cannot supply the missing information. In Part 9 (Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters) the same ideas return for nonlinear models, with the Jacobian in the role of S.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Aside: PCA is an SVD

Centre the data matrix X (samples × genes) by columns. Then X = U\Sigma V^T gives the principal axes v_i, the scores U\Sigma, and the variance explained \sigma_i^2/(n-1).
prcomp does exactly this (it calls svd, not eigen of the covariance matrix, for the reason on the A^TA slide).
The truncated SVD is the best rank-k approximation of a matrix (Eckart–Young): keeping the top k PCs is TSVD of the data.
For a large sparse cells × genes matrix, compute only the top k singular triplets with irlba (Python: scipy.sparse.linalg.svds), as in How eigen() works, and big problems.

The statistics of PCA (scaling, interpretation, biplots) are in the sister course.

One slide only, because PCA is taught elsewhere. The numerical points worth knowing: PCA is computed by the SVD of the centred data, not by eigen of the covariance (which would square the condition number); and for single-cell data with 1e5 cells nobody computes the full SVD, only the top 50 components with a Lanczos-type method (irlba), which is the subject of Part 5.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Summary

SVD A = U\Sigma V^T: rotate (V^T), stretch by \sigma_i, rotate (U). Av_i = \sigma_iu_i. Compute it with svd(), not via A^TA.
\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1, \kappa = \sigma_1/\sigma_n. Numerical rank = number of \sigma_i above a tolerance: \max(m,n)\varepsilon\sigma_1 for rounding, the noise level for data.
Least squares: x = \sum_i (u_i^Tb/\sigma_i)\, v_i. Noise is amplified by 1/\sigma_i; the small-\sigma directions v_i name what is not determined.
Pseudoinverse: minimum-norm solution, drops zero \sigma_i. Truncated SVD: drops \sigma_i below the noise. Ridge: filter factors \sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda^2); choose \lambda at the corner of the L-curve. Both trade noise for bias.
NNLS (nnls, scipy.optimize.nnls) enforces x \ge 0 by an active set, but does not resolve an undetermined split.
Deconvolution: CD4 + CD8 is well determined, the split is not. Check with the singular values and by refitting perturbed data.

Next: Part 5, Power iteration and friends: eigenvalues, starting from the simplest iteration.

The three ideas to keep: the SVD as a diagnostic (singular values and vectors tell you what the data determine), every regulariser as a filter on singular values, and the refit-with-noise check. The next part turns to eigenvalue problems, where the SVD returns as a close relative (singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of A^T A), and the Lanczos idea behind irlba appears.
crumbs: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute partial derivatives of a function of two variables, and check them with a difference quotient,
write down the Jacobian of a small system and explain what each entry means for the biology,
do a Newton step for a system by hand (one \(2\times2\) linear solve) and in code (solve(J, -F)),
recognise quadratic convergence in a table of errors,
build a finite-difference Jacobian and explain how the step \(h\) affects Newton’s convergence,
use a library routine (rootSolve::multiroot in R, scipy.optimize.root in Python) and check its answer,
find all steady states of the genetic toggle switch with many starts, and spot when Newton fails (nearly singular Jacobian, negative concentrations, NaN, a root you did not want).

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator. The code part checks your hand answers and then explores where only code works.

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
By hand
B1. Partial derivatives. (a) \(g(u, v) = u^2 v + 3v\). Compute \(\partial g/\partial u\) and \(\partial g/\partial v\), and evaluate both at \((u, v) = (1, 2)\). (b) An enzyme makes product at rate \(r(S, E) = \dfrac{k\,E\,S}{K + S}\) (Michaelis–Menten, with enzyme concentration \(E\) and substrate \(S\)). With \(k = 2\) and \(K = 1\), compute \(\partial r/\partial E\) and \(\partial r/\partial S\) at \(S = 1\), \(E = 0.5\). Say in words what each number means. (c) Check \(\partial r/\partial S\) from (b) with a difference quotient, \(h = 0.01\).
B2. The Jacobian of the toggle switch. (a) Derive the four entries of \(J\) for general \(\alpha\) and \(n\) (Fact 2) yourself, using the chain rule on \(\alpha(1 + v^n)^{-1}\). (b) Evaluate \(J\) at \((u, v) = (1, 2)\) for \(\alpha = 3\), \(n = 2\). (c) Which entries describe degradation, and which repression? Why is \(|\partial F_2/\partial u|\) at \((1, 2)\) larger than \(|\partial F_1/\partial v|\)? (d) Evaluate \(J\) and \(\det J\) at the middle steady state \(u = v = 1.2134\).
B3. The linear approximation. At \(\mathbf x = (1, 2)\), compute \(\mathbf F(\mathbf x)\). Use \(J\) from B2(b) to predict \(\mathbf F(1.1, 1.9)\), then compute the true value. How close is the prediction?
B4. Two Newton steps. Start at \(\mathbf x_0 = (3, 0)\), with \(\alpha = 3\), \(n = 2\). (a) Compute \(\mathbf F(\mathbf x_0)\) and \(J(\mathbf x_0)\). Why is this first step especially easy? (b) Solve \(J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F\) and give \(\mathbf x_1\). (c) Do a second step from \(\mathbf x_1\) (keep 4–5 significant digits). Compare \(\mathbf x_2\) with the steady state \((2.6180, 0.3820)\).
B5. All steady states, exactly. For the toggle switch with \(n = 2\): (a) Write the two steady-state equations as \(u(1 + v^2) = \alpha\) and \(v(1 + u^2) = \alpha\). Subtract them and show that \((u - v)(1 - uv) = 0\). (b) Case \(u = v\): show that \(u^3 + u - \alpha = 0\). For \(\alpha = 3\), find the root with two Newton steps from \(u_0 = 1\) (one variable). (c) Case \(uv = 1\): show that \(u + v = \alpha\). Find \(u\) and \(v\) for \(\alpha = 3\) exactly. (You need \(t^2 - \alpha t + 1 = 0\).) (d) For which \(\alpha\) does case (c) give real, positive solutions? What does that mean for the switch?
B6. A linear system. Suppose \(\mathbf F(\mathbf x) = A\mathbf x - \mathbf b\) with a fixed invertible matrix \(A\). What is \(J\)? Show that Newton reaches the exact root in one step, from any start.
B7. A finite-difference Jacobian by hand. At \(\mathbf x = (3, 0.5)\) use \(h = 0.01\) (not scaled). (a) Compute column 2: \(\big(\mathbf F(3, 0.51) - \mathbf F(3, 0.5)\big)/0.01\). Compare with the exact column \((-1.92, -1)\). (b) Compute column 1 the same way and compare with \((-1, -0.18)\). (c) How many evaluations of \(\mathbf F\) did the whole Jacobian cost? How many for a network of 100 genes?
B8. Symmetry and cost. (a) Suppose \(u_0 = v_0\). Show that \(F_1 = F_2\) and that \(J\) is symmetric with equal diagonal entries. Conclude that \(\delta_u = \delta_v\), so every Newton iterate stays on the line \(u = v\). Which steady state can Newton then find? (b) Solving a dense \(n\times n\) system costs about \(\tfrac23 n^3\) operations. At \(10^9\) operations per second, how long does one Newton step take for \(n = 2\), \(1000\) and \(20\,000\) genes? With a finite-difference Jacobian and an \(\mathbf F\) costing \(10n\) operations, how much does building the Jacobian cost in comparison?

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
In code
The solutions build on each other: the Background defines F and J, C1 defines fd_jacobian, C2 defines newton_sys and the exact root xstar. Each Rust file is a complete program.
C1. Check the Jacobian. Write F and J (Background) and a function fd_jacobian(F, x, h) that returns the finite-difference Jacobian (Fact 6). Check B2(b), and compare J(x) with fd_jacobian(F, x) at \((3, 0.5)\), \((1, 2)\), \((1.2, 1.2)\) and \((0.1, 4)\). What size of difference do you expect? Also compare with a library routine: R numDeriv::jacobian, Python scipy.optimize.approx_fprime.
C2. Newton for the toggle switch. Write newton_sys(F, J, x0, tol, maxit) that returns all iterates (one per row). Check your B4 answers with a start at \((3, 0)\). Then start at \((3, 0.5)\): print the error \(\|\mathbf x_k - \mathbf x^*\|\) (use the exact root from B5) and the residual \(\|\mathbf F(\mathbf x_k)\|\) per step, and the ratios \(e_{k+1}/e_k^2\). Is the convergence quadratic?
C3. All steady states from many starts. Run Newton from a \(10\times10\) grid of starts with \(u_0, v_0 \in \{0.2, 0.6, \dots, 3.8\}\). Collect the distinct roots (round to 6 decimals). What fraction of starts goes to each? Check the residual of every run. Compare with the basin picture in the lecture.
C4. A finite-difference Jacobian inside Newton. Run Newton from \((3, 0.5)\) with fd_jacobian in place of J, for \(h = \sqrt\varepsilon\), \(10^{-4}\), \(10^{-2}\) and \(0.3\). Print the number of steps and the first five errors. What happens to the convergence when \(h\) is large?
C5. The library routine. Solve the same problem with multiroot (R) or scipy.optimize.root (Python), first with the default settings and then with your J and a tighter tolerance. How large are the residual and the error at the default settings? Do the starts \((0.5, 3)\), \((1, 1)\) and \((1, 0.2)\) give the same roots as your Newton? (Rust: no library, so count how many evaluations of \(\mathbf F\) your Newton with a finite-difference Jacobian needs.)
C6. Failure: a nearly singular Jacobian. (a) Run Newton from \((1.9, 0.5)\) and from \((2.0, 0.55)\). For each, print \(\det J(\mathbf x_0)\) (R det, Python np.linalg.det), the length of the first step, the smallest \(u\) or \(v\) along the way, and where it ends. (b) Set the Hill coefficient to \(n = 2.5\) and take two plain Newton steps from \((2, 0.5)\). What happens, and why? (c) Write a damped Newton: after computing \(\boldsymbol\delta\), try \(t = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots\) and accept \(\mathbf x + t\boldsymbol\delta\) as soon as all entries are \(\ge 0\) and \(\|\mathbf F\|\) has not grown. Does it solve (b)?
C7. When is the switch bistable? For \(\alpha = 1, 1.5, 2, \dots, 5\), run Newton from an \(8\times 8\) grid of starts in \([0.25, 5]^2\) and count the distinct roots with residual below \(10^{-10}\). Also count the runs that hit maxit = 50. Compare with B5(d) and the formula \(u = (\alpha + \sqrt{\alpha^2 - 4})/2\) for the “U on” state. What goes wrong at \(\alpha = 2\)?

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — partial derivatives (B1, B2)





Pretend the other variable is a number like 7. For \(\alpha(1 + v^n)^{-1}\): the derivative of \((\cdot)^{-1}\) is \(-(\cdot)^{-2}\), times the derivative of the inside, \(n v^{n-1}\). For \(r(S, E)\) in \(S\), use the quotient rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dS}\dfrac{S}{K+S} = \dfrac{K}{(K+S)^2}\).









Hint 2 — a 2×2 linear solve (B4)





Write the two equations out. Use one equation to express one unknown in terms of the other, and substitute. For \(\begin{pmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\delta = \mathbf r\) the closed form is \(\delta_1 = (d r_1 - b r_2)/\det\), \(\delta_2 = (a r_2 - c r_1)/\det\) with \(\det = ad - bc\). Remember the right-hand side is \(-\mathbf F\).









Hint 3 — exact steady states (B5)





\(u(1 + v^2) - v(1 + u^2) = (u - v) + uv(v - u)\). Factor out \((u - v)\). With \(uv = 1\), \(u(1 + v^2) = u + v\,(uv) = u + v\). Two numbers with sum \(\alpha\) and product 1 are the roots of \(t^2 - \alpha t + 1 = 0\).









Hint 4 — Newton in code (C2, C3)





R: solve(A, b) solves \(A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\); collect the iterates with rbind. Python: np.linalg.solve, collect them in a list and convert with np.array. Rust: jac(&x).lu().solve(&(-f(&x))) returns None if the matrix is singular. For the grid of starts: R expand.grid and apply; distinct rows with unique after round. Python: np.unique(..., axis=0, return_counts=True).









Hint 5 — finite differences (C1, C4)





Copy x, add \(h_j\) to entry \(j\) only, and fill column \(j\) with the difference of the two \(\mathbf F\) vectors divided by \(h_j\). In R, .Machine$double.eps; in Python, np.finfo(float).eps; in Rust, f64::EPSILON. For C4, pass a small function function(x) fd_jacobian(F, x, h) (Python: lambda x: fd_jacobian(F, x, h)) as the Jacobian.









Hint 6 — library routines (C5)





multiroot(f, start, jacfunc = NULL, rtol, atol, ctol) returns a list with root, f.root (the residual), iter and estim.precis. scipy.optimize.root(fun, x0, jac=None, tol=None) returns an object with .x, .fun, .nfev and .success. Always look at the residual, not just at success.









Hint 7 — failures and damping (C6, C7)





A negative number raised to a non-integer power is NaN in R and numpy (and in Rust’s powf). For the damped step, a while loop that halves t; stop with an error if t becomes tiny. In C7, wrap the Newton call in tryCatch (Python: try/except np.linalg.LinAlgError) because the Jacobian can be exactly singular. At \(\alpha = 2\), compute \(\det J\) at the root \(u = v = 1\).

Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Where this leads

Gaussian elimination as LU (Part 3): what solve(J, -F) does inside, why it costs about \(\tfrac23 n^3\) operations, and why we never form solve(J). Pivoting, norms and conditioning: norms beyond the Euclidean length, and why a nearly singular \(J\) (C6) amplifies errors.
Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse (Part 3): gene networks give sparse Jacobians, which makes Newton feasible for thousands of genes.
Numerical differentiation (Part 7): central differences and Richardson extrapolation (what numDeriv does) for more accurate Jacobians.
Equilibria, stability and the phase plane (Part 8): the same toggle switch; the eigenvalues of \(J\) at each steady state decide which ones are stable, explaining why no cell sits in the middle state that Newton found so often.
Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton (Part 9): Newton applied to the gradient of a likelihood, with the Jacobian of the gradient (the Hessian); quasi-Newton methods build an approximate Jacobian cheaply, which C4 shows is enough.

title: Exercise: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the SVD of a 2×2 matrix by hand and explain it as rotate – stretch – rotate,
read the condition number and the numerical rank off the singular values, and name the badly determined combination of parameters from the smallest right singular vector,
write the least-squares solution as \(\sum_i (u_i^Tb/\sigma_i)\,v_i\) and predict how much noise each term picks up,
compute the pseudoinverse (minimum-norm) solution of a rank-deficient problem,
regularise with the truncated SVD and ridge, and choose \(k\) or \(\lambda\) from the residual and the L-curve,
solve a non-negative least-squares problem, check its optimality conditions, and recognise when its answer is not determined by the data.

The running example is the deconvolution of a bulk RNA-seq sample into cell-type proportions, with a simulated signature in which CD4 and CD8 T cells differ by 2 % on two genes. The by-hand part uses pen, paper and a calculator.

title: Exercise: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Background
A bulk sample is modelled as a mixture of pure cell types: \(b \approx S p\), where \(S\) (genes × cell types) is the signature matrix and \(p\) the vector of proportions. With more genes than cell types this is an overdetermined least-squares problem, \(\min_p \|Sp - b\|\).
Facts used below:

SVD. Every \(m\times n\) matrix (\(m \ge n\)) is \(A = U\Sigma V^T = \sum_i \sigma_i u_iv_i^T\), with orthonormal columns \(u_i\) (data space) and \(v_i\) (parameter space) and singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_n \ge 0\). Key relation: \(Av_i = \sigma_i u_i\).
By hand: the \(\sigma_i^2\) are the eigenvalues of \(A^TA\) and the \(v_i\) its eigenvectors; then \(u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i\). (In floating point, do not compute it this way: forming \(A^TA\) squares the condition number.)
\(\|A\|_2 = \sigma_1\) and the condition number is \(\kappa(A) = \sigma_1/\sigma_n\).
Numerical rank: the number of \(\sigma_i\) above a tolerance; for rounding errors \(\max(m,n)\,\varepsilon\,\sigma_1\), for measured data the noise level.
Least squares through the SVD: \(x = \sum_i \dfrac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}\,v_i\). Noise \(\delta b\) adds \(\dfrac{u_i^T\delta b}{\sigma_i}\,v_i\): divided by \(\sigma_i\).
Pseudoinverse: \(A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^T\) with \(1/\sigma_i\) replaced by 0 for (numerically) zero \(\sigma_i\). \(A^+b\) is the least-squares solution of minimum norm.
Truncated SVD: keep the first \(k\) terms of fact 5. Ridge (Tikhonov): \(\min_x \|Ax-b\|^2 + \lambda^2\|x\|^2\), solved by fact 5 with each term multiplied by the filter factor \(f_i = \sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda^2)\), or as least squares on the stacked system \(\begin{pmatrix}A\\ \lambda I\end{pmatrix}x \approx \begin{pmatrix}b\\0\end{pmatrix}\).
NNLS: \(\min_x\|Ax-b\|\) subject to \(x \ge 0\). With \(w = A^T(b - Ax)\), the solution satisfies \(w_j = 0\) where \(x_j > 0\) and \(w_j \le 0\) where \(x_j = 0\) (no held variable would reduce the residual by increasing).

The basic tools in each language:

RPythonRust


A <- matrix(c(3, 4, 0, 5), nrow = 2)     # filled by column: rows (3, 0) and (4, 5)
s <- svd(A)                              # list with d, u, v
s$d                                      # singular values, largest first
# [1] 6.708204 2.236068
s$d[1] / s$d[2]                          # condition number = kappa(A, exact = TRUE)
# [1] 3
max(abs(A - s$u %*% diag(s$d) %*% t(s$v)))   # A = U Sigma V^T
# [1] 1.33808e-15


import numpy as np

A = np.array([[3.0, 0.0],
              [4.0, 5.0]])
U, d, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)   # note: returns V^T, not V
print(d)                                 # singular values, largest first
# [6.70820393 2.23606798]
print(d[0] / d[1])                       # condition number = np.linalg.cond(A)
# 3.000000000000001
print(np.max(np.abs(A - U @ np.diag(d) @ Vt)))     # A = U Sigma V^T
# 1.3380796711988474e-15


// rust/examples/svd_background.rs  —  cargo run --example svd_background
// The SVD of a 2x2 matrix with nalgebra (R: svd; numpy: np.linalg.svd).
use nalgebra::{DMatrix, DVector};

fn main() {
    let a = DMatrix::from_row_slice(2, 2, &[3.0, 0.0,
                                            4.0, 5.0]);
    let svd = a.clone().svd(true, true);     // sorted, largest first
    let d: DVector<f64> = svd.singular_values.clone();
    let u = svd.u.unwrap();
    let vt = svd.v_t.unwrap();               // like numpy, nalgebra returns V^T
    println!("{} {}", d[0], d[1]);           // singular values
    println!("{}", d[0] / d[1]);             // condition number
    let rebuilt = &u * DMatrix::from_diagonal(&d) * &vt;
    println!("{:e}", (a - rebuilt).abs().max()); // A = U Sigma V^T
}

// Output:
// 6.708203932499368 2.236067977499789
// 3.0000000000000004
// 1.7763568394002505e-15



R’s svd returns \(V\); numpy’s np.linalg.svd and nalgebra’s SVD return \(V^T\). The signs of singular vectors are arbitrary and differ between programs; where we print singular vectors we fix a sign first. Rust prints numbers in its own format; the values agree with R and Python to the digits shown unless the text says otherwise.

title: Exercise: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
By hand
B1. The SVD of a 2×2 matrix. Let \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Compute \(A^TA\) and its eigenvalues. What are \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\)? (b) Find the eigenvectors \(v_1, v_2\) of \(A^TA\) (unit length, first entry positive), then \(u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i\). Check that \(u_1 \perp u_2\). (c) Check that \(\sigma_1u_1v_1^T + \sigma_2u_2v_2^T = A\). (d) What are \(\|A\|_2\) and \(\kappa(A)\)? Check that \(\sigma_1\sigma_2 = |\det A|\). (e) The unit circle is mapped by \(A\) onto an ellipse. Give the directions and lengths of its half-axes. Which unit vector \(x\) is stretched most?
B2. Two identical cell types. Two cell types have the same signature on three genes: \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\). (a) What is the rank of \(A\)? Compute \(A^TA\), its eigenvalues, and \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\). (b) Find \(v_1\), \(v_2\) and \(u_1\). Which combination of the two proportions is \(v_2\), and what does \(A\) do to it? (c) The bulk sample is \(b = (3, 6, 6)\). Describe all least-squares solutions \(x\). (d) Compute the pseudoinverse \(A^+ = \sigma_1^{-1}v_1u_1^T\) and the minimum-norm solution \(A^+b\). Is it the solution of (c) with the smallest \(\|x\|\)? (e) With a noisy sample \(b = (3, 6, 7)\), what is \(A^+b\)?
B3. Two nearly identical cell types. Now the second cell type is 2 % higher on gene 2: \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.02 \end{pmatrix}\). (a) \(A\) is symmetric with positive eigenvalues, so its singular values are its eigenvalues. Compute them (to 3 significant digits) and \(\kappa(A)\). (b) Solve \(Ax = (2, 2.02)\). (c) Now the measurement of gene 2 is off by \(0.01\): solve \(Ax = (2, 2.03)\). Compare the relative change in \(b\) with the relative change in \(x\). Is the amplification below \(\kappa\)? (d) Find the eigenvector belonging to the small eigenvalue. In which direction did \(x\) move in (c)? Interpret it biologically.
B4. Filtering the small singular value. Continue with B3 (\(\sigma_1 \approx 2.01\), \(\sigma_2 \approx 0.00995\), \(v_1 \approx u_1 \approx \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, 1)\), \(v_2 \approx \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1)\)). (a) Truncated SVD with \(k = 1\) for \(b = (2, 2.03)\): compute \(x_1 = \dfrac{u_1^Tb}{\sigma_1}v_1\). (b) Compute the ridge filter factors \(f_1, f_2\) for \(\lambda = 0.1\) and for \(\lambda = 1\). (c) In B3(c), the change \(\delta b = (0, 0.01)\) moved \(x\) by about \((-0.5, 0.5)\), almost exactly along \(v_2\). Roughly how far does it move the ridge solution with \(\lambda = 0.1\)? (d) If the two cell types really were present in different amounts, say \(x = (1.2, 0.8)\), what would TSVD with \(k = 1\) report? What is the price of regularisation?
B5. NNLS by hand. Three genes, two cell types: \(A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1.1 \end{pmatrix}\), \(b = (1, 1, 0.9)\). (a) Solve the unconstrained least-squares problem with the normal equations (\(A^TA\) is 2×2; this is fine by hand). Is the answer a valid set of proportions? (b) Hold \(x_2 = 0\) and solve the one-variable least-squares problem for \(x_1\). (c) Check the optimality condition (fact 8): compute \(w = A^T(b - Ax)\) at your answer from (b). Does increasing \(x_2\) from 0 help? (d) Compare the two answers with the “true” \(x_1 + x_2\), if the truth were a 50/50 mix of the two cell types.
B6. Where the noise goes in the deconvolution. In the simulated signature, the CD4T and CD8T columns are equal except on gene 1 (\(142.074\) and \(139.232\)) and gene 2 (\(145.465\) and \(148.374\)). The smallest singular value is \(\sigma_5 = 2.875\) with \(v_5 \approx \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(1, -1, 0, 0, 0)\). (a) Compute \(Sv_5 = (S_{\cdot,\mathrm{CD4}} - S_{\cdot,\mathrm{CD8}})/\sqrt2\). On which genes is it non-zero? Check that its length is \(\sigma_5\), and write down \(u_5 = Sv_5/\sigma_5\). (b) The bulk values of genes 1 and 2 are about 65 and 67, measured with 5 % independent noise. What is the typical size (standard deviation) of \(u_5^T\delta b\)? (c) How large an error does that cause in \(x\) along \(v_5\)? And in CD4 and in CD8 separately? In CD4 + CD8? (d) With CD8 made identical to CD4, R reports \(\sigma = (642.9, 340.6, 278.8, 269.1, 6.6\times10^{-14})\) for the \(40\times5\) matrix. Compute the tolerance \(\max(m,n)\,\varepsilon\,\sigma_1\) and the numerical rank. Why is \(\sigma_5\) not exactly 0?

title: Exercise: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — SVD by hand (B1, B2)





The eigenvalues of a symmetric 2×2 matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a & c\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}\) solve \(\lambda^2 - (a+d)\lambda + (ad - c^2) = 0\). For an eigenvector, solve \((A^TA - \lambda I)v = 0\): one equation is enough, then scale to length 1. For \(u_i\), multiply \(A\) by \(v_i\) and divide by \(\sigma_i\); if \(\sigma_i = 0\), there is no \(u_i\) to compute (and you do not need it for \(A^+\)).









Hint 2 — conditioning (B3, B4)





The inverse of \(\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}\) is \(\frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}\). Relative change = \(\|\delta b\|/\|b\|\) and \(\|\delta x\|/\|x\|\) in the 2-norm. Ridge acts on each SVD component separately: a change along \(v_2\) is multiplied by \(f_2\).









Hint 3 — NNLS by hand (B5)





Normal equations: \(A^TAx = A^Tb\). With \(x_2\) held at 0, the problem is \(\min_{x_1}\|a_1x_1 - b\|\), solved by \(x_1 = a_1^Tb/a_1^Ta_1\). \(w_2 = a_2^T(b - Ax)\) is minus half the derivative of \(\|Ax - b\|^2\) with respect to \(x_2\): if \(w_2 \le 0\), increasing \(x_2\) does not reduce the residual.









Hint 4 — noise along one direction (B6)





For independent noise \(\delta b_1, \delta b_2\) with standard deviations \(s_1, s_2\), the combination \(c_1\delta b_1 + c_2\delta b_2\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{c_1^2s_1^2 + c_2^2s_2^2}\). A change \(t\,v_5\) in \(x\) changes CD4 by \(t/\sqrt2\) and CD8 by \(-t/\sqrt2\), and leaves CD4 + CD8 unchanged.









Hint 5 — SVD in code (C1–C4)





R: s <- svd(A) gives s$d, s$u, s$v; crossprod(U, b) is \(U^Tb\). Python: U, d, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False); the \(v_i\) are the rows of Vt. Rust (nalgebra): let svd = a.clone().svd(true, true); gives svd.singular_values, svd.u.unwrap(), svd.v_t.unwrap() (rows are \(v_i\)), sorted largest first. To fix a sign, multiply a column of \(V\) and the matching column of \(U\) by \(-1\). Machine epsilon: .Machine$double.eps, np.finfo(float).eps, f64::EPSILON.









Hint 6 — ridge and the L-curve (C5)





Filter factors f <- d^2 / (d^2 + lambda^2), then \(x = V\,(f \cdot U^Tb/d)\). Stacked system in R: qr.solve(rbind(S, lambda * diag(5)), c(b, rep(0, 5))); Python: np.linalg.lstsq(np.vstack([S, lam * np.eye(5)]), np.concatenate([b, np.zeros(5)])). For the plot, use sapply (R) or a list comprehension (Python) over 10^seq(-1, 3, by = 0.05), and plot(..., log = "xy") / plt.loglog.









Hint 7 — NNLS (C6)





R: library(nnls); fit <- nnls(A, b); fit$x (nnls, install with install.packages("nnls")). Python: x, rnorm = scipy.optimize.nnls(A, b) (docs). Rust: there is no NNLS in the allowed crates; the solution has a hand-written Lawson–Hanson active-set method (the algorithm on the slides), built on the QR least-squares solve from the previous unit.









Hint 8 — replicates (C7)





R: replicate(500, { ... }) collects the results of a block into an array; apply(est, c(1, 2), sd) takes the standard deviation over the last dimension. Python: fill an array est[r, :, :] in a loop and use est.std(axis=0, ddof=1). Rust: rand_distr::StandardNormal with a seeded StdRng. The three languages use different random numbers, so the last digit differs.

text:
Where this leads

Part 5, Power iteration and friends and How eigen() works, and big problems: singular values are square roots of eigenvalues of \(A^TA\); the algorithms that compute both, and Lanczos-type methods (irlba) that compute only the top few singular triplets of a large sparse cells × genes matrix, as needed for PCA of single-cell data.
Part 9, Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters: the same diagnosis for nonlinear models. The Jacobian of the model takes the place of \(S\), and its small singular values name the parameter combinations the data cannot determine.
Part 9, Constraints and linear programming: the optimality conditions you checked for NNLS are a special case of the KKT conditions for constrained optimisation.
We used ridge with a penalty towards 0 and a single \(\lambda\) chosen by eye from the L-curve. Statistical treatments (cross-validation, Bayesian priors, penalties towards a prior guess) choose \(\lambda\) more carefully; the numerical core is the filter-factor formula of this exercise.

title: Quiz: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In one or two sentences each: what do \(V^T\), \(\Sigma\) and \(U\) in \(A = U\Sigma V^T\) do to a vector \(x\)? What does \(A\) do to the unit circle?






Hint





Apply the three factors to \(x\) one at a time, right to left.









Answer





\(V^T\) rotates (possibly with a reflection) so that the directions \(v_1, v_2, \dots\) line up with the coordinate axes. \(\Sigma\) stretches axis \(i\) by \(\sigma_i\). \(U\) rotates the axes onto the directions \(u_1, u_2, \dots\) in data space. The unit circle becomes an ellipse with half-axes \(\sigma_1u_1\) and \(\sigma_2u_2\); \(v_1\) is the unit vector stretched most, \(Av_1 = \sigma_1u_1\).




Q2. A \(100\times 3\) matrix has singular values \(50\), \(5\) and \(0.005\). What is its condition number? What is its numerical rank (a) for rounding errors only, (b) if the right-hand side has noise of relative size \(10^{-3}\)?






Hint





\(\kappa = \sigma_1/\sigma_n\). For (a), the tolerance is \(\max(m,n)\,\varepsilon\,\sigma_1\). For (b), compare \(\sigma_i/\sigma_1\) with the noise level.









Answer





\(\kappa = 50/0.005 = 10^4\). (a) The tolerance is \(100 \times 2.2\times10^{-16}\times 50 \approx 10^{-12}\): all three are above it, rank 3. (b) \(\sigma_3/\sigma_1 = 10^{-4}\) is below the noise level \(10^{-3}\): noise along \(u_3\) is amplified by \(1/\sigma_3\) and swamps the signal, so for practical purposes the rank is 2, and the combination \(v_3\) of the parameters is not determined by the data.




Q3. On paper, \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^TA)}\). Why do svd(), np.linalg.svd and nalgebra not compute singular values that way?






Hint





What is the condition number of \(A^TA\), compared with that of \(A\)?









Answer





\(\kappa(A^TA) = \kappa(A)^2\). Forming \(A^TA\) squares the small singular values: a \(\sigma_n = 10^{-9}\) becomes an eigenvalue \(10^{-18}\), below the rounding error of the entries of \(A^TA\), and is lost. The same reason makes the normal equations worse than QR. SVD routines work on \(A\) itself with orthogonal transformations.




Q4. You regress expression on a set of covariates with lm, and one coefficient comes back as NA. What does that mean, and is the coefficient next to it trustworthy?






Hint





lm uses a pivoted QR and checks the rank.









Answer





The design matrix is (numerically) rank-deficient: that covariate is a linear combination of others (for example two columns that are identical, or dummy variables that add up to the intercept). lm drops it. The remaining coefficients are one of infinitely many solutions; the coefficient of a column that is collinear with the dropped one now measures their combined effect (in the lecture, “CD4” = CD4 + CD8). Look at svd(X)$d and the right singular vector of the zero singular value to see which columns are involved.




Q5. What do these lines print, approximately, and why is the second number not exactly 0?

RPythonRust


svd(cbind(1:3, 1:3))$d


import numpy as np
A = np.column_stack([[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]]).astype(float)
print(np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False))


// rust/examples/svd_q5.rs  —  cargo run --example svd_q5
// Q5: singular values of a matrix with two identical columns.
use nalgebra::DMatrix;

fn main() {
    let a = DMatrix::from_row_slice(3, 2, &[1.0, 1.0, 2.0, 2.0, 3.0, 3.0]);
    println!("{:?}", a.singular_values().as_slice());
}









Hint





Both columns are \(c = (1, 2, 3)\). What is \(\|c\|\), and what is \(A\,(1, 1)/\sqrt2\)?









Answer





\(\sigma_1 = \|c\|\sqrt2 = \sqrt{28} = 5.2915\) and \(\sigma_2 = 0\) in exact arithmetic (rank 1). R prints 5.291503e+00 5.787113e-16, Python [5.29150262e+00 5.78711299e-16], Rust [5.2915026221291805, 0.0]. The SVD is computed with rounding errors of size about \(\varepsilon\,\sigma_1 \approx 10^{-15}\), so an exact zero comes out as a number of that size (or, by luck, 0). That is why the rank is decided with a tolerance, never with == 0.




Q6. In a least-squares problem, \(\sigma_4 = 0.01\), and the noise contributes about \(0.1\) to \(u_4^Tb\). How large an error does that cause in the solution, and in which direction?






Hint





\(x = \sum_i (u_i^Tb/\sigma_i)\,v_i\).









Answer





\(0.1/0.01 = 10\), along \(v_4\). Whatever \(v_4\) is (in the lecture, “more CD4, less CD8”), the solution moves by 10 units in that direction, even though the noise in \(b\) is only 0.1. The other components, with larger \(\sigma_i\), are hardly affected.




Q7. Two cell types have exactly the same signature. The pseudoinverse solution gives them the same proportion. Does this mean the data show they are equally abundant?






Hint





Which property singles out the pseudoinverse solution among all least-squares solutions?









Answer





No. Every split with the same total fits the data equally well. The pseudoinverse picks the solution with the smallest \(\|x\|\), which for two identical columns is the equal split. It is a convention, not information. Report the total, and say that the split is not determined.




Q8. Compute the ridge filter factors \(f_i = \sigma_i^2/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda^2)\) for \(\sigma = 100\), \(1\) and \(0.01\) with \(\lambda = 1\). What does ridge do to each component?






Hint





\(f \approx 1\) when \(\sigma \gg \lambda\) and \(f \approx (\sigma/\lambda)^2\) when \(\sigma \ll \lambda\).









Answer





\(f = 10^4/(10^4 + 1) = 0.9999\), \(f = 1/2 = 0.5\) and \(f = 10^{-4}/(1 + 10^{-4}) \approx 10^{-4}\). The first component is kept, the second halved, the third almost removed. The truncated SVD would use 1, 1 or 0 instead (a sharp cut) depending on where \(k\) is set; ridge is a smooth step at \(\sigma = \lambda\).




Q9. You increase \(\lambda\) in a ridge deconvolution from 10 to 1000. What happens to the residual, to \(\|x\|\) and to the sum of the estimated proportions? How do you pick \(\lambda\) without knowing the truth?






Hint





For large \(\lambda\), which singular values are above \(\lambda\)?









Answer





Once \(\lambda\) is comparable to the large singular values, ridge damps the well-determined components too: the residual grows fast, \(\|x\|\) shrinks, and all proportions are pulled towards 0 (in the lecture example the sum drops from 0.997 to 0.23). Choose \(\lambda\) at the corner of the L-curve (log solution norm against log residual norm), or as the largest \(\lambda\) whose residual is still about the noise level (discrepancy principle), or by cross-validation.




Q10. NNLS gives a CD8 T-cell proportion of exactly 0. A colleague concludes the sample has no CD8 T cells. What would you check?






Hint





What does the smallest singular vector of the signature look like? What happens if you refit with slightly different data?









Answer





Check whether CD8 is confounded with another cell type: look at the smallest singular values of the signature and their right singular vectors (in the lecture, \(v_5 \approx (1, -1, 0, 0, 0)/\sqrt2\), CD4 minus CD8). Then refit with perturbed data (new noise of the measured size, or a bootstrap over genes). If CD8 jumps between 0 and a large value while CD4 + CD8 stays fixed, the zero is set by noise: NNLS only clipped the split at the bound. It is not evidence of absence.




Q11. How is PCA related to the SVD, and why does prcomp use svd rather than eigen(cov(X))?






Hint





Write the centred data matrix as \(X = U\Sigma V^T\) and compute \(X^TX\).









Answer





For the column-centred data \(X = U\Sigma V^T\), the principal axes are the \(v_i\), the scores are \(U\Sigma\), and the variances are \(\sigma_i^2/(n-1)\), because the covariance matrix is \(X^TX/(n-1) = V\,\Sigma^2/(n-1)\,V^T\). Computing the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix instead squares the condition number, as in Q3, so small variances lose accuracy. Keeping the top \(k\) components is the truncated SVD of the data.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
About this lecture
Part 2 ended with Newton for systems of equations: one linear solve J\,\Delta\mathbf x = -\mathbf f per step. This part opens the black box behind solve().

Recap: Gaussian elimination, as in a first linear algebra course.
The new view: elimination is a factorisation A = LU, lower triangular times upper triangular.
With L and U in hand, A\mathbf x = \mathbf b is two cheap triangular solves: forward and back substitution.
Cost: factorising is O(n^3), each solve with the factors only O(n^2). So: factor once, solve many.
Never solve(A) %*% b: slower and less accurate.
Failure: a zero pivot stops elimination even when the system has a perfectly good answer (the fix, pivoting, is the next unit).
Biology: isotope mixing models: what fraction of an animal’s diet came from each source, for one animal or for thousands.


This is the first of three units on linear systems. Students know Gaussian elimination as a pen-and-paper procedure for solving one system. The point of this unit is to see it as an object, the factorisation A = LU, which can be stored and reused. That one change of view explains why solve() is fast, why R and Python offer lu functions at all, and why inverting a matrix is almost never the right thing to do. Pivoting and conditioning are deliberately left to the next unit, Pivoting, norms and conditioning; here we only show the zero-pivot failure as a teaser.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: A biology problem: what did they eat?
text:
A biology problem: what did they eat?




Stable isotope ratios in bone collagen record diet. Each source has a signature (\delta^{13}C, \delta^{15}N, corrected for trophic enrichment); a consumer is a mixture.

Three sources, unknown diet fractions f_1, f_2, f_3.
Two isotopes give two equations; the fractions summing to 1 gives the third.
3 equations, 3 unknowns: a linear system.
Consumer #4 lies outside the triangle; we come back to it.



This is the classic linear mixing model used in archaeology (human bone collagen), ecology (food webs, hair and feather samples) and microbial ecology (tracer studies). With k isotopes one can separate k + 1 sources exactly. The source values here are illustrative but realistic: C3 plants around -26 per mil carbon, C4 plants such as maize around -10, marine fish in between with high nitrogen because they sit higher in the food web. Real studies add uncertainty (Bayesian mixing models such as MixSIAR), but at their core is this linear system. Ask: where in the triangle would a pure maize eater be? Answer: at the maize corner.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
As a matrix equation
Mass balance for each isotope, plus “fractions sum to 1”:

\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ -26 & -10 & -18 \\ 2 & 6 & 14 \end{pmatrix}}_{A:\ \text{columns = sources}}
\begin{pmatrix} f_1 \\ f_2 \\ f_3 \end{pmatrix}
=
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -19.6 \\ 5.6 \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf b:\ \text{consumer \#1}}

A <- rbind(c(  1,   1,   1),      # fractions sum to 1
           c(-26, -10, -18),      # d13C of C3 plants, maize, fish
           c(  2,   6,  14))      # d15N
b <- c(1, -19.6, 5.6)             # consumer #1
solve(A, b)
# [1] 0.5 0.3 0.2
Half C3 plants, 30 % maize, 20 % fish. What did solve() do?

Row 2 reads: -26 f1 - 10 f2 - 18 f3 = -19.6, the consumer’s carbon signature as a weighted average of the sources. The matrix A depends only on the sources; the right-hand side b depends only on the consumer. That split is the key to the rest of the lecture. Check by hand: 0.5 * (-26) + 0.3 * (-10) + 0.2 * (-18) = -13 - 3 - 3.6 = -19.6.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Many consumers, one matrix
A study has hundreds of animals (or an isotope image has 10^5 pixels), all against the same sources:
B <- cbind(c(1, -19.6,  5.6),     # one column per consumer
           c(1, -14.8,  6.8),
           c(1, -17.2, 11.2),
           c(1, -24.0,  9.0))
X <- solve(A, B)                  # one column of fractions per consumer
X
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]  [,4]
# [1,]  0.5  0.2  0.1  0.55
# [2,]  0.3  0.6  0.2 -0.20
# [3,]  0.2  0.2  0.7  0.65

Same A, many right-hand sides \mathbf b. Can the work on A be done once?
Consumer #4: a negative fraction. The numerics are fine; the consumer lies outside the mixing triangle (a missing source, or wrong source values).


This is the situation the lecture is built around: A fixed, b changing. It is extremely common: calibration against the same set of standards, per-pixel unmixing in an image, the same matrix at every time step of an implicit ODE solver (Part 8) or diffusion solver (Part 10), Newton with a frozen Jacobian. Consumer 4 is a model check, not a numerical failure: fractions must lie between 0 and 1, and a negative one means the point is outside the polygon of sources. Always check this in a mixing model.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Keep the multipliers: L
Put each multiplier where it made its zero, with 1 on the diagonal:

L = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ \ell_{21} & 1 & 0 \\ \ell_{31} & \ell_{32} & 1 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -26 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & \tfrac14 & 1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 16 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 10 \end{pmatrix}

Then A = LU. Check row 3: 2\cdot(1, 1, 1) + \tfrac14 \cdot (0, 16, 8) + 1\cdot(0, 0, 10) = (2, 6, 14). ✓

Row i of A = (row i of U) + (the multiples of earlier U rows that elimination subtracted). L records exactly those multiples.
L is unit lower triangular, U is upper triangular. This is the LU factorisation.


The check is the whole proof in miniature: elimination subtracted l_ik times (new) row k from row i, so adding those multiples back reconstructs the original row. Students rarely see this in a first course, where the multipliers are computed and immediately forgotten. Point out that L and U together hold n^2 numbers, the same as A: in practice they are stored in the space of A (the 1s on the diagonal of L are not stored), which is exactly what LAPACK and the lu() functions return.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Why triangular is good
A\mathbf x = \mathbf b becomes L(U\mathbf x) = \mathbf b. Call \mathbf y = U\mathbf x and solve two triangular systems:


1. Forward substitution L\mathbf y = \mathbf b, top to bottom:
\begin{aligned}
y_1 &= 1 \\
y_2 &= -19.6 + 26\,y_1 = 6.4 \\
y_3 &= 5.6 - 2\,y_1 - \tfrac14 y_2 = 2.0
\end{aligned}

2. Back substitution U\mathbf x = \mathbf y, bottom to top:
\begin{aligned}
x_3 &= 2.0 / 10 = 0.2 \\
x_2 &= (6.4 - 8\,x_3)/16 = 0.3 \\
x_1 &= 1 - x_2 - x_3 = 0.5
\end{aligned}


Forward substitution replays on \mathbf b the row operations that elimination did on A (\mathbf y is the right-hand column of the augmented matrix after elimination).
Next consumer: new \mathbf b, same L and U, only these 6 lines again.


This is the same arithmetic the augmented matrix would have done to b, just done afterwards. That is why factorising does not cost anything extra: it is elimination, with the b part postponed. Count the work: forward substitution here is 3 multiply-subtract pairs, back substitution 3 pairs and 2 divisions. Compare with the elimination itself (next slides): that work does not depend on b, so it is done once.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Elimination in R, written out
lu_nopivot <- function(A) {
  n <- nrow(A); L <- diag(n); U <- A
  for (k in 1:(n - 1)) {                         # pivot column k
    for (i in (k + 1):n) {                       # rows below the pivot
      L[i, k] <- U[i, k] / U[k, k]               # multiplier l_ik
      U[i, k:n] <- U[i, k:n] - L[i, k] * U[k, k:n]   # row i - l_ik * row k
    }
  }
  list(L = L, U = U)
}
F <- lu_nopivot(A)
F$L %*% F$U                                      # gives back A exactly

Three nested loops (the third is the vector operation on k:n): that is where n^3 will come from.
diag(n) is the n \times n identity matrix; %*% is the matrix product.


Ten lines, exactly the board procedure. The inner vector operation updates only columns k to n, since the columns before k are already zero in those rows. This is a teaching implementation: R loops are slow, and real code calls LAPACK (next slides). The name lu_nopivot is a reminder that something is missing: it fails when U[k, k] is 0, as we see near the end of the lecture. Python and Rust versions are in the exercise.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: Forward and back substitution in R

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
What libraries do: Matrix::lu
library(Matrix)
Fm <- lu(A)                     # LAPACK's LU, stored compactly
e  <- expand2(Fm)               # A = P1. %*% L %*% U
e$L
#             [,1]        [,2]        [,3]
# [1,]  1.00000000           .           .
# [2,] -0.07692308  1.00000000           .
# [3,] -0.03846154  0.11764706  1.00000000
solve(Fm, b)                    # forward + back substitution only
# [1] 0.5 0.3 0.2

lu() gives different L and U from ours: it reorders the rows first (pivot -26, the largest in column 1). The permutation matrix P records the swaps: A = PLU.
Same answer. Why it reorders is the next unit, Pivoting, norms and conditioning.


The Matrix package ships with R. expand2 returns the three factors (in Matrix >= 1.6; older versions have expand). The pivot -26 was chosen because it is the largest entry in absolute value in the first column; dividing by large pivots keeps the multipliers at most 1 in size, and all entries of L here are below 1. That is partial pivoting, the topic of the next lecture. Python: scipy.linalg.lu_factor and lu_solve; Rust: nalgebra’s a.lu() and .solve(&b). Base solve(A, b) calls the same LAPACK routine and then substitutes, every time: solve(A, b) in base R is LAPACK dgesv: factorise with pivoting, then substitute; it does not keep the factors.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Counting the cost
Factorising. At step k there are n-k rows below the pivot; each needs 1 division and n-k multiply–subtract pairs:
\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} 2(n-k)^2 \;\approx\; 2\sum_{j=1}^{n} j^2 \;\approx\; \tfrac23 n^3 \text{ operations}
Substitution. Row i of forward substitution needs i-1 pairs: \sum_i 2(i-1) \approx n^2. Back substitution the same. Total \approx 2n^2.



n
factorise \tfrac23 n^3
substitute 2n^2
ratio




3

6.7\times10^5
2\times10^4

6.7\times10^8
2\times10^6

2\times10^8
3 333




Use sum of j^2 = n^3/3 + lower terms. The ratio is n/3: for small systems it does not matter, for a 1000 x 1000 system one factorisation costs as much as several hundred solves. Recall from Convergence and cost: at about 1e9 simple operations per second per core, 6.7e8 is under a second, 6.7e11 is ten minutes. For n = 3 the leading-term formulas are rough (the exact counts are 13 and 15 operations, see the exercise), but for large n only the leading term matters.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: Measured: slopes on a log–log plot
text:
Measured: slopes on a log–log plot


Substitution: slope ≈ 2. Factorising: slope ≈ 2.6, doubling ratio 5.5 → 6.3 → 6.5 (towards 8).
The gap grows with n: at n = 8000, one factorisation (6.4 s) = 145 solves (0.044 s).


Timed with a single BLAS thread (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, see the figure script), minimum of several runs, random dense matrices. The factorisation slope is below 3 because LAPACK’s blocked algorithm runs at more operations per second as n grows (it keeps blocks in cache), so the time grows slower than the operation count until the processor runs at full speed; the doubling ratio creeps up towards 8. This is the “When timing misleads” slide from Convergence and cost: count operations, then measure, and expect the measured exponent to approach the count only for large n. The substitution slope is close to 2: each entry of L and U is read once.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Factor once, solve many
Right-hand sides that arrive one at a time (a new sample, the next time step, the next Newton step with a frozen Jacobian):
set.seed(1)
n <- 1000; A <- matrix(rnorm(n * n), n)
Bm <- matrix(rnorm(n * 200), n)                    # 200 right-hand sides
system.time(for (j in 1:200) x <- solve(A, Bm[, j]))["elapsed"]
#  6.618                                           # factorises 200 times
system.time({ F <- lu(A); for (j in 1:200) x <- solve(F, Bm[, j]) })["elapsed"]
#  0.12                                            # factorises once
system.time(X <- solve(A, Bm))["elapsed"]
#  0.035                                           # all at once

55 times faster by keeping the factors. If all \mathbf b are known in advance, put them as columns of a matrix: solve(A, B) factorises once.


Single thread again (timings in seconds on our server; yours will differ, the ratios less so). The loop with solve(A, b) redoes the O(n^3) factorisation every time. Keeping the lu object costs one factorisation plus 200 cheap substitutions. solve(A, Bm) with a matrix right-hand side does one factorisation and then substitutes all 200 columns in one optimised LAPACK call, which is faster still. The one-at-a-time case is the important one in practice: in an implicit ODE or diffusion solver (Parts 8 and 10), the right-hand side of step t + 1 depends on the solution at step t, so they cannot be batched.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: How the total cost grows with m
text:
How the total cost grows with m


Refactorising: m \cdot \tfrac23 n^3. Factor once: \tfrac23 n^3 + m \cdot 2n^2. For m = 10\,000 samples: 4 min vs 4 s.
The orange dashed line (inverse once) runs parallel to the blue one, but higher. Next slide.


Built from measured single-call times at n = 1000 (see the figure script): solve(A, b) 0.024 s, lu(A) 0.018 s, one substitution 0.00042 s, solve(A) 0.068 s, one product Ainv %*% b 0.00083 s. For one right-hand side the two blue/red strategies are the same. For many, the cost of the factorisation is spread over all of them, and the curve is set by the cheap substitutions. The inverse curve starts higher (inverting costs about 3 to 4 times a factorisation) and stays higher.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Never solve(A) %*% b (1): cost
solve(A) with one argument returns A^{-1}. It computes it by solving A\,\mathbf x_j = \mathbf e_j for each column \mathbf e_j of the identity:

LU of A: \tfrac23 n^3, plus n right-hand sides: about \tfrac43 n^3 more. Total \approx 2n^3, 3 times one factorisation.
Then A^{-1}\mathbf b costs 2n^2, the same as forward + back substitution.

system.time(solve(A))["elapsed"]       # n = 1000, one thread
#  0.068
system.time(lu(A))["elapsed"]
#  0.018
So for one \mathbf b, the inverse is 3–4 times slower, and for many \mathbf b it gains nothing over keeping L and U.

The 4/3 n^3 for the n extra right-hand sides already uses the zeros in the identity columns; without that trick it would be 2 n^3. Memory too: the inverse is a full dense matrix even when A is sparse or banded (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse), while LU of a banded matrix stays banded. In formulas, x = A^{-1} b is fine notation. In code, it should always be read as “solve A x = b”.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Never solve(A) %*% b (2): accuracy
Four sources, three isotopes; sources 1 and 2 differ by only 0.01–0.02 ‰:
A4 <- rbind(1,
            c(-26, -25.99, -10, -18),   # d13C
            c(  2,   2.01,   6,  14),   # d15N
            c(  4,   4.02,   3,  19))   # d34S
f <- c(0.3, 0.2, 0.4, 0.1); b <- A4 %*% f
x_lu  <- solve(A4, b)
x_inv <- solve(A4) %*% b
c(max(abs(b - A4 %*% x_lu)), max(abs(b - A4 %*% x_inv)))   # residuals
# [1] 0.000000e+00 4.657608e-12
c(max(abs(x_lu - f)),        max(abs(x_inv - f)))          # errors
# [1] 2.060296e-13 4.786171e-13

The residual \mathbf b - A\mathbf x of solve(A, b) is at rounding level; the inverse’s is 10^4 times larger. The error is also larger.


Two sources with almost the same signature make the matrix nearly singular (kappa(A4) is about 8e4; that number and why it matters are the next unit). Both answers lose some digits because of that. But the LU solution is backward stable (as in Error, conditioning and stability): it is the exact solution for a matrix within rounding of A4, so its residual is at the level of epsilon. The inverse route is not: its residual grows with the condition number. The residual is the check you can always run, because it does not need the true answer.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: The residual check, on many matrices
text:
The residual check, on many matrices


Random 50 \times 50 matrices with condition number \kappa from 10 to 10^{15}. Residual relative to \max|A|\cdot\max|\mathbf x|.
solve(A, b): about \varepsilon, whatever \kappa. Inverse: grows like \kappa\,\varepsilon.


The blue points are the signature of a backward stable algorithm: the computed x solves a system within rounding of the given one, so the residual is tiny even when the error in x is large. The orange points are not: multiplying by a computed inverse adds error proportional to kappa. Conditioning (kappa, and why a small residual does not guarantee a small error) is the next unit.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: When elimination breaks: a zero pivot
text:
When elimination breaks: a zero pivot
Two sources with the same \delta^{13}C (C3 plants and freshwater fish, both -26 ‰), told apart by \delta^{15}N:
A0 <- rbind(c(  1,   1,   1),
            c(-26, -26, -10),       # d13C: C3 plants, freshwater fish, maize
            c(  2,  10,   6))       # d15N
lu_nopivot(A0)$U
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    1    1
# [2,]    0    0   16             # pivot U[2, 2] = 0
# [3,]    0  NaN -Inf
solve(A0, c(1, -20, 6.5))
# [1] 0.250 0.375 0.375

After step 1 the pivot is 0: division by zero gives Inf and NaN, no error message.
The system is fine (solve answers): swapping rows 2 and 3 fixes it.


A zero pivot does not mean the matrix is singular. Here it means only that the rows are in an unlucky order: the carbon row cannot tell sources 1 and 2 apart, but the nitrogen row can. Swap rows 2 and 3 and elimination goes through (the exercise does it by hand). Note again that R gives no error: 0/0 is NaN and x/0 is Inf, as in How computers store numbers. This is the first reason libraries reorder rows. The second reason is on the next slide.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: Worse: a tiny pivot gives a wrong answer silently
text:
Worse: a tiny pivot gives a wrong answer silently
\begin{pmatrix} 10^{-20} & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf x = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf x \approx (1, 1)
As <- rbind(c(1e-20, 1), c(1, 1))
Fs <- lu_nopivot(As)                  # l21 = 1e20, u22 = 1 - 1e20
back_sub(Fs$U, forward_sub(Fs$L, c(1, 2)))
# [1] 0 1                               # x1 is 100 % wrong
solve(As, c(1, 2))
# [1] 1 1

1 - 10^{20} rounds to -10^{20}: the “1” in a_{22} is lost, and with it x_1.
No NaN, no warning. Check: the residual, b - A %*% x, here (0, 1).
The cure is partial pivoting: Pivoting, norms and conditioning.


The matrix is perfectly well conditioned; the algorithm without pivoting is unstable. A huge multiplier (1e20) means that the second row of U is dominated by the first, and information in a22 vanishes in rounding (the epsilon of How computers store numbers). This is the teaser for the next lecture, which shows that choosing the largest available pivot keeps all multipliers at most 1 and makes elimination stable in practice. The residual check catches this failure: for x = (0, 1), A x = (1, 1), so b - A x = (0, 1), far from rounding level.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
section: Checks to run on a linear solve
text:
Checks to run on a linear solve

Residual: max(abs(b - A %*% x)) should be near \varepsilon \cdot \max|A| \cdot \max|\mathbf x|. If not, the algorithm failed (no pivoting, inverse).
Factors: max(abs(L %*% U - A)) for your own LU; is.finite() on the factors catches a zero pivot.
Use the library: solve(A, b), solve(A, B), or F <- lu(A) then solve(F, b). They pivot.
No inverses in code: solve(A) %*% b → solve(A, b).
Plausibility: diet fractions between 0 and 1. A negative fraction = consumer outside the source polygon, a model problem, not a numerical one.

A small residual does not prove a small error (A4 above): that depends on the condition number. Next unit.

Checks 1 and 2 detect algorithmic failure. Check 5 detects modelling failure. Neither detects an ill-conditioned problem, where a tiny residual can come with a large error; that is the topic of Pivoting, norms and conditioning, with flow cytometry spectral unmixing as the biology.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Summary

Gaussian elimination = LU factorisation. Keep the multipliers \ell_{ik} = a_{ik}/a_{kk} in a unit lower triangular L; the eliminated matrix is the upper triangular U; A = LU.
Solve A\mathbf x = \mathbf b as L\mathbf y = \mathbf b (forward substitution), then U\mathbf x = \mathbf y (back substitution).
Cost: factorising \approx \tfrac23 n^3, each solve with the factors \approx 2n^2. Factor once, solve many: F <- lu(A); solve(F, b), or solve(A, B) for many columns at once.
Never solve(A) %*% b: about 3 times the work, and a residual that grows with \kappa.
Libraries reorder rows (A = PLU). Without that, a zero pivot gives NaN, a tiny pivot a silently wrong answer. Check the residual.
Biology: isotope mixing models for many consumers against the same sources; negative fractions flag a consumer outside the source polygon.

Next: Pivoting, norms and conditioning: why libraries pivot, and how much a matrix amplifies noise.

Recap the change of view: elimination is not just a procedure that spits out x, it produces an object (L, U, and the permutation) that can be stored and reused. The cost split n^3 / n^2 is what makes implicit ODE solvers, Newton’s method for systems and implicit diffusion schemes affordable. The next unit explains pivoting, defines the condition number of a matrix and uses it to read off how many digits a solve can lose.

title: Exercise: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

run Gaussian elimination on a 3×3 matrix by hand and record the multipliers,
write the result as an LU factorisation \(A = LU\) and check it by multiplying out,
solve \(A\mathbf x = \mathbf b\) for a new \(\mathbf b\) by forward and back substitution alone,
count the operations: about \(\tfrac23 n^3\) to factorise, \(2n^2\) per solve, and use that to choose between factor once, solve many and refactorising,
explain why solve(A) %*% b is slower and less accurate than solve(A, b),
recognise a zero or tiny pivot, and run the checks (is.finite, the residual) that catch it.

The biology throughout is the isotope mixing model: which fraction of a consumer’s diet came from each source. The by-hand part uses pen and paper only.

title: Exercise: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:

The biology throughout is the isotope mixing model: which fraction of a consumer’s diet came from each source. The by-hand part uses pen and paper only.

title: Exercise: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Background
A consumer’s isotope signature is a weighted average of its diet sources (after correcting for trophic enrichment). With \(k\) isotopes and \(k+1\) sources, the mass balance for each isotope plus “fractions sum to 1” gives a square system \(A\mathbf f = \mathbf b\): the columns of \(A\) are the sources, \(\mathbf b\) is the consumer.
Facts used below:

Elimination. At step \(k\), the pivot is \(u_{kk}\); row \(i > k\) gets row \(k\) times the multiplier \(\ell_{ik} = u_{ik}/u_{kk}\) subtracted from it. After \(n-1\) steps the matrix is upper triangular, \(U\).
LU. Put the multipliers below the diagonal of a unit lower triangular \(L\) (1s on the diagonal). Then \(A = LU\).
Solving with the factors. \(L\mathbf y = \mathbf b\) by forward substitution (top to bottom), then \(U\mathbf x = \mathbf y\) by back substitution (bottom to top).
Cost. Factorising \(\approx \tfrac23 n^3\) operations; each forward + back substitution \(\approx 2n^2\). A computer does roughly \(10^9\) simple operations per second per core.
Inverse. Computing \(A^{-1}\) costs \(\approx 2n^3\), and multiplying by it is less accurate than substituting.
Pivots. A zero pivot stops elimination (division by zero); a tiny one gives huge multipliers and a wrong answer. Libraries reorder rows (partial pivoting): \(A = PLU\). Pivoting is the topic of Pivoting, norms and conditioning.
Residual \(\mathbf r = \mathbf b - A\mathbf x\). A good solver gives \(\max|r_i|\) near \(\varepsilon\cdot\max|a_{ij}|\cdot\max|x_j|\).

A salt-marsh example: a ribbed mussel feeds on Spartina (marsh grass, \(\delta^{13}\)C \(= -13\) ‰, \(\delta^{34}\)S \(= +6\) ‰), phytoplankton (\(-21\), \(+18\)) and upland C3 plant detritus (\(-27\), \(+2\)). The basic tools in each language:

RPythonRust


library(Matrix)
A <- rbind(c(  1,   1,   1),      # fractions sum to 1
           c(-13, -21, -27),      # d13C: Spartina, phytoplankton, upland C3
           c(  6,  18,   2))      # d34S
b <- c(1, -18.4, 11.6)            # one ribbed mussel
solve(A, b)                       # factorise + substitute, in one call
# [1] 0.4 0.5 0.1
F <- lu(A)                        # factorise once ...
solve(F, b)                       # ... substitute as often as needed
# [1] 0.4 0.5 0.1


import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import lu_factor, lu_solve

A = np.array([[  1,   1,   1],          # fractions sum to 1
              [-13, -21, -27],          # d13C: Spartina, phytoplankton, upland C3
              [  6,  18,   2]], float)  # d34S
b = np.array([1, -18.4, 11.6])          # one ribbed mussel
print(np.linalg.solve(A, b))            # factorise + substitute, in one call
# [0.4 0.5 0.1]
F = lu_factor(A)                        # factorise once ...
print(lu_solve(F, b))                   # ... substitute as often as needed
# [0.4 0.5 0.1]


// rust/examples/lu_background.rs  —  cargo run --example lu_background
use nalgebra::{dmatrix, dvector};

fn main() {
    let a = dmatrix![  1.0,   1.0,   1.0;      // fractions sum to 1
                     -13.0, -21.0, -27.0;      // d13C: Spartina, phytoplankton, upland C3
                       6.0,  18.0,   2.0];     // d34S
    let b = dvector![1.0, -18.4, 11.6];        // one ribbed mussel
    let f = a.clone().lu();                    // factorise once ...
    let x = f.solve(&b).expect("singular");    // ... substitute as often as needed
    println!("{:?}", x.as_slice());
}

// Output:
// [0.39999999999999997, 0.5, 0.1]



R prints 7 significant digits, numpy 8, and Rust’s {:?} prints every digit needed to identify the double, so Rust shows 0.39999999999999997 where R shows 0.4. They are the same number up to the last bit or two. Python’s library calls are numpy.linalg.solve, scipy.linalg.lu_factor and scipy.linalg.lu_solve; Rust uses nalgebra’s LU (.lu(), .solve()).

title: Exercise: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
By hand
B1. Elimination, as in your first course. The mussel above has signature \(\delta^{13}\)C \(= -18.4\) ‰, \(\delta^{34}\)S \(= 11.6\) ‰. (a) Write the system \(A\mathbf f = \mathbf b\) as an augmented matrix \([A \mid \mathbf b]\). (b) Eliminate below the diagonal. Write down each multiplier \(\ell_{ik}\) as you use it. (c) Back-substitute for \(f_1, f_2, f_3\). What fraction of the mussel’s diet is phytoplankton?
B2. The multipliers make \(L\). (a) From B1, write \(L\) (multipliers below the diagonal, 1s on it) and \(U\) (the eliminated \(A\), without the \(\mathbf b\) column). (b) Multiply out \(LU\) and check that you get \(A\). (c) Look at the \(\mathbf b\) column at the end of B1(b). Which triangular system with \(L\) does that column solve?
B3. A second mussel, without eliminating again. A second mussel has \(\delta^{13}\)C \(= -22.4\) ‰, \(\delta^{34}\)S \(= 7.6\) ‰. (a) Solve \(L\mathbf y = \mathbf b\) by forward substitution, then \(U\mathbf f = \mathbf y\) by back substitution. (b) Count the multiplications, additions/subtractions and divisions in (a). Then count those that eliminating \(A\) itself took in B1(b) (ignore the \(\mathbf b\) column). Which part would you redo for a third mussel?
B4. An LU with no biology. Factorise \[A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 & 3 \\ 8 & 7 & 9 \end{pmatrix}.\] (a) Give \(L\) and \(U\). (b) The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal, and \(\det(LU) = \det L \cdot \det U\). What is \(\det A\)? (c) Solve \(A\mathbf x = (4, 10, 24)^T\) with your factors.
B5. A zero pivot. Three diet sources: C3 plants (\(\delta^{13}\)C \(= -26\), \(\delta^{15}\)N \(= 2\)), freshwater fish (\(-26\), \(10\)) and maize (\(-10\), \(6\)). Rows: sum to 1, \(\delta^{13}\)C, \(\delta^{15}\)N. (a) Write \(A\) and do the first elimination step. What goes wrong at step 2? (b) Swap rows 2 and 3 of \(A\) (and of \(\mathbf b\)), and factorise again. Give \(L\) and \(U\). (c) Solve for a consumer with \(\delta^{13}\)C \(= -20\), \(\delta^{15}\)N \(= 6.5\). (d) Now suppose the fish had \(\delta^{15}\)N \(= 2\) as well (the same signature as the C3 plants in both isotopes). Eliminate. Does any row swap help? What does that mean for the diet estimate?
B6. Counting the cost. (a) Use B3(b) to give the exact operation counts for \(n = 3\). Compare with \(\tfrac23 n^3\) and \(2n^2\). (b) For \(n = 1000\), how many operations are one factorisation and one solve? Roughly how many seconds at \(10^9\) operations per second? (c) An implicit model of tracer diffusion in tissue (Part 10) solves a system with the same \(5000 \times 5000\) matrix at each of 1000 time steps. Estimate the time if you factorise at every step, and if you factorise once. (Treat the matrix as dense.) (d) A study has 10 000 consumers and a 3×3 mixing matrix. Does the choice between refactorising and factor-once matter for the operation count?
B7. Why not the inverse. (a) Accuracy, \(1 \times 1\). Work in decimal arithmetic with 3 significant digits (round after every operation). Solve \(7x = 63\) (i) by division, \(x = 63/7\), and (ii) via the inverse, \(x = (1/7) \cdot 63\). (b) Cost. Computing \(A^{-1}\) means solving \(A\mathbf x_j = \mathbf e_j\) for \(j = 1, \dots, n\). With the counts from the lecture, what does that cost, compared with one factorisation? (Use \(2n^2\) per column, ignoring that the \(\mathbf e_j\) are mostly zeros.) (c) For \(m\) right-hand sides, write the total cost of the inverse route and of the factor-once route. Does the inverse ever win?
