The bound holds; it is pessimistic because it uses the largest derivative.
The same nodes are 2.3 times worse near the ends: |w| is larger there.


f’‘(3) = 0.0592 is the same second derivative as in Convergence and cost, where it set the error constant of the forward difference. For linear interpolation the error at the midpoint is h^2/8 times f’’, here 4/8 times 0.059 = 0.030. For degree 4 the fifth derivative was computed with R’s D() (the exercise shows how). The actual error at 1 h is left as an exercise. The important observation is in the w column: the node polynomial is larger near the ends. With 5 nodes the factor is 2.3; with 13 nodes it is about 300, next slides.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: A longer run: 48 h, a reading every 4 h
text:
A longer run: 48 h, a reading every 4 h


13 readings, so a degree-12 interpolant. It passes through every reading, and dips to OD = −0.15 at 0.9 h: a negative cell density.
It also wiggles in stationary phase near 44–48 h. In the middle it is fine.
This is the Runge phenomenon (Carl Runge, 1901).


Same culture, a longer experiment, a typical plate-reader overnight run. Every reading is exact (no noise at all) and the interpolant still produces nonsense between the first two readings. The largest error, 0.25 OD, is right at the start, in lag phase, which is often exactly the part a biologist cares about (lag time). The classic textbook example is Runge’s function 1/(1 + 25 x^2) on [-1, 1], which the exercise reproduces. The cause is the same: equally spaced nodes and a function whose derivatives grow fast.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: Why the ends? The node polynomial
text:
Why the ends? The node polynomial


Equispaced (red): |w(t)| is about 300 times larger between the first two readings than in the middle.
The error is |f^{(13)}(\xi)|/13! \times |w(t)|: the same derivative factor, multiplied by a much larger w at the ends.
Chebyshev times (blue, ticks on top) are crowded towards the ends, and |w| is level across the whole run.


Log scale on the y axis. Each dip is a node, where w is zero. For equispaced nodes the arches grow towards both ends by orders of magnitude; this is a property of equal spacing, true for any curve. The Chebyshev arches all have the same height: that is the defining property of Chebyshev points, they make the largest value of |w| as small as possible. The derivative part also matters: the logistic has large high derivatives (its complex singularity is close to the steep part), which is why the 0-8 h run did not show the effect.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
More readings make it worse


0–8 h, equispaced (green): error falls with n, by a factor \approx 1.6 per extra reading, until rounding sets in near 10^{-8}.
0–48 h, equispaced (red): error jumps between 0.03 and 0.6 OD and does not converge.
0–48 h, Chebyshev (blue): falls steadily, 2\times10^{-5} at n = 40.


The error-vs-n plot for this method, on a log axis. Green: short interval relative to the curve’s steep part, so the error formula’s derivative factor is beaten by the (n+1)! in the denominator, and the polynomial converges, geometrically. Its upturn after n = 34 is rounding error amplified by the large basis polynomials of equispaced nodes: a second, independent reason to avoid high degree with equal spacing. Red: on the long run the node polynomial wins; the error oscillates and grows for larger n. Blue: the same curve and the same number of readings, only the times moved. Check for students: if adding readings does not reduce the change in your interpolant, you are in the red regime.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Chebyshev nodes
On [-1, 1]: x_k = \cos\!\left(\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n+2}\right), k = 0, \dots, n. On [a, b]: t_k = \tfrac{a+b}{2} - \tfrac{b-a}{2}\,x_k.
They are the projections of equally spaced points on a semicircle, so they crowd at the ends.
n <- 12; k <- 0:n
tc <- 24 - 24 * cos((2 * k + 1) * pi / (2 * n + 2))   # 13 times in [0, 48] h
round(tc, 2)
#  [1]  0.17  1.56  4.25  8.09 12.85 18.26 24.00 29.74 35.15 39.91 43.75 46.44
# [13] 47.83

They minimise \max |w(t)|: the smallest possible value is 2\left(\tfrac{b-a}{4}\right)^{n+1}.
For a smooth curve the error then falls geometrically with n.


Draw a semicircle over [-1, 1], mark n+1 equally spaced angles, drop them to the axis. These are Chebyshev points of the first kind, the zeros of the Chebyshev polynomial T_{n+1}; the second kind (extreme points, cos(k pi / n)) includes the endpoints and is equally good. numpy has chebpts1 and chebpts2. Experimental-design reading: sample densely at the beginning and end of the run and sparsely in the middle. That is rarely how anyone designs a growth experiment, which is the honest limitation of this fix.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: Chebyshev times on the same run
text:
Chebyshev times on the same run


Same 13 readings’ worth of effort, same degree 12. Largest error 0.039 OD instead of 0.25, no negative OD.
In practice you rarely choose the times freely. With the times you have, use low degree, locally: a line between neighbours (approx), or the cubic splines of the next lecture.

approx(t, y, xout = c(3, 5))$y        # piecewise linear, 0-8 h readings
# [1] 0.4159873 0.8141777             # errors 0.027, -0.030

The remaining error of 0.039 is at the end of the steep rise, near 6 h, where Chebyshev points are already sparse; with more Chebyshev points it keeps falling (blue curve two slides back). approx is base R’s piecewise linear interpolation; it can never overshoot the readings, which is its great virtue. Its error is h^2/8 times max |f’’| per interval, from the error formula with n = 1. Splines (next lecture) keep the locality and add smoothness.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Interpolation vs fitting


Hourly readings over 12 h with plate-reader noise (sd 0.02 OD). The degree-12 interpolant goes through the noise and swings to 0.39 OD off near the ends.
A degree-5 least-squares fit (blue) ignores the noise: error 0.032. Without noise, the interpolant’s error was only 0.008.


Interpolation assumes the readings are exact. Real readings are not. Each reading’s error is multiplied by the corresponding basis polynomial L_i, and for 13 equispaced points the largest single L_i reaches 18 near the ends, and the sum of all |L_i| (the Lebesgue constant) reaches 89; for 13 Chebyshev points it is only 2.6. That turns noise of 0.02 into swings of 0.4. A fit with fewer coefficients than points averages the noise out instead. Choosing the degree of a fit is a bias-variance question; the next lecture, Splines, makes it explicit with smoothing splines.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Interpolation vs fitting in R
set.seed(1)
t12 <- 0:12                                  # hourly for 12 h
y12 <- od(t12) + rnorm(13, sd = 0.02)        # plate-reader noise
f_int <- lm(y12 ~ poly(t12, 12))             # 13 coefficients: interpolation
f_fit <- lm(y12 ~ poly(t12, 5))              # 6 coefficients: least squares
max(abs(resid(f_int)))
# [1] 0                                       # passes through every point
tt <- seq(0, 12, by = 0.01)
max(abs(predict(f_int, data.frame(t12 = tt)) - od(tt)))
# [1] 0.3937819
max(abs(predict(f_fit, data.frame(t12 = tt)) - od(tt)))
# [1] 0.03161686

poly() builds orthogonal columns (a QR of the Vandermonde matrix), so even degree 12 is well conditioned.
Zero residuals are a warning sign, not a success: the model has as many parameters as data.


lm with as many coefficients as points is interpolation; with fewer it is least squares, exactly as in Least squares: normal equations vs QR. Using poly() rather than raw powers is what makes degree 12 possible at all (next slide). The diagnostic: compare the interpolant with a lower-degree fit; if they differ by much more than the measurement noise between the points, the interpolant is chasing noise.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Monomial coefficients lose digits

t48 <- seq(0, 48, by = 4)
solve(outer(t48, 0:12, "^"), od(t48))
# Error in solve.default(...) :
#   system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number = 5.66168e-23

In hours, t^{12} reaches 48^{12} \approx 10^{20}: \kappa(V) \approx 8\times10^{20}. R refuses from n = 9; forced (tol = 0, or numpy, which never refuses) the values go wrong from n \approx 22 (orange).
Rescaled to [-1, 1] (red) it lasts longer but stalls near 10^{-5}. Barycentric (blue) reaches 10^{-12}.


Even at Chebyshev nodes, the monomial basis is a bad basis: the Vandermonde matrix’s condition number grows exponentially with n, as in the least-squares lecture. Orange: times in hours, forced through with solve(…, tol = 0); R’s default solve gives up already at n = 9, which is cautious, because LU still reproduces the readings well (a small residual) for a while. From n of about 22 the values between readings are garbage. Red: rescaled to [-1, 1], also forced; the error follows the true interpolation error down to about 1e-5 and then stalls and wanders: kappa(V) reaches 1e18 to 1e19, so the coefficients have essentially no correct digits, and only the cancellation between them keeps the values roughly right. Blue: the same polynomial evaluated with the barycentric formula, which never forms coefficients; it reaches 1e-12. The problem is not the polynomial but how it is represented.

title: Polynomial interpolation
section: The barycentric form: the stable way to evaluate
text:
The barycentric form: the stable way to evaluate
Divide the Lagrange form by the Lagrange form of the constant 1:
p(t) = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_j \frac{w_j\, y_j}{t - t_j}}{\displaystyle\sum_j \frac{w_j}{t - t_j}}, \qquad w_j = \frac{1}{\prod_{k \ne j}(t_j - t_k)} \quad \left(\text{Chebyshev: } w_j = (-1)^j \sin\tfrac{(2j+1)\pi}{2n+2}\right)
bary_weights <- function(x) sapply(seq_along(x), function(j) 1 / prod(x[j] - x[-j]))
bary_eval <- function(x, y, w, xx) sapply(xx, function(z) {
  d <- z - x
  if (any(d == 0)) return(y[d == 0])          # z is a node
  sum(w * y / d) / sum(w / d)
})
bary_eval(t, y, bary_weights(t), c(3, 5))
# [1] 0.4026258 0.8312495

Weights O(n^2) once, then O(n) per point; a new reading updates the weights in O(n).
Rounding errors in numerator and denominator largely cancel: accurate to \approx\varepsilon times the Lebesgue constant. Python: scipy.interpolate.BarycentricInterpolator.


The trick: the weights w_j do not depend on t, and dividing by the same sum for y = 1 makes any common scaling of the weights cancel, which is why the simple Chebyshev formula (scaled weights) works. Higham (2004) proved the formula is numerically stable for nodes with a small Lebesgue constant such as Chebyshev points. This is what serious software does: scipy’s BarycentricInterpolator, and Chebfun in MATLAB, which routinely interpolates with degree 1000 at Chebyshev points. In R there is pracma::barylag; the five lines above are enough. Note the guard for t equal to a node, where the formula would divide by zero.

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Checklist: is my interpolant trustworthy?

Plot it on a fine grid, not only at the readings. Values outside the biology (negative OD, OD above the plateau) → Runge or noise.
Leave one reading out, interpolate from the rest, compare at the left-out time: the difference estimates the error.
Change the degree (drop the end readings, or add one): if the answer between readings changes a lot, do not trust it.
Noisy readings? Do not interpolate: fit (least squares, lower degree) or smooth (Splines).
Never extrapolate a polynomial beyond the first or last reading: |w(t)| grows like |t|^{n+1} outside.
Evaluate stably: barycentric formula or poly(); not solve() on raw powers.


Each item maps to a slide. Item 2 is the practical version of the error formula: with real data we do not know the truth, but leave-one-out tells us how much the answer depends on each reading. Item 5 deserves emphasis: outside the readings every factor of w grows, and a degree-12 polynomial goes to plus or minus infinity like t^12. Extrapolating a growth curve with a polynomial is a common error in lab spreadsheets (Excel’s trendline “polynomial order 6”).

title: Polynomial interpolation
text:
Summary

n+1 readings → one interpolating polynomial of degree \le n. Monomial (Vandermonde), Lagrange (\sum y_i L_i) and Newton (divided differences) are three ways to write the same polynomial.
Error: f(t) - p(t) = \dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\prod (t - t_i): a property of the curve times a property of the sampling.
Equispaced readings: |w| explodes near the ends, so a high degree diverges (Runge): a 48-h run read every 4 h gives a negative OD.
Chebyshev times (crowded at the ends) keep |w| level; the error then falls geometrically.
Readings are noisy: interpolation copies the noise and amplifies it; fit with fewer parameters instead.
Evaluate with the barycentric formula; raw powers of t are badly conditioned.

Next: Splines: low-degree pieces joined smoothly, the practical answer for real sampling times.

Recap the three messages: one polynomial, three representations; the error formula with its two factors; and the practical conclusion that high-degree global polynomials on equispaced or noisy data are a bad idea. The next lecture keeps polynomials but uses them locally: piecewise cubics (splines) through the same readings, and smoothing splines for noisy ones, with the growth rate as the derivative of the smoothed OD curve.

title: Exercise: bisection and fixed-point iteration
text:
Explore
The demo below iterates the population models of this exercise in your browser (\(K = 100\) throughout). The tab Iterate: cobweb shows (a) the cobweb plot of \(g\) with the diagonal \(y = x\) and (b) the same iterates as a time series. Click or drag in the cobweb plot (or use the slider) to set the starting population \(N_0\). Steady states are marked filled (attracting, \(|g'(N^*)| < 1\)) or open (repelling). The readout gives \(g'(N^*)\) at every steady state, the ratio of the last two steps \(d_{n-1}/d_{n-2}\) (Fact 5), and the long-run behaviour after 3000 years: a steady state, a \(k\)-cycle, collapse, or no repeat (chaos). The tab Bisection on f = g − N shows \(f(N) = g(N) - N\) with a starting bracket \([a, b]\) that you can drag. Press step to bisect, and watch the error bound and the actual error of the midpoint in panel (b).



E1. (two steady states, one visible) With the harvested Ricker model (\(r = 0.5\), \(H = 10\)), read both steady states and their \(g'(N^*)\) from the readout. Then use the presets \(N_0 = 30\), \(21\) and \(20\), and drag \(N_0\) slowly between 20 and 21. Which steady state does the iteration reach, and from which starting values? Is there any \(N_0\) from which the iteration converges to the lower steady state?






Answer E1





\(N^* = 74.95\) with \(g' = 0.709\) (attracting, monotone) and \(N^* = 20.48\) with \(g' = 1.336\) (repelling). From \(N_0 = 30\) the stock reaches \(74.941\) after 30 years and settles at \(74.952\); from \(21\) it climbs slowly at first (the cobweb steps away from 20.48) and also settles at \(74.952\). From \(20\) it shrinks: \(\dots, 10.48, 6.40, 0.21\), and it collapses in year 13. Dragging shows the threshold: \(N_0 = 20.5\) survives, \(20.4\) collapses in year 19; the closer \(N_0\) is to \(20.48\), the longer the stock hesitates before it decides. No starting value converges to the lower steady state: every start near it is pushed away, and the cobweb staircase leads away from the open circle on both sides. The lower root is a threshold that iteration can never find; bisection can (E4).



E2. (the rate is \(g'(N^*)\)) Keep \(N_0 = 30\) and 30 years, and compare the step ratio with \(g'\) at the upper steady state. Then switch to Beverton–Holt and use the presets \(R = 2\) and \(R = 3\) (step the years up to 30 with +1 year), and to Ricker with \(r = 0.5\) and \(r = 1.9\). For each, what does the step ratio approach, and how does the cobweb look when the ratio is negative?






Answer E2





Harvested stock: ratio \(0.709\), equal to \(g'(74.95) = 0.709\). Beverton–Holt \(R = 2\): \(0.506\) after 10 years, \(0.500\) after 30, which is \(g'(K) = 1/R\); \(R = 3\): \(0.333 = 1/3\) after 10 years. Ricker \(r = 0.5\): \(0.500 = 1 - r\), a staircase. Ricker \(r = 1.9\): \(-0.900 = 1 - r\); the cobweb is a slowly tightening spiral around \((100, 100)\) and the time series alternates above and below \(K\), still \(0.39\) off after 30 years. The step ratio measures \(g'(N^*)\) without knowing \(N^*\): a negative ratio means alternation, and a ratio near \(\pm 1\) means slow convergence.



E3. (from steady state to cycles to chaos) In the Ricker model, use the presets \(r = 1.5\), \(2.3\), \(2.6\), \(3\) and \(3.12\), and record \(g'(100)\) and the long-run behaviour for each. Then drag the \(r\) slider slowly from \(1.9\) to \(2.1\). At which \(r\) does the steady state \(N^* = 100\) stop attracting? At \(r = 2.3\) tick show g(g(N)): where does that curve cross the diagonal?






Answer E3





\(r = 1.5\): \(g' = -0.5\), settles at 100 (spiral). \(r = 2.3\): \(g' = -1.3\), repelling; a 2-cycle \(159.22, 40.78\). \(r = 2.6\): \(g' = -1.6\); a 4-cycle \(190.48, 18.12, 152.32, 39.08\). \(r = 3\): \(g' = -2\); no repeat within 64 years, chaos. \(r = 3.12\): a 3-cycle \(266.99, 1.46, 31.55\), a window of order inside the chaos. On the slider, \(r = 1.99\) settles at 100, \(r = 2.00\) is still creeping towards 100 after 3000 years (\(g' = -1\) exactly), and \(r = 2.01\) gives the 2-cycle \(112.19, 87.81\): the steady state stops attracting exactly where \(|g'(K)| = |1 - r|\) reaches 1. The curve \(g(g(N))\) crosses the diagonal at 0, 40.78, 100 and 159.22: the two points of the 2-cycle are fixed points of \(g \circ g\) that are not fixed points of \(g\). The steady state \(100\) still exists for every \(r\); it is just never reached.



E4. (bisection, step by step) Open the Bisection tab with the harvested stock and the bracket \([50, 100]\). Press step three times and write down the bracket and the midpoint each time. Then step on to 33 steps: compare the width with \(10^{-8}\) and the actual error with the bound \((b-a)/2\). Keep stepping: what happens in the 40s? Finally, try the brackets \([0, 100]\) and \([0, 50]\).






Answer E4





Midpoint \(75\) with \(f(75) = -0.0139\), so the new bracket is \([50, 75]\); then \(m = 62.5\), \(f = 2.89\), bracket \([62.5, 75]\); then \(m = 68.75\), \(f = 1.63\), bracket \([68.75, 75]\). The first midpoint happened to be within \(0.048\) of the root, but bisection does not know that and keeps halving. After 33 steps the width is \(5.8\times10^{-9} < 10^{-8}\), as the readout predicts (33 steps), and the actual error is \(6.8\times10^{-10}\), below the bound \(2.9\times10^{-9}\). In panel (b) the bound is a straight line (one binary digit per step, rate \(\tfrac12\)); the actual errors wobble below it. In the 40s the bracket reaches a few gaps between doubles near 75 (\(1.7\times10^{-13}\) after 48 steps), \(f(m)\) evaluates to exactly 0, and bisection stops: the floating-point floor. \([0, 100]\): \(f(0) = f(100) = -10\), no sign change, bisection cannot start although two roots lie inside. \([0, 50]\) finds the lower root \(20.482\), the one the iteration in E1 could never reach.



E5. (the double root) Still in the Bisection tab, use the catch buttons \(H = 14\), \(14.26\) and \(15\) with the brackets \([0, 50]\) and \([50, 100]\). Which ones work? At \(H = 14.26\), find a bracket that does work by dragging \(a\) and \(b\) (or use \([40, 47]\)). Then go to the cobweb tab with \(H = 14.26\) and \(H = 15\): what does the stock do, and how fast?






Answer E5





\(H = 14\): roots \(40.07\) (\(g' = 1.079\), repelling) and \(53.55\) (\(g' = 0.924\), attracting); \(f(50) = 0.20 > 0\), so both brackets work. \(H = 14.26\): \(f(0) = f(100) = -14.26\) and \(f(50) = -0.059\), so no bracket among the three has a sign change, but the readout shows two roots, \(46.22\) and \(47.28\): \(f\) is positive only on that interval of width 1.06, with a maximum of \(0.0016\). \([40, 47]\) works (\(f(47) = +0.0013\)) and finds \(46.22\). The maximum sustainable catch is \(14.2616\) at \(N = 46.75\); at \(H = 15\) there is no root at all. In the cobweb tab at \(H = 14.26\) from \(N_0 = 60\), the stock is still at \(48.33\) after 100 years with step ratio \(0.98\): the attracting root has \(g' = 0.994\), so convergence is very slow, and the repelling root \(46.22\) (the collapse threshold) is only 1 below. At \(H = 15\) the stock collapses (year 35 from \(N_0 = 60\)). Near a double root both methods struggle: bisection cannot find a bracket, and iteration is slow because \(g' \to 1\).

title: Newton for systems of equations
section: Try it: Newton in the plane
text:
Try it: Newton in the plane




The toggle switch with alpha = 3, n = 2, computed live in the browser. Blue and red solid curves: the nullclines F1 = 0 and F2 = 0; the dots are the three steady states. The orange dot is the start (3, 0.5). Click “+ 1”: the two dashed lines are the nullclines of the linear approximation at x0, each one straight; they cross at x1 = (2.6699, 0.3594), exactly the step by hand from earlier. Point at the readout: F = (-0.6, -0.2), J, det J = 0.654, delta = solve(J, -F). Keep clicking: the dashed lines hug the curves more and more, and the errors 0.4, 0.057, 2.1e-3, 2.9e-6, 5.9e-12 show the doubling exponent. Then click (1, 0.2): the first step jumps to the V-high state. Click (1.9, 0.5): det J = -0.03, the dashed lines are nearly parallel, x1 is off the plot at (-5.1, 4.4). Tick “basins”: 21 / 57 / 21 percent as in the figure; tick “det J = 0” and show that the thin bands follow the dotted curve. Finally drag alpha down to 2: the three states merge, the whole square becomes one colour, and the run from (3, 0.5) needs 39 steps because J is singular at the root. That leads into the next slide.

title: Exercise: Newton for systems of equations
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Newton on the toggle switch in your browser. The plot shows the \((u, v)\) plane with the two nullclines \(F_1 = 0\) (blue) and \(F_2 = 0\) (red); the steady states are where they cross (green: U high, white: middle, purple: V high). Click or drag in the plot to move the start \(\mathbf x_0\) (orange). The thin dashed grey line is the whole Newton path; the step buttons walk along it. At the current iterate \(\mathbf x_k\) the two dashed coloured lines are the linearised nullclines, \(F_i(\mathbf x_k) + J_i(\mathbf x_k)\,\boldsymbol\delta = 0\) (row \(i\) of Fact 3 set to zero): straight lines that touch the curved ones near \(\mathbf x_k\). Where they cross is the solution of \(J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F\), the next iterate (yellow dot). The readout gives \(\mathbf F\), \(J\), \(\det J\) and \(\boldsymbol\delta\) at \(\mathbf x_k\), where the run ends, and the error \(\|\mathbf x_k - \mathbf x^*\|\) of every iterate. The run stops when \(\|\mathbf F\| < 10^{-12}\) or after 50 steps.
basins colours every start by the steady state Newton reaches from it (black: no convergence), computed on a grid, and gives the shares for starts in \([0, 4]^2\), as in the lecture’s basin figure. det J = 0 draws the dotted curve where the Jacobian is singular. The sliders change \(\alpha\) and \(n\).



E1. (linearise, solve, repeat) Click the start (3, 0.5) and + 1 once. Read \(\mathbf F\), \(J\), \(\det J\), \(\boldsymbol\delta\) and \(\mathbf x_1\) and compare with the lecture’s step by hand. Where do the two dashed lines cross? Keep clicking + 1 until the run stops. How many steps does it take, and how do the errors per step show quadratic convergence?






Answer E1





\(\mathbf F(\mathbf x_0) = (-0.6, -0.2)\), \(J = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & -1.92\\ -0.18 & -1\end{pmatrix}\), \(\det J = 0.654\), \(\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.330073, -0.140587)\), \(\mathbf x_1 = (2.669927, 0.359413)\): the same as by hand. The dashed lines cross exactly at \(\mathbf x_1\): each dashed line is where one component of the linear approximation is zero, so their crossing is where both are, the solution of \(J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F\). Near the “U high” state the dashed lines lie almost on top of the curves, so their crossing is almost the root. The run ends at \((2.618034, 0.381966)\) after 5 steps, with errors \(0.400\), \(0.0566\), \(2.1\times10^{-3}\), \(2.9\times10^{-6}\), \(5.9\times10^{-12}\), \(\approx 0\): the exponent roughly doubles each step.



E2. (which root?) Click the starts (1, 0.2) and (1, 1) and step through each. Where does each run end, and why? Then tick basins. What shares do you read for starts in \([0, 4]^2\)? Drag the start slowly from \((1, 0.2)\) to the right along \(v = 0.2\): where does the answer switch to “U high”?






Answer E2





From \((1, 0.2)\) the first step jumps to \((0.334, 2.499)\) and the run ends in V high \((0.381966, 2.618034)\) after 5 steps, although \(u > v\) at the start: the crossing of the linearised nullclines happens to lie up on the left. From \((1, 1)\) every iterate stays on the diagonal (\((1.2, 1.2)\) after one step, B8) and the run ends in the middle state \((1.213412, 1.213412)\) after 4 steps. The basin shares are U high 21 %, middle 57 %, V high 21 %, no convergence 0 %, as in the lecture: the unstable middle state is Newton’s most common answer. Along \(v = 0.2\) the start stays in the purple (V high) region up to \(u \approx 1.4\); between about \(1.45\) and \(1.55\) the answer flips between middle, U high and V high in a thin band, and from \(u \approx 1.6\) on the run ends in U high. The boundaries are curved and have nothing to do with the diagonal \(u = v\) that separates the cell’s two fates.



E3. (a nearly singular Jacobian) Click (1.9, 0.5) and + 1. Read \(\det J\) and \(\mathbf x_1\), then follow the run to the end. Do the same for (2, 0.55). Now tick det J = 0. Where do the two starts lie relative to the dotted curve, and what does the basin picture look like near it?






Answer E3





At \((1.9, 0.5)\): \(\det J = -0.0299\) (“nearly singular”); the dashed lines are almost parallel, so they cross far away: \(\mathbf x_1 = (-5.14, 4.43)\), off the plot, with a negative concentration. From there the run comes back and ends in the middle state after 7 steps. At \((2, 0.55)\): \(\det J = 0.0663\), \(\mathbf x_1 = (5.106, -0.891)\), also a huge step, but it ends in U high after 7 steps. Both starts lie just on either side of the dotted curve \(\det J = 0\). Along that curve the basins break into thin interleaved bands of all three colours: a tiny change of the start sends the first step to a very different place.



E4. (bistability needs \(\alpha > 2\)) Keep basins on, start at (3, 0.5), and lower \(\alpha\): \(2.5\), \(2.2\), \(2.05\), \(2\), \(1.5\). For each, count the steady states and read the shares. Compare the “U high” state with \(u = (\alpha + \sqrt{\alpha^2 - 4})/2\) from B5. What is special about \(\alpha = 2\): the number of steps, the errors per step, and the black area?






Answer E4

The U-high states agree with \((\alpha + \sqrt{\alpha^2-4})/2\): \(2\), \(1.5583\), \(1.25\). As \(\alpha \to 2\) the three states move together and at \(\alpha = 2\) they merge at \((1, 1)\), where \(\det J = 0\): the Jacobian is singular at the root. From \((3, 0.5)\) the run then needs 39 steps instead of 5–8, and the errors per step shrink only by a factor of about \(2/3\) (\(0.67\), \(0.44\), \(0.28\), …): linear, not quadratic, convergence, like Newton at a multiple root in one variable. The 7 % black starts are runs that are still crawling after 50 steps. Below \(\alpha = 2\) there is one state, the circuit is no switch, and every start finds it.



E5. (the Hill coefficient) Reset, then set \(n = 2.5\) (with \(\alpha = 3\)) and click (2, 0.5). What happens after one step, and why? Tick basins: how large is the black area now? Finally set \(n = 1\) and try \(\alpha\) between 1 and 5. Is the switch ever bistable?






Answer E5





With \(n = 2.5\) the first step from \((2, 0.5)\) goes to \((9.72, -3.25)\); then \(v^{2.5}\) of a negative number is NaN, and the run ends with NaN after 1 step (the lecture’s Failure 1). The steady states still exist (“U high” at \((2.955096, 0.187363)\)), but the shares are U high 16 %, middle 33 %, V high 16 %, no convergence 34 %: every start whose path visits negative concentrations fails. With \(n = 1\) there is a single steady state for every \(\alpha\) (at \(\alpha = 3\): \(u = v = 1.302776\)): without cooperativity no bistability. The black regions there are runs that wander around the poles at \(u = -1\) or \(v = -1\), where \(1 + u^n = 0\).

title: Exercise: Newton and secant methods
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Newton, secant or bisection in your browser on the three equations of the lecture: the two-site dose–response \(f(c) = R(c) - 0.5\), the score \(S(\lambda)\) of the zero-truncated Poisson counts, and Michaelis–Menten in log substrate, \(\sigma(u) - \tfrac12\) (Newton step \(u - \sinh u\)). Drag or click in the plot to move the start value (two start values for secant, the bracket \([a, b]\) for bisection). Step takes one step and draws the tangent (Newton), the chord through the last two points (secant) or the halved bracket (bisection), and where it meets zero; Run keeps stepping, Back undoes a step. The table lists each iterate, \(f\) there, the error against the wanted root (\(c_{50}\), \(\hat\lambda\) or \(u^* = 0\)), the number of correct digits \(-\log_{10}\big(|e|/\max(|x^*|, 1)\big)\), and how the digit count changed from the previous step (column ×: the factor, for Newton and secant; column +: the digits added, for bisection). The digits of \(x_k\) that agree with the root are in bold. The demo stops like the lecture’s newton() and secant(): when a step is below \(10^{-12}\,|x|\), or after 60 steps.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R and Python, but exp and log may round differently in the last bit, so the last digit of an iterate can differ from the lecture.



E1. (digits double) Click Newton c₀ = 1 and press Step five times. After each step, write down the error, the number of correct digits and the factor in column ×. Watch the tangent of each step in the plot. How far is \(c_1\) from the root, and why is the first step still a big improvement? How many function evaluations did the run take?






Answer E1





Errors \(3.6\times10^{-1}\), \(6.5\times10^{-3}\), \(1.6\times10^{-6}\), \(9.1\times10^{-14}\), \(4.4\times10^{-16}\); correct digits \(1.0\), \(2.7\), \(6.3\), \(13.6\), all. From step 2 on the digit count is multiplied by about 2 each step (\(2.8\), \(2.3\), \(2.1\)): quadratic convergence. The bold part of \(c_k\) grows the same way. The first tangent, drawn at \(c_0 = 1\) where the curve is still flat and bending, overshoots to \(c_1 = 3.617\), \(0.36\) past the root; but the error fell from \(2.3\) to \(0.36\), and from there the tangent is a good model of the curve. The run stops after 5 steps with 10 evaluations (\(f\) and \(f'\) at each of \(c_0, \ldots, c_4\)), as in the lecture.



E2. (secant and bisection) Click secant 1, 2 and Run. Record the correct digits per step and the factors, the number of steps and of evaluations. Then click bisection [1, 10] and press Step ten times, recording the digits, then Run to the end. Which method needs the fewest evaluations of \(f\) for full precision?






Answer E2





Secant: digits \(1.3\), \(3.2\), \(5.3\), \(9.4\), all; factors \(2.4\), \(1.7\), \(1.8\), close to the golden ratio \(1.618\). It stops after 6 steps (the sixth step is too small to change \(c\)) with 8 evaluations: 2 for the start values and one per step. Bisection: digits \(0.2\), \(2.5\), \(0.5\), \(0.8\), \(1.1\), \(1.4\), \(1.7\), \(2.1\), \(2.7\), \(3.1\): about \(+0.3\) per step, with a lucky hit at step 2 (\(c = 3.25\)) that is lost again at step 3. Bisection needs 42 steps and 44 evaluations. Per evaluation the secant method (8) beats Newton (10 in E1), and both beat bisection by a factor of about 5.



E3. (the MLE and a bad start) Choose MLE from x̄ = 1.73 and Run. Read the digits and factors. Then drag \(\lambda_0\) to the right, in steps of 0.01, and find the largest start from which Newton still reaches \(\hat\lambda\). Finally click 2 bad start (\(\lambda_0 = 3\)) and Step through it. What happens to \(\lambda_k\), and how does the run end?






Answer E3





From \(\bar x = 1.73\): digits \(0.9\), \(1.8\), \(3.6\), \(7.2\), \(14.5\), all, with factors \(2.1\), \(2.0\), \(2.0\), \(2.0\): textbook quadratic convergence. 6 steps, 12 evaluations, \(\hat\lambda = 1.218469525830127\). The last start that works is \(\lambda_0 = 2.70\): its first tangent lands at \(\lambda_1 = 0.0056\), just right of 0, and Newton crawls back in 15 steps. From \(2.71\) on, \(\lambda_1 < 0\) (\(-0.009\) for \(2.71\)) and the run fails, in line with the lecture (“up to about 2.7”). From \(\lambda_0 = 3\): \(\lambda_1 = -0.47\) (the demo warns: negative rate), then \(-1.07\), \(-2.59\), \(-6.03\), \(-12.3\), \(-24.7\), …: each step roughly doubles \(\lambda\), because for negative \(\lambda\) the score behaves like \(173/\lambda\). At \(\lambda_{11} = -789\), \(e^{-\lambda}\) overflows, and \(\lambda_{12}\) is NaN: diverged.



E4. (a flat tangent) Click 1 flat tangent (\(c_0 = 10\)) and Run. Where does \(c_1\) land, what root does the run converge to, and what do the columns \(f(c_k)\), error and digits say at the end? Then drag \(c_0\) from \(6\) to \(12\) and watch where the runs end. Finally switch to bisection with \([a, b] = [1, 10]\).






Answer E4





\(f'(10)\) is small, so the tangent at \(c_0 = 10\) is nearly flat and meets zero at \(c_1 = -5.73\). Newton then converges in 6 steps to \(c = -3.04997\): the status says converged, \(f(c_k)\) drops to \(10^{-16}\), but the error against \(c_{50}\) stays at \(6.3\) and the digits at \(0\): a confident, wrong, negative dose. Dragging \(c_0\): every start up to \(7.85\) reaches \(c_{50}\). Above that the outcome jumps around: \(c_0 = 7.9\)–\(8.0\) ends at a second negative root, \(c = -0.2513\) (right of the pole at \(c = -0.1\)); \(8.05\)–\(8.2\) comes back to \(c_{50}\); \(8.25\) and \(8.3\) run off to \(-10^{300}\) and end in NaN; from \(8.35\) to \(10.3\) every start ends at \(-3.05\); most starts between \(10.4\) and \(11.15\) reach \(c_{50}\) again, and from \(11.35\) on the iterates run off to \(-\infty\). Nothing in Newton’s output warns you; only a range check does. Bisection on \([1, 10]\) cannot leave the bracket and always ends at \(c_{50}\), at the price of 44 evaluations.



E5. (cycling) Click 3 cycling (\(u_0 = 2.1773189849653\), \(S_0 = 8.82\,K_m\)) and Run. The demo pauses when it detects a cycle. Look at the late digits of \(u_k\) in the table, then press Run again and let it finish. Then drag \(u_0\) to \(2.30\) and to \(1.61\) (\(S_0 = 10\,K_m\) and \(5\,K_m\)).






Answer E5





The tangents bounce between \(u = 2.177\) and \(-2.177\) (\(S = 8.82\,K_m\) and \(K_m/8.82\)), and the demo pauses at step 3 with a cycling warning. The late digits are not constant: \(2.17731898496530\), \(\ldots 65228\), \(\ldots 64363\), \(\ldots 53958\): the distance from the exact cycle grows about 12-fold every two steps, because the cycle is unstable and the start is only correct to 13 digits. In this browser the iterates leave the cycle after about 25 steps and then converge to \(u = 0\) at step 31; whether a run escapes towards the root or towards infinity depends on the rounding, so R may behave differently. From \(u_0 = 2.30\) each step lands farther out: \(-2.64\), \(4.31\), \(-33.0\), \(1.1\times10^{14}\), then \(-\infty\): diverged. From \(u_0 = 1.61\): converged in 5 steps. In 0.01 steps the last start that converges is \(u_0 = 2.17\); from \(2.18\) on, Newton diverges. A cap on the number of steps (and printing the last iterates) is what turns an endless bounce into a message.

title: The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Try it: bias against noise




The same signature, truth and 5 percent noise pattern as on the slides, solved live in the browser; the SVD is a one-sided Jacobi on S. Panel (a): bars are the estimate for the lecture sample, dashed lines the truth, dots 100 samples with fresh random noise; the last group is CD4 + CD8. Panel (b): the filter factors. Panel (c): expected error over the noise, split into bias and noise. Start with least squares: CD8 at -0.09, the CD4 and CD8 dots spray from -0.6 to 1.2 (32 off the scale each), but the CD4 + CD8 dots are a tight band at 0.45: noise only goes along v5. Readout: f5/sigma5 = 0.35. Truncated SVD, k from 5 down to 1: k = 4 kills the noise (1.20 to 0.011) at a bias of 0.106, the equal split; smaller k only adds bias, and the residual jumps from 9.71 to 11.07. Ridge, slide lambda: f5 = 0.076 at 10, bias and noise cross near 10, the total is smallest near 30; at 316 and 1000 everything shrinks. Finally reset and drag “CD8 differs by” to 30 percent: sigma5 goes to 43, least squares is fine (0.32, 0.13). Better data beats better maths.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
About this lecture
A derivative is a rate: how fast a culture grows, how fast a drug is cleared, how steeply a log-likelihood rises. A computer only has function values, so it estimates the rate from a few nearby values.

Stencils from Taylor: forward, backward and central differences, a one-sided formula for the ends of a data set, and the second derivative.
The best step for each: \varepsilon^{1/2}, \varepsilon^{1/3}, \varepsilon^{1/4}, and why.
Richardson extrapolation: combine two poor estimates into a good one (what numDeriv::grad does).
Measured data: differentiating amplifies noise. Widen the stencil or smooth first.
Gradients for fitting by finite differences, how they fail inside optim, and the alternatives: the complex step and automatic differentiation.

Biology: the instantaneous growth rate from a noisy plate-reader OD curve; the gradient of a log-likelihood when fitting the growth curve.

This unit opens Part 7. In Convergence and cost we used the forward difference of the logistic OD curve to see the truncation/rounding V and only previewed the central difference. Here we do the systematic version: where every stencil comes from, how to pick the step, how to do better than any single stencil, and what happens with real, noisy data. The second half is about gradients, the multivariate version, because that is where most biologists meet numerical derivatives without noticing: every optimiser that is not given a gradient computes one by finite differences.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Recap: the V from Convergence and cost
text:
Recap: the V from Convergence and cost
Logistic OD curve N(t) = \dfrac{K}{1 + (K/N_0 - 1)\,e^{-rt}}, K = 1.2, N_0 = 0.05, r = 0.8 per hour. True growth rate at t = 3 h: N'(3) = 0.21026 OD/h.

Forward difference \dfrac{N(t+h) - N(t)}{h}: truncation error \tfrac{h}{2}N'', order 1.
Rounding error \approx \varepsilon|N|/h: the two values agree in almost all digits, and dividing by a small h blows up their rounding.
Total error: a V on log–log axes, best h \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8}, best error \approx 10^{-8}: half the digits lost.
The central difference \dfrac{N(t+h) - N(t-h)}{2h} had slope 2 and a deeper V.
The ratio check \dfrac{D(h) - D(h/2)}{D(h/2) - D(h/4)} \approx 2^p tells truncation regime from rounding regime without the exact answer.

Today: where these formulas come from, how to build any formula you need, and what changes when N is measured, not computed.

One slide only: students who skipped Convergence and cost should go back to it. The three facts to carry forward: truncation error falls like h^p, rounding error grows like eps/h, and the best step balances them. Everything in the first half of this lecture is a variation on that balance. The second half replaces eps by the measurement noise, which is about 10^13 times larger.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: The problem: growth rate from a plate reader
text:
The problem: growth rate from a plate reader
A plate reader measures OD600 every 10 minutes for 10 hours (61 values, 3 decimals, noise sd \approx 0.005). We want the growth rate N'(t) and its maximum.

The curve looks clean. Its central differences do not: they jump by \pm 0.03, and one is negative, a culture “shrinking” in mid-growth.

Simulated data: the same logistic curve, plus Gaussian noise of sd 0.005 OD (a realistic plate-reader noise level), rounded to three decimals as a plate reader exports them. Left panel: you cannot see the noise by eye. Right panel: the naive derivative, (y[i+1] - y[i-1]) / (20 min), is visibly noisy, overshoots the maximum (0.27 instead of 0.24) and goes negative near the end. The maximum specific growth rate, the number many papers report, is read off exactly this kind of curve. By the end of the lecture we know why the noise grows when we differentiate and two ways to tame it. First, though, the stencils themselves.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Taylor, three times
Write the neighbours of t as Taylor series around t (prime = derivative at t):

\begin{aligned}
N(t+h) &= N + h N' + \tfrac{h^2}{2} N'' + \tfrac{h^3}{6} N''' + \tfrac{h^4}{24} N'''' + \dots \\
N(t-h) &= N - h N' + \tfrac{h^2}{2} N'' - \tfrac{h^3}{6} N''' + \tfrac{h^4}{24} N'''' - \dots \\
N(t+2h) &= N + 2h N' + \tfrac{4h^2}{2} N'' + \tfrac{8h^3}{6} N''' + \dots
\end{aligned}

For the OD curve at t = 3:

Recipe: add multiples of these rows so that everything cancels except the derivative you want. What is left over is the error.

This is the only tool we need. Each row is the Taylor polynomial from first-year calculus, evaluated at a shifted point. The minus signs in the second row alternate because (-h)^k changes sign with k. The derivatives of the logistic come from differentiating N’ = r N (1 - N/K) repeatedly; students do not need to compute them, but having the numbers lets us check every error formula against the computer. Notation: N, N’, N’’ without an argument all mean “at t”.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Forward and backward differences
Forward: take row 1, subtract N, divide by h: \frac{N(t+h) - N(t)}{h} = N' + \underbrace{\tfrac{h}{2} N''}_{\text{error}} + O(h^2)
Backward: take row 2, the same way: \frac{N(t) - N(t-h)}{h} = N' - \tfrac{h}{2} N'' + O(h^2)

Both are first order. At t = 3: error \approx \pm 0.0296\,h; with h = 0.1 h, +0.0029 and -0.0030.
The errors have opposite signs: forward overestimates, backward underestimates (the curve bends upwards at t = 3).
Use: the backward difference needs only past values, the forward only future ones. At the last measurement of a time course, backward is all you have.


The leading error term is the first Taylor term we did not cancel. The O(h^2) collects the rest. For a curve that bends upwards (N’’ > 0), the forward secant is steeper than the tangent and the backward secant shallower. That the two errors are almost equal and opposite is the hint for the next slide: average them.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Central difference: let the errors cancel
text:
Central difference: let the errors cancel
Subtract row 2 from row 1: the even terms (N, N'', N'''') cancel. N(t+h) - N(t-h) = 2hN' + \tfrac{2h^3}{6} N''' + \dots
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{N(t+h) - N(t-h)}{2h} = N' + \underbrace{\tfrac{h^2}{6} N'''}_{\text{error}} + O(h^4)

Second order: halving h quarters the error. At t = 3: error \approx -0.00705\,h^2, so -7.0\times10^{-5} at h = 0.1, forty times smaller than forward.
Same cost as forward (two evaluations), if N(t) is not needed anyway.
It is the average of forward and backward; their \pm\tfrac{h}{2}N'' errors cancel.
It needs a point on each side: not available at the first and last time point.


Symmetry is what buys the extra order. Note the next error term is O(h^4), not O(h^3): only even powers of h appear in the central difference’s error. That fact is what makes Richardson extrapolation so effective later. One caveat about cost: if you need N(t) anyway (e.g. inside a Newton step), the forward difference costs one extra evaluation and the central two.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Any stencil you need: match Taylor terms
text:
Any stencil you need: match Taylor terms
At the first time point there is no t - h. Look for weights w_0, w_1, w_2 with w_0 N(t) + w_1 N(t+h) + w_2 N(t+2h) \approx h\,N'(t). Matching the N, hN' and h^2N'' terms of the Taylor rows gives a 3\times3 linear system:
s <- c(0, 1, 2)                            # offsets: t, t+h, t+2h
A <- outer(0:2, s, function(k, s) s^k / factorial(k))   # row k: Taylor term k
solve(A, c(0, 1, 0))                       # want: 0 N + 1 hN' + 0 h^2 N''
# [1] -1.5  2.0 -0.5
So N'(t) \approx \dfrac{-3N(t) + 4N(t+h) - N(t+2h)}{2h}, error -\tfrac{h^2}{3}N''': second order with one-sided data.

Same method with offsets (-1, 0, 1) and right-hand side (0, 0, 1) gives the second derivative.
np.gradient uses central differences inside and (with edge_order=2) this formula at the ends.


This is the method of undetermined coefficients. Row k of A holds s^k / k!, the Taylor coefficient of h^k N^(k) at offset s; the right-hand side says which derivative we want. Three points can match three terms, so the first unmatched term, k = 3, is the error. The linear system ties back to Part 3: it is a small Vandermonde-type matrix. More points give higher order: offsets -2..2 give the five-point formula (1, -8, 0, 8, -1)/12h with error O(h^4) (exercise C2). The same idea builds every stencil in the diffusion units.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
The second derivative
Add rows 1 and 2: now the odd terms cancel. N(t+h) + N(t-h) = 2N + h^2 N'' + \tfrac{2h^4}{24} N'''' + \dots
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{N(t+h) - 2N(t) + N(t-h)}{h^2} = N'' + \underbrace{\tfrac{h^2}{12} N''''}_{\text{error}} + \dots

Second order. At t = 3: error \approx -0.00514\,h^2.
Biology: N'' is the acceleration of growth. It changes sign at the inflection point, the time of fastest growth (t = 3.92 h here).
This (1, -2, 1)/h^2 stencil is the workhorse of Part 10: in space it becomes the diffusion term D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2, in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences.



The picture summarises the four stencils so far: dots are the points used, numbers the weights, right column the divisor. Filled dots only. For the second derivative the weights must sum to zero (a constant has no curvature) and the stencil is symmetric. Flag the forward reference clearly: the diffusion equation replaces t by a space coordinate x, and the second difference of concentrations on a grid of channels is exactly this formula. Its error, h^2/12 times the fourth derivative, is the spatial accuracy of every scheme in Part 10.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
All four in R
K <- 1.2; N0 <- 0.05; r <- 0.8
od <- function(t) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
gr <- function(t) r * od(t) * (1 - od(t) / K)            # exact N'(t)
t0 <- 3; exact <- gr(t0); d2 <- r * exact * (1 - 2 * od(t0) / K)  # N'(3), N''(3)
h   <- c(0.1, 0.05, 0.025)
fwd <- (od(t0 + h) - od(t0)) / h
bwd <- (od(t0) - od(t0 - h)) / h
cen <- (od(t0 + h) - od(t0 - h)) / (2 * h)
sec <- (od(t0 + h) - 2 * od(t0) + od(t0 - h)) / h^2
err <- cbind(fwd = fwd - exact, bwd = bwd - exact, cen = cen - exact, sec = sec - d2)
err[1, ] / err[2, ]                                      # halve h: error ratio
#      fwd      bwd      cen      sec
# 1.974603 2.022227 3.999432 3.997985

Ratios \approx 2 (first order) and \approx 4 (second order), as the Taylor errors predicted.
The errors themselves: 0.00289, -0.00303, -7.04\times10^{-5}, -5.14\times10^{-5} at h = 0.1: the leading terms \pm0.0296h, -0.00705h^2, -0.00514h^2.


Vectorised over h as in Convergence and cost. N’‘(3) is computed from the differentiated logistic equation, N’’ = r N’ (1 - 2N/K). The ratio of errors at h and h/2 is 2^p, the cheapest way to confirm the order when the exact answer is known; without it, use the difference-ratio check from the recap slide. The forward and backward ratios are not exactly 2 because the O(h^2) terms are still visible at h = 0.1.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Each stencil has its own V
text:
Each stencil has its own V

Rounding hits the second derivative hardest: it divides by h^2, not h. Its V is shifted far to the right.

Three curves, same OD function at t = 3. Right side: truncation, slopes 1, 2 and 2. Left side: rounding, slope -1 for the first-derivative formulas and -2 for the second derivative. The dotted lines mark eps^(1/2), eps^(1/3) and eps^(1/4), the rule-of-thumb best steps from the next slide; each is close to the bottom of its V. Note how much worse the second derivative is at small h: at h = 1e-8, where the forward difference is at its best, the second difference is wrong by about 1.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: The best step: balance the two errors
text:
The best step: balance the two errors
Truncation \approx C h^p, rounding \approx \varepsilon |N| / h^k for the k-th derivative. Setting them equal: h^* \approx \varepsilon^{1/(p+k)}, \qquad \text{best error} \approx \varepsilon^{p/(p+k)} \qquad (\text{if } C \text{ and } |N| \text{ are of order } 1).

Higher order and a larger step: the central difference wins twice.
Steps are relative: use h = \varepsilon^{1/3}\max(|t|, 1). Time in seconds (t = 10\,800 s) or a rate constant of size 10^{-4} needs a step scaled to it.


Derivation for the central case: minimise C h^2 + eps |N| / h; derivative 2 C h - eps |N| / h^2 = 0 gives h = (eps |N| / 2C)^(1/3). With C = |N’’’|/6 = 0.007 and |N| = 0.39 that is 1.8e-5, close to eps^(1/3) = 6e-6; the rule of thumb ignores the constants because they are rarely known. For the second derivative the rounding term is about 4 eps |N| / h^2 (weights 1, 2, 1). The relative step matters as soon as t (or a parameter) is far from 1: for a rate constant of 1e-4, an absolute step of 6e-6 changes it by 6 percent (truncation error), and for t = 10800 s, the truncation-optimal step is scaled up in proportion. Library codes scale every step by the size of the variable.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Failure: the second derivative with a tiny step
text:
Failure: the second derivative with a tiny step
h   <- 10^-(2:8)
sec <- (od(t0 + h) - 2 * od(t0) + od(t0 - h)) / h^2
print(data.frame(h, sec, err = abs(sec - d2)), digits = 3)
#       h     sec      err
# 1 1e-02  0.0592 5.14e-07
# 2 1e-03  0.0592 5.21e-09
# 3 1e-04  0.0592 7.82e-09
# 4 1e-05  0.0592 9.07e-07
# 5 1e-06  0.0591 1.49e-04
# 6 1e-07  0.0500 9.25e-03
# 7 1e-08 -0.5551 6.14e-01

At h = 10^{-8}, the step that is best for the forward difference, the curvature is -0.56: ten times too large, with the wrong sign. “Growth is slowing down”, confidently and falsely.
Check: vary h by factors of 10. The answer must stay put over a range of h; if it drifts or changes sign, you are in the rounding regime.


A typical way to hit this: copying the step 1e-8 (or sqrt(eps)) from a first-derivative code into a second-derivative code. The numerator is the difference of three numbers that agree in about 15 digits, so it is pure rounding noise of size 1e-16, divided by 1e-16. The check costs a few extra evaluations and is always worth it: a derivative estimate that is stable over two or three decades of h can be trusted; one that changes with h cannot. Same check as the difference ratios from Convergence and cost, without needing the exact answer.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Richardson extrapolation
The central difference has an error made of even powers only: D(h) = N' + c_2 h^2 + c_4 h^4 + \dots, \qquad D(h/2) = N' + \tfrac{c_2}{4} h^2 + \tfrac{c_4}{16} h^4 + \dots Take 4 D(h/2) - D(h): the h^2 term cancels. Divide by 3: R(h) = \frac{4 D(h/2) - D(h)}{3} = N' + O(h^4).
D <- function(h) (od(t0 + h) - od(t0 - h)) / (2 * h)
c(D(0.1), D(0.05), (4 * D(0.05) - D(0.1)) / 3) - exact      # errors
# [1] -7.043731e-05 -1.761183e-05 -3.336916e-09

Two second-order estimates with errors 10^{-4} and 10^{-5} give one with error 3\times10^{-9}. Fourth order, from the same four function values.
Repeat on the R’s (now dividing by 16 - 1, then 64 - 1): a table of ever higher order. Four levels from h = 0.4: error 3\times10^{-13}.


Richardson extrapolation is “use the known shape of the error to remove it”. We do not know c2, but we know how it scales with h, so two estimates are enough to eliminate it. This only works if the error really is c2 h^2 + …, i.e. in the truncation regime and for a smooth function. The repeated version is a triangular table, column j removing the h^(2j) term with weights 4j/(4j - 1) and -1/(4^j - 1); exercise C3 builds it. The same idea turns the trapezoid rule into Romberg integration in the next unit, Numerical integration.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
What numDeriv::grad does
library(numDeriv)
grad(od, 3) - exact                       # Richardson, the default
# [1] 2.060019e-13
grad(od, 3, method = "simple") - exact    # one forward difference
# [1] 2.960551e-06

grad takes central differences at a relative step h = 10^{-4}|x| and at h/2, h/4, h/8 (8 evaluations of f per variable) and runs the Richardson table: 12–13 correct digits.
method = "simple": one forward difference with h = 10^{-4}, error \approx 0.0296 \times 10^{-4}.
Python: scipy.differentiate.derivative (adaptive, Richardson-like); scipy.optimize.approx_fprime is a plain forward difference.
When Richardson fails: if f is not smooth (an if, abs, interpolated data, an adaptive ODE solver), or noisy, the error is not c_2h^2 + \dots and the extrapolation can make it worse.


numDeriv’s defaults: method.args = list(d = 1e-4, r = 4, v = 2): initial relative step d, r rounds of extrapolation, step reduction factor v. The large starting step keeps the whole table out of the rounding regime, and the extrapolation supplies the accuracy instead of a tiny step. That is the main practical lesson: accuracy should come from the formula’s order, not from shrinking h. On noise: the weights 4/3 and -1/3 add up to 1 but their absolute values sum to 5/3, so random errors in D grow at every level.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Measured data: the noise replaces \varepsilon
Each measurement is y_i = N(t_i) + e_i, noise sd \sigma = 0.005. The central difference of the noise has sd \frac{\sqrt{2}\,\sigma}{2\,\Delta t} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt2\,\Delta t} = \frac{0.005}{\sqrt2 \cdot \tfrac16} = 0.021 \text{ OD/h}.
set.seed(1)
t  <- seq(0, 10, by = 1/6)                            # every 10 min
y  <- round(od(t) + rnorm(length(t), sd = 0.005), 3)  # plate reader, 3 decimals
i  <- 2:(length(t) - 1)
cen <- (y[i + 1] - y[i - 1]) / (2 / 6)                # central, h = 10 min
sqrt(mean((cen - gr(t[i]))^2))                        # rms error
# [1] 0.02030602

The same \varepsilon/h term as before, with \varepsilon|N| \approx 10^{-16} replaced by \sigma = 5\times10^{-3}: 13 orders of magnitude larger.
Measuring more often makes it worse: every 2 min, the noise in N' is 0.11 OD/h, almost half the peak growth rate.


The derivation: the difference of two independent errors has variance 2 sigma^2; dividing by 2 dt divides the sd by 2 dt. The measured rms error 0.0203 matches the predicted 0.0212. Differentiation is an ill-conditioned operation in the language of Error, conditioning and stability: a small change in the data (0.005) gives a large change in the derivative, and the smaller the spacing, the larger the amplification. That is the opposite of most students’ intuition that more data is always better. More data helps only if we use it to average, which is what the next slides do. If you then compute the specific growth rate N’/N (or the slope of log OD), the noise is further divided by N, so it is worst at the low ODs of early growth.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
The V again, with noise
Use a wider central difference: \dfrac{y_{i+k} - y_{i-k}}{2k\,\Delta t}, half-width h = k\,\Delta t. Noise \sigma/(\sqrt2 h) falls, truncation \tfrac{h^2}{6}|N'''| grows.

Best near h = 40 min (k = 4): rms error 0.0053, four times smaller than neighbours. Predicted: h^* = \big(3\sigma / (\sqrt2\,|N'''|)\big)^{1/3} \approx 0.5 h.

Exactly the V of the recap slide, on a much larger scale: truncation on the right, noise on the left, and an optimal step that is now about half an hour instead of 1e-8. The formula for h* is the same balance as for rounding, with eps|N| replaced by sigma/sqrt(2) and |N’’‘| taken at its largest, 0.077 at the inflection point. In practice you do not know sigma or N’’’ precisely, but the lesson is robust: with noisy data the best stencil is much wider than the sampling interval. The price: fewer points at the ends (k values lost on each side) and some blurring of sharp features.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Smooth first, then differentiate
Fit a smooth curve to all the data, then differentiate the curve. A smoothing spline (Splines, Part 6) picks its smoothness from the data:
fit <- smooth.spline(t, y)                 # smoothness chosen by GCV
d   <- predict(fit, t, deriv = 1)$y        # derivative of the spline
sqrt(mean((d - gr(t))^2))                  # rms error
# [1] 0.004708606
c(max(d), t[which.max(d)])                 # max growth rate and when
# [1] 0.2366499 4.0000000

rms error 0.0047, and a value at every time point, ends included. Maximum growth rate 0.237 OD/h at 4.0 h (true: 0.240 at 3.92 h); raw central differences gave 0.270.
Python: scipy.interpolate.make_smoothing_spline, then .derivative().
Alternatives: a local polynomial fit (Savitzky–Golay), or fit a growth model and differentiate it (Part 9).


smooth.spline chooses its smoothing parameter by generalised cross-validation, which balances fit against roughness, the same bias-variance trade-off as the stencil width, made automatically. predict with deriv = 1 differentiates the fitted cubic pieces exactly. How smoothing splines work is the topic of Splines. Fitting a parametric model (logistic, Gompertz) and differentiating it is the most accurate option when the model is right, and the most misleading when it is wrong; the fitting methods are in Part 9 (Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting, whose example is a drug-concentration model rather than a growth curve, but the method is the same).

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Comparing the three


Raw neighbours (grey): noisy. Wider stencil (blue) and spline (orange): close to the truth, both slightly flatten the peak.
The spline is least reliable at the ends (here 0.056 instead of 0.038 at t = 0).
Check: compute the derivative with two different smoothing levels (stencil widths, spline df). Features that survive both are real; features that move are noise.


All smoothing trades noise for bias: a peak gets lower and wider. The spline errs at the ends because there are no data beyond them to pin down the slope; this is where the first growth rate (lag phase) is estimated, so be careful when reporting it. The two-smoothing-level check is the noisy-data version of “vary h by factors of 10”. Never report a derivative of raw data without having looked at this plot.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Gradients for fitting
Fit (r, K, N_0) to the plate-reader data by maximum likelihood (Gaussian noise, \sigma = 0.005): \ell(r, K, N_0) = -\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_i \big(y_i - N(t_i; r, K, N_0)\big)^2. The gradient \nabla\ell = (\partial\ell/\partial r, \partial\ell/\partial K, \partial\ell/\partial N_0): one central difference per parameter, nudging only that one.
logistic <- function(t, r, K, N0) K / (1 + (K / N0 - 1) * exp(-r * t))
loglik <- function(th) -sum((y - logistic(t, th[1], th[2], th[3]))^2) / (2 * 0.005^2)
cen_grad <- function(f, x, h = 6e-6) sapply(seq_along(x), function(j) {
  e <- replace(numeric(length(x)), j, h)          # nudge parameter j only
  (f(x + e) - f(x - e)) / (2 * h) })
th <- c(r = 0.75, K = 1.15, N0 = 0.06)            # a point on the way to the optimum
cen_grad(loglik, th)
# [1]  42388.45  57583.61 109411.83

Relative error against the analytic gradient: forward (h = 10^{-8}) 10^{-7}–10^{-6}; central 10^{-11}–10^{-7}; numDeriv::grad 10^{-12}.
Cost: p + 1 (forward), 2p (central), 8p (numDeriv) evaluations of \ell for p parameters.


A partial derivative is an ordinary derivative with the other parameters held fixed, so every formula of this lecture applies one coordinate at a time. This is the same construction as the finite-difference Jacobian in Newton for systems of equations, applied to a scalar function. The gradient components are large (1e4 to 1e5) because sigma is small; what matters is the relative error. The analytic gradient is in the exercise (C6). For three parameters the cost does not matter; for an ODE model with 50 parameters where one evaluation takes a second, 100 or 400 seconds per gradient does.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Failure: optim’s default gradient
Without a gradient, optim uses central differences with a fixed absolute step ndeps = 1e-3.
fit1 <- optim(th, loglik, method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1))
fit2 <- optim(th, loglik, gr = function(p) grad(loglik, p),
              method = "BFGS", control = list(fnscale = -1))
rbind(default = fit1$par, numDeriv = fit2$par)
#                  r        K         N0
# default  0.7948541 1.202606 0.05085940
# numDeriv 0.7954268 1.202457 0.05076077
grad(loglik, fit1$par)                    # should be ~0 at the maximum
# [1] 48.205320  7.205445 -8.363963

h = 10^{-3} is 2 % of N_0 = 0.05: at the true maximum the default gradient is still 290 in the N_0 direction. BFGS stops at the wrong place.
Here the error is about \tfrac15 of a standard error. For a parameter of size 10^{-3} (a rate constant in /s) the step is the size of the parameter.
Check: evaluate an accurate gradient at the returned optimum. Fix: pass gr, or set parscale/ndeps to the parameter sizes.


fnscale = -1 makes optim maximise. The default-gradient run stops after 16 gradient evaluations at a point where the true gradient is (48, 7, -8), compared with 1e-4 for the run with the numDeriv gradient. The parameter differences (6e-4 in r, 1e-4 in N0) are about 0.17 standard errors (standard errors 0.0035 and 0.0006 from the Hessian), so the conclusions here do not change. But it is a silent wrong answer, and it gets worse the further parameters are from size 1. scipy.optimize.minimize uses a relative forward step instead, so it fails differently (fewer digits, not a biased gradient). Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (Part 9) uses the Hessian, again by finite differences.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Optional: the complex step
If f is a formula that also works for complex numbers, step in the imaginary direction: f(x + ih) = f(x) + ih f'(x) - \tfrac{h^2}{2}f''(x) - \dots \;\Longrightarrow\; f'(x) = \frac{\operatorname{Im} f(x + ih)}{h} + O(h^2).
Im(od(t0 + 1e-20i)) / 1e-20 - exact       # 1e-20i: the complex number 10^-20 i
# [1] -2.775558e-17

No subtraction, so no cancellation: h = 10^{-20} is fine, and the result is exact to rounding.
Only for code that accepts complex input: no abs, max, if (x > 0), compiled solvers. One derivative per evaluation.


Optional slide; complex numbers are not assumed knowledge. The idea: the real part carries f(x), the imaginary part carries h f’(x), and they never have to be subtracted from each other. The O(h^2) truncation term is h^2 f’’’ / 6 times 1e-40: invisible. In R, exp, log, sin and arithmetic all work on complex numbers, so the logistic formula works unchanged. It breaks as soon as the code compares numbers or calls something that is real-only. It is a stepping stone to the next slide: carrying a derivative along with the value through the computation.

title: Numerical differentiation
section: Automatic differentiation: what Stan, JAX and torch do
text:
Automatic differentiation: what Stan, JAX and torch do
A program is a chain of elementary steps (+, \times, exp, …), each with a known derivative. Automatic differentiation (AD) applies the chain rule to the numbers as the program runs.









finite differences
AD




accuracy
half to two-thirds of the digits
exact up to rounding: no h


gradient of p parameters
p+1 to 8p evaluations
reverse mode: about 2–4 evaluations, any p


needs
only f as a black box
code written in an AD-aware library




Forward mode: carry (value, derivative) through every step; one pass per parameter.
Reverse mode (backpropagation): record the steps, then run the chain rule backwards once for the whole gradient.
Stan (gradients for HMC sampling), TMB/RTMB, JAX, PyTorch, Julia. A log-likelihood with 10 000 parameters: AD is the only option.


One slide, no code: the point is to know what these tools do and why they exist. Forward mode on the logistic: v1 = -r t, v2 = exp(v1), v3 = 1 + A v2, v4 = K / v3; carrying derivatives with respect to t gives dv1 = -r, dv2 = v2 dv1, dv3 = A dv2, dv4 = -K dv3 / v3^2 (exercise B7 does this by hand). Reverse mode is why deep learning is possible: a network with a million weights gets its whole gradient for the price of a few forward passes. Its cost is memory: every intermediate value is stored for the backward pass. For an ODE model inside a likelihood, the AD-aware tools differentiate through the solver (sensitivity equations or adjoints). Finite differences remain the right tool for black-box code and for checking an AD or hand-written gradient.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Checklist: detecting derivative trouble

Value changes when h changes by 10× → rounding regime (too small) or truncation (too large). Find the plateau.
Step not scaled to the variable → use h = \varepsilon^{1/3}\max(|x|, 1) (central), or parscale in optim.
Second derivative with a first-derivative step → use h \approx \varepsilon^{1/4}, never 10^{-8}.
Derivative of measured data → never difference neighbours; widen the stencil or smooth, and compare two smoothing levels.
Negative growth rates mid-growth, spiky curves → noise, not biology.
Optimiser stops with a non-zero gradient → check with numDeriv::grad at the result; supply an analytic or AD gradient.
Hand-written gradient → compare with a finite-difference gradient; agreement to ~10^{-7} relative, not \sim 1.
Function with if, abs, interpolation, or an adaptive ODE solve → not smooth: no Richardson, larger h.


Every item corresponds to a failure shown in this lecture or the exercise. The gradient check (last-but-one item) is standard practice before trusting any hand-coded or AD gradient: a sign error or missing factor gives a relative difference of order 1, not 1e-7. The last item: an adaptive ODE solver’s output changes in small jumps when a parameter changes, because the step sequence changes; its tolerance (say 1e-6) plays the role of eps, so the best step is around sqrt(1e-6) = 1e-3, not 1e-8.

title: Numerical differentiation
text:
Summary

Stencils from Taylor: forward/backward O(h), central O(h^2), second derivative \tfrac{N(t+h) - 2N(t) + N(t-h)}{h^2}, O(h^2). Any stencil: match Taylor terms with a small linear system.
Best step balances truncation Ch^p against rounding \varepsilon/h^k: \varepsilon^{1/2} (forward), \varepsilon^{1/3} (central), \varepsilon^{1/4} (second derivative). Steps are relative to the variable.
Richardson: \tfrac{4D(h/2) - D(h)}{3} removes the h^2 error; repeated, it gives 12–13 digits (numDeriv::grad). Needs a smooth function.
Measured data: noise \sigma replaces \varepsilon, and \sigma/h is huge. Widen the stencil or smooth first (Splines); check with two smoothing levels.
Gradients for fitting: one difference per parameter; watch the step size relative to each parameter (optim’s ndeps). AD gives exact gradients at the cost of a few evaluations.

Next: Numerical integration, the opposite operation: integrating averages the noise away, and Richardson returns as Romberg.

The single idea of the unit: every derivative estimate divides a difference by a small number, and that amplifies whatever error is in the values, rounding or measurement noise. The stencils tell us how fast truncation falls; the balance tells us where to stop. The second-derivative stencil returns in Part 10 as the diffusion term. Numerical integration is the friendly counterpart: errors average out instead of being amplified.

title: Exercise: the SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation
text:
Explore
The demo below solves the deconvolution of the lecture in your browser: the same signature \(S\) (CD4T and CD8T differ by 2 % on genes 1 and 2), true proportions \(p = (0.30, 0.15, 0.15, 0.10, 0.30)\), and a bulk sample \(b = b_0\,(1 + s \cdot \text{noise})\). With lecture pattern the noise is the fixed \(\sin(37g)\) of the slides, so at \(s = 5\%\) you get the slide numbers; random draws \(N(0,1)\) noise instead, and new random sample draws another one. The SVD is computed by one-sided Jacobi (rotations of pairs of columns of \(S\), never \(S^TS\)).

Panel (a): the estimate for this sample (bars), the truth (dashed) and the estimates from 100 further samples with fresh random noise of the same size (dots; arrows count dots off the scale). The last group is CD4 + CD8.
Panel (b): the filter factors \(f_i\) of the chosen method against \(\sigma\), with the five singular values as circles.
Panel (c): the error to expect over the noise, split into bias \(\|E[x] - p\|\) (what the method gets wrong without noise) and noise \(\sqrt{E\|x - E[x]\|^2}\) (the spread of the dots), against \(\lambda\) or \(k\); total \(= \sqrt{\text{bias}^2 + \text{noise}^2}\). Both use the truth, which only a simulation knows.




E1. (noise is divided by \(\sigma_i\)) Start with least squares at 5 % noise. Read the estimate, the expected noise and how many dots fall off the scale for CD4T and CD8T. Then set the noise to 1 % and to 0. How does the expected noise depend on \(s\)? Which estimates do the dots leave alone, and what does the readout give as the multiplier \(f_5/\sigma_5\) of \(u_5^Tb\)?






Answer E1





At 5 %: \(x = (0.543, -0.092, 0.149, 0.099, 0.299)\), as on the slides; expected noise 1.202, and 32 of 100 dots fall off the scale (\(-0.6\) to \(1.2\)) for CD4T and for CD8T. At 1 % the noise is 0.240 and the estimate \((0.349, 0.102, \dots)\); at 0 the estimate is exactly \(p\). The noise is proportional to \(s\) (1.202 / 5 = 0.240): least squares has no bias, only noise. The dots for B, NK, Mono and CD4 + CD8 stay in a tight band (CD4 + CD8 = 0.451 at 5 %): the noise lands only along \(v_5 \approx (1, -1, 0, 0, 0)/\sqrt2\), which changes the split but not the total. The multiplier is \(1/\sigma_5 = 1/2.87 = 0.348\), against at most \(1/269 = 0.0037\) for the other components: component 5 amplifies noise about 90 times more.



E2. (truncation: bias against noise) Back at 5 % noise, choose truncated SVD and move \(k\) from 5 down to 1. Note \(\|x - p\|\), \(\|Sx - b\|\), and the expected bias and noise for each \(k\). Where does the step in panel (b) sit for \(k = 4\)? Which \(k\) gives the smallest expected error, and which \(k\) would the residual alone point to?






Answer E2

These are the lecture’s table. For \(k = 4\) the step lies between \(\sigma_5 = 2.87\) and \(\sigma_4 = 269\), so only \(\sigma_5\) gets \(f = 0\). Dropping component 5 cuts the noise from 1.202 to 0.011 at the price of a bias of 0.106: that bias is the equal split \(0.226/0.226\) instead of \(0.30/0.15\), the part of \(p\) along \(v_5\) that TSVD sets to 0. Fewer components only add bias. The smallest expected error is at \(k = 4\) (0.107), and the residual says the same without the truth: it drops steeply until \(k = 4\) and then barely moves (9.71 to 9.62). All dots for CD4T and CD8T now sit on top of each other: very stable, and wrong in the same way every time.



E3. (ridge: a smooth filter) Choose ridge and move \(\lambda\) from 0.1 to 1000. Read \(f_5\) and the expected bias and noise at \(\lambda = 1\), 10, 31.6 and 316. Where do the bias and noise curves cross, and where is the total smallest? At \(\lambda = 10\), compare the error of the lecture sample with the expected error, then click random and new random sample a few times. What happens to all five proportions at \(\lambda = 316\) and 1000?






Answer E3





\(\lambda = 1\): \(f_5 = 0.892\), bias 0.011, noise 1.072. \(\lambda = 10\): \(f_5 = 0.076\), bias 0.098, noise 0.092, total 0.135: the curves cross close to \(\lambda = 10\). \(\lambda = 31.6\): \(f_5 = 0.008\), bias 0.105, noise 0.015, total 0.106, the smallest (the readout’s “smallest total”), as good as TSVD with \(k = 4\). \(\lambda = 316\): total 0.187, now all bias. The lecture sample at \(\lambda = 10\) has \(\|x - p\| = 0.072\), better than the expected 0.135: its noise pattern happens to push the split towards the truth (the lecture called this luck). Random samples (seeds 1–3) give 0.091, 0.092 and 0.067: the dots show a spread of about \(\pm0.07\) around 0.23 (CD4) and 0.22 (CD8), close to the equal split. At \(\lambda = 316\) (\(f_1 \ldots f_4\) are no longer near 1) every proportion shrinks, CD4 + CD8 = 0.384 and Mono 0.165; at 1000 the estimate is \((0.073, 0.073, 0.026, 0.022, 0.038)\) and the residual 193. Too much ridge is bias in everything, not just the split.



E4. (how much regularisation depends on the noise) Keep ridge and read the readout’s “smallest total” at noise 0.5 %, 1 %, 5 %, 10 % and 20 %. How does the best \(\lambda\) move, and why?






Answer E4





The best \(\lambda\) is about 3.2 at 0.5 %, 6.3 at 1 %, 32 at 5 %, 50 at 10 % and 63 at 20 % (total errors 0.080, 0.097, 0.106, 0.108, 0.115). More noise means component 5 must be damped harder, so the step \(\sigma = \lambda\) in panel (b) moves right, away from \(\sigma_5 = 2.87\). It can never pass \(\sigma_4 = 269\) without destroying the well-determined proportions, so even at 20 % noise the best \(\lambda\) stays far below it. With less noise, a smaller \(\lambda\) lets part of the true split through (\(f_5 = 0.45\) at \(\lambda = 3.2\)), and the best error drops below the 0.106 of TSVD. Regularisation must be matched to the noise level, which is why \(\lambda\) is chosen from the data (residual, L-curve) rather than fixed once.



E5. (better data, not better maths) Press reset. Move CD8 differs by (the difference between CD8T and CD4T on genes 1 and 2) to 0 (identical columns), then to 10 % and 30 %. Read \(\sigma_5\), \(\kappa\), the least-squares estimate and its expected noise. At 30 %, which method has the smallest expected error now?






Answer E5





At 0: \(\sigma_5 = 0\) and \(\kappa = \infty\). The demo, like pinv, drops singular values below the rounding tolerance, so “least squares” returns the minimum-norm answer \((0.226, 0.226, 0.149, 0.099, 0.299)\), identical to TSVD \(k = 4\). At 10 %: \(\sigma_5 = 14.4\), \(\kappa = 44.8\), \(x = (0.355, 0.097, \dots)\), expected noise 0.241. At 30 %: \(\sigma_5 = 43.0\), \(\kappa = 15.0\), \(x = (0.323, 0.128, \dots)\), noise 0.081, so least squares now beats TSVD \(k = 4\) (0.108), which still throws away the split. Ridge with \(\lambda \approx 32\) is best (0.065), and at \(\lambda = 10\) the estimate \((0.318, 0.133)\) is within 0.02 of the truth. \(\sigma_5\) grows in proportion to the difference (2.87 per 2 %), and the noise along \(v_5\) falls as \(1/\sigma_5\). A signature with genes that really separate the two cell types does what no choice of \(k\) or \(\lambda\) can.
