title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: Nullclines: where one variable stands still
text:
Nullclines: where one variable stands still





u-nullcline du/dt = 0: u = 3/(1 + v^2). On it the flow is vertical.
v-nullcline dv/dt = 0: v = 3/(1 + u^2). On it the flow is horizontal.
Fixed points (steady states) = where they cross.
The nullclines cut the plane into regions with a fixed sign pattern: below both, u and v grow; above both, both shrink. In the thin lenses, the flow points away from the middle state.



The nullclines are the two curves from Newton for systems of equations (F1 = 0 and F2 = 0), now read as the places where one concentration momentarily stops changing. Checking the sign of du/dt on each side is a pen-and-paper exercise: at (0, 0), du/dt = 3 > 0. Follow the arrows on the nullclines near the middle state: on both sides they point away from it along the lenses and towards the outer states. That already suggests the middle state is unstable, before any eigenvalue. Nullclines are the fastest sketch of a two-variable model and the first thing to draw for any new model.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Stability in one variable
Logistic growth (the running OD example, r = 0.8 h^{-1}, K = 1.2): \dfrac{dN}{dt} = f(N) = rN\left(1 - \dfrac{N}{K}\right).

Fixed points: f(N^*) = 0, so N^* = 0 or N^* = K.
Push a little: N = N^* + \delta. Taylor: f(N^* + \delta) \approx \underbrace{f(N^*)}_{0} + f'(N^*)\,\delta, so \frac{d\delta}{dt} \approx f'(N^*)\,\delta \quad\Rightarrow\quad \delta(t) \approx \delta_0\, e^{f'(N^*)\,t}
f'(N) = r(1 - 2N/K): f'(0) = 0.8 > 0, unstable (a few cells grow); f'(1.2) = -0.8 < 0, stable (a perturbation of the plateau halves every \ln 2/0.8 = 0.87 h).

Rule: f'(N^*) < 0 stable, f'(N^*) > 0 unstable, f'(N^*) = 0 undecided.

The one-variable case contains the whole idea. Near a fixed point the right-hand side is approximately linear, and a linear ODE d delta/dt = lambda delta has the solution delta_0 exp(lambda t). The sign of lambda decides growth or decay; its size sets the speed. The relaxation time 1/|lambda| = 1.25 h for the plateau. When f’ = 0 the linear term vanishes and the quadratic term decides: the linearisation is inconclusive, a case we meet again at the end. The logistic parameters are the shared running example from Convergence and cost.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Linearisation in two variables
Push the toggle away from a fixed point \mathbf x^*: \mathbf x = \mathbf x^* + \boldsymbol\delta. Exactly as for Newton,
\frac{d\boldsymbol\delta}{dt} = \mathbf F(\mathbf x^* + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \underbrace{\mathbf F(\mathbf x^*)}_{\mathbf 0} + J(\mathbf x^*)\,\boldsymbol\delta \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\frac{d\boldsymbol\delta}{dt} \approx J\,\boldsymbol\delta}
At U on, (2.618, 0.382):
J = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1.745 \\ -0.255 & -1 \end{pmatrix}: \qquad
\begin{aligned}
\dot\delta_u &= -\delta_u - 1.745\,\delta_v\\
\dot\delta_v &= -0.255\,\delta_u - \delta_v
\end{aligned}

Same J as in Newton for systems of equations; a new use. Newton solves J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F; stability asks how e^{Jt} acts on \boldsymbol\delta.
The two equations are coupled: \delta_v feeds \delta_u. To see growth or decay we need to uncouple them.


The derivation is the linear approximation F(x + delta) ≈ F(x) + J delta from Newton for systems of equations, applied at a point where F is zero. Read the entries as biology: -1 on the diagonal is degradation; -1.745 says a bit of extra V strongly reduces production of U (V = 0.38 is on the steep part of its Hill curve); -0.255 says extra U barely changes V’s production (U = 2.6 is far above threshold). Is the state stable? Not obvious from the entries: both diagonals are negative, but the off-diagonals couple the variables. Eigenvectors uncouple them.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Eigenvalues decide
If J\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v, then \boldsymbol\delta(t) = e^{\lambda t}\,\mathbf v solves \dot{\boldsymbol\delta} = J\boldsymbol\delta (check: both sides equal \lambda e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v). Any start is a mix:
\boldsymbol\delta(t) = c_1\, e^{\lambda_1 t}\,\mathbf v_1 + c_2\, e^{\lambda_2 t}\,\mathbf v_2
At U on: \lambda_1 = -5/3, \mathbf v_1 = (0.934, 0.357); \lambda_2 = -1/3, \mathbf v_2 = (0.934, -0.357).

Both negative: every small push dies out. U on is stable.
The slowest decay, e^{-t/3}, sets the recovery time: a perturbation halves every 3\ln 2 = 2.1 protein lifetimes.
Rule: stable if all eigenvalues have \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda < 0; unstable if any has \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda > 0.


This is the reason eigenvalues were worth a whole Part. Along an eigenvector the coupled system acts like the one-variable case: the matrix only stretches the vector by lambda. Write the start as a combination of the two eigenvectors and each part evolves independently. For complex eigenvalues lambda = a ± ib, e^{lambda t} = e^{at}(cos bt ± i sin bt): the real part decides growth or decay, the imaginary part gives rotation. The recovery time is a measurable prediction: after a pulse of inducer that slightly perturbs the U-on state, the cell returns with a time constant of 3 protein lifetimes. Exact values: tau = -2, det = 5/9, so lambda = -1 ± 2/3 (exercise).
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: The zoo of two-variable fixed points
text:
The zoo of two-variable fixed points









eigenvalues
type
stable?




real, both < 0
stable node
yes


real, opposite signs
saddle
no (one direction attracts, one repels)


complex a \pm ib, a < 0
stable spiral (damped oscillation)
yes


complex \pm ib, a = 0
centre
undecided by linearisation




Four linear systems dx/dt = A x, one per panel, with their eigenvalues below. Orange lines in the node and the saddle are the eigenvector directions: trajectories run straight along them. In the node, trajectories come in tangent to the slow direction (eigenvalue -0.5), the vertical one here. In the saddle, the horizontal eigenvector (lambda = 1) repels and the vertical one (lambda = -1) attracts: almost every trajectory comes in and then leaves. Spirals arise from complex eigenvalues; the imaginary part is the angular speed. Positive real parts give the unstable versions of node and spiral (arrows reversed). A centre is a borderline case: for the nonlinear system, small higher-order terms decide between a slow inward or outward spiral.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
A 2 × 2 shortcut: trace and determinant




For J = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix}: \tau = a + d, \Delta = ad - bc,
\lambda_{1,2} = \frac{\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}}{2}

\Delta < 0: saddle.
\Delta > 0, \tau < 0: stable; \tau > 0: unstable.
\tau^2 < 4\Delta: complex, a spiral.

Toggle, U on: \tau = -2, \Delta = 0.556. Middle: \tau = -2, \Delta = -0.419 → saddle.


The eigenvalues of a 2 by 2 matrix are the roots of lambda^2 - tau lambda + Delta = 0 (recap from Power iteration and friends). Delta is the product of the eigenvalues, tau their sum. A negative product means opposite signs: a saddle, whatever the trace. With positive product, both have the sign of the trace. The dashed parabola separates real from complex eigenvalues. The middle state of the toggle has det J = -0.4186, the number we computed in Newton for systems of equations, so it is a saddle. The Sel’kov point (orange) comes later in this lecture. This shortcut is only for 2 by 2; for more variables we need eigen().
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
The toggle’s three states, classified
J <- function(x) {
  u <- x[1]; v <- x[2]
  matrix(c(-1, -alpha * n * v^(n - 1) / (1 + v^n)^2,
           -alpha * n * u^(n - 1) / (1 + u^n)^2, -1), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
}
states <- rbind(U_on   = c(2.618034, 0.381966),
                middle = c(1.213412, 1.213412),
                V_on   = c(0.381966, 2.618034))
t(apply(states, 1, function(x) eigen(J(x))$values))
#              [,1]       [,2]
# U_on   -1.6666667 -0.3333333
# middle  0.1910584 -2.1910584
# V_on   -1.6666667 -0.3333333

U on and V on: stable nodes. Middle: a saddle, \lambda = 0.191 > 0: unstable. Two stable states = bistable.
eigen returns complex numbers when needed; test Re(values).


The Jacobian is exactly the one from Newton for systems of equations. eigen applies the QR algorithm (How eigen() works, and big problems) and works for any size. The steady states are rounded to 6 digits here; the eigenvalues change only in the 7th digit, because eigenvalues of this small matrix are well conditioned. This is the classification that Newton could not give: the root found most often, the middle state, is unstable, and a cell never sits there. Mind the order: for a non-symmetric matrix eigen sorts by decreasing modulus (U on: -1.67 before -0.33); at the middle state J happens to be symmetric, so eigen sorts by decreasing value (0.19 first). Never read stability from values[1]; use max(Re(values)).
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
The saddle up close




eigen(J(states["middle", ]))$vectors
#            [,1]      [,2]
# [1,] -0.7071068 0.7071068
# [2,]  0.7071068 0.7071068

\lambda = 0.19 along (1, -1): more U, less V grows. The cell decides.
\lambda = -2.19 along (1, 1): changing both equally decays.
Trajectories come in along the diagonal and leave along (1, -1), towards U on or V on.



The eigenvectors carry the biology. The unstable direction (1, -1) is “one protein up, the other down”: a small imbalance is amplified by mutual repression, which is the switch deciding. The stable direction (1, 1) is “both up or both down”: that is corrected by degradation. The figure shows trajectories starting near the diagonal: they slide in along the orange line towards the saddle, then turn and leave along the dashed red line. The eigenvectors are the columns of $vectors, normalised to length 1, in the same order as $values (0.19 first); the sign of an eigenvector is arbitrary.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Eigenvalues of big networks
A <- J(states["U_on", ])
eigen(A)$values                  # sorted by |lambda| for non-symmetric A
# [1] -1.6666667 -0.3333333
power_it <- function(B, k = 100) {
  x <- c(1, 0)
  for (i in 1:k) { x <- B %*% x; x <- x / sqrt(sum(x^2)) }
  sum(x * (B %*% x))             # Rayleigh quotient
}
power_it(A)                      # largest |lambda|: says nothing about stability
# [1] -1.666667
power_it(A + 2 * diag(2)) - 2    # shift: the rightmost eigenvalue now dominates
# [1] -0.3333333

Stability needs the eigenvalue with the largest real part, not the largest |\lambda| that power iteration finds (Power iteration and friends).
20 000 genes: do not call eigen (O(n^3)). Use a sparse iterative (Arnoldi) method for the rightmost eigenvalue: RSpectra::eigs(J, k = 1, which = "LR") (How eigen() works, and big problems).


Two lessons from Part 5. First, Power iteration and friends finds the eigenvalue of largest modulus. For stability that is the wrong one: here -5/3 is largest in size, but -1/3 is the eigenvalue that decides how slowly perturbations die out and which one would first cross zero. A shift B = A + cI moves all eigenvalues right by c; once they are all positive and real, the rightmost is also the largest. Complex eigenvalues make this harder, which is why library codes use Arnoldi with “largest real part” selection (How eigen() works, and big problems). Second, the same ordering trap applies to eigen() for non-symmetric matrices: values[1] is the largest in modulus. Always compute max(Re(values)).
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: The separatrix: the edge between two fates
text:
The separatrix: the edge between two fates
The saddle’s stable direction continues as a curve, the separatrix, between the two basins. Trace it by running the ODE backwards from the saddle along \mathbf v_{\text{stable}}. Biased switch (\alpha_v = 2.9):
library(rootSolve)
au <- 3; av <- 2.9
toggle2 <- function(t, x, parms)
  list(c(au / (1 + x[2]^2) - x[1], av / (1 + x[1]^2) - x[2]))
xs <- multiroot(function(x) toggle2(0, x, NULL)[[1]], start = c(1, 1.3))$root
e  <- eigen(jacobian.full(y = xs, func = toggle2))    # FD Jacobian
e$values
# [1] -2.176727  0.176727
vs <- e$vectors[, e$values < 0]                       # stable direction
tb <- seq(0, -7, by = -0.01)                          # backwards in time
up   <- ode(y = xs + 1e-6 * vs, times = tb, func = toggle2, parms = NULL)
down <- ode(y = xs - 1e-6 * vs, times = tb, func = toggle2, parms = NULL)

Why backwards? Forwards in time, the stable direction attracts: trajectories near the separatrix come towards the saddle, so we cannot follow the separatrix away from it. Reversing time turns the attracting direction into a repelling one, so a start a distance 1e-6 from the saddle along v_stable runs out along the separatrix. Two runs, one for each side. In the symmetric switch the separatrix is the diagonal u = v (by symmetry), but with alpha_v = 2.9 the saddle moves to (1.094, 1.320) and the separatrix bends: no symmetry argument helps, and we need this computation. jacobian.full from rootSolve gives a finite-difference Jacobian of a deSolve-style function. Note the selection e$values < 0: here eigen lists the negative eigenvalue first.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: Where Newton goes ≠ where the cell goes
text:
Where Newton goes ≠ where the cell goes


Left: Newton’s basins for the biased switch (the middle state takes 57 %). Right: the fate of the ODE from each start, by simulation: U on 58 %, V on 42 %. The orange separatrix from the backward runs lies exactly on the boundary.
Newton’s basins are a property of the algorithm; the ODE’s basins are a property of the cell.


This is the contrast promised in Newton for systems of equations, now for the biased switch. Left: each start coloured by the root Newton converges to: curved regions, thin interleaved bands, and the unstable middle state as the most common answer. Right: each start simulated to t = 100 (vectorised RK4, 90 000 starts) and coloured by where it ends; the boundary is a single smooth curve, and it coincides with the separatrix computed from just two backward runs. That is the check: two independent computations agree. A 3 % weaker V promoter shifts the boundary above the diagonal: more starts end in U on. The dotted diagonal is where the boundary would be in the symmetric switch.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: Failure: the simulation stops at the saddle
text:
Failure: the simulation stops at the saddle




ode(y = c(u = 2, v = 2), times = c(0, 20, 100),
    func = toggle, parms = NULL)
#   time        u        v
# 1    0 2.000000 2.000000
# 2   20 1.213412 1.213412
# 3  100 1.213412 1.213412

A start on the separatrix (u = v) converges to the saddle. A start 10^{-8} off stays there for \approx 100 time units.
“The simulation settled” does not mean “stable”.
Check: eigenvalues at the end point; restart from a perturbed end point.



A simulation run to “steady state” is a popular way to find steady states. It fails here in two ways. Starting exactly on the stable manifold, it converges, correctly, to the unstable state: the diagonal is invariant in the symmetric model, and floating-point rounding keeps u and v exactly equal. Starting very close, the trajectory spends a long time near the saddle, because the push away grows only like e^{0.19 t}: from 1e-4 it takes about ln(1e4)/0.19 ≈ 48 time units, from 1e-8 about twice that. Someone who stops at t = 20 and reads off (1.2134, 1.2134) reports an unstable state as “the steady state”. Symmetric models and symmetric initial conditions (all genes equal) make this more common than one would think.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Oscillations: glycolysis in yeast
Yeast cells and extracts show oscillating NADH and ADP levels, with periods of about a minute (Chance et al. 1964; Hess & Boiteux 1971). Sel’kov’s model (1968), dimensionless:
\frac{du}{dt} = -u + a v + u^2 v, \qquad \frac{dv}{dt} = b - a v - u^2 v, \qquad a = 0.08,\ b = 0.6

v = fructose-6-phosphate (F6P), fed in at rate b. u = ADP, removed at rate 1.
u^2 v: the enzyme phosphofructokinase turns F6P into ADP and is activated by ADP: positive feedback.
One fixed point, by hand: u^* = b = 0.6, v^* = b/(a + b^2) = 1.364.

Circadian clocks and the cell-cycle oscillator are larger models, but analysed the same way: find the fixed point, find it unstable, look for a cycle.

Glycolytic oscillations were among the first biochemical oscillations observed. Sel’kov’s two-variable model keeps only the key step: PFK, the enzyme that converts F6P to fructose bisphosphate, is allosterically activated by its downstream product ADP. Product activation plus substrate depletion gives a relaxation oscillation. The equations are in the dimensionless form popularised by Strogatz (Nonlinear dynamics and chaos, section 7.3). Fixed point: add the two equations to get -u + b = 0, so u = b; then the second gives v = b/(a + b^2). The same programme (unstable fixed point, then a closed orbit) underlies models of circadian clocks (Goldbeter) and the embryonic cell cycle (Novák–Tyson), and the repressilator.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
An unstable spiral
a <- 0.08; b <- 0.6
selkov <- function(t, x, parms) {
  u <- x[1]; v <- x[2]                   # u = ADP, v = F6P
  list(c(-u + a * v + u^2 * v,
          b - a * v - u^2 * v))
}
Jsel <- function(x) {
  u <- x[1]; v <- x[2]
  matrix(c(-1 + 2 * u * v,  a + u^2,
           -2 * u * v,     -(a + u^2)), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
}
eigen(Jsel(c(b, b / (a + b^2))))$values
# [1] 0.09818182+0.6560185i 0.09818182-0.6560185i

\tau = 0.196 > 0, \Delta = 0.44 > 0, \tau^2 < 4\Delta: unstable spiral. Perturbations rotate and grow like e^{0.098\,t}.
The flow points inwards far away (substrate is bounded), outwards near the fixed point. In between, trajectories must circle: a limit cycle.


Real part 0.098 > 0: unstable. Imaginary part 0.656: rotation with angular frequency 0.656, i.e. a period of 2 pi / 0.656 = 9.58 near the fixed point. Since nothing escapes to infinity (one can draw a box that trajectories enter but never leave) and the only fixed point inside repels, the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem says trajectories must approach a closed orbit. That theorem holds in two dimensions only; in three or more dimensions trajectories can also be chaotic. We do not prove anything here: we simulate.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
The limit cycle


From inside (orange, near the fixed point) the spiral grows; from outside (blue) the trajectory shrinks. Both end on the same closed orbit (black).
Its size and period are set by the model, not by the start: a property a biologist can measure.


Left: the nullclines (blue: du/dt = 0, v = u/(a + u^2); red: dv/dt = 0, v = b/(a + u^2)) cross once, at the white unstable fixed point. Right: u(t) from the two starts. After about 50 time units the two runs are on the same cycle, shifted only in phase. That is what distinguishes a limit cycle from the closed orbits of a centre, where every start gives a different amplitude. Stability of the cycle as a whole is decided by Floquet multipliers, the eigenvalues of the map “go once around the cycle”; we only check it by simulation.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Measuring the cycle
out <- ode(y = c(u = 0.61, v = 1.36), times = seq(0, 100, by = 0.01),
           func = selkov, parms = NULL)
late <- out[out[, "time"] > 60, ]                 # drop the transient
range(late[, "u"])                                # amplitude
# [1] 0.2452569 1.5175375
up <- which(diff(sign(late[, "u"] - b)) > 0)      # u crosses b upwards
diff(late[up, "time"])                            # period
# [1] 9.62 9.63 9.62

Period \approx 9.62 (time units of ADP turnover). Successive periods agree: the transient is over.
Checks: a second start gives the same range and period; halving rtol/atol changes nothing in the shown digits; the linear guess 2\pi/0.656 = 9.58 is only close because we are near the onset of oscillation.


The period is measured from successive upward crossings of the line u = b. The output grid of 0.01 limits the resolution to about 0.01; linear interpolation between grid points gives 9.6226. Discard the transient: the run from near the fixed point takes about 40 time units to grow onto the cycle. In the exercise students check the period against a start from outside the cycle and against tighter tolerances. Detecting oscillations automatically (in a parameter scan) is a common task; the robust check is that the max and min of late values differ by much more than the solver tolerance.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Failure: \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \approx 0
At \alpha = 2 the three toggle states merge at (1, 1):


alpha <- 2
F <- function(x) toggle(0, x, NULL)[[1]]
eigen(J(c(1, 1)))$values               # exact state
# [1]  0 -2
ss <- multiroot(F, start = c(3, 0.5))$root
ss                                     # J singular at root
# [1] 1.0017321 0.9982688
eigen(jacobian.full(y = ss, func = toggle))$values
# [1] -1.999998e+00 -1.964308e-06










\alpha
slowest \lambda = -1 + 2/\alpha
time to 1 %
u(100) vs steady

-0.333

-0.048

1.1686 vs 1.1051





\lambda \approx 0: linearisation cannot decide, and an error of 10^{-6} in the state or in J can flip the sign. Simulations relax very slowly (“critical slowing down”).


Two problems meet at a bifurcation. Newton loses quadratic convergence because J is singular at the root (as in Newton for systems of equations), so multiroot stops at its tolerance with an error of 0.002. The eigenvalue computed there, -2e-6, is a rounding-level number whose sign means nothing. Even with the exact state (1, 1) the eigenvalue is exactly 0 and the linearisation is inconclusive: the nonlinear terms decide (here, stable, but with algebraic not exponential decay). Near alpha = 2 the slowest eigenvalue -1 + 2/alpha is close to zero, so a simulation run for 100 time units is still far from the steady state. Check: compare |Re lambda| with the error you expect in J (about 1e-8 for a finite-difference J) and in the state; simulate much longer than 5/|lambda|.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: Outlook: following steady states as α changes
text:
Outlook: following steady states as α changes





Bifurcation diagram: steady states against a parameter, solid = stable, dashed = unstable.
At \alpha = 2 the middle branch loses stability and two stable branches appear: bistability begins (a pitchfork).
Numerical continuation: step \alpha, use the previous state as Newton’s start (predictor), correct with Newton, compute eigenvalues. Detect bifurcations where \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda crosses 0.
Tools: AUTO, MatCont, PyDSTool, BifurcationKit.jl.



One-slide outlook. The left panel is what Gardner et al. needed: the range of promoter strengths for which the circuit is a switch. Right: the largest eigenvalue on each branch; the bifurcation is where it crosses zero. Continuation software does more than our naive loop: it parametrises the branch by arclength so that it can go around folds (where the branch turns back and the naive loop fails because J is singular), and it detects Hopf bifurcations, where a pair of complex eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis and a limit cycle is born. For the Sel’kov model, decreasing b from 0.6 to about 0.4 brings the real part of the eigenvalues back below zero (exercise), and the oscillation disappears.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: Checklist: is this steady state real?
text:
Checklist: is this steady state real?

Find all fixed points: nullclines for two variables, Newton from many starts for more.
Classify each: eigenvalues of J at the fixed point; stable iff all \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda < 0. Use \max(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda), not values[1].
Is |\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda| large compared with the error in J and in the state? If not, linearisation cannot decide.
Do not trust “the simulation stopped”: check eigenvalues there, restart from a perturbed point, run longer than 5/|\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda|.
Basins: a separatrix from backward runs, checked against a grid of forward simulations.
Oscillations: unstable fixed point + bounded flow → look for a limit cycle; check period and amplitude are independent of the start and the tolerances.


A practical list for any ODE model in a paper or a thesis. The first two items are the minimum: list the steady states and their stability. Most mistakes in practice come from the third and fourth: a borderline eigenvalue reported as stable, or a simulation endpoint reported as a steady state.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Summary

Phase plane: the flow of a two-variable ODE as arrows and trajectories. Nullclines (\dot u = 0, \dot v = 0) cross at fixed points.
Linearisation: near \mathbf x^*, \dot{\boldsymbol\delta} \approx J(\mathbf x^*)\boldsymbol\delta, solved by e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v. Stable iff all \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda < 0. 2\times2: trace and determinant. Node, saddle, spiral, centre.
Toggle switch (\alpha = 3): U on and V on are stable nodes (\lambda = -5/3, -1/3); the middle state is a saddle (\lambda = 0.19, -2.19).
The separatrix (stable manifold of the saddle) separates the basins. Compute it by integrating backwards from the saddle. The cell’s basins are not Newton’s basins.
Limit cycle: an unstable spiral in a bounded flow. Sel’kov glycolysis: period 9.62.
Rightmost eigenvalue, not largest |\lambda|. Failures: simulations that stall at saddles; \mathrm{Re}\,\lambda \approx 0 near a bifurcation (\alpha = 2).
Tools: deSolve::ode / solve_ivp / ode_solvers; eigen / np.linalg.eigvals / nalgebra.

Next: Stochastic simulation: when molecule numbers are small, noise kicks the switch across the separatrix.

Recap the chain: fixed point (Newton), Jacobian (Newton for systems), eigenvalues (Part 5), trajectories (Part 8 solvers). The phase plane is where they meet. Next unit: Stochastic simulation, where noise makes the cell jump between the two stable states of the switch from time to time; the separatrix and the saddle decide how often.
crumbs: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a small DFT by hand, both as a matrix–vector product and with one even/odd FFT split, and write down the trigonometric interpolant it defines,
read fft() output correctly: the normalisation, which index holds which frequency, and how to get amplitude, period and peak time of a rhythm,
explain why the FFT costs \(O(n\log n)\) and the matrix \(O(n^2)\), and when a library FFT is slow,
predict from the sampling interval which rhythms are resolved and which are aliased, and to which period,
recognise leakage and reduce it with a window,
filter a noisy trace in frequency space, and see (and fix) what goes wrong at the edges,
use the convolution theorem, and tell circular from linear convolution.

The running example is a simulated clock-controlled gene measured every 2 h for 48 h, plus a simulated luciferase trace. The by-hand part uses pen, paper and a calculator.

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a small DFT by hand, both as a matrix–vector product and with one even/odd FFT split, and write down the trigonometric interpolant it defines,
read fft() output correctly: the normalisation, which index holds which frequency, and how to get amplitude, period and peak time of a rhythm,
explain why the FFT costs \(O(n\log n)\) and the matrix \(O(n^2)\), and when a library FFT is slow,
predict from the sampling interval which rhythms are resolved and which are aliased, and to which period,
recognise leakage and reduce it with a window,
filter a noisy trace in frequency space, and see (and fix) what goes wrong at the edges,
use the convolution theorem, and tell circular from linear convolution.

The running example is a simulated clock-controlled gene measured every 2 h for 48 h, plus a simulated luciferase trace. The by-hand part uses pen, paper and a calculator.

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
Background
\(n\) equispaced samples \(x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}\), taken every \(\Delta t\), over a record of length \(T = n\Delta t\).
Facts used below:

DFT. \(X_k = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} x_j\, w^{jk}\) with \(w = e^{-2\pi i/n}\), for \(k = 0, \dots, n-1\). Here \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), so \(|e^{i\theta}| = 1\). \(k\) counts cycles per record: period \(T/k\), frequency \(k/T\).
Inverse. \(x_j = \frac1n \sum_k X_k\, w^{-jk}\). As a matrix: \(X = Fx\) with \(F_{jk} = w^{jk}\), and \(F^{-1} = \bar F^{T}/n\).
Real data. \(X_{n-k} = \overline{X_k}\): only \(k = 0, \dots, n/2\) carry information.
Trigonometric interpolant (\(n\) even): \(p(t) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n/2-1}\big[a_k\cos\tfrac{2\pi kt}{T} + b_k \sin\tfrac{2\pi kt}{T}\big] + a_{n/2}\cos\tfrac{\pi n t}{T}\) with \(a_0 = X_0/n\), \(a_k = 2\,\mathrm{Re}X_k/n\), \(b_k = -2\,\mathrm{Im}X_k/n\), \(a_{n/2} = X_{n/2}/n\). It passes through every sample.
Reading a rhythm. For \(x_j = A\cos(2\pi k t_j/T - \theta)\): \(X_k = \tfrac{nA}{2}e^{-i\theta}\). Amplitude \(A = 2|X_k|/n\) (for \(0 < k < n/2\)); the peak is at \(t = \theta/(2\pi)\cdot T/k\) with \(\theta = -\arg X_k\).
FFT. With \(E\), \(O\) the DFTs of the even and odd samples (length \(n/2\)): \(X_k = E_k + w^kO_k\) and \(X_{k+n/2} = E_k - w^kO_k\) for \(k < n/2\). Cost \(n\log_2 n\) instead of \(n^2\).
Nyquist. Sampling every \(\Delta t\) resolves frequencies up to \(f_N = 1/(2\Delta t)\), i.e. periods down to \(2\Delta t\). A frequency \(f\) above \(f_N\) gives the same samples as its alias \(|f - m/\Delta t|\), for the whole number \(m\) that brings it into \([0, f_N]\).
Convolution theorem. For circular convolution \((h * y)_j = \sum_m h_m\,y_{(j-m) \bmod n}\): \(\mathrm{DFT}(h*y)_k = H_kY_k\). For ordinary (linear) convolution, pad both with zeros to length at least \(n_y + n_h - 1\) first.

Conventions differ between languages. R’s fft and numpy’s np.fft.fft both compute \(X_k\) exactly as in fact 1 (no \(1/n\)). R indexes from 1, so \(X_k\) is X[k + 1]; Python and Rust index from 0, so \(X_k\) is X[k]. R’s inverse fft(X, inverse = TRUE) does not divide by \(n\); numpy’s np.fft.ifft does. Rust’s rustfft works in place on complex vectors and divides by nothing in either direction. scipy.fft has the same functions as np.fft (and next_fast_len).

RPythonRust


x <- c(7.81, 8.81, 9.05, 9.98, 9.40, 8.50, 8.15, 7.47, 6.87, 6.41, 7.15, 7.37,
       7.81, 8.09, 9.64, 9.49, 9.29, 9.03, 8.25, 7.43, 6.98, 6.73, 6.72, 6.65)
n <- length(x)                          # 24 samples, every 2 h, T = 48 h
X <- fft(x)                             # unnormalised: X[1] = sum(x)
Re(X[1]) / n                            # mean
k <- 2                                  # 2 cycles per 48 h = 24-h period
2 * Mod(X[k + 1]) / n                   # amplitude (R index k + 1)
(-Arg(X[k + 1]) / (2 * pi) * 24) %% 24  # peak time (h)
max(abs(Re(fft(X, inverse = TRUE)) / n - x))   # inverse: divide by n

# Output:
# [1] 8.045
# [1] 1.464505
# [1] 6.452646
# [1] 3.552714e-15


import numpy as np

x = np.array([7.81, 8.81, 9.05, 9.98, 9.40, 8.50, 8.15, 7.47, 6.87, 6.41, 7.15, 7.37,
              7.81, 8.09, 9.64, 9.49, 9.29, 9.03, 8.25, 7.43, 6.98, 6.73, 6.72, 6.65])
n = len(x)                              # 24 samples, every 2 h, T = 48 h
X = np.fft.fft(x)                       # unnormalised: X[0] = sum(x)
print(X[0].real / n)                    # mean
k = 2                                   # 2 cycles per 48 h = 24-h period
print(2 * np.abs(X[k]) / n)             # amplitude (Python index k)
print((-np.angle(X[k]) / (2 * np.pi) * 24) % 24)   # peak time (h)
print(np.max(np.abs(np.fft.ifft(X).real - x)))      # ifft already divides by n

# Output:
# 8.045
# 1.4645046555493249
# 6.452646116071165
# 3.552713678800501e-15


// rust/examples/fourier_fft_background.rs  —  cargo run --example fourier_fft_background
// The circadian gene: fft, amplitude, peak time and the inverse (rustfft).
use rustfft::{num_complex::Complex, FftPlanner};

fn main() {
    let x = [7.81, 8.81, 9.05, 9.98, 9.40, 8.50, 8.15, 7.47, 6.87, 6.41, 7.15, 7.37,
             7.81, 8.09, 9.64, 9.49, 9.29, 9.03, 8.25, 7.43, 6.98, 6.73, 6.72, 6.65];
    let n = x.len();                     // 24 samples, every 2 h, T = 48 h
    let mut planner = FftPlanner::<f64>::new();
    // rustfft works in place on complex numbers: copy x into a complex buffer
    let mut xc: Vec<Complex<f64>> = x.iter().map(|&v| Complex::new(v, 0.0)).collect();
    planner.plan_fft_forward(n).process(&mut xc);   // unnormalised: xc[0] = sum(x)
    println!("{}", xc[0].re / n as f64); // mean
    let k = 2;                           // 2 cycles per 48 h = 24-h period
    println!("{}", 2.0 * xc[k].norm() / n as f64);  // amplitude (index k, 0-based)
    let peak = (-xc[k].arg() / (2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI) * 24.0).rem_euclid(24.0);
    println!("{}", peak);                // peak time (h)
    planner.plan_fft_inverse(n).process(&mut xc);   // inverse, also unnormalised
    let err = (0..n).map(|j| (xc[j].re / n as f64 - x[j]).abs()).fold(0.0, f64::max);
    println!("{:e}", err);
}

// Output:
// 8.045
// 1.464504655549325
// 6.452646116071164
// 3.552713678800501e-15



Rust prints numbers in its own format (e.g. inf rather than Inf); the values are the same unless the text says otherwise.

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
By hand
B1. A DFT of four samples. A gene is measured every 6 h for one day (\(n = 4\), \(T = 24\) h): \(x = (3, 1, 1, 3)\) at \(t = 0, 6, 12, 18\) h. (a) Write down \(F_4\) (use \(w = e^{-2\pi i/4} = -i\)) and compute \(X = F_4x\). (b) Check facts 1 and 3: is \(X_0\) the sum? Is \(X_3 = \overline{X_1}\)? (c) Compute \(a_0, a_1, b_1, a_2\) and write the trigonometric interpolant \(p(t)\). Check that \(p(6) = 1\). (d) What are the amplitude of the 24-h rhythm and the time of its peak? Use fact 5, then check by finding the maximum of \(p\). (e) Use fact 2 to recover \(x_1\) from \(X\).
B2. One FFT step. Same \(x = (3, 1, 1, 3)\). (a) Write down the even samples and the odd samples. Compute their 2-point DFTs \(E\) and \(O\) (for \(n = 2\), \(w = -1\), so the DFT of \((a, b)\) is \((a + b, a - b)\)). (b) Combine them with fact 6 into \(X_0, \dots, X_3\) and compare with B1. (c) Count complex multiplications: the matrix product for \(n = 4\) needs \(n^2 = 16\). How many does the FFT need for \(n = 4\)? (Count only multiplications by \(w^k\) with \(w^k \ne \pm 1\).) (d) Roughly how many operations do the matrix (\(n^2\)) and the FFT (\(n\log_2 n\)) need for \(n = 2^{10}\) and \(n = 2^{20}\)? If a computer does \(10^9\) per second, how long does each take for \(n = 2^{20}\)?
B3. Reading fft output. A gene is sampled every 2 h for 48 h (\(n = 24\)). In R, fft(x)[3] is 0-18i and fft(x)[1] is 192. (a) Which \(k\) is fft(x)[3]? What period? Which index holds it in Python? (b) What are the mean and the amplitude of this rhythm? (c) At what time does it peak? (d) What is fft(x)[23]? Which \(k\) is that? (e) A second gene has fft(x)[3] equal to -18+0i. Same amplitude? When does it peak?
B4. Nyquist and aliasing. (a) Sampling every 4 h: what is the Nyquist frequency, and the shortest period that is resolved? (b) For each true period, 24, 12, 8, 6, 4.8 and 4 h, say whether 4-h sampling resolves it. If not, compute the alias frequency (fact 7) and the period you would report. (c) Repeat (b) for 2-h sampling. (d) An 8-h rhythm sampled every 4 h (exactly at Nyquist): the samples are \(\cos(2\pi(4j - p)/8)\) for a peak at time \(p\). Write the samples for \(p = 0\) and \(p = 2\). What does this tell you about rhythms at exactly the Nyquist frequency? (e) A lab wants to detect 12-h rhythms. What is the largest sampling interval that is (in theory) enough? Why is that not a good design in practice?
B5. Convolution by hand. \(y = (1, 2, 3, 4)\), two-point average \(h = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0, 0)\). (a) Compute the circular convolution \((h * y)_j = \tfrac12(y_j + y_{j-1})\), with \(y_{-1} = y_3\). Which entry is affected by wrap-around? (b) Compute \(Y = F_4y\) and \(H = F_4h\), multiply entrywise, and transform back with fact 2. Do you get (a)? (c) \(|H_k|\) is the gain of the filter at frequency \(k\). What does the two-point average do to \(k = 1\) and to \(k = 2\) (the Nyquist frequency)? (d) Write down the linear convolution of \(y\) with \((\tfrac12, \tfrac12)\) (length 5). How long must you pad \(y\) and \(h\) so that the circular convolution gives it?
B6. Resolution and record length. With a 48-h record, the DFT frequencies are \(k/48\) per hour. (a) Which \(k\) (not necessarily whole) do a 24-h and a 22-h rhythm have? Can a 48-h experiment tell them apart? (b) How long must the record be for the two to land on neighbouring bins, i.e. for \(1/22 - 1/24 \ge 1/T\)? (c) Does sampling every 1 h instead of every 2 h help? Does zero-padding the 48-h record to 480 h help?

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
In code
C1. The DFT as a matrix. (a) Write dft_matrix(n) (fact 2) and check your answer to B1(a). Check that \(\bar F^TF = nI\) for \(n = 4\). (b) For \(n = 256, 512, 1024, 2048\), compare \(Fx\) with fft(x) (Python: np.fft.fft; Rust: rustfft) for a test signal: the largest difference, and the time of each. How does the time grow when \(n\) doubles? (c) The difference grows with \(n\). Which one is less accurate, and why might that be? (Hint: what is \(2\pi jk/n\) for \(j = k = 2047\)?)
C2. Your own FFT. (a) Write the recursive my_fft(x) from fact 6 for \(n\) a power of 2, and check B2 and \(n = 1024\) against the library. (b) Time fft for \(n = 65536\), \(65537\) (a prime) and nextn(65537) (Python: scipy.fft.next_fast_len). Which language suffers from the prime length?
C3. Is the gene circadian? Use the 48-h data from the Background. (a) Print the amplitude for \(k = 0, \dots, 7\) with the period of each. Which period dominates? (b) Fit the cosinor model \(x \approx c_0 + c_1\cos(2\pi t/24) + c_2\sin(2\pi t/24)\) by least squares (lm; Python np.linalg.lstsq; Rust nalgebra). Compare the coefficients with \(a_0, a_2, b_2\) from the FFT. Why are they equal? (c) Write trig_interp (fact 4), check that it passes through the data, and find its maximum on a fine grid. Compare with the largest data point and with the peak from fact 5. Which would you trust, and why?
C4. Aliasing in a sampling design. A gene has a circadian component and a fast ultradian one: \(x(t) = 8 + 1.5\cos(2\pi(t-6)/24) + \cos(2\pi t/4.8)\). (a) Sample it every 2 h and every 4 h over 48 h. For each design report the strongest \(k \ge 1\), and the amplitude and peak time of the 24-h component. Which design gives the true values (1.5 and 6 h)? Explain with B4. (b) For an 8-h rhythm sampled every 4 h, compute the amplitude seen at \(k = 6\) (use \(|X_6|/n\): \(k = n/2\)) for peak times \(p = 0, 1, 2\) h. Compare with B4(d).
C5. Leakage and the Hann window. A free-running clock (constant darkness) has period 25.5 h. A luciferase recording covers 120 h, sampled every 30 min. (a) Compute the amplitude spectrum of \(\cos(2\pi t/25.5)\) without a window and with the Hann window \(w_j = \tfrac12 - \tfrac12\cos(2\pi j/n)\) (amplitude \(= 2|X_k|/\sum_j w_j\) instead of \(2|X_k|/n\)). Print \(k = 1, \dots, 8, 10, 20\). (b) Zero-pad the windowed signal to 10 times its length and locate the peak. What period do you estimate? (c) Add a weak 12-h rhythm of amplitude 0.05 and look at \(k = 10\). Can you see it with and without the window? Compare with the leakage alone at \(k = 10\).
C6. Smoothing a luciferase trace. Simulate \(\text{truth}(t) = 20 + 60e^{-t/40} + 30e^{-t/80}\cos(2\pi(t-4)/24)\) every 30 min for 120 h, plus normal noise with sd 6. (a) Write lowpass(y, kmax): zero every coefficient with \(|k| > k_\text{max}\) (both halves!) and transform back. For \(k_\text{max} = 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 60\) print the root-mean-square error against the truth, over the whole trace and over the first and last 5 h. (b) Repeat with a straight-line trend removed before filtering and added back afterwards. (c) Which \(k_\text{max}\) would you choose? What goes wrong for small and for large \(k_\text{max}\)?
C7. The convolution theorem. (a) Check B5(a)–(b) by computer. (b) Compute the linear convolution of B5(d) by zero-padding and compare with the built-in (convolve(y, rev(h), type = "open"); Python np.convolve). (c) The gain of a moving average of width \(m = 8\) on \(n = 240\) samples (30 min apart) is \(|H_k|\). Print it for \(k = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 45, 50, 60\). Which periods are removed completely? Is a moving average a good low-pass filter?

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — DFT by hand (B1, B2, B5)





Powers of \(w = -i\): \(w^0 = 1\), \(w^1 = -i\), \(w^2 = -1\), \(w^3 = i\), \(w^4 = 1\), so \(F_{jk} = (-i)^{jk \bmod 4}\). Multiply out row by row; \(i \cdot i = -1\). For the inverse use \(w^{-1} = i\) and divide by 4. In B2, the 2-point DFTs need no multiplication at all, and the only twiddle factors for \(n = 4\) are \(w^0 = 1\) and \(w^1 = -i\).









Hint 2 — reading fft output (B3, C3)





\(k\) = index − 1 in R. Period \(= T/k\). Amplitude \(2|X_k|/n\); \(|a + bi| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\). \(\arg(-18i) = -\pi/2\), \(\arg(-18) = \pi\). The peak time is \(\theta/(2\pi)\) of a period, with \(\theta = -\arg X_k\); add a period if it is negative. In R: Mod, Arg, Re, Im, Conj; Python: np.abs, np.angle, .real, .imag, .conj(); Rust: z.norm(), z.arg(), z.re, z.im, z.conj() (from rustfft::num_complex).









Hint 3 — aliasing (B4, C4)





Work in cycles per hour. Sampling every 4 h: \(f_s = 1/\Delta t = 0.25\), \(f_N = 0.125\). A 6-h rhythm has \(f = 0.1667 > f_N\); subtract \(f_s\): \(|0.1667 - 0.25| = 0.0833\), i.e. period 12 h. If the result is still above \(f_N\), subtract \(f_s\) again.









Hint 4 — the DFT matrix and timing (C1, C2)





R: outer(j, j) gives all products \(jk\), and exp(-2i * pi * outer(j, j) / n) the matrix; system.time times an expression. Python: np.outer, time.perf_counter(). Rust: std::time::Instant; plan once with FftPlanner, then process a Vec<Complex<f64>> in place. For the recursion, x[seq(1, n, by = 2)] in R and x[0::2] in Python are the even samples.









Hint 5 — windows and zero-padding (C5)





Multiply the signal by the window before the FFT. R: pad with c(w * y, rep(0, N - n)); Python: np.fft.fft(w * y, N) pads for you; Rust: Vec::resize(N, 0.0). In the padded transform, index \(k\) means \(k\) cycles per padded length (\(N\Delta t\) = 1200 h).









Hint 6 — filtering (C6, C7)





The signed frequency of each entry is c(0:(n/2), -(n/2 - 1):-1) in R and np.fft.fftfreq(n, d=1/n) in Python; in Rust entry \(k > n/2\) has frequency \(n - k\). Take Re() / .real after the inverse. A straight-line trend: fitted(lm(y ~ t)) in R, np.polyval(np.polyfit(t, y, 1), t) in Python. R’s stats::filter computes moving averages directly.

title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
Where this leads

Numerical differentiation (Part 7): differentiating a sampled signal multiplies \(X_k\) by \(2\pi i k/T\), so it amplifies high-frequency noise; finite differences have the same problem, and smoothing first (C6) is a common remedy.
Numerical integration (Part 7): the trapezoid rule of that unit is, for smooth periodic functions over a whole period, far more accurate than its usual \(O(h^2)\), for the same reason trigonometric interpolation works well here.
The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences (Part 10): each Fourier mode of a concentration profile decays at its own rate, and the stability limit of the explicit scheme is decided by the fastest (Nyquist) mode.
Deconvolution (the blur slide) is the ill-conditioned problem of The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation (Part 4) in another basis: dividing by small \(|H_k|\) is dividing by small singular values.

title: Quiz: random numbers and Monte Carlo
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of random numbers and Monte Carlo. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. You run set.seed(42); runif(3) in R and np.random.default_rng(42).random(3) in Python. Do you get the same three numbers? Is that a problem for reproducibility?






Hint





Which generator does each language use by default?









Answer





No. R uses the Mersenne Twister, numpy’s default_rng uses PCG64 (and Rust’s StdRng uses ChaCha12), so the same seed gives different streams (R 0.915, 0.937, 0.286; numpy 0.774, 0.439, 0.859). Reproducibility means the same code, software and seed give the same numbers; it does not extend across languages. Results from different languages should agree within their Monte Carlo error bars, not digit by digit.




Q2. A colleague’s function simulate_once() starts with set.seed(1). They call it 1000 times in a loop and average the results. What goes wrong?






Hint





What does the generator produce right after set.seed(1)?









Answer





Every call restarts the stream at the same point, so all 1000 “replicates” use the same random numbers and give the identical result. The average is one simulation, and the sample sd is 0, so the standard error claims perfect precision. Set the seed once, at the top of the script.




Q3. What does this code print?

RPythonRust


x <- 0
for (i in 1:9) {
  cat(x, "")
  x <- (5 * x + 1) %% 8
}


x = 0
for i in range(9):
    print(x, end=" ")
    x = (5 * x + 1) % 8


// rust/examples/monte_carlo_q3.rs  —  cargo run --example monte_carlo_q3
// Q3: a tiny LCG, x_{n+1} = (5 x_n + 1) mod 8, seed 0.
fn main() {
    let mut x: u64 = 0;
    for _ in 0..9 {
        print!("{} ", x);
        x = (5 * x + 1) % 8;
    }
    println!();
}









Hint





Do the first few steps by hand: \(5 \cdot 0 + 1 = 1\), \(5 \cdot 1 + 1 = 6\), …









Answer





0 1 6 7 4 5 2 3 0. The sequence visits all 8 values and then repeats (period 8): a full-period linear congruential generator. It is completely deterministic, and its last bit alternates 0, 1, 0, 1, which is one of the reasons tiny LCGs are bad generators.




Q4. A density on \([0, 1]\) is \(f(x) = 2x\). Give a formula that turns a uniform number \(U\) into a draw from \(f\). What draw do you get for \(U = 0.25\)?






Hint





Find the CDF \(F(x)\), set \(U = F(x)\) and solve for \(x\).









Answer





\(F(x) = x^2\), so \(X = F^{-1}(U) = \sqrt U\). For \(U = 0.25\): \(X = 0.5\). This is inverse-transform sampling. (Check: \(P(X \le 0.5) = P(U \le 0.25) = 0.25 = F(0.5)\).)




Q5. A rejection sampler uses a uniform proposal and \(M = 20\). About how many proposals do you need for 1000 accepted draws? What happens if \(M\) is chosen smaller than \(\max f\)?






Hint





The acceptance rate is \(1/M\).









Answer





About \(1000 \cdot 20 = 20\,000\) proposals (acceptance rate 5%). If \(M < \max f\), the proposals near the peak are all accepted but should have been accepted more often than possible, so the peak is cut off and the samples come from the wrong distribution, without any error or warning. A large \(M\) is only wasteful; a too small \(M\) is wrong.




Q6. A Monte Carlo estimate with \(N = 10^4\) draws has a standard error of 0.02. How many draws do you need for an SE of 0.002? How would the answer change for a 1-D trapezoid rule, whose error falls like \(N^{-2}\)?






Hint





SE \(= s/\sqrt N\).









Answer





To make the SE 10 times smaller you need \(10^2 = 100\) times more draws: \(N = 10^6\). For the trapezoid rule, 10 times smaller error needs only \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) times more points. Monte Carlo is slow; its strengths are a free error bar and an error rate that does not depend on the dimension.




Q7. Why does Monte Carlo beat a grid rule for a 10-dimensional integral but not for a 1-dimensional one?






Hint





With \(N\) points in \(d\) dimensions, how many grid points are there per axis?









Answer





A grid with \(N\) points has only \(N^{1/d}\) points per axis, so a rule of order \(p\) has error \(\approx N^{-p/d}\). For \(d = 1\) the trapezoid rule gives \(N^{-2}\), far better than Monte Carlo’s \(N^{-1/2}\). For \(d = 10\) the same rule gives \(N^{-0.2}\) (and \(10^6\) points are only 3–4 per axis), while Monte Carlo still gives \(N^{-1/2}\). The rates break even at \(d = 2p\), so \(d = 4\) for the trapezoid rule. This is the curse of dimensionality.




Q8. You test whether ChIP-seq peaks are enriched in promoters by shuffling the peaks 1000 times. None of the 1000 shuffles has as many overlaps as the real data. What p-value do you report?






Hint





Is “0 out of 1000” the same as “probability 0”?









Answer





Not \(p = 0\). Report \((k + 1)/(B + 1) = 1/1001 \approx 0.001\), or say \(p < 0.001\). The data could still arise under the null with a probability below \(1/1000\); 1000 shuffles cannot resolve it. For a precise small p-value you need about \(100/p\) shuffles, or importance sampling.




Q9. Plain Monte Carlo with \(10^5\) standard normal draws estimates \(P(X > 5)\) as exactly 0 with standard error 0. What is wrong, and what is the fix?






Hint





\(P(X > 5) = 2.9 \times 10^{-7}\). How many draws above 5 do you expect?









Answer





You expect \(10^5 \cdot 2.9\times10^{-7} = 0.03\) draws above 5, so you almost always see none, and both the estimate and its SE are 0: a confident wrong answer. The SE formula is only meaningful when there are enough hits (about 100 for 10% error). Fix: importance sampling, drawing from a proposal such as \(N(5, 1)\) that puts half its draws above 5, and weighting each by \(\phi(x)/\phi(x - 5)\).




Q10. Which of these integrals can be estimated by plain Monte Carlo with a trustworthy standard error: \(\int_0^1 x^{-0.4}\,dx\) or \(\int_0^1 x^{-0.6}\,dx\)? Both are finite.






Hint





The SE needs a finite variance, i.e. a finite \(\int_0^1 f(x)^2\,dx\).









Answer





\(\int_0^1 x^{-0.8}\,dx = 5\) is finite, but \(\int_0^1 x^{-1.2}\,dx = \infty\). So \(x^{-0.4}\) has finite variance and a reliable SE; \(x^{-0.6}\) has infinite variance: its estimate converges, but slowly and in jumps, and the reported SE is usually too small. Check by plotting the running estimate and by repeating with several seeds.




Q11. An importance sampler reports an estimate with a small standard error, but the effective sample size is 40 out of 100 000 draws. Should you trust the estimate? What is the likely cause?






Hint





\(\text{ESS} = (\sum w)^2 / \sum w^2\). When is it small?









Answer





No. An ESS of 40 means a handful of draws carry almost all the weight, so the estimate rests on a few points, and the SE (computed from the same few large weights) is unreliable. The usual cause is a proposal with lighter tails than the target, or one centred in the wrong place: the rare draws in the region the proposal neglects get enormous weights. Use a wider proposal (heavier tails) and check the ESS again.

title: Exercise: numerical differentiation
text:
Explore
The demo below differentiates the plate-reader data of C4 (the same 61 values) in your browser, with one of three estimators of half-width \(k\) samples (\(h = k \cdot 10\) min): the central difference \((y_{i+k} - y_{i-k})/(2k\,\Delta t)\) (\(k = 1\) is the difference of neighbours), the local line of C5 (least-squares slope over the \(2k+1\) points) and Richardson \(\tfrac{4D(h) - D(2h)}{3}\) of two central differences. Panel (a) shows the data, the points the estimator uses at the selected time and the slope it finds; click or drag in (a) or (b) to move the selected time. Panel (b) compares the estimated growth rate with the true \(N'(t) = rN(1 - N/K)\), with the neighbour differences in grey. Panel (c) shows the rms error against \(h\) for every \(k\) from 1 to 12: the measured error (strong; the other two estimators faint), the noise model \(\sigma\sqrt{\sum_j w_j^2}\) for the estimator’s weights \(w_j\) (dashed) and the truncation error, the same estimator applied to the exact OD values (dotted). The switch exact OD replaces the data by the noise-free curve. As in C4, the rms error is taken over the time points where the stencil fits, and the readout says how many are lost at each end.



E1. (neighbours: noise wins) Click neighbours. Read the rms error, the predicted noise sd and the truncation rms, and the maximum growth rate. Then switch to exact OD. How much of the error of the neighbour differences is truncation? Where in panel (b) are the estimates least useful, relative to the growth rate itself?






Answer E1





rms error \(0.0203\) OD/h, noise sd \(0.021\) (B6(a)), truncation rms \(1.5\times10^{-4}\): the noise is more than 100 times the truncation error, so with exact OD values the same formula is almost perfect (rms \(1.5\times10^{-4}\), the curve in (b) lies on the truth). With the measurements the maximum is \(0.270\) at \(4.00\) h, 13 % above the true \(0.240\): the maximum of noisy estimates is biased upwards, because it picks the largest noise. The noise sd is the same everywhere, but in the first half hour the true rate is only \(0.04\)–\(0.05\) OD/h and after 8 h below \(0.035\) OD/h, so there the noise (\(0.021\)) is half the signal or more, and some estimates are even negative (\(-0.033\) in the stationary phase).



E2. (the V with noise) Stay with central on the plate-reader data and drag \(k\) from 1 to 12. Follow the marker in panel (c), and the dashed and dotted lines. At which \(k\) is the rms error smallest, and where do the noise model and the truncation cross? What happens to the peak in panel (b), and to the ends, at \(k = 12\)?






Answer E2





The error falls from \(0.0203\) (\(k = 1\)) to \(0.0092\), \(0.0065\) and a minimum of \(0.0053\) at \(k = 4\) (40 min), then rises again: \(0.0058\), \(0.0069\), …, \(0.023\) at \(k = 12\). The noise model falls like \(1/h\) (\(0.0053\) at \(k = 4\), \(0.0042\) at \(k = 5\)), the truncation rises like \(h^2\) (\(0.0025\) at \(k = 4\), \(0.0040\) at \(k = 5\)); they cross near \(k = 5\), and the measured minimum sits just before the crossing, as in B4(c). At \(k = 12\) the curve in (b) is smooth but too flat: the maximum is \(0.201\) OD/h instead of \(0.240\), and 12 points (2 h) are lost at each end, so the whole lag phase has no estimate. This is the V of Convergence and cost with the noise \(\sigma\) in the place of \(\varepsilon|N|\), and the best step is 40 minutes instead of \(10^{-8}\).



E3. (use all the points) Click local line k = 4 and compare its rms error, noise sd and truncation rms with those of central k = 4 (shown in the readout). Then vary \(k\): which \(k\) is best for the local line? Why does it have less noise at the same half-width?






Answer E3





Local line, \(k = 4\): rms \(0.00405\), noise sd \(0.0039\), truncation \(0.0019\); central, \(k = 4\): \(0.00528\), \(0.0053\), \(0.0025\). The local line is better on both counts. \(k = 4\) and \(k = 5\) tie at \(0.00405\) (\(k = 6\): \(0.0047\)). The central difference uses only the two outermost of the 9 points in the window; the least-squares slope uses all of them (panel (a) highlights 8 points with non-zero weight), so it averages more noise: its noise sd is \(\sigma / (\Delta t \sqrt{\sum j^2}) = 0.005 \cdot 6/\sqrt{60} = 0.0039\) instead of \(\sigma/(\sqrt2\, h) = 0.0053\). Maximum \(0.234\) at \(4.33\) h, as in C5.



E4. (Richardson and noise) Click Richardson and exact OD with \(k = 1\). Compare its rms error with the central difference at the same \(k\) (readout). How many digits does the extrapolation gain? Now switch back to the plate-reader data (or click Richardson k = 1). What happens, and why? Finally, find the \(k\) at which Richardson does best on the measured data, and read off which time span it covers.






Answer E4





Exact OD: \(1.0\times10^{-6}\) against \(1.54\times10^{-4}\) for the central difference, a factor 150, about two digits gained; the dotted line in (c) is much steeper (slope 4 instead of 2). On the measured data the rms error rises to \(0.0269\) (central: \(0.0203\)), and the maximum is \(0.281\): the noise sd grows from \(0.021\) to \(0.029\), since the weights \(\tfrac43\) and \(-\tfrac13\) amplify the noise of both differences (B5(c)), and the truncation it removes was negligible anyway. Richardson is best at \(k = 5\)–\(7\) (rms \(0.0044\), \(0.0043\), \(0.0042\)), no better than the local line at \(k = 4\), and at \(k = 7\) it needs 14 points on each side: estimates only from 2.33 h to 7.67 h. With noisy data, extrapolation spends its effort on the wrong error.

title: Quiz: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of the DFT and the FFT. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In R, x <- c(2, 4, 6, 8). What is fft(x)[1], and how do you get the mean of x from it?






Hint





Put \(k = 0\) in \(X_k = \sum_j x_j e^{-2\pi i jk/n}\).









Answer





20+0i, the sum of the samples (every \(e^0 = 1\)). R’s fft is unnormalised, so the mean is Re(fft(x)[1]) / length(x) \(= 5\). The same holds for np.fft.fft(x)[0] in Python.




Q2. A gene is sampled every hour for 72 h (\(n = 72\)). At which R index of fft(x) do you find the 24-h rhythm? At which Python index? And what period does R index 2 correspond to?






Hint





\(k\) counts cycles per record. R adds 1 to every index.









Answer





A 24-h rhythm makes \(k = 72/24 = 3\) cycles in 72 h: R index 4, Python index 3. R index 2 is \(k = 1\): one cycle per record, period 72 h.




Q3. Why is the FFT faster than multiplying by the DFT matrix, and by roughly what factor for \(n = 2^{20}\)?






Hint





Split the samples into even and odd ones. How many times can you halve \(2^{20}\)?









Answer





The DFT of length \(n\) is two DFTs of length \(n/2\) (even and odd samples) combined with \(n\) operations: \(X_k = E_k + w^kO_k\), \(X_{k+n/2} = E_k - w^kO_k\). Repeating gives \(\log_2 n\) levels of \(n\) operations: \(n\log_2 n\) instead of \(n^2\). For \(n = 2^{20}\) the ratio is \(n/\log_2 n = 2^{20}/20 \approx 50\,000\).




Q4. You sample every 3 h. What is the Nyquist frequency, and what is the shortest period you can resolve?






Hint





The fastest wave on the grid goes up and down in two samples.









Answer





\(f_N = 1/(2\cdot3) = 1/6\) cycles per hour: periods down to 6 h. A 6-h rhythm itself sits exactly at Nyquist, and its visible amplitude depends on its phase; in practice sample clearly faster than that.




Q5. A rhythm with a 5-h period is sampled every 4 h. What period will the FFT report?






Hint





Frequencies in cycles per hour: \(f = 0.2\), \(f_s = 0.25\). Fold \(f\) back into \([0, f_s/2]\).









Answer





\(f = 0.2 > f_N = 0.125\), so it is aliased to \(|0.2 - 0.25| = 0.05\) cycles per hour: a 20-h period. The samples are identical to those of a 20-h rhythm; no analysis of these samples can tell the difference.




Q6. A colleague recorded a free-running clock with period 25.5 h for 5 days. Its spectrum has a peak near 24 h and a raised “floor” at all other frequencies. What causes the floor, and what can she do about it?






Hint





How many cycles of 25.5 h fit into 120 h? What does the DFT assume about the signal outside the record?









Answer





Leakage. 120/25.5 = 4.7 cycles, not a whole number. The DFT treats the record as one period of a periodic signal, so there is a jump where the end wraps to the start, and a jump has energy at all frequencies. Multiply by a window (Hann) that tapers both ends to zero before the FFT: the floor drops by orders of magnitude and the peak becomes a little wider. Zero-padding then helps to locate the peak (about 25.5 h) on a finer grid.




Q7. To low-pass filter a trace, a student sets Y[(kmax + 2):n] <- 0 in R and transforms back. The result has a large imaginary part, and its real part is too small. What went wrong?






Hint





Which frequencies live in the second half of fft(y)?









Answer





The second half of fft(y) holds the negative frequencies \(-k\), the mirror images of the low ones (X[n + 2 - m] = Conj(X[m])). Zeroing them removes half of every low-frequency cosine, which leaves complex exponentials: a complex result with half the amplitude. Zero only entries with \(|k| > k_\text{max}\), i.e. both the high positive and the high negative frequencies, keeping the pairs intact.




Q8. You smooth a 5-day luciferase trace with a moving average computed via the FFT (fft(y) * fft(h), transform back). The middle looks fine but the first few points are pulled towards the values at the end of the trace. Why, and how do you fix it?






Hint





What kind of convolution does a product of DFTs give?









Answer





A product of DFTs is a circular convolution: the average at the first points includes samples from the end of the record (wrap-around). Pad \(y\) and \(h\) with zeros to length at least \(n + m - 1\) to get the ordinary (linear) convolution, and then decide how to treat the edges (fewer points, mirror the data, or drop them). Removing a trend first also helps, because the start and end values then agree better.




Q9. What does this print, and what is the amplitude of the cosine?

RPythonRust


x <- c(1, 0, -1, 0)
fft(x)
2 * Mod(fft(x)[2]) / 4

# Output:
# [1] 0+0i 2+0i 0+0i 2+0i
# [1] 1


import numpy as np

x = np.array([1.0, 0, -1, 0])
print(np.fft.fft(x))
print(2 * abs(np.fft.fft(x)[1]) / 4)

# Output:
# [0.+0.j 2.+0.j 0.+0.j 2.+0.j]
# 1.0


// rust/examples/fourier_fft_q9.rs  —  cargo run --example fourier_fft_q9
// Quiz: fft of one cycle of a cosine sampled 4 times.
use rustfft::{num_complex::Complex, FftPlanner};

fn main() {
    let mut x: Vec<Complex<f64>> = [1.0, 0.0, -1.0, 0.0].iter().map(|&v| Complex::new(v, 0.0)).collect();
    FftPlanner::<f64>::new().plan_fft_forward(4).process(&mut x);
    let s: Vec<String> = x.iter().map(|z| format!("{}{:+}i", z.re + 0.0, z.im + 0.0)).collect();
    println!("{}", s.join(" "));
    println!("{}", 2.0 * x[1].norm() / 4.0);
}

// Output:
// 0+0i 2+0i 0+0i 2+0i
// 1









Hint





\(x = (1, 0, -1, 0)\) is \(\cos(2\pi j/4)\): one cycle in four samples.









Answer





\(X = (0, 2, 0, 2)\): a cosine with \(k = 1\) appears at \(k = 1\) and at its mirror \(k = 3 \equiv -1\), each with \(nA/2 = 2\), and the phase is 0 (real, positive). The amplitude is \(2|X_1|/n = 1\). The mean (\(X_0\)) is 0.




Q10. In R, fft takes 0.003 s for \(n = 65536\) but over 4 s for \(n = 65537\). Why, and what is the quick fix?






Hint





Factor 65537.









Answer





65537 is prime. R’s mixed-radix FFT splits \(n\) into its prime factors; a factor \(p\) costs about \(np\) operations, so a prime \(n\) costs \(O(n^2)\). Pad with zeros to nextn(n) (here 65610 \(= 2\cdot3^8\cdot5\)) or trim the series to a length with only small factors. numpy/scipy and rustfft use Bluestein’s algorithm for primes and stay \(O(n\log n)\).




Q11. Does zero-padding a 48-h time course to 480 h let you separate a 24-h from a 22-h rhythm?






Hint





Padding adds zeros, not data. What sets the width of a peak?









Answer





No. Zero-padding evaluates the same spectrum on a 10× finer frequency grid, but each peak keeps its width of about \(1/T = 1/48\) cycles per hour. The two rhythms differ by \(1/22 - 1/24 = 1/264\), much less than that, so their peaks merge. Only a longer record (at least about 264 h) separates them.




Q12. Deblurring a microscope image by dividing fft(image) by fft(psf) gives pure noise. Why? What is the connection with the SVD?






Hint





How large is the Fourier transform of a Gaussian PSF at high frequencies?









Answer





The transform of a smooth PSF is tiny at high frequencies (around \(10^{-18}\) for a Gaussian of 2 pixels on a 128-pixel image). Dividing amplifies the measurement noise at those frequencies by the inverse of that. Blur is a linear map whose singular values are the \(|H_k|\) (the Fourier modes are its singular vectors), so this is the same problem as small singular values in least squares (The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation): regularise (Wiener filter = ridge in frequency space, or truncate high frequencies).

title: Exercise: power iteration and friends
text:
Explore
The demo below runs power iteration in your browser on the matrices of this unit: the 2 × 2 plants of the lecture and of B1–B3, a symmetric 2 × 2, the fish Leslie matrix, its semelparous variant, and the cell-state chain (as \(P^T\), so that the iteration is \(\mathbf x \leftarrow P^T\mathbf x\)). Panel (a) shows the current vector \(\mathbf x_k\): for a 2 × 2 matrix as a direction in the plane, with the two eigen-directions dashed (\(\mathbf v_1\) blue, \(\mathbf v_2\) red), the earlier iterates faded and \(A\mathbf x_k\) in green (drag the circle to move the start \(\mathbf x_0\)); for larger matrices as bars, with the eigenvector dashed. Panel (b) shows the error in \(\mathbf x_k\) and in the eigenvalue estimate against \(k\) on a log scale, with the predicted line \(C\,|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|^k\) (dashed). Nonnegative matrices are normalised by the sum (proportions, estimate = growth of the total), others by the 2-norm (estimate = Rayleigh quotient). Inverse iteration switches to \((A - \sigma I)^{-1}\); the \(\sigma\) buttons set useful shifts. The readout lists the eigenvalues, the predicted rate, the steps per digit, the measured rate over the last five steps and the residual.



E1. (swinging towards \(\mathbf v_1\)) With the lecture’s plant \(\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0.75 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) and the start “class 1”, click step +1 four times. Write down the eigenvalue estimate and the error in \(\mathbf x\) at each step, and watch where \(\mathbf x_k\) lies relative to the blue line. By what factor does the error fall per step, and why does \(\mathbf x_k\) land on alternate sides of \(\mathbf v_1\)? At which \(k\) does the error first drop below \(10^{-10}\)?






Answer E1





The estimates are \(1.75\), \(1.4286\), \(1.525\), \(1.4918\): the lecture’s table. The error in the proportions goes \(0.33\) (\(k = 0\)), \(0.095\), \(0.033\), \(0.011\), \(0.0037\): divided by 3 each step, and the measured rate settles at \(0.333 = |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| = 0.5/1.5\). The proportion of class 1 alternates around \(2/3\) (\(0.571\), \(0.700\), \(0.656\), \(0.670\)), so \(\mathbf x_k\) falls on one side of \(\mathbf v_1\), then the other: the \(\mathbf v_2\) part is multiplied by \(\lambda_2 = -0.5\) each step and changes sign. The readout predicts 2.1 steps per digit; the error is below \(10^{-10}\) at \(k = 20\), and the marker lies on the dashed line the whole way.



E2. (the rate decides) Read the predicted rate and the steps per digit for plant B1, early flowering and biennial. Predict for each how many steps it takes to reach an error of \(10^{-10}\), then move the \(k\) slider to find out. What happens for the biennial plant, and what does the eigenvalue estimate do?






Answer E2





Plant B1: rate \(0.6/1.2 = 0.5\), 3.3 steps per digit, so about 33 steps; the error first drops below \(10^{-10}\) at \(k = 33\). Early flowering: rate \(0.8198/1.2198 = 0.672\), 5.8 steps per digit, so about 58; it takes 55 (the constant \(C\) in front of \(0.672^k\) is below 1 here). Biennial: \(\lambda = \pm 1\), rate \(1.00\), and the readout warns that two eigenvalues share the largest modulus. The proportions jump between \((1, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\), the error stays at \(0.80\) and \(0.20\) forever, and the estimate alternates \(0.25\), \(4\), \(0.25\), \(4\): the population grows by \(0.25 \times 4 = 1\) per two years, as in B3, and there is no stable stage distribution to find.



E3. (the fish, and a fish that spawns once) Choose fish (start: age 1) and go to \(k = 20\), then \(k = 40\). Compare the bars with the dashed stable age distribution and the measured rate with \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|\). Why does the error curve wiggle? Then choose semelparous fish, press play, and describe what the bars and the estimate do. Does the start “equal” help?






Answer E3





At \(k = 20\) the bars read \(0.694\), \(0.177\), \(0.090\), \(0.038\), on top of the dashed outlines; the estimate is \(1.1771512\) (true \(1.1773586\)), the error in \(\mathbf x\) is \(5.8\times10^{-5}\) and the measured rate \(0.651\) (at \(k = 40\): \(9.5\times10^{-9}\) and \(0.652\)), close to \(|\lambda_2/\lambda_1| = 0.7699/1.177 = 0.654\) (5.4 steps per digit). The second eigenvalues are the complex pair \(-0.2663 \pm 0.7224i\), so the \(\mathbf v_2\) part rotates as it shrinks: the error wiggles under the dashed line, like the transient oscillation of the age structure. Semelparous fish: all fish sit in one age class, which moves one class per step (age 2, age 3, age 0, age 1, …); the estimate cycles \(0.6\), \(0.5\), \(12\), \(0.3\), the error stays between \(0.36\) and \(0.95\), the residual does not fall, and the readout says that four eigenvalues share the largest modulus \(1.0194\). The start “equal” does not help: after four steps \(\mathbf x_4 = (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25)\) again, because \(L^4 = 1.08\,I\), and the error stays at \(0.39\).



E4. (shift and invert) Choose cell states \(P^T\). With power iteration, read the rate and the error at \(k = 60\). Then switch to inverse iteration and try \(\sigma = 1\), \(0.82\), \(0.77\) and \(0.9\). For each: which eigenvalue is found, at what predicted rate, and after how many steps is the error below \(10^{-10}\)?






Answer E4





Power iteration: rate \(0.8\), 10.3 steps per digit; after 60 steps the error is still \(3.8\times10^{-7}\). \(\sigma = 1\): the shift is the eigenvalue itself; the readout warns that \(A - \sigma I\) is singular to working precision, yet one step gives \((0.200, 0.550, 0.250)\) with error \(10^{-16}\). \(\sigma = 0.82\): finds \(\lambda = 0.8\) with eigenvector \((0, 0.707, -0.707)\) (the B–L exchange), rate \(0.02/0.07 = 0.286\), error below \(10^{-10}\) at \(k = 20\). \(\sigma = 0.77\): finds \(0.75\), not \(0.8\), because \(0.75\) is nearer; rate \(0.02/0.03 = 0.667\), 54 steps. \(\sigma = 0.9\) lies exactly halfway between \(0.8\) and \(1\): rate \(1\), no single nearest eigenvalue, and the residual stays at \(0.062\). These are the lecture’s 21 and 58 iterations (counted there by a residual below \(10^{-12}\)).



E5. (complex eigenvalues) Choose the lecture’s plant again and set \(a_{21}\) to \(-0.75\) with its slider. What happens to the eigenvalues, to the dashed lines in panel (a), and to \(\mathbf x_k\) as you step?






Answer E5





The characteristic polynomial becomes \(\lambda^2 - \lambda + 0.75\), with eigenvalues \(0.5 \pm 0.7071i\): there are no real eigen-directions, so the dashed lines disappear. Both eigenvalues have the same modulus, so none dominates: \(\mathbf x_k\) keeps turning around the circle (on average by about 55° per step, the angle of \(0.5 + 0.7071i\)), the residual does not fall (still \(0.98\) at \(k = 60\)) and the readout says that the largest eigenvalues are a complex pair. A real matrix with a complex dominant pair cannot be handled by real power iteration at all; for nonnegative population matrices this cannot happen, because a nonnegative matrix always has a real, positive eigenvalue of largest modulus (Perron–Frobenius; it may still share that modulus with others, as for the semelparous fish).

Try it: power iteration

title: Exercise: how eigen() works, and big problems
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

do one step of the QR algorithm by hand and explain why it keeps the eigenvalues,
relate the speed of the QR algorithm to ratios of eigenvalues, recognise when it stalls, and show how a shift fixes that,
explain why a real nonsymmetric matrix can have complex eigenvalues and what they mean for a biological model,
show that eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric matrix can be very sensitive, and run the two checks: the condition number of the eigenvector matrix, and perturb-and-recompute,
write a short Lanczos iteration, see its Ritz values converge, and see ghost eigenvalues appear without reorthogonalisation,
compute the top principal components of a large sparse single-cell matrix without densifying or centring it, and check the result with residuals.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator for square roots. The code part checks your hand answers and then works at sizes where only code works. C6 and C7 build a 20 000 × 2 000 matrix: they need about 2 GB of memory and run for under a minute.
