title: Quiz: equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of nullclines, linearisation, eigenvalues and limit cycles. The toggle switch is \(\dot u = \dfrac{3}{1+v^2} - u\), \(\dot v = \dfrac{3}{1+u^2} - v\), with steady states U on \((2.618, 0.382)\), middle \((1.213, 1.213)\) and V on \((0.382, 2.618)\). Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A population follows \(\dot N = f(N)\) with a fixed point at \(N^* = 5\) and \(f'(5) = -0.2\) per day. Is \(N^*\) stable? Roughly how long does a small perturbation take to halve?






Hint





Near \(N^*\), \(\delta(t) \approx \delta_0 e^{f'(N^*)t}\).









Answer





Stable, because \(f'(5) < 0\). The perturbation halves when \(e^{-0.2t} = 1/2\), i.e. after \(\ln 2/0.2 \approx 3.5\) days.




Q2. On the u-nullcline of the toggle switch, in which direction does the flow point, and why?






Hint





What is \(du/dt\) on the u-nullcline?









Answer





Vertically (straight up or down): on the u-nullcline \(du/dt = 0\), so only \(v\) changes. Whether it is up or down depends on the sign of \(dv/dt\) there, i.e. on which side of the v-nullcline the point lies.




Q3. A Jacobian at a fixed point has trace \(\tau = 1\) and determinant \(\Delta = -2\). Classify the fixed point without computing the eigenvalues.






Hint





\(\Delta\) is the product of the two eigenvalues.









Answer





A saddle (unstable): a negative product means one positive and one negative real eigenvalue. The trace does not matter. (They are \(2\) and \(-1\).)




Q4. At the “U on” state the eigenvalues of \(J\) are \(-5/3\) and \(-1/3\). Which one decides how long the cell takes to recover from a small push, and how long is that roughly?






Hint





Each eigen-component decays like \(e^{\lambda t}\). Which one is still there after a while?









Answer





The eigenvalue closest to zero, \(-1/3\): the \(e^{-5t/3}\) part is gone quickly, and what remains decays like \(e^{-t/3}\), a time constant of 3 protein lifetimes (half-life \(3\ln 2 \approx 2.1\)). The eigenvalue largest in size (\(-5/3\)) is the less important one.




Q5. Newton found the middle state of the toggle switch from 57 % of starts in \([0, 4]^2\). Why does no cell ever sit there, and what number shows it?






Hint





Newton finds roots of \(\mathbf F\); stability is a property of \(J\) at the root.









Answer





The middle state is a saddle: \(J\) there has eigenvalues \(0.19\) and \(-2.19\). The positive one means a small imbalance between U and V (direction \((1, -1)\)) grows like \(e^{0.19t}\), so molecular noise always pushes a cell off it. Newton does not care about stability: it converges to unstable roots as happily as to stable ones.




Q6. You want the stability of a steady state of a 10 000-gene model. You run 100 steps of power iteration on its Jacobian and get \(\lambda = -4.2\). Can you conclude the state is stable?






Hint





Which eigenvalue does power iteration find, and which one decides stability?









Answer





No. Power iteration finds the eigenvalue of largest modulus; stability depends on the eigenvalue with the largest real part. Another eigenvalue could be \(+0.01\). Shift first (\(J + cI\) with \(c\) large enough that the rightmost eigenvalue becomes the largest), or use an Arnoldi-type routine that asks for the largest real part (RSpectra::eigs(J, k = 1, which = "LR"), scipy.sparse.linalg.eigs(J, k=1, which="LR")).




Q7. Why is the separatrix computed by integrating backwards in time from next to the saddle, rather than forwards?






Hint





What do the eigenvalues of \(-J\) look like?









Answer





The separatrix is the saddle’s stable manifold: forwards in time, points on it approach the saddle, and any small error is amplified by the unstable eigenvalue, so a forward run cannot stay on it. Backwards in time the eigenvalues change sign, the stable direction becomes repelling, and a start \(10^{-6}\) away along \(\mathbf v_{\text{stable}}\) runs out along the separatrix.




Q8. A student simulates the symmetric toggle switch from \(u_0 = v_0 = 2\) to \(t = 100\), finds \((1.213412, 1.213412)\), and reports it as “the steady state the cell reaches”. What went wrong, and what check would have caught it?






Hint





Where does a start with \(u_0 = v_0\) go in a symmetric model?









Answer





The diagonal \(u = v\) is invariant and is exactly the separatrix, so the run converges to the saddle, which no real cell can sit at. Checks: compute the eigenvalues of \(J\) at the end point (one is \(+0.19\)); or restart from a slightly perturbed end point, e.g. \((1.2134, 1.2135)\), and see it leave.




Q9. In the Sel’kov model the fixed point has eigenvalues \(0.098 \pm 0.656i\). What do the real and the imaginary part tell you, and why does \(u\) not grow for ever?






Hint





\(e^{(a + ib)t} = e^{at}(\cos bt + i \sin bt)\).









Answer





Real part \(> 0\): small perturbations grow (unstable spiral). Imaginary part: they rotate with angular frequency \(0.656\), a period of about \(2\pi/0.656 \approx 9.6\) near the fixed point. The linearisation only holds close to the fixed point; further out the nonlinear terms (substrate depletion) stop the growth, and trajectories settle on a limit cycle (period 9.62).




Q10. A computed eigenvalue at a steady state is \(\lambda_{\max} = -3\times10^{-9}\), from a finite-difference Jacobian. Is the state stable?






Hint





How accurate is a forward-difference Jacobian?









Answer





You cannot tell. A forward-difference Jacobian has errors of about \(\sqrt\varepsilon \approx 10^{-8}\), larger than \(|\lambda_{\max}|\), so even the sign is not reliable. This happens at a bifurcation (the toggle at \(\alpha = 2\), where the true value is 0). Use an exact Jacobian; if \(\lambda_{\max}\) is still \(\approx 0\), linearisation cannot decide and the nonlinear terms (or a long simulation) must.




Q11. The toggle switch is bistable for \(\alpha > 2\). In a bifurcation diagram of \(u^*\) against \(\alpha\), what happens at \(\alpha = 2\), and what does a continuation method do there?






Hint





Look at the eigenvalues of the middle state on either side of \(\alpha = 2\).









Answer





For \(\alpha < 2\) there is one stable steady state. At \(\alpha = 2\) its largest eigenvalue crosses 0: it becomes a saddle and two new stable branches (U on, V on) split off (a pitchfork). A continuation method steps \(\alpha\), predicts the new steady state from the old one, corrects it with Newton, computes the eigenvalues and flags the step where \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda_{\max}\) changes sign.

title: Random numbers and Monte Carlo
section: Try it: watch the error fall like 1/\sqrt{N}
text:
Try it: watch the error fall like 1/\sqrt{N}




Live in the browser, seed 1, with its own generator (numbers differ from R but agree within the SE). OD-curve area first: click +10, +100, +1000, +10 000, +100 000. Left: the running estimate wanders, the ±2 SE band narrows around the green exact value 7.244. Right: the error of this run follows the dashed line sigma/sqrt(N) with slope -1/2, with dips whenever the running mean crosses the truth. At N = 100: 6.93 ± 0.85; at N = 10 100: 7.230 ± 0.083, a hundred times more draws for one more digit. Then motif overlap, +10 000: 143 of 10 000 placements have K >= 18, 0.0143 ± 0.0024, exact 0.01314 inside the band, same as the simulation two slides back. Preview for later: rare event P(X > 5) without importance sampling, +100 000: estimate 0, SE 0, a confident wrong answer, and the dashed true SE lies above 100 %. Tick importance sampling and click +100 000: 0.75 % relative SE. Last, the second tab: grid against Monte Carlo at a budget of 1e5 evaluations; drag d from 1 to 10, the grid’s error passes Monte Carlo’s at d = 3 to 4, and at d = 10 the grid needs about 1e18 evaluations for 1 % error (43 000 years at 1 µs), Monte Carlo 213 000 draws.

title: Exercise: random numbers and Monte Carlo
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Monte Carlo in your browser on three problems with a known answer: the area under the OD curve on \([0, 10]\) h (exact \(7.2444\), C4), the motif-overlap p-value \(P(K \ge 18)\) for 200 randomly placed hits (exact \(0.01314\), B6 and C7; each draw places 200 hits and counts the overlaps), and the rare-event probability \(P(X > 5)\) (exact \(2.867\times10^{-7}\), B7 and C8), plain or by importance sampling from \(N(5, 1)\). The buttons add draws to the running sample. Panel (a) shows the running estimate with its \(\pm 2\) SE band and the exact value; panel (b) shows the relative error of this run against \(N\) on log–log axes, with the dashed line \(\sigma/\sqrt N\) (the true SE, slope \(-\tfrac12\)). The second tab, Curse of dimensionality, is the toy marginal likelihood of C6: a grid at the prior quantiles against Monte Carlo with the same budget, and the number of evaluations each needs for 1 % error.
The demo uses its own seeded generator, so its numbers differ from those of R, Python and Rust in the solutions, but they agree within the standard errors. All numbers below are for seed 1; the draws come in the same order however you click, so the readout depends only on \(N\) and the seed.



E1. (the \(1/\sqrt N\) law) With OD-curve area, click +100 and write down the estimate, the SE and the error. Click +10 000 (\(N = 10\,100\)) and then +100 000 (\(N = 110\,100\)) and do the same. By what factor does the SE shrink per factor 100 in \(N\)? In panel (b), how do the error dots relate to the dashed line, and why do they scatter around it?






Answer E1





\(N = 100\): \(6.929 \pm 0.85\), SE \(0.426\), error \(-0.32\) (4.3 %). \(N = 10\,100\): \(7.230 \pm 0.083\), SE \(0.0415\), error \(-0.015\) (0.20 %). \(N = 110\,100\): \(7.232 \pm 0.025\), SE \(0.0125\), error \(-0.013\) (0.18 %). From \(N = 100\) to \(10\,100\) the SE falls by \(0.426/0.0415 = 10.3 \approx \sqrt{101}\): 100 times more draws for one more digit. The dots in panel (b) follow the dashed line \(\sigma/\sqrt N\) (\(\sigma = 4.16\)) with slope \(-\tfrac12\), but the actual error is random: whenever the running mean crosses the exact value the error dips far below the line, and it rarely stays far above it. At \(N = 10\,100\) the error is a third of an SE, at \(N = 110\,100\) about one SE, so it barely changed while the SE fell threefold. The SE describes the typical size of the error, not the error of one run.



E2. (is the error bar honest?) Stay with the OD-curve area. For seeds 1 to 10, move the seed slider and click +1000 once each time. Note the estimate and whether the exact value is inside \(\pm 2\) SE. How often does the band miss, and how often should it?






Answer E2





All ten SEs are about \(0.13\) (\(4.16/\sqrt{1000} = 0.132\)), so the band is \(\pm 0.26\) or \(\pm 0.27\) every time. The estimates are 7.141, 7.242, 7.320, 7.485, 6.989, 7.200, 7.554, 7.242, 7.287, 7.285. Only seed 7 misses: \(7.554 \pm 0.26\) ends at \(7.29\), just above the exact \(7.244\) (seeds 4 and 5 are close to the edge). A \(\pm 2\) SE band is a 95 % interval, so about 1 run in 20 should miss; 1 in 10 is within chance. This is why a single seed that “looks good” proves nothing, and why the SE, not the agreement of one run with a known answer, is what you report.



E3. (the motif test) Click motif overlap P(K ≥ 18), then +10 000. Compare the simulated p-value, its SE and the number of placements with \(K \ge 18\) with the lecture (122 of 10 000 in R) and with the exact \(0.01314\). What is the relative SE, and how many placements would you need for 10 % relative SE? Click +100 000 and check.






Answer E3





\(N = 10\,000\): 143 placements with \(K \ge 18\), estimate \(0.0143 \pm 0.0024\), SE \(0.00119\), error \(0.0012\) (8.8 %); the exact value is inside the band. R’s 122 and the demo’s 143 differ by \(0.0021\), less than 2 SE: two different streams, both honest. The relative SE is \(0.00119/0.0143 \approx 8\%\). For 10 % you need \(B \approx 100/p \approx 7\,600\) placements (B6c), so \(10\,000\) is already enough. At \(N = 110\,000\): 1 482 hits, \(0.01347 \pm 0.00070\), SE \(3.48\times10^{-4}\) (2.6 %): 11 times more draws, \(\sqrt{11} = 3.3\) times smaller SE.



E4. (rare event and importance sampling) Click rare event P(X > 5) with importance sampling off, then +100 000. What do the estimate, the SE and the readout say? Where are the error dots in panel (b), and where is the dashed line? Now tick importance sampling (this restarts the run), click +1000, then +100 000 (\(N = 101\,000\)). Read the estimate, the relative SE and the number of draws above 5.






Answer E4





Plain: 0 draws above 5, estimate \(0 \pm 0\), SE 0, error 100 %; the readout warns that SE = 0 claims certainty. In panel (b) the error is stuck at 1 (100 %) for every \(N\), and the dashed true SE \(\sqrt{p(1-p)}/(p\sqrt N)\) lies above it (5.9 at \(N = 10^5\)): the true uncertainty is larger than the answer, but the sample cannot show it. With importance sampling: at \(N = 1000\), 509 draws above 5 and \(2.69\times10^{-7} \pm 4.1\times10^{-8}\) (SE 7.7 %); at \(N = 101\,000\), 50 582 draws above 5 and \(2.878\times10^{-7} \pm 4.3\times10^{-9}\), relative SE \(0.75\%\), error \(0.39\%\), as in the lecture. The relative sd of one draw drops from \(\sqrt{(1-p)/p} = 1868\) to \(2.38\): the variance falls by a factor \((1868/2.38)^2 \approx 6\times10^5\), so plain Monte Carlo would need about 600 000 times more draws for the same SE.



E5. (the curse of dimensionality) Open Curse of dimensionality (budget \(10^5\), seed 1). Move \(d\) from 1 to 10 and read the grid error, the expected Monte Carlo SE and the error of the Monte Carlo run. Where does Monte Carlo start to win? Then read panel (d) and the second readout line at \(d = 10\) and \(d = 20\): how many evaluations does each method need for 1 % error, and how long is that at 1 µs per evaluation?






Answer E5





Grid errors: \(< 10^{-8}\) (\(d = 1\)), 0.016 % (\(d = 2\)), 0.49 % (\(d = 3\)), 2.8 % (\(d = 4\)), 18 % (\(d = 6\)), 78 % (\(d = 10\), 3 points per axis), the numbers of C6. The expected Monte Carlo SE grows only slowly: 0.19 %, 0.29 %, 0.39 %, 0.50 %, 0.74 %, 1.5 %; the seed-1 run has error 1.2 % at \(d = 10\). The grid wins at \(d = 1, 2\), the two are level at \(d = 3\), and Monte Carlo wins from \(d = 4\), as B5(c) predicted for a second-order rule. For 1 % at \(d = 10\) the grid needs 65 points per axis, about \(10^{18}\) evaluations (43 000 years), Monte Carlo 213 110 draws (0.2 s). At \(d = 20\): grid 101 per axis, \(10^{40}\) evaluations (far beyond the age of the universe); Monte Carlo about 5 million draws (5 s). Monte Carlo’s cost also grows with \(d\), like \(1.364^d\), because the likelihood becomes more peaked relative to the prior, but exponentially more slowly than the grid’s.

title: Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

take one step of the midpoint, Heun and classical RK4 methods by hand, and write each as a short function,
read the order of a method off a table or a log–log plot of error against step size, and compare methods by the number of function evaluations,
use a conserved quantity (Lotka–Volterra) to detect the error of an ODE solver,
explain how an embedded pair estimates the error of a step, and how an adaptive solver accepts or rejects the step and chooses the next one,
say what rtol and atol mean, choose them for a model, and check a result by tightening them,
use the library solvers (deSolve::ode, scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, ode_solvers), and locate events such as the peak of an epidemic.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a pocket calculator. The code part checks the hand answers and then works at sizes where only code works.

title: Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
By hand
B1. Midpoint and Heun. Drug clearance \(C' = -0.8\,C\), \(C_0 = 10\) mg/L, one step of \(h = 0.5\) hours. (a) Take one Euler, one midpoint and one Heun step. Write down \(k_1\), \(k_2\) and the point where \(k_2\) is evaluated for each. (b) Compare with the exact \(C(0.5) = 10e^{-0.4} = 6.70320\). Give the error of each method. (c) Show that for \(C' = -kC\) midpoint and Heun both give \(C_1 = C_0(1 + z + z^2/2)\) with \(z = -kh\). Which Taylor polynomial is this?
B2. One RK4 step. Same problem and step. (a) Compute \(k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4\) (fill in a table: stage, point, slope) and \(C_1\). (b) Compare with the exact value. How many times smaller is the error than Heun’s? (c) The error of one step is \(\propto h^5\). Predict the error of a single RK4 step with \(h = 0.25\), then check it: the exact value is \(10e^{-0.2} = 8.187308\).
B3. Reading the order. Errors in \(N(10)\) for the logistic curve:









\(h\)
0.5
0.25
0.125




Heun
\(1.51\times10^{-3}\)
\(3.36\times10^{-4}\)
\(8.05\times10^{-5}\)


RK4
\(9.25\times10^{-6}\)
\(5.31\times10^{-7}\)
\(3.20\times10^{-8}\)




Estimate the order of each method from consecutive ratios.
Predict both errors for \(h = 0.0625\).
About how many function evaluations does each method need (from \(t = 0\) to \(10\)) for an error of \(10^{-8}\)?

B4. An embedded pair by hand. Clearance again, from \(C_0 = 10\) with \(h = 0.5\), using Euler (order 1) and Heun (order 2) from B1 as a pair, with rtol = 0.01 and atol = 0. (a) What is the error estimate? Compare it with the true errors of Euler and Heun. Which of the two does it estimate? (b) Compute \(\text{sc}\), the scaled error err and decide: accept or reject? Compute the next step size. (c) The error estimate of this pair is \(\propto h^2\). Predict err for the new step, then compute it.
B5. What rtol and atol mean. SIR at \(t = 0\): \(S = 9990\), \(I = 10\), \(R = 0\) people. (a) With rtol = 1e-3 and atol = 1e-6, what error is allowed in one step for each of \(S\), \(I\) and \(R\)? (b) A colleague writes the same model in fractions of the population (\(S = 0.999\), \(I = 0.001\)) and keeps atol = 1e-6. What error does this allow in \(I\), in people? Is that still fine? (c) Another colleague sets atol = 10 (“ten people do not matter in a town of 10 000”). What error does this allow in \(I\) at \(t = 0\), relative to \(I\) itself? What could go wrong? (d) A signalling model measures concentrations in mol/L; the important species is around \(10^{-9}\) M. What is wrong with atol = 1e-6? Give two fixes.
B6. A conserved quantity. Lotka–Volterra with \(V(x, y) = c x - d \ln x + b y - a \ln y\). (a) Use the chain rule, \(\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} x' + \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} y'\), to show that \(dV/dt = 0\) along every solution. (b) Compute \(V\) at the start \((10, 5)\) and at the equilibrium \((x^*, y^*) = (d/c,\ a/b)\). (Use \(\ln 2 = 0.6931\), \(\ln 5 = 1.6094\), \(\ln 10 = 2.3026\).) (c) \(V\) is smallest at the equilibrium, and the orbits are the curves $V = $ constant around it. Euler makes \(V\) increase. What does the plotted orbit do? Why is that a biologically misleading picture?
B7. Events. For SIR let \(g = \beta S/N - \gamma\). (a) Show that \(I' = g\, I\), so \(I\) peaks where \(g\) changes sign from \(+\) to \(-\). What is \(S\) at the peak? (b) An adaptive solver (rtol = 1e-4) takes two consecutive steps ending at \(t = 35.16\) with \(S = 4426.1\) and at \(t = 42.04\) with \(S = 2404.5\). Compute \(g\) at both, and locate the peak by linear interpolation of \(g\). The true peak time is \(38.355\) days; why is your estimate off, and what does a solver do instead? (c) Lynx numbers rise above 20 for about 0.8 years in each 5.5-year cycle. A program only checks \(y - 20\) at the end of each step, and its steps are 2.5 years long. Can it miss the event? What two remedies are there?

title: Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
In code
C1. Write the methods. (a) Write step functions euler_step, midpoint_step, heun_step, rk4_step with arguments (f, t, y, h), and a driver rk_solve(step, f, t0, y0, h, n) that takes n fixed steps and returns all times and states. Check your answers to B1 and B2. (b) For the logistic curve, compute the error in \(N(10)\) for \(h = 1, \tfrac12, \dots, \tfrac1{64}\) with Euler, Heun and RK4. Compute the observed order from consecutive ratios, and compare with B3. (c) Plot the errors against \(h\) on log–log axes. Read off the slopes.
C2. Cost versus accuracy. With \(n = 10\cdot 2^k\) steps (\(k = 0, \dots, 13\)), find for each of Euler, Heun and RK4 the smallest \(n\) that gives an error below \(10^{-6}\) in \(N(10)\), and the number of function evaluations that costs. Compare with your estimate in B3(c).
C3. Predator–prey. (a) Solve Lotka–Volterra for 50 years with Euler (\(h = 0.01\)), Heun (\(h = 0.01\)) and RK4 (\(h = 0.1\)), and report the largest \(|V(t) - V(0)|\) for each. (b) Do the same with the library’s Dormand–Prince solver, with rtol = atol = 1e-3 and 1e-6. In Python, also try the defaults of solve_ivp. Which setting would you trust for a 50-year simulation?
C4. An adaptive solver of your own. Write adapt_heun(f, t, y, tend, h, rtol, atol) using the Heun–Euler pair and the rules of Background item 6 (\(q = 1\)). Record every accepted step and count the rejected ones. (a) Logistic curve from \(h = 1\) to \(t = 10\) with rtol = 1e-3 and 1e-6 (atol = 1e-9): report the error in \(N(10)\), the number of accepted and rejected steps and of function evaluations. Does the first step get rejected, as in B4? (b) SIR to day 160 with rtol = atol = 1e-6: how many steps? Plot \(h\) against \(t\) (log scale) and find where the steps are smallest and largest. Why there?
C5. The library on the repressilator. (a) Solve the repressilator to \(t = 50\) with Dormand–Prince (ode45 / RK45 / Dopri5) and rtol = atol \(= 10^{-3}, \dots, 10^{-9}\). Report \(p_1(50)\) and the numbers of steps and function evaluations. How many digits of \(p_1(50)\) can you trust at each tolerance? How do the step counts grow? (b) Solve with fixed-step RK4 and \(h = 1\), \(0.2\), \(0.01\). In R, ode(..., method = "rk4") uses the spacing of times as the step unless you give hini. Which of the answers are usable?
C6. When atol is too large. Use your adapt_heun from C4 on SIR to day 60, with rtol \(= 10^{-3}, \dots, 10^{-6}\) and atol \(= 10\), \(1\) and \(10^{-6}\) people. Report the relative error in \(I(60)\); the reference value is \(I(60) = 998.2012187\). Explain the pattern with B5(c).
C7. Events. (a) Find the time and height of the epidemic peak as an event (\(g = \beta S/N - \gamma\) crosses zero), with tight tolerances (rtol = 1e-10). Compare with \(I_{\max} = 3007.961\). In R use ode(..., method = "lsoda", rootfunc = ...) (root finding is not available with ode45 in deSolve); in Python solve_ivp(..., events=...); in Rust, ode_solvers has no event location, so scan the dense output for a sign change and refine it by bisection. (b) Find the first time the lynx population reaches 20 (from below). (c) Now look only at the solution at \(t = 0, 2.5, 5, \dots, 15\). Is there a sign change of \(y - 20\)? Compare with B7(c).

title: Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — one step by hand (B1, B2)





Write a table with one row per stage: where the slope is evaluated (\(t\) and the point \(C\)), and the slope \(-0.8\,C\) there. Each point uses the previous slope: the point for \(k_2\) is \(C_0 + \tfrac h2 k_1\), for \(k_3\) it is \(C_0 + \tfrac h2 k_2\), for \(k_4\) it is \(C_0 + h k_3\). For B2(c), the single-step error shrinks by \(2^5 = 32\) when \(h\) is halved.









Hint 2 — order and cost (B3, C1, C2)





\(p \approx \log_2(\text{err}(h)/\text{err}(h/2))\). To get from error \(e_1\) at step \(h_1\) to error \(e_2\), take \(h_2 = h_1 (e_2/e_1)^{1/p}\). Number of steps \(= 10/h\); evaluations \(=\) steps \(\times\) stages. In code, log2 in R, np.log2 in Python, f64::log2 in Rust; log–log plots with plot(..., log = "xy"), plt.loglog.









Hint 3 — embedded pair and controller (B4, C4)





The estimate is \(|y^{\text{Heun}} - y^{\text{Euler}}| = \tfrac h2 |k_2 - k_1|\). With atol = 0, \(\text{sc} = \texttt{rtol}\cdot\max(|y_n|, |y_{n+1}|)\). For the Heun–Euler pair \(q = 1\), so \(h_{\text{new}} = h\cdot\min(5, \max(0.2, 0.9\,\text{err}^{-1/2}))\). In code, keep a while (t < tend) loop; shorten the last step with h <- min(h, tend - t); on rejection, do not advance t or y.









Hint 4 — tolerances (B5, C5, C6)





Allowed error per step \(= \texttt{atol} + \texttt{rtol}\cdot|y|\). Below \(|y| \approx \texttt{atol}/\texttt{rtol}\) the atol term dominates. In R, attributes(out)$istate[2:3] (or diagnostics(out)) gives the numbers of steps and function evaluations; in Python sol.t.size - 1 and sol.nfev; in Rust the Stats returned by integrate() (accepted_steps, num_eval). For Rust, set OutputType::Sparse to get the solver’s own steps.









Hint 5 — the conserved quantity (B6, C3)





\(\partial V/\partial x = c - d/x\) and \(\partial V/\partial y = b - a/y\). Factor \(x' = x(a - by)\) and \(y' = y(cx - d)\). In code, compute \(V\) for every row of the solution and take max(abs(v - v[1])).









Hint 6 — events (B7, C7)





In deSolve, give rootfunc = function(t, y, parms) ... returning \(g\); without an events argument the integration stops at the first root, whose time is in attributes(out)$troot (see lsoda and events). In solve_ivp, give events=g, and set the attributes g.terminal = True (stop) and g.direction = -1 (only \(+ \to -\)); results are in sol.t_events and sol.y_events. In Rust, integrate_with_continuous_output_model fills a ContinuousOutputModel whose evaluate(t) gives the dense output at any \(t\).

title: Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
Where this leads

Stiffness and implicit methods (Part 8): on stiff problems (fast and slow processes together) every explicit method, RK4 and Dormand–Prince included, needs tiny steps for stability, not accuracy; the adaptive solver then takes millions of steps. Implicit methods and LSODA (the lsoda used for events above) fix this.
Equilibria, stability and the phase plane (Part 8): the closed predator–prey orbits and the repressilator’s limit cycle are studied there with nullclines and the Jacobian; the solvers of this unit draw the trajectories.
Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting (Part 9): fitting ODE parameters to data calls the solver thousands of times; tolerances that are too loose make the fit noisy, tolerances that are too tight make it slow.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
About this lecture
Some models mix a reaction that is over in a millisecond with one that takes minutes. The fast part is finished almost at once, yet an explicit solver keeps taking millisecond steps to the very end. Such a model is called stiff.

The test equation y' = \lambda y and the stability region of a method: which step sizes h keep errors from growing.
Stiff = widely separated time scales. The step size of an explicit solver is set by stability, not by accuracy; even adaptive RK45 takes thousands of steps.
Implicit methods (backward Euler, BDF, Radau) are stable for any step on decaying problems. The price: a Newton solve in every step.
Library solvers: lsoda switches automatically between a non-stiff and a stiff method.
Biology: enzyme kinetics with fast binding and slow catalysis (and its Michaelis–Menten shortcut), and Robertson’s chemical kinetics problem, the classic stiff test case.


This is the third unit of Part 8. Students know Euler (with its instability on drug clearance), RK4 and adaptive RK45 with deSolve::ode and solve_ivp. Here we explain the one situation where those tools break down in practice: they still give the right answer, but take thousands or millions of steps to get it. Many biological models are stiff (any model with fast binding, fast degradation or a fine spatial grid), so this is not an exotic case. The fix, implicit methods, is also the place where Newton for systems (Part 2) and linear solves (Part 3) come back inside an ODE solver.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
A biology problem first
One enzyme, one substrate, mass action: E + S \rightleftharpoons C \to E + P.
library(deSolve)
p  <- c(kf = 100, kr = 100, kcat = 1)    # per uM per s, per s, per s
y0 <- c(S = 10, E = 1, C = 0, P = 0)     # uM
times <- seq(0, 30, by = 0.5)            # s
for (m in c("ode45", "lsoda")) {
  tm <- system.time(out <- ode(y0, times, enzyme, p, method = m))
  cat(m, ": steps", attr(out, "istate")[2], "  time", tm[["elapsed"]], "s\n")
}
# ode45 : steps 3585   time 0.288 s
# lsoda : steps 216   time 0.007 s

Same model, same default tolerances, same answer: 17 times more steps and 40 times the time for the Runge–Kutta solver.
The solution is a smooth curve over 30 s. Why does RK45 need 3585 steps for it?


The model function enzyme is on the next slide. ode45 is the adaptive Dormand–Prince RK45 from Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size; lsoda is the default method of deSolve::ode. attr(out, “istate”)[2] is the number of steps the solver took; deSolve’s diagnostics(out) prints this and more. Timings are from our laptop and will differ on yours; the step counts will not. With 30 s instead of 3 h of simulated time, or a model with 1000 such reactions, the factor decides whether a parameter fit runs in a minute or a day.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
The shortcut: Michaelis–Menten


Assume C is always in balance with S (quasi-steady state, QSSA: C' \approx 0). Then S' = -\frac{V_{\max} S}{K_m + S}, V_{\max} = k_{cat} E_0 = 1\ \mu\text{M/s}, K_m = \frac{k_r + k_{cat}}{k_f} = 1.01\ \mu\text{M}.

One ODE, no fast time scale: ode45 needs 61 steps (one per output interval).
But it is an approximation: P(10\text{ s}) = 8.24 vs 8.00 in the full model (3 %). Good when E_0 \ll S_0 + K_m.





This is the textbook route: remove the fast variable by assuming it is always at its quasi-equilibrium. Mathematically, setting C’ = 0 gives C = E0 S / (Km + S), and substituting gives the Michaelis–Menten rate. The QSSA solution misses the first millisecond (the substrate that is bound in C is counted as free) and runs slightly ahead. With E0 = 1 and S0 + Km = 11 the error is a few per cent; with enzyme comparable to substrate (common inside cells, or in signalling cascades) it gets much worse, which the exercise shows. Also, many models have no clean separation into fast and slow variables, or have dozens of fast reactions. Then we want a solver that handles the full model directly. That is what the rest of the lecture builds.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Recap: Euler’s stability limit
From Initial value problems and Euler’s method: drug clearance C' = -0.8\,C.
C_{n+1} = C_n + h(-0.8\,C_n) = (1 - 0.8h)\,C_n



h (hours)

0.6
−0.6
−1.4


behaviour

oscillates, decays
blows up




Errors shrink only if |1 - 0.8h| < 1, that is h < 2/0.8 = 2.5 hours.
A rate 1000 times faster would need steps 1000 times smaller, even after that component has decayed to nothing.


One slide only: the instability slide of the Euler unit. The key observation to carry into this lecture: the bound depends on the rate k only, not on how large the solution is or how accurate we want to be. If the model contains one component that decays with rate 1200 per second, Euler needs h < 2/1200 s for the whole simulation, even when that component has long since settled. This is the whole phenomenon of stiffness in one line.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
The test equation y' = \lambda y
Every method, applied to y' = \lambda y with step h, multiplies by a fixed factor R(z) per step, where z = h\lambda:








method
one step
R(z)




Euler
y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n
1 + z


RK4
(four stages)
1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24}




Stable if |R(z)| \le 1: errors do not grow. The set of such z is the method’s stability region.
Why this tiny equation? Near any state, a system \mathbf y' = \mathbf f(\mathbf y) behaves like \mathbf y' = J\mathbf y, and J splits into modes y' = \lambda y, one per eigenvalue \lambda of the Jacobian J.
Every eigenvalue must satisfy h\lambda \in stability region. \lambda can be complex (oscillation), so the region lives in the complex plane.


The RK4 factor is the Taylor series of e^z cut after the z^4 term: each stage adds one more term. The justification for the test equation is linearisation: f(y) near a point is approximately f(y) + J (y - y), the same linearisation that Newton for systems of equations uses, and a linear system with a diagonalisable J decouples into independent scalar equations, one per eigenvalue (Part 5, Power iteration and friends). A real negative lambda is a decaying mode (clearance, binding), a complex lambda with negative real part is a damped oscillation. Do not dwell on the complex plane: for most of this lecture only the negative real axis matters.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Stability regions


On the negative real axis: Euler needs h|\lambda| \le 2, RK4 h|\lambda| \le 2.79. Both regions are bounded.
Backward Euler (next slides) is stable everywhere except inside the white disc: the whole left half-plane.


Shaded = stable. Euler: the disc of radius 1 around -1. RK4: a larger, kidney-shaped region that reaches -2.79 on the real axis and about ±2.83 on the imaginary axis (that is why RK4 is fine for oscillations, unlike Euler). Every explicit method has a bounded stability region: R(z) is a polynomial, and a polynomial grows without bound for large z. Higher order buys a bit more room, never an unlimited amount. Backward Euler, the right panel, is stable for every z with negative real part, whatever the step. The exercise asks you to draw these three regions yourself.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
What “stiff” means
Eigenvalues of the enzyme model’s Jacobian at the start (reduced to S, C using E = 1 - C):
J <- rbind(c(-100, 1100), c(100, -1101))   # d(S', C') / d(S, C) at S = 10, C = 0
eigen(J)$values
# [1] -1.200917e+03 -8.326972e-02

Two time scales: 1/1201 \approx 0.8 ms (binding) and 1/0.083 \approx 12 s (catalysis). Ratio \approx 14\,000.
Stiff: the fast mode has decayed, yet it still limits an explicit step to h < 2.79/1201 = 2.3 ms (RK4). Covering 30 s takes 13 000 steps.
Accuracy alone would allow steps of tenths of a second: lsoda’s steps reach 0.5 s (the output spacing).


A problem is stiff when the step size of an explicit method is set by stability, not by accuracy.


The Jacobian entries come from differentiating S’ = -kf (1 - C) S + kr C and C’ = kf (1 - C) S - (kr + kcat) C at S = 10, C = 0; the exercise does this by hand. Trace -1201 and determinant 100 give the eigenvalues roughly as -1201 and -100/1201. The definition in the box is the practical one; there is no sharp mathematical definition. Stiffness is a property of the problem together with the time span and the tolerance: if you only wanted to simulate the first 5 ms, the problem would not be stiff, because then the fast mode is what you are resolving.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Adaptive RK45 cannot escape


The error controller keeps pushing h up, gets rejected, pushes again: h rides the stability limit 3.3/|\lambda_\text{fast}| (dashed).
Adaptivity does not help: it finds the stability limit by trial and error, not a way past it.


This is our own hand-written Dormand–Prince RK45 (the method in deSolve’s ode45 and scipy’s RK45) on the enzyme model with rtol = atol = 1e-6. The blue line is the accepted step size, the red dashed line is 3.3 divided by the fast eigenvalue of the Jacobian at that time (3.3 is where the RK45 stability region crosses the negative real axis). They coincide. As substrate is used up, the fast eigenvalue drops from about 1200 to about 200 per second, so the limit grows from 3 ms to 16 ms, but it never gets near the 0.5 s that the smooth curve allows. If the solver steps above the limit, the fast mode starts to grow, the error estimate notices and rejects the step. So the answer is still correct, which is why stiffness often goes unnoticed: it shows up only as slowness.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Backward Euler
Use the slope at the end of the step instead of the start:
y_{n+1} = y_n + h\, f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1})
On y' = \lambda y: y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_{n+1}, so y_{n+1} = \frac{1}{1 - h\lambda}\, y_n, \qquad R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}.
z <- -0.8 * c(0.5, 2, 3, 10)            # h * lambda for C' = -0.8 C, h = 0.5, 2, 3, 10
rbind(euler = 1 + z, rk4 = 1 + z + z^2/2 + z^3/6 + z^4/24, beuler = 1 / (1 - z))
#         [,1]   [,2]   [,3]    [,4]
# euler  0.600 -0.600 -1.400  -7.000
# rk4    0.670  0.270  0.558 110.333
# beuler 0.714  0.385  0.294   0.111

For any \lambda < 0 and any h > 0: 0 < R < 1. Decay stays decay. (A-stable.)
y_{n+1} appears on both sides: each step is an equation to solve. That is what “implicit” means.


Graphically: Euler follows the tangent at the start of the step, backward Euler picks the end point whose tangent points back to the start. For the linear test equation the equation is trivial to solve. Note the RK4 column at h = 10: factor 110, an explosion, while backward Euler still decays (too fast: e^-8 would be 0.0003, it gives 0.11, so it is stable but not accurate at that step). Like Euler, backward Euler has order 1. A-stable means: the stability region contains the whole left half-plane. Any explicit method fails that.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Backward Euler by hand
Drug clearance C' = -0.8\,C, C_0 = 10 mg/L, h = 3 hours:
C_1 = \frac{C_0}{1 + 0.8\cdot 3} = \frac{10}{3.4} = 2.94, \qquad C_2 = \frac{2.94}{3.4} = 0.865

Stable and positive, but not accurate at this step: order 1, and h|\lambda| = 2.4 is large.
Stability lets us pick h for accuracy only. On a stiff problem that is the win: the fast mode only needs to stay damped, not resolved.


Pen-and-paper: the student can check every number. Backward Euler errs in the safe direction for decay (it decays too slowly) but it is not magic: with steps comparable to the fast time scale it is inaccurate for that component. The point for stiff problems: we do not care about the fast component’s details after it has decayed; we only need it not to blow up, and backward Euler damps it. The slow component, which we do care about, is resolved accurately by a step chosen for it.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
section: Implicit = one nonlinear solve per step
text:
Implicit = one nonlinear solve per step
For a nonlinear \mathbf f, each step must solve for \mathbf y = \mathbf y_{n+1}: \mathbf G(\mathbf y) = \mathbf y - \mathbf y_n - h\,\mathbf f(\mathbf y) = \mathbf 0
This is a root-finding problem: use Newton, from Newton for systems of equations.

Jacobian of \mathbf G: \;I - hJ, where J is the Jacobian of \mathbf f. Newton: solve (I - hJ)\,\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf G(\mathbf y), set \mathbf y \leftarrow \mathbf y + \boldsymbol\delta.
Start from \mathbf y_n: the previous value is close, so 1–4 iterations suffice.

By hand — dimerisation M' = -kM^2, k = 10, M_0 = 1, h = 0.1: solve G(y) = y + h k y^2 - 1 = y + y^2 - 1 = 0, G'(y) = 1 + 2y.










iteration

0.6667 - \frac{0.1111}{2.333} = 0.6190

This is the slide that ties Part 8 back to Part 2. A Newton solve per step, each needing the Jacobian and a linear solve (Gaussian elimination as LU). In one variable the Jacobian of G is 1 - h f’(y). The exact backward Euler value here is (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 = 0.618034, the golden ratio again; the exact ODE solution at t = 0.1 is 1/(1 + kt) = 0.5, so the backward Euler step itself is not very accurate at this h, but Newton solved its equation to 5 digits in 3 iterations. Quadratic convergence: errors 0.38, 0.049, 0.00097, 4e-7.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
section: Backward Euler with Newton in R

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Backward Euler on the enzyme




Y <- beuler(f, jac, c(10, 1, 0, 0),
            h = 0.1, n = 300)
Y[c(11, 101, 301), ]       # t = 1, 10, 30 s
#           [,1]   [,2]      [,3]    [,4]
# [1,] 8.2153795 0.1095 0.8905306  0.8941
# [2,] 1.4245101 0.4145 0.5854757  7.9900
# [3,] 0.0001077 0.9999 0.0001072  9.9998

300 steps of 0.1 s; on average 3.4 Newton iterations each.
Explicit Euler: fine at h = 1 ms (30 000 steps), NaN at h = 3 ms.
Reference (lsoda): P(10) = 8.0027. Backward Euler: 7.9900.



The figure shows the complex C over the first 3 s. Explicit Euler with 1 ms steps tracks the reference; with 3 ms steps it goes negative within a few steps and overflows to NaN. Backward Euler with steps 100 times larger than Euler’s stability limit follows the curve. Its first step jumps from C = 0 to the slow curve in one go: it cannot resolve the 1 ms binding phase with a 0.1 s step, and it does not need to. The error 0.013 in P(10) is the order-1 error of backward Euler; halve h and it halves (next slide).

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Error against step size




Error in P after 10 s (from t = 0.1 s, after the binding transient):

Explicit Euler: order 1, but only left of the stability limit. To the right: no answer at all.
Backward Euler: order 1 at any h.
BDF2 (next slide): order 2, still stable at any h.



Slopes read off as in Convergence and cost: backward Euler loses a factor 10 in h and gains a factor 10 in error, BDF2 gains a factor 100. At h = 0.01 s backward Euler has error 1.3e-3 with 1000 steps. Explicit Euler cannot take that step at all; its largest stable step, 1.5 ms, gives 4.6e-4 with 6700 steps. BDF2 reaches 2e-6 at h = 0.01. We started at t = 0.1 s from the reference solution so that the plot shows the order on the smooth part; including the 1 ms transient adds a hump for intermediate h, where the step is comparable to the fast time scale.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Higher order: BDF
Backward differentiation formulas: fit a polynomial through y_{n+1}, y_n, y_{n-1}, \dots and require that its slope at t_{n+1} equals f(y_{n+1}).







order
formula




BDF1 = backward Euler
y_{n+1} - y_n = h f(y_{n+1})


BDF2
y_{n+1} - \tfrac43 y_n + \tfrac13 y_{n-1} = \tfrac23 h f(y_{n+1})




Still one Newton solve per step (Jacobian I - \tfrac23 hJ for BDF2); uses old values instead of extra stages.
BDF1 and BDF2 are A-stable. BDF3–5 lose a sliver near the imaginary axis (fine for decay, less so for weakly damped oscillations). Above order 6 they are unstable.
bdf in deSolve, "BDF" in solve_ivp: orders 1–5, step and order chosen automatically (Gear’s method).


The idea parallels the finite-difference formulas of Numerical differentiation: the left-hand side of BDF2, divided by h, is the one-sided second-order difference approximation of y’ at t_{n+1}. A multistep method needs past values, so it starts with BDF1 and builds up order; the exercise checks BDF2’s order. Radau (method “radau” in deSolve, “Radau” in solve_ivp) is the other family: an implicit Runge–Kutta method of order 5, stable on the whole left half-plane, with more work per step (three coupled stages, so a 3n by 3n Newton system) but fewer steps.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
What one implicit step costs








per step
explicit (RK45)
implicit (BDF, Radau)




evaluations of \mathbf f
6
1–4 per Newton iteration


Jacobian J (n \times n)
—
analytic, or n extra \mathbf f calls by finite differences


linear solve
—
LU of I - hJ: \approx \tfrac23 n^3


number of steps (stiff)
huge
small




Solvers reuse J and its LU over many steps; they refactorise only when Newton slows down.
Large models (gene networks, spatial grids) have sparse J: banded or sparse LU keeps the cost near O(n).
Non-stiff problem: explicit wins. Use an implicit method only when stiffness makes the explicit one slow.


The trade-off: fewer, more expensive steps. For n = 4 the linear algebra is trivial; for a model with 1000 species a dense LU per step costs about 7e8 flops, and the Jacobian 1000 extra f calls. That is why reusing J matters and why deSolve has the stiff solvers lsodes (sparse) and the bandwidth arguments, scipy has jac_sparsity. The cost of LU and the role of sparsity are from Gaussian elimination as LU and Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse. A finite-difference Jacobian is built exactly as in Newton for systems of equations. When the problem is not stiff, an implicit method wastes its Newton solves: RK45 is then the better choice.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
LSODA: switch automatically
LSODA starts with a non-stiff method (Adams, explicit-style multistep), watches its step sizes, and switches to BDF when it detects stiffness (and back again if it fades).
out <- ode(y0, times, enzyme, p, method = "lsoda")
attr(out, "istate")[15]      # method of the last step: 1 = Adams, 2 = BDF
# [1] 2
attr(out, "rstate")[5]       # time of the last switch (s)
# [1] 0.01679162

Adams through the binding transient (where small steps are needed for accuracy anyway), BDF from 17 ms on.
diagnostics(out) prints all counters: steps, \mathbf f calls, Jacobians, method.
That is why lsoda is the default of deSolve::ode: you do not need to know in advance whether your model is stiff.


LSODA is from ODEPACK (Petzold and Hindmarsh, 1983) and still the default in deSolve; scipy’s solve_ivp has it as method “LSODA” (its default is RK45, explicit). The switch time 17 ms is a few times the binding time scale: by then the fast mode has decayed and the Adams method’s steps would be set by stability. The switching is a heuristic: it estimates the largest eigenvalue from the solver’s own data. diagnostics works on the output of every deSolve solver.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
The solvers you can call
ode(y0, times, enzyme, p)                     # lsoda: switches Adams <-> BDF
ode(y0, times, enzyme, p, method = "bdf")     # BDF, orders 1-5
ode(y0, times, enzyme, p, method = "radau")   # implicit Runge-Kutta, order 5
ode(y0, times, enzyme, p, method = "ode45")   # explicit RK45: non-stiff only



deSolve::ode
scipy.integrate.solve_ivp
type




"lsoda" (default)
method="LSODA"
switches non-stiff ↔︎ stiff


"bdf"
method="BDF"
implicit multistep


"radau"
method="Radau"
implicit Runge–Kutta


"ode45"
method="RK45" (default)
explicit




Give the Jacobian (jacfunc / jac=) if you have it: fewer \mathbf f calls, more reliable Newton.
Rust’s ode_solvers crate has no stiff solver; its Dopri5 stops with “stiffness detected”. The exercise writes backward Euler with Newton by hand.


Note the defaults differ: R defaults to lsoda, which handles stiff problems; Python’s solve_ivp defaults to RK45, which does not. A Python user who never changes method= will meet stiffness as “my simulation takes forever”. Without a Jacobian, the stiff solvers build one by finite differences, which costs n extra function calls each time. For big sparse problems deSolve has lsodes and ode.1D/ode.2D, scipy has the jac_sparsity argument. In Rust, Dopri5 actually runs a stiffness test every 1000 steps and returns an error when it fires repeatedly; that is honest, but there is no implicit solver to switch to in the crate.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Robertson’s problem


Three species, three reactions (Robertson 1966): A \xrightarrow{0.04} B, \quad B + B \xrightarrow{3\times10^7} C + B, \quad B + C \xrightarrow{10^4} A + C
rober <- function(t, y, p) {
  r1 <- 0.04 * y[1]; r2 <- 3e7 * y[2]^2
  r3 <- 1e4 * y[2] * y[3]
  list(c(-r1 + r3, r1 - r2 - r3, r2))
}

Rate constants span 9 orders of magnitude; y_1 + y_2 + y_3 = 1.
B stays tiny (\le 3.7\times10^{-5}) and fast; A \to C takes 10^5 time units and more.





H. H. Robertson’s 1966 example of an autocatalytic reaction network, and the standard test problem for stiff solvers ever since. It is a chemistry problem, but its structure (one intermediate with a very short lifetime, made and consumed by fast reactions, embedded in a slow overall conversion) is everywhere in biochemistry: reactive intermediates, short-lived complexes, radicals. The plot uses a log time axis from 1e-6 to 1e11 and shows y2 scaled by 1e4. B rises within 1e-3 time units to its quasi-steady level and then follows the slow conversion of A to C, which is still not complete at 1e5.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Robertson: steps and time
for (m in c("ode45", "lsoda", "bdf", "radau")) {
  tm <- system.time(out <- ode(c(1, 0, 0), c(0, 40), rober, NULL, method = m,
                               hini = 1e-4, maxsteps = 1e5))
  is <- attr(out, "istate")
  cat(m, is[2], "steps", is[3], "f-evals", tm[["elapsed"]], "s  y2:", out[2, 3], "\n")
}
ode45 59284 steps 377479 f-evals 1.202 s  y2: 8.887885e-06 
lsoda 98 steps 200 f-evals 0.002 s  y2: 9.18632e-06 
bdf 92 steps 188 f-evals 0.002 s  y2: 9.187624e-06 
radau 26 steps 269 f-evals 0.002 s  y2: 9.185542e-06 

600 times more steps for RK45, and its y_2 is 3 % off: 59 000 steps at the edge of stability pile up error (a tighter atol does not cure it).
To t = 10^{11}: lsoda takes 1595 steps. RK45, held at h \approx 10^{-3}, would need about 10^{14}.


The fast eigenvalue at t = 40 is about -3400, so RK45 is limited to h of about 3.3/3400, 1e-3, for the whole run: 40 / 1e-3 is 40 000 steps plus the early phase. The stiff solvers take 26 to 98 steps. Radau takes the fewest steps but each one costs more f calls (three implicit stages). Timings are from our laptop; on a second run ode45 took 2.8 s, the stiff solvers stay at a few milliseconds. ode45 is also less accurate in y2: with atol = 1e-10 it still returns 8.89e-6, so this is not just a loose tolerance; scipy’s RK45 gets y2 right with 34 500 steps (exercise), so the deSolve number is a warning rather than a law. deSolve’s ode45 needs hini = 1e-4 here: with its automatic first step it can stall on this problem. For the run to 1e11 the stiff solvers’ step grows to 1e9 and more; an explicit method stays at 1e-3 for ever.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
When implicit methods mislead




The 24-hour oscillator x'' = -\omega^2 x from Initial value problems and Euler’s method, backward Euler:

|R(i\omega h)| = 1/\sqrt{1 + \omega^2 h^2} < 1: every step shrinks the amplitude.
After 10 days at h = 1 h: amplitude 3.5\times10^{-4} instead of 1. (Euler: 2850.)
A biologist would conclude the clock is damped. The damping is the method’s.



Backward Euler’s stability region includes the whole imaginary axis and even most of the right half-plane: it damps things that should not decay at all, and even makes growing solutions (y’ = +y with h > 2) look like decay. Euler multiplies the amplitude by sqrt(1 + w^2 h^2) per step, backward Euler divides by the same factor: 2850 versus 1/2850. This is the mirror image of the Euler spiral. The fix: higher-order implicit methods (BDF2 damps far less; Radau and the trapezoidal rule better still), smaller steps, and above all a non-stiff method for a non-stiff oscillator. Check: halve the step, and compare with a second method of a different type; a damping that changes with h is numerical.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Checks for stiff problems

Count steps (diagnostics, attr(out, "istate"), sol.nfev): thousands of steps for a smooth curve, step size flat at a small value → stiff. Switch to lsoda, bdf or radau.
Eigenvalues of the Jacobian: a ratio of 10^3 or more between the largest and smallest |\text{Re}\,\lambda|, over the time span you simulate → stiff.
Compare two solvers of different type and tighten the tolerances: the answer must not move.
atol below the smallest concentration you care about (y_2 \approx 10^{-5} needs atol \ll 10^{-5}).
Conservation laws (E + C, S + C + P, y_1 + y_2 + y_3) and positivity. A negative y_2 in Robertson makes the true ODE blow up: y_2' \approx -3\times10^7 y_2^2 drives it to -\infty.
Newton failures (“repeated convergence failures”, “step size too small”): often a wrong hand-coded Jacobian, or a model with a real singularity.


The first check is the cheapest and catches most cases: if a library solver is slow, look at its step count before buying a faster computer. The positivity point is specific to kinetic models with second-order reactions: an explicit step that overshoots zero puts y2 on the wrong side, where the quadratic term pushes it further away; this is how a slightly unstable solver turns into NaN rather than a small error. A wrong analytic Jacobian does not change the answer of an implicit solver (the equation G = 0 is the same) but slows Newton down or makes it fail; check it against a finite-difference Jacobian as in Newton for systems of equations.

title: Stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Summary

Test equation y' = \lambda y: a method multiplies by R(h\lambda) per step. Stability region: |R| \le 1. Euler h|\lambda| \le 2, RK4 \le 2.79: bounded for every explicit method.
Stiff: fast and slow time scales together; the explicit step is set by stability, not accuracy. Adaptive RK45 rides the stability limit: 3585 steps for the enzyme, 59 284 for Robertson to t = 40.
Backward Euler y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(y_{n+1}): R = 1/(1-z), stable for all decaying modes. Order 1. BDF2–5 for higher order, Radau for implicit RK.
Implicit = a Newton solve per step with Jacobian I - hJ: the cost of a step goes up, the number of steps goes down by orders of magnitude.
LSODA switches between Adams and BDF automatically (default in deSolve::ode; method="LSODA" in solve_ivp, whose default RK45 is non-stiff).
Failure: implicit methods damp oscillations that should persist. Checks: step counts, Jacobian eigenvalues, two solvers, atol, conservation, positivity.

Next: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane: the same Jacobian eigenvalues decide whether a steady state of the model is stable.

Recap. The common thread with the next unit: eigenvalues of the Jacobian. Here they set the time scales and decide whether a solver is stable; there they decide whether a steady state of the biology is stable. The Michaelis–Menten QSSA is the modeller’s alternative to an implicit solver: remove the fast variable by hand. Both are legitimate, but only the stiff solver keeps the full model.

title: Quiz: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of Runge–Kutta methods and adaptive step size. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Heun’s method uses two slopes per step. Which two, and how are they combined?






Hint





The first is Euler’s slope. Where is the second one evaluated?









Answer





\(k_1 = f(t_n, y_n)\) at the start, and \(k_2 = f(t_n + h, y_n + h k_1)\) at the point an Euler step would reach. The step uses their average: \(y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac h2 (k_1 + k_2)\), the trapezoid rule applied to the slope. Two evaluations, order 2.




Q2. One step of RK4 with \(h = 0.5\) on \(C' = -0.8\,C\), \(C_0 = 10\) gave \(k_1 = -8\), \(k_2 = -6.4\), \(k_3 = -6.72\), \(k_4 = -5.312\). What is \(C_1\)?






Hint





Weights \(1, 2, 2, 1\), divided by 6, times \(h\).









Answer





\(C_1 = 10 + \tfrac{0.5}{6}(-8 - 2\cdot6.4 - 2\cdot6.72 - 5.312) = 10 - \tfrac{0.5}{6}\cdot 39.552 = 6.704\). Exact: \(10e^{-0.4} = 6.7032\), so the error is \(8\times10^{-4}\) (Euler: \(-0.70\)).




Q3. You halve the step size and the error of your ODE solver drops from \(3.2\times10^{-6}\) to \(2.0\times10^{-7}\). What is the order of the method? Which method could it be?






Hint





Error \(\approx C h^p\); halving \(h\) divides it by \(2^p\).









Answer





The ratio is 16 \(= 2^4\), so order 4: for example classical RK4. On a log–log plot of error against \(h\) this is a slope of 4. If you expected RK4 and got a ratio of 2 or 4, there is a bug in one of the stages.




Q4. RK4 costs four function evaluations per step, Euler one. Why is RK4 nevertheless much cheaper for a given accuracy?






Hint





How does the number of steps needed scale with the target error \(\varepsilon\) for order 1 and order 4?









Answer





For error \(\varepsilon\), Euler needs \(h \propto \varepsilon\) and RK4 \(h \propto \varepsilon^{1/4}\). For \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\) on the logistic curve that was about 61 000 evaluations for Euler and 140 for RK4. Four times the work per step is a small price for steps that can be hundreds of times longer. Only for very rough answers (one digit) is Euler competitive.




Q5. In the Lotka–Volterra model, how can you tell from a numerical solution, without knowing the exact solution, that it is inaccurate?






Hint





What should stay constant along every true orbit?









Answer





The quantity \(V = cx - d\ln x + by - a\ln y\) is conserved by the exact solution. Compute \(V\) along the numerical solution: if it drifts (Euler: by 0.5 over 50 years; RK4 with \(h = 0.1\): by \(6\times10^{-6}\)), the solution has that much error, and an outward drift shows up as an orbit that spirals out. Any conserved quantity of a model (total mass, total number of molecules) can be used this way, although linear ones like \(S + I + R\) are kept exactly by every Runge–Kutta method and are therefore no test.




Q6. What is an embedded pair, and why is it useful?






Hint





Heun’s first stage is an Euler step.









Answer





Two Runge–Kutta formulas of different order (e.g. 1 and 2, or 4 and 5) that share the same stages, so one step gives two answers at almost no extra cost. Their difference estimates the error of the step. An adaptive solver uses that estimate to accept or reject the step and to choose the next step size. Dormand–Prince 5(4), behind ode45, RK45 and Dopri5, is the standard example.




Q7. An adaptive solver with a pair of orders 4 and 5 finds the scaled error \(\text{err} = 32\) for a step of \(h = 0.1\). Is the step accepted? What step does it try next (safety factor 0.9, exponent \(-1/5\), change at most a factor 5)?






Hint





\(32^{-1/5} = 1/2\).









Answer





\(\text{err} > 1\), so the step is rejected. New step: \(0.1\cdot\max(0.2,\ 0.9\cdot 32^{-1/5}) = 0.1\cdot 0.45 = 0.045\). The solver retries from the same point with \(h = 0.045\). The exponent \(-1/5\) comes from the local error of the order-4 member, which is \(\propto h^5\).




Q8. You solve an SIR model in counts of people (\(S \approx 10\,000\), \(I(0) = 10\)) with rtol = 1e-6. A colleague says atol = 10 is fine, “ten people do not matter”. What do you answer?






Hint





Allowed error per step \(=\) atol \(+\) rtol \(\cdot|y|\). How large is that for \(I\) at the start, compared with \(I\)?









Answer





At the start the allowed error in \(I\) is about 10 people, the size of \(I\) itself: the solver may get the seed of the epidemic wrong by 100%, and that error grows with the epidemic. In our runs it left a 3–5% error in \(I\) at day 60 that no value of rtol removed. atol must be well below the smallest value you care about in every variable (here, say, atol = 1e-6). It has the units of the variable, so it must change when you change units.




Q9. What does rtol = 1e-6 guarantee about the answer at \(t = 50\)?






Hint





Is the tolerance about one step or about the whole run?









Answer





Nothing directly. It controls the estimated error per step; errors from many steps add up and can be amplified (in an oscillator they shift the phase). For the repressilator, tolerance \(10^{-6}\) gave 4 correct digits of \(p_1(50)\), not 6. The practical check is to solve again with 10–100 times smaller tolerances and keep the digits that agree.




Q10. In deSolve, ode(y0, times = 0:50, func, parms, method = "rk4") gave \(p_1(50) = 3\times10^{58}\) for the repressilator, while method = "ode45" with the same times was fine. Why?






Hint





What step size does a fixed-step method in deSolve use?









Answer





deSolve’s fixed-step methods step from one output time to the next unless hini is given, so "rk4" used \(h = 1\), which is unstable for this model and blew up. "ode45" chooses its own steps (capped at the output spacing) to meet the tolerance. Choose fixed steps deliberately, and check them by halving.




Q11. What is dense output, and why does it matter for finding the peak of an epidemic?






Hint





Adaptive steps can be several days long.









Answer





A polynomial through each step, built from the stages already computed, that gives the solution at any time inside the step at no extra cost. Without it, the solution is known only at the solver’s steps (or at your output grid): taking max(I) over a daily grid misses the true SIR peak (3007.96) by 1.7 people, and joining long steps with straight lines cuts the peak. Event location (finding where \(\beta S/N - \gamma = 0\)) applies a root finder to the dense output.




Q12. Why can an event solver miss a population briefly crossing a threshold, and what can you do about it?






Hint





The solver only checks the sign of \(g\) at the ends of each step.









Answer





If \(g\) crosses zero and back within one step, it has the same sign at both ends, and no event is reported (lynx above 20 for 0.8 years, steps of 2.5 years). Remedies: limit the maximum step (hmax in deSolve, max_step in solve_ivp) to below the shortest excursion that matters, or watch a quantity that changes sign once per excursion, such as the derivative at a maximum.

title: Exercise: initial value problems and Euler’s method
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Euler’s method in your browser. The tab One equation has the lecture’s logistic OD curve (\(K = 1.2\), \(N_0 = 0.05\), \(r = 0.8\) per hour) and drug clearance (\(C' = -0.8\,C\), \(C_0 = 10\) mg/L). Panel (a) shows the direction field, the exact solution (blue) and the Euler steps (red); Step takes one step at a time, Run animates, Reset goes back to \(t = 0\), All steps jumps to the end. At the current point, the dashed orange segment is the next step (the tangent, of length \(h\)) and the dashed grey curve is the exact solution through the current Euler point. Panel (b) shows the global error at a fixed time (\(t = 5\) h for the logistic, \(t = 6\) h for clearance) against \(h\) on log–log axes, with a slope-1 line and the unstable range \(h > 2/k\) shaded; the large dot is the current \(h\). The readout gives the current step, the factor \(1 - kh\) (or \(1 - rh\)), the error and the ratio \(\text{error}(h)/\text{error}(h/2)\). The tab Systems runs the SIR epidemic and the 24-hour oscillator from the lecture.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R, Python and Rust, so the numbers agree with the lecture to the digits shown.



E1. (follow the slope) With logistic growth and \(h = 1\), click Reset and then Step three times. After each step write down \(N_n\), the slope \(f(N_n)\) and the exact value, and compare with your table from B3. Where does the dashed grey curve go after each step, and why does Euler fall behind?






Answer E1





\(N_1 = 0.08833\), \(N_2 = 0.15380\), \(N_3 = 0.26107\) against the exact \(0.10587\), \(0.21263\), \(0.38879\): the hand table. The slopes used are \(0.03833\), \(0.06547\), \(0.10727\). Each step follows the tangent at its start, but the curve bends upwards (it is convex below \(N = K/2 = 0.6\)), so the true slope increases during the step and Euler lands below the curve. The dashed grey curve is the exact solution through the current Euler point: after the first step Euler is on a different solution curve, lower than ours, and each further step moves to yet another one. The gap between that curve and the next Euler point is the local error; the gap to the blue curve is the global error.



E2. (order 1) Set \(h = 1\), \(0.5\), \(0.1\) and \(0.01\) with the slider. For each, read the error at \(t = 5\) and the ratio \(\text{error}(h)/\text{error}(h/2)\). Where does the large dot sit in panel (b)? How many steps would four correct digits at \(t = 5\) cost?






Answer E2





Errors \(-0.2004\), \(-0.09399\), \(-0.01703\), \(-0.001660\); ratios \(2.13\), \(2.12\), \(2.03\), \(2.00\). Dividing \(h\) by 10 divides the error by 10, and halving \(h\) halves it: order 1. The dot moves down the slope-1 line \(0.17\,h\), so an error of \(10^{-4}\) needs \(h \approx 10^{-4}/0.17 = 6\times10^{-4}\), about 8300 steps to reach \(t = 5\) (C2(c)). At \(h = 1\) the ratio is not yet 2 and the dot lies slightly off the line: the step is too large for the leading error term to dominate.



E3. (instability) Switch to drug clearance. Try \(h = 0.5\), \(1.25\), \(2\), \(2.4\) and \(3\), and use Step to watch the first few steps. Read the factor \(1 - kh\) and \(C\) at \(t = 12\) h. Which runs decay, which change sign, which grow? What happens in panel (b) as \(h\) passes \(2/k = 2.5\)?






Answer E3





\(h = 0.5\): factor \(0.60\), monotone decay, \(C(12) = 5\times10^{-5}\) (exact \(6.8\times10^{-4}\)). \(h = 1.25\): factor \(0\), the first step lands exactly on \(C = 0\) and stays there. \(h = 2\): factor \(-0.60\), the sign flips every step but the size decays (\(C(12) = 0.467\)). \(h = 2.4\): factor \(-0.92\), still decaying but slowly (\(C(12) = -6.59\)). \(h = 3\): factor \(-1.40\), the sign flips and the size grows; after two steps the solution leaves the plot, and \(C(12) = 38.4\) (the introduction’s example). In panel (b) the error at \(t = 6\) follows the slope-1 line for small \(h\), bends away for \(h\) around 1–2, and jumps to \(19.5\) in the shaded range \(h > 2.5\). A small \(h\) is accurate; a large one is not even stable, and the limit \(2/k\) depends only on the rate.



E4. (a confident wrong answer) Back on logistic growth, click the preset logistic h = 3, 60 h and step through it. What does Euler settle into? Compare \(h = 2.6\), \(2.4\) and \(1.5\) (time span 60 h). Which step sizes give the wrong long-term behaviour, and what single check would have shown it without the exact solution?






Answer E4





With \(h = 3\) (\(1 - rh = -1.40\)) the culture first grows like the true curve, then overshoots \(K = 1.2\) and settles into a boom–bust cycle between about \(0.75\) and \(1.44\) (the lecture’s 2-cycle \(0.77 \leftrightarrow 1.43\), reached after more steps). With \(h = 2.6\) (\(-1.08\)) there is a smaller cycle, \(1.01 \leftrightarrow 1.34\). With \(h = 2.4\) (\(-0.92\)) the oscillation around \(K\) is damped, \(1.18 / 1.22\) after 60 h, and with \(h = 1.5\) (\(-0.20\)) the run sits at \(K\). Above \(h = 2/r = 2.5\) the long-term behaviour is wrong: a regular cycle that the logistic ODE does not have. The check: halve the step. The cycle at \(h = 3\) disappears at \(h = 1.5\); a real oscillation would not.



E5. (systems) Open the Systems tab. For the SIR epidemic, click \(h = 4\), \(1\), \(0.1\) and \(0.01\) days and read the Euler peak, its day, the error and the conservation check. Then switch to the 24-hour oscillator, choose the 10-day span, and compare \(h = 1\), \(0.1\) and \(0.01\) h. Is either error check (conservation, amplitude) an accuracy check?






Answer E5





SIR peaks \(3535.245\) (day 48), \(3127.315\) (day 41), \(3019.556\) (day 38.6), \(3009.117\) (day 38.38) against the exact \(3007.961\): errors \(527\), \(119\), \(11.6\), \(1.16\), falling in proportion to \(h\) (order 1, panel (b)). \(S + I + R\) stays within about \(10^{-11}\) of \(10\,000\) for every \(h\), so conservation says nothing about accuracy. The oscillator’s amplitude after 10 days is \(2850\), \(2.2755\) and \(1.0857\); the orbit in the \((x, x'/\omega)\) plane spirals outwards instead of closing, growing by \(\sqrt{1 + \omega^2h^2}\) per step (\(1.0337\) for \(h = 1\) h, a factor \(2.2\) per day). The amplitude should be exactly 1, so its drift is an accuracy check: it shrinks in proportion to \(h\), but never vanishes, whatever the step.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
About this lecture
Part 9 is about fitting models: finding the parameter value that makes a model agree best with data. This lecture does it for one parameter.

A minimum of f is a root of f', but you can also search for the minimum directly, using only values of f: no derivative, and harder to fool.
Golden-section search keeps a three-point bracket and shrinks it by 0.618 per function evaluation: slow, but it cannot fail on a unimodal function.
Brent’s method (R’s optimize) adds fast parabolic steps. Newton for minimisation uses f'/f''.
Two limits: a minimum can only be located to about \sqrt{\varepsilon} \approx 10^{-8} (the bottom is flat), and every method here finds a local minimum, not necessarily the global one.

Biology: the decay rate of an mRNA from a time course (maximum likelihood with one parameter), and the period of a circadian rhythm, whose likelihood has two local maxima.

This opens Part 9. Everything here is one-dimensional, so we can draw every function we optimise, and see exactly what each method does. The next unit (Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton) moves to several parameters, where we can no longer draw the function and the ideas from today (brackets, local models, local versus global) are what keeps us safe. The link to Part 2 is direct: a minimum of a smooth function is a root of its derivative, and the methods mirror each other (golden section ~ bisection, parabolic interpolation ~ secant, Brent ~ Brent, Newton ~ Newton).

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: Recap: an MLE as the root of the score
text:
Recap: an MLE as the root of the score
From Newton and secant methods: UMI counts of a gene in the 100 cells where it was detected, modelled as a zero-truncated Poisson with rate \lambda.
\ell(\lambda) = 173\log\lambda - 100\,\lambda - 100\log(1 - e^{-\lambda}) + \text{const}, \qquad S(\lambda) = \ell'(\lambda) = \frac{173}{\lambda} - \frac{100}{1 - e^{-\lambda}}

The maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) \hat\lambda = 1.218 was found as the root of the score S, with Newton and with uniroot.
But the question was never “where is S = 0?”. It was “which \lambda makes the data most likely?”
Today: answer that question directly, by maximising \ell, and see what is gained and what is lost.


A quick reminder of the second running example of the Newton unit. 100 cells, counts 1 to 5 in 52, 30, 12, 5 and 1 cells, so the sum is 173. The truncation term (zeros are never seen) is what makes the MLE a transcendental equation. Newton from the mean converged in 6 steps; Newton from 3 ran off to negative rates; uniroot on a wide bracket found it safely.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Minimum versus root

Maximising \ell is the same as minimising f = -\ell (the convention of every optimiser). At a smooth minimum f'(x^*) = 0, so the minimum is a root of f'.
nll <- function(l) -(173 * log(l) - 100 * l - 100 * log(-expm1(-l)))  # minus log-lik
optimize(nll, interval = c(0.01, 10), tol = 1e-10)
# $minimum
# [1] 1.21847
#
# $objective
# [1] 52.61033

Same answer as uniroot on the score, without writing down the derivative. “nll” is the usual abbreviation for negative log-likelihood. optimize minimises by default; optimize(loglik, …, maximum = TRUE) maximises instead, which is the same thing. Python’s minimize_scalar and Rust’s argmin only minimise: pass the negative log-likelihood. $objective is the value of nll at the minimum.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: Why search for the minimum directly?
text:
Why search for the minimum directly?









root of f'
minimum of f

a minimum (lower values are always better)

Often there is no formula for f': f comes out of an ODE solver, a simulation, or a long likelihood.
Comparing two values of f tells you which one is better. A value of f' only tells you which way is downhill.
The price: we lose half of the digits. Usually that is fine for a parameter estimate.


The table is the plan of the lecture. Each method for minimisation has a root-finding twin: bisection becomes golden section, the secant method becomes parabolic interpolation, Newton stays Newton (on f’), and Brent combines the safe and the fast method in both cases. The last row is the surprise of the lecture, and we will see it on a plot. In practice, a rate estimated to 8 significant digits is far more precise than any data justify (the standard error is in the second digit), so the lost digits rarely matter; they matter when the optimum feeds another computation, such as a finite-difference derivative.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: A biology problem: how fast does an mRNA decay?
text:
A biology problem: how fast does an mRNA decay?
Transcription is stopped at t = 0 (actinomycin D); qPCR measures the fraction of the mRNA left.




Model: y_i = e^{-k t_i} + \text{noise}, one unknown, the decay rate k.
With Gaussian noise of constant size, the MLE of k minimises the sum of squared errors
\text{SSE}(k) = \sum_i \left(y_i - e^{-k t_i}\right)^2 .
\text{SSE}'(k) = 0 has no closed form.


The numbers are simulated with k = 0.35 per hour plus noise (sd 0.03), rounded to 3 decimals, so that we know the truth. The Gaussian log-likelihood is -SSE/(2 sigma^2) plus a constant, so for Gaussian noise “maximum likelihood” and “least squares” are the same fit; that is why we can minimise SSE. A common shortcut is to regress log(y) on t with lm, which is linear and has a formula. It gives k = 0.348, not 0.375: taking logs gives the small, noisy late points much more weight. It is a different statistical model (multiplicative noise), not a wrong one, but if the noise is additive the nonlinear fit is the MLE. The half-life is log(2)/k.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
The objective function
t <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8)                            # hours
y <- c(1.000, 0.804, 0.684, 0.484, 0.217, 0.094, 0.083)  # fraction left
sse <- function(k) sum((y - exp(-k * t))^2)
k <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 5)
round(sapply(k, sse), 4)
# [1] 2.6793 0.0723 0.0329 0.1678 0.3152 0.5726 0.7708 1.2769


One low valley near k = 0.4. For large k the curve flattens (all predictions near 0) and bends the other way (yellow).


The objective function (also cost, loss) is what we minimise. sse takes a single k, so we use sapply to evaluate it on a vector of k values. Evaluating on a coarse grid is always the first thing to do: it shows where the minimum is, roughly, and whether there is more than one. The yellow region, where SSE’’ < 0, will matter for Newton. For k -> infinity the model predicts 0 for every t > 0, and SSE tends to (1-1)^2 plus the sum of the other y^2, about 1.47.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Brackets for a minimum
A function is unimodal on [a, b] if it decreases to a single minimum x^* and increases after it.

A bracket for a minimum is three points a < c < b with f(c) < f(a) and f(c) < f(b): a low point between two higher ones. If f is continuous, a (local) minimum lies in (a, b).
From the grid on the previous slide: f(0) = 2.68 > f(0.5) = 0.033 < f(0.75) = 0.168. So (0, 0.5, 0.75) is a bracket; so is [0, 1] with c = 0.5.
Compare with root finding: there a sign change at two points was enough. Here two values say nothing: is the minimum between them, or beyond the lower one?

Recipe: evaluate f on a grid, take the lowest grid point and its two neighbours.

The analogy with the intermediate value theorem: a continuous function on a closed interval takes a minimum somewhere, and if the middle value is lower than both ends, that minimum is not at an end, so it is a local minimum inside. Unimodal is the property that makes it the only one. Two points are not enough: f(0.25) > f(0.5) is consistent with a minimum at 0.4 and with one at 3. Brent’s method in optimize assumes that the interval you give contains one minimum; it does not check.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Golden-section search: the idea
Place two points x_1 < x_2 inside [a, b] and compare f(x_1) with f(x_2):

f(x_1) < f(x_2): the minimum cannot be right of x_2. Keep [a, x_2].
otherwise: keep [x_1, b].


The trick is where to put x_1 and x_2: so that one old point is reused, and each step costs one new evaluation.

The analogue of bisection, but we need two interior points instead of one midpoint, because comparing two values is how we learn which part to throw away. If we put the two points anywhere, each step costs two evaluations. With the golden-ratio placement the surviving interior point is exactly in the right place for the next step, so each step costs one evaluation. In the figure: step 1 compares 0.382 and 0.618 and keeps [0, 0.618]; step 2 reuses 0.382 and adds 0.236; and so on.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Why 0.618?
Put the points symmetrically at fractions 1 - g and g of the interval, L = b - a:
x_1 = a + (1 - g)L, \qquad x_2 = a + gL .
Keep [a, x_2], of length gL. The old x_1 should be the new x_2, at fraction g of the new interval:
(1 - g)L = g \cdot gL \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g^2 + g - 1 = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} = 0.6180\ldots

The bracket shrinks by 0.618 per evaluation: L_k = 0.618^k L_0. That is linear convergence with rate 0.618.
Bisection for roots: 0.5 per evaluation (\log_{10} 2 = 0.30 digits). Golden section: \log_{10}(1/0.618) = 0.21 digits per evaluation.


g is 1 over the golden ratio phi = 1.618, hence the name. 1 - g = g^2 = 0.382. The symmetric case (keep [x1, b]) gives the same equation. Linear convergence in the sense of Convergence and cost: the error bound is multiplied by a fixed factor each evaluation. From width 1 to 1e-8 takes log(1e-8)/log(0.618) = 38 evaluations, plus the two to start. Golden section is optimal among methods that only compare function values, in the worst case; it is slower than bisection because comparing two values carries less information than a sign.
