Bold: the only new evaluation in each step. The other point is reused.
After 4 evaluations the minimum (\hat k = 0.3754) is in [0.2361, 0.4721].
0.382 is already close; golden section does not know that, and keeps shrinking at 0.618 per step.


Do this with the students. New points: in step 2, b - g(b - a) = 0.618 - 0.6180.618 = 0.2361. In step 3, a + g(b - a) = 0.2361 + 0.6180.3820 = 0.4721. Each comparison throws away the outer part on the side of the larger value. The exercise has the same by hand on a function you can evaluate with a calculator. Note that golden section uses only the order of the two values, not their size: f(0.382) is 40 times smaller than f(0.618), but that information is not used. Parabolic interpolation will use it.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
Optimisation in one dimension
text:
How fast?


Golden section: a straight line on a log scale, slope \log_{10} 0.618 = -0.21 per evaluation. Linear.
Brent and Newton: superlinear, but they stall near 10^{-9} and 10^{-13}. Why the floors differ comes in a few slides.


Error of the best point found so far, against the number of function evaluations, all on SSE(k). Golden section’s staircase follows 0.618^n; it reaches 1e-9 after about 42 evaluations. Brent (optimize with tol = 1e-12) and Newton (from 0.2, counting two evaluations per step for SSE’ and SSE’’) reach 1e-8 in about 10 evaluations. Brent stalls at about 5e-10: it compares values of f, and those values stop changing near the minimum. Newton works with the derivative and gets further. Keep this picture in mind for the slide on the flat bottom.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Parabolic interpolation
Use the sizes of the three values: fit a parabola through (a, f_a), (b, f_b), (c, f_c) and jump to its vertex,
x_\text{new} = b - \frac12\,\frac{(b-a)^2(f_b - f_c) - (b-c)^2(f_b - f_a)}{(b-a)(f_b - f_c) - (b-c)(f_b - f_a)} .


Near the minimum f looks like a parabola, so the vertex is very close: order about 1.32, superlinear.
Far away it can jump anywhere, even to a maximum (a parabola opening downwards). From (0, 0.5, 1) the next steps go to -1.51, then wander off to k = 34.


The minimisation twin of the secant method: there we fitted a line to two values of f and found its root; here we fit a parabola to three values of f and find its vertex. Repeating it with the three latest points is successive parabolic interpolation. From (0.2, 0.3, 0.5): errors 0.020, 0.014, 0.008, 7e-6, 2e-4, 2e-6, 2e-9: fast but not smooth. From (0, 0.5, 1), the first vertex 0.70 is already worse than 0.5, and the iteration then runs away: no bracket is kept. Like the secant method: fast when close, unsafe when not.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: Brent’s method: a fast step on a leash
text:
Brent’s method: a fast step on a leash
The minimiser twin of uniroot (Brent 1973):

Keep a bracket [a, b] and the three best points so far.
Try a parabolic step. Accept it if it lands inside the bracket and the steps are shrinking.
Otherwise take a golden-section step.


As safe as golden section; superlinear near the minimum. No derivative.
R: optimize (alias optimise). Python: scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar. Rust: argmin’s BrentOpt.
Also inside optim(method = "Brent") for one parameter.


Exactly the idea of the safeguarded root finder from Newton and secant methods: a fast method that is allowed to act only while it behaves, and a slow guaranteed method as a fallback. Brent’s minimiser starts at the golden-section point a + 0.382(b - a), which matters for the circadian example later. Python: minimize_scalar(f, bounds=(a, b), method=“bounded”) is the version with an interval like optimize; method=“brent” (the default) wants a bracket triple or finds one itself. In Rust, BrentOpt::new(a, b) from the argmin crate.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
optimize in practice
count <- 0
fc <- function(k) { count <<- count + 1; sse(k) }   # counts evaluations
optimize(fc, c(0, 1))$minimum; count
# [1] 0.3754002
# [1] 11
count <- 0; optimize(fc, c(0, 1), tol = 1e-10)$minimum; count
# [1] 0.3753873
# [1] 14
count <- 0; golden(fc, 0, 1, tol = 1e-10); count
# [1] 0.3753873
# [1] 50

Default tol is \varepsilon^{1/4} \approx 1.2\times10^{-4}, an absolute tolerance: the default answer is off in the 5th digit. Set tol.
Brent: 14 evaluations; golden section: 50, for the same accuracy.


The same default as uniroot, and the same advice. 0.3754002 versus the true 0.3753873: fine for reporting a half-life of 1.85 h, not fine if the estimate feeds into anything else. With tol = 1e-10 Brent takes only three more evaluations. Golden section needs 50, as predicted: log(1e-10)/log(0.618) = 48, plus 2. The counter uses <<- to change a variable outside the function, the same trick as in the Newton exercise. For the record: the half-life is log(2)/0.3754 = 1.85 hours.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: How precisely can we locate a minimum?
text:
How precisely can we locate a minimum?
Back to the zero-truncated Poisson, where the root of the score is known to full precision:
S <- function(l) 173 / l - 100 / (-expm1(-l))       # score = -nll'
lhat <- uniroot(S, c(0.01, 10), tol = 1e-15)$root
d <- 10^-(5:10)                                      # step away from lhat
nll(lhat + d) - nll(lhat)
# [1]  2.845923e-09  2.845013e-11  2.629008e-13  0.000000e+00  7.105427e-15
# [6] -2.842171e-14
S(lhat + d)
# [1] -5.691820e-04 -5.691856e-05 -5.691860e-06 -5.691860e-07 -5.691859e-08
# [6] -5.691874e-09
optimize(nll, c(0.01, 10), tol = 1e-15)$minimum - lhat
# [1] 6.859067e-10

1e-8 away from \hat\lambda, f has not changed at all; at 1e-10 it is even lower. The score still sees every step.
Asking optimize for tol = 1e-15 does not help: about 9 digits is all there is.


The values of nll near the minimum are around 52.6, and the change in nll over a distance of 1e-8 is about 3e-15: that is smaller than the gap between doubles near 52.6 (7e-15). So the computer literally cannot tell those two points apart by their f values. The differences we see for d <= 1e-8 are rounding noise: one of them is even negative, so a point 1e-10 away “looks better” than the minimum. The score, by contrast, is linear in the distance near its root, so its values keep shrinking in proportion: -5.69e-4, -5.69e-5, … all the way down.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
The flat bottom: why \sqrt{\varepsilon}

Taylor at the minimum, where f'(x^*) = 0: \;f(x^* + \delta) \approx f(x^*) + \tfrac12 f''(x^*)\,\delta^2.
The change is lost in rounding when \tfrac12 f''\delta^2 < \varepsilon\,|f(x^*)|, that is, for
|\delta| \lesssim \sqrt{\varepsilon}\,\sqrt{2|f(x^*)|/f''(x^*)} = 1.5\times10^{-8} \cdot \sqrt{2\cdot 52.6/56.9} \approx 2\times10^{-8} .

Left: nll minus its minimum on a 1e-8 scale, in units of 1e-14: a noisy staircase in steps of about 7e-15 (the gap between doubles near 52.6), around the true parabola (red). Any point in the middle region is as good as any other, as far as the computer can tell. Right: the score near the root is a clean straight line. A root changes f’ linearly in delta, so it is resolved to about epsilon; a minimum changes f quadratically in delta, so only to about sqrt(epsilon). This is a general limit, not a weakness of optimize: every method that compares values of f has it, including Nelder-Mead and the line searches in the next unit. If you need more digits, find the root of f’. And never set tol below about sqrt(eps)*|x|: R’s optimize and argmin’s BrentOpt both use a relative part sqrt(eps) internally for exactly this reason.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Newton for minimisation
Fit the local parabola (second-order Taylor) at x_k and jump to its vertex:
q(x) = f(x_k) + f'(x_k)(x - x_k) + \tfrac12 f''(x_k)(x - x_k)^2, \qquad x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{f'(x_k)}{f''(x_k)} .

This is Newton’s method on f': quadratic convergence near a minimum with f''(x^*) > 0.
For the zero-truncated Poisson, f = -\ell, f' = -S, f'' = -S': exactly the Newton iteration on the score from Newton and secant methods (6 steps from \bar x).
It needs f' and f'', and it works on f', so it reaches full precision (no \sqrt\varepsilon floor).
f''(\hat x) is the curvature at the minimum. For a likelihood, it gives the standard error.


The derivation in one line: q’(x) = f’(x_k) + f’‘(x_k)(x - x_k) = 0 gives the step. Newton for minimisation is not a new method; it is Newton for roots applied to f’. Everything from Part 2 carries over: digits double near the minimum, a wrong derivative makes it linear, a bad start can diverge. One new failure appears: f’’ can be negative, and then the local parabola opens downwards and its vertex is a maximum. Standard errors from the curvature are the topic of Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Newton on the decay rate
d1 <- function(k) sum(2 * (y - exp(-k * t)) * t * exp(-k * t))        # SSE'
d2 <- function(k) sum(2 * t^2 * exp(-k * t) * (2 * exp(-k * t) - y))  # SSE''
newton_min <- function(d1, d2, x0, n = 6) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in 1:n) x[i + 1] <- x[i] - d1(x[i]) / d2(x[i])
  x
}
print(newton_min(d1, d2, 0.2), digits = 10)
# [1] 0.2000000000 0.2778001915 0.3394487230 0.3697526835 0.3752380818
# [6] 0.3753872034 0.3753873095
newton_min(d1, d2, 0.7)
# [1]  0.700000 -1.659596 -1.597081 -1.534561 -1.472036 -1.409503 -1.346962
newton_min(d1, d2, 1.0)
# [1]  1.000000  3.956008  5.844671  7.797795  9.779586 11.772747 13.770211

From 0.2: digits double after a slow start. From 0.7: a negative rate. From 1.0: off to k = \infty.


Check d1 and d2 against numDeriv::grad and numDeriv::hessian before trusting them (the exercise does). The fixed number of steps keeps the slide short; a real implementation has a stopping rule as in the Newton unit. From 0.7, SSE’’ = 0.25 is small and positive: the local parabola is very flat and its vertex far to the left. From 1.0, SSE’’ is negative (-0.19): see the next slide.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
When Newton heads uphill


Left: f'' > 0, the local parabola opens upwards; its vertex is a good guess for the minimum.
Right: f'' < 0, the parabola opens downwards; its vertex is a maximum of q, and Newton walks away from the minimum, towards the flat plateau at k \to \infty.
Checks: f''(x_k) > 0 at every step, and f(x_{k+1}) < f(x_k). If either fails, do not take the step.


Root-finding Newton does not care whether a root of f’ is a minimum or a maximum; it heads for whatever stationary point the local model suggests. From k = 1 the nearest “stationary point” of the local model is a maximum at 3.96, and beyond that SSE keeps rising slowly towards its limit 1.47 at infinity, so Newton follows it out. The two checks are the start of the safeguards in the next unit: if f’’ <= 0 use a different direction, and if f does not decrease, shorten the step (line search). Or bracket first and let Brent do the work.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Convexity
f is convex on an interval if f''(x) \ge 0 there: the graph bends upwards everywhere, every chord lies above it.

A convex function has no separate local minima: a local minimum is the global one.
Newton’s local parabola always opens upwards, so each step points downhill. (It can still overshoot: see the exercise.)
-\ell for the zero-truncated Poisson is convex for all \lambda > 0 (-S' > 0). Any reasonable method finds \hat\lambda.
\text{SSE}(k) for the decay is convex only for k < 0.80 (the yellow region on the earlier plot). Start right of it and Newton fails.

Many likelihoods are convex in the right parameterisation (Poisson and logistic regression, in their coefficients). Nonlinear models (decay curves, ODEs, periods) usually are not.

Convexity is the property that turns “a local minimum” into “the answer”. It is why fitting a GLM never needs a starting value in practice, and why fitting an ODE model always does. Convexity depends on the parameterisation: SSE as a function of log(k) has a different shape. The exercise has f(x) = x - 2 log x, which is convex for all x > 0 and still sends Newton out of its domain from x0 = 4: convexity guarantees the direction, not the step length.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: Local versus global: a circadian period
text:
Local versus global: a circadian period
A bioluminescence reporter of a clock gene, every 4 h for 6 days. Fit a sine wave with unknown period T.
t <- seq(0, 140, by = 4)                           # 36 time points (h)
set.seed(15)                                       # simulated, true period 24.5 h
y <- round(2 + 0.6 * cos(2 * pi * (t - 6) / 24.5) + rnorm(36, sd = 0.3), 2)
rss <- function(T) {                               # best sine wave with period T
  X <- cbind(1, cos(2 * pi * t / T), sin(2 * pi * t / T))
  sum(lm.fit(X, y)$residuals^2)                    # linear least squares for fixed T
}

For a fixed T, mean, amplitude and phase come from a linear least-squares fit. What is left, \text{RSS}(T), depends on T only.
With Gaussian noise, \log L(T) = -\tfrac{n}{2}\log \text{RSS}(T) + \text{const}: minima of RSS are maxima of the likelihood.


Circadian periods are estimated like this all the time (cosinor fits, and periodograms, which are the same idea on a grid). The data are simulated so that we know the truth: period 24.5 h, peak at 6 h, amplitude 0.6, noise sd 0.3. Writing a cos + b sin instead of A cos(2 pi t/T - phi) makes the model linear in a and b, so for each T the best a, b and mean come from lm.fit (Least squares: normal equations vs QR). The remaining one-dimensional problem in T is the hard, nonlinear part: we “profile out” the linear parameters.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
optimize returns the wrong period

optimize(rss, c(10, 40))$minimum       # a plausible search range
# [1] 32.40162                         # a local minimum: as bad as no rhythm at all
optimize(rss, c(15, 35))$minimum
# [1] 24.63047                         # the global minimum

RSS(T) is flat at about 10.5 (the RSS of a flat line is 10.72) with small wiggles, and has one narrow, deep dip near the true period. Brent’s first two golden-section points on [10, 40] are 21.5 and 28.5, both on the flat part (orange crosses). RSS(28.5) = 10.31 is a bit lower than RSS(21.5) = 10.36, so the method keeps [21.5, 40]; the next comparison (28.5 against 32.9) keeps [28.5, 40], and the dip is gone for good. The method then converges, correctly, to a local minimum at 32.4 h. No warning: as far as optimize knows, the function is unimodal, because we promised it was.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Grid first, then refine
Tg <- seq(10, 40, by = 0.25)                # grid finer than the dip (about 3 h wide)
r  <- sapply(Tg, rss)
T0 <- Tg[which.min(r)]; T0
# [1] 24.75
optimize(rss, c(T0 - 0.5, T0 + 0.5), tol = 1e-6)$minimum
# [1] 24.63047
c(rss(24.63047), rss(32.40162))
# [1]  1.908081 10.225063

A grid finds the right basin; a local method (Brent, Newton) then polishes it. 121 + 10 evaluations.
The grid spacing must be smaller than the narrowest dip you care about. Too coarse and it can miss it too.
Alternatives: multistart (run from many starting points, keep the best), and always compare the objective at the candidates.


For one parameter a grid is cheap and the most reliable method there is; in ten parameters a grid is impossible (10^10 points for 10 per axis), which is why multistart and good starting values matter so much in the next units. The width of the dip is about the period squared divided by the length of the record, 24^2/140 = 4 h: longer recordings give narrower dips, which are both more precise and easier to miss. A periodogram (Fourier series and the FFT) is exactly this grid scan, computed fast. Comparing the objective at the two candidates settles it: 1.9 against 10.2.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
section: Checklist: before you trust a minimum
text:
Checklist: before you trust a minimum

Plot f over the whole plausible range. How many valleys?
Bracket: give optimize an interval that contains one minimum (grid first).
Set tol (default 1.2\times10^{-4}, absolute). Do not ask for more than \sim\sqrt{\varepsilon}\,|x|.
Check the answer: not at the edge of the interval? f at the answer lower than at nearby grid points? Biologically sensible (positive rate, period near 24 h)?
Hand-written Newton: check f' and f'' against finite differences; require f'' > 0 and f decreasing at each step.
Local vs global: try several intervals or starting points; compare f at every candidate.


A minimum at the edge of the interval almost always means the interval was wrong (or the true optimum is a boundary, which is a constrained problem: Constraints and linear programming). The “compare f at every candidate” check is what caught the 32.4 h period. These checks carry over unchanged to many parameters, where you can no longer plot f, which makes them more important there, not less.

title: Optimisation in one dimension
text:
Summary

A smooth minimum is a root of f', but minimising directly needs only values of f, never confuses a minimum with a maximum, and keeps a three-point bracket.
Golden section: shrink by 0.618 per evaluation (linear), safe on any unimodal function. Parabolic interpolation: superlinear (order ~1.32) but unsafe. Brent = both: optimize, minimize_scalar, BrentOpt. Set tol.
Newton: x_{k+1} = x_k - f'/f'', quadratic, needs f'' > 0; otherwise it heads for a maximum.
A minimum can only be located to about \sqrt\varepsilon relative: the bottom is flat. For more digits, find the root of f'.
Convex \Rightarrow local = global. Otherwise (a circadian period) a local method can return a local minimum without warning: grid first, compare candidates.

Next: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton: many parameters, the gradient and the Hessian, and line searches.

The one-dimensional methods return in the next unit as the line search inside every multivariate optimiser: choose a direction, then do a one-dimensional minimisation along it. The decay-rate fit returns with two parameters (initial amount and rate) in Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting, and the curvature at the minimum returns as standard errors in Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
About this lecture
Fitting a model means finding the parameters that make a misfit (a sum of squares, a negative log-likelihood) as small as possible. With more than one parameter we need new tools.

The gradient (the slopes in every direction) and the Hessian (the curvatures). Both are Jacobians, which you met in Newton for systems of equations.
Steepest descent with a backtracking line search, and why it zig-zags when the Hessian is badly conditioned.
Newton’s method for minimisation: fast near the minimum, unreliable far from it.
Quasi-Newton (BFGS, L-BFGS): build the curvature from gradients. Nelder–Mead: no derivatives at all.
What optim and scipy.optimize.minimize do, and why scaling and starting values matter. One slide on stochastic gradient descent.
Biology: fitting a 4-parameter logistic dose–response curve (EC50, Hill slope, top, bottom). We also explain the growth-curve failure from Why numerical analysis?.


This is the central unit of Part 9. Everything the students do when they call optim, nls or scipy.optimize.minimize happens here. The previous unit, Optimisation in one dimension, gave the one-variable picture: a minimum has f’ = 0 and f’’ > 0, golden section and Brent need no derivatives, and a line search picks a step along a direction. Today we go to several variables. The new mathematics is small: the gradient and the Hessian are Jacobians, so the students already know how to compute and check them. The real content is the behaviour of the methods: which ones are slow, which ones fail, and how to tell.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: A biology problem: a dose–response curve
text:
A biology problem: a dose–response curve




A reporter assay: 9 doses of an agonist, 2 wells each. The 4-parameter logistic (4PL):
m(c) = b + \frac{t - b}{1 + (\mathrm{EC50}/c)^{h}}

b, t: bottom and top plateaus (% of max)
\mathrm{EC50}: dose at half response (µM)
h: Hill slope



Find the 4 numbers that minimise the sum of squared errors \mathrm{SSE}(\mathbf p) = \sum_i (y_i - m(c_i))^2. There is no formula: we must search.


The 4PL (also called the Hill equation with baseline, or the four-parameter logistic of GraphPad Prism) is the standard model for dose-response data: drug screens, receptor assays, ELISA standard curves. The data are simulated (bottom 5, top 100, EC50 1.5 µM, Hill 1.2, noise sd 4), so we know what a good answer looks like. In Newton and secant methods we had a known curve and solved for the dose with R = 0.5; here the curve is unknown and we solve for its parameters from measurements. Four parameters means a search in four dimensions: we cannot plot the SSE, and grid search with 100 values per parameter would need 10^8 evaluations.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Fitting is minimising
dose <- rep(10^seq(-2, 2, by = 0.5), each = 2)        # µM: 9 doses, 2 wells each
y <- c(12.9, 9.8, 2.9, 0.1, 4.2, 9.7, 17.7, 22.3, 49.7, 42.1,
       67.3, 72.6, 97.4, 91.8, 94.6, 93.3, 92.9, 95.1)  # % of max response
f4 <- function(p, c)                     # p = (bottom, top, EC50, hill)
  p[1] + (p[2] - p[1]) / (1 + (p[3] / c)^p[4])
sse <- function(p) sum((y - f4(p, dose))^2)
p0 <- c(0, 100, 1, 1)                    # a first guess, read off the plot
sse(p0)
# [1] 558.9029

sse is an ordinary R function of a vector p of length 4. Every method today only needs to call it (and perhaps its gradient).
The best fit has \mathrm{SSE} = 314.924 at \mathbf p^* = (5.39,\ 96.17,\ 1.271,\ 1.240). How do we get there from \mathbf p_0?


The starting guess comes from the plot: the response runs from about 0 to about 100, crosses 50 near 1 µM, and a Hill slope of 1 is the usual default. Later in the lecture we see what happens with a worse guess. The answer quoted here is what every method in this lecture should agree on; we use it to measure errors. Note that p is a vector, and p[3] is EC50: R indexes from 1.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
What we already have
From Optimisation in one dimension:

At a minimum of f(x): f'(x^*) = 0 and f''(x^*) > 0. A line search finds a good step along one direction.

From Newton for systems of equations:

The Jacobian J of \mathbf F: \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^m has entries J_{ij} = \partial F_i / \partial x_j (row = output, column = input).
Newton for \mathbf F(\mathbf x) = \mathbf 0: solve J\,\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F, set \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \boldsymbol\delta. Quadratic convergence near the root.
A finite-difference Jacobian costs n+1 evaluations of \mathbf F, step h \approx \sqrt\varepsilon; numDeriv::jacobian does it more accurately.

Today: minimum of f(\mathbf x) = a point where all slopes are zero and the surface curves up in every direction.

One slide of recap. Two facts carry over: the one-variable conditions for a minimum, and Newton’s method as “linearise, then solve a linear system”. The plan for the rest of the lecture is to write “all slopes zero” as a system of n equations, the gradient equal to zero, and to reuse the Jacobian machinery on it. The idea of a line search from the previous unit comes back as the safeguard that makes every method in this lecture work from a poor start.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: The gradient: all slopes at once
text:
The gradient: all slopes at once


For f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 + x_1x_2 + 3x_2^2 at (2, 1):
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = 2x_1 + x_2 = 5, \quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = x_1 + 6x_2 = 8
\nabla f(2, 1) = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 8 \end{pmatrix}

The gradient \nabla f is the Jacobian of a scalar function: one row, written as a column.
It points uphill, perpendicular to the contour lines; -\nabla f is the steepest descent direction.
At a minimum: \nabla f(\mathbf x^*) = \mathbf 0.



Arrows: -\nabla \mathrm{SSE} for the 4PL, bottom and top held at their best values.


Pen and paper first: a partial derivative is the ordinary derivative with the other variable frozen, as in Newton for systems. A scalar function has a 1 by n Jacobian; by convention we write it as a column vector and call it the gradient, with the symbol nabla. Why uphill: the change of f for a small step d is approximately the gradient dotted with d, which is largest when d points along the gradient and zero when d runs along a contour. The figure shows the SSE of the dose-response fit as a function of EC50 and Hill, with the two plateaus frozen at their best values; every arrow is the negative gradient, normalised to the same length. All arrows cross the contours at right angles (the axes have the same scale) and point roughly, but not exactly, at the minimum.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: The gradient of the SSE: the chain rule
text:
The gradient of the SSE: the chain rule
\mathrm{SSE}(\mathbf p) = \sum_i r_i^2 with residuals r_i = y_i - m(c_i; \mathbf p), so
\nabla \mathrm{SSE} = -2\, J^\mathsf{T} \mathbf r, \qquad J_{ij} = \frac{\partial m(c_i)}{\partial p_j} \quad (18 \times 4)
grad_sse <- function(p) {
  u <- (p[3] / dose)^p[4];  D <- 1 + u
  J <- cbind(u / D,                                       # dm/d bottom
             1 / D,                                       # dm/d top
             -(p[2] - p[1]) * p[4] * u / (p[3] * D^2),    # dm/d EC50
             -(p[2] - p[1]) * u * log(p[3] / dose) / D^2) # dm/d hill
  -2 * drop(t(J) %*% (y - f4(p, dose)))
}
grad_sse(p0)
# [1]    -1.729861    48.929861 -1125.637873    59.964774
library(numDeriv);  grad(sse, p0)             # check with finite differences
# [1]    -1.729861    48.929861 -1125.637873    59.964774

The SSE is a sum of squares of the residuals, so each partial derivative is -2 times the sum of residual times the derivative of the model prediction. Collect the model derivatives in the 18 by 4 Jacobian of the predictions and the whole gradient is one matrix product. The four model derivatives are first-year calculus: with u = (EC50/c)^h and D = 1 + u, the derivative of D with respect to EC50 is h u / EC50 and with respect to h is u log(EC50/c). numDeriv::grad uses Richardson extrapolation of central differences (Numerical differentiation) and agrees to all printed digits. Always run this check before trusting a hand-coded gradient: a wrong sign or a missing factor shows up as a difference of order 1. Read the numbers: the slope along EC50 is 20 times larger than any other; we come back to that.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: The Hessian: the Jacobian of the gradient
text:
The Hessian: the Jacobian of the gradient
The gradient is a vector function of \mathbf x, so it has a Jacobian: the Hessian, H_{ij} = \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\,\partial x_j}.
For f = x_1^2 + x_1x_2 + 3x_2^2: \nabla f = (2x_1 + x_2,\ x_1 + 6x_2), so H = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 \end{pmatrix} (symmetric).
Quadratic model (Taylor in several variables):
f(\mathbf x + \mathbf s) \approx f(\mathbf x) + \nabla f^\mathsf{T}\mathbf s + \tfrac12\, \mathbf s^\mathsf{T} H\, \mathbf s
Test for a minimum: \nabla f = \mathbf 0 and H positive definite (all eigenvalues > 0): the surface curves up in every direction.

Here: eigenvalues 4 \pm \sqrt5 = 6.24,\ 1.76, both positive. One positive, one negative: a saddle. Both negative: a maximum.


The one-variable conditions f’ = 0, f’’ > 0 become gradient = 0 and Hessian positive definite. The Hessian is symmetric because mixed partial derivatives do not depend on the order (for smooth f). For a 2 by 2 matrix: positive definite if and only if the determinant and the trace are both positive; here det = 11, trace = 8. The quadratic model is the one from the Taylor table in Why numerical analysis?, now with vectors: s^T H s is the curvature along the direction s, times the length squared. Eigenvectors of H are the directions of largest and smallest curvature, the axes of the elliptical contours.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
The Hessian at the 4PL minimum
hess <- function(p) jacobian(grad_sse, p)      # Jacobian of the gradient
H <- hess(pstar);  round(H, 1)                 # pstar = best fit
#        [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4]
# [1,]   16.0    2.8 -123.8 -100.8
# [2,]    2.8   14.4 -123.6   99.6
# [3,] -123.8 -123.6 3611.5   12.5
# [4,] -100.8   99.6   12.5 3701.6
ev <- eigen(H, symmetric = TRUE)$values;  ev
# [1] 3708.824707 3618.223881    9.741189    6.737673
max(ev) / min(ev)
# [1] 550.4608

All four eigenvalues positive: a true minimum.
Curvature differs by a factor 550 between directions: the valley is long and narrow. This is the condition number \kappa(H) from Pivoting, norms and conditioning.


We get the Hessian as the finite-difference Jacobian of the analytic gradient: four extra gradient evaluations. This is exactly the finite-difference Jacobian of Newton for systems, applied to F = gradient. numDeriv::hessian(sse, p) also works and needs only sse, at more cost. The eigenvalues say: along EC50 and Hill (the large entries 3611 and 3701), the SSE is steep; along bottom and top, it is shallow, with curvature about 7 to 10. Part of this is units: a change of 1 µM in EC50 is a huge change, a change of 1 % in top is a small one. Condition number of a symmetric positive definite matrix = largest over smallest eigenvalue. We will see that kappa decides the speed of steepest descent, and in Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters, the same Hessian gives the standard errors.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: Steepest descent with a fixed step
text:
Steepest descent with a fixed step
Go downhill: \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k - \alpha\, \nabla f(\mathbf x_k), with a fixed step size \alpha.
x <- p0
for (k in 1:5000) x <- x - 1e-4 * grad_sse(x)
sse(x)
# [1] 315.1635                            # 5000 steps, still not at 314.924
x <- p0
for (k in 1:20) x <- x - 6e-4 * grad_sse(x)
sse(x)
# [1] NaN                                 # overshoots, EC50 < 0, NaN after 11 steps

Too small: slow. Too large: each step overshoots the valley and the iteration blows up.
On a quadratic, steepest descent is stable only for \alpha < 2/\lambda_{\max}; here 2/3709 = 5.4\times10^{-4}. Nobody knows \lambda_{\max} in advance.


This is the simplest possible method, and the one used (with tricks) to train neural networks. With alpha = 1e-4 it creeps; with 6e-4 the steps along the steep EC50 direction overshoot, grow, EC50 goes negative, (negative)^h is NaN in R, and everything after is NaN. The bound 2 / lambda_max is the same stability condition as for Euler’s method on y’ = -lambda y (Initial value problems and Euler’s method): steepest descent with a fixed step is Euler’s method on the gradient flow x’ = -grad f. A step that suits the steep direction is far too small for the shallow one, which is the whole problem.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Backtracking line search (Armijo)
Try \alpha = 1; halve it until the step decreases f enough: f(\mathbf x - \alpha \mathbf g) \le f(\mathbf x) - c\,\alpha\, \|\mathbf g\|^2, with c = 10^{-4}.
sd_armijo <- function(f, g, x, tol = 1e-4, maxit = 1e4) {
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    gk <- g(x)
    if (sqrt(sum(gk^2)) < tol) break           # gradient ~ 0: stop
    a <- 1
    while (!isTRUE(f(x - a * gk) <= f(x) - 1e-4 * a * sum(gk^2)))
      a <- a / 2                                # backtrack
    x <- x - a * gk
  }
  list(par = x, steps = k - 1)
}
sd_armijo(sse, grad_sse, p0)$steps
# [1] 3453

isTRUE also rejects a step that gives NaN. Never diverges; but 3453 steps.


The Armijo (sufficient decrease) condition asks for a decrease of at least a small fraction c of what the linear model predicts: alpha times the squared gradient length. Halving guarantees that some step is accepted, because for small enough alpha the linear model is accurate. This is the backtracking line search from Optimisation in one dimension, used here along the direction -g. Production codes also enforce a curvature condition (the Wolfe conditions) so that steps are not too short, and interpolate rather than halve. The stopping tolerance 1e-4 on the gradient length is about 1e-7 of its starting size; asking for much less runs into rounding, because a line search on f cannot see decreases below about eps times f (about 7e-14 here). A real code should also cap the number of halvings.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Why steepest descent zig-zags


On a long narrow valley, -\nabla f points across the valley, not along it. Each step overshoots to the other side.
With exact line search the error shrinks per step by about \dfrac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}. For the 4PL, \kappa = 550: 0.9964 per step, about 3800 steps per 6 digits.


Left: f = (x1^2 + 10 x2^2)/2, kappa = 10, exact line search: the best step along the current gradient. Successive directions are at right angles, so the path zig-zags across the valley and makes slow progress along it. Right: the error after k steps for kappa = 10, 100, 1000, from the worst-case start (1, 1/kappa). The rate depends only on kappa: (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1) per step for the error (its square for f - f*), so kappa = 10 needs about 70 steps per 6 digits and kappa = 1000 about 7000. The 4PL with kappa = 550 predicts about 3800 steps per 6 digits; our Armijo version took 3453, from a start where part of the error was in the steep directions. This is the same condition number as in Pivoting, norms and conditioning: there it bounded error amplification in a linear solve, here it bounds the speed of the simplest optimiser. Rescaling the parameters changes kappa, which is why scaling matters (later slide).

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Newton’s method for minimisation
Minimum \Rightarrow \nabla f = \mathbf 0: a system of n equations. Apply Newton for systems with \mathbf F = \nabla f and J = H:
H(\mathbf x_k)\, \mathbf s = -\nabla f(\mathbf x_k), \qquad \mathbf x_{k+1} = \mathbf x_k + \mathbf s







Newton for systems
Newton for minimisation




\mathbf F(\mathbf x) = \mathbf 0
\nabla f(\mathbf x) = \mathbf 0


Jacobian J
Hessian H (= Jacobian of \nabla f)


solve(J, -F)
solve(H, -g)




Same step = the minimum of the quadratic model. On a quadratic f, one step is exact. Toy example from (2, 1): \mathbf s = -H^{-1}(5, 8)^\mathsf{T} = (-2, -1), straight to (0, 0).
Quadratic convergence near the minimum. The condition number does not slow it down.


This slide is the bridge. Setting the derivative of the quadratic model to zero, grad f + H s = 0, gives the same step as Newton on the gradient. In one variable this is x - f’(x)/f’’(x), from Optimisation in one dimension. By hand: H = [2 1; 1 6], det 11, inverse = (1/11)[6 -1; -1 2]; H^-1 (5, 8) = (1/11)(30 - 8, -5 + 16) = (2, 1); the step is (-2, -1). Newton uses the curvature in every direction, so it rescales the long narrow valley into a round one: kappa no longer matters. The cost: second derivatives (n^2 of them) and a linear solve, O(n^3), per step.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Newton in R
newton_min <- function(f, g, H, x, tol = 1e-4, maxit = 50) {
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    gk <- g(x)
    if (sqrt(sum(gk^2)) < tol) break
    s <- solve(H(x), -gk)                      # Newton direction
    a <- 1                                     # line search, as before
    while (!isTRUE(f(x + a * s) <= f(x) + 1e-4 * a * sum(gk * s))) a <- a / 2
    x <- x + a * s
  }
  list(par = x, steps = k - 1)
}
newton_min(sse, grad_sse, hess, p0)$steps

Five steps instead of 3453. Every step here has a = 1, the full Newton step; the line search is only a safety net. Read the gradient row: 0.735, 1.4e-4, 2.2e-11, the exponent roughly doubles, which is quadratic convergence as in Newton and secant methods. The Hessian is the finite-difference Jacobian of the analytic gradient, with about 8 correct digits; that is enough for quadratic convergence in practice. Each step costs one gradient plus four more for the Hessian, plus a 4 by 4 solve: trivial here, expensive for thousands of parameters.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: Three methods on the same fit
text:
Three methods on the same fit


Newton: 5 steps. BFGS (in a few slides): 13 steps, gradients only. Steepest descent: a straight line on a log axis, linear convergence, slope set by \kappa.


Distance to the best parameters, log scale, all from the same start p0. The steepest descent curve on the right is a straight line after an initial phase: linear convergence, a fixed fraction per step, as in Convergence and cost. The slope corresponds to about 0.995 per step, close to the (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1) = 0.9964 predicted from kappa = 550. Newton bends down ever faster (quadratic). BFGS starts like steepest descent, because its first approximation of the Hessian is the identity, then learns the curvature and accelerates (superlinear convergence). In terms of work: steepest descent used 3453 gradients and many more function values for the backtracking.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
When Newton fails
Start from a worse guess, \mathrm{EC50} = 10 µM: \mathbf p = (0, 100, 10, 1).
eigen(hess(c(0, 100, 10, 1)), symmetric = TRUE)$values
# [1]   115.27332    13.13729   -42.62776 -2422.74914

Two negative eigenvalues: the quadratic model has no minimum (a saddle). Pure Newton steps head for any point with \nabla f = 0; after 20 steps: EC50 = 86, hill = 16, \mathrm{SSE} = 21188.
Check: eigenvalues of H, or \nabla f^\mathsf{T}\mathbf s < 0 (a descent direction); a line search only helps if \mathbf s goes downhill.
Fixes: make H positive definite (add \mu I; 9 steps to the minimum from here), a trust region, or quasi-Newton.


Far from the minimum the SSE is not shaped like a bowl. With EC50 = 10 µM the model curve sits to the right of most of the data, and the curvature along the Hill direction is negative. Newton’s method only looks for a zero of the gradient, so it is just as happy with a saddle or a maximum: the same lesson as in Newton for systems, where Newton found the unstable middle steady state. The fix “add mu times I” with mu larger than the most negative eigenvalue makes the model a bowl again; for huge mu the step becomes a short steepest descent step. That interpolation between Newton and steepest descent is the Levenberg-Marquardt idea of Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting. A trust region instead limits the step length to a region where the quadratic model is trusted.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: Quasi-Newton: learn the curvature from gradients
text:
Quasi-Newton: learn the curvature from gradients
The secant idea from Newton and secant methods: replace f'' by a slope of f' between two points. In n dimensions, with step \mathbf s_k = \mathbf x_{k+1} - \mathbf x_k and gradient change \mathbf y_k = \nabla f_{k+1} - \nabla f_k:
\textbf{secant condition:}\quad B_{k+1}\,\mathbf y_k = \mathbf s_k \qquad (B \approx H^{-1})
BFGS (Broyden, Fletcher, Goldfarb, Shanno, 1970) picks the update closest to B_k that satisfies it:
B_{k+1} = V^\mathsf{T} B_k V + \rho\, \mathbf s_k \mathbf s_k^\mathsf{T}, \qquad V = I - \rho\, \mathbf y_k \mathbf s_k^\mathsf{T}, \quad \rho = 1/(\mathbf y_k^\mathsf{T}\mathbf s_k)

Start from B_0 = I (first step = steepest descent). Direction -B_k \nabla f_k: no Hessian, no linear solve.
If \mathbf y_k^\mathsf{T}\mathbf s_k > 0, B stays positive definite: every direction goes downhill.


In one variable the secant condition says B times (change of f’) equals the step, which is the secant method applied to f’. In n variables one secant condition gives only n equations for the n^2 entries of B, so there are many solutions; BFGS takes the one closest to the previous B (in a weighted norm), which turns out to be a rank-2 update. The four authors found it independently in 1970. Keeping the inverse Hessian means no linear solve: the direction is a matrix-vector product, O(n^2). y^T s > 0 says the slope increased along the step, i.e. the function curves up along it; the Wolfe line search guarantees this, our simpler Armijo version checks it and skips the update otherwise. Broyden’s method for root finding, mentioned in Newton for systems of equations, is the same idea for a nonsymmetric Jacobian.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
BFGS in R
bfgs <- function(f, g, x, tol = 1e-4, maxit = 200) {
  n <- length(x); B <- diag(n); gk <- g(x)     # B ~ inverse Hessian
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    if (sqrt(sum(gk^2)) < tol) break
    s <- -drop(B %*% gk);  a <- 1
    while (!isTRUE(f(x + a*s) <= f(x) + 1e-4 * a * sum(gk*s))) a <- a / 2
    s <- a * s;  x <- x + s;  gn <- g(x);  yv <- gn - gk;  gk <- gn
    if ((sy <- sum(yv * s)) > 0) {             # curvature check
      V <- diag(n) - outer(yv, s) / sy
      B <- t(V) %*% B %*% V + outer(s, s) / sy }
  }
  list(par = x, steps = k - 1)
}
bfgs(sse, grad_sse, p0)$steps
# [1] 13

13 steps, one gradient each, plus backtracking. Superlinear convergence; no second derivatives.


Thirteen lines. The update is the formula from the previous slide; outer(s, s) is the matrix s s^T. Without a gradient function, the gradient is taken by finite differences, which is what optim does when you do not pass gr. Compare the costs: steepest descent 3453 gradients; Newton 5 gradients plus 5 Hessians (20 gradients with finite differences); BFGS 13 gradients. For four parameters all are instant; for an ODE model where each SSE evaluation takes a second, the difference is hours.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: L-BFGS: when there are many parameters
text:
L-BFGS: when there are many parameters

BFGS stores an n \times n matrix. For n = 10^6 parameters (an image, a genome-wide model, a neural network) that is 8 \times 10^{12} bytes.
L-BFGS (limited-memory BFGS) never forms B. It keeps the last m pairs (\mathbf s_k, \mathbf y_k), typically m = 5 to 20, and computes -B\nabla f from them in O(mn) operations.
Each step costs about as much as a steepest-descent step, but converges almost as fast as BFGS.
In R: optim(method = "L-BFGS-B") (the B is for bounds, e.g. lower = 0). In Python: minimize(method="L-BFGS-B"), the default when bounds are given.


The memory argument is the whole story: n^2 storage and n^2 work per step are fine for 4 or 400 parameters and impossible for a million. L-BFGS applies the last m updates to a scaled identity using a short recursion (the two-loop recursion), never storing a matrix. In practice it is the default large-scale smooth optimiser. L-BFGS-B adds simple bounds, lower <= p <= upper, which is useful for parameters that must be positive; Constraints and linear programming treats constraints properly.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Nelder–Mead: no derivatives at all


Keep n + 1 points (a simplex: a triangle in 2-D). Replace the worst by its reflection through the others; expand if that was very good, contract if bad, shrink if nothing helps.
Needs only f: works for noisy or non-smooth functions. optim’s default. Slow, and it can stop at a non-minimum, especially in many dimensions.


Nelder and Mead, 1965. No gradients, no line search, just comparisons of function values, so it does not care about rounding noise in f, kinks, or discontinuities that would wreck a finite-difference gradient. Right: the points R’s optim evaluates when fitting only EC50 and Hill (63 evaluations); the simplex tumbles downhill, then shrinks around the minimum. Weaknesses: in more than a handful of dimensions it becomes very slow, and the simplex can collapse into a flat shape and stop where the gradient is not zero; there are known examples (McKinnon 1998) where it converges to a non-stationary point. Its stopping rule is “the function values at the corners agree to reltol”, which is also satisfied on a plateau: that is what happened to the growth curve in Why numerical analysis?.
