No gradient given → finite differences: R’s optim uses central differences with ndeps = 1e-3 (an absolute step!); scipy uses forward differences with h \approx \sqrt\varepsilon\max(1, |x|).
Stopping: relative change in f below reltol \approx 1.5\times10^{-8} (R), gradient norm below gtol = 10^{-5} (scipy BFGS). maxit = 500 for Nelder–Mead, 100 for BFGS in R.
convergence = 0 means “a stopping rule was met”, not “this is the minimum”.


The point of this table is that the library methods are the ones we just wrote, plus careful engineering: better line searches (Wolfe conditions, interpolation), scaling of the first B, and stopping rules. Defaults matter. optim’s ndeps = 1e-3 is an absolute step: fine for parameters near 1, terrible for a parameter of size 1e-6 or 1e4, which is one more reason to scale. R’s nlm is a Newton-type method with finite-difference Hessian; nlminb (PORT library) is another common choice. Python users: minimize returns an OptimizeResult with x, fun, nfev, njev, success, message. The Rust argmin crate provides the same solvers; we use it in the exercises.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
The 4PL with optim
for (m in c("Nelder-Mead", "BFGS", "CG", "L-BFGS-B")) {
  o <- optim(p0, sse, method = m)
  cat(sprintf("%-11s  SSE %.4f  EC50 %.4f  fn %3d  gr %3s  conv %d\n",
              m, o$value, o$par[3], o$counts[1], o$counts[2], o$convergence))
}
# Nelder-Mead  SSE 314.9240  EC50 1.2711  fn 335  gr  NA  conv 0
# BFGS         SSE 314.9240  EC50 1.2711  fn  40  gr  11  conv 0
# CG           SSE 321.2024  EC50 1.2765  fn 333  gr 101  conv 1
# L-BFGS-B     SSE 314.9240  EC50 1.2710  fn  36  gr  36  conv 0

fn, gr: calls of sse and of the (finite-difference) gradient; each gr costs 8 more sse calls.
Conjugate gradients hit maxit = 100 (conv 1): another victim of \kappa = 550.
Passing the analytic gradient, optim(p0, sse, grad_sse, method = "BFGS"), saves the finite-difference calls.


All but CG agree on the minimum to the printed digits. Nelder-Mead needs 335 function calls; BFGS 40 plus 11 gradients, each of which is 8 function calls by central differences, so 128 in total. CG is a method between steepest descent and quasi-Newton that needs only O(n) memory; it is also slowed down by a bad condition number and stops at its iteration limit with a worse SSE. It at least says so: convergence = 1 means maxit reached. Always print the convergence code and the counts.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: Scaling: the same data in nM
text:
Scaling: the same data in nM




dose_nM <- dose * 1000
sse_nM <- function(p) sum((y - f4(p, dose_nM))^2)
o <- optim(c(0, 100, 1, 1), sse_nM, method = "BFGS")
round(o$par, 2); o$value; o$convergence
# [1]  48.69 127.67   2.24 -13.82
# [1] 25807.26
# [1] 0


“EC50 is about 1” is now 1000 times too small. The curve sits left of every dose; BFGS slides to a flat line at the mean (hill = -13.8) and reports success.
Even from a good start (EC50 = 1000), \kappa(H) = 1.9\times10^{6} and BFGS stops early: SSE 314.9246, 109 calls. With control = list(parscale = c(1, 100, 1000, 1)): 314.9240, 36 calls.


Same data, same model, only the dose unit changed. Two separate problems. First, the habit of starting at 1: with doses from 10 to 100000 nM, an EC50 of 1 nM means every well is on the top plateau, and the optimiser goes to a degenerate fit where the curve is flat over the data (a negative Hill slope with EC50 below all doses gives the constant 48.69, the mean of y). The SSE is then flat in EC50 and hill, the gradient is zero there, and BFGS stops. Second, scaling: the EC50 entry of the Hessian shrinks by a factor 10^6, the condition number grows from 550 to 1.9 million, and the finite-difference step ndeps = 1e-3 is now tiny relative to EC50 = 1271. parscale tells optim to work with p / parscale internally, so all parameters are of size 1. Fitting log10(EC50) instead of EC50 does the same job and also keeps EC50 positive.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Back to the growth curve
Why numerical analysis?: logistic fit, time in minutes, start r = 0.5 (“per hour” by habit).
grad(sse_min, c(r = 0.5, K = 1, N0 = 0.05))      # time in minutes
# [1] 0.000 3.940 0.098
optim(c(r = 0.5, K = 1, N0 = 0.05), sse_min, method = "BFGS")$par
#            r            K           N0
# 0.5000000000 0.8358333304 0.0009999665
optim(c(r = 0.5, K = 1, N0 = 0.05), sse_h)$par   # time in hours
#         r         K        N0
# 0.5241071 1.1913604 0.0165278

At r = 0.5/min the model reaches K within minutes, long before the first reading: \partial\,\mathrm{SSE}/\partial r \approx 4\times10^{-23}. BFGS never moves r; Nelder–Mead wanders on the plateau until its corner values agree.
In hours the natural guess is right, and \kappa drops from 1.2\times10^4 to 1.0\times10^3. Choose units so parameters are near 1.


Now we can explain the opening failure of the course. The model at r = 0.5 per minute predicts e^(-60) of the way from K at the first measurement (120 minutes), so it is K at every time point after zero. Changing r changes nothing: the exact partial derivative is 3.8e-23, numDeriv prints 0. A gradient method moves only in directions where the slope is nonzero, so r stays exactly 0.5 and only K and N0 are fitted (K to the mean of the later points). Nelder-Mead’s reflections in r also change nothing, the corner values agree to reltol and it stops. With time in hours the same starting value is in the right region, both Nelder-Mead and BFGS find r = 0.524 per hour (doubling time 79 minutes), and the Hessian is better conditioned because r is no longer 100 times smaller than the other parameters.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Starting values and multistart

Start from the data: bottom ≈ min(y), top ≈ max(y), EC50 ≈ dose where y crosses halfway, hill ≈ 1. R’s SSfpl self-start model for nls does this for you.
Multistart: run from many starts, keep the best, and look at how many agree.

starts <- expand.grid(EC50 = 10^(-2:2), hill = c(0.5, 1, 3))   # 15 starts
nm <- apply(starts, 1, function(s) optim(c(0, 100, s), sse)$value)
table(round(nm, 1))
#  314.9 1344.4 1557.2 1926.8 2453.2
#     10      2      1      1      1

Nelder–Mead from 15 starts: 5 end far from the minimum, 4 of them with convergence = 0. BFGS with the analytic gradient finds 314.9 from all 15.


These are the generic defences, and they are cheap. A data-based start is what commercial curve-fitting software does. SSfpl uses log dose and a scale parameter (1/Hill on the natural log scale), which also takes care of scaling. Multistart costs 15 fits here, a fraction of a second. If all starts agree, you have some confidence it is the global minimum (no proof!); if they disagree, look at the bad ones: here Nelder-Mead ends with a step-like curve (Hill 11 to 14) from two of the Hill = 3 starts, and with a very shallow one (Hill 0.17 to 0.45, plateaus far outside the data) from three others; only one of the five says so (convergence = 1, maxit reached). Different local minima, or the same minimum found with poor accuracy, are both worth knowing about. The rows of starts are (EC50, hill); bottom and top start at 0 and 100.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
section: Stochastic gradient descent, in one slide
text:
Stochastic gradient descent, in one slide
When the objective is a sum over many data points, f(\mathbf p) = \sum_{i=1}^N f_i(\mathbf p), with N in the millions (images, sequences, cells):
\mathbf p_{k+1} = \mathbf p_k - \alpha_k \sum_{i \in \text{batch}_k} \nabla f_i(\mathbf p_k)

Each step uses the gradient of a small random minibatch (say 32 points): a noisy but cheap estimate of \nabla f.
No line search: the learning rate \alpha_k is set by hand and decreased over time; variants (momentum, Adam) adapt it per parameter, a cheap form of scaling.
This is how neural networks are trained (gradients by automatic differentiation). For an 18-point dose–response curve, use BFGS.


One slide only, because students will meet it in machine learning. The noise is a feature for huge data sets: a full gradient over 10 million images costs 10 million evaluations; a minibatch gradient costs 32, so you get hundreds of thousands of rough steps for the price of one exact one. The disadvantages are those of steepest descent (condition number, step size) plus noise: it converges slowly to an exact minimum, which in machine learning is not the goal. Adam divides each gradient component by a running estimate of its size, which is a diagonal rescaling, the same idea as parscale. Automatic differentiation computes exact gradients by applying the chain rule to the program; it is the third way, next to hand-derived and finite differences.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Checklist for a fit

Check the gradient against numDeriv::grad before using it (agreement to ~10^{-6} relative, not ~1).
Look at the convergence code and the counts; maxit reached means “not finished”.
Plot the fitted curve over the data. A flat line or a step is a degenerate fit.
Units and scale: parameters near 1 (µM, hours, log EC50), or parscale.
Start from the data, and multistart: do the answers agree?
At the answer: gradient near 0 and Hessian eigenvalues all positive (a minimum, not a saddle or plateau). A huge \kappa warns of poorly determined parameters.
Method: smooth with gradient → BFGS (L-BFGS for many parameters); noisy or non-smooth → Nelder–Mead; sum of squares → Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting.


A list to keep next to the keyboard. Each item caught one of today’s failures: the wrong gradient (exercise), the iteration limit (CG), the flat fits (nM start, growth curve), the bad conditioning (nM, minutes), the bad starts (Nelder-Mead multistart), and the saddle (Newton from EC50 = 10). The Hessian at the answer comes back in Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters, where its inverse gives standard errors; a near-zero eigenvalue means a parameter combination the data do not determine.

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Summary

Gradient \nabla f: Jacobian of a scalar function, points uphill. Hessian H: Jacobian of the gradient. Minimum: \nabla f = \mathbf 0, H positive definite.
Steepest descent + backtracking (Armijo): always goes downhill, but converges linearly at a rate set by \kappa(H); it zig-zags in narrow valleys.
Newton: solve H\mathbf s = -\nabla f. Quadratic convergence near the minimum; can head for saddles when H is not positive definite.
BFGS builds H^{-1} from gradient differences; L-BFGS stores only a few of them. Nelder–Mead uses only f.
optim (default Nelder–Mead) and minimize (default BFGS) report “converged” when a stopping rule is met. Scale the parameters, start from the data, multistart, check.

Next: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting: Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt use the structure of a sum of squares.

Recap the three families: first-order (steepest descent, SGD), second-order (Newton), and in between (quasi-Newton), plus the derivative-free simplex. The SSE has special structure: its Hessian is approximately 2 J^T J, using only the model Jacobian we already computed for the gradient. That is Gauss-Newton, and adding mu I to it is Levenberg-Marquardt, the method behind nls and minpack.lm: the next unit.

title: How eigen() works, and big problems
section: Try it: the QR algorithm, live
text:
Try it: the QR algorithm, live




The QR algorithm computed live in the browser, with deflation below 1e-12 exactly as in exercise C2. Left: A_k as a heat map (blue positive, orange negative, paler = smaller, white below 1e-12; the diagonal outlined, deflated eigenvalues in green). Right: the subdiagonal entries on a log axis, with the dashed rates |lambda_{i+1}/lambda_i|^k when there is no shift. Start with the lecture’s 3 x 3, no shift: step +1 gives the A_1 of the background (4.41, 0.691, 3.15, -0.538, 1.43); press play: a32 follows 0.423^k and deflates at k = 33, a21 follows 0.634^k, all three eigenvalues at k = 62 (fig02). Switch to Rayleigh: 7 steps, |a32| goes 7e-3, 1e-7, 6e-22 (fig03); Wilkinson: 4 steps. Then “close lambda1, lambda2”: rate 0.932, 367 steps unshifted, 6 with Wilkinson. B with the Rayleigh shift: mu = 2 sits halfway between 1 and 3 and nothing moves; Wilkinson finds both in one step. Predator-prey J: the 2 x 2 block keeps rotating (next slides). 4 x 4 community: a43 deflates (-0.5), a21 goes to 0 (-3), the block for -1 +- i stays and repeats every 4 steps. If time allows, the second tab belongs to the sensitivity slides: n = 10, eps = 1e-10 moves the chain’s eigenvalues by 0.1 and the symmetric matrix’s by 4e-11.

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
About this lecture
In Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting we fitted a pharmacokinetic model and got numbers for k_a, k_e and V. This lecture asks how much those numbers can be trusted.

Structural non-identifiability: the model itself cannot tell parameters apart (a product F\!\cdot\!D/V; the k_a/k_e flip-flop). No amount of data helps.
Practical non-identifiability: the model could, but these data do not.
Near the optimum the sum of squares is a bowl. Its curvature, the Hessian \approx 2J^TJ, gives standard errors \sqrt{\operatorname{diag}(s^2(J^TJ)^{-1})} and a correlation matrix.
Small singular values of J name the badly determined combinations, as in The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation.
The profile likelihood checks the bowl picture, and shows flat directions the standard errors hide. Sloppy models have many of them.
Fixes: better sampling times, reparameterisation, priors.


This closes the loop of Part 9: we can now fit a nonlinear model, and the question is what the fitted numbers mean. The numerical content is small (a Jacobian, a matrix inverse or SVD, a loop of re-fits), but the consequences are large: a model that fits the data perfectly can still have parameters that are not determined at all. The running example is the one-compartment oral pharmacokinetic model from the previous unit. Everything here applies equally to growth curves, enzyme kinetics and signalling models.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: A biology problem: the fit is fine
text:
A biology problem: the fit is fine


One oral dose of 100 mg; the first blood sample is taken at 3 h. Three fits with absorption rate k_a = 1.12, 3 and 20 /h (each with k_e and V re-fitted) pass equally well through the data.
The grey circles are what early samples would have shown. Without them, the data cannot say how fast the drug was absorbed.
nls happily reports k_a = 1.12 \pm 0.41 /h. Is that number worth anything?


This is the situation the lecture is about. The model fits, the residuals look fine, the software prints an estimate and a standard error, and yet the parameter is not determined: any absorption rate from about 0.7 per hour to infinity (instant absorption) fits the late data. The curves only differ before the first sample. In clinical pharmacokinetics this is common: outpatients come in hours after the dose. The data are the simulated measurements of the previous unit (true ka = 1, ke = 0.2, V = 20, noise SD 0.1 mg/L) so that we know the truth; the grey points are the early samples of the same simulated subject.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Recap: the model and the fit
text:
Recap: the model and the fit
One-compartment model, oral dose D, bioavailability F (fraction absorbed):
C(t) = \frac{F\,D\,k_a}{V\,(k_a - k_e)}\left(e^{-k_e t} - e^{-k_a t}\right)
pk <- function(t, ka, ke, V, D = 100) D * ka / (V * (ka - ke)) * (exp(-ke * t) - exp(-ka * t))
t <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)                          # h
y <- c(1.02, 1.88, 2.34, 2.98, 3.27, 3.26, 3.17, 2.77, 1.92, 1.23, 1.00, 0.61)  # mg/L
fit <- nls(y ~ pk(t, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 0.5, ke = 0.1, V = 10))
coef(fit)
#         ka         ke          V
#  1.0150721  0.1906157 20.2162113
deviance(fit)                          # residual sum of squares
# [1] 0.06646744

The data of the previous unit: 12 samples, F = 1 assumed. Truth: k_a = 1, k_e = 0.2 /h, V = 20 L, noise SD 0.1 mg/L.


The same model as in the previous unit: first-order absorption from the gut with rate ka, first-order elimination with rate ke, one well-mixed compartment of volume V. The fit with all 12 samples recovers the truth well. The rest of the lecture asks how well, and what goes wrong with fewer or worse-placed samples. D = 100 mg, so D/V has units mg/L. nls uses Gauss-Newton by default; the details are in the previous unit.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Two kinds of trouble
A parameter is identifiable if the data determine it: different values give different predictions.









Structural
Practical




Cause
the model equations
the data (too few, too noisy, badly placed)


Perfect, noise-free data
still not determined
determined


Example
F and V only as F/V; flip-flop
k_a with first sample at 3 h


Symptom
J exactly rank-deficient; equal-SSE minima
huge SE, |r| \to 1, flat profile


Fix
reparameterise, add a different experiment
better design, more data, prior




Structural identifiability is a property of the model and the measured output alone; one can check it with algebra before any experiment. Practical identifiability depends on how many samples, where, and how noisy. A structurally identifiable model can be practically non-identifiable (our sparse design); a structurally non-identifiable model stays so whatever the data. Both show up in the same numerical objects: the Jacobian and the shape of the sum of squares.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Structural (1): parameters that only appear as a product
text:
Structural (1): parameters that only appear as a product
If the bioavailability F is unknown, F and V enter only through F/V: doubling both changes nothing.
nls(y ~ pk(t, ka, ke, V / F), start = list(ka = 0.5, ke = 0.1, V = 10, F = 0.8))
# Error in nlsModel(...) : singular gradient matrix at initial parameter estimates
library(numDeriv)                     # numerical Jacobian and Hessian
p4 <- c(coef(fit), F = 1)
J4 <- jacobian(function(p) pk(t, p[1], p[2], p[3] / p[4]), p4)
svd(J4 %*% diag(p4))$d                # columns scaled: d C / d log p
# [1] 1.189228e+01 3.483442e+00 1.047785e+00 2.252039e-11
round(svd(J4 %*% diag(p4))$v[, 4], 3)
# [1]  0.000  0.000 -0.707 -0.707      # log V and log F together

The Jacobian has an exact null direction: \sigma_4 \approx 10^{-11} (rounding), v_4 \propto (0, 0, 1, 1) in (\log k_a, \log k_e, \log V, \log F).
Fix: fit and report the identifiable combination, the apparent volume V/F. Separating F needs a different experiment (an IV dose).


“Singular gradient” is how nls reports that the columns of the Jacobian are linearly dependent; Gauss-Newton cannot solve for a step. The SVD tells us exactly which combination is missing: the right singular vector for the zero singular value says increase log V and log F by the same amount, i.e. V/F stays fixed. We use log parameters (each column multiplied by its parameter) so that the singular vectors are about relative changes. jacobian is from the numDeriv package. Pharmacokineticists report V/F and CL/F after oral dosing for exactly this reason; F itself needs an intravenous reference dose.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Structural (2): the flip-flop

Recap from Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting: swap k_a \leftrightarrow k_e, set V' = V\,k_e/k_a, and C(t) is identical for every t.

Two exact minima, same SSE (0.066467): (1.015, 0.191, 20.2) and (0.191, 1.015, 3.80). Each is locally identifiable (right: fix k_a, re-fit the rest: two wells of equal depth); globally the data cannot choose.
Check: multistart. Equal SSE at different parameters = a symmetry, not a convergence problem. Fix: outside knowledge: an IV dose gives k_e; or impose k_a > k_e by fitting k_a = k_e + e^{\delta}.


The previous unit found the two minima with a multistart and checked the algebra: with ka and ke swapped the prefactor becomes ke/(V’(ke-ka)) and the bracket changes sign, so the curve is unchanged if ke/V’ = ka/V. What is new here is the classification and the right-hand panel. It is a profile, which we define properly later: for each fixed ka, re-fit ke and V and record the rise in SSE. The two wells have exactly equal depth; the hump between them is what keeps an optimiser on one side, so which minimum you get depends on the start (and, exercise C2 shows, on the algorithm). Slow-release formulations really do show flip-flop kinetics, so the constraint ka > ke is a modelling decision: make it explicitly and say so.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
The flip-flop in practice
fit2 <- nls(y ~ pk(t, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 0.1, ke = 0.5, V = 5))
coef(fit2)
#        ka        ke         V
# 0.1906156 1.0150718 3.7963082
c(deviance(fit), deviance(fit2))
# [1] 0.06646744 0.06646744

Same residuals, different parameters. Neither run warns.
Check: multistart (previous unit). Equal-SSE minima at different parameter values mean a structural problem, not a convergence problem.
Fix: use outside knowledge. An IV dose gives k_e directly; or impose k_a > k_e by fitting k_a = k_e + e^{\delta}.


The multistart check from the previous unit was a guard against local minima. Here it finds two minima with identical SSE to all printed digits, which is the signature of a symmetry in the model. The second solution has V = 3.8 L, which is physiologically odd for many drugs, but only outside knowledge can say that. Constraining ka > ke is a modelling decision: make it explicitly and say so.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Near the optimum the SSE is a bowl
text:
Near the optimum the SSE is a bowl
Taylor expansion of S(\theta) = \sum_i r_i(\theta)^2 around the optimum \hat\theta (gradient = 0):
S(\hat\theta + \delta) \approx S(\hat\theta) + \tfrac12\,\delta^T H\,\delta, \qquad H = \nabla^2 S
With residuals r_i = y_i - C(t_i;\theta) and the Jacobian J_{ij} = \partial C(t_i)/\partial\theta_j (12\times3):
H = 2J^TJ \;-\; 2\sum_i r_i\,\nabla^2 C(t_i) \;\approx\; 2J^TJ

The second term is small when residuals are small and random: this is the Gauss–Newton approximation from the previous unit.
Steep directions of the bowl (large eigenvalues of H) are well determined; flat ones are not.


This is the multivariate version of the parabola from Optimisation in one dimension: near a minimum every smooth function looks quadratic, and the curvature tells how sharply the minimum is defined. The Hessian of the sum of squares has two parts; the one with second derivatives of the model is multiplied by residuals, which are small and of both signs at a good fit, so it nearly cancels. That is why J^T J (which needs only first derivatives) is used everywhere. We will check the approximation numerically in two slides.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Standard errors from the Jacobian
If the noise is independent with variance \sigma^2, the estimate is approximately normal with
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\theta) \approx \sigma^2 (J^TJ)^{-1}, \qquad \hat\sigma^2 = s^2 = \frac{S(\hat\theta)}{n - p} = \frac{0.06647}{12 - 3} = 0.00739
th <- coef(fit)
J  <- jacobian(function(p) pk(t, p[1], p[2], p[3]), th)   # 12 x 3
s2 <- deviance(fit) / (length(y) - 3)
sqrt(diag(s2 * solve(crossprod(J))))          # standard errors by hand
# [1] 0.06243155 0.01040041 0.71647066
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))                         # what nls reports
#         ka         ke          V
# 0.06243155 0.01040041 0.71647070

The same formula as for linear regression, with J in place of the design matrix.


For a linear model y = X beta + noise, Cov(beta-hat) = sigma^2 (X^T X)^{-1} exactly. For a nonlinear model we linearise around the optimum: J plays the role of X. So the standard errors printed by summary(nls) are only as good as that linearisation, which is the point of the profile slides. vcov uses the QR factor of the gradient matrix rather than solve(crossprod(J)), for the conditioning reason a few slides on. numDeriv::jacobian uses Richardson extrapolation of central differences (Numerical differentiation unit), so it is accurate to many digits. Python: scipy.optimize.least_squares returns jac, and the covariance is s2 * inv(jac.T @ jac).
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: The Hessian and the Fisher information
text:
The Hessian and the Fisher information
sse <- function(p) sum((y - pk(t, p[1], p[2], p[3]))^2)
H <- hessian(sse, th)                         # numDeriv: full second derivatives
round(H, 2)                                   # round(2 * crossprod(J), 2):
#       [,1]   [,2]  [,3]                     #       [,1]   [,2]  [,3]
# [1,] 20.84  -6.08 -1.72                     # [1,] 20.78  -6.08 -1.72
# [2,] -6.08 823.98 11.42                     # [2,] -6.08 825.40 11.42
# [3,] -1.72  11.42  0.32                     # [3,] -1.72  11.42  0.32
sqrt(diag(2 * s2 * solve(H)))
# [1] 0.06216416 0.01040070 0.71504108

H and 2J^TJ agree to 0.3 %: the Gauss–Newton approximation is good here.
In likelihood language: -\log L = S/(2\sigma^2) + \text{const}, so the Fisher information is \mathcal I = J^TJ/\sigma^2 and \operatorname{Cov} \approx \mathcal I^{-1}. For a general likelihood: invert the Hessian of -\log L (optim(..., hessian = TRUE)).


numDeriv::hessian computes all second derivatives numerically. This is the route to use when the objective is not a sum of squares, e.g. a Poisson or binomial likelihood: minimise the negative log-likelihood with optim, ask for the Hessian, and invert it. For least squares with Gaussian noise the two routes agree up to the residual term. The observed Fisher information is the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood at the optimum; its inverse is the asymptotic covariance. The standard errors differ by less than 0.5 % here, which is irrelevant for reporting.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
The correlation matrix
r_{jk} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{jk}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Cov}_{jj}\operatorname{Cov}_{kk}}}
round(cov2cor(vcov(fit)), 2)
#       ka    ke     V
# ka  1.00 -0.82  0.90
# ke -0.82  1.00 -0.91
# V   0.90 -0.91  1.00

r(k_a, V) = 0.90: a larger k_a can be compensated by a larger V. The bowl is a tilted, elongated valley.
|r| > 0.95 is a warning; |r| \to 1 means one parameter can replace another.
A standard error alone hides this: each SE is the width of the valley after the others have moved along.


cov2cor divides each covariance by the product of the two standard errors. High correlation between estimates is not a property of the biology (the true ka and V are not “correlated”), it is a property of the experiment: the data constrain a combination of ka and V much better than either alone. With all 12 samples the correlations are high but below 0.95. Python: np.corrcoef does not apply here; compute C / np.outer(se, se).
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: The SVD of J: which combinations are determined
text:
The SVD of J: which combinations are determined
Scale the columns (\partial C/\partial \log\theta_j = \theta_j\,\partial C/\partial\theta_j) so all parameters are compared in relative terms:
Jl <- J %*% diag(th)                  # sensitivities to log ka, log ke, log V
sv <- svd(Jl)
sv$d
# [1] 8.779119 3.478099 1.005166
round(sv$v[, 3], 2)                   # the worst direction
# [1] -0.69  0.60 -0.40
sqrt(s2) / sv$d                       # SE along each direction (log units)
# [1] 0.009788864 0.024708208 0.085495889

As in The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation: noise along v_i is amplified by 1/\sigma_i. Here the SE along v_3 is s/\sigma_3 = 0.085, about 9 %.
v_3: increase k_a, decrease k_e, increase V together (the sign of v_3 is arbitrary). The data barely notice.


This is the link to Part 4. There the matrix was the signature S and v5 said “CD4 minus CD8”; here the matrix is the Jacobian and v3 names the combination of rate constants that the data constrain least. In log units, an SE of 0.085 means a factor exp(0.085) = 1.09, so about 9 % relative uncertainty in that combination, against 1 % along v1. Exact zero singular values are structural non-identifiability (the F/V slide); small ones are practical non-identifiability.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Scaling and conditioning
kappa(J, exact = TRUE)                # columns in 1/h, 1/h and L
# [1] 169.9302
kappa(Jl, exact = TRUE)               # columns per unit log-parameter
# [1] 8.733995
kappa(crossprod(J), exact = TRUE)     # forming J^T J squares kappa
# [1] 28876.26

Part of a large \kappa(J) is just units (V in litres vs rates per hour). Log-parameters remove that part; what is left is real.
As in Pivoting, norms and conditioning: solving with J^TJ loses about \log_{10}\kappa(J)^2 digits. vcov uses the QR factor R of J: (J^TJ)^{-1} = R^{-1}R^{-T}.
solve(crossprod(J)) on a sloppy model can return garbage or fail: use chol2inv(qr.R(qr(J))) or the SVD.


Two separate issues. First, scaling: a parameter measured in litres has a much smaller derivative than a rate per hour, so the raw kappa is inflated by units. Multiplying each column by its parameter value (equivalent to fitting log parameters) makes the comparison fair. Second, numerical: the covariance matrix is (J^T J)^{-1}, and forming J^T J squares the condition number, exactly as in the normal equations of Least squares: normal equations vs QR. With kappa = 1e8 that leaves no correct digits. chol2inv(qr.R(qr(J))) computes (R^T R)^{-1} from the QR factor without forming J^T J.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Practical non-identifiability: samples from 3 h
late <- t >= 3                                    # first sample at 3 h
fits <- nls(y ~ pk(t, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 1, ke = 0.2, V = 20),
            subset = late)
summary(fits)$coefficients[, 1:2]
#      Estimate Std. Error
# ka  1.1220379 0.40551186
# ke  0.1882042 0.01525188
# V  20.1639648 0.76727489
round(cov2cor(vcov(fits)), 3)
#        ka     ke      V
# ka  1.000 -0.852  0.522
# ke -0.852  1.000 -0.835
# V   0.522 -0.835  1.000

After 3 h the curve is \approx A\,e^{-k_e t} with A = D k_a/(V(k_a - k_e)): only two numbers, for three parameters.
The SE says k_a = 1.12 \pm 0.41; Wald 95 % interval (0.33, 1.92). The truth (1.0) is inside, but is this interval right?


The model is structurally fine; the problem is where the samples are. Once absorption is complete, exp(-ka t) is negligible and the data only see the elimination phase, which has two features: an amplitude and a slope. ka enters only through the amplitude, together with V, so ka can be traded against ke and V. No correlation is alarming here, and the SE is not absurd, which makes it dangerous: it suggests ka is known to about 35 %. The next slides show that the truth is much worse.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Where the bowl picture fails


Contours of \Delta S/s^2 over (k_a, V), with k_e re-fitted at each point; red: the ellipse that the SEs and correlations describe.
All samples: the ellipse matches the valley. From 3 h: the valley is open to the right: k_a \to \infty (instant absorption) fits as well. The ellipse cannot show that.


The Wald ellipse is the quadratic approximation drawn at the 3.84 level; the blue 3.84 contour is the real thing. With the rich design they coincide: the quadratic picture is fine and the standard errors are trustworthy. With the sparse design the region of acceptable fits is a long channel that never closes: as ka grows, V settles at a value (the IV-bolus volume) and the fit stays acceptable. The ellipse, being an ellipse, must close, and it even extends to negative ka on the left (cut off here). A standard error cannot describe a one-sided, unbounded uncertainty.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
The profile likelihood
To check one parameter, fix it on a grid and re-optimise all the others:
\text{PL}(k_a) = \min_{k_e,\,V} S(k_a, k_e, V), \qquad \text{95 \% interval: } \frac{\text{PL}(k_a) - S(\hat\theta)}{s^2} \le 3.84
prof <- function(ka, t, y) {           # fix ka, re-fit ke and V
  f <- nls(y ~ pk(t, ka, ke, V), start = list(ke = 0.2, V = 20))
  deviance(f)
}
crit <- function(ka) (prof(ka, t, y) - deviance(fit)) / s2 - 3.84
ka_hat <- coef(fit)[["ka"]]
c(uniroot(crit, c(0.3, ka_hat))$root, uniroot(crit, c(ka_hat, 30))$root)
# [1] 0.8971499 1.1417900                         # profile interval
ka_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * sqrt(vcov(fit)["ka", "ka"])
# [1] 0.8927063 1.1374380                         # Wald interval

3.84 = 1.96^2 is the 95 % point of \chi^2_1. For a linear model the two intervals are identical.


The profile is the honest version of the standard error: instead of assuming the valley is a parabola, we walk along it. Each grid point is a full nonlinear fit with one parameter held fixed, so it costs as many fits as grid points, which is cheap for small models. The threshold: with Gaussian noise, -2 log L = S/sigma^2 + const, and the likelihood-ratio test says a drop of chi^2_1(0.95) = 3.84 is the 95 % boundary. We plug in s^2 for sigma^2; with few degrees of freedom an F-based threshold is a bit wider, which does not change the picture. With all 12 samples the two intervals agree to within 0.005: the profile confirms the SE. uniroot finds where the profile crosses the threshold, as in Bisection and fixed-point iteration.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Profiles show what the SE hides
text:
Profiles show what the SE hides


All samples (blue): a clear well, close to the Wald parabola (dotted). k_a \in (0.90, 1.14).
From 3 h (orange): a lower bound (0.68), but on the right the profile levels off at 1.07, far below 3.84: no upper bound. The Wald interval (0.33, 1.92) is wrong at both ends.


This is the main diagnostic of the lecture. A profile that rises above the threshold on both sides gives a confidence interval (possibly asymmetric). A profile that flattens below the threshold on one side means the parameter is practically non-identifiable in that direction: here, any ka above 0.68 fits, and the curve stays at 1.07 all the way to infinity (instant absorption). A profile that is flat everywhere means the parameter is not determined at all. Compare the dotted Wald parabola for the sparse design: too wide on the left, far too narrow on the right. Raue et al. (2009, Bioinformatics) popularised profiles for exactly this use in systems biology.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Sloppy models

Eigenvalues \lambda_i of J^TJ (log-parameters, so units do not matter), relative to the largest.

Two-compartment version (5 parameters: k_a, k_{10}, k_{12}, k_{21}, V), same 12 sample times: eigenvalues spread over 4.5 decades, with no gap.
SE along each eigenvector \propto 1/\sqrt{\lambda_i}: the stiffest combination is known 180× better than the sloppiest.
Typical of biochemical network models (Gutenkunst et al. 2007): a few stiff combinations, many sloppy ones, no clear gap.


The eigenvalues of J^T J are the squared singular values of J. A gap between large and small (as with the F/V product) says “this many combinations are determined, the rest are not”. Sloppy models have no gap: the eigenvalues are roughly evenly spaced on a log scale, often over 6 or more decades in signalling models with dozens of parameters. Here sqrt(10^4.5) is about 180. The two-compartment curves are computed from the closed-form tri-exponential solution at the true parameters, no data needed. The point of Gutenkunst et al. was that this is the norm, not the exception, in systems biology: individual rate constants are rarely determined by time-course data, even when the fit is excellent.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Sloppy parameters, good predictions
Prediction SE at time t^*: with g = \partial C(t^*)/\partial\theta, \operatorname{Var}\hat C(t^*) \approx g^T\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\theta)\,g.










t^* (h)
0.5
1
6
12




truth
1.86
2.82
1.87
0.57


all samples: \hat C \pm SE
1.87 ± 0.04
2.83 ± 0.04
1.93 ± 0.04
0.62 ± 0.04


from 3 h: \hat C \pm SE
2.02 ± 0.51
3.00 ± 0.54
1.92 ± 0.05
0.62 ± 0.05




From 3 h: predictions inside the sampled window are as good as with all samples; before 3 h they are 12× less certain.
Ask what you need the model for. A sloppy model can predict well where the data constrain it, while its parameters are not determined.


This is the constructive side of sloppiness. If the question is “what is the concentration at 6 h”, the sparse design answers it with SE 0.05 mg/L, close to the rich design. If the question is “what is ka” or “what is the peak concentration”, it cannot. The delta-method formula g^T Cov g propagates the parameter covariance to any derived quantity: a prediction, the AUC, the half-life ln 2 / ke. It inherits the linearisation, so for the sparse design the 0.5 h and 1 h SEs are only rough (the profile of ka is far from a parabola). For those, profile the prediction itself or simulate.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Fix 1: choose the sampling times


Relative sensitivities \theta_j\,\partial C/\partial\theta_j: k_a matters only in the first 3 h; k_e late; V near the peak. Ticks: all samples (black), from 3 h (red).
J needs only a guess of \theta, not data: compare designs before the experiment.


The columns of the Jacobian are these sensitivity curves evaluated at the sample times. A parameter is well determined if its column is large and not proportional to the others at the chosen times. ka has a large positive sensitivity early (faster absorption, faster rise) and a small negative one later, which is almost proportional to the V sensitivity: that is the ka-V trade-off on the sparse design. Optimal experimental design formalises this: choose times to maximise det(J^T J) (D-optimal) or minimise the variance of a parameter of interest.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Design in code: same cost, earlier samples
text:
Design in code: same cost, earlier samples
se_design <- function(tt, p = c(1, 0.2, 20), sigma = 0.1) {
  J <- jacobian(function(lp) pk(tt, exp(lp[1]), exp(lp[2]), exp(lp[3])), log(p))
  sigma * sqrt(diag(solve(crossprod(J))))   # predicted SE of log ka, log ke, log V
}
round(se_design(c(3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)), 3)
# [1] 0.398 0.115 0.061
round(se_design(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12)), 3)
# [1] 0.101 0.087 0.059

Six samples either way. Moving three of them before 3 h cuts the SE of \log k_a from 0.40 (a factor 1.5) to 0.10 (10 %); k_e even improves.
The guess \theta need not be right, only roughly right. Check several guesses.
These are linearised SEs; for the first design the profile showed the truth is worse still.


This is the cheapest fix of all: it costs nothing but thought before the experiment. sigma is the assay SD (known from calibration). We use the true parameters as the guess here; in practice one uses a literature value or a pilot study, and checks that the conclusion does not depend much on the guess. Note the Jacobian is evaluated at the guess, with no data at all: the identifiability of a design can be computed before a single blood sample is taken.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Fix 2: reparameterise

Log-parameters \theta = \log k: positivity for free, columns of J on the same scale (\kappa 170 → 8.7), and the bowl is often more nearly quadratic (better SEs, as factors).
Fit what is identifiable. Unknown F: estimate V/F, not F and V. From 3 h only: the late curve A e^{-k_e t} determines k_e, A, and the clearance-type quantity \text{AUC} = FD/(k_eV).
Remove a symmetry. k_a = k_e + e^{\delta} allows only the branch k_a > k_e: no flip-flop.
Reparameterising does not create information. It moves the undetermined part into one named parameter and keeps the rest clean.


The general strategy: find the combinations that the data determine (from the SVD of J, the profiles, or algebra), and make them the parameters. Then the fit converges more easily, the covariance matrix is well conditioned, and what you report is meaningful. AUC (area under the curve) and clearance CL = ke V are exactly the quantities clinical pharmacokinetics reports, partly for this reason: they are determined by the elimination phase. Note that log parameters change the Wald interval (symmetric in log ka means asymmetric in ka) but not the profile interval, which is invariant to reparameterisation.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Fix 3: a prior is an extra residual
text:
Fix 3: a prior is an extra residual
Prior knowledge “k_a is about 1.2 /h, within a factor e^{0.5} = 1.65” becomes one more residual, (\log k_a - \log 1.2)/0.5:
library(minpack.lm)
res <- function(lp, t, y) c((y - pk(t, exp(lp[1]), exp(lp[2]), exp(lp[3]))) / 0.1,
                            (lp[1] - log(1.2)) / 0.5)
fp <- nls.lm(par = log(c(1, 0.2, 20)), fn = res, t = t[late], y = y[late])
exp(fp$par)
# [1]  1.1563835  0.1871582 20.1940289
Ja <- jacobian(res, fp$par, t = t[late], y = y[late])   # 7 x 3 (6 data + 1 prior)
sqrt(diag(solve(crossprod(Ja))))                        # SE of log ka, log ke, log V
# [1] 0.34998612 0.08243784 0.04434703

This is ridge regularisation (The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation) on \log k_a, and the maximum a posteriori estimate with a log-normal prior.
SE of \log k_a: 0.35, against 0.50 in the prior alone. The data added little: the answer is mostly the prior. Say so.


Dividing the data residuals by the noise SD (0.1 mg/L, known from the assay) and the prior residual by the prior SD puts them on the same footing: the sum of squares is then -2 log of likelihood times prior. nls.lm (Levenberg-Marquardt, from the previous unit) takes a residual function, so adding a row is trivial. Python: scipy.optimize.least_squares with the extra residual. The SE now has a finite value, but compare it with the prior SD: the posterior is only a little narrower than the prior, so the estimate is mostly assumption. A prior removes the numerical symptom (flat valley, huge SE) but not the lack of information, the same lesson as NNLS and ridge in Part 4.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
section: Checklist: can I trust these parameters?
text:
Checklist: can I trust these parameters?

Multistart. Equal SSE at different parameter values → structural symmetry (flip-flop). Different SSE → local minima.
nls says “singular gradient”, or svd(J) has a \sigma near rounding level → structural: find the combination in v_n and reparameterise.
Standard errors from vcov / s^2(J^TJ)^{-1}, computed by QR or SVD, and the correlation matrix: |r| > 0.95 is a warning.
SVD of J in log-parameters: name the badly determined combinations; look for a gap or an even (sloppy) spread.
Profile each parameter you will report. Flat on one side → no bound in that direction; do not quote the SE.
Before the experiment: compute J at a guessed \theta for candidate sampling times.
Report what is determined (predictions, V/F, AUC), and any prior you used.


Every line maps to one of the slides. The order is roughly the order of cost: a multistart and a look at vcov are free once you have a fit; the SVD of J is one line; profiles cost one fit per grid point per parameter. The last line matters most in a paper: if ka is not identifiable from your design, report the quantities that are, and say that ka was fixed or given a prior.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Summary

Structural non-identifiability is in the model: products like F/V (exact null direction of J), symmetries like the k_a/k_e flip-flop (equal-SSE minima). Practical non-identifiability is in the data.
Near \hat\theta, S is a bowl with Hessian H \approx 2J^TJ. Covariance \approx s^2(J^TJ)^{-1} = inverse Fisher information; vcov(nls), numDeriv::hessian. Correlations near ±1 = parameters that trade off.
Small singular values of J = badly determined directions, SE s/\sigma_i. Scale to log-parameters; never form J^TJ when \kappa is large.
Profile likelihood (fix one, re-fit the rest) checks the bowl; a flat profile means no bound, whatever the SE says.
Sloppy models: eigenvalues of J^TJ spread over decades. Predictions can be good where data constrain them.
Fixes: design (sampling times, computable in advance), reparameterise (log, identifiable combinations), priors (= ridge; say how much they did).

Next: Constraints and linear programming: bounds, Lagrange multipliers, and flux balance analysis.

The one-sentence version: a good fit is necessary but not sufficient; look at J (its SVD and the covariance it implies) and at profiles before reporting any fitted parameter. The capstone of the course (if used) asks for exactly this analysis on a real time course.
crumbs: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters

title: Exercise: Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the methods of this unit in your browser. The tab One step, four slopes takes one step from \(t = 0\) on the logistic OD curve (\(K = 1.2\), \(N_0 = 0.05\), \(r = 0.8\)) or on drug clearance (\(C' = -0.8\,C\), \(C_0 = 10\)). Panel (a) draws every stage as a dot with its slope, the dashed line that leads to it, and the combined step (green square) next to the exact value (open circle). next stage reveals the stages one at a time. Panel (b) shows the error at \(t = 10\) for all four methods against \(h\), or against the number of \(f\) evaluations, with the current method and \(h\) as a large dot. The tab Adaptive steps solves predator–prey (50 years) or the repressilator (\(t = 0 \dots 50\)) with an embedded pair and the controller from the lecture (rtol = atol, first step \(h = 0.01\)). Panel (c) puts a dot at every accepted step over a tight reference solution (grey), panel (d) shows the step size with rejected attempts as red crosses, and panel (e) shows the phase plane.
The browser uses the same IEEE doubles as R, Python and Rust, so the fixed-step numbers match the lecture to the digits shown. The adaptive solver is the controller of the slides, not deSolve’s or scipy’s, so its step counts are close to those of ode45/RK45 but not identical (first step, error norm and step limits differ).



E1. (four slopes) On the logistic curve with RK4 and \(h = 1\), press next stage four times. For each stage, write down where the slope is evaluated and its value, and say which earlier slope leads to the point. Why is \(k_3\) larger than \(k_2\), although both are taken at \(t = 0.5\)? Compare the combined value with the exact one, then switch to Euler, Midpoint and Heun at the same \(h\) and compare the errors of the single step.






Answer E1





\(k_1 = f(0, 0.05) = 0.03833\); \(k_2 = f(0.5, 0.06917) = 0.05214\), reached along slope \(k_1\); \(k_3 = f(0.5, 0.07607) = 0.05700\), reached along \(k_2\); \(k_4 = f(1, 0.10700) = 0.07797\), reached along \(k_3\). The curve bends upwards, so \(k_1\) (the slope at the start) underestimates the rise; the point for \(k_3\) is built with the steeper \(k_2\), so it lies higher, where the logistic curve is steeper. The weighted slope \((k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4)/6\) gives \(N_1 = 0.1057646\) against the exact \(0.1058708\): error \(-1.1\times10^{-4}\). One step of Euler is off by \(-0.018\), midpoint by \(-3.7\times10^{-3}\) and Heun by \(-4.0\times10^{-3}\): RK4 is 160 times better than Euler for 4 times the work.



E2. (order) Still on the logistic curve, set \(h = 1\), \(0.5\) and \(0.25\) for Euler, Heun and RK4, and note the error at \(t = 10\) and the readout “halving h divides it by”. What does each ratio approach, and which slope does the big dot follow in panel (b)? Why is Heun worse than Euler at \(h = 2\) (the right end of the curves)?






Answer E2





Euler: \(7.45\times10^{-3}\), \(3.41\times10^{-3}\), \(1.61\times10^{-3}\); ratios \(2.2, 2.1, 2.1 \to 2 = 2^1\). Heun: \(8.80\times10^{-3}\), \(1.51\times10^{-3}\), \(3.36\times10^{-4}\); ratios \(5.8, 4.5, 4.2 \to 4 = 2^2\). RK4: \(1.83\times10^{-4}\), \(9.25\times10^{-6}\), \(5.31\times10^{-7}\); ratios \(19.8, 17.4, 16.6 \to 16 = 2^4\). The dots lie on lines of slope 1, 2 and 4. At \(h = 2\) Heun’s error is \(0.099\), Euler’s \(0.037\): the methods are outside the asymptotic regime: the \(h^2\) term is not yet small compared with the higher terms, and the order only says how errors behave for small \(h\).



E3. (what accuracy costs) Switch panel (b) to f evaluations. For each of Euler, Heun and RK4, read off roughly how many evaluations of \(f\) are needed for an error of \(10^{-6}\) (the dotted line); extrapolate along the slope if the curve does not reach it. Which method is cheapest when one digit is enough?






Answer E3





RK4 crosses \(10^{-6}\) between 80 evaluations (\(h = 0.5\), \(9.3\times10^{-6}\)) and 160 (\(h = 0.25\), \(5.3\times10^{-7}\)), so about 140. Heun crosses between 1280 (\(1.2\times10^{-6}\)) and 2560 (\(3.1\times10^{-7}\)) evaluations, so about 1400. Euler is still at \(2.4\times10^{-5}\) at the end of its curve (2560 evaluations); along slope \(-1\) it needs about 25 times more, roughly 60 000. These are the numbers of the lecture. For an error of about \(10^{-2}\) all three need 10–20 evaluations (Euler \(7.5\times10^{-3}\) with 10, Heun \(8.8\times10^{-3}\) and RK4 \(5.5\times10^{-3}\) with 20): if one digit is enough, Euler is as cheap as any.



E4. (adaptive steps on predator–prey) Open Adaptive steps, choose predator–prey and Dormand–Prince 5(4) with rtol = 1e-3. Read the numbers of accepted and rejected steps, of \(f\) evaluations, and the drift of the conserved quantity \(V\). Where in the cycle are the steps short, and where long? Then go to 1e-6. By what factor did the number of steps grow, and what did you get for it?






Answer E4





rtol = 1e-3: 67 accepted steps, 19 rejected, 517 evaluations, \(\max|V(t) - V(0)| = 0.032\); the orbit in (e) is visibly polygonal and wanders off the grey reference. The steps grow from \(0.01\) to about \(1.4\) years when both populations are low (hares about 12, lynx about 4) and shrink to about \(0.35\) when they are high and changing fast (hares crashing, lynx peaking); the rejections (red crosses) come where the step had grown too far before such a phase. rtol = 1e-6: 229 accepted, 55 rejected, 1705 evaluations, drift \(2.1\times10^{-6}\); steps from \(0.14\) (hares about 26, lynx 22) to \(0.42\) (lynx about 4). A factor 1000 in tolerance costs only 3.4 times more steps (for an order-5 method, \(1000^{1/5} = 4\)) and makes the drift 15 000 times smaller. Compare with fixed steps in C3: Euler with 5000 steps drifts by 0.51.



E5. (higher order pays) Choose the repressilator at rtol = 1e-6 and try all three pairs. Record the accepted steps, \(f\) evaluations and the error in \(p_1(50)\). Then go to 1e-5 and 1e-7 with each pair: by what factor does the number of steps grow per factor 10 in rtol? Finally try Heun–Euler at 1e-9. What happens, and what would you use in practice?






Answer E5





At 1e-6: Heun–Euler 39 065 steps, 78 138 evaluations, error \(3.7\times10^{-4}\); Bogacki–Shampine 1689 steps, 5074 evaluations, error \(-1.3\times10^{-2}\); Dormand–Prince 492 steps, 2959 evaluations, error \(-2.5\times10^{-4}\) (deSolve’s ode45 takes 487 steps). Per factor 10 in rtol the step count grows by about \(3.2 = 10^{1/2}\) (Heun–Euler: 12 355, 39 065, 123 530), \(2.2 = 10^{1/3}\) (Bogacki–Shampine: 784, 1689, 3667) and \(1.6 = 10^{1/5}\) (Dormand–Prince: 317, 492, 769): the exponent is \(1/(q+1)\) from the controller. The same rtol does not mean the same error at \(t = 50\): the tolerance controls the error per step, and the errors add up over the cycles (Bogacki–Shampine is 50 times worse here). Heun–Euler at 1e-9 needs steps of about \(10^{-6}\) and stops at \(t = 6.6\) after 150 000 attempts. In practice, use Dormand–Prince (ode45, RK45, Dopri5), and check the answer by tightening the tolerance.

text:
Explore
The demo below runs the QR algorithm in your browser, with deflation below \(10^{-12}\) exactly as qr_eig in C2, on the matrices of this unit: the 3 × 3 \(A\) of the Background, a symmetric 5 × 5, a symmetric 4 × 4 with two close eigenvalues, \(B\) of C2, the switch \(P\) of B2, the predator–prey Jacobian \(J\), and the Jacobian of a 4-species community (eigenvalues \(-3\), \(-1 \pm i\), \(-0.5\)). Panel (a) shows \(A_k\) as a heat map: blue for positive and orange for negative entries, paler for smaller ones, white below \(10^{-12}\); the diagonal is outlined, a deflated eigenvalue turns green, and the dashed box is the active block that is still being iterated. Panel (b) shows the subdiagonal entries \(|a_{i+1,i}|\) against the step \(k\) on a log axis; without a shift, the dashed lines are the rates \(|\lambda_{i+1}/\lambda_i|^k\) of fact 2. The shift buttons switch to the Rayleigh shift \(\mu = a_{nn}\) or the Wilkinson shift (fact 3), computed from the active block. The readout gives the shift, the diagonal, the true eigenvalues and the rates. The second tab, Sensitivity of eigenvalues, perturbs the transit chain of fact 5 (and a symmetric matrix of the same size) by \(\varepsilon\) and computes the eigenvalues live.



E1. (power iteration on all columns) With the 3 × 3 lecture matrix and no shift, press step +1 and compare \(A_1\) with the Background output. Then move to \(k = 10\), \(20\) and \(30\) and read \(|a_{21}|\) and \(|a_{32}|\) off the heat map. Compare with the dashed lines in (b). Which eigenvalue is found first, at which step, and when are all three found? Why does the diagonal look converged long before that?






Answer E1





\(A_1\) has \(4.41\), \(3.15\), \(1.43\) on the diagonal and \(0.691\) and \(-0.538\) beside it: the Background’s R %*% Q (same signs as R and numpy). At \(k = 10\), \(20\), \(30\) the entries are \(|a_{21}| = 0.0133\), \(1\times10^{-4}\), \(1\times10^{-6}\) and \(|a_{32}| = 2\times10^{-4}\), \(4\times10^{-8}\), \(8\times10^{-12}\): the points lie on straight lines parallel to the dashed \(0.634^k\) and \(0.423^k\) (C1 prints \(1.33\times10^{-2}\), \(1.39\times10^{-4}\), \(1.46\times10^{-6}\) and \(2.31\times10^{-4}\), \(4.19\times10^{-8}\), \(7.63\times10^{-12}\)). \(|a_{32}|\) is faster because \(\lambda_3/\lambda_2 = 1.268/3 = 0.423\) is the smaller ratio; it crosses \(10^{-12}\) at \(k = 33\), and \(1.267949\) turns green. \(a_{21}\) needs \(k = 62\), the 62 steps of C2. The readout shows the diagonal \(4.732051\), \(3.000000\), \(1.267949\) already at \(k = 20\): for a symmetric matrix the error on the diagonal is about the square of the off-diagonal entries, so six correct decimals need off-diagonals of only about \(10^{-3}\)–\(10^{-4}\).



E2. (close eigenvalues, and what a shift buys) Choose close λ₁, λ₂. Read the three rates. Predict from the first one how many steps \(a_{21}\) needs to fall below \(10^{-12}\), then press +100 until it is done. Repeat with the Rayleigh and the Wilkinson shift and watch \(\mu\) in the readout. Do the same count for the 5 × 5 symmetric matrix.






Answer E2





The eigenvalues are \(2.309\), \(2.151\), \(1.191\), \(0.349\) and the rates \(0.932\), \(0.554\), \(0.293\). From \(0.932^k = 10^{-12}\), \(k = 12/0.0306 \approx 390\); the demo finds all eigenvalues after 367 steps (\(a_{43}\) deflates at 23 and \(a_{32}\) at 49, \(a_{21}\) at 367; at \(k = 100\) it is still \(1.5\times10^{-4}\), at \(k = 300\) \(1.1\times10^{-10}\)). With the Rayleigh shift: 11 steps; with Wilkinson: 6. With a shift the curves in (b) are no longer straight lines but plunge (several digits per step), and \(\mu\) settles on the eigenvalue being deflated: at \(k = 4\) the Rayleigh shift is \(\mu = 1.190983\), the eigenvalue \(1.190983\) to all six decimals shown. After each deflation the shift is taken from the smaller block and moves to the next eigenvalue. The 5 × 5 matrix (rates \(0.523\), \(0.777\), \(0.885\), \(0.299\)): 213 steps unshifted, 13 Rayleigh, 8 Wilkinson. LAPACK uses shifts for exactly this reason: the cost no longer depends on how close the eigenvalues are.



E3. (a shift that fails) Choose B (2 × 2) and try the three shifts. How many steps does each take? What does the Rayleigh shift do, and what value of \(\mu\) does the readout show? Then choose switch P and try the three shifts again. Compare with B2.






Answer E3





\(B\): no shift 26 steps (B1(c) predicted about 26), Wilkinson 1 step. The Rayleigh shift is \(\mu = a_{22} = 2\) at every step, exactly halfway between the eigenvalues 1 and 3: \(B - 2I = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(\pm 1\) of equal modulus, so \(A_k\) never changes; the curve in (b) is flat at 1 and after 30 steps the readout warns that \(|a_{21}|\) has not shrunk. The stop at 600 steps is C2’s “500 steps and the values 2, 2”. \(P\): no shift and Rayleigh (\(\mu = a_{22} = 0\)) both stall, because \(\lambda = \pm 1\) have the same modulus (the readout says so). Wilkinson gives \(\mu = -1\), an exact eigenvalue: \(P + I\) is singular, one step gives \(\operatorname{diag}(1, -1)\). As in B2(c), any shift that makes \(|\lambda_1 - \mu| \ne |\lambda_2 - \mu|\) works, and one close to an eigenvalue works best; the Wilkinson shift is chosen so that this always holds for a symmetric matrix.



E4. (a complex pair never splits) Choose predator–prey J, no shift, and go to \(k = 50\) and then \(k = 51\). Compare with C3. Then choose 4 × 4 community and press play. Which subdiagonal entries go to zero, which eigenvalues appear on the diagonal, and what happens to the rest? Look at \(A_{40}\), \(A_{41}\), \(A_{42}\), \(A_{43}\), \(A_{44}\). Does the Wilkinson shift help?






Answer E4





\(J\) at \(k = 50\): \(a_{21} = 0.571\), diagonal \(-0.231\), \(0.131\); at \(k = 51\): \(a_{21} = -0.752\), diagonal \(0.205\), \(-0.305\) (the numbers of C3). The curve in (b) jumps around at about 1 and never falls; the readout says that \(-0.05 \pm 0.705i\) have equal modulus. The 4 × 4: \(a_{43}\) falls along \(0.354^k\) and deflates at \(k = 26\) (\(-0.5\) turns green); \(a_{21}\) falls roughly along \(0.471^k\) (with jumps, because the pair below it rotates) and \(-3\) appears in position (1, 1). \(a_{32}\) stays of order 1: rows and columns 2–3 keep a full 2 × 2 block. Its entries change every step (\(-1.2\), \(2.6\), \(-0.4\), \(-0.8\) at \(k = 40\); \(-0.5\), \(-2.5\), \(0.5\), \(-1.5\) at \(k = 41\)) and repeat after 4 steps (\(A_{44} = A_{40}\)), but every version has trace \(-2\) and determinant \(2\), so its eigenvalues are always \(-1 \pm i\) (fact 4). The result is the real Schur form: triangular except for one 2 × 2 block per complex pair. Wilkinson deflates \(-0.5\) already at \(k = 7\), but a real shift cannot separate the pair either: \(a_{32}\) still does not shrink. LAPACK uses two complex-conjugate shifts at once (the Francis double shift) and reads the pair off the block.



E5. (sensitivity) Open the Sensitivity of eigenvalues tab. With \(n = 10\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-10}\), how far do the eigenvalues of the chain and of the symmetric matrix move? Read the slopes of the two lines in panel (b). Change \(n\) to 2, 3 and 20 at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-10}\). Then set \(\varepsilon = 10^{-16}\): what does the solver return, and what changes when you switch to ε × random matrix (a perturbation of every entry, like rounding)? Use \(n = 10\) and \(n = 20\), and compare with B4.






Answer E5





\(n = 10\), \(\varepsilon = 10^{-10}\): the chain’s ten eigenvalues sit on the dashed circle around \(-1\), moved by \(0.100 = \varepsilon^{1/10}\); the symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues move by \(3.6\times10^{-11}\), less than \(\varepsilon\), and the readout gives a ratio of \(2.8\times10^{9}\). In (b) the symmetric points lie on a line of slope 1 (change \(\approx \varepsilon\)), the chain’s on a line of slope \(1/n\): almost flat for \(n = 10\). At \(\varepsilon = 10^{-10}\): \(n = 2\) moves the chain’s eigenvalues by \(10^{-5} = \sqrt\varepsilon\) (B4(a)), \(n = 3\) by \(4.64\times10^{-4}\), \(n = 20\) by \(0.316\). At \(\varepsilon = 10^{-16}\) with a single entry, the solver returns exactly \(-1\) for every eigenvalue: a change of \(10^{-16}\) is below the rounding of the other entries, and the readout notes that any point inside the circle of radius \(0.025\) would be an equally good answer. With \(\varepsilon\) times a random matrix, the eigenvalues spread to \(0.0205\) for \(n = 10\) and \(0.154\) for \(n = 20\), close to \(\varepsilon^{1/n} = 0.025\) and \(0.158\) (B4(c)): rounding alone makes each eigenvalue of a 20-compartment chain uncertain by about 15 %, while the symmetric matrix moves by \(10^{-15}\).

section: Try it: four slopes, then adaptive steps

Try it: four slopes, then adaptive steps




Live in the browser; the adaptive solver is the controller of the previous slide with Dormand-Prince 5(4), first step 0.01, rtol = atol. Start on predator-prey at rtol 1e-3: 67 accepted steps, 19 rejected (red crosses), 517 f evaluations; the dots in (c) are sparse, the orbit in (e) is a polygon that wanders off the grey reference, V drifts by 0.032. Point at panel (d): long steps (about 1.4 years) when both populations are low, short ones when they are high and changing fast; the crosses come just after the step has grown too far. Click 1e-6: 229 steps, drift 2e-6, the orbit closes. Switch to the repressilator at 1e-6 and compare the three pairs: Heun-Euler 39 000 steps, Bogacki-Shampine 1700, Dormand-Prince 492 (the same as deSolve’s ode45 to within 1 %). Heun-Euler at 1e-9 gives up after 150 000 attempts. If there is time, go back to the first tab: RK4 on the logistic curve with h = 1, press “next stage” four times to build k1..k4 (the table of “One RK4 step by hand”), then show panel (b) against h (slopes 1, 2, 4) and against f evaluations (RK4 about 140 evaluations for 1e-6, Euler about 60 000).

title: Exercise: equilibria, stability and the phase plane
text:
Explore
The demo below draws the phase plane of the toggle switch (\(\alpha_u = 3\), \(n = 2\), \(\alpha_v\) on the slider) or of the Sel’kov model (\(a = 0.08\), \(b\) on the slider) in your browser. Grey arrows show the direction of the flow (all the same length), blue is the nullcline \(du/dt = 0\), red is \(dv/dt = 0\). Fixed points are black if stable and white if unstable, labelled with their type; the readout lists their eigenvalues. Click anywhere (or use a start button) to launch a trajectory. It is integrated with classical RK4, \(h = 0.01\), up to \(t = 100\) (toggle) or \(t = 200\) (Sel’kov), and it stops when it comes within \(10^{-3}\) of a stable fixed point. Below the buttons you see \(u(t)\) and \(v(t)\) of the latest trajectory. Basins of the flow colours each of \(160 \times 160\) starts in \([0, 4]^2\) by the stable state its trajectory reaches. Separatrix draws the saddle’s stable manifold, computed as in C4 by running backwards in time from the saddle \(\pm 10^{-6}\,\mathbf v_{\text{stable}}\). The demo Newton for systems of equations shows the same plane coloured by where Newton goes. This one shows where the cell goes.



E1. (two neighbours, two fates) In the symmetric toggle, click the starts \((0.5, 0.3)\) and \((0.3, 0.5)\). Where does each end, and when? Read the fixed-point readout: which types and eigenvalues does it give, and do they agree with B4 and B5? In the \(u(t)\) panel of the run from \((0.3, 0.5)\), why does \(u\) first rise and then fall?






Answer E1





\((0.5, 0.3)\) ends in U on, \((0.3, 0.5)\) in V on, each within \(10^{-3}\) at \(t = 30.6\): the two runs are mirror images. The readout gives V on and U on as stable nodes with \(\lambda = -0.333, -1.667\) (\(-1 \pm 2/3\), B4), and the middle state \((1.213, 1.213)\) as a saddle with \(\lambda = 0.191, -2.191\) (\(-1 \pm g\), B5). Both starts lie below both nullclines, where both proteins are produced faster than they decay, so at first \(u\) and \(v\) both rise, roughly along the saddle’s stable direction \((1, 1)\), and the runs pass within 0.27 of the saddle at \(t \approx 1\). Then the unstable direction \((1, -1)\) takes over: the protein that was slightly ahead wins and the other is shut off. In the run from \((0.3, 0.5)\), \(u\) rises to 1.00 at \(t \approx 1.7\) and then falls to 0.38.



E2. (the trap at the saddle) Click \((2, 2)\), then \((2, 2.0001)\). What does the readout say for each? For the second run, how long does it spend near the saddle, and why does it end where it ends? Compare with the estimate \(\ln(0.1/10^{-4})/0.191\).






Answer E2





\((2, 2)\) lies on the diagonal, the stable manifold of the saddle. The run slides into the middle state and stays within \(10^{-3}\) of it from \(t = 3.3\) to \(t = 100\); the readout warns that this is an unstable state. A simulation that “settled” here proves nothing about stability. \((2, 2.0001)\) also reaches the saddle quickly, but the tiny excess of V grows like \(e^{0.191 t}\). It takes \(\ln(0.1/10^{-4})/0.191 \approx 36\) time units to grow to a visible \(0.1\), and the run reaches V on only at \(t = 75.0\) (U on from \((0.5, 0.3)\) took 30.6). It ends in V on because \(v_0 > u_0\): it starts above the separatrix \(u = v\). This is the lecture’s failure slide, live.



E3. (basins of the flow versus Newton’s basins) Tick basins of the flow and separatrix. Read the shares for the symmetric switch, then click biased toggle (\(\alpha_v = 2.9\)). Read the shares again and check the separatrix against C4 at \(u = 1\) and \(u = 2\). How does this picture differ from Newton’s basins for the same plane (Newton for systems of equations: 21.8 / 57 / 21.2 % for the biased switch)?






Answer E3





Symmetric: U on 50 %, V on 50 %, middle 0.6 %. The “middle” share is exactly the 160 grid cells on the diagonal \(u = v\) (160 of 25 600 = 0.625 %), whose runs stay on the stable manifold and end at the saddle. The separatrix is the diagonal. Biased: U on 58 %, V on 42 %, middle 0 %. The separatrix now bends above the diagonal: it passes \(u = 1\) at \(v \approx 1.21\) and \(u = 2\) at \(v \approx 2.35\) (C4: 1.2144 and 2.3486). It is exactly the edge between green and purple. The flow’s basins are two smooth regions separated by one curve, and the saddle has no basin of positive area. Newton’s basins of the same equations interleave in thin bands, and the unstable middle state takes the largest share (57 %). Newton’s basins belong to the algorithm, the flow’s basins to the cell.



E4. (losing the switch) With the basins on, lower \(\alpha_v\) with the slider: 2.8, 2.75, 2.72, 2.71, 2.70. Record the share of V on and the small eigenvalues of V on and of the saddle. What happens to the two states, and where does bistability disappear? Then click \((0.3, 0.5)\) at \(\alpha_v = 2.70\).






Answer E4

V on and the saddle move towards each other: (0.628, 1.944) and (0.767, 1.707) at \(\alpha_v = 2.71\). Their eigenvalues closest to zero both approach 0, and between 2.70 and 2.71 the two states collide and vanish (a saddle-node bifurcation, where the blue and red nullclines stop crossing in the upper left). At 2.70 only one state is left, a stable node at (2.718, 0.322). A cell that starts with more V, at \((0.3, 0.5)\), now ends in U on (\(t = 25.9\)). V on never became unstable on the way: the readout calls it a stable node until it disappears. A weaker promoter shrinks its basin first and then removes it.



E5. (a limit cycle is born and dies) Click Sel’kov. Launch both start buttons and compare the late range of \(u\) and the period. Then set \(b = 0.4,\ 0.35,\ 0.34,\ 0.3\) and \(b = 0.8,\ 0.84,\ 0.85,\ 0.9\), and launch inside for each. Use the type and eigenvalues in the readout and the range of \(u\). Where do the oscillations appear and disappear, and how does that compare with B7(c)? What is odd at \(b = 0.34\)?






Answer E5





At \(b = 0.6\) the fixed point is an unstable spiral, \(\lambda = 0.098 \pm 0.656i\). Both starts end on the same cycle: after \(t = 100\), \(u\) runs from 0.245 to 1.518 with period 9.62, as in the lecture. The size and period are set by the model, not by the start.

The cycle exists between the two Hopf points \(b = 0.3464\) and \(b = 0.8485\) of B7(c), where the real part of the eigenvalues changes sign. Near each end the cycle shrinks to a point, and the period approaches \(2\pi/\mathrm{Im}\,\lambda\) (\(2\pi/0.450 = 14.0\) at \(b = 0.35\); \(2\pi/0.886 = 7.09\) at \(b = 0.84\)). At \(b = 0.34\) the fixed point is stable, yet \(u\) still swings by 0.09 between \(t = 100\) and 200. With \(\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda = -0.007\), a perturbation decays only like \(e^{-0.007 t}\), which takes about 300 time units per factor 10. This is critical slowing down again: a finite simulation cannot tell a slowly dying oscillation from a small cycle, but the eigenvalues can. At \(b = 0.85\) the demo refuses to classify (\(|\mathrm{Re}\,\lambda| < 10^{-3}\)), as the lecture’s failure slide recommends.

title: Equilibria, stability and the phase plane
section: Try it: where does the cell go?
text:
Try it: where does the cell go?




The toggle switch and the Sel’kov oscillator, live in the browser: normalised velocity arrows, the nullclines (blue du/dt = 0, red dv/dt = 0), the fixed points with their type from the Jacobian’s eigenvalues (black stable, white unstable), and trajectories by RK4 with h = 0.01 wherever I click. Symmetric switch first. Click (0.5, 0.3) and (0.3, 0.5): both rise towards the saddle, then split, U on and V on at t = 30.6. Read the readout: outer states stable nodes, -1/3 and -5/3; middle a saddle, 0.191 and -2.191. Click (2, 2): it slides into the saddle and stays there; the readout warns. Click (2, 2.0001): it sits at the saddle for a long time and reaches V on only at t = 75, which previews the next slide. Tick basins of the flow and separatrix: 50/50, the diagonal is the boundary. Click biased toggle: 58/42, the orange separatrix bends above the diagonal and is exactly the colour boundary; contrast with Newton’s banded basins on the previous slide. Drag alpha_v down: the V-on basin shrinks, V on and the saddle approach each other, and between 2.71 and 2.70 they vanish together. Then Sel’kov: inside and outside starts end on the same cycle (u 0.245 to 1.518, period 9.62); drag b to 0.3 (stable spiral, the oscillation dies) and back over 0.35 (a small cycle is born, a Hopf bifurcation).

title: Exercise: Gaussian elimination as LU
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the lecture’s mixing model (C3 plants, maize, fish) in exact fractions. Tab 1. Factorise A = LU does elimination one multiplier at a time: each multiplier \(\ell_{ik}\) is written into \(L\) at the spot where it makes the new 0 in \(U\) (green in both), and the product \(L\cdot U\) is shown beside them. Tab 2. Solve for samples keeps \(L\) and \(U\) and solves each consumer by forward and back substitution only, written out line by line. It marks the consumer among the sources in isotope space, and counts operations for two strategies: factor once (13 to factorise, then 15 per sample) and re-eliminate for every sample (13 + 15 = 28 each time). The zero pivot button loads the matrix from B5.



E1. (the multipliers fill \(L\)) In tab 1, click next ▶ through the elimination. For each step write down the multiplier, where it lands in \(L\), the new row of \(U\) and the running operation count. Look at the check panel at every step, including the middle ones where \(L\) still has grey zeros. What does it show, and why does it hold even halfway?






Answer E1





Step 1: \(\ell_{21} = -26 \div 1 = -26\), row 2 of \(U\) becomes \((0, 16, 8)\), 5 operations. Step 2: \(\ell_{31} = 2 \div 1 = 2\), row 3 becomes \((0, 4, 12)\), 10 so far. Step 3: \(\ell_{32} = 4 \div 16 = \tfrac14\), row 3 becomes \((0, 0, 10)\), 13 in total. These are the \(L\) and \(U\) of the lecture. The check panel shows \(L\cdot U = A\) ✓ at every step. Each step subtracts \(\ell_{ik}\) times row \(k\) from row \(i\) of \(U\) and at the same time writes \(\ell_{ik}\) into \(L\), and multiplying by \(L\) adds that multiple back. The two changes cancel in the product, so no information is lost at any point. The grey zeros are multipliers not computed yet; those rows have not been touched.



E2. (forward substitution replays elimination) Switch to tab 2. Consumer #1 is solved. Read off \(\mathbf y\) and compare it with the slide “Why triangular is good”. Then click consumers #2 and #3. Write down \(\mathbf y\) and the diet for each. How many operations does each sample cost, and which numbers stay the same from one consumer to the next?






Answer E2





Consumer #1: \(\mathbf y = (1, 6.4, 2)\), \(\mathbf f = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\), as on the slide. Consumer #2: \(\mathbf y = (1, 11.2, 2)\), \(\mathbf f = (0.2, 0.6, 0.2)\). Consumer #3: \(\mathbf y = (1, 8.8, 7)\), \(\mathbf f = (0.1, 0.2, 0.7)\). Each sample costs 15 operations: 6 in forward substitution (3 multiply–subtract pairs) and 9 in back substitution (3 pairs and 3 divisions). \(L\) and \(U\), and so the multipliers \(-26\), \(2\), \(\tfrac14\) and the pivots \(1\), \(16\), \(10\), are the same every time. Only \(\mathbf b\), \(\mathbf y\) and \(\mathbf f\) change. \(\mathbf y\) is exactly the \(\mathbf b\) column that the augmented matrix \([A \mid \mathbf b]\) would hold after elimination, so the forward substitution step replays the row operations on \(\mathbf b\).



E3. (a consumer outside the triangle) Click consumer #4. Which fraction is negative? Where is the consumer in the isotope plot? Did anything go wrong numerically?






Answer E3





\(\mathbf y = (1, 2, 6.5)\) and \(\mathbf f = (0.55, -0.20, 0.65)\): maize gets \(-20\) %. The point \((-24, 9)\) lies outside the source triangle (red dot), to the upper left of the C3–fish edge. The arithmetic is exact and \(A\mathbf f = \mathbf b\) holds; the substitutions are the same 15 operations as before. The negative fraction is a model problem: a missing source or wrong source values. It is not a numerical failure.



E4. (when does factor once pay?) Click reset count, then solve another sample ▶ ten times. Read both totals and the ratio for \(n = 3\). Then click \(n = 1000\) (the same counts for a \(1000\times1000\) matrix). Why does keeping \(L\) and \(U\) gain so little for the \(3 \times 3\) mixing model and so much for \(n = 1000\)? What does the ratio approach for very many samples in each case?






Answer E4





After 10 samples with \(n = 3\): re-eliminating costs \(10 \cdot 28 = 280\) operations, factor once \(13 + 10\cdot 15 = 163\), 1.72 times fewer. With \(n = 1000\): \(6.7\cdot10^9\) against \(6.9\cdot10^8\), 9.74 times fewer. For \(n = 3\) the factorisation (13) costs about as much as one solve (15), so skipping it saves at most a factor \(28/15 = 1.87\). For \(n = 1000\) one factorisation (\(\approx \tfrac23 n^3 = 6.7\cdot10^8\)) costs as much as 333 solves (\(2n^2 = 2\cdot10^6\)). For \(m \ll 333\) the saving is about \(m\), and for very many samples it approaches \((F + S)/S \approx 334\). This is the \(n/3\) ratio from the lecture’s cost table. A 10 000-consumer study with a \(3\times3\) matrix does not care (B6(d)). A \(1000\times1000\) implicit time step does.



E5. (a zero pivot) Click zero pivot (two sources at −26 ‰) and then run to end in tab 1. Where does elimination stop, and what would lu_nopivot store in row 3? Try tab 2. Then go back, click the swap button, and step through again. Give \(L\) and \(U\), and solve consumer #1 in tab 2.






Answer E5





After step 1, \(U\) has rows \((1, 1, 1)\), \((0, 0, 16)\), \((0, 8, 4)\): the pivot \(u_{22}\) is 0, and \(\ell_{32} = 8 \div 0\) is impossible. In doubles, \(\ell_{32} = \text{Inf}\) and row 3 becomes \((0, \text{NaN}, -\text{Inf})\), as on the lecture slide, with no error message. Tab 2 has no factors to reuse. After swapping rows 2 and 3: \(\ell_{21} = 2\), \(\ell_{31} = -26\), \(\ell_{32} = 0 \div 8 = 0\), so \(L = \begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-26&0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(U = \begin{pmatrix} 1&1&1\\0&8&4\\0&0&16\end{pmatrix}\), again 13 operations and \(L\cdot U\) equal to the reordered \(A\). Consumer #1, reordered to \(P\mathbf b = (1, 6.5, -20)\), gives \(\mathbf y = (1, 4.5, 6)\) and \(\mathbf f = (0.25, 0.375, 0.375)\), the answer of B5(c). The matrix was never singular; the rows were only in an unlucky order. Choosing that order automatically is partial pivoting, in the next unit.

title: Gaussian elimination as LU
