title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
About this lecture
So far every optimiser was free to try any parameter value. Biology says no: rates are positive, proportions sum to 1, a cell takes up at most so much glucose.

Simple fixes for simple constraints: bounds (L-BFGS-B) and reparameterisation (e^\theta, softmax). Each has a failure.
Lagrange multipliers in one picture: at the optimum the gradient of f is parallel to the gradient of the constraint, and the multiplier is a shadow price.
Linear programming: linear objective, linear constraints. The optimum is at a corner; the simplex method walks from corner to corner.
Biology: flux balance analysis (FBA). Which fluxes maximise growth of a toy metabolic network, which fluxes are not determined, what a knock-out does, and which nutrient limits growth.


This is the last unit of Part 9. Units 26 to 29 minimised a smooth function with no restrictions on the parameters. Here the restrictions come in. The first third is a short tool kit for fitting problems (bounds, reparameterisation, the Lagrange picture); the rest is linear programming, which is a different kind of optimisation problem with its own algorithm, and its main biological use, FBA. FBA is used on genome-scale models with thousands of reactions; we use a toy network with 9 reactions that can be solved by hand, so every number on the slides can be checked.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Three kinds of constraint








constraint
example
written as




sign / bound
a degradation rate, a background signal
k \ge 0, c \ge 0


sum to one
diet fractions, cell-type proportions
p_i \ge 0,\ \sum_i p_i = 1


capacity
uptake of glucose, enzyme or ribosome budget
v_\text{glc} \le 10


balance
metabolites at steady state
S\mathbf v = \mathbf 0



We have already met answers that break them:

Gaussian elimination as LU: a consumer’s diet came out as (0.55, -0.20, 0.65), a negative fraction of maize.
The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation: least squares gave a CD8 T-cell proportion of -0.09.

A constraint is active at a solution if it holds with equality there (c = 0, v_\text{glc} = 10). Inactive constraints do not change the answer.

Equality constraints (sum to 1, steady state) cut the search space down to a surface; inequality constraints (signs, capacities) cut off a region. The set of parameter values that satisfy all constraints is the feasible set. The word active matters throughout the lecture: an inactive inequality could be deleted without changing the solution, an active one decides it. The two earlier examples are both cases where the unconstrained answer is impossible, which is the usual way students discover they need constraints.

title: Constraints and linear programming
section: A fit that wants a negative background
text:
A fit that wants a negative background
mRNA decay after a transcription block: signal y = A e^{-kt} + c, background c \ge 0 (synthetic data).
t <- 0:8                                          # hours
y <- c(1.020, 0.577, 0.378, 0.243, 0.125, 0.062, 0.020, 0.010, -0.012)
sse <- function(p) sum((y - (p[1] * exp(-p[2] * t) + p[3]))^2)   # p = (A, k, c)
fit <- optim(c(1, 0.3, 0.1), sse, method = "BFGS")
round(fit$par, 4)
# [1]  1.0366  0.4788 -0.0294

The best unconstrained fit has a negative background. The noise in the last points pulled it down.
That is not a numerical error: the minimum of the SSE really is at c < 0. The model needs to be told that c \ge 0.


The data are synthetic: true A = 1, k = 0.5, c = 0, plus a fixed noise vector. Background-subtracted signals can go slightly negative, so this happens with real qPCR or fluorescence decay data too. The fitted half-life also depends on c (next slide), so this is not cosmetic. optim with BFGS is what Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton used.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Fix 1: bounds

fitb <- optim(c(1, 0.3, 0.1), sse, method = "L-BFGS-B", lower = c(0, 0, 0))
round(fitb$par, 4)
# [1] 1.0152 0.5214 0.0000

optim(method = "L-BFGS-B") takes lower and upper: steps that would leave the box are cut back (projected) onto it.
The background sits at the bound, and the half-life changes from 1.45 h to 1.33 h.


L-BFGS-B is the limited-memory BFGS from Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton with box constraints added: at each step, any parameter that would cross its bound is held at the bound. In Python it is scipy.optimize.minimize(method=“L-BFGS-B”, bounds=…). The free fit has a lower SSE (0.0023 vs 0.0038), as it must: it searches a bigger set. The quantity of interest, the half-life ln 2 / k, moves by 8%. Which answer is right is a modelling decision; the numerics only tell you that the bound is active.

title: Constraints and linear programming
section: At a bound, the gradient is not zero
text:
At a bound, the gradient is not zero
round(numDeriv::grad(sse, fitb$par), 4)
# [1] 0.0000 0.0000 0.1054

In A and k (free) the gradient is 0, as usual. In c it is positive: the SSE would fall if c could decrease, but the bound stops it.
That number is the multiplier of the bound: how fast the SSE would fall per unit we relax c \ge 0.
Check: after a bounded fit, list the parameters that sit at a bound. Their usual standard errors are meaningless (Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters), and the result depends on the bound you chose.


“Converged” no longer means “gradient zero”. The condition at a bounded minimum is: gradient zero in every free parameter, and pointing outward (into the forbidden region) in every parameter held at a bound. A gradient pointing inward would mean the optimiser stopped too early. This is the simplest case of the KKT conditions, which we meet again with NNLS (The SVD, rank deficiency and regularisation) and in linear programming. The Hessian-based standard errors of the previous unit assume an interior minimum with zero gradient, so they do not apply to a parameter at its bound.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Fix 2: reparameterise
Optimise an unconstrained \theta and map it into the allowed set:

Positive: c = e^{\theta}, as for rate constants in Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting.
Proportions: p = \text{softmax}(\theta) = e^{\theta_i} / \sum_j e^{\theta_j}, with \theta_1 = 0 fixed. Every p_i > 0 and they sum to 1.

sse_log <- function(q) sse(c(q[1], q[2], exp(q[3])))      # c = exp(theta)
fitl <- optim(c(1, 0.3, log(0.1)), sse_log, method = "BFGS")
round(fitl$par, 3); signif(exp(fitl$par[3]), 3); fitl$convergence
# [1]  1.015  0.523 -7.116
# [1] 0.000812
# [1] 1                         # 1 = hit the iteration limit

Failure: the best c is 0, which needs \theta = -\infty. BFGS walks towards it until it runs out of iterations; \theta is wherever it stopped (Python stops at -14, Rust at -29).


Reparameterisation is the right tool when the true value is well inside the allowed region: it removes the constraint and also helps scaling (rates spanning decades become theta spanning a few units). It is the wrong tool when the answer is on the boundary: e^theta can only approach 0, the SSE becomes flat in theta, and the optimiser drifts. c is still about right (8e-4), but theta is meaningless, convergence is not reported, and anything based on the curvature in theta is nonsense. Softmax has the same problem when a proportion should be exactly 0; the exercise shows it on the diet example. Check: if a reparameterised parameter runs off to large negative values, the constraint is active; switch to a bound.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Lagrange multipliers in one picture




Counts n = (30, 10) of two cell types. Maximise the log-likelihood f(p) = 30 \log p_1 + 10 \log p_2 subject to g(p) = p_1 + p_2 = 1.

Grey curves: contours of f. Blue line: the constraint.
At the orange point, \nabla f has a component along the line: sliding along it improves f.
At the optimum the contour touches the line: \nabla f is parallel to \nabla g: \nabla f = \lambda \nabla g



This one picture is the whole idea of Lagrange multipliers. On the constraint we can only move along the line. If the gradient of f has any component along the line, moving that way increases f, so we are not at the optimum. At the optimum the gradient of f must therefore be perpendicular to the line, which is the direction of the gradient of g. Parallel gradients: grad f = lambda grad g, for some number lambda. Together with the constraint itself that gives as many equations as unknowns.

title: Constraints and linear programming
section: The multiplier is a shadow price
text:
The multiplier is a shadow price
\nabla f = (30/p_1,\ 10/p_2) and \nabla g = (1, 1), so 30/p_1 = 10/p_2 = \lambda. With p_1 + p_2 = 1: \lambda = 40, p = (0.75, 0.25).
n <- c(30, 10)
f <- function(p) sum(n * log(p))
p_hat <- n / sum(n)
n / p_hat                            # gradient of f at the optimum
# [1] 40 40                          # = lambda * (1, 1)
f(1.01 * p_hat) - f(p_hat)           # relax the constraint: sum = 1.01
# [1] 0.3980132                      # about lambda * 0.01 = 0.4

\lambda = how much the best f improves per unit the constraint is relaxed. Economists call it the shadow price of the constraint.
Inequalities: the multiplier is \ge 0, and zero if the constraint is inactive (relaxing it changes nothing). These are the KKT conditions; the bounded decay fit and NNLS are examples.


The answer p = n/N is no surprise, but the multiplier is the new object. Its meaning, the rate of change of the optimal value when the constraint level changes, carries over to every constrained problem, and in linear programming it becomes the answer to biological questions: which nutrient limits growth? For inequality constraints: an active constraint has a multiplier that tells you how much it costs you; an inactive one has multiplier 0. KKT stands for Karush, Kuhn and Tucker. We do not need the general theory; the gradient of 0.105 at the bounded decay fit was such a multiplier.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Linear programming
Objective and constraints all linear. A cell makes ATP by respiration (x_1) or fermentation (x_2) (toy numbers):
\max\ 6x_1 + 3x_2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_2 &\le 6 &&\text{carbon supply}\\
4x_1 + x_2 &\le 12 &&\text{proteome: respiration enzymes are costly}\\
x_1,\ x_2 &\ge 0
\end{aligned}

Respiration gives twice the ATP per carbon, but needs four times the enzyme per unit flux.
A linear function has no interior maximum: its gradient (6, 3) is never zero. The answer is always on the boundary.
Gradient methods are the wrong tool; LP has its own algorithms, exact in a finite number of steps.


This is a caricature of a real model of overflow metabolism (fast-growing E. coli or yeast ferment even with oxygen present, because respiration costs more protein per unit of flux). We will see that the best strategy is a mix, which is the biological point of such models. Note the absence of a minimum in the interior: no gradient method stopping rule (gradient near zero) can ever be satisfied, so we need a different idea.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
The feasible polygon





Each constraint keeps one side of a line. Together: a convex polygon (in n dimensions a polytope).
Orange: lines of equal ATP, 6x_1 + 3x_2 = z. Push z up until the line leaves the polygon.
The last point touched is a corner (vertex): (2, 4), ATP = 24. A mix of both pathways.
Fundamental fact: if an LP has an optimum, one of the corners is optimal.



Draw this on the board. The level lines of a linear objective are parallel straight lines; sliding them in the direction of the gradient, the last contact with a convex polygon is a corner, or a whole edge if the objective is parallel to that edge. So we only need to check the corners, a finite set. The corners here: (0,0) ATP 0, (3,0) ATP 18, (2,4) ATP 24, (0,6) ATP 18. Pure respiration is limited by the proteome, pure fermentation by carbon, the mix uses both resources fully.

title: Constraints and linear programming
section: The simplex idea: walk along edges
text:
The simplex idea: walk along edges





Start at a corner: (0, 0), ATP 0.
Along which edge does ATP increase? x_1: +6 per unit. Go until a constraint stops you: proteome at x_1 = 3 (carbon would allow 6). Corner (3, 0), ATP 18.
Along the proteome edge, x_2 up by 1 means x_1 down by \tfrac14: ATP changes by 3 - 6/4 = +1.5. Go until carbon stops you: (2, 4), ATP 24.
Along the carbon edge: x_2 up 1, x_1 down 1: 3 - 6 = -3. No improving edge: optimal.



This is Dantzig’s simplex method (1947) without the tableau. Each step: from the current corner, look at the edges leaving it; the rate of change of the objective along an edge is the reduced cost. Pick an improving edge, walk along it until the first constraint becomes active (the ratio test), and you are at a new corner. Stop when no edge improves. Because the polygon is convex, a corner with no improving edge is the global optimum: there are no local optima in LP. In n dimensions the corners are found by solving n x n linear systems of active constraints, which is where LU factorisations come in; real solvers update the factorisation from step to step.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
How many corners?

With n variables and m constraints, a corner is where n constraints are active: up to \binom{m}{n} candidates.
\binom{4}{2} = 6 here, \binom{100}{50} \approx 10^{29} for a modest problem. Checking every corner is hopeless.
The simplex method visits only a short path of improving corners: in practice a small multiple of m steps (in rare worst cases exponentially many).
Interior-point methods cut through the inside of the polytope with Newton steps (Newton for systems of equations) and are polynomial in the worst case.
Modern solvers (HiGHS, GLPK, Gurobi) have both and pick one.


The exercise has students write the brute-force corner enumeration for 2 variables, and then count how many candidates a larger problem would need. Klee and Minty (1972) built cube-shaped LPs on which the textbook simplex visits all 2^n corners, but on real problems it is fast, and that was a famous puzzle in the theory of algorithms. Interior-point methods (Karmarkar 1984) follow a smooth path through the interior; each step solves a large sparse linear system. For FBA on genome-scale models either kind solves in well under a second.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
LP in R: lpSolve::lp
library(lpSolve)
res <- lp("max", objective.in = c(6, 3),
          const.mat = rbind(c(1, 1), c(4, 1)),
          const.dir = c("<=", "<="), const.rhs = c(6, 12),
          compute.sens = TRUE)
res$status; res$solution; res$objval
# [1] 0                    # 0 = success
# [1] 2 4
# [1] 24
res$duals[1:2]             # shadow prices of carbon and proteome
# [1] 2 1

lp assumes x \ge 0. Python: scipy.optimize.linprog (HiGHS, minimises); Rust: the minilp crate.
Shadow prices: one more unit of carbon gives +2 ATP, one more unit of proteome +1 ATP.


Check the shadow prices by hand: with carbon 7 the corner moves to (5/3, 16/3), ATP 26, so +2. With proteome 13: (7/3, 11/3), ATP 25, so +1. These are the Lagrange multipliers of the two active constraints: they solve (6, 3) = y1 (1, 1) + y2 (4, 1), the LP version of grad f = lambda grad g. linprog only minimises, so Python users pass -c and flip the sign of the objective and of the marginals; the exercise shows how. compute.sens = TRUE asks lpSolve for the sensitivity analysis; the first entries of duals belong to the constraints, the rest are reduced costs of the variables.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
When an LP goes wrong


Tie (objective 8x_1 + 2x_2): a whole edge is optimal. The solver returns one corner and does not tell you.
Unbounded: a missing constraint. Infeasible: constraints that contradict each other.
Check the status every time. lpSolve is not reliable here: on the middle LP it returns status 0 (“success”) with x_2 = 10^{30}, its internal infinity. Look for absurd values.


Each failure has a biological counterpart in FBA. A tie means alternative optimal flux distributions: the next slides show them. Unbounded means a forgotten uptake bound or a cycle that makes ATP from nothing; real genome-scale models are checked for such energy-generating cycles. Infeasible means the model cannot do what you demand (e.g. a measured growth rate higher than the model allows), often a missing reaction. The lpSolve behaviour is real: for this two-variable LP it reports success with 1e30, while on the FBA problem later it correctly reports status 3. scipy reports status 3 (unbounded) or 2 (infeasible) with a message. Degenerate corners (more than n constraints meeting at a point) are a fourth, milder case: the simplex can stall there for a few steps, and the shadow prices are not unique.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Flux balance analysis: the network

Toy network: 6 metabolites, 9 reactions. Glucose (G) is split into pyruvate (P) by two routes (GLY, or BYP1 + BYP2 via X). P is respired (RES, needs O2), fermented to acetate (FER), or built into biomass (BIO).

Fluxes v_j are reaction rates in mmol per gram dry weight per hour; we keep toy units. EX_glc and EX_o2 are exchange reactions: uptake from the medium, with upper bounds 10 and 15. EX_ac secretes acetate. BIO is a pseudo-reaction that drains the precursors and energy needed to make new cells; its flux is the growth rate. ATP is drawn as numbers next to each reaction, not as a node, to keep the picture readable; it is a metabolite like the others. The two parallel routes are on purpose: real networks have isozymes and bypasses, and they make the optimum non-unique. The yields are invented (real respiration yields more ATP), but the structure is that of textbook FBA examples.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
The stoichiometric matrix
Row = metabolite, column = reaction, entry = how many molecules the reaction makes (+) or uses (−).
rxn <- c("EX_glc", "EX_o2", "GLY", "BYP1", "BYP2", "RES", "FER", "EX_ac", "BIO")
S <- rbind(G   = c(1, 0, -1, -1,  0,  0,  0,  0,  0),
           O2  = c(0, 1,  0,  0,  0, -2,  0,  0,  0),
           X   = c(0, 0,  0,  1, -1,  0,  0,  0,  0),
           P   = c(0, 0,  2,  0,  2, -1, -1,  0, -1),
           ATP = c(0, 0,  2,  0,  2, 11,  1,  0, -5),
           Ac  = c(0, 0,  0,  0,  0,  0,  1, -1,  0))
colnames(S) <- rxn
qr(S)$rank
# [1] 6

\frac{d}{dt}(\text{concentrations}) = S\mathbf v. Steady state: S\mathbf v = \mathbf 0: every metabolite is made as fast as it is used.
6 independent equations, 9 unknowns: a 3-dimensional null space of solutions, the same null space as in Gaussian elimination as LU.


Read one row: P (pyruvate) is made twice by GLY and twice by BYP2, used once by each of RES, FER and BIO. Steady state is the key assumption of FBA: intracellular metabolites turn over in seconds, growth takes an hour, so on the slow time scale the metabolite pools are constant. We do not know the kinetics (no rate laws, no parameters), only the stoichiometry, which is known from biochemistry. That is why FBA works on genome-scale models where kinetic models would need thousands of unknown parameters. Elimination of S v = 0 leaves 3 free fluxes (for example glucose uptake, the split between the two routes, and respiration); the bounds and the objective choose among them.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
FBA as a linear program
\max_{\mathbf v}\ v_\text{BIO} \quad\text{subject to}\quad S\mathbf v = \mathbf 0,\quad \mathbf v \ge \mathbf 0,\quad v_\text{glc} \le 10,\quad v_{\text{O}_2} \le 15
fba <- function(ub = c(10, 15), ko = integer(0)) {
  B <- diag(9)[c(1, 2, ko), , drop = FALSE]     # rows picking v_glc, v_o2, knock-outs
  lp("max", objective.in = c(rep(0, 8), 1),      # maximise v_BIO
     const.mat = rbind(S, B), const.dir = c(rep("=", 6), rep("<=", nrow(B))),
     const.rhs = c(rep(0, 6), ub, rep(0, length(ko))), compute.sens = TRUE)
}
sol <- fba(); sol$objval
# [1] 15
setNames(sol$solution, rxn)
# EX_glc  EX_o2    GLY   BYP1   BYP2    RES    FER  EX_ac    BIO
#     10     10     10      0      0      5      0      0     15

All glucose used, pure respiration, no acetate; oxygen uptake 10 of the 15 allowed.


The objective “maximise growth” is an assumption: that evolution has tuned the cell to grow as fast as possible in this medium. It works well for bacteria in exponential growth, less well elsewhere, and other objectives (maximal ATP, minimal total flux) are used too. lpSolve has no variable bounds other than v >= 0, so the uptake limits are extra rows; a knock-out is a row forcing that flux to 0. scipy’s linprog takes bounds directly. By hand: with no fermentation, P balance gives 20 = RES + BIO, ATP balance gives 20 + 11 RES = 5 BIO; so BIO = 15, RES = 5. Check with S %*% sol$solution: zero up to rounding.

title: Constraints and linear programming
section: The optimum is not unique: flux variability
text:
The optimum is not unique: flux variability




Flux variability analysis (FVA): fix growth at its maximum (15), then minimise and maximise each flux in turn, 2 \times 9 more LPs.

GLY and the bypass can share the glucose in any ratio: each ranges over [0, 10].
The solver’s GLY = 10 was one arbitrary corner.
Like a non-identifiable parameter (Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters): the objective cannot tell the routes apart. Report ranges, not one flux vector.



This is the tie case of the failure slide, in biology. Growth only depends on the sum GLY + BYP1, so every split is optimal. In real genome-scale models a large fraction of the fluxes have non-trivial ranges at optimal growth. Comparing a single FBA solution with measured fluxes (from 13C labelling) is therefore misleading; FVA ranges are the honest comparison. Other ways to pick one solution: minimise total flux among optimal solutions (parsimonious FBA), or sample the optimal face. The exercise computes the FVA table.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Knock-outs
ko <- sapply(1:9, function(j) fba(ko = j)$objval)    # remove one reaction at a time
round(setNames(ko, rxn), 3)
# EX_glc  EX_o2    GLY   BYP1   BYP2    RES    FER  EX_ac    BIO
#  0.000  6.667 15.000 15.000 15.000  6.667 15.000 15.000  0.000
fba(ko = c(3, 4))$objval                              # GLY and BYP1 together
# [1] 0

Essential: glucose uptake (and BIO itself). No respiration: growth drops to 6.67, by fermentation alone (anaerobic growth).
GLY and BYP1 are each dispensable, but together lethal: a synthetic lethal pair, from redundancy.


Knock-out predictions are the main use of FBA in practice: gene essentiality screens in E. coli and yeast are predicted with roughly 90% accuracy by genome-scale models, and the errors point to missing knowledge. Each prediction is one more LP. A gene knock-out removes all reactions that need that gene (through gene-protein-reaction rules); here one reaction is one gene. Without RES the cell ferments: P balance 20 = FER + BIO and ATP balance 20 + FER = 5 BIO give BIO = 20/3. Acetate secretion is the measurable signature.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Shadow prices: what limits growth?
fba()$duals[7:8]                        # rows 7, 8: glucose and oxygen bounds
# [1] 1.5 0.0
round(fba(ub = c(10, 4))$duals[7:8], 3)   # less oxygen
# [1] 0.667 0.833

Plenty of oxygen: one more glucose gives +1.5 growth, oxygen has price 0 (its bound is inactive: 10 used of 15). Glucose limits growth.
Oxygen limited to 4: both limit; growth 10, and acetate is secreted (8): overflow metabolism.


The shadow price is the Lagrange multiplier again: the rate at which the best growth changes if one bound is relaxed. Experimentally that is the question: would adding more of this nutrient help? Rows 7 and 8 of the constraint matrix are the two uptake bounds, so duals[7:8] are their prices. With plenty of oxygen, the cell respires all its pyruvate and only glucose is short. With oxygen 4, respiration is capped at 2, the rest of the pyruvate is fermented, and acetate leaves the cell, as E. coli does in oxygen-limited cultures.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Scanning the oxygen limit


Below 10: each unit of oxygen gives 5/6 = 0.833 more growth and less acetate. Above 10: oxygen is in excess, price 0.
Shadow prices are local: they hold until another constraint becomes active (the kink at 10), where the price is not unique.


This is the one-dimensional version of a phenotype phase plane (growth as a function of two uptake rates). Each point is one LP. At exactly 10 the price is ambiguous (0.833 from the left, 0 from the right); solvers report either one, and the exercise shows lpSolve and HiGHS disagreeing there. To predict the effect of a large change, re-solve instead of multiplying by the price.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
FBA checklist

Status first. Infeasible: the bounds contradict each other or the model misses a reaction. Unbounded: a forgotten uptake bound or an ATP-making cycle.
S\mathbf v = \mathbf 0 check on the returned fluxes, with a tolerance (fluxes of 10^{-12} are zeros).
Never trust one flux vector. Run FVA; a flux is determined only if its range is narrow.
Read the shadow prices to see which bounds matter; they only hold until the next kink.
Units and bounds decide the answer: an uptake bound of 10 vs 15 is a modelling choice, not a fact.


The same failures as on the LP failure slide, translated into model-building practice. Genome-scale models come with standard tests (the MEMOTE test suite checks for mass imbalance, energy-generating cycles and blocked reactions). A practical warning: LP solvers work in floating point with feasibility tolerances around 1e-9, so a flux of 3e-15 is zero and an S v of 1e-12 is a balanced metabolite.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Production tools

COBRA Toolbox (MATLAB) and cobrapy (Python) are the standard: they read models in SBML, set bounds, run FBA, FVA, knock-out screens and parsimonious FBA, and call an LP solver (GLPK, HiGHS, Gurobi, CPLEX).
Genome-scale models: E. coli iML1515 has 2712 reactions and 1877 metabolites; human Recon3D about 13 000 reactions. S is sparse (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse): a reaction touches a handful of metabolites.
The toy model is exactly what these tools do, at a size where you can check every number by hand.


cobrapy: model.optimize() runs FBA, cobra.flux_analysis.flux_variability_analysis runs FVA, single_gene_deletion runs the knock-out screen, and solution.shadow_prices gives the shadow prices of the metabolites. In R the sybil package did the same but is no longer maintained; most R users call cobrapy or use the COBRA Toolbox. The models are curated over years from the literature; the numerical part is a sparse LP, solved in milliseconds.

title: Constraints and linear programming
text:
Summary

Biological constraints: signs, sums to 1, capacities, steady state. A constraint is active if it holds with equality.
Bounds (L-BFGS-B): the answer can sit at a bound, where the gradient is not zero. Reparameterisation (e^\theta, softmax) fails when the answer is on the boundary: \theta runs to -\infty.
Lagrange: at a constrained optimum \nabla f = \lambda \nabla g; \lambda is the shadow price, 0 for inactive constraints.
LP: the optimum is at a corner of the feasible polytope; simplex walks along improving edges; solvers: lpSolve::lp, scipy.optimize.linprog (HiGHS), minilp. Check the status: tie, unbounded, infeasible.
FBA: maximise growth subject to S\mathbf v = \mathbf 0 and bounds. Optimal fluxes are often not unique (FVA), knock-outs are one LP each, shadow prices show which nutrient limits growth.

Next: Part 10, The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences.

The two ideas that carry furthest: constraints change what “converged” means (gradient not zero at an active constraint), and multipliers measure how much each constraint costs. In FBA both become biology: the active bounds are the limiting nutrients, the multipliers their value to the cell. Part 10 moves from ordinary to partial differential equations.

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
About this lecture
Fitting a model to data means choosing parameters that make the residuals small. When the model is nonlinear in its parameters (a rate inside an exponential), lm cannot do it and there is no formula: we iterate.

Gauss–Newton: linearise the model, solve one linear least-squares problem per step (by QR), repeat. Fast near the answer, wild far from it.
Levenberg–Marquardt: damped Gauss–Newton, sliding between Gauss–Newton and gradient descent. What minpack.lm::nlsLM and scipy.optimize.least_squares use.
Practicalities: nls and its “singular gradient”, log-parameters for positive rates, multistart.
ODE models: the ODE solver sits inside the residual function. Its tolerance and the finite-difference step must fit together.
Biology: a drug taken orally. From 12 plasma samples, estimate the absorption rate, the elimination rate and the volume of distribution.


This unit puts together three earlier ones: linear least squares by QR (Part 4), Newton for systems with its Jacobian (Part 2) and the ODE solvers of Part 8. It also runs alongside Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton: Levenberg-Marquardt is the special-purpose method for sums of squares, and its two limits are Gauss-Newton and gradient descent. The PK model is the running example; it has a closed form, which lets us check every ODE-based fit exactly. The flip-flop at the end leads into the next unit, Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: A biology problem first: a drug in plasma
text:
A biology problem first: a drug in plasma


One oral dose D = 100 mg. Plasma sampled 12 times over 12 hours.
Questions: how fast is the drug absorbed (k_a), how fast eliminated (k_e), and in what volume (V) does it distribute? These decide the dosing schedule.
The data are simulated from k_a = 1/h, k_e = 0.2/h, V = 20 L, plus noise with SD 0.1 mg/L, so we know the truth.


This is the standard one-compartment model with first-order absorption, the first model fitted in any pharmacokinetics course. Real data would come from a phase 1 study. The data were simulated with set.seed(1), rounded to 2 decimals and typed in, so R, Python and Rust use the same 12 numbers (they are in the exercise and in the figure script). The fitted curve (orange) differs slightly from the true one (dashed) because of the noise: least squares finds the best curve for these data, not the truth. How close the estimates are to the truth is the topic of the next unit.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: The model: an ODE with a closed form
text:
The model: an ODE with a closed form


Amount in gut A_g, in the central compartment (plasma) A_c:
A_g' = -k_a A_g, \qquad A_c' = k_a A_g - k_e A_c
A_g(0) = D, A_c(0) = 0, and we measure C = A_c / V.

Solved by hand (the Bateman function):
C(t) = \frac{D\,k_a}{V(k_a - k_e)}\left(e^{-k_e t} - e^{-k_a t}\right)

D  <- 100
tt <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)
y  <- c(1.02, 1.88, 2.34, 2.98, 3.27, 3.26, 3.17, 2.77, 1.92, 1.23, 1.00, 0.61)
bateman <- function(t, ka, ke, V) D * ka / (V * (ka - ke)) * (exp(-ke * t) - exp(-ka * t))

k_a and k_e sit inside exponentials: the model is nonlinear in its parameters. No transformation turns it into lm.
Most ODE models have no closed form. We use the formula first, then fit the ODE directly and check against it.


The ODE is linear in the state, which is why it can be solved by hand: first A_g = D exp(-ka t), then a linear first-order ODE for A_c. Taking logs helps for a single exponential (log C = log C0 - k t is a straight line, as in the intro), but not for a difference of two exponentials. Note the formula is 0/0 at ka = ke: R returns NaN there. The ODE has no such problem; the exercise looks at this. Bioavailability F is absorbed into V here (strictly, V is V/F).
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
The least-squares problem
Parameters \mathbf p = (k_a, k_e, V), model values m_i(\mathbf p) = C(t_i), residuals r_i = y_i - m_i(\mathbf p):
\min_{\mathbf p}\ \text{RSS}(\mathbf p) = \sum_{i=1}^{12} r_i(\mathbf p)^2





RSS over (k_a, k_e), with V at its best value for each pair.
A curved valley, two minima with the same RSS (stars), and a line k_a = k_e where the formula is 0/0.
A start in the wrong place can end in the wrong minimum. We come back to this at the end.



Contours of RSS on log axes; V is “profiled out”: for fixed ka and ke the model is linear in D/V, so the best V comes from a one-line linear least-squares fit. The valley is long and curved, which is typical for rate constants: the data mainly determine a combination of them. The second minimum is not a numerical artefact; it is the flip-flop solution, an exact symmetry of the model, discussed at the end. For now: nonlinear least squares can have several minima, and a local method finds the one whose valley it starts in.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: Recap: linear least squares by QR
text:
Recap: linear least squares by QR
For a linear model A\mathbf x \approx \mathbf b (unit Least squares: normal equations vs QR):

minimise \|\mathbf b - A\mathbf x\|^2; factor A = QR and back-substitute R\mathbf x = Q^T\mathbf b. In R: qr.solve(A, b).
The normal equations A^TA\mathbf x = A^T\mathbf b give the same \mathbf x in exact arithmetic, but square the condition number: \kappa(A^TA) = \kappa(A)^2.

And from Newton for systems of equations: the Jacobian J_{ij} = \partial m_i / \partial p_j is the matrix of slopes, and
\mathbf m(\mathbf p + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \mathbf m(\mathbf p) + J\,\boldsymbol\delta.
Gauss–Newton = these two ideas together.

One slide of recap only. The student should remember: QR for least squares, never form A^T A if you can avoid it, and the Jacobian as the matrix that turns a small change in the parameters into the change in the model. Here the Jacobian is 12 x 3: one row per measurement, one column per parameter. Unlike in Newton for systems, J is not square, which is why each step is a least-squares problem rather than a linear system.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Linearise the model
At the start \mathbf p_0 = (0.5, 0.1, 10), by forward differences (rows t = 0.25, 2, 12 h):
model <- function(p) bateman(tt, p[1], p[2], p[3])
jac <- function(p, h = 1e-7) sapply(1:3, function(j) {      # forward differences
  e <- replace(numeric(3), j, h * p[j]); (model(p + e) - model(p)) / e[j] })
J <- jac(c(0.5, 0.1, 10));  round(J[c(1, 6, 12), ], 3)
#        [,1]    [,2]   [,3]
# [1,]  2.178  -0.147 -0.116
# [2,]  6.379  -6.379 -0.564
# [3,] -1.495 -35.844 -0.373

Column 1: raising k_a raises early concentrations and lowers late ones (faster in, faster gone).
Column 2: raising k_e lowers everything, most at 12 h. Column 3: raising V dilutes.
Step h = 10^{-7}\,p_j is relative to each parameter, as in Newton for systems of equations.


Each column is a sensitivity: how much each predicted concentration moves per unit change of one parameter. Read the signs with the students; they are pharmacology. The forward-difference step of about sqrt(eps) times the parameter balances truncation and rounding error (Convergence and cost). We could differentiate the Bateman function by hand, but for an ODE model we cannot, so we use the generic finite-difference Jacobian from the start. Keep the 0.373 in mind: V’s column is small because V is large, a scaling issue that the log-parameters slide comes back to.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
The Gauss–Newton step
Replace the model by its linearisation and minimise the RSS of that:
\min_{\boldsymbol\delta}\ \|\mathbf r - J\boldsymbol\delta\|^2, \qquad \mathbf r = \mathbf y - \mathbf m(\mathbf p_k), \qquad \mathbf p_{k+1} = \mathbf p_k + \boldsymbol\delta
A linear least-squares problem with design matrix J (12 × 3) and data \mathbf r: solve it by QR.
r <- y - model(c(0.5, 0.1, 10))
qr.solve(J, r)                                  # delta
# [1]  0.35245282 -0.01478552  8.03484167

In the normal-equation form, J^TJ\,\boldsymbol\delta = J^T\mathbf r. Same \boldsymbol\delta here, but at the minimum \kappa(J) = 170 while \kappa(J^TJ) = 2.9\times10^4: QR keeps 2 more digits.
Compare Newton for systems of equations: there J was square and we solved J\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F. Here J is tall and we solve in the least-squares sense.


This is the whole method: linearise, solve a linear least-squares problem, update, repeat. Gauss used it for orbits of asteroids around 1800. Many textbooks write the step with the normal equations; libraries do not form J^T J. With three well-scaled parameters the difference is small, but with 20 parameters of very different size, or a nearly non-identifiable model, kappa(J) can be 1e7 and then kappa squared is 1e14, and the normal equations lose everything. qr.solve uses Householder QR (Part 4).
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
One Gauss–Newton step by hand
One parameter: after an IV bolus, C(t) = 10\,e^{-kt}. Data t = 1, 2, 4 h: y = 6.0,\ 3.7,\ 1.3 mg/L. Start k_0 = 0.3.



t
m = 10e^{-0.3t}
J = -10\,t\,e^{-0.3t}
r = y - m




1
7.408
−7.408
−1.408


2
5.488
−10.976
−1.788


4
3.012
−12.048
−1.712



With one column, the least-squares solution is a ratio:
\delta = \frac{\sum J_i r_i}{\sum J_i^2} = \frac{50.68}{320.51} = 0.158, \qquad k_1 = 0.458.
RSS: 8.11 → 0.285. Next steps: 0.5021, 0.504413, 0.5044173 (the minimum).

Do this on the board. The one-column least-squares formula is the slope of a line through the origin, from the qPCR unit. The RSS drops by a factor 28 in one step. The exercise repeats this and does the second step, then the same step in log k. The number of correct digits roughly doubles in the last steps: GN behaves like Newton here because the residuals at the minimum are small (RSS 0.0052).
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Gauss–Newton in R
gauss_newton <- function(p, maxit = 30, tol = 1e-8) {
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    r <- y - model(p)
    delta <- qr.solve(jac(p), r)               # linear least squares by QR
    p <- p + delta
    cat(sprintf("%2d %10.6f %10.6f %10.4f %12.8f\n", k, p[1], p[2], p[3], sum((y - model(p))^2)))
    if (sqrt(sum(delta^2)) < tol * sqrt(sum(p^2))) break
  }
  p
}
p_hat <- gauss_newton(c(0.5, 0.1, 10))
 1   0.852453   0.085214    18.0348  15.91083738
 2   1.124562   0.128428    22.3757   0.97745046
 3   1.056583   0.176306    20.8165   0.09134721
 4   1.016284   0.189795    20.2448   0.06656857
 5   1.015102   0.190607    20.2166   0.06646745
 6   1.015072   0.190616    20.2162   0.06646744
Two more iterations change nothing visible: \hat k_a = 1.0151, \hat k_e = 0.1906, \hat V = 20.216, RSS 0.0665.

Ten lines. The stopping rule is a relative step size; the RSS itself cannot go to zero because of the noise, so “RSS small” is not a usable criterion. Iterations 7 and 8 are not shown. With a forward-difference Jacobian, the step stalls at about 1e-9 relative, so asking for tol = 1e-10 would never stop: the stopping tolerance must sit above the accuracy of the Jacobian.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
nls is Gauss–Newton
fit <- nls(y ~ bateman(tt, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 0.5, ke = 0.1, V = 10),
           trace = TRUE)
# 93.53426    (2.65e+01): par = (0.5 0.1 10)
# 15.91084    (1.43e+01): par = (0.8524528 0.08521448 18.03484)
# 0.9774509   (3.57e+00): par = (1.124562 0.1284276 22.37571)
# 0.09134723  (6.10e-01): par = (1.056583 0.1763063 20.81648)
# 0.06656857  (3.89e-02): par = (1.016284 0.1897946 20.24476)
# 0.06646745  (3.05e-04): par = (1.015102 0.1906071 20.21665)
# 0.06646744  (1.67e-06): par = (1.015072 0.1906157 20.21621)

Exactly our iterates. nls uses Gauss–Newton with a QR solve and a numerical Jacobian, plus step halving if the RSS goes up.
The number in brackets is its convergence criterion (the size of the predicted RSS decrease); it stops below 10^{-5}.


The first column is the RSS, the second nls’s relative-offset convergence criterion, then the parameters. The match with our 10 lines is digit for digit: nls computes the gradient with numericDeriv (forward differences) and solves with qr. Step halving: if the full step increases the RSS, nls tries half, a quarter, and so on, down to minFactor = 1/1024. That is a crude form of damping. Python: scipy.optimize.curve_fit does the same job, but uses Levenberg-Marquardt (MINPACK) by default.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: How fast? Gauss–Newton is almost Newton
text:
How fast? Gauss–Newton is almost Newton


Newton for minimising RSS needs the Hessian 2\left(J^TJ - \sum_i r_i \nabla^2 m_i\right). Gauss–Newton drops the second term: it needs only first derivatives.
Small residuals (good fit) or a nearly linear model → the dropped term is small → convergence close to quadratic. Large residuals → only linear convergence.


Relative error in (ka, ke, V) against a reference fit, per accepted iteration, on a log axis. Gauss-Newton (blue) needs 3 slow steps and then gains 2-3 digits per step; the curve bending downwards is the signature of superlinear convergence. It flattens at 1e-10 because the Jacobian is a forward difference. The green and orange curves are Levenberg-Marquardt, which comes next. The Hessian formula connects to Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton: Gauss-Newton is a quasi-Newton method whose Hessian approximation J^T J comes for free from the Jacobian.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: Failure: Gauss–Newton from a bad start
text:
Failure: Gauss–Newton from a bad start
Start \mathbf p_0 = (3, 0.05, 50): fast absorption, very slow elimination, large volume. RSS 9.5.
p0 <- c(3, 0.05, 50)
p1 <- p0 + qr.solve(jac(p0), y - model(p0));  p1        # one Gauss-Newton step
# [1] -2.22468806  0.17865474  0.04427022
sum((y - model(p1))^2)
# [1] 6.742435e+29
nls(y ~ bateman(tt, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 3, ke = 0.05, V = 50))
# Error in nls(y ~ bateman(tt, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 3, ke = 0.05,  :
#   singular gradient

The linearisation is only good near \mathbf p_0; the full step goes far outside: a negative absorption rate and a volume of 44 mL.
nls evaluates the Jacobian at that point, finds it numerically rank deficient (\kappa \approx 10^{12}) and stops: “singular gradient”.


“Singular gradient” is the most common nls error and it rarely means the model is wrong. It means: at some trial point the columns of the Jacobian became (numerically) dependent. Typical causes: a bad start (here), a parameter that wandered to a place where it no longer affects the model (V = 0.04 makes everything huge; ka negative makes the exponentials blow up), or a model that really is over-parameterised. The remedies: better starting values, bounds or log-parameters, or a damped method. The damped method is next.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Levenberg–Marquardt: damped Gauss–Newton
Add a penalty on the step length:
\min_{\boldsymbol\delta}\ \|\mathbf r - J\boldsymbol\delta\|^2 + \lambda\,\|D_g\boldsymbol\delta\|^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \min_{\boldsymbol\delta} \left\| \begin{pmatrix} J \\ \sqrt{\lambda}\,D_g \end{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\delta - \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf r\\ \mathbf 0\end{pmatrix}\right\|^2

Still a linear least-squares problem, 3 rows taller: solve by QR. (D_g = diagonal of column lengths of J, Marquardt’s scaling, so the units of V do not matter.)
\lambda \to 0: the Gauss–Newton step. \lambda large: \boldsymbol\delta \approx D_g^{-2}J^T\mathbf r/\lambda, a short step downhill (-J^T\mathbf r is half the gradient of the RSS): gradient descent.
Rule: if the RSS went down, accept and divide \lambda by 10; if up, reject and multiply \lambda by 10.


Levenberg (1944) and Marquardt (1963). The normal-equation form is (J^T J + lambda D^2) delta = J^T r; the stacked form on the slide is the same thing without squaring the condition number. Far from the minimum, where the linearisation is poor, steps are rejected and lambda grows until the step is short enough to go downhill: gradient descent is slow but safe. Near the minimum lambda shrinks and the method becomes Gauss-Newton with its fast convergence. This is a trust-region idea: lambda controls how far we trust the linear model. Gradient descent and trust regions in general are in Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Levenberg–Marquardt in R
lev_mar <- function(p, lambda = 0.01, maxit = 200, tol = 1e-8) {
  rss <- sum((y - model(p))^2)
  for (k in 1:maxit) {
    J <- jac(p); r <- y - model(p)
    Dg <- diag(sqrt(colSums(J^2)))              # Marquardt's scaling
    delta <- qr.solve(rbind(J, sqrt(lambda) * Dg), c(r, 0, 0, 0))
    rss_new <- sum((y - model(p + delta))^2)
    if (is.finite(rss_new) && rss_new < rss) {  # accept: trust the linear model more
      p <- p + delta; rss <- rss_new; lambda <- lambda / 10
      if (sqrt(sum(delta^2)) < tol * sqrt(sum(p^2))) break
    } else lambda <- lambda * 10                # reject: shorter, more downhill step
  }
  p
}

From (3, 0.05, 50): 15 passes, 10 steps accepted, 5 rejected (the first two among them); ends at (1.0151, 0.1906, 20.216).


Fourteen lines, and the core is the same qr.solve as Gauss-Newton with three extra rows. The is.finite check matters: a trial point with ka negative may give Inf or NaN, which must count as a rejection. The fixed factor 10 is the simplest rule; MINPACK adjusts lambda more cleverly through a trust-region radius, but the behaviour is the same. Iteration counts: 15 loop passes; passes 1, 2 and 4 are rejected far from the minimum, passes 13 and 14 near the end, where the RSS can hardly decrease any more within rounding.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
The two paths


Gauss–Newton (orange) jumps out of the region where the model makes sense.
Levenberg–Marquardt (green) first takes short downhill steps along the valley, then Gauss–Newton steps: error curve in orange on the convergence plot.


Projected on the (ka, ke) plane; contours are the profiled RSS of the earlier slide in linear axes. The first two LM trial steps were rejected (not drawn), so lambda went up to 1 before a step was accepted. Steps 3-5 move along the valley floor, then the method switches to almost pure Gauss-Newton and converges in four more steps. On the convergence plot the orange LM curve has the same steep end as Gauss-Newton: near the minimum, LM is Gauss-Newton.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
The library versions
library(minpack.lm)
fit <- nlsLM(y ~ bateman(tt, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 3, ke = 0.05, V = 50))
coef(fit)
#         ka         ke          V
#  1.0150722  0.1906157 20.2162105

nlsLM has the nls interface but uses MINPACK’s Levenberg–Marquardt; nls.lm takes a residual function instead of a formula.
Python: scipy.optimize.curve_fit (LM by default) and least_squares (trust region by default, method="lm" for MINPACK). Rust: nalgebra + 40 hand-written lines (exercise).
Same answer as nls when both converge. LM converges from more starts, not from all.


MINPACK (Moré, 1980) is the Fortran library behind both minpack.lm and scipy’s “lm” option. scipy’s default for least_squares is “trf”, a trust-region reflective method that also handles bounds. curve_fit wraps least_squares with a model-function interface like nls and also returns a covariance matrix; standard errors are for the next unit. The Rust argmin crate has a Gauss-Newton solver, but it needs extra trait plumbing; in the exercise we write LM ourselves with nalgebra’s QR, which is shorter and shows everything.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Positive rates: fit the logarithms
Rates and volumes must be positive. Fit \mathbf q = \log\mathbf p and use k_a = e^{q_1}, …:
fit <- nlsLM(y ~ bateman(tt, exp(lka), exp(lke), exp(lV)),
             start = list(lka = log(3), lke = log(0.05), lV = log(50)))
exp(coef(fit))
#        lka        lke         lV
#  1.0150721  0.1906157 20.2162104

Positivity for free: any step in \mathbf q gives \mathbf p > 0. No negative k_a, no V = 0.04 with a negative sign next.
Scale-free: a step of 0.1 in q is a 10 % change in any parameter, whatever its units. \kappa(J) at the minimum: 170 in (k_a, k_e, V), 8.7 in logs.
Chain rule: \partial m/\partial q_j = p_j\,\partial m/\partial p_j.
Not a cure-all: plain Gauss–Newton in logs from (3, 0.05, 50) still diverges (k_a \to 2\times10^{-4}, k_e \to 617). Damping is still needed.


The log-parameterisation is standard in pharmacometrics and systems biology (it also makes the multistart grid natural: starts spread over orders of magnitude). The conditioning improvement comes from the column scaling: V’s column was small because V is large; in log form all columns measure relative sensitivities. Bounds are the other option (least_squares(bounds=…), nlsLM(lower=…)); they are covered in Constraints and linear programming. Log-parameters cannot express a parameter that is truly zero; if a rate might be zero, you will see q drifting to minus infinity.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Fitting an ODE model
Most models (saturable elimination, viral dynamics, gene circuits) have no closed form. Then the residual function solves the ODE:
library(deSolve)
pk_rhs <- function(t, A, p) list(c(-p[1] * A[1],                 # gut
                                    p[1] * A[1] - p[2] * A[2]))   # central compartment
pk_ode <- function(p, tol = 1e-10) {
  out <- ode(c(D, 0), c(0, tt), pk_rhs, p, rtol = tol, atol = tol)
  out[-1, 3] / p[3]                       # amount in the central compartment / V
}
resid <- function(q, ...) y - pk_ode(exp(q), ...)
fit <- nls.lm(log(c(0.5, 0.1, 10)), fn = resid,
              control = nls.lm.control(epsfcn = 1e-10))
exp(fit$par)
# [1]  1.0150721  0.1906157 20.2162095

Matches the closed-form fit to 7 digits. Cost: each residual = one ODE solve; each Jacobian = 3 more.


deSolve’s ode with its default method lsoda (Stiffness and implicit methods). The output matrix has time in column 1 and the states after it; we drop the t = 0 row and take column 3 (A_c). Python: solve_ivp inside the function passed to least_squares; Rust: ode_solvers’ Dopri5 inside a hand-written LM. The epsfcn setting is explained two slides on. Saturable (Michaelis-Menten) elimination, ke A_c replaced by Vmax C/(Km + C), has no closed form and is fitted exactly like this. Viral dynamics (target cells, infected cells, virus) likewise.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: The optimiser sees the solver error
text:
The optimiser sees the solver error


What the optimiser minimises is \text{RSS}_\text{exact} plus the solver error: smooth stretches with jumps where the solver changes its step sequence.
With rtol = atol = 1e-3 the error (10^{-4}) is as large as the RSS change from a 0.3 % change in k_a: the fitted k_a is wrong in the 4th digit, and the reported RSS (0.06641) is below the true minimum (0.06647).


RSS computed through deSolve minus the exact RSS from the Bateman formula, along a line in ka (ke and V fixed at the estimate). Left, tolerance 1e-3: an error of about 1e-4 with visible jumps (step rejections and order changes in lsoda). Right, 1e-6: three orders smaller, still with one small kink. The optimiser cannot tell solver error from model misfit, so it partly fits the solver error. For this mild model the effect on the estimate is small even at 1e-3 (4 digits); for stiff models, or models where a small state drives a big one, the noise is larger and the optimiser can stall, stop early or report a wrong convergence. Table in exercise C6: estimates and RSS for rtol from 1e-2 to 1e-10.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Inner tolerance vs finite-difference step


The Jacobian is a difference quotient: solver error \varepsilon_\text{ode} divided by the step h. MINPACK’s default step 1.5\times10^{-8}|q| is tiny (here |q_1| = |\log k_a| = 0.015): the error jumps around whatever the tolerance.
Rule (from Convergence and cost): h \approx \sqrt{\varepsilon_\text{ode}}, and the solver tolerance 100–1000 times tighter than the accuracy you want from the fit. Then refit with a tighter tolerance and keep only the digits that agree.


Relative error of the fitted ka against the exact fit, for deSolve tolerances from 1e-3 to 1e-12 (tighter to the right) and two finite-difference steps. Orange: MINPACK’s default, sqrt(machine eps) times |q|. Because log ka is close to 0, the absolute step for ka is 2e-10, smaller than the solver error, and the Jacobian is garbage at random tolerances (3.5e-3 error at 1e-9!). Blue: epsfcn = 1e-10 gives step 1e-5 |q|; the error falls with the tolerance until it reaches the 1e-7 level set by the optimiser’s own stopping rule. scipy’s least_squares (default “trf”) uses a step relative to max(1, |q|), which avoids the trap. Alternative: forward sensitivity equations (deSolve’s companion packages, SUNDIALS) compute the Jacobian by solving extra ODEs; mention only.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Multistart


resid <- function(q) y - bateman(tt, exp(q[1]), exp(q[2]), exp(q[3]))
g <- c(0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10)
starts <- expand.grid(ka = g, ke = 1.5 * g)
ends <- t(apply(starts, 1, function(s) {
  fit <- nls.lm(log(c(s, 10)), fn = resid,
                control = nls.lm.control(maxiter = 200))
  c(exp(fit$par), rss = fit$deviance)
}))




36 starts over 2.5 orders of magnitude (log grid). 14 end at (1.02, 0.19, 20.2), 21 at (0.19, 1.02, 3.8), 1 runs off (k_a \to 10^{15}, RSS 64.5 = no model at all).
Always compare the RSS of the ends: a failed run has a much larger RSS. Here the two good ends have the same RSS: 0.06646744.


Multistart is the simplest global strategy: many local fits from spread-out starts, keep the best. A grid on log axes (or random log-uniform starts) covers the plausible range. Starts above the diagonal ka = ke go to the mirror solution: each start finds the minimum on its side of the ridge. The one failure started close to the diagonal and drifted to ka huge, ke tiny, V huge: the model predicts essentially 0, RSS = sum(y^2) = 64.5. Cost: 36 fits of about 8 iterations each, about 1500 model evaluations; with an ODE inside each costs one solve. Other global methods (simulated annealing, evolutionary algorithms, scatter search) are popular in systems biology; multistart with a good local method is hard to beat in benchmarks.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: The flip-flop: two answers, one curve
text:
The flip-flop: two answers, one curve


Swap k_a \leftrightarrow k_e and set V' = V\,k_e/k_a: the Bateman function is exactly the same. Plasma data alone cannot tell “fast in, slow out” from “slow in, fast out”.
Pharmacology: flip-flop kinetics (e.g. slow-release tablets). Decide with other data (an IV dose gives k_e directly) or prior knowledge (V = 3.8 L is plasma volume only).
No optimiser fixes this: the parameters are not identifiable. Next unit.


Check the algebra: D ka / (V (ka - ke)) times (e^{-ke t} - e^{-ka t}); swapping ka and ke flips the sign of both the denominator and the bracket, and the prefactor ka/V becomes ke/V’, which equals ka/V when V’ = V ke / ka. So the two parameter sets give identical concentrations at every time; the RSS values agree to all printed digits. The difference is in the gut, which is not measured. This is structural non-identifiability: a symmetry of the model, not a lack of data. The next unit, Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters, takes this up with the same model and data, together with practical non-identifiability (flat valleys) and standard errors.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
section: Checklist: is my nonlinear fit trustworthy?
text:
Checklist: is my nonlinear fit trustworthy?

“singular gradient” / no convergence → better starts, log-parameters, or Levenberg–Marquardt (nlsLM, least_squares).
A parameter at a strange value (negative rate, 10^{15}, 10^{-27}) → the fit ran off; restart, reparameterise, or the data do not determine it.
Plot the fitted curve over the data, and the residuals against time: a systematic pattern means a wrong model, not a numerical problem.
Multistart: several local fits from a log grid; compare the RSS of the ends. Equal RSS at different parameters → non-identifiable.
ODE inside: set rtol/atol explicitly and tight (1e-8 to 1e-10); refit with 100× tighter tolerance; finite-difference step \gg solver error.
Stopping: ask for a tolerance above the accuracy of your Jacobian; read the convergence message.


Each item is a failure from this lecture: the bad start, the run-off to infinity, the flip-flop, the solver error and the finite-difference step. The plot-the-fit item is the one that catches model errors, which no optimiser can detect: a perfect minimisation of the wrong model is still the wrong answer.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Summary

Nonlinear least squares: minimise \sum_i (y_i - m_i(\mathbf p))^2 when \mathbf p enters nonlinearly. No formula: iterate.
Gauss–Newton: linearise, \mathbf m(\mathbf p + \boldsymbol\delta) \approx \mathbf m + J\boldsymbol\delta, then one linear least-squares solve per step, by QR. Nearly quadratic near a good fit; can jump far away from a bad start. nls is Gauss–Newton with step halving (“singular gradient”).
Levenberg–Marquardt: add \lambda\|D_g\boldsymbol\delta\|^2; \lambda small = Gauss–Newton, \lambda large = gradient descent. nlsLM, nls.lm, curve_fit, least_squares.
Log-parameters for positive rates: positivity for free, better conditioning (170 → 8.7).
ODE fitting: the solver runs inside the residual; its error is part of the objective. Tight tolerance, a finite-difference step well above the solver error, refit to check.
Multistart finds several minima; the PK model has two with equal RSS (flip-flop).

Next: Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters: which parameters the data determine, and how well.

The methods of this unit are the workhorse of quantitative biology: almost every published rate constant from a time course came out of a Levenberg-Marquardt or trust-region fit with an ODE solver inside. The next unit asks how much to trust the numbers: standard errors from J^T J, profile likelihoods, and the structural non-identifiability we just met. After that, Constraints and linear programming deals with bounds and linear constraints.
crumbs: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting

title: Quiz: stochastic simulation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of stochastic simulation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Two genes follow the same birth–death model, one with a steady state of 10 mRNA per cell, the other with 1000. By about what percentage do single cells fluctuate around the mean in each case? For which one is the ODE a good description of a single cell?






Hint





The steady state is Poisson: variance = mean.









Answer





The relative fluctuation is sd/mean \(= \sqrt{\text{mean}}/\text{mean} = 1/\sqrt{\text{mean}}\): \(1/\sqrt{10} = 32\%\) and \(1/\sqrt{1000} = 3.2\%\). The ODE describes a single cell well only for the abundant gene. For the gene with 10 copies, the ODE gives the mean over cells, but no single cell sits at it.




Q2. A cell has \(m = 5\) mRNA and \(p = 40\) proteins. Transcription has rate 10, mRNA decay 1 per molecule, translation 2 per mRNA, protein decay 0.2 per protein (all per hour). What is the probability that the next reaction is a translation, and what is the mean waiting time until the next reaction?






Hint





Compute all four propensities and their sum \(a_0\).









Answer





\(a = (10, 5, 10, 8)\), \(a_0 = 33\) per hour. Translation: \(10/33 = 0.30\). Mean waiting time \(1/a_0 = 0.030\) h \(= 1.8\) min.




Q3. In an SSA step the total propensity is \(a_0 = 4\) per hour and the uniform number for the waiting time is \(u_1 = 0.5\). How long until the next reaction? Why is the waiting time exponential?






Hint





Inverse transform: \(\tau = -\log(u_1)/a_0\).









Answer





\(\tau = -\ln(0.5)/4 = 0.693/4 = 0.173\) h (10.4 min); \(u_1 = 0.5\) gives the median waiting time. Each reaction happens with a constant probability per unit time (\(a_j\,dt\)) as long as the state does not change; a constant hazard means an exponential waiting time, and the first of several independent exponential events is exponential with the summed rate \(a_0\).




Q4. You simulate 2000 cells with the SSA and compare the mean with the ODE. For which of these models should the two agree exactly (up to the Monte Carlo error): (a) birth–death mRNA, (b) the telegraph gene with protein, (c) an SIR epidemic, (d) dimerisation \(2P \to D\)?






Hint





Look at the propensities: are they linear in the counts?









Answer






and (b): all propensities are linear in the counts (\(k\), \(\delta m\), \(k_\text{on}(1 - g)\), \(k_m g\), …), so the mean obeys the ODE exactly. (c) and (d) have propensities with products of counts (\(\beta S I/N\), \(c\,p(p - 1)/2\)); the mean of a product is not the product of the means, so the ODE is only an approximation, good when all counts are large. In (c), outbreaks that die out early make the mean very different from the ODE.





Q5. What does this code print? It chooses the reaction in an SSA step.

RPythonRust


a <- c(2, 0, 3)                         # propensities of reactions 1, 2, 3
a0 <- sum(a)
for (u in c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.9))
  cat(u, "->", findInterval(u * a0, cumsum(a)) + 1, "\n")
# 0.3 -> 1
# 0.4 -> 3
# 0.5 -> 3
# 0.9 -> 3


import numpy as np

a = np.array([2.0, 0.0, 3.0])           # propensities of reactions 1, 2, 3
a0 = a.sum()
for u in [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.9]:
    print(u, "->", np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(a), u * a0, side="right") + 1)
# 0.3 -> 1
# 0.4 -> 3
# 0.5 -> 3
# 0.9 -> 3


// rust/examples/gillespie_q5.rs  —  cargo run --release --example gillespie_q5
// Q5: which reaction does the discrete inverse transform pick?
fn main() {
    let a = [2.0, 0.0, 3.0]; // propensities of reactions 1, 2, 3
    let a0: f64 = a.iter().sum();
    let cum: Vec<f64> = a.iter().scan(0.0, |s, &x| { *s += x; Some(*s) }).collect();
    for u in [0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.9] {
        let j = cum.partition_point(|&c| c <= u * a0) + 1; // like findInterval + 1
        println!("{} -> {}", u, j);
    }
}

// Output:
// 0.3 -> 1
// 0.4 -> 3
// 0.5 -> 3
// 0.9 -> 3









Hint





The cumulative sums are \((2, 2, 5)\), and \(u a_0 = 5u\). A value exactly on a boundary goes to the next piece.









Answer





0.3 -> 1, 0.4 -> 3, 0.5 -> 3, 0.9 -> 3. Reaction 1 owns \([0, 2)\), reaction 2 the empty piece \([2, 2)\), reaction 3 \([2, 5)\). \(u a_0 = 2\) (for \(u = 0.4\)) is on the boundary and goes to reaction 3. A reaction with propensity 0 is never chosen, as it must be.




Q6. Gene A has mRNA mean 12 and variance 13; gene B has mean 12 and variance 250 (smFISH counts). What are the Fano factors, and what do they suggest about how each gene is transcribed? Would the conclusion change if the data were fluorescence intensities in arbitrary units?






Hint





Poisson: Fano factor 1. What happens to var/mean if every value is multiplied by \(c\)?









Answer





\(F_A = 13/12 = 1.08\), \(F_B = 250/12 = 20.8\). Gene A is consistent with constitutive (Poisson) transcription: molecules made one at a time, independently. Gene B is much wider than Poisson, suggesting bursts of transcription (in the telegraph model, roughly bursts of about 20 mRNA). With intensities \(c\) times the counts, the Fano factor is multiplied by \(c\), so the comparison with 1 means nothing until the intensities are converted to molecule numbers.




Q7. You run the same SSA with seed 1 in R and in Python and get different trajectories and a slightly different mean (10.12 vs 9.99, each with SE 0.07). Is one of the programs wrong?






Hint





Which generator does each language use? How far apart are the means in SEs?









Answer





Not on this evidence. R (Mersenne Twister), numpy (PCG64) and Rust (ChaCha12) produce different random streams from the same seed, so single trajectories always differ. Compare statistics with their standard errors: the difference 0.13 has SE \(\sqrt{0.07^2 + 0.07^2} = 0.10\), so 1.3 SE: consistent. A bug would show as differences of many SEs, or as a disagreement with a known answer (Poisson, the ODE mean for linear propensities).




Q8. A student stores every event of a long SSA run of the birth–death model (\(k = 10\), \(\delta = 1\)) in a table and reports the mean of the m column: 10.5. The correct mean is 10. What went wrong, and how should the mean be computed?






Hint





In which states do events happen more often?









Answer





Events happen at rate \(a_0 = 10 + m\), so states with many molecules produce more rows in the table: averaging over rows weights each state by how often it changes, not by how long it lasts. Fix: weight each state by its duration (the waiting time until the next event), or record the state at fixed, equally spaced times, as ssa() does with its times argument.




Q9. Tau-leaping with step \(\tau = 2\) h gives some cells a negative number of mRNA molecules (\(\delta = 1\) per hour). Why, and what are two ways to avoid it?






Hint





How many degradations does one leap expect when \(m = 2\)?









Answer





In one leap the number of degradations is Poisson$(m ) = $ Poisson\((2m)\), which does not know how many molecules exist: with \(m = 2\) it expects 4 degradations. Fixes: a smaller \(\tau\) (so that \(\delta\tau \ll 1\): each propensity changes little within a leap), or exact SSA steps for species with few molecules (what adaptive tau-leaping codes do). Clipping at zero hides the problem and biases the distribution. Even without negatives, a large \(\tau\) gives the wrong variance (20 instead of 10 at \(\tau = 1\)).




Q10. An Euler–Maruyama simulation of the chemical Langevin equation \(dm = (k - \delta m)\,dt + \sqrt{k + \delta m}\,dW\) returns NaN for a gene with mean 0.5 molecules but works fine for mean 100. Explain.






Hint





When is \(k + \delta m\) negative?









Answer





The normal kicks can push \(m\) below zero, and below \(-k/\delta\) the square root is of a negative number: NaN, which then spreads through every later step. With mean 100 and sd 10 this essentially never happens; with mean 0.5 it happens in several percent of the runs. The Langevin equation replaces whole-number jumps by continuous noise, an approximation that holds only for large copy numbers. For small numbers, use the SSA.




Q11. An infection with \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma = 3\) enters a large population with 2 infected people. What is the probability that it dies out without a large outbreak? What does the SIR ODE say?






Hint





Each initial case starts an independent chain that dies out with probability \(1/R_0\).









Answer





\((1/3)^2 = 1/9 = 0.11\) (simulation: 0.109 with SE 0.003). The ODE always predicts an epidemic with a peak of about 3000 infected in 10 000: it has no state “extinct”, because \(I\) only decays exponentially towards zero and never reaches it.

title: Exercise: numerical integration
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute an integral with the left Riemann, midpoint, trapezoid and Simpson rules, by hand for a few points and in code as composite rules,
read the order of a rule off a log–log plot of error against the number of intervals, and recognise when a non-smooth integrand lowers it,
improve the trapezoid rule with Richardson extrapolation (Romberg), and write a short adaptive Simpson routine,
explain why integrate / scipy.integrate.quad can return a confident wrong answer, and fix it by splitting the interval, transforming it or giving the scale,
remove an infinite interval or an endpoint singularity by substitution,
compute an AUC from blood samples (linear and linear-up/log-down, extrapolated to infinity), a chromatography peak area, and the normalising constant of a posterior density.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a pocket calculator (for exp, ln and square roots).

title: Exercise: numerical integration
text:
Background
Every rule replaces the integral by a weighted sum of function values, \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx \sum_i w_i f(x_i)\). With \(n\) intervals of width \(h = (b-a)/n\) and \(f_i = f(a + ih)\):









rule
formula
error
order




left Riemann
\(h\,(f_0 + f_1 + \dots + f_{n-1})\)
\(\approx \tfrac{(b-a)h}{2} f'\)
1


midpoint
\(h \sum_i f(a + (i - \tfrac12) h)\)
\(-\tfrac{(b-a)h^2}{24} f''\)
2


trapezoid \(T(h)\)
\(h\,(\tfrac12 f_0 + f_1 + \dots + f_{n-1} + \tfrac12 f_n)\)
\(\tfrac{(b-a)h^2}{12} f''\)
2


Simpson (\(n\) even)
\(\tfrac{h}{3}(f_0 + 4f_1 + 2f_2 + 4f_3 + \dots + 4f_{n-1} + f_n)\)
\(\tfrac{(b-a)h^4}{180} f''''\)
4



(The derivatives are evaluated at some unknown point in \([a, b]\).) A rule of order \(p\) has error \(\approx C h^p\): halving \(h\) divides the error by \(2^p\), and on a log–log plot of error against \(n\) the slope is \(-p\). The orders hold only if the derivative in the error term exists and is bounded.
Richardson extrapolation (from Numerical differentiation): if \(T(h) \approx I + Ch^2\), then \(\big(4T(h/2) - T(h)\big)/3\) cancels the \(h^2\) term. Repeating it column by column is Romberg integration. Adaptive Simpson compares Simpson on one panel (\(S_1\)) and on two half-panels (\(S_2\)) of each piece: \(|S_2 - S_1|/15\) estimates the error of \(S_2\); pieces that fail are split in two. Gaussian quadrature chooses the points as well: \(n\) points integrate polynomials up to degree \(2n-1\) exactly.
Libraries. R’s integrate and Python’s scipy.integrate.quad both call QUADPACK: a 21-point Gauss–Kronrod rule on \([a, b]\), then repeated bisection of the piece with the largest estimated error; infinite intervals are mapped to \((0, 1]\). They stop when the estimated error is below \(\max(\text{abs.tol}, \text{rel.tol}\cdot|\text{value}|)\); R’s defaults are rel.tol = abs.tol \(\approx 1.2\times10^{-4}\), SciPy’s epsabs = epsrel \(= 1.49\times10^{-8}\). Rust’s quadrature crate uses the double-exponential (tanh–sinh) rule, whose points crowd towards both ends of the interval; it takes a target absolute error and has no infinite limits. For data, NumPy has np.trapezoid and SciPy scipy.integrate.trapezoid and simpson; base R has no trapezoid function (pracma::trapz exists), but it is one line.
Substitution. \(x = t/(1-t)\) maps \(t \in [0, 1)\) to \(x \in [0, \infty)\) with \(dx = dt/(1-t)^2\). \(x = u^2\) turns \(\int_0^1 g(x)/\sqrt{x}\,dx\) into \(\int_0^1 2g(u^2)\,du\).
The running example. An oral dose of 500 mg; one-compartment model with volume 50 L, absorption rate 1.5 /h and elimination rate 0.2 /h: \[C(t) = \frac{500}{50}\cdot\frac{1.5}{1.5 - 0.2}\left(e^{-0.2t} - e^{-1.5t}\right) \text{ mg/L}, \qquad \mathrm{AUC}_{0-6} = 32.6243601574044, \quad \mathrm{AUC}_{0-24} = 49.5252069010181, \quad \mathrm{AUC}_{0-\infty} = 50.\] The blood samples are \(C(t)\) at 10 times, rounded to 2 decimals:

RPythonRust


t_h  <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24)                         # hours
conc <- c(0, 4.99, 6.87, 7.16, 6.20, 5.16, 3.47, 2.33, 1.05, 0.09)  # mg/L
auc_trap <- function(t, y) sum(diff(t) * (head(y, -1) + tail(y, -1)) / 2)
auc_trap(t_h, conc)                       # trapezoid rule on data
# [1] 51.6175
model <- function(t) 500 / 50 * 1.5 / 1.3 * (exp(-0.2 * t) - exp(-1.5 * t))
res <- integrate(model, 0, 24)            # adaptive quadrature on a function
res$value
# [1] 49.52521
res$abs.error
# [1] 1.034305e-07


import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad

t_h  = np.array([0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24])                         # hours
conc = np.array([0, 4.99, 6.87, 7.16, 6.20, 5.16, 3.47, 2.33, 1.05, 0.09])  # mg/L
def auc_trap(t, y):
    return np.sum(np.diff(t) * (y[:-1] + y[1:]) / 2)
print(auc_trap(t_h, conc))                 # same as np.trapezoid(conc, t_h)
# 51.61750000000001
def model(t):
    return 500 / 50 * 1.5 / 1.3 * (np.exp(-0.2 * t) - np.exp(-1.5 * t))
value, abserr = quad(model, 0, 24)         # adaptive quadrature on a function
print(value)
# 49.52520690101807
print(abserr)
# 1.0343052501277095e-07


// rust/examples/quadrature_background.rs  —  cargo run --example quadrature_background
// Background: trapezoid rule on the blood samples (hand-written) and the
// quadrature crate's integrate (double-exponential rule) on the model.
fn auc_trap(t: &[f64], y: &[f64]) -> f64 {
    (1..t.len()).map(|i| (t[i] - t[i - 1]) * (y[i - 1] + y[i]) / 2.0).sum()
}
fn model(t: f64) -> f64 {
    500.0 / 50.0 * 1.5 / 1.3 * ((-0.2 * t).exp() - (-1.5 * t).exp())
}

fn main() {
    let t_h = [0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 12.0, 24.0]; // hours
    let conc = [0.0, 4.99, 6.87, 7.16, 6.20, 5.16, 3.47, 2.33, 1.05, 0.09]; // mg/L
    println!("{}", auc_trap(&t_h, &conc));
    let out = quadrature::integrate(model, 0.0, 24.0, 1e-10); // target absolute error
    println!("{}", out.integral);
    println!("{:e}", out.error_estimate);
}

// Output:
// 51.6175
// 49.525206901018045
// 8.958167541095463e-12

title: Exercise: numerical integration
text:
By hand
B1. Four rules on a cubic. Take \(\int_0^2 x^3\,dx = 4\). (a) Compute the left Riemann, midpoint and trapezoid approximations with \(h = 1\) (two intervals), and Simpson’s rule with the three points \(0, 1, 2\). (b) Which rule is exact? Why is that not a coincidence? (c) Compute the trapezoid rule with \(h = 0.5\). By what factor did the error shrink? Which order does that suggest? (d) Combine the two trapezoid values by Richardson extrapolation, \((4T(h/2) - T(h))/3\). Compare with (a).
B2. AUC from seven blood samples. A sparser version of the data: \(t = 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 24\) h, \(C = 0, 6.87, 7.16, 5.16, 2.33, 1.05, 0.09\) mg/L. (a) Compute \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-24}\) with the linear trapezoid rule (interval by interval). (b) For the falling intervals, use the log-down rule \(\Delta t\,(C_1 - C_2)/\ln(C_1/C_2)\) instead. Useful values: \(\ln(7.16/5.16) = 0.3276\), \(\ln(5.16/2.33) = 0.7951\), \(\ln(2.33/1.05) = 0.7971\), \(\ln(1.05/0.09) = 2.4567\). (c) Estimate the terminal slope \(\lambda_z\) from the last two samples and the extrapolated area \(C_\text{last}/\lambda_z\). What fraction of \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-\infty}\) is extrapolated? (d) The true area from 12 h to 24 h is 4.76. Which interval contributes most of the error of the linear rule, and why is the log-down rule so much better there? The true area from 0 to 1 h is 4.48: what do both rules do there, and what would you change in the sampling plan?
B3. Order from a table. For \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-6}\) the absolute errors are:
