Compute the ratios of consecutive errors and the order of each rule.
Assuming error \(= C h^p\) from \(n = 16\) on, how many intervals does each rule need for an error of \(10^{-6}\)?

B4. Two-point Gauss. The 2-point Gauss–Legendre rule on \([-1, 1]\) is \(f(-1/\sqrt3) + f(1/\sqrt3)\). (a) Check that it is exact for \(1, x, x^2, x^3\), and find its result for \(x^4\) (exact: \(2/5\)). (b) Map it to \([0, 2]\) (points \(1 \pm 1/\sqrt3\), weights \(1\)) and apply it to \(\int_0^2 x^3\,dx\). Compare the cost with B1(a).
B5. Why integrate(dnorm, 0, 20000) returns 0. The 21-point Gauss–Kronrod rule on \([-1, 1]\) has its two outermost points at \(\pm 0.99566\) and \(\pm 0.97391\). (a) Map them to \([0, 20000]\) with \(x = 10000(1 + s)\). Where are the two points closest to 0? Estimate \(\log_{10}\) of dnorm at the closest one (\(\text{dnorm}(x) = e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\)). What does a double make of it? (b) Same for \([0, 20]\). (c) For which upper limits \(b\) does the closest point lie within 5 standard deviations of 0? Predict whether integrate(dnorm, 0, 2000) and integrate(dnorm, 0, 5000) work. (C5 checks.)
B6. Substitution. (a) Write \(\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx\) as an integral over \(t \in [0, 1)\) with \(x = t/(1-t)\). Evaluate the new integrand at \(t = 0, 0.5, 0.9\) and find its limit as \(t \to 1\). (b) The Jeffreys prior for a proportion is \(\propto 1/\sqrt{x(1-x)}\). Show with \(x = \sin^2\theta\) that its normalising constant \(\int_0^1 dx/\sqrt{x(1-x)}\) is \(\pi\). (c) Turn \(\int_0^1 e^{-x}/\sqrt{x}\,dx\) into a smooth integral with \(x = u^2\), and apply the trapezoid rule with \(h = 0.5\) to the new integral. (Exact: \(1.49365\).) Why could you not apply the trapezoid rule to the original?

title: Exercise: numerical integration
text:
In code
C1. (Composite rules and their order) Write functions left, mid, trap and simpson(f, a, b, n) for the composite rules. Apply them to \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-6}\) of the model for \(n = 2, 4, \dots, 1024\), plot the absolute errors against \(n\) on log–log axes, and fit the slopes for \(n \ge 32\). Do they match the table in the Background and your answers to B3?
C2. (Order needs smoothness) (a) Repeat C1 for \(\int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx = 2/3\) with the trapezoid and Simpson rules. What slopes do you get? (b) \(\int_0^1 e^{-x}/\sqrt{x}\,dx = \sqrt{\pi}\,\mathrm{erf}(1)\). What does the trapezoid rule return? Compute the midpoint rule for \(n = 16, 256, 4096\). (c) Use the substitution of B6(c) and Simpson’s rule with \(n = 2, 4, 8, 16\). Compare with integrate (Python: quad; Rust: quadrature::integrate) on the original integrand.
C3. (Romberg) Write romberg(f, a, b, k) that fills the \(k \times k\) table (row \(i\): trapezoid with \(2^{i-1}\) intervals, then Richardson column by column). (a) For \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-6}\), print the error of the last diagonal entry for \(k = 4, \dots, 9\), with the number of function values used. Compare with Simpson and 1024 intervals from C1. (b) Apply it to \(\sqrt{x}\) on \([0, 1]\). Why does extrapolation hardly help?
C4. (Adaptive Simpson) Write the adaptive Simpson routine from the slides. (a) Integrate the model from 0 to 24 h with tolerances \(10^{-4}, 10^{-6}, 10^{-8}\); count the function evaluations and print the errors. How many points would uniform Simpson need for the same accuracy (use C1’s order)? (b) A chromatogram: one peak at 340 s with \(\sigma = 3\) s and height 1000, run from 0 to 600 s: peak(t) = 1000 * exp(-(t - 340)^2 / (2 * 3^2)). Its area is \(1000 \cdot 3\sqrt{2\pi}\). What does your adaptive routine return, and why? (c) Fix it by starting from 60 pieces of 10 s.
C5. (Inside a library routine) (a) Wrap dnorm (Python: scipy.stats.norm.pdf; Rust: statrs’s Normal) in a function that records every \(x\) it is called with, and integrate from 0 to 20000. How many points are used, and where are the smallest ones? Compare with B5. (b) Integrate dnorm from 0 to \(b\) for \(b = 20, 200, 2000, 5000, 20000, \infty\), printing the value and the error estimate. (c) Fix \([0, 20000]\) by splitting at 10. (Python’s quad has an argument points for this.) (d) Integrate the chromatogram of C4 over a one-hour run, \([0, 3600]\) s, and over the peak \(\pm 10\sigma\).
C6. (Peak area versus peak height) A Gaussian peak with \(\sigma = 3\) s and height 1000 centred at 300 s is sampled every \(h\) seconds from 240 s on, with a sampling offset (phase) between 0 and \(h\). For \(h = 9, 6, 4.5, 3, 1.5\) s and 40 offsets each, compute the trapezoid area and the largest sample (the measured height). Report the worst relative area error and the worst height error. How many points across the peak (about \(4\sigma\) wide) do you need for 1 % area? For 5 % height?
C7. (AUC from the blood samples) Use the 10 samples from the Background. (a) For each interval, compute the error of the linear trapezoid and of the linear-up/log-down rule against the exact area of the model on that interval (integrate). Where are the errors? (b) Compute \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-24}\) with both rules, and \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-\infty}\) by adding \(C_\text{last}/\lambda_z\), with \(\lambda_z\) from a straight-line fit to \(\log C\) over the last three samples (R: lm; Python: np.polyfit). (c) The model route: integrate the model from 0 to \(\infty\) and compare with Dose\(/(V k_e) = 50\).
C8. (Normalising a posterior) For the zero-truncated Poisson UMI data of Newton and secant methods (100 cells), the log-likelihood is \(\ell(\lambda) = 173\log\lambda - 100\lambda - 100\log(1 - e^{-\lambda})\), with maximum at \(\hat\lambda = 1.2184695258301268\) and standard error 0.1325. With a flat prior, the posterior density is \(e^{\ell(\lambda)}/Z\). (a) Integrate \(e^{\ell(\lambda)}\) over \((0, b)\) for \(b = 10, 100, \infty\). Do the answers agree? (b) Integrate \(g(\lambda) = e^{\ell(\lambda) - \ell(\hat\lambda)}\) instead. Report \(Z_g\), \(\log Z = \ell(\hat\lambda) + \log Z_g\), and the posterior mean \(\int \lambda\,g(\lambda)\,d\lambda / Z_g\). (c) With 10 000 cells (every count multiplied by 100: \(\ell\) times 100, same \(\hat\lambda\), standard error 10 times smaller), integrate the scaled \(g\) over \((0, b)\) for \(b = 10, 100, \infty\), and over \(\hat\lambda \pm 10\) standard errors. Which answers can you trust?

title: Exercise: numerical integration
text:
Hints






Hint B1–B4 — the rules by hand





With \(h = 1\) on \([0, 2]\): \(f_0 = 0\), \(f_1 = 1\), \(f_2 = 8\); midpoints \(0.5^3 = 0.125\) and \(1.5^3 = 3.375\). Trapezoid: \(h(\tfrac12 f_0 + f_1 + \tfrac12 f_2)\). Simpson: \(\tfrac{h}{3}(f_0 + 4f_1 + f_2)\). For the order, divide each error by the next (step halved): 4 means order 2, 16 means order 4. For a target error, solve \(e_{16}\,(16/n)^p = 10^{-6}\) for \(n\). In B4, \((1/\sqrt3)^2 = 1/3\) and \((1/\sqrt3)^4 = 1/9\).









Hint B2 — linear-up/log-down





A falling interval uses \(\Delta t\,(C_1 - C_2)/\ln(C_1/C_2)\); this is the exact area under an exponential through the two samples. Rising intervals (0→1, 1→2) keep the trapezoid. \(\lambda_z = \ln(C_{12}/C_{24})/12\).









Hint B5–B6 — mapping points and substituting





B5: a point \(s\) near \(-1\) maps to \(x = 10000(1 + s)\), so \(s = -0.99566\) gives \(x = 10000 \cdot 0.00434\). \(\log_{10} e^{-y} = -0.4343\,y\). The smallest positive double is about \(5\times10^{-324}\). B6: replace \(x\) and \(dx\); for (a) \(dx = dt/(1-t)^2\); for (b) \(dx = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta\), \(1 - \sin^2\theta = \cos^2\theta\); for (c) \(dx = 2u\,du\) and \(\sqrt{x} = u\).









Hint C1–C3 — composite rules, slopes, Romberg





seq(a, b, length.out = n + 1) (Python: np.linspace(a, b, n + 1)) gives the grid. Simpson weights: c(1, rep(c(4, 2), n/2 - 1), 4, 1) (Python: np.r_[1, np.tile([4, 2], n//2 - 1), 4, 1]). Loop over rules with sapply over a list of functions. Slope: coef(lm(log(e) ~ log(n)))[2] (Python: np.polyfit(np.log(n), np.log(e), 1)[0]). Plot with matplot and log = "xy" (Python: plt.loglog). Romberg: R[i, j] <- R[i, j-1] + (R[i, j-1] - R[i-1, j-1]) / (4^(j-1) - 1). SciPy 1.15 removed its romberg function; scipy.integrate.romb works on \(2^k + 1\) equally spaced samples. In C2(b), pnorm gives \(\mathrm{erf}(1) = 2\,\Phi(\sqrt2) - 1\); Python has scipy.special.erf, Rust statrs::function::erf::erf.









Hint C4–C5 — counting and recording calls





A function that changes a variable outside itself: in R calls <<- calls + length(t) or seen <<- c(seen, x) (the <<- assigns in the enclosing environment); in Python a global counter or seen.append(x) on a list; in Rust a Cell or RefCell captured by the closure. R’s integrate passes a whole vector of points at once, so count length(t), not calls. The adaptive routine is recursive: it calls itself on the two halves.









Hint C6–C8 — biology tasks





C6: for each offset off, x <- seq(240 + off, 360, by = h); area is the trapezoid on peak(x); height is max(peak(x)). C7: ifelse(y2 < y1 & y2 > 0, logdown, linear) picks the rule per interval; the slope of lm(log(conc[8:10]) ~ t_h[8:10]) is \(-\lambda_z\). C8: compute \(\ell\) with log1p(-exp(-l)) (Python np.log1p), and remember the default absolute tolerance of integrate (\(1.2\times10^{-4}\)) and quad (\(1.5\times10^{-8}\)).

title: Exercise: numerical integration
Exercise: numerical integration
text:
Where this leads

Random numbers and Monte Carlo (next): integrals over many dimensions (a marginal likelihood with 10 parameters), where any grid is far too large and random points with error \(1/\sqrt{N}\) take over.
Initial value problems and Euler’s method and Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size (Part 8): solving \(y' = f(t, y)\) is integration in which the integrand depends on the answer. Euler is the left Riemann sum, Heun the trapezoid rule, and adaptive step-size control is the adaptive idea of C4.
Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting (Part 9): fitting the same one-compartment oral model (\(k_a\), \(k_e\), \(V\)) to blood samples (its own simulated study), which is what the model route of C7 needs. Overlapping chromatography peaks are fitted with the same methods.
Gauss–Kronrod rules, the double-exponential rule and QUADPACK’s extrapolation are used here as black boxes; their derivations are beyond this course.

title: Quiz: numerical integration
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of numerical integration. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. In one sentence: what do all quadrature rules (trapezoid, Simpson, Gauss, the 21-point rule inside integrate) have in common, and what does that imply about what they can miss?






Hint





Write the rule as a formula with function values in it.









Answer





Each is a weighted sum \(\sum_i w_i f(x_i)\) of finitely many function values. Whatever \(f\) does between the points is invisible to the rule, so a feature narrower than the spacing of the points (a narrow peak, a spike) can be missed completely, and the error estimate, computed from the same points, will not notice.




Q2. Blood samples at 0, 2 and 4 h give 0, 8 and 4 mg/L. Compute the AUC from 0 to 4 h with the trapezoid rule. Will the true AUC more likely be larger or smaller?






Hint





Two trapezoids of width 2. Is the curve between 0 and 2 h, during absorption, bent upwards or downwards?









Answer





\(2\cdot(0 + 8)/2 + 2\cdot(8 + 4)/2 = 8 + 12 = 20\) mg·h/L. During absorption the curve rises steeply and then flattens (concave), and near the peak it is concave too, so the straight lines lie below the curve: the true AUC is probably larger. (In the elimination phase, which is convex, the trapezoid rule overestimates.)




Q3. The trapezoid rule with step \(h\) has error \(0.8\). Roughly what is the error with step \(h/4\)? What would it be for Simpson’s rule if Simpson also had error 0.8 at \(h\)?






Hint





Error \(\approx C h^p\), with \(p = 2\) for the trapezoid and \(p = 4\) for Simpson.









Answer





Trapezoid: \(0.8/4^2 = 0.05\). Simpson: \(0.8/4^4 = 0.8/256 \approx 0.003\). This assumes \(h\) is already small enough for the leading error term to dominate and that the integrand is smooth.




Q4. You test Simpson’s rule on your integrand by halving \(h\) several times. The log–log plot of the error against \(n\) has slope \(-1.5\), not \(-4\). What does that tell you, and what can you do?






Hint





Which assumption behind the order 4 can fail?









Answer





The integrand is not smooth on the interval: Simpson’s \(h^4\) error needs a bounded fourth derivative. Slope \(-1.5\) is typical of a \(\sqrt{x}\)-type endpoint (an infinite slope). Find the point (plot the integrand), then either put a grid point there and split the interval, or remove the bad behaviour with a substitution (e.g. \(x = u^2\)). An adaptive routine (integrate, quad) will also cope, at the cost of many points near the bad spot.




Q5. Trapezoid estimates of an integral are \(T(h) = 2.10\) and \(T(h/2) = 2.03\). Give a better estimate. What is it called, and which classical rule does it reproduce?






Hint





The trapezoid error is \(\approx Ch^2\), so halving \(h\) divides it by 4.









Answer





\(\big(4\cdot 2.03 - 2.10\big)/3 = (8.12 - 2.10)/3 = 2.0067\). This is Richardson extrapolation, as for difference quotients in Numerical differentiation; one step of it turns two trapezoid sums into Simpson’s rule with step \(h/2\). Repeating it is Romberg integration.




Q6. A chromatogram is recorded for one hour (0–3600 s). It contains one peak at 340 s with \(\sigma = 3\) s and height 1000; its area is \(1000\cdot3\sqrt{2\pi} \approx 7520\). Explain the output of the code below. Why is the first result wrong, and what is the fix?

RPythonRust


peak <- function(t) 1000 * exp(-(t - 340)^2 / (2 * 3^2))
integrate(peak, 0, 3600)
# 1.199796e-59 with absolute error < 2.3e-59
integrate(peak, 310, 370)                  # the peak +- 10 sigma
# 7519.885 with absolute error < 0.56


import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import quad
peak = lambda t: 1000 * np.exp(-(t - 340)**2 / (2 * 3**2))
print(quad(peak, 0, 3600))
# (1.1997955764401264e-59, 2.2683315422332952e-59)
print(quad(peak, 310, 370))                # the peak +- 10 sigma
# (7519.8848238929795, 6.520516427577228e-06)


// rust/examples/quadrature_q6.rs  —  cargo run --example quadrature_q6
// Q6: a 3 s wide chromatography peak in a one-hour run, with the quadrature
// crate (double-exponential rule), over the whole run and over the peak.
fn main() {
    let peak = |t: f64| 1000.0 * (-(t - 340.0).powi(2) / (2.0 * 9.0)).exp();
    let o = quadrature::integrate(peak, 0.0, 3600.0, 1e-6);
    println!("{:e} with error estimate {:.1e}", o.integral, o.error_estimate);
    let o = quadrature::integrate(peak, 310.0, 370.0, 1e-6); // the peak +- 10 sigma
    println!("{} with error estimate {:.1e}", o.integral, o.error_estimate);
}

// Output:
// 6.526074485307542e-179 with error estimate 6.5e-179
// 7519.884823892994 with error estimate 3.4e-12









Hint





The first 21-point rule on \([0, 3600]\) has its points roughly every 100–200 s.









Answer





Over the whole run all three return essentially 0 (between \(10^{-179}\) and \(10^{-59}\)) with a tiny error estimate: no point lands within a few \(\sigma\) of the peak, the rule sees a flat zero function and stops. Over the peak \(\pm 10\sigma\) (310–370 s) all three return 7519.88. Fixes: integrate over the region where the peak lives (give the scale), split the run into pieces no wider than the peak (as a peak detector would), or for sampled data use the trapezoid rule on the samples, which sees every point.




Q7. Up to which polynomial degree is a 5-point Gauss–Legendre rule exact? And Simpson’s rule on 5 points (4 intervals)?






Hint





Gauss chooses both points and weights: \(2n\) free numbers.









Answer





Gauss with \(n = 5\) points: degree \(2n - 1 = 9\). Composite Simpson on 5 points: degree 3 (each panel integrates cubics exactly, not quartics). That is why libraries use Gauss-type rules on each piece: more accuracy per function value for smooth integrands.




Q8. integrate returns 0 with absolute error < 0. Is a zero error estimate reassuring?






Hint





How is the error estimate computed?









Answer





No. The error estimate is the difference between two rules (10-point Gauss and 21-point Kronrod) evaluated at the same points. If every point sees the same thing (for instance \(f = 0\) because the peak is elsewhere), both rules agree perfectly and the estimate is 0. An estimate of exactly 0, or one as large as the value, is a reason to plot the integrand and change the limits.




Q9. You want the normalising constant of a likelihood whose maximum is about \(10^{-40}\). Why may integrate(L, 0, Inf) give a meaningless answer, and what do you do instead?






Hint





Look at the stopping rule: estimated error < max(abs.tol, rel.tol × |value|), with abs.tol \(\approx 10^{-4}\) in R.









Answer





The whole integral is far below the absolute tolerance, so the first rough estimate already passes the test: different limits give different answers. Integrate the scaled function \(e^{\ell(\theta) - \ell_{\max}}\) (maximum 1) and add \(\ell_{\max}\) back on the log scale: \(\log Z = \ell_{\max} + \log \int e^{\ell - \ell_{\max}}\). Also give the scale of the axis: integrate over the mode \(\pm\) about 10 standard errors.




Q10. Which substitution makes each integral easy for any rule? (a) \(\int_0^1 \dfrac{\cos x}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx\) (b) \(\int_0^\infty \dfrac{dx}{(1+x)^3}\)






Hint






The trouble is \(1/\sqrt{x}\) at 0. (b) Map \([0, \infty)\) to a finite interval.










Answer






\(x = u^2\), \(dx = 2u\,du\): \(\int_0^1 2\cos(u^2)\,du\), smooth. (b) \(x = t/(1-t)\): \(1 + x = 1/(1-t)\) and \(dx = dt/(1-t)^2\), so the integrand becomes \((1-t)^3/(1-t)^2 = 1 - t\), and \(\int_0^1 (1 - t)\,dt = 1/2\). Even the trapezoid rule is exact on that.





Q11. In non-compartmental pharmacokinetics, why is the log-down rule used for falling concentrations, and why is it not used for rising ones or when a concentration is 0?






Hint





Which shape does each rule assume between two samples?









Answer





After the peak, elimination is roughly first order, so concentrations fall exponentially; the log-down rule assumes exactly that shape between samples, whereas a straight line overestimates a convex decline (by +44 % over a 12 h gap in the lecture example). During absorption the curve is not exponential decay, and the formula \(\Delta t\,(C_1 - C_2)/\ln(C_1/C_2)\) breaks down when \(C_1 = C_2\) (0/0) or when either is 0 (\(\ln 0\)), so the linear trapezoid is used there.




Q12. Two LC-MS runs of the same sample are sampled at different rates (every 6 s and every 2 s) for a peak with \(\sigma \approx 3\) s. The peak heights differ by 30 %, the areas by 1 %. Is something wrong with the instrument?






Hint





Does a sample land on the apex?









Answer





Probably not. With a 6 s spacing (\(2\sigma\)) the largest sample can miss the apex by up to 3 s, which lowers the measured height by up to 39 %, depending on the sampling phase. The trapezoid area of a whole peak is much more robust: about 1.4 % worst case at \(h = 2\sigma\) and far less for denser sampling. Quantify with areas, and sample densely enough (6–10 points across the peak) if heights or peak shapes matter.

title: Numerical integration
text:
About this lecture
In Why numerical analysis? integrate(dnorm, 0, 20000) returned 0, with an error estimate of 0. This lecture explains why, and how integrals are computed.

An integral is an area. Every method adds up finitely many function values with weights: \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \approx \sum_i w_i f(x_i).
Riemann, trapezoid and Simpson rules, made composite; their order read off a log–log plot. Order needs a smooth integrand.
Romberg (Richardson again), adaptive quadrature and Gaussian quadrature: what integrate and scipy.integrate.quad do inside.
Why a library misses a peak, and the fixes: split the interval, transform it, give the scale. Infinite intervals and singularities by substitution.
Biology: AUC in pharmacokinetics from blood samples, peak areas in chromatography and mass spectrometry, normalising a probability density.


Two kinds of integration problem appear in biology. Either we have samples (a concentration measured at 10 time points, a chromatogram sampled by a detector) and we must integrate data, or we have a formula (a model, a density) and can evaluate it wherever we like. The first kind fixes the points; the second lets the method choose them. Most of the lecture is about the second kind, but we start and end with data. The thread through the whole lecture: a rule only sees the function at the points it samples. Everything between the points is an assumption.

title: Numerical integration
text:
A biology problem first
An oral drug, 500 mg. Ten blood samples over 24 h. The area under the curve (AUC, mg·h/L) measures total exposure; bioequivalence of two formulations is judged on the ratio of their AUCs (accepted range 80–125 %).
t_h  <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24)                         # hours
conc <- c(0, 4.99, 6.87, 7.16, 6.20, 5.16, 3.47, 2.33, 1.05, 0.09)  # mg/L
auc_trap <- function(t, y) sum(diff(t) * (head(y, -1) + tail(y, -1)) / 2)
auc_trap(t_h, conc)
# [1] 51.6175
model <- function(t) 500 / 50 * 1.5 / 1.3 * (exp(-0.2 * t) - exp(-1.5 * t))
integrate(model, 0, 24)
# 49.52521 with absolute error < 1e-07

The data are the model rounded to 2 decimals, so the true AUC is 49.53. Straight lines between samples give 4 % too much. Why, and which method should we trust?


The model is the standard one-compartment model with first-order absorption: dose 500 mg, volume 50 L, absorption rate 1.5 per hour, elimination rate 0.2 per hour (half-life 3.5 h). We generated the data from it, so we know the right answer; in a real study you do not. The sum is the trapezoid rule, which we build on the next slides. diff(t) gives the interval widths, head(y, -1) drops the last value and tail(y, -1) drops the first, so the two vectors are the left and right ends of each interval. A 4 % bias is inside the 80-125 % window, but it is systematic: a formulation that is absorbed faster gets a different bias.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Where the 4 % comes from


Between 12 h and 24 h the straight line lies far above the curve: the curve bends upwards (convex), the chord cuts across.
Near the peak the line lies below. The errors partly cancel; here the tail wins.


A rule only knows the function at the sample points. Between them the trapezoid rule assumes a straight line. Where the true curve bends, the line is wrong, and the error is largest where the gap between samples is wide and the curvature is large: 12 to 24 h is a 12 h gap on an exponential decline. We come back to this at the end, with the linear-up/log-down rule that pharmacokineticists use.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Integrals as sums: four rules

Split [a, b] into n intervals of width h = (b-a)/n. Within each interval, replace f by something simple:

Left Riemann: a constant, f at the left end. Midpoint: a constant, f at the middle.
Trapezoid: a straight line through both ends. Simpson: a parabola through both ends and the middle.


This is the AUC from 0 to 6 h of the drug model, with h = 1.5 h. The Riemann sum is the definition of the integral from the first calculus course: let h go to 0 and the sum converges to the integral. All four rules have the form sum of weights times function values; they differ only in the weights and in where f is evaluated. Note the Simpson panel: a parabola through 0, 1.5 and 3 h overshoots the peak. With few points, a higher-order rule is not automatically better.

title: Numerical integration
text:
The trapezoid rule
One interval: the area of a trapezoid, \int_{x_0}^{x_1} f\,dx \approx \tfrac{h}{2}\,(f_0 + f_1).
Composite: add up n of them. Inner points are shared by two trapezoids:
T(h) = h\left(\tfrac12 f_0 + f_1 + f_2 + \dots + f_{n-1} + \tfrac12 f_n\right)
By hand, the first two samples of the drug data (h = 0.5 h; 0, 4.99, 6.87 mg/L):
T = 0.5\,(\tfrac12 \cdot 0 + 4.99 + \tfrac12 \cdot 6.87) = 0.5 \cdot 8.425 = 4.2125 \text{ mg·h/L}
On data the intervals can have different widths; then add \tfrac{h_i}{2}(f_{i-1} + f_i) one interval at a time, as auc_trap does.

The weights are h/2, h, h, …, h, h/2. Do the hand example on the board. The exact AUC from 0 to 1 h of the model is 4.48, so the trapezoid gives 6 % too little here: the curve bends downwards (concave) during absorption, and the chord lies under it. The composite rule with equal spacing is what we use when we can choose the points (a formula); with data we take the points we have.

title: Numerical integration
section: Trapezoid on a formula: halve h
text:
Trapezoid on a formula: halve h
trap <- function(f, a, b, n) {
  x <- seq(a, b, length.out = n + 1);  h <- (b - a) / n
  y <- f(x)
  h * (sum(y) - (y[1] + y[n + 1]) / 2)
}
exact <- 32.6243601574044                  # AUC 0-6 h of the model
err <- sapply(c(4, 8, 16, 32), function(n) trap(model, 0, 6, n) - exact)
err
# [1] -2.69839410 -0.71902293 -0.18284181 -0.04590877
err[-4] / err[-1]
# [1] 3.752862 3.932486 3.982721

Halving h divides the error by 4: error \approx C h^2, order 2.
Theory: T(h) - I = \tfrac{(b-a)\,h^2}{12} f''(\xi) for some \xi in [a, b]. Concave (f'' < 0): too small; convex (f'' > 0): too large.


The exact value comes from the closed-form integral of the model. Here, from 0 to 6 h, the curve is mostly concave and the rule underestimates; from 0 to 24 h with sparse samples the convex tail dominated and the rule overestimated. The error formula is the same idea as the Taylor remainder in Convergence and cost: the error of a straight-line fit over an interval of width h is about f’’ h^2 / 8 at worst, integrated over the interval and summed over n = (b-a)/h intervals. Ratios approaching 4 = 2^2 is the experimental check of order 2.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Simpson’s rule
A parabola through three equally spaced points x_0, x_1, x_2 integrates to
\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f\,dx \approx \tfrac{h}{3}\,(f_0 + 4 f_1 + f_2)
Composite (even n): weights \tfrac{h}{3}(1, 4, 2, 4, 2, \dots, 4, 1).
simpson <- function(f, a, b, n) {          # n must be even
  x <- seq(a, b, length.out = n + 1);  h <- (b - a) / n
  w <- c(1, rep(c(4, 2), n / 2 - 1), 4, 1)
  h / 3 * sum(w * f(x))
}
err <- sapply(c(4, 8, 16, 32), function(n) simpson(model, 0, 6, n) - exact)
err[-4] / err[-1]
# [1] 11.21479 14.39510 15.56133

Ratios approach 16 = 2^4: order 4. Same function values as the trapezoid, other weights.
Bonus: Simpson is exact for cubics, not just parabolas (the exercise checks it by hand).


Derivation sketch: put x1 = 0 and fit p(x) = A + Bx + Cx^2 through (-h, f0), (0, f1), (h, f2). The integral from -h to h is 2Ah + 2Ch^3/3, and solving for A and C gives h/3 (f0 + 4 f1 + f2). Exactness for cubics is a lucky symmetry: the x^3 term integrates to zero over the symmetric interval. That is why the order is 4 and not 3. Ratios of 11, 14, 15.6 converge to 16 only for small h; at h = 1.5 the parabola cannot follow the absorption peak.

title: Numerical integration
section: Reading the order off a log–log plot
text:
Reading the order off a log–log plot

n <- 2^(2:10)
e_trap <- sapply(n, function(k) abs(trap(model, 0, 6, k) - exact))
coef(lm(log(e_trap) ~ log(n)))[2]
#    log(n)
# -1.989719

Same plot as in Convergence and cost: error against n on log-log axes is a straight line with slope minus the order. Left Riemann: order 1. Midpoint and trapezoid: order 2, with the midpoint error about half the trapezoid error and of opposite sign (one is too small, the other too large). Simpson: order 4; 1000 intervals give 10 digits. With these orders you can predict how many points you need: to go from error 1e-4 to 1e-8 the trapezoid needs 100 times more points, Simpson 10 times.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Failure: order needs smoothness


\sqrt{x} has an infinite slope at 0: trapezoid and Simpson drop to order 1.5. 1/\sqrt{x(1-x)} is infinite at both ends: the midpoint rule crawls at order 0.5 (and the trapezoid gives NaN).
Check: halve h and compute \log_2 of the error ratio (or of the ratio of successive differences, if the answer is unknown). If it is not the promised order, the integrand is not smooth: a kink, a jump, an infinite slope.


The error formulas assume f’’ (trapezoid) or f’’’’ (Simpson) exists and is bounded. sqrt(x) has f’’ infinite at 0, so near 0 both rules make an error of order h^1.5 in the first interval, and that error dominates. Kinks are common in biology: a drug infusion that stops at t = 1 h gives a concentration with a kink there; a threshold model has a jump. The fix is to put a grid point at the kink (split the interval there) or to remove the singularity with a substitution, which we do later. Without the exact answer, use three estimates with h, h/2, h/4: the ratio (T(h) - T(h/2)) / (T(h/2) - T(h/4)) approaches 2^p.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Recap: Richardson extrapolation
From Numerical differentiation: if an estimate has error \approx C h^2, two estimates cancel the h^2 term.
T(h) \approx I + C h^2, \quad T(h/2) \approx I + C h^2/4 \quad\Rightarrow\quad I \approx \frac{4\,T(h/2) - T(h)}{3}
T16 <- trap(model, 0, 6, 16);  T32 <- trap(model, 0, 6, 32)
c(T16, T32) - exact
# [1] -0.18284181 -0.04590877
(4 * T32 - T16) / 3 - exact
# [1] -0.0002644228
simpson(model, 0, 6, 32) - exact
# [1] -0.0002644228

One extrapolation turns two trapezoids into Simpson, exactly. The new error is O(h^4).


In Numerical differentiation we combined two central differences with steps h and h/2 to cancel the h^2 term. The same arithmetic works for any estimate whose error is a power series in h. For the trapezoid the error expansion contains only even powers h^2, h^4, h^6, … (the Euler-Maclaurin formula), so we can repeat the trick. That repetition is Romberg’s method. Point out that we got 3 more digits from the same 33 function values.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Romberg integration
Halve h again and again, and extrapolate column by column: column j removes the h^{2j} term.
romberg <- function(f, a, b, k) {
  R <- matrix(NA, k, k)
  for (i in 1:k) {
    R[i, 1] <- trap(f, a, b, 2^(i - 1))          # h halved each row
    for (j in seq_len(i - 1) + 1)                # Richardson, column by column
      R[i, j] <- R[i, j-1] + (R[i, j-1] - R[i-1, j-1]) / (4^(j-1) - 1)
  }
  R
}
signif(abs(romberg(model, 0, 6, 6) - exact), 2)[6, ]
# [1] 4.6e-02 2.6e-04 7.7e-06 8.7e-07 2.9e-07 2.0e-07

With the same 33 function values: trapezoid error 5\times10^{-2}, Romberg 2\times10^{-7}.
Fails when the error is not a series in h^2: for \sqrt{x} the last row only improves from 1\times10^{-3} to 4\times10^{-4}. And on data you cannot halve h.


Each row halves h, so row i uses 2^(i-1) + 1 points; reusing the old points makes each new row cost only the new midpoints (our simple version recomputes them). The last row shows the gain per column. Gains slow down in later columns here because h is still large compared with the absorption time scale (1/1.5 h). For sqrt(x) the error has a term h^1.5 that Richardson does not know about, so extrapolation removes the wrong term (exercise). For measured data, the sample times are fixed, and extrapolating noisy values amplifies the noise, the same problem as with difference quotients of noisy data in Numerical differentiation.

title: Numerical integration
section: Adaptive quadrature: points where they are needed
text:
Adaptive quadrature: points where they are needed
Estimate the error on each piece from two rules; split only the pieces where they disagree.
adapt <- function(f, a, b, fa, fm, fb, tol) {
  m <- (a + b) / 2;  fl <- f((a + m) / 2);  fr <- f((m + b) / 2)
  S1 <- (b - a) / 6 * (fa + 4 * fm + fb)                    # 1 Simpson panel
  S2 <- (b - a) / 12 * (fa + 4 * fl + 2 * fm + 4 * fr + fb)  # 2 panels
  if (abs(S2 - S1) < 15 * tol) return(S2 + (S2 - S1) / 15)  # accept
  adapt(f, a, m, fa, fl, fm, tol / 2) + adapt(f, m, b, fm, fr, fb, tol / 2)
}
adapt(model, 0, 24, model(0), model(12), model(24), 1e-6) - 49.5252069010181
# [1] -8.981687e-10

S_2 - S_1 \approx 15 \times (error of S_2): the same Richardson idea gives a free error estimate.
The function calls itself on each half (recursion) until every piece passes.


Simpson’s error is C h^4. Halving h divides it by 16, so S1 - S2 is about 15 times the error of S2. If that is below the tolerance (times 15), accept the piece, and add the Richardson correction (S2 - S1)/15 for free. Otherwise split the interval in two and give each half half the tolerance. Passing fa, fm, fb down means no point is evaluated twice. This is about 10 lines and is a fair model of what library routines do, minus the bookkeeping. Recursion may be new to some students: a function that calls itself on a smaller problem, with a stopping rule (the accept line).

title: Numerical integration
section: Where adaptive quadrature puts its points
text:
Where adaptive quadrature puts its points


Dense where the curve bends sharply (absorption, first 2 h), sparse in the slow tail.
Failure: the first 5 points decide where to look. If all of them miss a narrow feature, S_1 = S_2 and the piece is accepted. Next: the library version of that failure.


The ticks at the bottom are the 269 evaluation points. Uniform Simpson needs 513 points for an error of 1e-6, while the adaptive version reaches 9e-10 with 269. The gain is bigger the more uneven the integrand: a spike, a narrow peak, a fast transient. And the failure is the price: the adaptive rule trusts its own error estimate, which is computed from the same few points. If those points do not see a feature, nothing tells the method to look. The exercise builds a chromatogram on which our adapt returns 0.

title: Numerical integration
section: Gaussian quadrature: choose the points too
text:
Gaussian quadrature: choose the points too
So far the points were equally spaced. Choosing where to evaluate as well as the weights doubles the power: n points integrate polynomials up to degree 2n - 1 exactly.



n
points on [-1, 1]
weights
exact up to degree




2
\pm 1/\sqrt{3} = \pm 0.5774
1, 1

3
0,\ \pm\sqrt{3/5} = \pm 0.7746
8/9, 5/9, 5/9
5



x3 <- c(-sqrt(3/5), 0, sqrt(3/5));  w3 <- c(5, 8, 5) / 9      # on [-1, 1]
3 * sum(w3 * model(3 + 3 * x3)) - exact                       # map to [0, 6]
# [1] 0.3688888

3 points: error 0.37 (trapezoid with 3 points: 8.8). 10 points: 7\times10^{-12} (trapezoid: 0.57).
Points for any n: pracma::gaussLegendre(n, a, b) in R, numpy.polynomial.legendre.leggauss in Python.


Gauss-Legendre points are the roots of Legendre polynomials; we do not derive them. To use them on [a, b], map x in [-1, 1] to (a+b)/2 + (b-a)/2 x and multiply the weights by (b-a)/2; here (b-a)/2 = 3. For smooth functions Gaussian quadrature is very efficient, which is why libraries use it on each piece. The catch: the points of the n-point rule and the 2n-point rule are different, so you cannot reuse points to estimate the error. Gauss-Kronrod rules fix that: they add n+1 points to an n-point Gauss rule, so the difference between the two is an error estimate. QUADPACK uses 10 Gauss points plus 11 Kronrod points: 21 points.

title: Numerical integration
section: What integrate, quad and quadrature do
text:
What integrate, quad and quadrature do

rel.tol = abs.tol \approx 1.2\times10^{-4}

All return a value and an error estimate. The estimate comes from the same points as the value.
Stopping rule: stop when the estimated error < max(abs.tol, rel.tol × |value|). An integral smaller than abs.tol is accepted at once.


QUADPACK is a Fortran library from 1983 (Piessens, de Doncker and others) and is still what R and SciPy call. QAGS starts with one 21-point Gauss-Kronrod rule on [a, b]; if the error estimate is too large it bisects the piece with the largest error, and repeats, up to subdivisions = 100 pieces. It also applies an extrapolation (Wynn’s epsilon algorithm) to the sequence of results, which is what lets it handle endpoint singularities. QAGI maps an infinite interval to (0, 1] with x = (1 - t)/t and uses a 15-point rule. The Rust crate is a port of John D. Cook’s double-exponential code; it also offers Clenshaw-Curtis. The last bullet is a trap we meet when normalising a density.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Why integrate(dnorm, 0, 20000) is 0
seen <- NULL
spy <- function(x) { seen <<- c(seen, x); dnorm(x) }   # record every x asked for
integrate(spy, 0, 20000)
# 0 with absolute error < 0
length(seen);  round(sort(seen)[1:4], 1)
# [1] 21
# [1]   43.4  260.9  698.4 1349.4


The 21 points lie at 43.4 and beyond, where dnorm underflows to exactly 0. Gauss and Kronrod agree (both 0), so the error estimate is 0 and QAGS stops.


This is the full explanation of the example in Why numerical analysis. The outermost Kronrod point on [-1, 1] is at 0.99566, so on [0, 20000] it sits at 10000 * (1 - 0.99566) = 43.4. dnorm(43.4) is about e^-943, far below the smallest double (How computers store numbers), so it is 0. Twenty-one zeros: the 10-point Gauss estimate and the 21-point Kronrod estimate agree perfectly, the error estimate is 0, and there is no reason to subdivide. The <<- operator assigns to the variable outside the function, so seen collects every x. In Python, use a list and append inside the function.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Three fixes, and the check
integrate(dnorm, 0, 10)$value + integrate(dnorm, 10, 20000)$value  # split
# [1] 0.5
integrate(dnorm, 0, Inf)                                          # transform
# 0.5 with absolute error < 4.7e-05
integrate(dnorm, 0, 20)                                           # give the scale
# 0.5 with absolute error < 3.7e-05
integrate(dnorm, 0, 5000)                                         # the check
# 2.326323e-06 with absolute error < 4.6e-06

Split at the feature; transform (an infinite interval is mapped so that its points spread over many scales); give the scale: limits where the function lives.
Check: change the limits or the tolerance a little; the answer must not move. An error estimate as large as the value is a warning.
The Rust crate packs its points at the ends, so it finds the peak at 0, but returns 0 for a peak at 5000 in [0, 20000]. Every finite rule can miss a narrow peak.


Splitting works because the piece [0, 10] has points near 0. The infinite version works because QAGI maps (0, Inf) to (0, 1] and the 15 points then land at x between 0.004 and 233. Giving the scale: the normal density is negligible beyond 10 standard deviations. The check line is the useful habit: 5000 is not a silly upper limit, and the answer is wrong without being 0 - but the error estimate is larger than the value. Comparing answers with different limits catches it. The last bullet refers to the Rust solution of C5 in Why numerical analysis: different rules miss different things.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Infinite intervals: substitute
\int_0^\infty f(x)\,dx with x = \dfrac{t}{1-t}: t \in [0, 1) covers x \in [0, \infty), and dx = \dfrac{dt}{(1-t)^2}.
\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = \int_0^1 \frac{e^{-t/(1-t)}}{(1-t)^2}\,dt = 1

integrate(function(x) dnorm(x, mean = 5000), 0, Inf)
# 0 with absolute error < 0

The transform fixes the range, not the scale: its points reach only x \approx 233. A peak at 5000 is missed. Give the scale: integrate(..., 4950, 5050) returns 1.


Right panel: the transformed integrand on [0, 1) is smooth and goes to 0 at t = 1, so any finite rule works. R uses x = (1 - t)/t instead, which maps t in (0, 1] to x in [0, Inf); the idea is the same. The transform assumes the interesting part of f is near x = 1, where t = 0.5. If f lives at x = 5000, its interesting part sits in a tiny piece of t near 1. Distributions with a known location (a posterior centred at its mode, a peak at a known retention time) should be integrated around that location.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Singularities: substitute again
The Jeffreys prior for a proportion (e.g. an allele frequency) is \propto 1/\sqrt{x(1-x)}, infinite at both ends. Its normalising constant is \int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x(1-x)}} = \pi.
jeff <- function(x) 1 / sqrt(x * (1 - x))
jeff(0)
# [1] Inf                                      # trapezoid: NaN
mid <- function(f, a, b, n) { h <- (b - a) / n;  h * sum(f(a + (1:n - 0.5) * h)) }
sapply(c(16, 256, 4096), function(n) mid(jeff, 0, 1, n)) - pi
# [1] -0.30148615 -0.07559745 -0.01890285     # order 0.5
integrate(jeff, 0, 1)
# 3.141593 with absolute error < 9.4e-06

Substitute x = \sin^2\theta: dx = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta and \sqrt{x(1-x)} = \sin\theta\cos\theta, so the integral is \int_0^{\pi/2} 2\,d\theta = \pi. Smooth (here constant).
For a single 1/\sqrt{x} at 0: x = u^2 turns \int_0^1 \frac{g(x)}{\sqrt{x}}dx into \int_0^1 2\,g(u^2)\,du.


An integrable singularity: the integrand is infinite, the area finite. Rules that evaluate at the endpoints fail outright (Inf times a weight). Open rules like the midpoint rule work, slowly: 4096 points for 2 digits. integrate copes because QUADPACK’s extrapolation is designed for endpoint singularities, and its Gauss-Kronrod points never touch the endpoints. Substitution is the robust fix: it is pen-and-paper work that makes any rule fast. The same appears in densities: a Gamma density with shape below 1 (waiting times between transcriptional bursts are sometimes fitted with one) is infinite at 0.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Biology: normalising a probability density
Posterior for the UMI rate \lambda of the zero-truncated Poisson model (Newton and secant methods; 100 cells, flat prior). The density is \propto L(\lambda), and we need Z = \int_0^\infty L\,d\lambda.
loglik <- function(l) 173 * log(l) - 100 * l - 100 * log1p(-exp(-l))
L <- function(l) exp(loglik(l))
sapply(c(10, 100, Inf), function(b) integrate(L, 0, b)$value)
# [1] 4.450271e-24 3.226339e-26 4.708206e-24        # three answers!
g <- function(l) exp(loglik(l) - loglik(1.2184695))   # scaled: max = 1
sapply(c(10, 100, Inf), function(b) integrate(g, 0, b)$value)
# [1] 0.3322104 0.3322104 0.3322104

L \approx 10^{-23} is far below abs.tol \approx 10^{-4}: integrate accepts its first rough answer. Scale the values: divide by the maximum (log scale, as in How computers store numbers); \log Z = \log L_{\max} + \log 0.3322.
Scale the axis too: integrate(g, 0, 1000) gives 2\times10^{-9}. The peak (width 0.13) is invisible at that scale.


This is the situation in Bayesian work and in likelihood-based model comparison: a likelihood is a tiny number, and its integral is a normalising constant or a marginal likelihood. Two scale problems. First the values: the absolute tolerance is a fixed number, so an integrand of size 1e-23 meets it with any answer. Python’s quad has the same problem (epsabs = 1.5e-8). Subtracting the maximum log-likelihood makes the peak height 1, and all limits now agree. Second the axis: with 10000 cells the posterior would be 10 times narrower, and even (0, 100) misses it (exercise). The cure is to integrate over the mode plus or minus 10 standard errors, using the standard error from Newton and secant methods.

title: Numerical integration
section: Biology: chromatography and mass-spec peak areas
text:
Biology: chromatography and mass-spec peak areas


A peak (Gaussian, \sigma = 3 s) sampled by the detector every h seconds; area by the trapezoid rule.
Every 6 s (h = 2\sigma, 2–3 points across the peak): area within 1.4 %, but the height is off by up to 39 %. Every 3 s: area exact to 5\times10^{-9}, height still off by up to 12 %.
Area is far more robust than height. Real errors come from noise, the baseline and overlapping peaks (fit those: Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting).


Quantification in LC-MS and HPLC uses peak areas. The trapezoid rule on a full peak that starts and ends at baseline is far more accurate than the h^2 rule suggests: its error depends on the derivatives at the two ends (Euler-Maclaurin), and for a peak those are all zero. The error then falls faster than any power of h, here exp(-2 pi^2 sigma^2 / h^2). The height depends on whether a sample lands on the apex, so it jumps with the sampling phase. The usual advice of 8 to 10 points across a peak is about noise, peak detection and shape, not the integration rule. This is why software integrates peaks rather than using heights, and why the baseline subtraction step deserves more attention than the rule.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Biology: AUC with linear-up / log-down
After the peak, concentrations fall roughly exponentially. Interpolate \log C linearly there; the area of an exponential segment is \dfrac{(C_1 - C_2)\,\Delta t}{\ln(C_1 / C_2)}.
auc_lul <- function(t, y) {
  dt <- diff(t);  y1 <- head(y, -1);  y2 <- tail(y, -1)
  lin <- dt * (y1 + y2) / 2                     # rising or flat: trapezoid
  logd <- dt * (y1 - y2) / log(y1 / y2)         # falling: exponential decay
  sum(ifelse(y2 < y1 & y2 > 0, logd, lin))
}
auc_lul(t_h, conc)
# [1] 48.91575                                  # linear: 51.6175, true: 49.52521


This is a domain-specific rule: it builds in what pharmacokineticists know about the shape of the curve, the same way the substitution builds in what we know about a singularity. On the log-scale panel the elimination phase is a straight line, so the log-down interpolation (green) follows it, while linear interpolation (blue) bulges far above it between 12 and 24 h. Here linear-up/log-down errs by -1.2 % instead of +4.2 %; the remaining error is in the absorption phase, where both rules use straight lines and the samples are too sparse. Non-compartmental analysis software (for example Phoenix WinNonlin or the R package PKNCA) offers both rules; check which one a report used.

title: Numerical integration
section: Data or model? AUC to infinity
text:
Data or model? AUC to infinity
Total exposure is \mathrm{AUC}_{0-\infty}. Extrapolate the tail with the terminal slope \lambda_z: \int_{t_\text{last}}^\infty C_\text{last}\,e^{-\lambda_z (t - t_\text{last})}\,dt = C_\text{last}/\lambda_z.
last <- 8:10                                    # terminal phase: 8, 12, 24 h
lz <- -coef(lm(log(conc[last]) ~ t_h[last]))[[2]]
lz
# [1] 0.2036783
auc_lul(t_h, conc) + conc[10] / lz              # AUC 0-infinity
# [1] 49.35762
500 / 50 / 0.2                                  # model: Dose / (V ke)
# [1] 50

Data route (non-compartmental): no model, but error from sparse sampling. Model route: fit, then integrate exactly; but only as right as the model.
Check: compare the two; the extrapolated part should be small (< 20 % of the total). Here: 0.09/0.204 = 0.44, under 1 %.


The terminal slope is a straight-line fit to log concentration over the last points (Least squares: normal equations vs QR). Extrapolation to infinity is the infinite-interval problem again, solved analytically because we assume an exponential tail. The model route needs a fit (Part 9) and then the integral is either closed form (here Dose/(V ke) = 50) or a call to integrate on a smooth function, which is easy. Disagreement between the two routes points to either sparse sampling (data route) or a wrong model (model route). Regulators accept the data route; the 20 % rule of thumb protects against a result that is mostly extrapolation.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Checklist: detecting integration trouble

Plot the integrand over the whole interval before integrating. Is there a narrow peak, a kink, a singularity?
Change the limits (and rel.tol) a little: the answer must not move.
Error estimate ≳ value, or exactly 0 → distrust the result.
Tiny values (likelihoods): scale to a maximum of 1 first; abs.tol is absolute.
Wide interval, narrow feature → split at the feature or integrate around it.
Order lower than promised on a halving test → not smooth: split at the kink or substitute.
Data: the rule assumes a shape between samples. Sparse samples where the curve bends are the main error.


A list to keep next to the keyboard. Each item is one of the failures in this lecture: the dnorm example (plot, change limits), the posterior (tiny values, wide interval), sqrt and the Jeffreys prior (order test), the AUC tail (shape between samples). Note that none of these produce an error or a warning: integrate and quad return a number in every case.

title: Numerical integration
text:
Summary

Every quadrature rule is \sum_i w_i f(x_i): it sees only the points it samples.
Composite rules: left Riemann order 1, trapezoid and midpoint order 2, Simpson order 4. Read the order off a log–log plot; it needs a smooth integrand.
Romberg = repeated Richardson on the trapezoid. Adaptive quadrature splits where two rules disagree. Gaussian quadrature chooses the points: n points, degree 2n-1.
integrate / quad: 21-point Gauss–Kronrod, bisect the worst piece. They can miss a narrow feature with a confident error estimate of 0. Fixes: split, transform, give the scale.
Infinite intervals and singularities: substitute (x = t/(1-t), x = u^2, x = \sin^2\theta).
Biology: AUC from samples (trapezoid, linear-up/log-down, extrapolation C_\text{last}/\lambda_z), peak areas (robust; heights are not), normalising a density (scale first).

Next: Random numbers and Monte Carlo, for integrals in many dimensions, where grids are hopeless.

Recap: rules, orders, the three improvements (Romberg, adaptive, Gauss), and the library failure with its three fixes. In one dimension these methods are hard to beat. In ten dimensions a grid with 10 points per axis already needs 10^10 evaluations; that is where Monte Carlo takes over, with an error of 1/sqrt(N) whatever the dimension.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
About this lecture
So far in Part 8 a model was an ODE: one smooth curve, the same in every cell. With 10 mRNA molecules per cell that picture breaks.

When copy numbers are small, reactions are random events. Each has a propensity: its probability per unit time.
The chemical master equation describes the probabilities of all states, but it is far too large to solve. We sample it instead.
Gillespie’s algorithm (the SSA): draw when the next reaction happens (an exponential waiting time) and which one it is (in proportion to its propensity). Exact, and 10 lines of code.
Many runs give a distribution. Its mean is compared with the ODE; its spread is the biology.
When the SSA is too slow: tau-leaping, and Euler–Maruyama for stochastic differential equations, each with its failure.
Biology: transcriptional bursting and the cell-to-cell variability it causes; the Fano factor.


This is the last unit of Part 8. The previous four units treated an ODE as the model and asked how to solve it accurately. Here the model itself changes: a cell with ten copies of an mRNA does not have a concentration that changes smoothly; it has a whole number of molecules that jumps up and down at random times. The numerical method is a Monte Carlo method (Random numbers and Monte Carlo), and its accuracy is a statistical question: how many runs, what standard error. We hand-write the algorithm in R; packages exist (GillespieSSA2, adaptivetau in R; gillespy2 in Python), but the algorithm is the point and is short.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Recap: the mRNA ODE
From Initial value problems and Euler’s method: mRNA made at rate k, each molecule degraded at rate \delta:
m'(t) = k - \delta\, m, \qquad m(0) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad m(t) = \frac{k}{\delta}\left(1 - e^{-\delta t}\right).









value
meaning




k
10 per hour
transcription rate


\delta
1 per hour
degradation rate per molecule (mean lifetime 1 h)


k/\delta
10 molecules
steady state




The ODE says: every cell reaches exactly 10.0 molecules after a few hours, and stays there.
A single-molecule FISH (smFISH) experiment counts mRNA in single cells. Do all cells have 10?


Same model as in the Euler unit (there with alpha = 10 per minute and delta = 0.2 per minute, steady state 50); here a gene expressed at a lower level, with times in hours, so that the steady state is 10 molecules. smFISH counts individual mRNA molecules as fluorescent dots, so it gives a whole number per cell for thousands of cells: a distribution, not a curve. The question of this lecture: what does the model predict for that distribution?

title: Stochastic simulation
section: A biology problem first: two genes, same mean
text:
A biology problem first: two genes, same mean


Two genes, both with a mean of 10 mRNA per cell. Gene A: a narrow peak. Gene B: one cell in five has none, a few have 40+.
The ODE gives the same answer, 10, for both. It cannot tell them apart.


These are simulated cells (1000 per gene), made with the two models of this lecture; real smFISH data look like this (Raj et al. 2006, mammalian cells; Zenklusen et al. 2008, yeast). Gene A is transcribed at a steady rate. Gene B is transcribed in bursts: the promoter switches on now and then, makes a burst of mRNA, and switches off. Such bursting is common in mammalian genes and is one source of cell-to-cell variability in genetically identical cells in the same environment: a clonal population is not uniform. Whether a cell has 0 or 40 copies of a transcription factor can decide its fate. The mean, which is all an ODE predicts, is identical.

title: Stochastic simulation
section: When copy numbers are small, the ODE is not enough
text:
When copy numbers are small, the ODE is not enough


The same model, scaled by its steady state. With 10 molecules, single cells fluctuate by \pm 30\%; with 1000, by \pm 3\%.
The relative fluctuation is about 1/\sqrt{\text{mean}}: 1/\sqrt{10} = 0.32, 1/\sqrt{1000} = 0.032.


The ODE is the limit of many molecules: when every species is present in thousands of copies, the random fluctuations average out and the deterministic curve describes each cell well. Bacteria have about 1 mRNA copy per gene on average, mammalian cells a few to a few hundred; many transcription factors are present in tens to hundreds of copies; a gene has 1 or 2 copies of its promoter. So in gene expression the small-number case is the rule. The 1/sqrt(mean) law is the Poisson law (variance = mean), which we will see is exact for this model.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Reactions as random events
A reaction j has a propensity a_j(\mathbf x): in a short time dt it happens with probability a_j(\mathbf x)\,dt. It changes the state \mathbf x by a fixed stoichiometry vector.










reaction

Total propensity a_0 = \sum_j a_j = 60 per hour: a reaction every minute on average.
The ODE uses the same rates: m' = k - \delta_m m, p' = k_p m - \delta_p p, i.e. (change vectors) × (propensities).


The propensity is the rate of the ODE, read as a probability per unit time. “Each mRNA is degraded at rate 1 per hour” means each molecule has probability delta dt of being degraded in the next dt, so with m molecules the probability that one of them goes is delta m dt. A protein is made from an mRNA: translation does not use up the mRNA, so its change vector is (0, +1). Steady state of the ODE: m = 10, p = k_p m / delta_p = 100. For a reaction between two molecules (A + B), the propensity is c times a times b; for two molecules of the same kind, c a (a - 1)/2. These combinatorial factors are where the stochastic and the deterministic model start to differ.

title: Stochastic simulation
section: The chemical master equation, in words
text:
The chemical master equation, in words
P_n(t) = probability that a cell has n mRNA molecules at time t. Probability flows into state n from n-1 (a molecule made) and n+1 (one degraded), and out of n by any reaction:
\frac{dP_n}{dt} = \underbrace{k\,P_{n-1} + \delta\,(n+1)\,P_{n+1}}_{\text{in}} - \underbrace{(k + \delta n)\,P_n}_{\text{out}}.
For n = 3: \;P_3' = 10\,P_2 + 4\,P_4 - 13\,P_3.

A linear ODE system, one equation per state. Its steady state here is Poisson(10).
But one equation per state: (promoter, mRNA ≤ 100, protein ≤ 500) has 2 \cdot 101 \cdot 501 \approx 10^5 states; an epidemic in 10 000 people about 5 \cdot 10^7.
So we do not solve the master equation; we sample from it, one cell at a time.


The chemical master equation (CME) is the exact description of a well-mixed reacting system: it is the Kolmogorov forward equation of a continuous-time Markov chain whose states are the molecule counts. It is linear in the P’s, so in principle we know how to solve it: a matrix exponential, or for the steady state a null vector of the rate matrix (an eigenvector for eigenvalue 0, as for the Markov chains in Power iteration and friends). The problem is size: one unknown per possible state, and the number of states is the product of the ranges of all species. Detailed balance gives the steady state of the one-species case by hand: k P_{n-1} = delta n P_n, so P_n = (k/delta)^n / n! P_0, the Poisson distribution (exercise B3).

title: Stochastic simulation
section: Gillespie’s idea: two questions per step
text:
Gillespie’s idea: two questions per step


When? With total propensity a_0, the waiting time is exponential with rate a_0: inverse transform \tau = -\log(u_1)/a_0.
Which? Reaction j with probability a_j/a_0: cut [0, a_0) into pieces of length a_j, see where u_2 a_0 falls.


Gillespie (1976, 1977) showed that these two draws produce exact sample paths of the master equation: no time step, no approximation beyond the model itself. Why exponential: each reaction j would fire after an exponential time with rate a_j if nothing else happened; the first of several independent exponentials is exponential with the sum of the rates, and it is reaction j with probability a_j / a0. Both draws are inverse-transform sampling from Random numbers and Monte Carlo: the continuous one for the exponential (with u in place of 1 - u, since both are uniform), the discrete one for the reaction, exactly the base-composition example there. After the reaction the propensities change, so they are recomputed before the next step.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
One step by hand
State m = 10: a_1 = k = 10 (make), a_2 = \delta m = 10 (degrade), a_0 = 20 per hour.

degrade: m \to 9



Next step: a = (10, 9), a_0 = 19; with u_1 = 0.9, u_2 = 0.2: \tau = 0.105/19 = 0.0055 h; 0.2 \cdot 19 = 3.8 < 10: make, m \to 10.

The time advances by random, unequal steps, one reaction per step. There is no step size h to choose.
Mean waiting time 1/a_0: 3 minutes here. A busier cell takes more, smaller steps.


Do this on the board. The time axis is not a grid: the algorithm jumps from event to event. Between events nothing happens, so the state is a step function of time. Compare with Euler: there we chose h and the error depended on it; here the only error is the randomness, which we control by the number of runs. The expected number of steps in a time T is about a0 T; that is the cost of the method, and it is large when molecule numbers are large (the propensities grow with them).

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Gillespie’s algorithm in R
k <- 10; delta <- 1                      # per hour: transcription, mRNA decay
set.seed(1)
t <- 0; m <- 0; tt <- 0; mm <- 0         # no mRNA at t = 0
while (t < 10) {
  a <- c(k, delta * m); a0 <- sum(a)     # propensities: make, degrade
  t <- t - log(runif(1)) / a0            # 1. when? waiting time ~ Exp(a0)
  m <- m + if (runif(1) * a0 < a[1]) 1 else -1   # 2. which? make or degrade
  tt <- c(tt, t); mm <- c(mm, m)         # record every event
}
length(tt) - 1                           # reactions in 10 h
# [1] 223

mm jumps by \pm 1 at the times tt: 0, 0.133, 0.183, 0.317, … h. Plot it as a step function, plot(tt, mm, type = "s").
With a_0 \approx 20 per hour, 10 hours take about 200 steps.


runif never returns exactly 0 in R, so the log is safe; in Python and Rust the generators can return 0, so the exercise uses 1 - u there. The comparison runif(1) * a0 < a[1] is the discrete inverse transform for two reactions. Growing a vector with c() inside a loop is slow for long runs (it copies every time); fine for a few hundred events, and the general function on the next slide records only at chosen times. Starting at m = 0, the first propensities are (10, 0), so the first reaction must be a transcription.

title: Stochastic simulation
Stochastic simulation
section: Many cells: a distribution, and its mean
text:
Many cells: a distribution, and its mean
S1 <- matrix(c(1, -1), nrow = 1)          # 1 species (m), 2 reactions
bd <- function(x) c(10, 1 * x)            # propensities: k, delta * m
set.seed(1)
tm <- c(0.5, 1, 2, 10)
M <- replicate(2000, ssa(0, S1, bd, tm)[, 1])   # 4 times x 2000 cells
rbind(ssa = rowMeans(M), se = apply(M, 1, sd) / sqrt(2000),
      ode = 10 * (1 - exp(-tm)))
#           [,1]      [,2]       [,3]        [,4]
# ssa 3.85750000 6.3285000 8.66400000 10.11850000
# se  0.04415962 0.0558243 0.06451847  0.06981881
# ode 3.93469340 6.3212056 8.64664717  9.99954600
c(mean = mean(M[4, ]), var = var(M[4, ]))       # Poisson: var = mean
#      mean       var
# 10.118500  9.749332

The SSA mean agrees with the ODE within 2 SE at every time. Variance ≈ mean: Fano factor ≈ 1.


replicate runs 2000 independent cells; each column of M is one cell at the four times. The mean over cells is a Monte Carlo estimate, so it comes with a standard error sd / sqrt(N), exactly as in Random numbers and Monte Carlo. The largest deviation is 1.7 SE (at t = 10), which is ordinary. For this model (all propensities linear in the state) the mean of the master equation obeys the ODE exactly; that is a check we can always run when the propensities are linear. In Python and Rust the streams differ (different generators), so the numbers in the exercise differ in the second decimal; compare them with their SEs, not digit by digit.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Runs, mean and distribution


Single cells wander around 10; the average of many follows the ODE.
At t = 10 h the counts follow Poisson(10), the steady state of the master equation. A check with a known answer.


Left: five single-cell trajectories (grey steps), the mean of 2000 runs on a grid of times (dots) and the ODE (blue). Right: the histogram of the 2000 counts at t = 10 h (from the slide before) against the Poisson(10) probabilities. Always test a stochastic simulator on such a case before trusting it on a model without a known answer, exactly as we tested Monte Carlo on the binomial overlap count.

title: Stochastic simulation
section: A classic bug: averaging over events
text:
A classic bug: averaging over events
One long run, mean of m after a 10 h burn-in, computed two ways:
set.seed(1); t <- 0; m <- 0
n_ev <- 0; sum_ev <- 0; area <- 0
while (t < 5000) {
  a <- c(10, 1 * m); a0 <- sum(a)
  tau <- -log(runif(1)) / a0
  if (t > 10) area <- area + m * tau          # m holds for a time tau
  t <- t + tau
  m <- m + if (runif(1) * a0 < a[1]) 1 else -1
  if (t > 10) { n_ev <- n_ev + 1; sum_ev <- sum_ev + m }   # one record per event
}
c(per_event = sum_ev / n_ev, time_weighted = area / (t - 10))
#     per_event time_weighted
#     10.455514      9.957675

Events happen more often when m is large (a_0 = 10 + m), so averaging over events overweights large m: 10.5 instead of 10.
Check: weight each state by how long it lasts, or sample at fixed times (as ssa does).


A confident wrong answer that runs without any warning. The expected per-event mean is exactly 10.5 here: the event-sampled distribution is proportional to P_n times (10 + n), with mean (100 + 110) / 20. The error is 5% for this model and can be much larger when propensities vary a lot (bursty genes). The same bug appears when people take every row of an SSA output table as an equally likely snapshot. Packages that return all events (rather than fixed output times) invite it.

Bursting: the telegraph promoter
The promoter switches between off and on; it is transcribed only when on.

g \in \{0, 1\} is the promoter state. Each burst makes on average k_m/k_{\text{off}} = 22 mRNA.
ODE for the means: g^* = \frac{k_{\text{on}}}{k_{\text{on}} + k_{\text{off}}} = 0.1, \;m^* = \frac{k_m g^*}{\delta_m} = 10, \;p^* = 100: the same as the constitutive gene.


The two-state or “telegraph” model (Peccoud and Ycart 1995): the name comes from the on-off signal of the promoter. Biologically, “on” can be a state with the right transcription factors and chromatin opened; many mammalian genes are on only a small fraction of the time and fire bursts of transcripts. We chose the rates so that the mean mRNA and protein levels equal those of the constitutive gene: k_m g* = 10 per hour on average. So the two genes have the same ODE, and the difference is entirely in the noise. The single promoter copy (g is 0 or 1) is the extreme case of a small copy number.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
The telegraph model in R
S3 <- rbind(g = c(1, -1, 0,  0, 0,  0),   # promoter: on, off
            m = c(0,  0, 1, -1, 0,  0),   # mRNA: make, degrade
            p = c(0,  0, 0,  0, 1, -1))   # protein: make, degrade
telegraph <- function(x) c(0.5 * (1 - x[1]), 4.5 * x[1], 100 * x[1],
                           1 * x[2], 2 * x[2], 0.2 * x[3])
set.seed(1)
Y <- t(replicate(1000, ssa(c(0, 0, 0), S3, telegraph, 30)[1, ]))  # ~20 s
fano <- function(v) var(v) / mean(v)
c(mean_m = mean(Y[, 2]), Fano_m = fano(Y[, 2]),
  mean_p = mean(Y[, 3]), Fano_p = fano(Y[, 3]))
#    mean_m    Fano_m    mean_p    Fano_p
#  10.10700  15.26168 100.21200  32.92882

Same ssa, new S and propensities. 1000 cells at t = 30 h (six protein lifetimes: steady state).
Means 10 and 100, as the ODE says. The variance is 15 times the mean for mRNA, 33 times for protein.


Nothing in the algorithm changes; only the model description. Starting values: promoter off, no mRNA, no protein; t = 30 h is long enough to forget the start (protein lifetime 5 h, e^-6 = 0.25% of the initial transient left). The constitutive gene in the same set-up (exercise C2) gives means 10.15 and 100.9 and Fano factors 1.02 and 2.64. 1000 cells take about 20 s in R, because every one of about 1800 reactions per cell is a trip through an R loop; the Rust version in the exercise takes under a second.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Bursts in time


Green bands: promoter on. mRNA jumps up in a burst, then decays; long stretches with zero mRNA.
The protein (lifetime 5 h) averages over several mRNA bursts, but still swings from 20 to 110.


Same mean, very different single-cell behaviour. The constitutive gene (left) stays near 10 mRNA and 100 proteins. The bursty gene (right) has long silent periods and short bursts. The protein integrates over its lifetime, which smooths the mRNA bursts, but a few hours without a burst still drain it. A cell that needs this protein above a threshold will sometimes fall below it by chance: this is how bursting turns into different fates for identical cells (e.g. persistence to antibiotics, competence in Bacillus subtilis, lineage choice).

F = 1: molecules made one at a time, independently. F > 1: made in bursts; roughly 1 + burst size.
A measured F \gg 1 for an mRNA is evidence for transcriptional bursting.


The exact formulas come from the master equation (for linear propensities the mean and variance satisfy closed linear ODEs; the exercise uses only the results). Even a constitutive promoter gives protein F > 1: each mRNA makes a burst of proteins (on average k_p / delta_m = 2 per mRNA lifetime), so protein noise has a translational-burst part. The SE of a simulated Fano factor is roughly F sqrt(2/N), about 5% with 1000 cells, so 15.3 against 16 is fine. Caveat for data: the Fano factor depends on units. Fluorescence in arbitrary units, a times the molecule count, has F multiplied by a; only counts of molecules can be compared with 1.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Protein distributions


Constitutive: a little wider than Poisson(100) (Fano 2.6). Bursty: spread from 0 to 300 (Fano 33), with the same mean.
Many genes, many cells: a plot of F against the mean separates bursty genes from Poisson-like ones.


The 1000 cells of the previous two slides. The dashed curve is the Poisson distribution with the same mean, the narrowest a birth-death process can give. This is the kind of comparison made in single-cell studies of gene expression noise (e.g. Taniguchi et al. 2010, E. coli, protein and mRNA in single cells). Note how badly the ODE describes the bursty population: the “typical” cell is not at 100.

title: Stochastic simulation
section: When the mean is not the ODE: extinction
text:
When the mean is not the ODE: extinction
The SIR epidemic from Initial value problems and Euler’s method (N = 10\,000, \beta = 0.3, \gamma = 0.1 per day, R_0 = 3), but starting from one case:
sir_fate <- function(I0, N = 10000, beta = 0.3, gamma = 0.1) {
  S <- N - I0; I <- I0
  while (I > 0 && I < 100) {                 # stop: extinct, or 100 infected
    a1 <- beta * S * I / N; a2 <- gamma * I  # infection, recovery
    if (runif(1) * (a1 + a2) < a1) { S <- S - 1; I <- I + 1 } else I <- I - 1
  }
  I == 0                                     # TRUE if the outbreak died out
}
set.seed(1); ext <- replicate(10000, sir_fate(1))
c(extinct = mean(ext), se = sd(ext) / sqrt(10000))
#     extinct          se
# 0.334800000 0.004719441

The ODE always predicts an epidemic. One in three outbreaks dies out early (1/R_0 = 0.333).


The infection propensity beta S I / N is nonlinear (a product of two counts), but that is not the main point; the main point is the absorbing state I = 0, which the ODE never reaches. Early on, the first case recovers before infecting anyone with probability gamma / (beta + gamma) = 1/4, and the full extinction probability of the branching process is 1/R0 (exercise B7). Once 100 people are infected, extinction is practically impossible, so we stop there; we need only the order of events, not the times, for this question. The same kind of question: does a new mutant lineage survive drift, does a noise kick switch the toggle switch to its other stable state (Equilibria, stability and the phase plane)? The ODE answers none of them.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Single outbreaks vs the ODE


Runs that take off look like the ODE, but shifted in time by a random delay. Their average is lower and wider than the ODE curve.
The ODE is the mean only for linear propensities. Otherwise: simulate, and compare.


The 20 outbreaks that take off all peak at about 3000 infected, like the ODE, but the time to reach a few hundred cases varies by weeks, because the early phase with a handful of cases is dominated by chance. Averaging over runs, including the ones that died out, gives a curve with a lower and wider peak than any single run: the mean of the stochastic model is not the solution of the ODE. Fitting an ODE to a stochastic outbreak can therefore give wrong rates (Part 9). For linear propensities the ODE is exactly the mean (the mRNA examples); for nonlinear ones it is an approximation that is good when all counts are large.

The work grows with the number of molecules, not with the accuracy wanted. Abundant species make the SSA slow, even when nothing interesting happens to them.
Rust or C is 20–50 times faster than an R loop (exercise). Beyond that, approximate: many reactions per step.


The SSA is exact but simulates every single reaction. In the third row, 10 000 proteins with lifetime 5 h means 2000 degradation events per hour, and as many translations. Compiled code helps by a constant factor. The algorithmic way out is to stop simulating each event: fire many reactions in one step when the propensities hardly change during that step. That is tau-leaping. The numbers in the last column are estimates from the measured cost of about 10 microseconds per step in R.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Tau-leaping, and its failure
Take a fixed step \tau; reaction j fires a Poisson(a_j \tau) number of times, propensities frozen during the step.
tau_leap <- function(tau, t_end = 10, k = 10, delta = 1) {
  m <- 0; went_negative <- FALSE
  for (n in 1:round(t_end / tau)) {
    m <- m + rpois(1, k * tau) - rpois(1, delta * m * tau)   # many reactions per leap
    if (m < 0) { went_negative <- TRUE; m <- 0 }             # impossible: clip
  }
  c(m, went_negative)
}

Large \tau: wrong variance and negative molecule numbers. Check: \delta\tau \ll 1 (each propensity changes little per leap); count negatives; halve \tau.


Tau-leaping (Gillespie 2001) is to the SSA what Euler’s method is to the exact ODE solution: a fixed step, frozen rates, an error that grows with the step. The Poisson number of degradations does not know how many molecules there are: with m = 3 and delta tau = 1.5 it removes 4.5 on average. Clipping to zero hides the failure and biases the result. The variance is wrong even without negatives: for this model the tau-leap variance is 2k/(delta (2 - delta tau)), 20 instead of 10 at tau = 1 (exercise C4). Production codes choose tau adaptively and switch to exact SSA steps for species with few molecules (rpois; the adaptivetau package in R).

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Euler–Maruyama for stochastic differential equations
With many molecules, replace the Poisson numbers by normals with the same mean and variance: the chemical Langevin equation \;dm = (k - \delta m)\,dt + \sqrt{k + \delta m}\;dW. Euler–Maruyama: an Euler step plus a random kick of size \sqrt h.
em <- function(h, k, t_end = 10, delta = 1) {
  m <- 0
  for (n in 1:round(t_end / h))
    m <- m + (k - delta * m) * h + sqrt((k + delta * m) * h) * rnorm(1)
  m
}
set.seed(1); m <- replicate(2000, em(h = 0.01, k = 10))
c(mean = mean(m), var = var(m))
#     mean      var
# 9.917764 9.817142
m <- replicate(2000, em(h = 0.01, k = 0.5)); mean(is.nan(m))   # mean 0.5 molecules
# [1] 0.076          (Warning: NaNs produced)

Mean 10, variance 10: right. With a mean of 0.5 molecules, m goes negative and \sqrt{\cdot} gives NaN in 8% of runs. Continuous noise needs large numbers.


The drift term is the ODE right-hand side; the diffusion term has variance (sum of propensities) per unit time, matching the Poisson numbers of a tau-leap step. Euler-Maruyama is Euler’s method with a normal kick of standard deviation sqrt(h) times the noise strength; it has weak order 1 (for means and variances) and strong order 1/2 (for single paths), lower than the order 1 of Euler for ODEs. SDEs also model noise outside chemistry: fluctuating environments, Brownian motion of particles, population sizes with environmental noise. The failure is the opposite of the SSA’s cost problem: the approximation is only valid when every species has many copies.

title: Stochastic simulation
section: Checklist: is my stochastic simulation right?
text:
Checklist: is my stochastic simulation right?

Test on a known answer: birth–death should give Poisson(k/\delta); for linear propensities the mean must follow the ODE.
Every estimate has an error bar: mean \pm 2\,\text{SE} over cells; a Fano factor from 1000 cells is uncertain by about 5%.
Sample at fixed times, or weight by duration: never average over events.
Run long enough to forget the start (several lifetimes of the slowest species).
Seeds: set once; R, numpy and Rust have different generators, so trajectories differ between languages. Compare statistics, not trajectories.
Tau-leaping and Euler–Maruyama: no negative counts, no NaN; halve the step and compare.


A stochastic simulation always returns plausible-looking numbers, so the checks are about the statistics. The cross-language point is practical: the exercise solutions in R, Python and Rust give different numbers for every run (and the Python seed for one task happens to give a mean 3 SE from the truth, which is what happens now and then). Agreement means agreement within the standard errors. A result that depends on the seed by more than its error bar is not a result.

title: Stochastic simulation
text:
Summary

Small copy numbers: reactions are random events with propensities; the ODE describes only the mean, and only for linear propensities.
The chemical master equation is exact but has one equation per state; we sample it.
Gillespie’s SSA: \tau = -\log(u_1)/a_0, reaction j with probability a_j/a_0. Exact, no step size, cost one step per reaction.
Many runs → distribution: mean \pm SE against the ODE; sample at fixed times.
Tau-leaping (Poisson numbers per step) and Euler–Maruyama (normal kicks) are faster; they fail with negative counts or NaN when numbers are small.
Biology: transcriptional bursting (telegraph promoter) gives Fano factor \gg 1; constitutive transcription gives Poisson, F = 1. Early extinction of an outbreak, which no ODE shows.

Next: Part 9, Optimisation in one dimension: from simulating models to fitting them.

The SSA closes Part 8: from ODEs solved accurately to the stochastic models behind them. Part 9 turns to fitting model parameters to data; Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting fits ODE models, and the variability seen here is one reason why an ODE fitted to single-cell data can mislead. The Monte Carlo ideas (standard errors, seeds, known-answer tests) from Random numbers and Monte Carlo carried over unchanged.

title: Exercise: stochastic simulation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write down the propensities and stoichiometry of a small reaction network, and the ODE for its mean,
write the chemical master equation of a birth–death process and find its steady state (Poisson) by hand,
carry out steps of Gillespie’s direct method by hand, and hand-write the algorithm in code,
run many simulated cells, compare the mean with the ODE (with a standard error) and the distribution with a known answer,
explain how a two-state (telegraph) promoter gives transcriptional bursting, and compute and interpret the Fano factor,
spot the event-averaging bug, the negative counts of tau-leaping and the NaNs of Euler–Maruyama at small numbers,
estimate the probability that an epidemic started by one case dies out.

The by-hand part uses pen, paper and a pocket calculator (for log and exp). The code part hand-writes the SSA in each language: no simulation package is needed.
