title: Exercise: stochastic simulation
Exercise: stochastic simulation
text:
By hand
B1. Propensities and the ODE. The constitutive gene has the reactions \(\varnothing \to M\) (\(k = 10\)), \(M \to \varnothing\) (\(\delta_m m\), \(\delta_m = 1\)), \(M \to M + P\) (\(k_p m\), \(k_p = 2\)), \(P \to \varnothing\) (\(\delta_p p\), \(\delta_p = 0.2\)), all per hour. (a) Write the stoichiometry matrix \(S\) (rows \(m\), \(p\); one column per reaction). (b) In the state \((m, p) = (4, 30)\), compute the four propensities, \(a_0\), the probability that each reaction is the next one, and the mean waiting time in minutes. (c) Write the ODE \(\mathbf x' = S\,\mathbf a(\mathbf x)\) and its steady state. (d) The telegraph gene in the state \((g, m, p) = (0, 4, 30)\): which reactions are possible, and what is \(a_0\)?
B2. Gillespie by hand. Birth–death with \(k = 10\), \(\delta = 1\) per hour, starting at \(t = 0\) with \(m = 2\). (Useful: \(\ln 0.5 = -0.693\), \(\ln 0.2 = -1.609\).) (a) Step 1 with \(u_1 = 0.5\), \(u_2 = 0.3\): the waiting time, the reaction, the new \(t\) and \(m\). (b) Step 2 with \(u_1 = 0.2\), \(u_2 = 0.9\). (c) Starting from \(m = 0\): which reaction is certainly the first, and what is its mean waiting time? (d) What plays the role of Euler’s step size \(h\) here?
B3. The master equation of a small gene. Birth–death with \(k = 2\), \(\delta = 1\) per hour. (a) Write \(P_0'\) and \(P_1'\) from Fact 2. (b) At steady state all \(P_n' = 0\). Show that \(P_1 = 2P_0\) and \(P_2 = 2P_0\), and guess \(P_n\). Normalise and compute \(P_0, \dots, P_3\). Which distribution is this? (c) A model with three species, each between 0 and 199 molecules: how many equations does its master equation have? Why does that favour simulation?
B4. The telegraph gene. \(k_\text{on} = 0.5\), \(k_\text{off} = 4.5\), \(k_m = 100\), \(\delta_m = 1\) per hour. (a) Write the ODE for the mean promoter state \(g\) (the fraction of time on) and for \(m\), and find their steady states. Then the protein steady state (\(k_p = 2\), \(\delta_p = 0.2\)). (b) How long is the promoter on, and off, on average? How many mRNA does one burst make on average? (c) Compute the Fano factor of the mRNA (Fact 4) and compare it with the constitutive gene. (d) Keep the mean at 10 but make bursts half as large: \(k_\text{on} = 1\), \(k_\text{off} = 9\), \(k_m = 100\). Compute the mean and the Fano factor.
B5. Fano factors from counts. smFISH counts of two genes in 8 cells: gene A: 6, 12, 8, 14, 10, 7, 13, 10; gene B: 0, 0, 31, 2, 0, 45, 1, 1. (a) Compute the mean, the sample variance (divide by \(n - 1\)) and the Fano factor of each. (b) For a Poisson(10) gene, what is the probability that a cell has no mRNA? How many of the 8 cells of gene B have none? (c) A colleague measures gene A by fluorescence, 50 units per molecule. What Fano factor do they get, and what is wrong with comparing it with 1?
B6. Tau-leaping goes negative. After transcription has stopped (\(k = 0\)), a cell has \(m = 3\) mRNA, \(\delta = 1\) per hour. (a) In one tau-leap of \(\tau = 1.5\) h, how many degradations are expected? (b) The number of degradations is Poisson(4.5); \(P(N \le 3) = 0.342\). What is the probability that the count becomes negative? (c) Why can the exact SSA never produce a negative count? (d) Choose \(\tau\) so that at most 10% of the molecules are expected to go in one leap. What is then the chance of going negative? (\(P(\text{Poisson}(0.3) \ge 4) = 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\).)
B7. Will the outbreak die out? SIR with \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\) per day in a large population (\(S \approx N\)), starting with \(I = 1\). (a) With \(S \approx N\) the infection propensity is \(\beta I\) and the recovery propensity \(\gamma I\). What is the probability that the next event is a recovery? (b) Each infected person independently starts a chain that dies out with probability \(q\). Explain why \(q = 0.25 + 0.75\,q^2\), and solve it. (c) What is the extinction probability with 3 initial cases? With 10 (the start of the SIR example in Initial value problems and Euler’s method)? (d) What does the ODE predict in each case?

title: Exercise: stochastic simulation
text:
In code
C1. Gillespie’s algorithm, hand-written. Birth–death, \(k = 10\), \(\delta = 1\) per hour, \(m(0) = 0\). (a) Write a function that simulates one cell up to \(t = 10\) h and returns all event times and counts. How many reactions happen? (Expected: \(\int_0^{10}(10 + m(t))\,dt \approx 190\).) (b) Simulate 2000 cells and record \(m\) at \(t = 0.5, 1, 2, 10\) h (the count after the last event at or before \(t\): findInterval; Python np.searchsorted). Compare the mean \(\pm\) SE with the ODE \(m(t) = 10(1 - e^{-t})\). (c) At \(t = 10\) h: the variance and Fano factor, and the fractions of cells with 5, 10 and 15 molecules against Poisson(10) (dpois; Python scipy.stats.poisson.pmf).
C2. A general SSA: constitutive versus bursty. Write ssa(x, S, propensity, times) that takes a start state, a stoichiometry matrix (species × reactions), a propensity function and output times, and returns the state at each output time. (a) Simulate 1000 cells of the constitutive gene with protein (B1) from \((0, 0)\) to \(t = 30\) h. Compare the means with the ODE (10 and 99.7 at \(t = 30\) h) and the Fano factors with 1 and \(1 + k_p/(\delta_m + \delta_p) = 2.67\). (b) Simulate 1000 cells of the telegraph gene from \((g, m, p) = (0, 0, 0)\). Compare the means with (a), and the Fano factors with 16 (mRNA, B4) and 32.5 (protein, exact value from the moment equations). (c) What fraction of cells has no mRNA in each model? Compare with Poisson(10).
C3. A bug: averaging over events. Simulate one cell of the birth–death process for 5000 h. After a burn-in of 10 h, compute the mean of \(m\) in two ways: (i) the average of \(m\) after each event, (ii) the time-weighted average \(\frac{1}{T}\int m\,dt\) (each state weighted by how long it lasts). Which is right? Explain the value 10.5 that (i) approaches.
C4. Tau-leaping. Birth–death, \(k = 10\), \(\delta = 1\) per hour, from \(m = 0\) to \(t = 10\) h, with steps \(\tau = 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 1.5\) h. In each step, add Poisson\((k\tau)\) and subtract Poisson\((\delta m \tau)\) molecules (rpois; Python rng.poisson); if \(m < 0\), record it and set \(m = 0\). Over 2000 runs, print the mean and variance at \(t = 10\) h, the theoretical tau-leap variance \(2k/(\delta(2 - \delta\tau))\) (the exact SSA value is 10), and the fraction of runs that went negative.
C5. Euler–Maruyama. Simulate the chemical Langevin equation of Fact 5 with \(h = 0.01\) h to \(t = 10\) h, 2000 runs (rnorm; Python rng.standard_normal). (a) With \(k = 10\): compare the mean and variance with Poisson(10). (b) With \(k = 0.5\) (mean 0.5 molecules): what fraction of runs end in NaN? Of the others, what fraction ends negative?
C6. Early extinction of an epidemic. SIR with \(N = 10\,000\), \(\beta = 0.3\), \(\gamma = 0.1\) per day. Simulate only the order of events (no times needed): infection with probability \(a_1/(a_1 + a_2)\), \(a_1 = \beta S I/N\), \(a_2 = \gamma I\). Stop when \(I = 0\) (extinct) or \(I = 100\) (established). With 10 000 runs each, estimate the extinction probability for \(I_0 = 1, 2, 3\) with its SE, and compare with \((1/3)^{I_0}\) from B7.

title: Exercise: stochastic simulation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — propensities and the master equation (B1, B3)





A column of \(S\) is “what this reaction does to each species”: translation does not use up the mRNA. The probability that reaction \(j\) is next is \(a_j/a_0\), and the waiting time has mean \(1/a_0\). For B3, set \(P_0' = 0\) first: it involves only \(P_0\) and \(P_1\). Then use \(P_1' = 0\). The guess \(P_n = (2^n/n!)\,P_0\) sums to \(e^2 P_0\).









Hint 2 — the SSA (B2, C1, C2)





One loop: compute the propensities, \(a_0\), \(\tau = -\log(u_1)/a_0\), then choose the reaction by comparing \(u_2 a_0\) with the cumulative sums (cumsum, findInterval; Python np.cumsum, np.searchsorted(..., side="right"); Rust a running sum or partition_point). Uniforms: R runif; Python rng.random() with rng = np.random.default_rng(1); Rust rng.random::<f64>() with StdRng::seed_from_u64(1) from rand. To record the state at output times, note that the state does not change between events: every output time before the next event time sees the current state. Repeat runs with replicate in R or a list comprehension in Python.









Hint 3 — Fano factors (B4, B5, C2)





\(F = \text{var}/\text{mean}\) with the sample variance: R var, Python x.var(ddof=1) (numpy’s default ddof=0 divides by \(n\)). Multiplying every value by \(c\) multiplies the mean by \(c\) and the variance by \(c^2\). With 1000 cells, a Fano factor is uncertain by roughly \(F\sqrt{2/1000} \approx 4.5\%\) of its value; the mean of a bursty gene is uncertain by \(\sqrt{F \cdot \text{mean}/1000}\).









Hint 4 — events versus time (C3)





For the time-weighted mean, add \(m \cdot \tau\) (the current count times the waiting time) before the jump. Events happen at rate \(a_0 = 10 + m\), so states with large \(m\) are left more often. If a fraction \(P_n\) of the time is spent in state \(n\), a fraction proportional to \(P_n (10 + n)\) of the events happens there. Use \(\mathrm E[m] = 10\), \(\mathrm E[m^2] = 110\) (Poisson).









Hint 5 — tau-leaping and Euler–Maruyama (B6, C4, C5)





\(P(\text{negative}) = P(N > m) = 1 - P(N \le m)\). In Rust, rand_distr::Poisson::new(lambda) refuses lambda = 0, so return 0 yourself in that case; normal numbers from rand_distr::StandardNormal. In R, sqrt of a negative number gives NaN with a warning; in numpy a RuntimeWarning (silence it with np.errstate(invalid="ignore")); in Rust f64::sqrt silently returns NaN. Once a value is NaN, every later step is NaN too.









Hint 6 — extinction (B7, C6)





A chain of infections dies out if the first person recovers before infecting anyone (probability 0.25), or infects someone first and then both the new chain and their own continued chain die out (probability \(0.75\,q \cdot q\)). Solve the quadratic \(3q^2 - 4q + 1 = 0\). In code, the propensities change after every event, so recompute them in the loop; the waiting times are not needed for this question.

title: Exercise: stochastic simulation
Exercise: stochastic simulation
text:
Where this leads

Optimisation in one dimension and Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting (Part 9): fitting rates such as \(k_\text{on}\), \(k_\text{off}\) and \(k_m\) to measured mean and Fano factor, or ODE parameters to time courses; the cell-to-cell variability of this unit is one reason why an ODE fitted to single-cell data can mislead.
Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (Part 9): from a mean and a Fano factor alone, burst size and burst frequency can be estimated, but not all four telegraph rates.
Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation (Part 10): reactions plus space. Stochastic versions (molecules hopping between compartments) use the same SSA with diffusion as an extra “reaction”.
Not covered in this course: solving the master equation directly for small systems (finite state projection), the next-reaction method and adaptive tau-leaping, and the theory of stochastic differential equations (Itô calculus, strong and weak order).

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write a model fit as nonlinear least squares, with residuals \(r_i = y_i - m_i(\mathbf p)\) and a Jacobian \(J_{ij} = \partial m_i/\partial p_j\),
do a Gauss–Newton step by hand for one parameter, and in code for three, with each step a linear least-squares problem solved by QR,
show how Gauss–Newton fails from a bad start, and how Levenberg–Marquardt (damping \(\lambda\)) fixes it, and say what the two limits of \(\lambda\) are,
read nls’s “singular gradient” and use minpack.lm::nlsLM / nls.lm, scipy.optimize.curve_fit / least_squares, or a hand-written LM in Rust,
fit log-parameters to keep rates positive and improve the conditioning,
fit an ODE model with the solver inside the residual function, and choose the solver tolerance and the finite-difference step so that they fit together,
run a multistart and recognise two minima with the same RSS (the flip-flop).

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator with exp. The code part checks your hand answers and then fits the three-parameter model, first in closed form, then as an ODE.

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Background
After an oral dose \(D\), a drug moves from the gut (\(A_g\)) into the plasma, or central compartment (\(A_c\)), and is eliminated from there:
\[A_g' = -k_a A_g, \qquad A_c' = k_a A_g - k_e A_c, \qquad A_g(0) = D,\ A_c(0) = 0,\]
and we measure the concentration \(C = A_c/V\). This linear ODE has a closed form, the Bateman function
\[C(t) = \frac{D\,k_a}{V(k_a - k_e)}\left(e^{-k_e t} - e^{-k_a t}\right).\]
The data: \(D = 100\) mg, plasma sampled at 12 times over 12 hours. They were simulated from \(k_a = 1\)/h, \(k_e = 0.2\)/h, \(V = 20\) L with noise of SD 0.1 mg/L (set.seed(1) in R, then rounded to 2 decimals), so we know the truth.
Facts used below:

Nonlinear least squares. Parameters \(\mathbf p\), model \(m_i(\mathbf p) = C(t_i)\), residuals \(\mathbf r = \mathbf y - \mathbf m(\mathbf p)\). Minimise \(\text{RSS}(\mathbf p) = \|\mathbf r\|^2\).
Jacobian. \(J_{ij} = \partial m_i / \partial p_j\) (12 × 3). Forward differences: column \(j \approx (\mathbf m(\mathbf p + h_j\mathbf e_j) - \mathbf m(\mathbf p))/h_j\) with \(h_j \approx 10^{-7}\max(1, |p_j|)\).
Gauss–Newton. \(\boldsymbol\delta = \arg\min \|\mathbf r - J\boldsymbol\delta\|^2\), solved by QR (qr.solve(J, r)), then \(\mathbf p \leftarrow \mathbf p + \boldsymbol\delta\). For one parameter: \(\delta = \sum_i J_i r_i / \sum_i J_i^2\).
Levenberg–Marquardt. \(\boldsymbol\delta = \arg\min \|\mathbf r - J\boldsymbol\delta\|^2 + \lambda\|D_g\boldsymbol\delta\|^2\), i.e. \((J^TJ + \lambda D_g^2)\boldsymbol\delta = J^T\mathbf r\), solved as the stacked least-squares problem \(\begin{pmatrix}J\\ \sqrt\lambda D_g\end{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\delta \approx \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf r\\ \mathbf 0\end{pmatrix}\). \(D_g\) = diagonal of the column lengths of \(J\) (or \(I\)). Accept the step and divide \(\lambda\) by 10 if the RSS goes down; otherwise reject it and multiply \(\lambda\) by 10.
Log-parameters. Fit \(\mathbf q = \log\mathbf p\); \(\partial m/\partial q_j = p_j\,\partial m/\partial p_j\).
Flip-flop. \((k_a, k_e, V)\) and \((k_e, k_a, V k_e/k_a)\) give the same \(C(t)\).
Finite differences with noise. If the model values carry an error of size \(\varepsilon\) (rounding, or an ODE solver’s error), the forward-difference error is about \(\tfrac{h}{2}|m''| + 2\varepsilon/h\), smallest near \(h \approx 2\sqrt{\varepsilon/|m''|}\) (Convergence and cost).

The data, the model and a first library fit in each language. All solutions below assume this code has been run.

RPythonRust


D  <- 100                                                  # oral dose, mg
tt <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)   # hours after the dose
y  <- c(1.02, 1.88, 2.34, 2.98, 3.27, 3.26, 3.17, 2.77, 1.92, 1.23, 1.00, 0.61)  # mg/L
bateman <- function(t, ka, ke, V) D * ka / (V * (ka - ke)) * (exp(-ke * t) - exp(-ka * t))
rss <- function(p) sum((y - bateman(tt, p[1], p[2], p[3]))^2)
rss(c(1, 0.2, 20))                           # at the simulation parameters
# [1] 0.08346328
fit <- nls(y ~ bateman(tt, ka, ke, V), start = list(ka = 0.5, ke = 0.1, V = 10))
coef(fit)
#         ka         ke          V
#  1.0150721  0.1906157 20.2162113
deviance(fit)                                # RSS at the fitted parameters
# [1] 0.06646744


import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import curve_fit

D = 100.0                                                  # oral dose, mg
tt = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12])   # hours
y = np.array([1.02, 1.88, 2.34, 2.98, 3.27, 3.26, 3.17, 2.77, 1.92, 1.23, 1.00, 0.61])  # mg/L

def bateman(t, ka, ke, V):
    return D * ka / (V * (ka - ke)) * (np.exp(-ke * t) - np.exp(-ka * t))

def rss(p):
    return np.sum((y - bateman(tt, *p))**2)

print(rss([1, 0.2, 20]))                    # at the simulation parameters
# 0.0834632806408188
p, cov = curve_fit(bateman, tt, y, p0=[0.5, 0.1, 10])
print(p)
# [ 1.01507215  0.19061569 20.21621051]
print(rss(p))                               # RSS at the fitted parameters
# 0.06646743904580547


// rust/examples/nonlinear_least_squares_background.rs  —  cargo run --example nonlinear_least_squares_background
// Background: the PK data, the Bateman function and the residual sum of squares
const D: f64 = 100.0; // oral dose, mg
const TT: [f64; 12] = [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0, 10.0, 12.0]; // h
const Y: [f64; 12] = [1.02, 1.88, 2.34, 2.98, 3.27, 3.26, 3.17, 2.77, 1.92, 1.23, 1.00, 0.61]; // mg/L

fn bateman(t: f64, ka: f64, ke: f64, v: f64) -> f64 {
    D * ka / (v * (ka - ke)) * ((-ke * t).exp() - (-ka * t).exp())
}

fn rss(p: [f64; 3]) -> f64 {
    TT.iter().zip(Y.iter()).map(|(&t, &y)| (y - bateman(t, p[0], p[1], p[2])).powi(2)).sum()
}

fn main() {
    println!("{}", rss([1.0, 0.2, 20.0]));                       // at the simulation parameters
    // no nls in Rust: we write Gauss-Newton ourselves in C2; here the RSS at nls's estimate
    println!("{}", rss([1.0150721, 0.1906157, 20.2162104]));
}

// Output:
// 0.0834632806408188
// 0.06646743904589647



In R, nls is Gauss–Newton; minpack.lm::nlsLM has the same formula interface with Levenberg–Marquardt, and minpack.lm::nls.lm takes a residual function. In Python, scipy.optimize.curve_fit takes a model function like nls (Levenberg–Marquardt by default) and scipy.optimize.least_squares takes a residual function (trust-region "trf" by default, method="lm" for MINPACK). In Rust there is no nls: we write Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt ourselves with nalgebra’s QR (the argmin crate has a Gauss–Newton solver, but it needs more plumbing than the method itself). ODEs: deSolve::ode, scipy.integrate.solve_ivp, and ode_solvers::Dopri5 in Rust.

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
By hand
B1. Sensitivities. After an IV bolus, a one-compartment model gives \(C(t) = C_0 e^{-kt}\). (a) Write down \(\partial C/\partial C_0\) and \(\partial C/\partial k\). (b) Evaluate the \(3\times 2\) Jacobian at \(C_0 = 10\) mg/L, \(k = 0.3\)/h for samples at \(t = 1, 2, 4\) h. (c) At which time \(t\) is \(|\partial C/\partial k|\) largest? What does that say about when to sample if you want \(k\)? (d) For the oral model on the slides, the Jacobian column for \(k_a\) is positive at \(t = 0.25\) h and negative at \(t = 12\) h. Explain the sign change in words.
B2. Gauss–Newton by hand. Fit only \(k\) in \(C(t) = 10\,e^{-kt}\) to \(y = (6.0, 3.7, 1.3)\) mg/L at \(t = (1, 2, 4)\) h. (a) From \(k_0 = 0.3\): compute \(\mathbf m\), \(J\), \(\mathbf r\), the step \(\delta = \sum J_i r_i/\sum J_i^2\) and \(k_1\). Compare with the slide. (b) Do the second step from \(k_1\). Compute the RSS at \(k_0\), \(k_1\), \(k_2\). (c) The minimum is at \(k^* = 0.504417\). How many correct digits do \(k_0\), \(k_1\), \(k_2\) have? What kind of convergence does that suggest?
B3. A linear model needs one step. Suppose \(k_e = 0.2\) is known and the model is \(m(t) = a\,e^{-0.2t} + b\) (a decay on top of a baseline \(b\)). (a) Write the Jacobian with respect to \((a, b)\). Does it depend on \((a, b)\)? (b) Explain why Gauss–Newton reaches the least-squares solution in one step from any start. Which unit’s method is it then?
B4. Levenberg–Marquardt between two limits. Take \(J = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\1 & 1\\1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\), \(\mathbf r = (1, 0, 1)\) and \(D_g = I\). (a) Compute \(J^TJ\) and \(J^T\mathbf r\). (b) The Gauss–Newton step: solve \(J^TJ\boldsymbol\delta = J^T\mathbf r\). (c) The LM step with \(\lambda = 1\): solve \((J^TJ + I)\boldsymbol\delta = J^T\mathbf r\). (d) The LM step with \(\lambda = 100\). Compare it with \(J^T\mathbf r/\lambda\). In which direction does a large-\(\lambda\) step point, and why is that “downhill”? (The gradient of \(\|\mathbf r\|^2\) with respect to \(\mathbf p\) is \(-2J^T\mathbf r\).) (e) Order the three steps by length. What does \(\lambda\) control?
B5. Log-parameters. Same data as B2; now fit \(q = \log k\). (a) Use the chain rule to write \(\partial m/\partial q\) in terms of \(\partial m/\partial k\). (b) Do one Gauss–Newton step in \(q\) from \(k_0 = 0.3\) (reuse \(\mathbf r\) and \(J\) from B2(a)). What is \(k_1 = e^{q_1}\)? Is it closer to \(k^*\) than the step in \(k\)? (c) Now start far away, at \(k_0 = 1.5\). There \(\mathbf m = (2.231, 0.498, 0.025)\), \(\partial m/\partial k = (-2.231, -0.996, -0.099)\) and \(\mathbf r = (3.769, 3.202, 1.275)\). Do one Gauss–Newton step in \(k\) and one in \(q\). What is wrong with the first one, biologically?
B6. The flip-flop. (a) Show that swapping \(k_a \leftrightarrow k_e\) and replacing \(V\) by \(V' = V k_e/k_a\) leaves \(C(t)\) unchanged. (b) The fit gives \((\hat k_a, \hat k_e, \hat V) = (1.0151, 0.1906, 20.216)\). What is the mirror solution? (c) The two parameter sets give the same plasma curve. What do they predict differently? Name one experiment that would tell them apart.
B7. Tolerance and finite-difference step. A residual function solves an ODE with an error of about \(\varepsilon_\text{ode}\) in each model value. Take \(|m''| \approx 1\) in the units of the problem. (a) With \(\varepsilon_\text{ode} = 10^{-6}\) (deSolve’s default tolerance), what is the error of a forward-difference derivative with \(h = 10^{-8}\)? With \(h = 10^{-3}\)? (b) Which \(h\) minimises the error, and what is the smallest error? Repeat for \(\varepsilon_\text{ode} = 10^{-10}\). (c) A Levenberg–Marquardt fit of 3 parameters with a forward-difference Jacobian solves the ODE once for the residual, 3 times for the Jacobian, and once for the trial point, per iteration. A multistart from 36 starts takes about 10 iterations each. How many ODE solves is that? At 5 ms per solve, how long?

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
In code
C1. The data and the model. (a) Plot the data and the curve with the simulation parameters \((1, 0.2, 20)\). Compute the RSS there and at the start \((0.5, 0.1, 10)\). (b) Compute \(t_\text{max} = \ln(k_a/k_e)/(k_a - k_e)\), \(C_\text{max} = C(t_\text{max})\) and \(\text{AUC} = D/(V k_e)\) for the simulation parameters. C3. Gauss–Newton fails, Levenberg–Marquardt does not. (a) Take one Gauss–Newton step from \((3, 0.05, 50)\). Where does it go, and what is the RSS there? (b) Write Levenberg–Marquardt with Marquardt’s scaling \(D_g\) (Fact 4), solving the stacked problem by QR. Start at \((3, 0.05, 50)\) with \(\lambda = 0.01\) and print every accepted step with its \(\lambda\). (c) Run nls and nlsLM from the same start (Python: curve_fit and least_squares).
C4. Log-parameters. (a) Rewrite the Jacobian so that it takes any model function f and uses \(h_j = 10^{-7}\max(1, |p_j|)\). Check it against the Bateman function at \((1, 0.2, 20)\) with tol = 1e-10. (b) Fit \(\log(k_a, k_e, V)\) from \((0.5, 0.1, 10)\) with the ODE inside the residual function: nls.lm with control = nls.lm.control(epsfcn = 1e-10) (Python: least_squares; Rust: your LM with Dopri5). Compare with the closed-form fit.
C6. How tight must the inner solver be? (a) Repeat C5(b) with tol \(= 10^{-2}, 10^{-3}, 10^{-4}, 10^{-6}, 10^{-8}, 10^{-10}\). For each, print the estimates, the RSS the optimiser reports, the true RSS (Bateman function) at the returned parameters, and the number of iterations. In Python, include the solve_ivp default rtol = 1e-3, atol = 1e-6. (b) Along the line \(k_a \in [0.9, 1.1]\) (401 points; \(k_e\), \(V\) at the estimate), compute \(\max|\text{RSS}_\text{ode} - \text{RSS}_\text{exact}|\) for tol \(= 10^{-3}, 10^{-6}, 10^{-10}\). Compare with the RSS change caused by a 1 % change in \(k_a\).
C7. Multistart. Fit from the 36 starts \(k_a \in \{0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10\}\), \(k_e \in 1.5\times\{0.03, \dots, 10\}\), \(V = 10\), in log-parameters. Tabulate where the fits end (parameters and RSS, rounded to 4 digits). How many minima are there? Are they equally good? Which one would you report, and why?

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Jacobian and one-parameter Gauss–Newton (B1, B2, B5)





\(\frac{d}{dk} e^{-kt} = -t\,e^{-kt}\). With one parameter, \(J\) is a single column and the least-squares solution of \(J\delta \approx \mathbf r\) is \(\sum J_i r_i/\sum J_i^2\) (the slope of a line through the origin). Keep 4 significant digits. For \(q = \log k\): \(k = e^q\), so \(dk/dq = k\).









Hint 2 — Levenberg–Marquardt by hand (B4)





A \(2\times2\) system \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\delta = \mathbf g\) has \(\delta_1 = (d g_1 - b g_2)/(ad - bc)\), \(\delta_2 = (a g_2 - c g_1)/(ad - bc)\). Adding \(\lambda I\) only changes \(a\) and \(d\).









Hint 3 — finite differences with noise (B7)





Truncation error \(\approx \tfrac{h}{2}|m''|\), noise error \(\approx 2\varepsilon/h\) (two noisy values, divided by \(h\)). Set the derivative of the sum with respect to \(h\) to zero. This is the V-shaped error curve of Convergence and cost, with \(\varepsilon_\text{ode}\) in place of machine epsilon.









Hint 4 — QR least squares in each language (C2–C4)





R: qr.solve(A, b) solves a tall system in the least-squares sense; rbind stacks the damping rows under \(J\). Python: Q, R = np.linalg.qr(A) then np.linalg.solve(R, Q.T @ b) (np.linalg.qr); np.vstack stacks. Rust: a.clone().qr(), q_tr_mul and solve_upper_triangular, as in Least squares: normal equations vs QR. Condition numbers: kappa(A, exact = TRUE), np.linalg.cond, ratio of nalgebra’s singular_values().









Hint 5 — library fitters (C2–C4, C7)





R: nls (trace = TRUE prints iterates), nlsLM (same interface), nls.lm(par, fn) where fn returns the residual vector; fit$par, fit$deviance (RSS), fit$niter. Wrap a call that may fail in tryCatch(..., error = conditionMessage). Python: curve_fit(f, t, y, p0) returns (p, cov); least_squares(fun, x0) returns an object with .x, .cost (half the RSS), .nfev.









Hint 6 — an ODE inside the residual (C5, C6)





R: ode(y, times, func, parms, rtol, atol) with func(t, y, parms) returning list(dy); give times = c(0, tt) because the first time is the start, and drop the first row of the output; column 1 is time. Python: solve_ivp(fun, (0, 12), y0, t_eval=tt, args=(ka, ke), rtol=, atol=), solution in sol.y. Rust: Dopri5::new(system, t0, t_end, dx, y0, rtol, atol) and integrate_with_continuous_output_model give the solution at any \(t\) (see Runge–Kutta and adaptive step size). In nls.lm, the finite-difference step is \(\sqrt{\texttt{epsfcn}}\,|q_j|\); with \(\log k_a \approx 0\) the default is far below the ODE error, so set epsfcn = 1e-10.

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Where this leads

Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (next unit): the flip-flop is a structural non-identifiability; the same PK model and data are used there for standard errors from \(J^TJ\), profile likelihoods and practical non-identifiability (long flat valleys like the one in the RSS landscape).
Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton: Levenberg–Marquardt’s two limits; Gauss–Newton as Newton with the Hessian approximated by \(J^TJ\); general-purpose optimisers (optim, scipy.optimize.minimize) for objectives that are not sums of squares, such as Poisson or negative-binomial likelihoods.
Constraints and linear programming: bounds on parameters as an alternative to log-parameters.
Stiffness and implicit methods: a stiff model inside a fit needs an implicit solver (lsoda, BDF, Radau) with tight tolerances; explicit solvers then become the slow part of the fit.
Exact Jacobians of ODE models from sensitivity equations or automatic differentiation are not covered here; they replace the finite differences of C5–C6 in professional fitting tools.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
About this lecture
So far every unknown was a number or a list of numbers that changed in time. Inside a microfluidic chip, a concentration also changes from place to place: it is a function of space and time, c(x, t). Its model is a partial differential equation (PDE).

Fick’s law and a mass balance give the diffusion equation \partial c/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2. Heat conduction obeys the same equation.
Put x and t on a grid: the (1, -2, 1)/\Delta x^2 stencil in space, an Euler step in time. This is the FTCS scheme, five lines of code.
Stability limit D\,\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2: break it and a zigzag explodes. It is Euler’s |1 - kh| \le 1 again, with k from the eigenvalues of the grid.
Boundary conditions: fixed concentration (a reservoir) or no flux (a wall). They change the answer completely.
Biology: a chemotaxis chamber between a source and a sink. How long until cells see a linear gradient? Why does doubling the channel length quadruple the wait?


This opens Part 10, the first PDE of the course. Almost nothing here is new mathematics: the second-difference stencil comes from Numerical differentiation (Part 7), the time step is Euler’s method from Initial value problems and Euler’s method (Part 8), the stability analysis uses eigenvalues (Part 5, Power iteration and friends) and the partial derivative was introduced in Newton for systems of equations (Part 2). The new thing is putting them together on a grid in space and time. Units 32 to 35 reuse the grid set up today (nodes x_i = i dx, µm and seconds; later units say where and why they deviate from it); Implicit schemes and the method of lines also reuses the chamber itself.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
Biology: a flow-free chemotaxis chamber


A channel joins a source reservoir (chemoattractant) to a sink reservoir (plain medium). No flow, so the molecules move only by diffusion [G1, G3].
At steady state the profile is a straight line: every cell in the channel sees the same gradient. How long until then?


Diffusion-based gradient generators are one of the two families described in the reviews [G1] (Kim, Kim and Jeon 2010) and [G3] (Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology 2015); the other family uses flow, which we meet in Flow plus diffusion. The advantage of a flow-free chamber is that cells, especially non-adherent ones such as neutrophils, are not pushed by shear and secreted signals are not washed away. The price is time: one waits for diffusion to set up the gradient. Our version is simplified: a single straight channel, L = 500 µm, reservoirs large enough that their concentrations stay fixed. These numbers are typical values, not taken from one specific device; the reviews were only skimmed, so treat them as order-of-magnitude. The profiles at the bottom are computed with today’s method. The orange dots are cells.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Recap: two tools you already have
text:
Recap: two tools you already have


Second difference (Numerical differentiation): \frac{u(x+h) - 2u(x) + u(x-h)}{h^2} = u''(x) + \tfrac{h^2}{12}u''''(x) + \dots

Weights (1, -2, 1)/h^2, error O(h^2).
A straight line has second difference 0.


Euler (Initial value problems and Euler’s method): y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f(t_n, y_n)

On y' = -ky: each step multiplies by 1 - kh.
Stable only if |1 - kh| \le 1, i.e. h \le 2/k.


Today: the stencil handles space, Euler handles time, and the stability rule comes back with k = the fastest rate on the grid.

One slide only. Both results were derived and tested in their own units; students who skipped them should go back. In Numerical differentiation the variable was time t and the function was an OD growth curve; today the variable is position x and the function is a concentration profile. The stencil does not care. From the Euler unit, the key fact is the amplification factor 1 - kh for the decay equation, and the systems version from Stiffness and implicit methods: for y’ = Jy the rule must hold for every eigenvalue of J.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: A function of space and time
text:
A function of space and time


c(x, t): one number for each position and time. Hold t fixed: a profile with slope \partial c/\partial x. Hold x fixed: a time course with slope \partial c/\partial t.
The curly \partial means “the other variable held fixed”, exactly as in Newton for systems of equations.


Left: the concentration in the channel as a heat map, position across, time up; dark is high. The orange line is a slice at t = 30 s: the profile across the channel, whose slope at x = 100 µm is the partial derivative with respect to x (about -0.003 per µm: the gradient the cells feel). The red line is a slice at x = 100 µm: the concentration seen by one cell over time, whose slope is the partial derivative with respect to t. Nothing new beyond Newton for systems of equations, where partial derivatives were slopes of slices of F(u, v). A PDE is an equation that links these partial derivatives to each other.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
Fick’s law: flux goes downhill
Molecules spread from high to low concentration. The flux J (amount crossing unit area per second) is proportional to the slope:
J = -D\,\frac{\partial c}{\partial x}



molecule
D in water (typical)
in µm²/s




small molecule (sugar, dye, fMLP)
\approx 10^{-9} m²/s
1000

\approx 2\cdot10^{-9} m²/s

Steady linear profile, source c_0, L = 500 µm: J = D\,c_0/L = 1000/500 = 2\,c_0 µm/s.
Convert once: 1\ \text{m}^2/\text{s} = 10^{12}\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s}. We work in µm and s.


The minus sign says flux runs from high to low concentration. D has units of length squared per time. The values are the standard textbook orders of magnitude listed in the plan for this part; a specific chemokine such as IL-8 (about 8 kDa) is somewhere around 1e-10 m^2/s, and larger proteins (antibodies, 150 kDa) are nearer 4e-11. Do not quote these to two digits; the exercise uses D = 1000 and 100 µm^2/s as round numbers. Working in µm and seconds keeps numbers near 1: a 10 µm grid spacing and D = 1000 µm^2/s give D/dx^2 = 10 per second.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: From Fick to the diffusion equation
text:
From Fick to the diffusion equation
Mass balance in a thin slice [x, x + \Delta x]: what flows in on the left minus what flows out on the right.
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}\,\Delta x = J(x) - J(x + \Delta x) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = -\frac{\partial J}{\partial x} = D\,\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}

Rate in − rate out, as for every ODE model, now per slice.
Concentration rises where the profile curves upward (\partial^2 c/\partial x^2 > 0) and falls where it bends down. A straight line does not change.
Heat obeys the same equation: \partial T/\partial t = \alpha\,\partial^2 T/\partial x^2, thermal diffusivity \alpha \approx 1.4\cdot10^{-7} m²/s for water. Hence “the heat equation”.


The derivation is the ODE principle from the Euler unit applied to each slice: rate in minus rate out. Divide by dx and let it shrink: the difference of the fluxes becomes a derivative. Substitute Fick’s law (D constant) to get the second derivative. The curvature rule is the intuition to keep: a bump (curving down at the top) flattens, a dip fills in, a straight line stays. That is why the steady state between two reservoirs is a straight line. The heat equation is the same equation with temperature for concentration; Implicit schemes and the method of lines uses it for a Drosophila embryo held between two temperatures.

The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: A PDE needs initial and boundary conditions
text:
A PDE needs initial and boundary conditions
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = D\,\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}, \quad 0 < x < L,\ t > 0

Initial condition: the channel is empty, c(x, 0) = 0.
Boundary conditions, one at each end:

Dirichlet (fixed value): a large reservoir holds the concentration. Source c(0, t) = 1, sink c(L, t) = 0.
No flux (Neumann): a wall, nothing crosses. J = 0, so \partial c/\partial x = 0 at the wall.

Steady state with two reservoirs: \partial^2 c/\partial x^2 = 0, so c = 1 - x/L. With a wall at x = L instead: c = 1 everywhere, no gradient at all.


An ODE needed one start value. A PDE needs a whole start profile (initial condition) and, for all time, something at each end of the domain (boundary conditions). Concentrations are scaled by the source concentration, so c runs from 0 to 1. The two boundary types are the two physical situations at the end of a channel: open to a reservoir, or closed by a wall. The last bullet is the whole reason a chemotaxis chamber has a sink: without it, the attractant fills the channel and the gradient disappears. We simulate both cases later.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
The diffusion time scale L^2/D
The only time you can make from a length L and D is L^2/D:




L = 500 µm
L = 1 mm




small molecule, D = 1000 µm²/s
250 s
1000 s


protein, D = 100 µm²/s
2500 s (42 min)
10 000 s (2.8 h)




Doubling L quadruples the time; a ten times smaller D means ten times longer.
Random-walk view: after time t a molecule has moved about \sqrt{2Dt}. Over 10 µm (a cell): 0.05 s. Over 1 mm: minutes to hours.
So far this is a guess at the scale. The simulation will give the factor in front.


Dimensional analysis: D is in µm^2/s, so L^2/D is in seconds, and any time the equation produces must be a multiple of it. The square is the point: diffusion is fast over short distances and slow over long ones, which is why cells do not need pumps internally but organisms need blood vessels. For chamber design it means that halving the channel length gives a gradient four times sooner, but also a four times steeper one with the same reservoirs. The protein numbers explain why diffusion chambers are pre-equilibrated for tens of minutes to hours before imaging.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Space and time on a grid
text:
Space and time on a grid


Grid points x_i = i\,\Delta x (i = 0, \dots, N) and times t_n = n\,\Delta t. Unknowns c_i^n \approx c(x_i, t_n).
Blue/grey squares: boundary values (given). Yellow: initial values (given). White: to compute.


Superscript n is the time level, subscript i the position; the superscript is a label, not a power. For our chamber N = 50 intervals of dx = 10 µm, so 51 points, of which 49 interior unknowns. The edges of the grid are known: the bottom row from the initial condition, the left and right columns from the boundary conditions. The scheme on the next two slides fills in the white points row by row, each from the row below: the red point from the three orange ones.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
Step 1, space: the second difference
At each interior point replace \partial^2 c/\partial x^2 by the stencil:
\frac{d c_i}{dt} = \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}\,\bigl(c_{i-1} - 2c_i + c_{i+1}\bigr), \qquad i = 1, \dots, N-1

One ODE per grid point: 49 coupled ODEs, each linked to its two neighbours.
In matrix form \mathbf c' = \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A\,\mathbf c + \mathbf b, with A tridiagonal: -2 on the diagonal, 1 beside it. \mathbf b holds the boundary values.
Spatial error \tfrac{\Delta x^2}{12}\,\partial^4 c/\partial x^4: second order in \Delta x.


This is the “method of lines”: discretise space only, and you are left with a system of ODEs in time, one per grid line. Implicit schemes and the method of lines takes this literally and hands the system to an ODE solver from Part 8. Read the ODE as a compartment model: each grid cell exchanges with its neighbours at rate D/dx^2 = 10 per second. It is the same tridiagonal pattern as the morphogen in a row of cells in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse (there written with the opposite sign, 2D + k on the diagonal and -D beside it, exchange rate D = 1 per minute plus degradation k). The vector b has D/dx^2 times c_0 = 1 in its first entry (the source) and zeros elsewhere (the sink holds 0).

Step 2, time: one Euler step = FTCS
Euler on these ODEs with step \Delta t gives Forward Time, Centred Space:
c_i^{n+1} = c_i^n + r\,\bigl(c_{i-1}^n - 2c_i^n + c_{i+1}^n\bigr), \qquad r = \frac{D\,\Delta t}{\Delta x^2}
By hand: L = 500 µm, N = 4 (\Delta x = 125 µm), r = 0.25; start (1, 0, 0, 0, 0):

Explicit: each new value comes straight from three old ones. Ends stay at 1 and 0. \Delta t = 0.25 \cdot 125^2/1000 = 3.9 s per step.


r, the “mesh ratio”, is the only number the scheme sees: it combines D, the time step and the grid spacing. Work the first row on the board. The attractant creeps one grid point per step: after n steps only the first n interior points are non-zero, the numerical version of “it takes time to diffuse”. The steady state on this grid is 0.75, 0.5, 0.25: the straight line, which FTCS leaves unchanged because its second difference is zero. title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
FTCS in R
D <- 1000                        # µm^2/s  (1e-9 m^2/s)
L <- 500; N <- 50; dx <- L / N   # 51 points, 10 µm apart
x <- seq(0, L, by = dx)
r <- 0.4; dt <- r * dx^2 / D     # 0.04 s
ftcs <- function(c, r, nsteps) {
  i <- 2:(length(c) - 1)                       # interior points
  for (k in seq_len(nsteps))
    c[i] <- c[i] + r * (c[i - 1] - 2 * c[i] + c[i + 1])
  c
}
c60 <- ftcs(c(1, rep(0, N)), r, 60 / dt)       # 1500 steps to 60 s
round(c60[seq(1, 51, by = 10)], 3)             # x = 0, 100, ..., 500
# [1] 1.000 0.765 0.543 0.343 0.165 0.000

Vectorised over space: c[i - 1], c[i], c[i + 1] are shifted copies. The loop over time stays.


Point out the R detail that makes this correct: the whole right-hand side is evaluated with the old vector before anything is assigned, so every point is updated from time level n. A loop over i that overwrites c[i] in place would use the already-updated c[i - 1]: a different (and here not intended) method. In Rust or C you therefore keep a copy of the old level; the exercise shows it. The time loop cannot be vectorised: each level needs the previous one. Boundary values are simply never touched, which is how the Dirichlet conditions are imposed. After one minute the profile is already close to the line 1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, 0.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
When is the gradient established?
Criterion: the profile is within 5 % (of the source concentration) of the line 1 - x/L.
t_grad <- function(D, L, N = 50, r = 0.4) {
  dx <- L / N; dt <- r * dx^2 / D; x <- seq(0, L, by = dx)
  c <- c(1, rep(0, N)); n <- 0
  while (max(abs(c - (1 - x / L))) > 0.05) { c <- ftcs(c, r, 1); n <- n + 1 }
  c(D = D, L = L, steps = n, t = n * dt, L2_D = L^2 / D)
}
rbind(t_grad(1000, 500), t_grad(1000, 1000), t_grad(100, 500), t_grad(100, 1000))
#         D    L steps       t  L2_D
# [1,] 1000  500  1611   64.44   250
# [2,] 1000 1000  1611  257.76  1000
# [3,]  100  500  1611  644.40  2500
# [4,]  100 1000  1611 2577.60 10000

Small molecule, 500 µm: 1 minute. Protein chemokine, 1 mm: 43 minutes. Doubling L: exactly ×4.


The 5 % criterion is a choice; 1 % takes about 1.6 times longer (exercise). The striking line is the steps column: 1611 every time. With N and r fixed, all four runs do exactly the same arithmetic; only the meaning of one time step changes, dt = r dx^2 / D. The next slide says why. For the experimentalist: a protein gradient over a millimetre needs most of an hour, and cells that start migrating before then see a gradient that is still changing.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
One simulation fits all chambers


Plotted against t\,D/L^2 the four curves are one curve. The gradient is established at t \approx 0.26\,L^2/D.
Rescale \tilde x = x/L, \tilde t = tD/L^2: the equation becomes \partial c/\partial \tilde t = \partial^2 c/\partial \tilde x^2, with no parameters left.


This is nondimensionalisation. With x = L x~ and t = (L^2/D) t~, the chain rule gives dc/dt = (D/L^2) dc/dt~ and d2c/dx2 = (1/L^2) d2c/dx~2, and D and L cancel. So there is only one problem: the chamber of length 1 with D = 1. Every chamber and every molecule is a rescaled copy. Practical value: one simulation (or one exact solution) answers the design question for all of them, and the answer to “why does doubling L quadruple the wait?” is: because time only appears as t D / L^2. The factor 0.258 is what the L^2/D slide could not give.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
Check against the exact solution
For this initial and boundary data there is a Fourier-series solution:
c(x, t) = 1 - \frac{x}{L} - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2}{n\pi}\,\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\;e^{-n^2\pi^2 D t/L^2}





Halve \Delta x with r = 0.4 fixed: the error falls 4×. Slope 2.
\Delta t \propto \Delta x^2, so the O(\Delta t) of Euler and the O(\Delta x^2) of the stencil shrink together.
Each halving costs 8× the work: 2× the points, 4× the steps.



The series: a straight line (steady state) minus a sum of sine modes that each decay at their own rate n^2 pi^2 D / L^2. At t = 0 the sum reproduces 1 - x/L, so c = 0 inside. The slowest mode, n = 1, decays with time constant L2/(pi2 D) = 25.3 s for our chamber; that mode alone explains the factor 0.258: (2/pi) exp(-pi^2 t~) = 0.05 gives t~ = 0.258. The error plot is the order check of Part 8 (Initial value problems and Euler’s method) in a new setting: error at t = 30 s against dx on log-log axes, slope 2. The step counts are printed under the points: 120 steps for dx = 25 µm, 30 720 steps for dx = 1.56 µm. The cost is what Implicit schemes and the method of lines attacks.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Failure: a slightly larger time step
text:
Failure: a slightly larger time step


r = 0.50: smooth. r = 0.52 (4 % larger \Delta t): a zigzag starts at the steep front and grows. After 30 s values reach \pm 4\cdot10^{15}.
Symptoms: values outside [0, 1], sign alternating from point to point.


The two runs differ only in dt: 0.050 s versus 0.052 s. At r = 0.52 the profile looks fine for the first 30 steps, then a point-to-point oscillation appears where the profile is steepest and grows by about 8 % per step. By 30 s (577 steps) the values are of order 1e15, by 60 s they overflow. The check is cheap and physical: diffusion can never create a concentration above the highest or below the lowest value present (maximum principle), so any value outside [0, 1] here is a numerical failure. Run this check in every diffusion simulation.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Why exactly 1/2: the zigzag by hand
text:
Why exactly 1/2: the zigzag by hand
Put a zigzag c_i = \varepsilon\,(-1)^i into one FTCS step:
c_{i-1} - 2c_i + c_{i+1} = \varepsilon(-1)^i\,(-1 - 2 - 1) = -4\,c_i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; c_i^{n+1} = (1 - 4r)\,c_i^n



r
0.25
0.4
0.5
0.52
0.6




factor 1 - 4r
0
−0.6
−1
−1.08
−1.4




Stable only if |1 - 4r| \le 1, i.e. \boxed{r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2}, i.e. \Delta t \le \Delta x^2/(2D).
Same as Euler’s |1 - kh| \le 1 with k = 4D/\Delta x^2: the zigzag decays fastest, and the step must resolve it.
Another view: for r \le 1/2 the new value (1 - 2r)c_i + r\,c_{i-1} + r\,c_{i+1} is an average with weights \ge 0, so it stays inside [0, 1].


The zigzag is the shortest wave the grid can hold (the Nyquist mode from Fourier series and the FFT). Its second difference is -4 times itself, the most negative possible, so it is the fastest-decaying mode of the true dynamics: rate 4D/dx^2 = 40 per second here, a lifetime of 0.025 s. Euler with step dt multiplies it by 1 - 40 dt, the drug clearance example of Initial value problems and Euler’s method with k = 40 per second. For r between 1/4 and 1/2 the factor is negative but smaller than 1 in size: the zigzag flips sign each step but decays, exactly like Euler with 1/k < h < 2/k. The averaging argument is the cleanest stability proof: weights 1 - 2r, r, r add to 1 and are non-negative only if r <= 1/2. With r = 1/2 the update is c_i = (c_{i-1} + c_{i+1})/2, the plain average of the neighbours.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
The eigenvalue view
n <- 49                                          # interior points
A <- diag(-2, n)
A[cbind(1:(n - 1), 2:n)] <- 1; A[cbind(2:n, 1:(n - 1))] <- 1
lam <- D / dx^2 * eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE)$values   # per second
range(lam)
# [1] -39.96053457  -0.03946543
2 / max(abs(lam))                                # Euler: dt <= 2 / |lambda|
# [1] 0.05004938

Formula: eigenvalues of A are -4\sin^2\!\bigl(\tfrac{k\pi}{2N}\bigr), k = 1, \dots, N - 1. All negative, all real.
Euler on \mathbf c' = \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A\mathbf c needs \Delta t\,|\lambda| \le 2 for every eigenvalue: eigenvalues from Part 5, the rule from Part 8 (Stiffness and implicit methods). The largest, \approx 4D/\Delta x^2, gives r \le 1/2.


This connects the zigzag argument to the general theory from Part 8 (Euler’s |1 - kh| <= 1 in Initial value problems and Euler’s method, applied eigenvalue by eigenvalue in Stiffness and implicit methods): a linear ODE system decouples into one scalar equation per eigenvalue, and Euler must be stable on each. eigen() from How eigen() works, and big problems (Part 5); the matrix is symmetric, so all eigenvalues are real. The formula can be checked against eigen() in the exercise. The largest magnitude is 4 sin^2(49 pi / 100) = 3.996, slightly less than 4, which is why the exact limit here is r <= 0.5005 rather than 0.5. Python: numpy.linalg.eigvalsh.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Slow modes, fast modes, and the cost
text:
Slow modes, fast modes, and the cost


Slowest mode: half a sine, rate \approx \pi^2D/L^2 = 0.039 per s. This is the biology (25 s time constant).
Fastest mode: the zigzag, 40 per s. It is gone in a few hundredths of a second, yet it sets the step. Ratio ≈ 1000: a stiff system (Stiffness and implicit methods).
Refine to \Delta x = 1 µm: ratio ≈ 100 000 and \Delta t \le 0.5 ms. Fix: Implicit schemes and the method of lines.


The eigenvectors are sine waves, the same modes as in the exact Fourier series: the grid has a discrete version of each. The slowest one carries the physics (how fast the gradient settles); the fastest ones are grid artefacts that a sensible method should simply damp. This is exactly the definition of stiffness from Stiffness and implicit methods: the step is set by stability, not by accuracy. The ratio of fastest to slowest rate grows like (2N/pi)^2, so it gets worse with every refinement. The next unit uses backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson, with one tridiagonal (Thomas) solve per step, and no step limit.

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
No-flux boundary: the ghost point
A wall at x_N = L: \partial c/\partial x = 0. Invent a ghost point c_{N+1} outside and set c_{N+1} = c_{N-1} (central difference of the slope = 0). The FTCS update at the wall becomes
c_N^{n+1} = c_N^n + r\,\bigl(c_{N-1}^n - 2c_N^n + c_{N+1}^n\bigr) = c_N^n + 2r\,\bigl(c_{N-1}^n - c_N^n\bigr).
ftcs_closed <- function(c, r, nsteps) {         # wall at x = L
  n <- length(c); i <- 2:(n - 1)
  for (k in seq_len(nsteps)) {
    cn <- c[n] + 2 * r * (c[n - 1] - c[n])       # uses old values
    c[i] <- c[i] + r * (c[i - 1] - 2 * c[i] + c[i + 1])
    c[n] <- cn
  }
  c
}

The wall point is now an unknown, not a given value. The ghost point is a device to reuse the central stencil at the boundary; it keeps the boundary condition second-order accurate. The simpler choice c_N = c_{N-1} also says “zero slope”, but only to first order. Note the order of operations: the new wall value is computed from old values before the interior update overwrites c[n - 1]. The stability limit is unchanged (r <= 1/2; the weights 1 - 2r and 2r are still non-negative).

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Sink or wall: a gradient or none
text:
Sink or wall: a gradient or none


Sink at x = L: the straight line after ~1 minute, kept for as long as the reservoirs last.
Wall at x = L (a dead-end channel): the attractant piles up and the channel fills to c = 1. The far end reaches 0.95 only after 328 s, 5× longer, and then there is no gradient.


Same channel, same molecule, only the right boundary condition differs. With the wall, the slowest mode is a quarter sine instead of a half sine, with rate pi^2 D / (4 L^2): four times slower, as if the channel were twice as long (the wall acts as a mirror). Two practical points. First, a dead-end side channel in a device is not a gradient generator: any gradient in it is transient. Second, real reservoirs are finite, so in real diffusion chambers source and sink slowly equilibrate and the gradient decays over hours to days; the reviews [G1, G3] list this as a limitation of flow-free devices (stated cautiously: we skimmed them). Our model with fixed boundary values assumes reservoirs that are much larger than the channel.

The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
section: Before you trust a diffusion simulation
text:
Before you trust a diffusion simulation

Stability: compute r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2 before running. FTCS needs r \le 1/2, for every species (the fastest D decides).
Maximum principle: no value above the largest or below the smallest boundary/initial value. Zigzags or negative concentrations mean r is too large or there is a bug.
Steady state: the run should settle to the solution of D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2 = 0 (a line between two reservoirs).
Conservation: with walls at both ends the total amount must stay constant (exercise).
Grid refinement: halve \Delta x (and quarter \Delta t). Changes should shrink about 4× per halving.
Units: D in µm²/s with x in µm; 10^{-9} m²/s is 1000 µm²/s, not 1000 m²/s.


The six checks of this unit. The second and fourth are physical invariants and need no exact solution; the fifth is the step-halving check of Part 8 (Initial value problems and Euler’s method) in two variables. A unit error in D (m^2/s used with a grid in µm) changes r by 1e12 and blows up at once; the reverse mistake gives a simulation in which nothing seems to happen. When a model has several species, for example a small drug and a protein, the small one with the larger D sets the time step for all.

The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences

title: The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
Summary

A concentration in a channel is a function of space and time, c(x, t). Fick’s law J = -D\,\partial c/\partial x plus a mass balance gives the diffusion (heat) equation \partial c/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2.
It needs an initial profile and a boundary condition at each end: fixed value (reservoir) or no flux (wall, ghost point).
FTCS: (1, -2, 1) stencil in space, Euler in time: c_i^{n+1} = c_i^n + r(c_{i-1}^n - 2c_i^n + c_{i+1}^n), r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2. Error O(\Delta x^2) with r fixed.
Stable only for r \le 1/2: the zigzag mode has the largest eigenvalue \approx 4D/\Delta x^2; Euler’s |1 - kh| \le 1 again. Violated: an exploding zigzag; check that values stay within bounds.
Time scale L^2/D: a linear gradient takes \approx 0.26\,L^2/D: 1 minute for a small molecule over 500 µm, 43 minutes for a protein over 1 mm. Doubling L quadruples the wait. Without a sink there is no lasting gradient.

Next: Implicit schemes and the method of lines: no step limit, one tridiagonal solve per step.

Recap the modelling step, the scheme, its accuracy, its failure and the checks. The step limit dt <= dx^2 / (2D) is the price of an explicit method: fine resolution is paid for twice. The next unit removes the limit with implicit time stepping, using the Thomas algorithm from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse, and hands the method-of-lines system to the stiff solvers of Part 8 (Stiffness and implicit methods). Steady state in two dimensions takes the grid to 2D (oxygen under a lid, a steady state with uptake), Flow plus diffusion adds flow, Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation adds uptake and production.

The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
About this lecture
The last two units followed a concentration in time until it settled. Often only the settled state matters: where does the oxygen end up once supply and consumption balance? Then time drops out, and what is left is one large linear (or nonlinear) system.

Steady diffusion with sources and sinks is a boundary value problem: D\,\nabla^2 c = r(c) (Poisson; Laplace if r = 0). No initial condition, only boundary conditions.
1D first: the (-1, 2, -1) stencil gives a tridiagonal system, solved in O(n).
2D: the five-point Laplacian, assembled from 1D pieces with Kronecker products, and solved with a sparse direct solver.
Numbering the grid: R is column-major, numpy row-major. Get the order wrong and the answer is wrong, with no error message.
Nonlinear uptake (Michaelis–Menten): Newton, with Jacobian = Laplacian + a diagonal.
Biology: oxygen under a lid over a cell layer. Where do the cells go hypoxic, and at what cell density?


This is the third unit of Part 10. The pieces are all old: the second-difference stencil (The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences), tridiagonal and sparse solves with fill-in (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse), and Newton with a Jacobian (Newton for systems of equations). New today: going from one to two space dimensions, which means turning a 2D grid into one vector, and doing that consistently. Grid: nodes x_i = i h as in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences (h is its Δx; here the same h in x and y), unknowns at the interior nodes, a ghost point for a wall (exercise), and in 2D the numbering k = i + (j − 1) n_x. Two deliberate differences from the two earlier diffusion units: the matrix is written as minus the second difference, (D/h²) tridiag(−1, 2, −1) instead of tridiag(1, −2, 1), so that it is symmetric positive definite and Cholesky and CG apply; and oxygen is in µM rather than scaled to 0..1, because the hypoxia threshold and K_m are absolute concentrations. Units µm and s as before.

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
Biology: oxygen under a lid


Cells on the floor of a chamber with a gas-impermeable lid. Oxygen enters only from the open edges and diffuses inwards; every cell on the way consumes some [O1].
Question: where do the cells go hypoxic, and how does that depend on cell density?


The setting is a simplified version of devices in which cells’ own respiration creates the oxygen gradient: a gas-impermeable barrier over a monolayer, with oxygen supplied from the side [O1]. A related approach supplies oxygen from below through a gas-permeable PDMS membrane [O2]. We did not rebuild a specific device: geometry and parameters here are our own round numbers, and every result is computed from the model, not measured (synthetic). Chamber 4 mm x 2 mm seen from above, lid 100 µm above the cells, edges open to air-saturated medium (about 200 µM O2 at 37 °C). The right panel is today’s final answer for a dense layer: a hypoxic core. Check numbers against [O1, O2] before using them for anything real: our sources list was compiled from abstracts.

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
The model and its numbers
Depth-averaged over the 100 µm gap: oxygen c(x, y) in µM obeys, at steady state,
D\left(\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial y^2}\right) = r(c), \qquad c = c_0 \text{ on the edges.}








quantity
value
status




D (O₂ in water, 37 °C)
2\times10^{-9} m²/s = 2000 µm²/s
standard value


c_0 (air-saturated medium)
200 µM
standard value


consumption per cell
50 amol/s (10–100 is typical)
order-of-magnitude assumption


cell density \rho
10^5 cells/cm² (about confluent)
varied, 0.25–4 × 10^5


R_0 = per cell × \rho / gap
0.5 µM/s at 10^5 cells/cm²
derived




The lid gap is thin compared with the chamber width (100 µm against 2 mm), so oxygen is nearly uniform over the height and we average over it: the cells’ uptake per area becomes a volume rate R0 = q rho / h_gap. With q = 50 amol/s = 5e-17 mol/s, rho = 1e5 cells/cm^2 = 1e-3 cells per µm^2 and a 100 µm gap: 5e-20 mol/(s µm^2) / 100 µm = 5e-22 mol/(s µm^3); one µM is 1e-21 mol/µm^3, so R0 = 0.5 µM/s. Per-cell consumption varies by more than a factor 10 between cell types; treat it as an assumption to vary, not a constant. r(c) is the uptake rate; we will try three forms: constant, linear, Michaelis–Menten.

title: Steady state in two dimensions
section: Recap: three tools you already have
text:
Recap: three tools you already have


Second difference (The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences)
\frac{c_{i-1} - 2c_i + c_{i+1}}{h^2} \approx c''(x_i)
error O(h^2); boundary values are known numbers.

Sparse solves (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse)

tridiagonal: O(n) (Thomas)
sparse: Matrix::solve
2D grid: some fill-in is unavoidable; a good ordering helps.


Newton (Newton for systems of equations)
J(\mathbf c)\,\boldsymbol\delta = -\mathbf F(\mathbf c), \quad \mathbf c \leftarrow \mathbf c + \boldsymbol\delta
quadratic convergence near a root; may find the wrong root.


One slide only. In the diffusion units the stencil was combined with a time step; today there is no time. In Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse, the fill-in demo ended with a 2D grid: 30 x 30 points, A with 4380 non-zeros, the Cholesky factor 27 029 in natural order and 10 231 after reordering. That grid was the five-point Laplacian of today. From Newton for systems of equations: one linear solve per step, and the root found depends on the starting point (the toggle switch had three).

title: Steady state in two dimensions
section: Steady state = a boundary value problem
text:
Steady state = a boundary value problem
Set \partial c/\partial t = 0 in the diffusion equation with uptake:
\underbrace{\frac{\partial c}{\partial t}}_{=\,0} = D\,\nabla^2 c - r(c) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D\,\nabla^2 c = r(c), \qquad \nabla^2 c = \frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial y^2}

Poisson equation when r does not depend on c; Laplace equation when r = 0.
No initial condition. The boundary conditions alone fix the answer: fixed value (open edge) or no flux (wall).
Could we just time-step until nothing changes? Explicit 2D with h = 50 µm needs \Delta t \le h^2/(4D) = 0.31 s, and settling takes \sim L^2/D: thousands of steps, 16\times more at h/2. A steady-state solve is one linear system.


A boundary value problem (BVP) is the opposite of the initial value problems of Part 8: information comes from the edges, all at once, not from a starting time. The 2D stability limit for FTCS is D dt / h^2 <= 1/4 (twice as strict as in 1D, because each point has four neighbours; derived the same way as in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences). Halving h divides dt by 4 and multiplies the number of points by 4, so the cost of time-stepping to steady state grows 16-fold. Implicit time steps (Implicit schemes and the method of lines) would remove the step limit, but if you only want the end state, ask for it directly.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
section: 1D first: one line across the chamber
text:
1D first: one line across the chamber
A long chamber: only y matters. Grid y_i = i\,h, i = 0, \dots, N (nodes as in the 1D chamber, h = \Delta x), with c_0 = c_N = 200 µM known. At each interior point:
\frac{D}{h^2}\bigl(-c_{i-1} + 2c_i - c_{i+1}\bigr) = -R_0, \qquad i = 1, \dots, N-1.
By hand, L = 2000 µm, N = 4 (h = 500 µm, D/h^2 = 0.008 /s), R_0 = 0.5 µM/s. Move known values to the right:
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 200 - 62.5 \\ -62.5 \\ 200 - 62.5\end{pmatrix} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathbf c = (106.25,\ 75,\ 106.25).

Sign convention: we write the operator as minus the second difference, so the matrix has a positive diagonal and is symmetric positive definite. The two earlier diffusion units wrote tridiag(1, −2, 1), the second difference itself, because there it sat on the right-hand side of an ODE; for a steady solve the minus sign is the natural choice, since Cholesky and CG need a positive definite matrix. It is the pattern of the morphogen row in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse, without the decay term on the diagonal and with fixed values instead of closed ends. R0 / (D/h^2) = 0.5 / 0.008 = 62.5. Solve by symmetry: c1 = c3, so 2c1 - c2 = 137.5 and -2c1 + 2c2 = -62.5; adding gives c2 = 75, then c1 = 106.25. The known boundary values appear only in the first and last equations: they move to the right-hand side, which is where all the boundary information lives.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
1D in R
library(Matrix)
lap1 <- function(n) bandSparse(n, k = -1:1,        # tridiag(-1, 2, -1)
  diagonals = list(rep(-1, n - 1), rep(2, n), rep(-1, n - 1)))
D <- 2000; c0 <- 200; R0 <- 0.5     # µm^2/s, µM, µM/s
L <- 2000; N <- 4; h <- L / N; n <- N - 1
A1 <- D / h^2 * lap1(n)
b1 <- rep(-R0, n); b1[c(1, n)] <- b1[c(1, n)] + D / h^2 * c0
as.vector(solve(A1, b1))
# [1] 106.25  75.00 106.25
y <- h * (1:n); c0 - R0 * y * (L - y) / (2 * D)    # exact parabola
# [1] 106.25  75.00 106.25

Exact to the last digit, even with 3 points: the second difference is exact for parabolas, and constant uptake gives a parabola.
bandSparse + solve: the sparse solver finds the band itself (O(n), as Thomas).


The exact solution of D c’’ = R0 with c = c0 at both ends is c0 - R0 y (L - y) / (2D): check by differentiating twice. The Taylor error term of the stencil involves the fourth derivative, which is zero for a parabola, so the grid solution is exact at the grid points for any h. That makes this a weak test of a solver: it cannot reveal the order. The next slides give a better test. The thomas function from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse would do the same job; we use Matrix because the 2D case needs it anyway.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
Failure: oxygen below zero


Double the density (R_0 = 1 µM/s): \mathbf c = (12.5,\ -50,\ 12.5). The solver is right; the model is wrong. Cells cannot consume oxygen that is not there.
Check: min(c) >= 0 for every concentration. Constant uptake is only valid while c stays well above zero.


The numerical method did its job perfectly (exact at the nodes, as on the previous slide). The failure is in the modelling assumption that every cell consumes at its maximal rate R0 regardless of how much oxygen is left. In reality uptake slows down as c approaches zero (Michaelis–Menten, later in this lecture). The depth of the dip is R0 L^2 / (8D): it grows linearly with density and with the square of the chamber width. Setting it equal to c0 gives the largest chamber that stays oxygenated under constant uptake: L = sqrt(8 D c0 / R0) = 2530 µm at 1e5 cells/cm^2.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
section: Check a solver: exact solution and refinement
text:
Check a solver: exact solution and refinement




Test problem with a non-polynomial solution: linear uptake r = k\,c, k = R_0/c_0 = 0.0025 /s:
c(y) = c_0\,\frac{\cosh\bigl((y - L/2)/\lambda\bigr)}{\cosh\bigl(L/(2\lambda)\bigr)}, \quad \lambda = \sqrt{D/k} = 894 \text{ µm}.

Add k to the diagonal: A1 + Diagonal(n, k).
h = 200 \to 6.25 µm: max error 0.22 \to 2.2\times10^{-4} µM, slope 2.



Linear (first-order) uptake keeps the system linear and has an exact solution: c’’ = c / lambda^2 is solved by cosh, symmetric around the middle. lambda = sqrt(D/k) is the same length scale that appears for morphogens in Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation. The error halves twice per halving of h: second order, as the Taylor expansion of the stencil promises. When no exact solution exists (the usual case), refine the grid and watch the changes shrink by 4x: that is the check we use for the 2D oxygen map later.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
Two dimensions: the five-point stencil
Grid x_i = i\,h, y_j = j\,h (same h in both directions). Add the two second differences:
\nabla^2 c\,(x_i, y_j) \approx \frac{c_{i-1,j} + c_{i+1,j} + c_{i,j-1} + c_{i,j+1} - 4\,c_{i,j}}{h^2}


Each equation links a point (red) to its four neighbours (orange). Neighbours on the edge (blue) are known.


The five-point Laplacian: the 1D stencil in x plus the 1D stencil in y, with -2 - 2 = -4 in the middle. Its error is again O(h^2). The chamber of the running example is 4000 x 2000 µm; with h = 50 µm there are 79 x 39 = 3081 interior unknowns. The figure shows a toy grid with nx = 5, ny = 3 interior points, and the numbering we use for the rest of the lecture, explained on the next slide.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
One vector from a grid
A solver wants a vector \mathbf c of length n_x n_y. Number the points row of the grid by row, x running fastest:
k = i + (j - 1)\,n_x \qquad (i = 1..n_x,\ j = 1..n_y)

In the toy grid (n_x = 5): point (3, 2) is k = 8. Its neighbours: k \pm 1 = 7, 9 in x, and k \pm n_x = 3, 13 in y.
In R this is exactly what as.vector(C) does to a matrix C[i, j] with nx rows: R stores matrices column by column (column-major), so the first index runs fastest.
So: keep the field as an n_x \times n_y matrix C[i, j] = c(x_i, y_j), and convert with as.vector(C) and matrix(cvec, nx, ny).


Any numbering works, as long as the matrix and every vector use the same one. This one is natural in R: as.vector stacks the columns of C, so C[1,1], C[2,1], …, C[nx,1] come first (all x at the first y), then the second column. Neighbours in y are nx apart in the vector: this distance is the bandwidth of the matrix, and it is why the 2D matrix is banded but not tridiagonal. A 1-based formula; in 0-based languages (Python, Rust) it is k = i + j nx with i, j from 0.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
The matrix has blocks


x-neighbours: the 1D matrix T_{n_x} repeated along the diagonal, one block per y-row (orange).
y-neighbours: -1 at distance n_x from the diagonal (green). The diagonal (blue) gets 2 + 2 = 4.


Pattern of the toy matrix, 15 x 15, without the factor D / h^2. The dotted lines separate the three y-rows of the grid. Left: no coupling between rows, each row is a 1D problem in x. Middle: each point is coupled to the same x-position in the row above and below, a 1D problem in y for each x. Right: the sum, the five-point Laplacian, block tridiagonal. Its rows near the edge have fewer than four off-diagonal entries; the missing neighbours are boundary points and go into the right-hand side. The two pieces have a name: Kronecker products.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
Kronecker products
A \otimes B: replace each entry a_{pq} of A by the block a_{pq} B. Size: (m_A m_B) \times (n_A n_B).
T3 <- matrix(c(2, -1, 0,  -1, 2, -1,  0, -1, 2), 3)
kronecker(diag(2), T3)              # I_2 (x) T_3: two copies of T_3
#      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
# [1,]    2   -1    0    0    0    0
# [2,]   -1    2   -1    0    0    0
# [3,]    0   -1    2    0    0    0
# [4,]    0    0    0    2   -1    0
# [5,]    0    0    0   -1    2   -1
# [6,]    0    0    0    0   -1    2

I_{n_y} \otimes T_{n_x}: the x-blocks (left panel). T_{n_y} \otimes I_{n_x}: each entry of T_{n_y} becomes a multiple of I_{n_x}, so the -1s sit n_x apart (middle panel).
With x running fastest: \;A = \dfrac{D}{h^2}\bigl(I_{n_y} \otimes T_{n_x} + T_{n_y} \otimes I_{n_x}\bigr).


kronecker works on dense matrices in base R and on sparse ones with Matrix loaded (the result stays sparse). Python: scipy.sparse.kron; Rust: sprs has a kronecker product too, but in the exercise we build the triplets by hand, which makes the index formula explicit. The order of the two factors is tied to the numbering: the factor on the right acts on the index that runs fastest. With y running fastest (numpy’s default, next slides) the formula becomes T_nx (x) I_ny + I_nx (x) T_ny.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Steady state in two dimensions
text:
Assembling the 2D matrix in R
Lx <- 4000; Ly <- 2000; h <- 50            # chamber and grid, µm
nx <- Lx / h - 1; ny <- Ly / h - 1         # 79 x 39 interior points
A <- D / h^2 * (kronecker(Diagonal(ny), lap1(nx)) +    # x-neighbours
                kronecker(lap1(ny), Diagonal(nx)))     # y-neighbours
dim(A)
# [1] 3081 3081
nnzero(A)                                  # about 5 per row
# [1] 15169
isSymmetric(A)
# [1] TRUE

Dense, this matrix would hold 9.5 million entries (76 MB); 99.8 % are zero.
Diagonal is the sparse identity. Never build the dense one at this size.


15169 = 5 x 3081 minus the missing neighbours along the four edges (2 x 79 + 2 x 39 = 236): 15405 - 236 = 15169. Symmetric because the stencil is symmetric (my neighbour’s coupling to me equals mine to it). The matrix is also positive definite, like its 1D parts, so Cholesky works. With h = 12.5 µm the chamber has 50 721 unknowns: 20 GB dense, about 3 MB sparse.

title: Steady state in two dimensions
section: The edges go into the right-hand side
text:
The edges go into the right-hand side
B <- matrix(0, nx, ny)              # B[i, j] belongs to point (x_i, y_j)
B[1, ]  <- B[1, ]  + c0;  B[nx, ] <- B[nx, ] + c0      # left, right edge
B[, 1]  <- B[, 1]  + c0;  B[, ny] <- B[, ny] + c0      # bottom, top edge
b <- D / h^2 * as.vector(B)         # stacks columns: x runs fastest
R0 <- 0.5                           # 1e5 cells/cm^2
C <- matrix(as.vector(solve(A, b - R0)), nx, ny)
range(C)
# [1]  86.14604 198.58301
which(C == min(C), arr.ind = TRUE)  # the centre: x = 2000, y = 1000 µm
#      row col
# [1,]  40  20

A corner point has two known neighbours, so it gets c_0 twice.
Sources and sinks enter the same way: subtract the uptake (or add the production) in \mathbf b, point by point.


Building b as a matrix with the same shape as the grid, then flattening with as.vector, is the safest way: the boundary rows and columns are visible in the code, and the flattening uses the same rule as the matrix. The uptake here is the same R0 everywhere, so subtracting a scalar is enough; a patterned cell layer (cells only in part of the chamber) would subtract a vector R0 * as.vector(cells). A point source (a single cell secreting something) adds its rate divided by the cell area h^2 at one k.

title: Steady state in two dimensions
section: Check the assembly with a known field
text:
Check the assembly with a known field
x <- h * (1:nx); y <- h * (1:ny)
U <- outer(sin(pi * x / Lx), sin(pi * y / Ly))      # 0 on all four edges
AU <- D * pi^2 * (1 / Lx^2 + 1 / Ly^2) * U          # exact -D * Laplacian
max(abs(as.vector(A %*% as.vector(U)) - as.vector(AU))) / max(AU)
# [1] 0.0004368497

Small and O(h^2): the matrix applies the Laplacian correctly. With the Kronecker factors in the wrong order the same check gives 253.9.
Use a field that differs in x and y, on a grid with n_x \ne n_y. A square grid and a symmetric test field hide orientation bugs.


A manufactured solution: pick a smooth function, compute its Laplacian by hand, and compare with A times its grid values. sin(pi x / Lx) sin(pi y / Ly) vanishes on the edges, so no boundary terms are needed, and its Laplacian is -pi^2 (1/Lx^2 + 1/Ly^2) times itself. The relative error 4.4e-4 is about (pi h)^2 / (12 L^2), the Taylor term. This check costs one matrix-vector product and catches most assembly bugs: wrong kronecker order, missing factor D / h^2, wrong sign, wrong grid spacing in one direction. A bug that swaps x and y on a square grid with a field symmetric in x and y is invisible, so test on a rectangle.

Right panel: the same solve with the Kronecker factors in the order that matches numpy’s default flattening, while b and the reshaping follow R’s column-major rule. Every size matches, nothing warns, and the answer has nothing to do with the chamber: stripes, values above the boundary value of 200 (impossible for a pure sink). This happens in practice when code is translated from Python to R or back, or when a formula is copied from a textbook that numbers y first. Plotting adds a second trap: R’s image(x, y, C) puts C[i, j] at (x_i, y_j), while matplotlib’s imshow(C) puts rows vertically and starts at the top, so use imshow(C.T, origin=“lower”) or pcolormesh(x, y, C.T). Rust has no matrix type with a built-in order: you write k = i + nx * j yourself, which is the safest of the three.

text:
Sparse direct solve

solve(A, b) on a sparse matrix: sparse LU. Tell it the matrix is symmetric (forceSymmetric(A)) and it uses sparse Cholesky (CHOLMOD) with a fill-reducing ordering.
2D grid, natural order: the band of width n_x fills in. Cholesky factor of the chamber matrix:

At h = 12.5 µm one solve took ~3 s as general LU, 0.16 s with forceSymmetric.
Python: scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve. Rust: sprs has no direct solver; the exercise uses a hand-written conjugate gradient.


Natural order: nnz(L) is about (number of unknowns) x nx, because everything inside the band fills in; refining h by 2 multiplies it by 8. Reordering (approximate minimum degree / nested dissection, chosen automatically by Cholesky(A, perm = TRUE) and by solve on a dsCMatrix) cuts it by a factor 5 to 11 here, and the gap grows with the grid. This is the 2D case of the fill-in discussion in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse. Timings are from one run on one machine and vary; the factor matters, not the seconds. Matrix caches the factorisation inside the matrix object, so repeated solves with the same A are almost free: time a fresh matrix. sprs-ldl (a separate crate, not in our Cargo.toml) would give a sparse Cholesky in Rust; CG needs only matrix-vector products and works because A is SPD. Full treatment of CG and preconditioning: Iterative linear solvers in depth (Part 11).
