title: Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
text:
By hand
B1. Amplification factors. Drug clearance \(C' = -0.8\,C\) (per hour), as in Initial value problems and Euler’s method. (a) For \(h = 0.5, 2, 3, 10\) hours compute \(z = h\lambda\) and the factor per step of Euler and of backward Euler. Compare with the exact factor \(e^{z}\) (given: \(e^{-0.4} = 0.670\), \(e^{-1.6} = 0.202\), \(e^{-2.4} = 0.0907\), \(e^{-8} = 0.000335\)). Which steps are stable? Which are accurate? (b) The enzyme model’s fastest eigenvalue at the start is \(\lambda = -1201\ \text{s}^{-1}\). What is the largest stable step of Euler and of RK4? How many steps does each need to cover 30 s? (c) What factor does backward Euler apply to this fast mode with \(h = 0.1\) s? What is the exact factor \(e^{-120.1}\), roughly? Does the difference matter?
B2. Backward Euler by hand. A drug is infused at 2 mg/L per hour and cleared at rate 0.8 per hour: \(C' = 2 - 0.8\,C\), \(C(0) = 0\). Exact solution: \(C(t) = 2.5\,(1 - e^{-0.8t})\). (a) Write the backward Euler step and solve it for \(C_{n+1}\) (it is linear: no Newton needed). (b) Take two steps with \(h = 1\) hour, by backward Euler and by Euler. Compare with the exact \(C(1) = 1.377\), \(C(2) = 1.995\). (c) Take one step with \(h = 10\) hours by each method. Compare with \(C(10) = 2.499\). (d) Show that the steady state \(C = 2.5\) is a fixed point of the backward Euler step for every \(h\).
B3. Newton inside a step. Protein monomers dimerise, \(2M \to D\), with \(M' = -kM^2\), \(k = 10\) per \(\mu\)M per s, \(M(0) = 1\ \mu\)M. Exact: \(M(t) = 1/(1 + kt)\). (a) Write the backward Euler equation \(G(y) = 0\) for \(y = M_1\) with \(h = 0.1\) s, and \(G'(y)\). (b) Do two Newton iterations from \(y = M_0 = 1\). (c) Solve \(G(y) = 0\) exactly with the quadratic formula. How many correct digits did two iterations give? Compare \(M_1\) with the exact \(M(0.1)\) and with one Euler step. (d) Repeat (c) with \(h = 0.2\) s. What does Euler give now? (e) Why is \(y = M_n\) a good starting point for Newton?
B4. Eigenvalues of the enzyme model. Use \(E = E_0 - C\) to reduce the model to \[S' = -k_f(E_0 - C)S + k_r C, \qquad C' = k_f(E_0 - C)S - (k_r + k_{cat})C.\] (a) Compute the \(2\times2\) Jacobian \(\partial(S', C')/\partial(S, C)\) in general, then at \(S = 10\), \(C = 0\). (b) Compute its trace and determinant, and the two eigenvalues (exactly, and with the approximations of fact 2). What are the two time scales, and their ratio? (c) Repeat at the end of the reaction, \(S = 0\), \(C = 0\). Is the model still stiff? What is the Euler step limit now?
B5. Robertson’s Jacobian. \(y_1' = -0.04y_1 + 10^4y_2y_3\), \(y_2' = 0.04y_1 - 10^4y_2y_3 - 3\times10^7y_2^2\), \(y_3' = 3\times10^7y_2^2\). (a) Write the \(3\times3\) Jacobian \(J\). (b) Evaluate \(J\) at the start, \(\mathbf y = (1, 0, 0)\). What are its eigenvalues? Is the problem stiff at \(t = 0\)? (c) Evaluate \(J\) at \(t = 40\), where \(\mathbf y \approx (0.7158,\ 9.19\times10^{-6},\ 0.2842)\). Each column of \(J\) sums to 0: what does that say about one eigenvalue (think of \(y_1 + y_2 + y_3\))? The slow eigenvalue is about \(-0.02\). Use the trace to estimate the fast one. (d) RK45 is stable for \(h|\lambda| \lesssim 3.3\). Estimate how many steps it needs from \(t = 0\) to \(40\). (e) Write the Newton matrix \(I - hJ\) of a backward Euler step with \(h = 1\) at \(t = 40\).
B6. BDF2 by hand. Drug clearance \(C' = -0.8\,C\), \(C_0 = 10\), \(h = 1\) hour. (a) Solve the BDF2 formula for \(C_{n+1}\) on this linear equation. (b) Take \(C_1\) from the exact solution, \(C_1 = 10e^{-0.8} = 4.493\), and compute \(C_2\) by BDF2. (c) Compute \(C_1, C_2\) by backward Euler. Compare both with the exact \(C_2 = 2.019\).
B7. Damping and classification. (a) For the oscillator \(x'' = -\omega^2 x\) (fact: the eigenvalues are \(\pm i\omega\)), backward Euler multiplies the amplitude by \(|1/(1 - i\omega h)| = 1/\sqrt{1 + \omega^2h^2}\) per step. With \(\omega = 2\pi/24\) per hour (\(\omega = 0.2618\)) and \(h = 1\) h, what is the factor per step, per day and after 10 days? (b) Stiff or not? Logistic growth of a culture (\(r = 0.8\) per hour) over 24 h; the SIR epidemic over a season; the enzyme model over 30 s; the enzyme model over its first 5 ms; Robertson’s problem to \(t = 10^{5}\); a circadian oscillator over 10 days; diffusion on a fine grid of 1000 points (Implicit schemes and the method of lines). For each, which deSolve/solve_ivp method would you choose?

title: Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
text:
In code
C1. Stability regions. On a grid of \(z\) values with \(\text{Re}\,z \in [-5, 3]\), \(\text{Im}\,z \in [-4, 4]\), compute \(|R(z)|\) for Euler, RK4 and backward Euler and draw the contour \(|R| = 1\) of each (R: contour with levels = 1; Python: plt.contour with levels=[1]). Which side of each curve is stable? Then find where the RK4 region crosses the negative real axis and the positive imaginary axis with a root finder (uniroot / scipy.optimize.brentq).
C2. Explicit vs backward Euler on the enzyme. Write the enzyme rates f(y) for \(\mathbf y = (S, E, C, P)\) and their \(4\times4\) Jacobian jac(y). (a) Run explicit Euler to \(t = 10\) s with \(h = 1\) ms and with \(h = 3\) ms. (b) Write beuler(f, jac, y0, h, n) with Newton (fact 4) and run it to \(t = 10\) s with \(h = 1\), \(0.1\) and \(0.01\) s. Compare \(P(10)\) with the reference \(8.002674\) from the background. (c) Count the Newton iterations per step, and check both conservation laws.
C3. Library solvers: count steps and time. Solve the enzyme model to \(t = 30\) s with rtol = 1e-6, atol = 1e-9 using ode45, lsoda, bdf and radau (R; use output times seq(0, 30, by = 0.5)) or RK45, LSODA, BDF, Radau (Python). Print steps, \(\mathbf f\) evaluations, wall time (system.time / time.perf_counter) and \(P(30)\). Which solver is fastest, and why does the step count not tell the whole story?
C4. When is Michaelis–Menten good enough? For \(E_0 = 0.1\), \(1\) and \(5\ \mu\)M (with \(S_0 = 10\)), solve the full model and the QSSA model (fact 6) on \(t \in [0, 20/E_0]\) and print the largest difference in \(P(t)\), with \(P_\text{QSSA} = S_0 - S_\text{QSSA}\). Compare with the ratio \(E_0/(S_0 + K_m)\).
C5. Order of backward Euler and BDF2. Start at \(t = 0.1\) s from the reference solution (after the binding transient) and integrate 10 s with backward Euler and with BDF2 (fact 5; take the second start value from the reference solution too), for \(h = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01\). Print the error in \(P(10.1)\) and read off the order of each method.
C6. Robertson’s problem. (a) Solve it from \(t = 0\) to \(40\) with rtol = 1e-6, atol = 1e-10 with an explicit and three stiff solvers; print steps, \(\mathbf f\) evaluations, time and \(y_2(40)\). (R: pass hini = 1e-4, without which deSolve’s ode45 can stall on this problem, and maxsteps = 1e5.) Compare the step count of the explicit solver with your estimate from B5(d). (b) Solve it to \(t = 10^{11}\) with a stiff solver (rtol = 1e-8, atol = 1e-12), print \(\mathbf y\) at \(t = 10^{-3}, 1, 10^4, 10^{11}\) and check the conservation law \(y_1 + y_2 + y_3 = 1\).
C7. Backward Euler damps a clock. Run backward Euler on the 24-hour oscillator \(y_1' = y_2\), \(y_2' = -\omega^2 y_1\), \(\mathbf y(0) = (1, 0)\), \(\omega = 2\pi/24\), for 10 days with \(h = 1, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01\) hours, and print the amplitude \(\sqrt{y_1^2 + (y_2/\omega)^2}\) (exact: 1). Then solve the same problem with an explicit library solver and with BDF at rtol = 1e-8, atol = 1e-10, and compare amplitudes and step counts. What would you conclude about the clock from the \(h = 1\) run alone?

title: Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — amplification factors (B1, B6, B7)





Compute \(z = h\lambda\) first: \(\lambda = -0.8\), so \(z = -0.4, -1.6, -2.4, -8\). Stable means \(|R| \le 1\); accurate means \(R\) close to \(e^z\). For the step limits in B1(b), solve \(h|\lambda| = 2\) and \(h|\lambda| = 2.785\). In B6, move every \(C_{n+1}\) term to the left: \(C_{n+1}(1 - \tfrac23 h\lambda) = \tfrac43 C_n - \tfrac13 C_{n-1}\).









Hint 2 — an implicit step (B2, B3)





Write the formula with \(C_{n+1}\) on both sides, then collect: B2 is linear, \(C_{n+1}(1 + 0.8h) = C_n + 2h\). In B3 the equation is quadratic: \(y + hky^2 - M_0 = 0\). Newton: \(y \leftarrow y - G(y)/G'(y)\), as in Newton and secant methods.









Hint 3 — Jacobians and eigenvalues (B4, B5)





Row \(i\) of \(J\) holds the partial derivatives of the \(i\)-th rate with respect to each variable, holding the others fixed (Newton for systems of equations). For a \(2\times2\) matrix, \(\lambda = \tfrac12\big(\text{tr} \pm \sqrt{\text{tr}^2 - 4\det}\big)\). In B5(c), if the columns of \(J\) sum to 0, then \((1, 1, 1)\,J = \mathbf 0\), so \(J\) is singular; the eigenvalues add up to the trace.









Hint 4 — backward Euler in code (C2, C5, C7)





Inner loop: delta <- solve(I - h * jac(y), -(y - yold - h * f(y))), stop when the length of delta is below 1e-10. R: solve, diag; Python: np.linalg.solve, np.eye; Rust: (&id - h * jac(&y)).lu().solve(&(-g)) with nalgebra. For BDF2 replace the equation by fact 5 and the matrix by \(I - \tfrac23 hJ\). On the linear oscillator Newton converges in one iteration (a second one confirms it).









Hint 5 — library solvers and counters (C3, C4, C6, C7)





R: attr(out, "istate")[2] is the number of steps, [3] the number of \(\mathbf f\) evaluations; diagnostics(out) prints everything. deSolve limits the step to the spacing of the output times (hmax), so compare step counts for the same times. Python: without t_eval, sol.t holds every step; use dense_output=True and sol.sol(t) to get values at chosen times. Python’s BDF and Radau are written in Python, LSODA in Fortran, so compare their wall times with care. Rust: Dopri5::from_param(..., n_stiff, ...) with n_stiff = u32::MAX switches the stiffness test off; the returned Stats has accepted_steps and num_eval.

title: Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Where this leads

Equilibria, stability and the phase plane (Part 8): the eigenvalues of the Jacobian come back, now to decide whether a steady state of the biology is stable, not whether a solver is.
Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting (Part 9): fitting rate constants solves the model hundreds of times; with a stiff model, choosing lsoda or bdf decides whether that takes seconds or hours.
Implicit schemes and the method of lines (Part 10): a diffusion equation on a grid becomes a large, sparse, stiff ODE system; backward Euler then needs one sparse (tridiagonal) solve per step.
We wrote backward Euler with a fixed step and full Newton iterations. Production solvers (lsoda, bdf, radau) also estimate their error, adapt step and order, and reuse the Jacobian and its LU factorisation over many steps.

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
About this lecture
Part 10 put every chip on a rectangular grid. Real chips have round pillars, curved channels and cells of any shape. This lecture is an outlook: what the tools used for real chip design do differently, with one small piece done by hand.

Why finite differences struggle with curved and irregular geometry: staircase walls, refinement that spreads everywhere.
Finite volumes in one picture: conservation in every cell, whatever its shape.
Finite elements in 1D: the unknown is a sum of hat functions; the weak form; a 2 × 2 matrix per element, assembled into a tridiagonal matrix. On a uniform mesh it is the finite-difference matrix again; on a non-uniform mesh we put the points where the solution changes.
Meshes of triangles in 2D, and solving for the flow itself: Stokes flow, with the Poiseuille profile as its exact solution in a straight channel.
What COMSOL, FEniCS / Firedrake, scikit-fem and deal.II do, and when to reach for them instead of our own codes.


This is optional further reading after Part 10. It assumes the diffusion units of Part 10 (the grid, the second difference, the Thomas algorithm, grid refinement as a check) and does not teach any of the big packages: the aim is that students know what they are doing when they open COMSOL or FEniCS, and can check it. The only new hand-written method is a 1D finite element code of about 15 lines, which turns out to need nothing beyond the tridiagonal solve of Implicit schemes and the method of lines.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
A chamber with pillars


Pillars hold up the roof of a wide culture chamber, or trap cells. On a square grid each round wall becomes a staircase: its position is wrong by up to \Delta x/2, and “no flux through the wall” has no clean stencil on a slanted wall.
Finer near the pillars means finer everywhere: a grid line runs across the whole chamber. Halving \Delta x costs 4× the unknowns in 2D, 8× in 3D.


The same chamber returns at the end of the lecture as a triangle mesh. Finite differences can be pushed to handle curved walls (cut cells, immersed boundaries, curvilinear coordinates), and research codes do, but each fix is a project of its own. The two methods below start from a mesh that follows the wall. 72 of the 384 grid cells are inside a pillar here; the staircase is visible even at 25 um, half the pillar radius. For transport near a wall (a drug taken up by cells on the pillar surface) the flux through the wall is exactly what we want to know, and it is what the staircase gets worst.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Finite volumes in one picture


Cut the domain into cells of any shape. For each cell: flux in − flux out = uptake (or accumulation) inside. One equation per cell.
Flux through a face between cells i and j: D\,(u_j - u_i)/d_{ij} × face area. On a uniform square grid this gives back the five-point stencil.
What leaves one cell enters its neighbour, so the total amount is conserved exactly. This is why most flow (CFD) codes are finite-volume codes: OpenFOAM, Ansys Fluent.


Finite volumes are the mass balance with which we derived the diffusion equation in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences, before taking the limit: keep the cells finite and write one balance per cell. The cells can be triangles, polygons or cut cells at a wall. The approximation sits in the face flux, which is a difference quotient between cell centres. Conservation holds to rounding error whatever the mesh, which matters for flow, where small leaks in mass add up downstream.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
section: Finite elements: a sum of hats
text:
Finite elements: a sum of hats


Pick nodes x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_N, any spacing. Hat function \varphi_j: 1 at node j, 0 at every other node, straight lines in between.
Approximate u(x) \approx u_h(x) = \sum_j u_j\,\varphi_j(x): the piecewise linear interpolant through the nodal values u_j. The unknowns are the u_j, as in finite differences.


This is piecewise linear interpolation from Splines, written as a sum of basis functions. Each hat lives on only two elements (the intervals next to its node), and that will make the matrix tridiagonal. In 2D the hats become pyramids over triangles; with quadratic or cubic pieces instead of straight lines one gets higher-order elements. The difference from finite differences is not the unknowns but how we choose the equations for them.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
The weak form in words
Model: -(D\,u')' + k\,u = f on 0 < x < L. Instead of asking it to hold at each node, ask it to hold on average against every hat \varphi_i:

Multiply the equation by \varphi_i and integrate over the domain.
Integrate by parts: -\int (D u')'\varphi_i\,dx = \int D\,u'\varphi_i'\,dx - \big[D u' \varphi_i\big]_0^L. Now only first derivatives appear, so piecewise linear u_h is allowed.
The boundary term is the flux. At a no-flux wall it is zero, so the condition is built in (natural boundary condition). Where u is prescribed, we do not test.
Insert u_h = \sum_j u_j\varphi_j: a linear system K\mathbf u = \mathbf b with K_{ij} = \int D\,\varphi_i'\varphi_j'\,dx + \int k\,\varphi_i\varphi_j\,dx, \qquad b_i = \int f\,\varphi_i\,dx.


Say it slowly: “weak” because we only ask for the equation in an averaged sense, which is also why kinks in u_h are fine. The no-flux wall is the nice surprise: in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences it needed a ghost point; here we do nothing at all. Galerkin’s choice is to test with the same hats used to build u_h, which makes K symmetric. Since each hat overlaps only its two neighbours, K_ij is zero unless |i - j| <= 1: tridiagonal. Nothing in steps 1-4 needs a uniform mesh or a straight wall, and that is the point.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Element by element


On one element of length h_e the two hats have slopes \pm 1/h_e, so \int D\varphi_i'\varphi_j' = \pm D/h_e; and \int \varphi_i\varphi_j = h_e/3 (same hat) or h_e/6.
Assembly: loop over elements and add each 2 × 2 block into rows and columns e, e+1. The same loop, over triangles with 3 × 3 blocks, builds the 2D matrix.


Every finite element code, from 15 lines of R to COMSOL, has this structure: compute a small matrix per element from its geometry and material (D and k may differ from element to element, at no extra cost), and add it into the big sparse matrix. The h/3 and h/6 come from integrating products of two straight lines: ∫ (x/h)^2 dx = h/3 and ∫ (x/h)(1 - x/h) dx = h/6 over [0, h]. The load vector gets f h_e / 2 per node of each element for constant f.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Same matrix as finite differences
For -D u'' = f on a uniform mesh, an interior row of K\mathbf u = \mathbf b reads \frac{D}{h}\,(-u_{i-1} + 2u_i - u_{i+1}) = f\,h \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D\,\frac{-u_{i-1} + 2u_i - u_{i+1}}{h^2} = f, the second difference from Numerical differentiation. Check with assemble() (next slides), 5 elements of h = 100, D = 1, f = 1:
S <- assemble(seq(0, 500, by = 100), D = 1, k = 0, f = 1)
S$di * 100;  S$off * 100;  S$b          # K times h, and b
# [1] 1 2 2 2 2 1
# [1] -1 -1 -1 -1 -1
# [1]  50 100 100 100 100  50

Interior: (-1, 2, -1) and f h. The last row has half weights: exactly the ghost-point no-flux row, divided by 2.
With uptake, FEM gives \tfrac{kh}{6}(u_{i-1} + 4u_i + u_{i+1}) where FD has k h\,u_i: a weighted average. Lumping it onto the diagonal gives FD exactly.


So on a rectangle with a uniform grid, finite elements bring nothing new: the matrix is the one from Part 10, row by row, up to a factor h. The last row is (D/h)(u_N - u_{N-1}) = f h / 2; the ghost-point row from The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences is D (2u_{N-1} - 2u_N)/h^2 = -f, i.e. the same equation times 2/h. Mass lumping (replacing the h/6, h/3 weights by a diagonal h/2) is a common trick; we will see on the failure slide why it can matter. The gain from finite elements comes when the mesh is not uniform, which the exercise B2 shows also reproduces the non-uniform finite-difference formula in 1D.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
section: The 1D example: drug into a hydrogel slab
text:
The 1D example: drug into a hydrogel slab
A hydrogel slab, L = 1 mm thick on a glass bottom, with cells embedded in it. A drug in the medium above diffuses in (D = 100 µm²/s) and the cells take it up (k = 0.04 s⁻¹).
-D\,u'' + k\,u = 0, \qquad u(0) = 1 \text{ (bath)}, \qquad u'(L) = 0 \text{ (glass)}

Exact steady state: u(x) = \dfrac{\cosh\big((L - x)/\lambda\big)}{\cosh(L/\lambda)} with \lambda = \sqrt{D/k} = 50 µm.
The drug reaches only the top ~150 µm. All the action is in a thin layer; the lower 800 µm need almost no points.
Questions a biologist asks: how deep do cells see the drug? How much is in the gel (\int u\,dx \approx \lambda = 50 µm × bath concentration)?


λ = sqrt(D/k) is the same length scale as the synthesis-diffusion-degradation morphogen gradient in Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation: here the source is the bath at the top and the sink is uptake by the cells. The numbers are round but realistic: a drug or growth factor in a soft gel has D of order 10-100 um^2/s; strong uptake or binding gives penetration depths of tens of um, which is why cells deep in thick gels or spheroids can be untreated. The total amount λ tanh(L/λ) = 50 um (in units of bath concentration) is the flux into the gel divided by k.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
FEM in R: assembly
assemble <- function(x, D, k, f = 0) {        # nodes x, any spacing
  n <- length(x); h <- diff(x)
  di <- numeric(n); off <- numeric(n - 1); b <- numeric(n)
  for (e in 1:(n - 1)) {                     # element e: nodes e and e + 1
    kd <- D / h[e] + k * h[e] / 3            # diagonal entries of the 2 x 2
    ko <- -D / h[e] + k * h[e] / 6           # off-diagonal entries
    di[e:(e + 1)] <- di[e:(e + 1)] + kd
    off[e] <- off[e] + ko
    b[e:(e + 1)] <- b[e:(e + 1)] + f * h[e] / 2
  }
  list(di = di, off = off, b = b)            # tridiagonal K, load b
}

di is the diagonal, off the off-diagonal (the matrix is symmetric). No ghost point: the no-flux end needs nothing.


Eleven lines, and no assumption about the spacing: h[e] is the length of element e. To let D or k vary from element to element (a two-layer gel, cells only in the lower layer), write D[e] and k[e]; the exercise does that with rep_len. Note how small the loop body is: this is the R version of the assembly picture. Python users: the same loop with numpy arrays; Rust: a plain for loop over Vec.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
section: FEM in R: solve and check
text:
FEM in R: solve and check
fem1d <- function(x, D, k, f = 0, u0 = 1) {  # u(x[1]) = u0, u' = 0 at the end
  S <- assemble(x, D, k, f); off <- S$off
  rhs <- S$b[-1]; rhs[1] <- rhs[1] - off[1] * u0     # move known u0 to the right
  c(u0, thomas(off, S$di[-1], c(off[-1], 0), rhs))
}
L <- 1000; D <- 100; k <- 0.04; lam <- sqrt(D / k)
exact <- function(x) cosh((L - x) / lam) / cosh(L / lam)
xu <- seq(0, L, length.out = 11)                 # uniform, h = 100 um
xg <- L * (0:10 / 10)^2                          # graded: 0, 10, 40, 90, ...
max(abs(fem1d(xu, D, k) - exact(xu)))
# [1] 0.06353851
max(abs(fem1d(xg, D, k) - exact(xg)))
# [1] 0.0138701

Same 10 elements, 4.6 times smaller error, by moving nodes to where u changes. The uniform mesh needs 20 elements (error 0.0169) to come close.


thomas() is the tridiagonal solver from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse, with the convention used in Implicit schemes and the method of lines: a, b, c, d all of length m, a[1] and c[m] unused. The Dirichlet value at x = 0 is removed from the unknowns and its column moved to the right-hand side, exactly as boundary values were handled in Part 10. The graded mesh x_i = L (i/N)^2 has its first element 10 um long and its last 190 um. The error is measured at the nodes against the exact cosh solution.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Refine where the solution changes


The uniform mesh puts one node inside the layer (x = 100 µm) and nine where u \approx 0. The graded mesh puts four nodes in the top 100 µm.


The right panel zooms in on the top 300 um. The uniform mesh misses the curvature of the profile at the surface and undershoots at 100 um (0.072 instead of 0.135). Where u is flat, long elements cost nothing in accuracy. In 1D a finite-difference code could also use a non-uniform grid (exercise B2 shows the formulas agree), so the 1D example only shows the mechanics; the real payoff of a mesh that follows the solution and the geometry comes in 2D and 3D, where a grid cannot be refined locally.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Error against number of elements


Both meshes are second order: doubling N divides the error by 4. Grading changes the constant, not the order.
The check is the one from Part 10: refine and watch the error fall at the expected rate. Real codes adapt the mesh automatically, refining where an error estimate is large.


Slope -2 on log-log axes, as for the second difference: piecewise linear elements have error of order h^2 in the values. On the graded mesh the first element is L/N^2 long, N times shorter than on the uniform mesh, and the error constant drops by a factor of about 4.5 at every N. Adaptive refinement (deal.II, COMSOL, FEniCS with error estimators) automates “put nodes where the error is”: solve, estimate the error per element, split the worst elements, solve again. Without an exact solution, compare successive refinements, as in the grid refinement slide of Implicit schemes and the method of lines.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
section: Failure: elements too long, negative drug
text:
Failure: elements too long, negative drug


With 4 elements (h = 250 µm) FEM returns u = -0.17 at 250 µm: a negative concentration. The off-diagonal -D/h + kh/6 turns positive once h > \sqrt6\,\lambda = 122 µm.
Check: look for negative or non-monotone values; keep h below ~\lambda in layers; refine and compare. Lumping (= FD) stays positive (0.037 vs exact 0.0067) but is still wrong.


The exact u at 250 um is 0.0067. With positive off-diagonals the matrix is no longer an M-matrix, and the discrete maximum principle (no new minima or maxima inside) is lost; the oscillation is the same kind of non-physical wiggle as central differences at high cell Péclet number in Flow plus diffusion. The fix is not a cleverer solver but a finer mesh where the solution changes over lengths shorter than h. Lumping restores the sign, at the price of a different (and here still large) error. In 2D the analogous warning sign is a mesh with very flat or very obtuse triangles; mesh generators report a quality measure for this.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Meshes in 2D: triangles


Triangles follow round walls; small triangles where the solution changes fast (near walls), large ones elsewhere. Same assembly loop, 3 × 3 element blocks.
Mesh generators (Gmsh, the meshers inside COMSOL) build this from a CAD drawing of the chip. The matrix is sparse but no longer banded: a sparse direct or iterative solver does the work.


This mesh has 2304 triangles, graded towards each pillar; a real mesher would make it less regular. The matrix has one row per node, and each row has as many non-zeros as the node has neighbours (about 7). It is solved with the sparse direct solvers of Steady state in two dimensions or, in 3D, with the iterative solvers of Iterative linear solvers in depth. Bad triangles (angles near 0 or 180 degrees) hurt accuracy and conditioning, so the first thing to look at in any simulation is the mesh.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Solving for the flow itself
So far the flow was given. To compute it, solve for velocity \mathbf u and pressure p: Navier–Stokes, mass + momentum.

Reynolds number Re = \rho U \ell/\mu: inertia against viscosity. Water (\rho = 1000 kg/m³, \mu = 10^{-3} Pa s) at U = 1 mm/s in a 100 µm channel: Re = 0.1.
At Re \ll 1 inertia drops out, leaving Stokes flow: \mu\nabla^2\mathbf u = \nabla p, \nabla\cdot\mathbf u = 0. Linear: no turbulence, flow follows walls smoothly, and reverses if the pressure reverses.
Numerically: three unknown fields coupled, the incompressibility constraint makes the linear system a saddle-point problem, and velocity and pressure need matched element types (e.g. quadratic velocity, linear pressure).


Navier–Stokes in words: mass is conserved (divergence of u is zero for water), and momentum changes by pressure forces, viscous friction and inertia (the nonlinear term u·grad u). Microfluidics lives at small Re, which is why the flow there is laminar and predictable: the T-sensor works because two streams flow side by side without mixing except by diffusion. Stokes flow is a linear system per solve, so it fits everything in Part 3. We do not solve 2D Stokes here: the saddle-point structure and the choice of element pairs are where library code earns its keep. Navier–Stokes at larger Re adds the nonlinear term, handled with Newton’s method from Newton for systems of equations.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Straight channel: the Poiseuille profile

In a long straight channel between walls w apart, Stokes reduces to 1D: -\mu u'' = G (pressure gradient G). Exact: u(y) = \frac{G}{2\mu}\,y\,(w - y), peak 1.5 × mean. Flow plus diffusion took this as given. Our 1D code, half channel, wall u(0) = 0, symmetry u'(w/2) = 0, w = 100 µm, mean 1000 µm/s:
fem1d(seq(0, 50, by = 10), D = 1, k = 0, f = 1.2, u0 = 0)   # f = G/mu = 12 * mean / w^2
# [1]    0  540  960 1260 1440 1500

These are exactly the values 0.6 y (100 - y): for this 1D problem linear elements happen to be exact at the nodes. The same flow in physical units needs G = 12 mu ubar / w^2 = 1200 Pa/m, about 1.2 Pa per mm of channel. In a rectangular channel of finite depth the profile is a series solution; around pillars or in a curved channel there is no formula, and that is the job for a 2D or 3D Stokes solver. Once the velocity field is computed it is fed into the advection-diffusion equation of Flow plus diffusion, on the same mesh; COMSOL calls this coupling “laminar flow” plus “transport of diluted species”.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
What the tools do
All of them: geometry → mesh → weak form → assemble → sparse solve → plots. They differ in how you talk to them.



Tool
What it is
Typical use




COMSOL Multiphysics
commercial, graphical, many physics modules
microfluidic chip design: draw or import the chip, flow + transport + heat


FEniCS / Firedrake
open source, Python; write the weak form almost as on paper
custom models, research codes, large parallel runs


scikit-fem
small pure-Python (numpy/scipy) library
learning, modest 2D problems


deal.II
C++ library, adaptive mesh refinement
large and adaptive simulations



Meshing: Gmsh. Finite-volume flow solvers: OpenFOAM, Ansys Fluent.

Mention, do not teach. COMSOL is what most microfluidics papers report for chip design, because it couples laminar flow, species transport and heat transfer in a graphical interface from a CAD drawing. FEniCS and Firedrake let you type the weak form (the K_ij formula of the weak form slide) in a Python-like language and generate the assembly code; scikit-fem does the same in plain numpy and is easy to install next to scipy. deal.II is for people writing their own large solvers. There is no mainstream finite element library in R; R users call Python or export results. Whatever the tool: it hides the same steps we did by hand, and it can go wrong in the same ways.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Summary

Square grids turn round walls into staircases, and refine everywhere at once.
Finite volumes: one balance per cell of any shape; conservation is exact.
Finite elements: u_h = \sum_j u_j\varphi_j with hat functions; the weak form needs only first derivatives and builds no-flux walls in; each element adds a small block to a sparse matrix (assembly).
On a uniform 1D mesh the FEM matrix is the finite-difference matrix. Its strength is freedom of the mesh: refine where the solution changes. Too-long elements across a layer give negative concentrations.
At low Reynolds number the flow obeys the linear Stokes equations; in a straight channel the answer is the Poiseuille parabola. Around pillars it must be computed.
COMSOL, FEniCS / Firedrake, scikit-fem and deal.II do mesh → assemble → solve; check them with mesh refinement, conservation and a 1D special case.

Next: Iterative linear solvers in depth, for the large sparse systems that 2D and 3D meshes produce.

The one idea to keep: finite elements are not a different kind of mathematics, they are the same sparse linear algebra on a mesh that follows the geometry and the solution. Everything students learned about checking a finite-difference solution applies unchanged. The next further-reading unit is about how such systems are solved when they are too big for a direct solve.
crumbs: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow

title: Quiz: stiffness and implicit methods
Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a gradient and a Hessian by hand for a function of two variables, and check a coded gradient against finite differences,
decide from the Hessian whether a point with zero gradient is a minimum, a maximum or a saddle,
take steepest descent steps with an exact and with a backtracking (Armijo) line search, and predict from the condition number how slow steepest descent will be,
take a Newton step for minimisation, and recognise when the Hessian is not positive definite,
explain what the BFGS update does and why it needs only gradients, and do one Nelder–Mead move by hand,
fit a 4-parameter logistic dose–response curve with your own methods and with optim / scipy.optimize.minimize / argmin, and detect the usual failures: a wrong gradient, bad scaling, a bad start.

The by-hand part needs pen and paper (a calculator helps in B7). The code part uses the dose–response data from the lecture.

title: Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute a gradient and a Hessian by hand for a function of two variables, and check a coded gradient against finite differences,
decide from the Hessian whether a point with zero gradient is a minimum, a maximum or a saddle,
take steepest descent steps with an exact and with a backtracking (Armijo) line search, and predict from the condition number how slow steepest descent will be,
take a Newton step for minimisation, and recognise when the Hessian is not positive definite,
explain what the BFGS update does and why it needs only gradients, and do one Nelder–Mead move by hand,
fit a 4-parameter logistic dose–response curve with your own methods and with optim / scipy.optimize.minimize / argmin, and detect the usual failures: a wrong gradient, bad scaling, a bad start.

The by-hand part needs pen and paper (a calculator helps in B7). The code part uses the dose–response data from the lecture.

title: Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
By hand
B1. Gradient and Hessian. Let \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1^2 - 2x_1x_2 + 2x_2^2 - 2x_2\). (a) Compute \(\nabla f\) and evaluate it at \((0, 0)\) and at \((3, 1)\). (b) Compute the Hessian \(H\). Does it depend on \(\mathbf x\)? (c) Find the point where \(\nabla f = \mathbf 0\). (d) Is it a minimum? Use the determinant and trace, then find the eigenvalues of \(H\) and its condition number \(\kappa\). (e) Take one Newton step from \((0, 0)\). Where do you land, and why?
B2. Minimum, maximum or saddle? Let \(f(x, y) = x^3 - 3x + y^2\). (a) Find all points with \(\nabla f = \mathbf 0\). (b) Classify each with the Hessian. (c) Take one Newton step from \((-0.5, 1)\). Does it move towards the minimum? Is \(\nabla f^\mathsf T\mathbf s < 0\) (a descent direction)?
B3. Steepest descent zig-zags. Let \(f(\mathbf x) = \tfrac12(x_1^2 + 9x_2^2)\), start \(\mathbf x_0 = (9, 1)\). (a) Give \(H\) and \(\kappa\). (b) For a quadratic \(f = \tfrac12\mathbf x^\mathsf T H\mathbf x\), the exact line search step along \(-\mathbf g\) is \(\alpha = \mathbf g^\mathsf T\mathbf g / \mathbf g^\mathsf T H\mathbf g\). Take two steepest-descent steps with exact line search. (c) Show that the two search directions are perpendicular. (d) By what factor did the distance to the minimum shrink per step? Compare with \((\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)\). (e) How many steps does it take to reduce the distance by \(10^6\)? How many does Newton need?
B4. Backtracking by hand. Same \(f\) and \(\mathbf x_0 = (9, 1)\). Run the Armijo rule with \(c = 10^{-4}\): try \(\alpha = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \ldots\) and stop at the first \(\alpha\) with \(f(\mathbf x_0 - \alpha\mathbf g) \le f(\mathbf x_0) - c\,\alpha\,\|\mathbf g\|^2\). Which \(\alpha\) is accepted, and how does the new \(f\) compare with the exact line search of B3?
B5. A fixed step size. Same \(f\), steepest descent with a fixed \(\alpha\). (a) Show that each component evolves separately: \(x_{1,k+1} = (1-\alpha)x_{1,k}\), \(x_{2,k+1} = (1-9\alpha)x_{2,k}\). (b) For which \(\alpha\) does the iteration converge? Relate the bound to the largest eigenvalue of \(H\). (c) Which \(\alpha\) makes the slower of the two factors as small as possible, and what is that factor?
B6. The BFGS secant condition. Same \(f\). The first BFGS step (with \(B_0 = I\) and exact line search) is the first steepest-descent step of B3: \(\mathbf s = (-1.8, -1.8)\). (a) Compute \(\mathbf y = \nabla f(\mathbf x_1) - \nabla f(\mathbf x_0)\) and \(\mathbf y^\mathsf T\mathbf s\). (b) Show that for any \(B_0\), the update \(B_1 = V^\mathsf TB_0V + \rho\,\mathbf s\mathbf s^\mathsf T\) with \(V = I - \rho\,\mathbf y\mathbf s^\mathsf T\), \(\rho = 1/\mathbf y^\mathsf T\mathbf s\) satisfies \(B_1\mathbf y = \mathbf s\). (Hint: compute \(V\mathbf y\) first.) (c) In one variable, what does \(B_1 y = s\) say? Which method from Newton and secant methods is this?
B7. Units and the condition number. At the best 4PL fit with dose in µM, the diagonal of the SSE Hessian is \((16.0,\ 14.4,\ 3611.5,\ 3701.6)\) for (bottom, top, EC50, hill). (a) If EC50 is measured in nM instead (\(q = 1000\,\mathrm{EC50}\)), how do \(\partial\,\mathrm{SSE}/\partial q\) and \(\partial^2\mathrm{SSE}/\partial q^2\) relate to the µM versions? (Chain rule.) (b) Use the ratio of the largest to the smallest diagonal entry as a rough guess for \(\kappa\), in µM and in nM. (The true values are 550 and \(1.9\times10^6\).) (c) R’s optim takes finite-difference gradient steps of \(10^{-3}\) in every parameter. What is that as a relative change of EC50 = 1271 nM, and of hill = 1.24? (d) What happens to \(\partial^2\mathrm{SSE}/\partial p^2\) for EC50 if you fit \(\ell = \log_{10}\mathrm{EC50}\) instead (at the minimum)? Use \(d\,\mathrm{EC50}/d\ell = \ln(10)\,\mathrm{EC50}\).
B8. Nelder–Mead by hand. Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2\) and the simplex \((1, 1), (2, 1), (1, 2)\). (a) Evaluate \(f\) at the three points; which is the worst? (b) Reflect the worst point through the centroid of the other two. Is the reflection accepted? (c) Do a second move: identify the new worst point, reflect, and decide whether to expand.

title: Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
In code
C1. Check the gradient. (a) Compare grad_sse(p0) with a forward-difference gradient (step \(h_j = \sqrt\varepsilon\max(|p_j|, 1)\)) and with numDeriv::grad (Python: approx_fprime; Rust: central differences). Print the relative error of each component. Which is more accurate? (b) Write grad_bad, a copy of grad_sse in which the factor \(h\) (hill) is missing in \(\partial m/\partial\mathrm{EC50}\). Compare it with a finite-difference gradient at \(\mathbf p_0\) and at \(\mathbf p_1 = (5, 95, 2, 1.5)\). Why does the check at \(\mathbf p_0\) not see the bug? (c) Now flip the sign of the log in \(\partial m/\partial h\) and give that gradient to BFGS (optim(p0, sse, grad_sign, method = "BFGS")). What SSE does it return, and does it report success?
C2. Zig-zag and the condition number. Write sd_armijo(f, g, x) (steepest descent with backtracking, stop when \(\|\mathbf g\| < 10^{-8}\)). Run it on \(f = \tfrac12(x_1^2 + \kappa x_2^2)\) from \((1, 1)\) for \(\kappa = 1, 10, 100, 1000\). Count the steps and compare with \(\log(10^{-8})/\log\frac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\).
C3. Steepest descent on the 4PL, and the Hessian. (a) Run sd_armijo on the SSE from \(\mathbf p_0\) with tolerance \(10^{-4}\). How many steps? (b) Compute the Hessian at the result as the forward-difference Jacobian of grad_sse (as in Newton for systems of equations). How symmetric is it? (c) Find its eigenvalues and \(\kappa\). Is the point a minimum? How many steps does \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\) predict for 6 digits?
C4. Newton. (a) Write Newton with backtracking (Hessian = Jacobian of the gradient; R: numDeriv::jacobian). From \(\mathbf p_0\), print the SSE and \(\|\nabla\mathrm{SSE}\|\) at each step. Is the convergence quadratic? (b) Start from \((0, 100, 10, 1)\). Print the eigenvalues of the Hessian. Then take 20 pure Newton steps (no line search). Where do you end? (c) Make the Hessian positive definite before each solve: if its smallest eigenvalue \(\lambda_{\min} \le 0\), add \((10^{-3}\max_i|H_{ii}| - \lambda_{\min})\,I\). How many steps from \((0, 100, 10, 1)\) now?
C5. BFGS, yours and the library’s. Write bfgs(f, g, x) as on the lecture slide. Count the calls of the SSE and of the gradient (wrap them in functions that increment a counter). Compare with optim(p0, sse, grad_sse, method = "BFGS") (Python: minimize(..., jac=grad_sse, method="BFGS"); Rust: argmin’s BFGS with MoreThuenteLineSearch). In R, also run optim with control = list(reltol = 1e-12): why does the default stop at a slightly higher SSE?
C6. Library methods, units and scaling. (a) Fit the 4PL from \(\mathbf p_0\) with Nelder–Mead, BFGS, CG and L-BFGS-B, without a gradient function. Print the SSE, EC50, the number of function calls and the convergence code. (b) Multiply the doses by 1000 (nM). Fit with BFGS from \((0, 100, 1, 1)\) (“EC50 is about 1”) and from \((0, 100, 1000, 1)\). Then repeat the second fit with parscale = c(1, 100, 1000, 1) (Python and Rust: optimise \(\mathbf q = \mathbf p / \text{scale}\)). (c) Fit \(\log_{10}\mathrm{EC50}\) instead of EC50 (dose in nM, start 3). Compare the number of calls.
C7. The growth curve from Why numerical analysis?. The data: OD at t_min = seq(0, 1440, by = 120) minutes, od = c(0.001, 0.047, 0.139, 0.282, 0.581, 0.859, 1.049, 1.161, 1.152, 1.217, 1.182, 1.176, 1.185), model \(N(t) = K/(1 + (K/N_0 - 1)e^{-rt})\), start \((r, K, N_0) = (0.5, 1, 0.05)\). (a) Compute the gradient of the SSE at the start, time in minutes. (b) Fit with Nelder–Mead and BFGS, with time in minutes and in hours. Which fits are right? (c) (R) Compare the condition number of the Hessian at the good fit in minutes and in hours.
C8. Multistart. Fit the 4PL from the 15 starts bottom = 0, top = 100, EC50 \(\in \{0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100\}\), hill \(\in \{0.5, 1, 3\}\), once with Nelder–Mead and once with BFGS with the analytic gradient. How many reach SSE = 314.92? Do the failures say so?

title: Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — gradients and Hessians by hand (B1, B2)





Differentiate with respect to one variable while treating the other as a constant. The Hessian is the matrix of derivatives of the two gradient components: row \(i\) = derivatives of \(\partial f/\partial x_i\). For a \(2\times2\) symmetric matrix the eigenvalues are \(\tfrac12\left(\operatorname{tr} \pm \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}^2 - 4\det}\right)\). A Newton step solves \(H\mathbf s = -\nabla f\); for a \(2\times 2\) matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac1{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}\).









Hint 2 — line searches (B3, B4, B5)





For \(f = \tfrac12(x_1^2 + 9x_2^2)\): \(\mathbf g = (x_1, 9x_2)\) and \(\mathbf g^\mathsf TH\mathbf g = g_1^2 + 9g_2^2\). For B5, the iteration in each component is \(x \leftarrow (1 - \alpha\lambda)x\) with \(\lambda\) the curvature in that direction; it converges if \(|1 - \alpha\lambda| < 1\).









Hint 3 — BFGS (B6, C5)





\(V\mathbf y = \mathbf y - \rho\,\mathbf y(\mathbf s^\mathsf T\mathbf y)\) and \(\rho\,\mathbf s^\mathsf T\mathbf y = 1\). In code, outer(s, s) (Python np.outer) is the matrix \(\mathbf s\mathbf s^\mathsf T\). Skip the update when \(\mathbf y^\mathsf T\mathbf s \le 0\).









Hint 4 — checking a gradient (C1)





Compare component by component, relative to the size of each component. A forward difference is good to about \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-8}\) relative, numDeriv::grad (Richardson extrapolation, see Numerical differentiation) to about \(10^{-10}\). A bug gives errors of order \(10^{-1}\) or 1. Check at a “generic” point: one where no parameter is 0 or 1.









Hint 5 — the Hessian and its eigenvalues (C3, C4)





R: eigen(H, symmetric = TRUE)$values, solve(H, -g). Python: np.linalg.eigvalsh (ascending order), np.linalg.solve. Rust: nalgebra::SymmetricEigen, DMatrix::lu().solve. Symmetrise a finite-difference Hessian with \((H + H^\mathsf T)/2\) before taking eigenvalues.









Hint 6 — library calls (C5–C8)





optim returns par, value, counts (calls of fn and gr, not counting finite-difference calls) and convergence (0 = a stopping rule was met, 1 = maxit reached). minimize returns x, fun, nfev, njev, success, message. In argmin, the starting point goes in configure(|s| s.param(...)), BFGS also needs inv_hessian (start with the identity), and Nelder–Mead needs the whole starting simplex. Python has no parscale: write lambda q: sse_nM(q * scale) and start from p / scale.

title: Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Where this leads

Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting (Part 9): the SSE has extra structure: its Hessian is approximately \(2J^\mathsf TJ\), built from the same model Jacobian as the gradient. That gives Gauss–Newton, and adding \(\mu I\) (as in C4(c)) gives Levenberg–Marquardt, the method behind nls, minpack.lm and scipy.optimize.least_squares. There we also fit ODE models, use log-parameters for positive rates, and multistart systematically.
Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (Part 9): the Hessian at the minimum (C3) gives standard errors of the fitted parameters; a near-zero eigenvalue means a direction the data cannot pin down.
Constraints and linear programming (Part 9): bounds (as in L-BFGS-B) and general constraints.
Our line searches only enforce sufficient decrease (Armijo). Library codes add a curvature condition (Wolfe) and interpolate the step; trust-region methods replace the line search altogether. We use those through the libraries rather than writing them.

title: Fourier series and the FFT
section: Try it: sampling, aliasing and leakage
text:
Try it: sampling, aliasing and leakage




Live in the browser: the clock gene 8 + 1.5 cos(2 pi (t - 6)/24), optionally plus a fast rhythm cos(2 pi t / Pu), sampled every Delta t over the chosen duration; the DFT is computed directly in JS. Top: true signal (grey), samples (blue), and the Fourier curve through the samples (orange dashed, the trigonometric interpolant). Bottom: amplitude 2|X_k|/n against cycles per day, Nyquist as a black line, grey beyond it. Start on “course data”: with noise sd 0.3 the samples are exactly the 24 values of the lecture, and the readout gives 8.045, amplitude 1.465, peak 6.45 h, as fft() did. Click “+ 4.8 h, every 2 h”: a second peak at 5 per day = 4.8 h, below Nyquist (6 per day), 24-h bin still 1.5 at 6 h. Click “every 4 h”: Nyquist drops to 3 per day, the purple arrow folds 5 per day onto 1 per day, the orange curve is a smooth 24-h wave through the samples, and the 24-h bin now reads 1.80 with peak 3.75 h: confident and wrong. Drag the sampling interval to 3 h: the alias moves to 8 h. Then “leakage”: a 25.5-h rhythm over 120 h on a log scale, energy in every bin; tick Hann window and the far bins fall by orders of magnitude (12-h bin from 0.07 to 0.003). Note the orange curve jumping back at the end of the record: the wrap-around. Last, “low-pass”: noisy trace sd 1, keep periods of 8 h and more; rms error 0.97 -> 0.41; drag the cut-off to 24 h (0.24) and to 48 h (1.07: the rhythm itself is removed).

title: Exercise: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write one backward Euler and one Crank–Nicolson step for the diffusion equation as a tridiagonal system, solve it by hand for three unknowns and in code with the Thomas algorithm,
compute the growth factor of each scheme for a Fourier mode and use it to explain unconditional stability, and why Crank–Nicolson oscillates after a sharp start,
verify a solver against an exact solution (a decaying sine mode) and read the order in time and in space from error ratios; recognise an error floor and lucky cancellation,
estimate the order by grid refinement when there is no exact solution,
hand the grid to a stiff ODE solver (method of lines) and tell it that the Jacobian is banded,
answer two microfluidic heat questions: how sharp a temperature step a Drosophila embryo feels between a cold and a warm stream [M1, M2], and why the wall of a PCR chip should be thin and not made of PDMS [H1, H2].

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator. The code part checks the hand answers and then goes to grids where only code works.

title: Exercise: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
By hand
B1. Implicit steps by hand. The chamber with \(N = 4\) (\(\Delta x = 125\) µm), empty at \(t = 0\), source \(c_0 = 1\), sink \(c_4 = 0\), \(r = 1\) (\(\Delta t = 15.6\) s). (a) The lecture gives the first backward Euler step: \(\mathbf c^1 = \tfrac1{21}(8, 3, 1)\). Write the system for the second step and solve it with Thomas (keep fractions or use 4 decimals). (b) Do one Crank–Nicolson step from the empty channel with \(r = 1\). Write the \(3\times3\) system first. (c) The exact values at \(t = 15.6\) s are \((0.480, 0.157, 0.034)\) and at \(t = 31.25\) s \((0.617, 0.315, 0.121)\). Which scheme is closer after one step? Is either of them accurate?
B2. Growth factors. (a) Fill in the growth factor of the zigzag mode (\(z = 4r\)) for \(r = 0.25, 1, 10, 100\) for FTCS, backward Euler, Crank–Nicolson and the exact solution. (b) A zigzag of amplitude 1 is present at \(t = 0\). How large is it after 10 Crank–Nicolson steps with \(r = 100\)? After 10 backward Euler steps? (c) The slowest mode of the chamber decays at rate \(0.0395\) per s. With \(\Delta t = 4\) s, compute \(z\) and the three factors (exact, backward Euler, Crank–Nicolson). What is left of that mode after 15 steps (60 s) in each case? (d) Which scheme is best for the slow mode and which for the zigzag? What does that suggest for a sharp start?
B3. What a step costs. The embryo grid of the lecture: \(N = 200\) (\(\Delta x = 2.5\) µm), \(D = 1.4\times10^5\) µm²/s, simulate 1 s. (a) FTCS needs \(\Delta t \le \Delta x^2/(2D)\). How many steps, and roughly how many operations at about 5 per grid point per step? (b) Backward Euler with \(\Delta t = 5\) ms and Thomas (about 8 operations per point): how many operations? (c) Same, but with a dense solve, \(\tfrac23 N^3\) per step. And if you factorise once and reuse the factors (\(2N^2\) per step for the two triangular solves)? (d) Repeat (a) and (b) for \(\Delta x = 0.25\) µm.
B4. Reading orders. On the sine-mode test (fine grid, \(N = 400\)), Crank–Nicolson gives error \(4.22\times10^{-4}\) at \(\Delta t = 3\) s and \(1.04\times10^{-4}\) at \(\Delta t = 1.5\) s; backward Euler gives \(2.06\times10^{-2}\) at \(\Delta t = 3\) s. (a) What is the observed order of Crank–Nicolson? Predict its error at \(\Delta t = 0.75\) s. (b) On the coarse grid \(N = 50\) the space error is about \(1.2\times10^{-4}\). What happens to the Crank–Nicolson error there if you keep halving \(\Delta t\) below 1.5 s? (c) How small must \(\Delta t\) be for backward Euler to reach an error of \(10^{-4}\), and how many steps is that up to \(t = 30\) s? Compare with Crank–Nicolson.
B5. The embryo between two streams. Model of the lecture: \(\partial T/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 T/\partial x^2 + (T_\text{out} - T)/\tau\), \(\tau = R^2/(2.405^2 D)\), steady length scale \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\). (a) Compute \(\tau\) and \(\lambda\) for \(R = 100\) µm and water. (b) The steady profile on the warm side is \(T = 27 - 3.5\,e^{-d/\lambda}\) at distance \(d\) from the middle. Show that the 10–90 % width (20.7 °C to 26.3 °C) is \(2\lambda\ln 5\) and compute it. What fraction of the 500 µm embryo is that? (c) Show that \(\lambda = R/2.405\). Would a medium with half the thermal diffusivity make the step sharper? What would change? (d) How long does the profile take to form (about \(4\tau\))? Why may [M1] treat the temperature inside the embryo as steady during development?
B6. The wall of a PCR chip. A chip sits on a heater; heat reaches the sample channel through a wall of thickness \(H\). Values as in [H1]: PDMS \(k = 0.15\) W/(m K), \(\rho = 970\) kg/m³, \(c_p = 1460\) J/(kg K); glass \(k = 1.1\), \(\rho = 2200\), \(c_p = 700\) (approximate; real glasses and PDMS mixes vary). (a) Compute the thermal diffusivity of each in m²/s and in mm²/s. (b) The heater jumps from 65 °C to 95 °C (annealing to denaturation). With an insulated channel side, the slowest mode decays with time constant \(4H^2/(\pi^2 D)\) and the channel-side temperature lags by about \(\tfrac{4}{\pi}\cdot 30\,e^{-t\pi^2D/(4H^2)}\) °C. How long until it is within 0.5 °C of 95 °C, for \(H = 1\) and 2 mm, PDMS and glass? (c) Now the channel side loses heat to air, \(h \approx 10\) W/(m² K), air at 25 °C. At steady state the profile is linear; balance the conducted flux \(k(95 - T_\text{top})/H\) with the loss \(h(T_\text{top} - 25)\) and find the temperature drop \(95 - T_\text{top}\) for each case. (d) A denaturation step lasts 15–30 s. Which designs work?

title: Exercise: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
In code
C1. Backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson. (a) Check your answers to B1 with be_step and cn_step on the vector c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0). (b) On the chamber (\(N = 50\)), run both schemes to \(t = 60\) s with \(\Delta t = 4\), 1 and 0.25 s, and print the largest error against exact. Which scheme wins at which step? Why is Crank–Nicolson worse at \(\Delta t = 4\) s?
C2. Verification against an exact sine mode. (a) Write sine_err(N, dt, step): start from \(\sin(\pi x/L)\) with both ends at 0, take step up to \(t = 30\) s, and return the largest error against fact 6. (b) With \(N = 400\), halve \(\Delta t\) from 6 s down to 0.094 s. Print the errors of both schemes and the observed orders \(\log_2(e_{k}/e_{k+1})\). Plot error against \(\Delta t\) on log–log axes. (c) Repeat Crank–Nicolson with \(N = 50\). Where is the floor? Explain the one point that is far below the floor. (d) Fix \(\Delta t = 0.01\) s and refine space, \(N = 10, 20, \dots, 160\). Observed order?
C3. Crank–Nicolson after a sharp start. Chamber, \(N = 50\), empty at \(t = 0\), \(\Delta t = 4\) s (\(r = 40\)). (a) Record \(c\) at \(x = 10\) µm after each of 15 Crank–Nicolson steps. Describe what you see. (b) Write two checks that catch it automatically: the number of sign changes of the step-to-step increments, and values above the source concentration. (c) Try two fixes and compare the error at \(t = 60\) s: (i) four backward Euler steps of 1 s, then Crank–Nicolson with 4 s; (ii) Crank–Nicolson with \(\Delta t = 0.4\) s.
C4. Method of lines. The chamber on a fine grid, \(N = 200\) (\(\Delta x = 2.5\) µm), from empty to \(t = 60\) s. The interior points obey \(\mathbf c' = \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A\mathbf c + \mathbf b\). (a) Write the right-hand side (pad the vector with the boundary values 1 and 0 and take a second difference). In R solve it with ode.1D and lsoda, bdf and ode45; in Python with solve_ivp and "BDF" (with jac_sparsity), "LSODA" (with lband = uband = 1) and "RK45". Report steps, right-hand-side evaluations and the largest error against exact. (b) Now set rtol = atol = 1e-10 and compare \(N = 50\) with \(N = 200\). What limits the error in each case? (c) Rust: ode_solvers has only explicit solvers. Run its Dopri5 on the same system and compare with your own Crank–Nicolson (four backward Euler start steps, then \(\Delta t = 0.25\) s).
C5. How sharp is the step inside the embryo? Use the model of B5 with \(L = 500\) µm, nodes \(x_i = i\,L/N\), no flux through the tips, \(T_\text{out} = 20\) °C for \(x < L/2\), 27 °C for \(x > L/2\) and 23.5 °C at the middle node. (a) The steady state solves \(T_i - \lambda^2\,\frac{T_{i-1} - 2T_i + T_{i+1}}{\Delta x^2} = T_{\text{out},i}\) (backward Euler with \(\Delta t \to \infty\)). Write embryo_steady(N, R) that solves it with one call to thomas (end rows from fact 8). (b) For \(N = 200\) compute \(\tau\), \(\lambda\) and the 10–90 % width (interpolate the crossing of 20.7 and 26.3 °C with approxfun / np.interp). Compare with B5 and with the formula profile. (c) Grid refinement: the temperature at \(x = 200\) µm for \(N = 25, 50, 100, 200, 400\). Compute the ratios of successive differences. Observed order? Which pair do you ignore, and why? (d) Widths for \(R = 50\), 100 and 150 µm. Compare with B5(c).
C6. Heat through the wall of a PCR chip. Nodes \(z_i = i\,H/N\), \(N = 50\); \(z_0\) is the heater (fixed temperature), \(z_N\) the channel side. Start at 65 °C everywhere; at \(t = 0\) the heater jumps to 95 °C. Backward Euler, \(\Delta t = 0.05\) s. (a) Insulated channel side (\(h = 0\)): the time until the channel side reaches 94.5 °C, for PDMS and glass, \(H = 1\) and 2 mm. Compare with B6(b). (b) Heat loss to air with \(h = 10\) W/(m² K) (fact 8; careful with mm and m): run 600 s and report the steady drop \(95 - T_\text{top}\). Compare with B6(c).

title: Exercise: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — the implicit systems (B1, C1)





Write one equation per interior point with the unknowns \(c_1, c_2, c_3\) on the left. Known values (the old level and the boundary values \(c_0 = 1\), \(c_4 = 0\)) go to the right. For Crank–Nicolson the right-hand side contains the explicit half: at \(i = 1\) it is \(c_1^n + \tfrac r2(c_0 - 2c_1^n + c_2^n)\), plus \(\tfrac r2 c_0\) for the boundary on the new level. Thomas by hand: \(w = a_i/b_{i-1}\), \(b_i \leftarrow b_i - w\,c_{i-1}\), \(d_i \leftarrow d_i - w\,d_{i-1}\), then back substitution.









Hint 2 — growth factors and cost (B2, B3)





After \(n\) steps a mode is multiplied by \(g^n\). \(|g| < 1\) means it shrinks; a negative \(g\) means it flips sign every step. For the cost, count steps = simulated time / \(\Delta t\), then multiply by the work per step.









Hint 3 — orders (B4, C2)





Error \(\approx C\,\Delta t^p\), so halving \(\Delta t\) divides it by \(2^p\), and \(p = \log_2(e(\Delta t)/e(\Delta t/2))\). In R use log2, in Python np.log2. When two error contributions have opposite sign, their sum can be accidentally small at one step size: always look at a sequence, never at one run. Plot with plot(..., log = "xy") (R) or plt.loglog (Python).









Hint 4 — oscillation checks (C3)





diff(c1) gives the increments, sign() their signs, and a second diff of the signs is non-zero wherever the direction changes. Python: np.diff, np.sign. A smooth filling curve has no sign changes at all.









Hint 5 — method of lines (C4)





R: diff(x, differences = 2) or diff(diff(x)) is the second difference. ode.1D(y, times, func, parms, nspec = 1, method = ...) returns a matrix whose first column is time; attr(out, "istate")[2:3] are steps and function evaluations. Increase maxsteps for ode45. Python: np.diff(x, 2); pass jac_sparsity=scipy.sparse.diags([1, 1, 1], [-1, 0, 1], shape=(n, n)) (scipy.sparse.diags) to "BDF", and lband=1, uband=1 to "LSODA"; sol.t.size - 1 steps, sol.nfev evaluations. Rust: ode_solvers accepts a DVector<f64> state.









Hint 6 — the embryo and the wall (B5, B6, C5, C6)





On the warm side, \(27 - 3.5e^{-d/\lambda} = 26.3\) gives \(e^{-d/\lambda} = 0.2\). For the wall, \(\ln(120/(0.5\pi)) = 4.34\). With heat loss the last row of backward Euler is \(-2r\,T_{N-1} + (1 + 2r + r\beta)\,T_N = T_N^\text{old} + r\beta\,T_\text{air}\) with \(\beta = 2\Delta z\,h/k\); \(h/k\) is in 1/m, so with \(\Delta z\) in mm divide by 1000. The no-flux rows of embryo_steady have \(-2s\) next to the diagonal, \(s = (\lambda/\Delta x)^2\).

title: Exercise: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Where this leads

Steady state in two dimensions (next unit): drop time completely and solve $D^2 c = $ sources in one step, as embryo_steady did in 1D. In 2D the matrix is sparse but no longer tridiagonal.
Flow plus diffusion: adding flow gives a non-symmetric matrix and new failure modes (numerical diffusion, wiggles); backward Euler with one Thomas solve per step carries over, as the step that marches the flow down a channel.
Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation: the exchange term of the embryo is a linear reaction; with nonlinear reactions one treats diffusion implicitly (one Thomas solve) and the reaction explicitly. The decay length \(\sqrt{D/k}\) returns for morphogen gradients, including the Drosophila experiment of [M1].
Iterative linear solvers in depth (optional): when a 2D or 3D grid is too large for a direct solve at each implicit step.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
About this lecture
FTCS is simple, but its time step must shrink with the square of the grid spacing. On a fine grid that means millions of steps for a few seconds of biology. Implicit schemes remove the limit.

Backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson for the diffusion equation: one tridiagonal solve per step, O(N) work with the Thomas algorithm.
Stable for every \Delta t. But Crank–Nicolson oscillates when the data are sharp and the step is large.
Accuracy: O(\Delta t) (backward Euler) or O(\Delta t^2) (Crank–Nicolson) in time, O(\Delta x^2) in space. Verify with an exact solution and with grid refinement.
Method of lines: the grid turns the PDE into a large, stiff ODE system; give it to lsoda or bdf.
Biology: a Drosophila embryo held between a cold and a warm stream [M1, M2]. How sharp is the temperature step inside it?


Second unit of Part 10. Everything here is assembled from earlier parts: the chamber, the grid and FTCS from The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences; the Thomas algorithm from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse; backward Euler, stiffness and BDF from Stiffness and implicit methods. The new things are Crank–Nicolson, the separation of time and space errors, and the habit of verifying a PDE solver before believing it. The biology switches from concentration to temperature: same equation, different D.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
A biology problem first


Two laminar streams, 20 °C and 27 °C, flow past a live embryo, one on each half [M1]. The warm half develops faster: even-skipped stripes appear out of order.
Heat crosses 500 µm of water in about a second, so why does the embryo not just settle at the average? How sharp is the step inside it?


[M1] Lucchetta, Lee, Fu, Patel and Ismagilov (2005), Nature 434: 1134–1138. [M2] Lucchetta, Munson and Ismagilov (2006), Lab on a Chip 6: 185–190, characterised the same device. Numbers from [M2]: channel 850 µm wide, embryo about 500 × 200 × 200 µm, inlet temperatures 20 and 27 °C, mean flow 5 cm/s. [M2] also estimates the time for heat to cross the embryo, x^2 / (2 D), as about 0.9 s for cytoplasm approximated by water, and solved the full 3D flow and heat problem with a commercial finite-element package; their simulated profile inside the embryo is step-like. We build a much cruder 1D model of our own. Its numbers are ours, not the paper’s.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Explicit is too slow here
Heat obeys the diffusion equation \partial T/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 T/\partial x^2, with D the thermal diffusivity; water: D \approx 1.4\times10^{-7} m²/s = 1.4\times10^{5} µm²/s, 140 times a small molecule.
D  <- 1.4e-7 * 1e12             # µm^2/s
L  <- 500; N <- 200; dx <- L / N # embryo, 2.5 µm grid
dx^2 / (2 * D)                  # FTCS limit on dt (s)
# [1] 2.232143e-05
L^2 / D                         # time scale L^2/D (s)
# [1] 1.785714
(L^2 / D) / (dx^2 / (2 * D))    # FTCS steps to cover it
# [1] 80000

22 µs steps for a process that takes a second; halve \Delta x and it is 4 × as many steps.


The thermal diffusivity is k / (rho c_p): conductivity 0.6 W/(m K), density 1000 kg/m^3, heat capacity 4180 J/(kg K) give 1.4e-7 m^2/s, the value [M2] uses for water. Heat diffuses about 100 times faster than a small molecule, which is why temperature steps are hard to keep sharp on a chip. 2.5 µm is not an extravagant grid: the transition we look for turns out to be about 130 µm wide, and we want 50 points across it. The FTCS limit r <= 1/2 is from the previous unit. The number of steps grows like N^2 for a fixed simulated time: 80 000 here, 320 000 at 1.25 µm. In 2D (Steady state in two dimensions) the limit is even stricter.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Recap: FTCS and its limit
On the chamber of The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences, with r = D\,\Delta t/\Delta x^2:
c_i^{n+1} = c_i^n + r\,\bigl(c_{i-1}^n - 2c_i^n + c_{i+1}^n\bigr) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \mathbf c^{n+1} = (I + rA)\,\mathbf c^n + \dots

A is tridiagonal (1, -2, 1). Its eigenvalues run from \approx -\pi^2\Delta x^2/L^2 (slow, the biology) to \approx -4 (the zigzag).
Each FTCS step multiplies a mode by 1 - 4r\sin^2(\theta/2). For the zigzag that is 1 - 4r: stable only if r \le 1/2.
The zigzag is gone in milliseconds, but it sets the step: the system is stiff.


One slide only: everything here was derived in the previous unit (L = 500 µm, D = 1000 µm^2/s, N = 50, dx = 10 µm, source c = 1 at x = 0, sink c = 0 at x = L). The grid is also the same: nodes x_i = i dx, i = 0..N, the boundary values sit on the two end nodes and the N - 1 interior nodes are the unknowns; units µm and s. theta is the wavenumber of the mode times dx, from 0 (smooth) to pi (zigzag). The dots stand for the boundary values, which enter the first and last equations. The stiffness argument is the one from Stiffness and implicit methods: the explicit step is set by the fastest mode, which we do not care about, rather than by the slow one we do care about. The remedy there was backward Euler.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Backward Euler for diffusion
Take the second difference at the new time level:
c_i^{n+1} = c_i^n + r\,\bigl(c_{i-1}^{n+1} - 2c_i^{n+1} + c_{i+1}^{n+1}\bigr)
Collect the unknowns on the left:
-r\,c_{i-1}^{n+1} + (1 + 2r)\,c_i^{n+1} - r\,c_{i+1}^{n+1} = c_i^n \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad (I - rA)\,\mathbf c^{n+1} = \mathbf c^n + \mathbf b

Every step is a linear system. The matrix is tridiagonal, diagonally dominant, the same every step.
\mathbf b: the boundary values, r\,c_0 in the first row and r\,c_N in the last.
Linear problem, so no Newton iteration (unlike the enzyme in Stiffness and implicit methods).


This is backward Euler from Stiffness and implicit methods applied to the ODE system c’ = (D / dx^2) A c + boundary terms: y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(y_{n+1}), and f is linear, so the “Newton solve” is a single linear solve with matrix I - h J = I - r A. Diagonal dominance: 1 + 2r > r + r, so Thomas needs no pivoting (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse). The matrix is also symmetric positive definite. Because it does not change from step to step, one could even factorise it once and reuse the factors; with Thomas the factorisation costs as much as the solve, so we simply call it every step.

text:
Backward Euler by hand
The chamber with N = 4 (\Delta x = 125 µm), empty at t = 0, source c_0 = 1, sink c_4 = 0. One step with r = 1 (\Delta t = 15.6 s):
\begin{pmatrix} 3 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 + 1\cdot 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mathbf c^1 = \tfrac{1}{21}(8, 3, 1) = (0.381, 0.143, 0.048)

One implicit step reaches all points at once and stays between 0 and 1. FTCS overshoots to the source value and would then explode.


Thomas by hand (as in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse): w = -1/3, b2 = 3 - 1/3 = 8/3, d2 = 1/3; w = -3/8, b3 = 3 - 3/8 = 21/8, d3 = 1/8; back substitution c3 = (1/8) / (21/8) = 1/21, c2 = (1/3 + 1/21) / (8/3) = 1/7 = 3/21, c1 = (1 + 3/21) / 3 = 8/21. The exact values come from the Fourier series of the previous unit. Backward Euler is not accurate with a single 15.6 s step (it smears too much near the source and lets too much reach the sink), but it has the right shape. FTCS at r = 1 is outside its limit: the attractant only reaches the first point, and that point already holds the source value. The exercise does one more step by hand.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
One tridiagonal solve per step
be_step <- function(c, r) {           # c includes the two boundary values
  m <- length(c) - 2; i <- 2:(m + 1)  # m interior unknowns
  d <- c[i]
  d[1] <- d[1] + r * c[1]             # source enters the first row
  d[m] <- d[m] + r * c[m + 2]         # sink enters the last row
  c[i] <- thomas(rep(-r, m), rep(1 + 2 * r, m), rep(-r, m), d)
  c
}

thomas(a, b, c, d) from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse: sub-diagonal, diagonal, super-diagonal, right-hand side. About 8N operations.
So one implicit step costs a few times an explicit step, not N^3. Never build a dense N\times N matrix and call solve().


The convention is the one from the structured-sparse unit: all four vectors have length m, a[1] and c[m] are not used, so rep(-r, m) is fine for both off-diagonals. The boundary values stay in c[1] and c[m + 2] and are never changed, exactly as in the ftcs function of the previous unit. With a dense matrix the solve costs about (2/3) m^3: for m = 199 that is 5 million operations per step instead of 1600. Python users: scipy.linalg.solve_banded does the same job; the exercise shows it. Rust: we write Thomas by hand.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Fifteen steps instead of 1500
The chamber (N = 50, \Delta x = 10 µm), empty at t = 0, to t = 60 s:
r <- D * 4 / dx^2                       # dt = 4 s: r = 40, FTCS needs r <= 0.5
c <- c(1, rep(0, N))
for (k in 1:15) c <- be_step(c, r)
round(c[c(6, 11, 26, 41)], 4)           # x = 50, 100, 250, 400 µm
# [1] 0.8781 0.7583 0.4294 0.1587
round(exact(x[c(6, 11, 26, 41)], 60, L, D), 4)
# [1] 0.8816 0.7650 0.4404 0.1650

FTCS (r = 0.4, 1500 steps) agrees with the exact values to 4 digits. Backward Euler with 15 steps is off by about 0.01.
Stable is not accurate. The error is now the time error of a 4 s step: order 1.


Here D = 1000 µm^2/s, L = 500, N = 50, x and exact() are from the previous unit (exact is the Fourier series). With r = 40 FTCS would blow up in a few steps; backward Euler gives a smooth, bounded and slightly too slow profile (backward Euler decays every mode a little too slowly, so the filling front lags). The 1500 FTCS steps are cheaper per step, but backward Euler wins on total work only if the accuracy we need allows large steps. For this chamber, with the gradient forming over a minute, a 1 s step (60 steps) would give about 0.003; we come back to how to choose dt after Crank–Nicolson.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Stable for every time step


Per step a mode is multiplied by: FTCS 1 - z, backward Euler \frac{1}{1 + z}, with z = 4r\sin^2(\theta/2) \ge 0.
Backward Euler: 0 < g < 1 for every z: unconditionally stable, and fast modes are killed (g \to 0).


z is dt times the decay rate of the mode; the exact solution multiplies the mode by e^{-z} per step (black). For small z (smooth modes, small steps) all methods agree with the exact factor. FTCS leaves the band [-1, 1] at z = 2, i.e. r = 1/2 for the zigzag. Backward Euler never does: this is the A-stability of Stiffness and implicit methods on the negative real axis. It damps the fast modes even more strongly than the exact solution would in the limit (both go to 0). The red curve is Crank–Nicolson, the next slide; note where it ends up for large z.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Crank–Nicolson
Average the second difference over the old and the new level (the trapezoidal rule in time):
c_i^{n+1} = c_i^n + \tfrac{r}{2}\bigl(c_{i-1}^{n} - 2c_i^{n} + c_{i+1}^{n}\bigr) + \tfrac{r}{2}\bigl(c_{i-1}^{n+1} - 2c_i^{n+1} + c_{i+1}^{n+1}\bigr)
cn_step <- function(c, r) {
  m <- length(c) - 2; i <- 2:(m + 1)
  d <- c[i] + r / 2 * (c[i - 1] - 2 * c[i] + c[i + 1])   # explicit half
  d[1] <- d[1] + r / 2 * c[1]; d[m] <- d[m] + r / 2 * c[m + 2]
  c[i] <- thomas(rep(-r / 2, m), rep(1 + r, m), rep(-r / 2, m), d)
  c
}

Same cost as backward Euler: one tridiagonal solve. Growth factor g = \frac{1 - z/2}{1 + z/2}: |g| \le 1 for every z, and second order in time.


Crank and Nicolson (1947) introduced it for heat conduction. Centred in time around t_{n+1/2}, which is why it is second order: the time error of backward Euler cancels between the two halves, like the trapezoidal rule against the rectangle rule in Numerical integration. It is A-stable too: |g| <= 1 for every z >= 0. But look at fig02 again: for large z, g tends to -1, not to 0. That is the catch on the next slide.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Crank–Nicolson fails on sharp data

“Stop the flow”: the embryo starts with a sharp 20/27 °C step, no heat exchange, \Delta t = 0.05 s (r = 1120). Crank–Nicolson flips the step every time step; backward Euler is smooth and close to the exact curve.

A thought experiment on the embryo grid (N = 200, dx = 2.5 µm, insulated tips): at t = 0 the anterior half is at 20 °C and the posterior at 27 °C, and from then on heat only redistributes inside. The exact solution (grey, a cosine series) is a smooth S-curve after 0.1 s. Crank–Nicolson with the same step as backward Euler gets the smooth part roughly right, but the sharp part of the initial step (made of high-frequency modes) survives with factor close to -1: after one step the jump points the wrong way, after two the right way, and so on. It decays only slowly. Note that the values stay between 20 and 27, so a simple range check does not catch it here.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Why, and what to do

High modes (z \gg 1) get g = \frac{1 - z/2}{1 + z/2} \approx -1 + \frac{4}{z}: they are not damped, only flipped. Sharp data (a step, an empty channel next to a full reservoir) is made of exactly these modes.
Chamber, empty at t = 0, 15 CN steps of 4 s: c at x = 10 µm is 1.1775, above the source value 1.




fix
chamber, c(10\text{ µm}, 60\text{ s}) (exact 0.9763)




plain CN, \Delta t = 4 s
1.1775


4 backward Euler steps of 1 s, then CN
0.9762


CN with \Delta t = 0.4 s (r = 4)
0.9763




Check: values outside the initial/boundary range; changes that alternate in sign from step to step; disagreement with backward Euler.


The fix in row 2 is known as Rannacher time-stepping: a few strongly damping backward Euler steps at the start (and after any sudden change of a boundary value) remove the sharp high modes; after that CN’s second-order accuracy takes over. Row 3: with r = 4 the zigzag has z = 16, g = -0.78, which still flips but now dies within a few steps. A safe rule of thumb for CN with sharp data is to keep r of order 1 near the start. Backward Euler never oscillates (g between 0 and 1), which is why stiff ODE solvers start with BDF1 and why the method of lines solvers later in this lecture handle sharp starts well. The maximum principle check from the previous unit catches the chamber case but not the embryo case of the previous slide.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Accuracy in time and space
The error at a fixed time has two parts:
\text{error} \approx C_t\,\Delta t^{\,p} + C_x\,\Delta x^2, \qquad p = 1 \text{ (backward Euler)},\quad p = 2 \text{ (Crank–Nicolson)}









scheme
time
space
stable for




FTCS
O(\Delta t)
O(\Delta x^2)
r \le 1/2


backward Euler
O(\Delta t)
O(\Delta x^2)
all \Delta t


Crank–Nicolson
O(\Delta t^2)
O(\Delta x^2)
all \Delta t (oscillates if r \gg 1)




Refining only one of them hits a floor set by the other.
Balance: backward Euler needs \Delta t \sim \Delta x^2 for equal errors (the FTCS step size again!); Crank–Nicolson only \Delta t \sim \Delta x.


The space error comes from the (1, -2, 1) stencil, the same for all three schemes. FTCS at its stability limit has dt proportional to dx^2 automatically, so its time error is of the same order as its space error; that is why the previous unit could refine with r fixed and see order 2. For backward Euler, a large step buys stability but the time error then dominates: to make it as small as the space error you are pushed back to dt ~ dx^2, but now with a free choice of the constant. Crank–Nicolson is the scheme that actually lets you take large steps and stay accurate, as long as the data are smooth. That is why it is the textbook default for diffusion.
