Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Verify against an exact solution
Both reservoirs at 0, start with one sine: c(x, 0) = \sin(\pi x/L). The exact solution keeps its shape and decays: c = e^{-D(\pi/L)^2 t}\sin(\pi x/L).
sine_err <- function(N, dt, step, tend = 30) {
  dx <- L / N; x <- seq(0, L, by = dx); c <- sin(pi * x / L)
  for (k in 1:round(tend / dt)) c <- step(c, D * dt / dx^2)
  max(abs(c - exp(-D * (pi / L)^2 * tend) * sin(pi * x / L)))
}
dts <- c(6, 3, 1.5, 0.75)                   # halve dt, fine grid N = 400
e <- rbind(be = sapply(dts, function(h) sine_err(400, h, be_step)),
           cn = sapply(dts, function(h) sine_err(400, h, cn_step)))
round(e[, -4] / e[, -1], 2)                 # error ratio per halving
#    [,1] [,2] [,3]
# be 1.92 1.96 1.98
# cn 4.03 4.06 4.23

Halving \Delta t halves the backward Euler error (order 1) and quarters the Crank–Nicolson error (order 2).


Any single Fourier mode is an exact solution of the diffusion equation with zero boundary values, with decay rate D k^2, k = pi / L. Here 1/(D k^2) = 25 s, and at t = 30 s the amplitude is 0.306. The fine grid (dx = 1.25 µm) keeps the space error small (about 1e-6) so that the time error dominates. The errors themselves: backward Euler 0.040, 0.021, 0.010, 0.0053; Crank–Nicolson 1.7e-3, 4.2e-4, 1.0e-4, 2.5e-5. The last CN ratio (4.23) is already drifting because the time error approaches the space-error floor. Why test on such a simple problem? Because it is exact, and a bug in the boundary rows or a factor 2 in r shows up at once as a wrong order.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Error against step size


Left: slopes 1 and 2, then a floor at the space error (open circles: \Delta x = 10 µm). The dip: time and space errors of opposite sign cancel by luck.
Right: refine space with a tiny \Delta t: slope 2.


Read the order off the slope, as in Convergence and cost. The open circles are Crank–Nicolson on the chamber’s own grid, N = 50: below dt of about 1 s the error stops at 1.2e-4, the space error of the 10 µm grid. The dip at dt = 1.5 s is a warning: Crank–Nicolson decays the sine slightly too fast, the grid slightly too slowly, and at one particular dt the two cancel. A single run at that dt would look ten times more accurate than it is. Only a sequence of runs (refinement) shows the true behaviour. The right panel uses CN with dt = 0.01 s so that the time error is negligible.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
section: Grid refinement without an exact solution
text:
Grid refinement without an exact solution
For the real problem there is no formula. Refine and watch the differences shrink:
T200 <- sapply(c(25, 50, 100, 200, 400), embryo_steady)   # T at x = 200 µm
T200
# [1] 21.03408 21.05464 21.05237 21.05180 21.05166
d <- diff(T200)
round(d[-4] / d[-1], 2)            # should approach 2^p = 4
# [1] -9.05  3.98  4.00

Ratio 4 per halving: order 2, as designed. The answer is 21.0517 \pm 0.0002 °C.
The first ratio is not 4: \Delta x = 20 µm is too coarse to be in the asymptotic range. Never trust the order from the two coarsest grids.


embryo_steady (on the embryo slides; full code in the exercise) computes the steady temperature profile of the embryo model on N intervals and returns the value at x = 200 µm, 50 µm on the cold side of the middle. With observed order p, the error of the finest grid is about d / (2^p - 1) = 0.00014 / 3 = 5e-5; Richardson extrapolation (Numerical differentiation, used again in Numerical integration) adds that correction. If the ratios wander instead of settling, the solver is not converging at its design order: look for a bug, a boundary condition of lower order, or a non-smooth input. A sign change in the differences, as in the first one here, means the coarsest grid is outside the asymptotic range, not that the method is wrong.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Method of lines
Discretise space only. The PDE becomes N - 1 coupled ODEs, one per grid line:
\frac{d\mathbf c}{dt} = \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A\,\mathbf c + \mathbf b

Backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson are just two ODE methods applied to it. Any ODE solver from Part 8 can take their place.
Eigenvalues of \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A on the chamber: -0.039 to -40 per s. Ratio \approx (2N/\pi)^2 \approx 1000, and it grows 4 × with every halving of \Delta x.
A fine grid is always stiff: use a stiff solver (lsoda, bdf, radau), and tell it the Jacobian is banded.


The name: the grid lines x = x_i in the (x, t) plane; along each line we solve an ODE in t. The ODE system is the compartment model of the previous unit, cells exchanging with neighbours at rate D / dx^2. Its Jacobian is exactly (D / dx^2) A, tridiagonal. A stiff solver needs to solve with I - h gamma J at each Newton step; if it treats J as dense that costs N^3 and N extra right-hand-side evaluations to build J by finite differences. With the band structure, the Jacobian can be built from 3 evaluations (one per diagonal, by grouping columns) and solved in O(N). The eigenvalue range is from the previous unit’s eigenvalue slide.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
section: Method of lines in R: ode.1D
text:
Method of lines in R: ode.1D
The embryo (next slides) as 201 ODEs, from 20 °C to t = 0.1 s:
library(deSolve)
rhs <- function(t, T, p) {
  Tg <- c(T[2], T, T[N])                 # ghost points: no flux through the tips
  list(D * diff(diff(Tg)) / dx^2 + (Tout - T) / tau)
}
for (m in c("lsoda", "bdf", "ode45")) {
  out <- ode.1D(rep(20, N + 1), c(0, 0.1), rhs, NULL, nspec = 1, method = m)
  cat(m, ": steps", attr(out, "istate")[2], " f-evals", attr(out, "istate")[3], "\n")
}
# lsoda : steps 128  f-evals 279
# bdf : steps 85  f-evals 158
# ode45 : steps 3563  f-evals 22235

ode.1D tells the stiff solver the Jacobian is banded (nspec = 1: one species per grid point).
Plain ode() with lsoda: same 128 steps but 2655 f-evals, to build a dense 201\times201 Jacobian.


diff(diff(Tg)) is the second difference of the vector with ghost points, exactly the stencil (1, -2, 1). The ghost points T[2] and T[N] are the mirror images for the no-flux condition (previous unit). Tout and tau are defined on the embryo slides. ode45, the explicit Dormand–Prince solver, takes 3563 steps: it rides its stability limit, just like on the enzyme model in Stiffness and implicit methods. The library solvers choose dt and the order themselves and control the time error to the tolerance; the spatial error is fixed by the grid you chose. In Python the same thing is solve_ivp(method=“BDF”, jac_sparsity=…) with a tridiagonal sparsity pattern; the exercise compares them.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
section: What the library controls, and what it does not
text:
What the library controls, and what it does not

rtol, atol control the time error only. The space error is fixed by \Delta x before the solver starts: tightening the tolerance cannot fix a coarse grid.
Verify the two separately: refine the grid at tight tolerance; tighten the tolerance on a fixed grid.
Adaptive BDF starts with order 1 (backward Euler) and small steps: it handles sharp starts without CN’s oscillations.
Python: solve_ivp(rhs, ..., method="BDF", jac_sparsity=S) with S the tridiagonal pattern. Rust: no stiff solver in ode_solvers; write backward Euler or CN with Thomas by hand.


The method of lines is how most production PDE codes for diffusion-like problems work: a spatial discretisation (finite differences here, finite volumes or finite elements in Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow) plus a good stiff ODE solver. Its weak point is the false sense of accuracy: the solver reports success at rtol = 1e-8 while the answer is wrong in the third digit because of the grid. The two refinements are independent, which is the practical meaning of error = C_t dt^p + C_x dx^2. BDF’s first steps are backward Euler steps with tiny h; the step grows as the sharp modes die out, which is the automatic version of the Rannacher start.

Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
section: Back to the embryo: a 1D model
text:
Back to the embryo: a 1D model
Along the long axis x (0 to 500 µm), heat diffuses and leaks to the stream just outside, T_\text{out}(x) = 20 or 27 °C:
\frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = D\,\frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2} + \frac{T_\text{out}(x) - T}{\tau}

\tau: time for heat to cross the 200 µm thickness. For a cylinder of radius R = 100 µm: \tau = R^2/(2.405^2 D) = 12 ms.
No flux through the tips (ghost points). Still tridiagonal: the leak only adds \Delta t/\tau to the diagonal.
Steady state: T = T_\text{out} \mp 3.5\,e^{-|x - L/2|/\lambda} with length scale \lambda = \sqrt{D\tau} = 42 µm.


This is our simplification, not the model of [M2]: we replace the 3D embryo by a cylinder whose surface is held at the temperature of the stream it touches, and keep only the slowest radial mode (2.405 is the first zero of the Bessel function J0; take it as given). The leak term is then exactly a linear “exchange” with rate 1/tau. The steady-state formula ignores the tips (they are 6 lambda away, so their effect is e^{-6}, under 0.01 °C) and comes from solving T - lambda^2 T’’ = Tout on each side with T and T’ continuous at the middle. lambda = R / 2.405: the step cannot be sharper than about the embryo’s own radius. The same structure, decay length sqrt(D / k), comes back for morphogens in Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation, and appeared as sqrt(D/k) cells for the morphogen in a row of cells in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse. Grid: the same nodes x_i = i dx as for the chamber, but N = 200 (dx = 2.5 µm, to put about 50 points across the transition), both tips are no-flux ends handled with ghost points, so all 201 nodes are unknowns, and the variable is temperature in °C instead of a scaled concentration.

Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
How sharp is the step?


The 10–90 % transition is 2\lambda\ln 5 \approx 134 µm, about a quarter of the embryo. Each half is within 0.5 °C of its stream over its outer 170 µm.
Numerical solution (line) and formula (circles) agree to 0.01 °C (the formula ignores the tips).


Backward Euler, N = 200, dt = 5 ms, 40 steps from a uniform 20 °C: by 0.2 s the profile has reached steady state. The answer to the biology question: inside the embryo the step is about 130 µm wide, not zero and not the whole embryo. That supports the experimental design of [M1]: each half really is at its stream’s temperature except for a band around the middle. [M2] found a step-like profile inside the embryo in their 3D finite-element simulation, and showed that offsetting the embryo by 20–36 µm across the channel shifts the profile by 8–16 % of the embryo length; our 1D model cannot say anything about such placement effects. Treat 134 µm as an order of magnitude.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
How fast does it form?


Streams on: steady within about 50 ms (\approx 4\tau). Development takes minutes, so the embryo always sees the steady profile.
Flow stopped (thought experiment): the step is gone within 1 s, the time scale L^2/(\pi^2 D) = 0.18 s of the slowest mode. The flow is what keeps the step.


Left: Crank–Nicolson with dt = 1 ms (r = 22) from 20 °C everywhere, no oscillations because the initial data are smooth relative to dt and the leak damps quickly. The posterior point rises with time constant tau; the anterior point warms by 0.2 °C because of conduction from the warm half. Right: backward Euler with dt = 1 ms on the stop-flow problem from the CN slide. [M2] justified their steady-state simulation with the same argument: heat transfer across the embryo (about 0.9 s by their estimate) is fast compared with the other time scales. The time scale for the PDMS walls is much longer, which is the subject of the exercise on PCR chips.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Checks before you trust it

Exact solution: a sine mode decays as e^{-Dk^2t}. Check the order (error ratio 2 or 4 per halving), not just a small error.
Refine time and space separately; expect a floor from the other one. Watch for lucky cancellation.
Observed order from three grids without an exact solution; ignore the coarsest pair.
Crank–Nicolson: sign-alternating changes or values beyond the data range → smaller \Delta t near the start, or a few backward Euler steps first.
Method of lines: tolerance controls the time error only. Count steps: thousands of tiny steps mean an explicit solver on a stiff grid.
Physical checks: steady state, conservation with no-flux ends, values between the boundary temperatures.


These extend the checklist of the previous unit. The exact-solution test is cheap enough to run every time you change a solver: put it in a test file. In practice the most common bugs in an implicit solver are in the first and last rows (boundary terms forgotten or added with the wrong factor, r instead of r / 2 for CN) and in r itself (units, dx defined as L / N vs L / (N - 1)); the order test catches both. The physical checks need no exact solution at all.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Summary

Backward Euler: (I - rA)\mathbf c^{n+1} = \mathbf c^n + \mathbf b. Crank–Nicolson: (I - \tfrac r2 A)\mathbf c^{n+1} = (I + \tfrac r2 A)\mathbf c^n + \mathbf b. One Thomas solve per step, O(N).
Both are unconditionally stable. Backward Euler damps fast modes (g \to 0); Crank–Nicolson flips them (g \to -1): oscillations with sharp data and large r. Fix: backward Euler start steps or smaller \Delta t.
Error \approx C_t\Delta t^p + C_x\Delta x^2, p = 1 (BE) or 2 (CN). Verify with an exact sine mode and by refinement; read the order from the ratios.
Method of lines: the grid gives a stiff ODE system; ode.1D with lsoda/bdf, or solve_ivp(method="BDF", jac_sparsity=...). The tolerance does not control the grid error.
Embryo: the temperature step inside is set by \lambda = \sqrt{D\tau} \approx 42 µm: about 130 µm wide, formed within 50 ms.

Next: Steady state in two dimensions: no time at all, one big sparse solve.

Recap. The pattern of this unit, a tridiagonal solve per step with a stiff solver in the background, carries over to every later unit of Part 10: in 2D the matrix becomes sparse rather than tridiagonal (Steady state in two dimensions), flow adds a non-symmetric term (Flow plus diffusion), and reaction terms are handled by splitting diffusion (implicit) from reaction (explicit) in Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation. Note that the embryo steady state was computed as one tridiagonal solve: the limit of backward Euler as dt goes to infinity. That is the starting point of the next unit.

title: Quiz: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of implicit schemes for diffusion. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. You halve the grid spacing \(\Delta x\) of an FTCS simulation and keep the simulated time the same. By what factor does the work grow, and why? What changes if you use backward Euler with a fixed \(\Delta t\) instead?






Hint





FTCS needs \(r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2\). Count grid points times steps.









Answer





FTCS: twice as many grid points and, because \(\Delta t \le \Delta x^2/(2D)\), four times as many steps: 8 times the work. Backward Euler has no step limit, so the number of steps stays the same and only the grid points double (Thomas is \(O(N)\)): 2 times the work. Whether \(\Delta t\) is still small enough for the accuracy you want is a separate question (Q5).




Q2. Write the backward Euler equation for an interior grid point \(i\). What kind of linear system do you have to solve per step, and how much does it cost for \(N\) unknowns?






Hint





The second difference is taken at the new time level.









Answer





\(-r\,c_{i-1}^{n+1} + (1 + 2r)\,c_i^{n+1} - r\,c_{i+1}^{n+1} = c_i^n\), \(r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2\). The matrix \(I - rA\) is tridiagonal, symmetric and diagonally dominant, so the Thomas algorithm solves it without pivoting in about \(8N\) operations. A dense solve() would cost \(\tfrac23N^3\).




Q3. With \(r = 100\), by what factor is the zigzag mode (\(z = 4r = 400\)) multiplied per step by FTCS, backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson? What does each factor mean in practice?






Hint





FTCS \(1 - z\), backward Euler \(1/(1 + z)\), Crank–Nicolson \((1 - z/2)/(1 + z/2)\).









Answer





FTCS \(-399\): the zigzag explodes, flipping sign each step. Backward Euler \(0.0025\): it is gone after one step, as it should be (the exact factor is \(e^{-400} \approx 0\)). Crank–Nicolson \(-0.990\): stable, but the zigzag survives for many steps and flips sign every step. That is the oscillation seen after sharp starts.




Q4. You start the chamber simulation from an empty channel next to a full reservoir and use Crank–Nicolson with \(r = 40\). Near the source the concentration is 1.6 after one step, 0.36 after two, 1.46 after three. What is happening, and give two fixes.






Hint





Which modes make up a sharp step, and what does Crank–Nicolson do with them at large \(r\)?









Answer





The sharp jump between reservoir and empty channel contains many high-frequency modes, which Crank–Nicolson multiplies by almost \(-1\) when \(r\) is large: they flip every step and decay slowly. The values above 1 violate the maximum principle and are a sure sign. Fixes: (1) take a few backward Euler steps first (they kill the high modes), then switch to Crank–Nicolson; (2) use a smaller \(\Delta t\) (here \(r = 4\) is enough) at least near the start. A stiff ODE solver (BDF) does the first automatically.




Q5. A solver gives errors 0.020, 0.010, 0.005 when you halve \(\Delta t\) twice; another gives \(4.2\times10^{-4}\), \(1.0\times10^{-4}\), \(2.5\times10^{-5}\). Which is backward Euler and which Crank–Nicolson? To reach \(10^{-4}\), about how many times more steps does the first one need?






Hint





Look at the ratio of successive errors: \(2^p\).









Answer





Ratio 2: order 1, backward Euler. Ratio 4: order 2, Crank–Nicolson. Backward Euler needs to go from 0.005 to \(10^{-4}\), another factor 50 in \(\Delta t\) beyond its third step size. Crank–Nicolson reaches \(10^{-4}\) already at the second step size, which is 2 times larger than the third: so backward Euler needs about \(2 \times 50 = 100\) times more steps, at the same cost per step.




Q6. You keep halving \(\Delta t\) in a Crank–Nicolson run, but below some step the error stays at \(1.2\times10^{-4}\). At one step size it was even \(1.3\times10^{-5}\). Explain both observations. What should you change?






Hint





Error \(\approx C_t\Delta t^2 + C_x\Delta x^2\).









Answer





The floor is the space error of the grid, which no time step can remove: refine \(\Delta x\). The single small value is cancellation: the time and space errors have opposite signs and nearly cancel at that one step size. It is luck, not accuracy; only a sequence of refinements shows the real behaviour.




Q7. Without an exact solution you compute a temperature on grids with \(N = 50, 100, 200\) and get 21.05464, 21.05237, 21.05180. Estimate the order of the method and the error of the finest result.






Hint





Compare successive differences. With order \(p\) the next difference is \(2^{-p}\) times the previous one.









Answer





Differences \(-0.00227\) and \(-0.00057\), ratio 3.98: order \(p = 2\). The remaining error of the finest value is about the last difference divided by \(2^p - 1 = 3\): \(0.00057/3 \approx 0.0002\) °C (the limit is about 21.0516). Use grids fine enough to be in the asymptotic range: with \(N = 25\) in the sequence the first ratio is \(-9\), which says nothing about the order.




Q8. What is the method of lines, and why should you hand the resulting system to lsoda/bdf (or solve_ivp(method="BDF")) rather than ode45/RK45? What does ode.1D (or jac_sparsity) add?






Hint





Eigenvalues of \(\frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A\) run from \(\approx -\pi^2D/L^2\) to \(\approx -4D/\Delta x^2\).









Answer





Discretise space only: the PDE becomes a system of ODEs, one per grid point, \(\mathbf c' = \frac{D}{\Delta x^2}A\mathbf c + \mathbf b\), which any ODE solver can integrate. Its eigenvalues span a ratio of about \((2N/\pi)^2\): the system is stiff, so an explicit solver is limited by stability to \(\Delta t \sim \Delta x^2/D\) (15 000 steps instead of about 200 on the chamber). ode.1D and jac_sparsity tell the stiff solver that the Jacobian is banded, so it is built from a few function evaluations and solved in \(O(N)\) instead of as a dense matrix.




Q9. You solve a method-of-lines problem at rtol = atol = 1e-10, but the error against the exact solution is \(2.7\times10^{-5}\). Is the solver broken?






Hint





What does the tolerance control?









Answer





No. The tolerance controls only the time error of the ODE solver. The space error is fixed by \(\Delta x\) before the solver starts: \(2.7\times10^{-5}\) is the error of the 10 µm grid. Refine the grid (halving \(\Delta x\) divides it by about 4) and keep the tolerance below the spatial error.




Q10. In the 1D embryo model the temperature step has width \(\approx 2\lambda\ln 5\) with \(\lambda = \sqrt{D\tau}\) and \(\tau = R^2/(2.405^2 D)\). Why does the width not depend on the thermal diffusivity \(D\)? What does \(D\) control?






Hint





Insert \(\tau\) into \(\lambda\).









Answer





\(\lambda^2 = D\tau = R^2/2.405^2\): \(D\) cancels, so \(\lambda = R/2.405 \approx 42\) µm for \(R = 100\) µm, and the width (about 134 µm) is set by the embryo’s thickness alone. Heat spreads along the embryo and leaks out through its surface at rates that are both proportional to \(D\). \(D\) sets how fast the profile forms (\(\tau \approx 12\) ms, steady within about 50 ms), not its shape.




Q11. A PCR chip’s wall is made twice as thick. What happens to (a) the time the channel side needs to follow a heater step and (b) the steady temperature drop due to heat loss at the top? Why is glass better than PDMS?






Hint





Diffusion time \(\propto H^2/D\); at steady state the profile is linear.









Answer






The time grows as \(H^2\): 4 times longer (PDMS: 17 s → 66 s to come within 0.5 °C). (b) The steady drop \(\approx (T_\text{heater} - T_\text{air})\,hH/k\) for small \(hH/k\) roughly doubles (PDMS: 4.4 → 8.2 °C). Glass has a thermal diffusivity about 7 times and a conductivity about 7 times that of PDMS, so it is faster and loses less: 2 mm of glass follows in about 10 s with a drop of about 1.3 °C. [H1] reaches the same recommendation from a 3D simulation.

title: Exercise: optimisation in one dimension
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the three minimisers of the lecture on the running examples, one function evaluation per Step, in your browser. Panel (a) shows the objective with the current bracket \([a, b]\) (shaded), the interior points, every point evaluated so far, and, for a parabolic step, the parabola (dashed) and its vertex. Drag the handles a and b below the axis to change the starting bracket. Panel (b) shows the bracket width \(b - a\) and the error \(|x - \hat x|\) of the current estimate against the number of evaluations on a log scale, with the line \(0.618^n(b_0 - a_0)\) and the flat-bottom level \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon|f(\hat x)|/f''(\hat x)}\); the table lists every step. Brent is the algorithm of R’s optimize, step for step (R counts one evaluation more, because optimize evaluates \(f\) once more to return $objective). multistart runs Brent on five equal sub-intervals of \([a, b]\); zoom: flat bottom plots \(f(x) - f(\hat x)\) in a tiny window around the minimiser.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R, Python and Rust; in the flat bottom the last digits can differ, because exp and log may be rounded differently.



E1. (golden section, step by step) On the decay rate \(\text{SSE}(k)\) with golden section and the bracket \([0, 1]\), press Step four times. Write down the new point and the width after each step and compare with B2 and the lecture’s table by hand. What is the ratio of consecutive widths? Then press To end with the default tolerance, and again with tol \(10^{-10}\). How many evaluations, and how large is the error at the end? Which line in panel (b) does the width follow, and what does the error do in the last steps?






Answer E1





The first step evaluates \(x_1 = 0.3820\) and \(x_2 = 0.6180\); then \(0.2361\), \(0.4721\) and \(0.3262\), with widths \(1, 0.618, 0.382, 0.236\): the same points as the table by hand, and a ratio of \(0.618\) per evaluation. With the default tolerance (\(1.2\times10^{-4}\)) golden section stops after 21 evaluations at \(0.37537\) with error \(2.0\times10^{-5}\); with tol \(10^{-10}\) after 50 evaluations (as in C2) with error \(2.4\times10^{-10}\). The width lies exactly on the dashed \(0.618^n\) line. The error falls with it down to \(2.4\times10^{-10}\) (after 43 evaluations, near the flat-bottom line at \(4\times10^{-10}\)) and then stops, while the width keeps shrinking: the last rows all show \(f = 0.002042809\), and the comparisons are decided by rounding. The final bracket, \(9.3\times10^{-11}\) wide, does not even contain \(\hat k\) any more. With tol \(10^{-15}\) the width keeps shrinking to \(10^{-15}\) (74 evaluations) and the error stays at \(2.4\times10^{-10}\).



E2. (parabolic steps and Brent) Switch to parabolic and press Step three times from \([0, 1]\). Where do the vertices land, and what happens if you press To end? Now switch to Brent, tol \(10^{-10}\), and press Step repeatedly. Which steps are golden and which are parabolic? How many evaluations does Brent need, and how does that compare with E1? Finally drag b to about \(0.6\) and run Brent again.






Answer E2





Parabolic interpolation from \(0, 0.5, 1\) jumps to \(0.7018\), already worse than \(0.5\), and then to \(-1.509\), where \(\text{SSE} = 3\times10^{10}\): the parabola through those points opens so steeply that its vertex is far outside. To end shows it wandering off to \(k \approx 72\), out on the flat plateau, where the points end up on a line and some parabolas open downwards (the table notes “a maximum”). There is no bracket to stop it. Brent starts at \(0.382\), takes two golden steps (\(0.618\), \(0.236\)) and then only parabolic steps (\(0.428\), \(0.347\), \(0.3775\), …); the error drops by several digits per step and it stops after 13 evaluations with error \(4.9\times10^{-11}\), against 50 for golden section (R reports 14). The parabolic steps are safe here because each one must land inside the bracket and shrink; the bracket shrinks from 1 to \(10^{-8}\). On \([0, 0.6]\) Brent starts at \(0.229\) and still finds \(\hat k = 0.3753873\) in 11 evaluations.



E3. (the wrong period) Choose circadian RSS(T) (the curve is hidden: the method only sees its own points) and golden section on \([10, 40]\). Press Step three times and follow the decisions with B6(c). Then press To end. What period is returned, and does anything warn you? Press plot the curve, then multistart. Finally drag a to 15 and b to 35 and run Brent.






Answer E3





The first step evaluates \(21.46\) (RSS \(10.363\)) and \(28.54\) (\(10.312\)); \(28.54\) is lower, so \([21.46, 40]\) is kept. The next point is \(32.92\) (\(10.249\)), lower again, so \([28.54, 40]\) is kept and the dip at 24.6 h is outside the bracket for good. Golden section converges in 28 evaluations to \(T = 32.4016\) h, RSS \(10.225\) (Brent: 14 evaluations, same answer). Nothing in the run itself warns you: the width shrinks as nicely as on the decay problem, only the error stays at 7.8 h. With the curve plotted, the narrow, deep dip near 24.6 h (RSS \(1.91\)) is obvious. Multistart (Brent on \([10, 16], [16, 22], \dots\), 76 evaluations) finds interior minima at \(14.59, 19.79, 24.63\) and \(32.40\) h with RSS \(10.39, 10.47, 1.908, 10.23\): comparing them picks \(24.63\) h. On \([15, 35]\) Brent starts at \(22.64\) (RSS \(7.18\)), already in the dip, and converges to \(24.6305\) h in 11 evaluations.



E4. (the flat bottom) Choose ZTP −log L(λ), Brent, tol \(10^{-15}\), and press To end. How large is the final error, compared with the flat-bottom line? Do the same with golden section. Then press zoom: flat bottom. How many of the 401 points in the window \(\pm3\times10^{-8}\) have exactly the same \(f\) as \(f(\hat\lambda)\)? Zoom in and out by a factor 10 and explain the picture with B5(c).






Answer E4





Brent stops after 12 evaluations with error \(1.8\times10^{-8}\), golden section after 77 evaluations with error \(1.2\times10^{-8}\), although its final bracket is only \(9\times10^{-16}\) wide: asking for tol \(10^{-15}\) does not help. Both errors are at the flat-bottom level \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon \cdot 52.61/56.92} = 2.0\times10^{-8}\). (R’s optimize on \([0.01, 10]\) happens to land closer, \(6.9\times10^{-10}\), but that is luck inside the same band.) In the zoom, 76 of the 401 points have \(f(\lambda) = f(\hat\lambda)\) exactly, spread from \(-3.0\times10^{-8}\) to \(3.1\times10^{-8}\); the others differ by one or a few gaps between doubles (\(7.1\times10^{-15}\) near 52.6), a staircase around the red parabola \(\tfrac12 f''\delta^2\). Zoomed in to \(\pm3\times10^{-9}\), the parabola is far below one gap and the dots are pure rounding noise: no method that compares values of \(f\) can tell these points apart. Zoomed out to \(\pm3\times10^{-7}\), the dots follow the parabola and only 11 points in the middle are equal to \(f(\hat\lambda)\). About 8 digits of \(\hat\lambda = 1.218469\ldots\) are all a minimiser can deliver; for more, find the root of the score (C3).

title: Exercise: identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

recognise structural non-identifiability (parameters that only appear as a product; the \(k_a/k_e\) flip-flop) from the model equations and from the Jacobian,
compute standard errors and the correlation matrix of fitted parameters from \(s^2(J^TJ)^{-1}\), and check them against the Hessian of the sum of squares,
read the badly determined parameter combinations off the SVD of the Jacobian (in log-parameters),
compute a profile likelihood by re-fitting with one parameter fixed, and spot a flat profile that the standard error hides,
recognise a sloppy model from the spread of the eigenvalues of \(J^TJ\),
compare sampling designs before an experiment, and add a prior as an extra residual.

The running example is the pharmacokinetic model and the simulated plasma concentrations of Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting: one oral dose of 100 mg, true \(k_a = 1\) /h, \(k_e = 0.2\) /h, \(V = 20\) L, noise SD 0.1 mg/L. The by-hand part uses pen, paper and a calculator.

title: Exercise: identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
By hand
B1. Two parameters that only appear as a product. An enzyme assay measures the initial rate \(v(S) = k_\text{cat}E_0\,S/(K_m + S)\) at substrate concentrations \(S = 1, 2, 5\) mM. The enzyme concentration \(E_0\) is not known. Take \(k_\text{cat} = 10\) /s, \(E_0 = 0.1\) µM, \(K_m = 2\) mM. (a) Write down the three columns of the Jacobian, \(\partial v/\partial k_\text{cat}\), \(\partial v/\partial E_0\), \(\partial v/\partial K_m\), and evaluate them at the three values of \(S\). (b) Show that the first two columns are proportional. What is the rank of \(J\)? What happens to \(J^TJ\)? (c) In log-parameters (fact 2), what do the first two columns become? Give the null direction \(v\) in \((\log k_\text{cat}, \log E_0, \log K_m)\). (d) Which combinations of the three parameters are identifiable? What extra measurement would separate \(k_\text{cat}\) from \(E_0\)?
B2. The flip-flop. (a) Show that swapping \(k_a \leftrightarrow k_e\) in the model and replacing \(V\) by \(V' = V k_e/k_a\) leaves \(C(t)\) unchanged for every \(t\). (b) For \(k_a = 1\), \(k_e = 0.2\) /h, \(V = 20\) L, \(F = 1\), \(D = 100\) mg: what is the flip-flop parameter set? Compute \(C(2)\) for both sets (\(e^{-0.4} = 0.6703\), \(e^{-2} = 0.1353\)). (c) An intravenous bolus of the same drug gives \(C(t) = (D/V)e^{-k_e t}\). Why does that experiment break the symmetry? What half-lives would the two parameter sets predict? (d) Is each of the two parameter sets locally identifiable? What does a multistart fit show?
B3. Standard errors for a 2-parameter fit. After an intravenous dose the concentration falls as \(C(t) = A e^{-kt}\). Samples at \(t = 0, 1, 2\) h, \(A = 10\) mg/L, \(k = 0.5\) /h, noise SD \(\sigma = 0.2\) mg/L (\(e^{-0.5} = 0.6065\), \(e^{-1} = 0.3679\)). (a) The columns of \(J\) are \(\partial C/\partial A = e^{-kt}\) and \(\partial C/\partial k = -At\,e^{-kt}\). Write down \(J\) (\(3\times2\)). (b) Compute \(J^TJ\) and its inverse. (c) Compute the standard errors of \(\hat A\) and \(\hat k\) (fact 4, \(\sigma\) known) and their correlation. Explain the sign of the correlation. (d) Move the third sample from \(t = 2\) to \(t = 4\) h (\(e^{-2} = 0.1353\)). Recompute \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat k)\). Did a longer time course help?
B4. Where to sample. In B3, suppose \(A = 10\) is known and only \(k\) is fitted, from a single sample at time \(t\). (a) Show that \(\mathrm{SE}(\hat k) = \sigma/|A t e^{-kt}|\). (b) Evaluate it at \(t = 0.5\), \(2\) and \(8\) h (\(e^{-0.25} = 0.7788\), \(e^{-4} = 0.0183\)). Which time is best? (c) Find the best \(t\) by setting the derivative of \(t e^{-kt}\) to zero. Use the answer to explain B3(d). (d) In the PK model, \(\partial C/\partial k_a\) is large only during the first 2–3 hours (lecture, “Fix 1”). What does that predict for a study whose first sample is at 3 h?
B5. A profile by hand. Same model as B3, data \(y = (10.2, 5.9, 3.8)\) at \(t = 0, 1, 2\), noise SD \(\sigma = 0.2\) known. The best fit is \(\hat A = 10.145\), \(\hat k = 0.5115\) with \(S(\hat\theta) = 0.0598\). (a) With \(k\) fixed, \(C = A e^{-kt}\) is linear in \(A\). Show that the best \(A\) is \(\hat A(k) = \sum_i y_i e^{-kt_i}/\sum_i e^{-2kt_i}\). (b) Compute \(\hat A(k)\) and \(\text{PL}(k) = S(\hat A(k), k)\) for \(k = 0.4\), \(0.5\) and \(0.6\) (\(e^{-0.4} = 0.6703\), \(e^{-0.8} = 0.4493\), \(e^{-0.6} = 0.5488\), \(e^{-1.2} = 0.3012\)). (c) With \(\sigma\) known, the 95 % criterion is \((\text{PL}(k) - S(\hat\theta))/\sigma^2 \le 3.84\). Which of the three \(k\) values lie inside the interval? (d) The Wald interval is \(\hat k \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}\) with \(\mathrm{SE} \approx 0.025\) from B3. Compare.
B6. Reading \(J^TJ\). A model has two positive parameters \(a, b\). At the fit, in log-parameters, \(J^TJ = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 3.9\\ 3.9 & 4\end{pmatrix}\), and \(\sigma = 0.1\). (a) Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(J^TJ\). (b) What is the standard error along each eigenvector? Which combinations, \(\log a + \log b\) or \(\log a - \log b\), are well and badly determined? What are they in terms of \(a\) and \(b\)? (c) Compute \(\operatorname{Cov} = \sigma^2(J^TJ)^{-1}\), the standard errors of \(\log a\) and \(\log b\), and their correlation. (d) What would you report from this fit?

title: Exercise: identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
In code
C1. Standard errors three ways. Continue from the Background block. (a) Compute the Jacobian \(J\) (\(12\times3\)) at the fit (numDeriv::jacobian; Python: the jacobian helper, or res.jac). Compute the standard errors with solve(crossprod(J)) and with the QR route \((J^TJ)^{-1} = R^{-1}R^{-T}\) (qr, chol2inv; Python: np.linalg.qr(J, mode="r")), and compare with vcov. (b) Print the correlation matrix. Which pair of parameters is most strongly correlated, and what does the sign mean? (c) Check your answers to B3(c) in code.
C2. The Hessian. (a) Compute the Hessian \(H\) of \(S(\theta)\) at the fit with numDeriv::hessian (Python: scipy.differentiate.hessian; Rust: central differences). How close is it to \(2J^TJ\)? Compute the standard errors from \(2s^2H^{-1}\). (b) Now take \(\sigma = 0.1\) as known and minimise the negative log-likelihood \(S/(2\sigma^2)\) with optim(..., method = "BFGS", hessian = TRUE) (Python: scipy.optimize.minimize(..., method="BFGS")) from the start \((1, 0.2, 20)\), and from \((0.5, 0.1, 10)\). Invert the Hessian of the negative log-likelihood to get standard errors. What do you get from each start? (c) Python only: BFGS returns an approximation hess_inv of \(H^{-1}\). Compare the standard errors from it with those from the real Hessian.
C3. Structural non-identifiability in code. (a) Let \(F\) be a free parameter: fit \(C(t) = \text{pk}(t, k_a, k_e, V/F)\) with four parameters. What does nls say? What does least_squares (Python) or the hand-written LM (Rust) return? Compute the singular values of the log-parameter Jacobian (svd; Python: np.linalg.svd) at \((1.0151, 0.1906, 20.22, 1)\) and the right singular vector of the smallest one. (b) Fit the three-parameter model from the starts \((k_a, k_e) = (0.5, 0.1), (2, 0.1), (0.1, 0.5), (2, 0.5)\), all with \(V = 10\). Report the estimates and the SSE. How many different answers, and how do they differ?
C4. The SVD of the Jacobian, two designs. Write a function that fits the model to given samples, computes \(J\), its log-parameter version \(J_\text{log}\) (fact 2), the singular values of \(J_\text{log}\), \(\kappa(J)\) and \(\kappa(J_\text{log})\) (kappa(..., exact = TRUE); Python: np.linalg.cond), the SE along each \(v_i\) (fact 5, with \(s\)), and \(v_3\). (a) Run it on all 12 samples and on the samples from 3 h only (late). (b) Which combination is worst determined in each design? Compare with the slide “Practical non-identifiability”.
C5. Profile likelihood. (a) Write profile_ka(ka, t, y): fix \(k_a\), fit \(k_e\) and \(V\) (start \(0.2, 20\)), return the SSE. For \(k_a = 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1, 1.5, 2, 5, 10, 30\), print \(\Delta = (\text{PL}(k_a) - S(\hat\theta))/s^2\) for both designs. (b) For all 12 samples, find the profile interval (where \(\Delta = 3.84\)) with uniroot (Python: scipy.optimize.brentq; Rust: bisection). Compare with the Wald interval \(\hat k_a \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}\), and with the Wald interval for \(\log k_a\), \(\hat k_a e^{\pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}/\hat k_a}\). (c) For the samples from 3 h: what is the 95 % profile interval? What would you write in a report?
C6. A sloppy model. The two-compartment version of the model has a peripheral compartment exchanging with the central one at rates \(k_{12}\), \(k_{21}\), and elimination rate \(k_{10}\). Its solution is a sum of three exponentials (code below). Take \(k_a = 1\), \(k_{10} = 0.2\), \(k_{12} = 0.3\), \(k_{21} = 0.15\) /h, \(V = 20\) L. (a) Check your implementation: \(C(1), C(6), C(24) = 2.4087, 0.9606, 0.2882\) mg/L. (b) At the 12 sample times, compute the eigenvalues of \(J^TJ\) in log-parameters (eigen; Python: np.linalg.eigh), how many decades they span, and the SE along each eigenvector for \(\sigma = 0.1\). Print the sloppiest eigenvector. (c) Add samples at 24, 36 and 48 h. Which eigenvalues change, and is the model still sloppy?
C7. Fixes: design and prior. (a) Write se_design(tt, p, sigma) that returns the predicted SE of \(\log k_a, \log k_e, \log V\) for sample times tt at a guessed \(\theta\) (no data needed). Compare three 6-sample designs: late \((3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)\), early \((0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12)\), peak \((1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12)\), at \(\theta = (1, 0.2, 20)\), \(\sigma = 0.1\). (b) Fit the samples from 3 h with a prior \(\log k_a \sim N(\log 1.2, \tau^2)\) as an extra residual (fact 8), for \(\tau = 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2\). Use minpack.lm::nls.lm with a residual function (Python: least_squares; Rust: the LM helper). Report \(\hat k_a\) and the SE of \(\log k_a\) from the augmented Jacobian. Compare the SE with \(\tau\): when is the answer mostly prior?

title: Exercise: identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Jacobians by hand (B1, B3)





Differentiate the model with respect to one parameter, holding the others fixed. For B1, \(\partial v/\partial k_\text{cat} = E_0 S/(K_m+S)\) and \(\partial v/\partial K_m = -k_\text{cat}E_0S/(K_m+S)^2\). Two columns are proportional if their ratio is the same in every row.









Hint 2 — inverting a 2×2 matrix (B3, B6)





\(\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ b & d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{ad - b^2}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\ -b & a\end{pmatrix}\). Eigenvalues of \(\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ b & a\end{pmatrix}\) are \(a \pm b\), with eigenvectors \((1, \pm1)/\sqrt2\).









Hint 3 — the flip-flop algebra (B2)





Write \(C\) as (prefactor) × (bracket). Swapping \(k_a\) and \(k_e\) changes the sign of both \(k_a - k_e\) and the bracket \(e^{-k_et} - e^{-k_at}\). What is left to match is the prefactor \(k_a/V\).









Hint 4 — profile of a linear parameter (B5)





For fixed \(k\), minimising \(\sum_i(y_i - Ae^{-kt_i})^2\) over \(A\) is a one-parameter linear least-squares problem: set the derivative with respect to \(A\) to zero.









Hint 5 — fitting and standard errors (C1, C2)





R: vcov(fit), cov2cor(vcov(fit)), chol2inv(qr.R(qr(J))) is \((J^TJ)^{-1}\). Python: least_squares minimises half the sum of squares of the residual vector you return; res.jac is the Jacobian of the residuals (\(= -J\)), which gives the same \(J^TJ\). scipy.differentiate.hessian calls your function with an array of shape (3, ...), so loop over the extra axes (as in the solution) or write a vectorised SSE. optim(..., hessian = TRUE) returns the numerical Hessian at the solution in $hessian.









Hint 6 — singular gradient and the SVD (C3, C4)





Multiply column \(j\) of \(J\) by \(\theta_j\) (R: J %*% diag(th); Python: J * th; Rust: DMatrix::from_fn). The signs of singular vectors are arbitrary; fix them (e.g. first entry positive) before comparing. nalgebra’s svd does not sort the singular values: sort them yourself.









Hint 7 — profiles (C5)





In R, a parameter that is not in start is taken from the calling environment, so nls(y ~ pk(t, ka, ke, V), start = list(ke = 0.2, V = 20)) inside a function with argument ka fits only ke and V. In Python, write the residual as a function of q = (ke, V) with ka fixed. If a fit fails at an extreme grid point, start it from the solution at the neighbouring point.









Hint 8 — a prior as a residual (C7)





Divide the data residuals by \(\sigma\) and append \((\log k_a - \mu)/\tau\). Then the sum of squares is \(-2\log(\text{likelihood} \times \text{prior})\) + constant, and the covariance is \((J_a^TJ_a)^{-1}\) without a factor \(s^2\), where \(J_a\) is the Jacobian of the augmented residual vector. Fit in log-parameters so that the prior is a plain difference.

title: Exercise: identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Where this leads

Part 9, Constraints and linear programming: bounds such as \(k_a > k_e\) or \(F \le 1\) as constraints in the optimiser, and what the Lagrange multipliers of active bounds say.
The capstone (if used): fit an ODE model to a real time course and report what is determined, using the checklist of the lecture (multistart, SVD of \(J\), profiles, prediction uncertainty).
We linearised (Wald SEs) and profiled with a \(\chi^2_1\) threshold, both large-sample approximations. Bootstrap and Bayesian sampling (MCMC) give uncertainty without them; they need many model fits, which is where fast and robust fitting (Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting) pays off.
Structural identifiability can also be decided symbolically, before any data, for ODE models of moderate size (differential algebra, as in the tools DAISY or StructuralIdentifiability.jl). We did it by hand and from the rank of \(J\).

title: Exercise: constraints and linear programming
text:
Explore
The demo below solves the lecture’s LPs in your browser. The first tab, LP in 2 variables, draws the ATP LP: the feasible polygon (blue), each limit as a coloured line (tick a limit to switch it on, drag its slider to move it), and the objective \(c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2\) as dashed orange level lines; the solid orange line is the best level. Set \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) with the sliders or drag the orange arrow (the gradient of the objective). The optimum is the large red corner, or a red edge in a tie. step ▶ walks the simplex path from \((0, 0)\), one corner per click, and the readout gives the rate of every edge leaving the current corner: the change in ATP per unit of the variable or the slack that the move frees. The shadow prices are measured by re-solving with the limit moved a little down and a little up; at a kink the two differ, and the readout shows both. The small plot on the right scans the best ATP against one limit (choose it with scan): its slope is the shadow price. The second tab, FBA toy network, solves the 9-reaction network of the lecture with a small simplex method written for the demo, including knock-outs, the flux variability ranges and an oxygen scan.



E1. (the simplex walk) Click ATP LP, then step ▶ until the button stops. Write down the corners visited, the ATP at each and the rate of the edge taken. At the last corner, what are the rates of the two edges leaving it? Compare them with the shadow prices in the readout.






Answer E1





\((0, 0)\), ATP 0 → \((3, 0)\), ATP 18, along \(x_2 = 0\) at \(+6\) per unit \(x_1\) (proteome stops it before carbon) → \((2, 4)\), ATP 24, along the proteome line at \(+1.5\) per unit \(x_2\). From \((2, 4)\) both edges lose ATP: \(-2\) per unit of carbon freed (back along the proteome line) and \(-1\) per unit of proteome freed (along the carbon line), so \((2, 4)\) is optimal. The lecture slide counts the same two edges per unit of \(x_2\) instead: \(-1.5\) and \(-3\) (moving one unit of \(x_2\) along the carbon line frees 3 units of proteome, and back along the proteome line frees \(\tfrac34\) of a unit of carbon). The shadow prices are carbon 2 and proteome 1: at the optimum, the rate of leaving a constraint is minus its shadow price. Freeing a unit of carbon costs 2 ATP, and getting one more unit of carbon gains 2 ATP; that is why the multipliers decide optimality.



E2. (the objective chooses the corner) Keep \(c_1 = 6\) and lower \(c_2\) (the ATP per unit of fermentation) in steps of 0.5, down to 1. At which value does the optimum leave \((2, 4)\), and what does the readout say exactly at that value? Then set \(c_2 = 3\) again and raise it to 6. Finally click tie: 8x₁+2x₂ and walk the simplex path. How does the walk notice a tie?






Answer E2





For \(c_2 = 2, 2.5, 3\) the optimum stays at \((2, 4)\). At \(c_2 = 1.5\) the level lines are parallel to the proteome line (\(6/1.5 = 4/1\)): tie, the whole edge \((3, 0)\)–\((2, 4)\) is optimal with ATP 18. At \(c_2 = 1\) the optimum is pure respiration, \((3, 0)\), ATP 18. Raising \(c_2\) to 6 makes the level lines parallel to the carbon line: tie on the edge \((2, 4)\)–\((0, 6)\), ATP 36; above that ratio pure fermentation would win. The optimal corner changes only when the level lines turn past an edge, so the mix \((2, 4)\) is robust to quite large changes in the yields. With \(8x_1 + 2x_2\) the walk stops at \((3, 0)\), ATP 24, and reports the edge along the proteome line with rate \(0\): no improving edge, so the corner is optimal, but a zero rate means the neighbour \((2, 4)\) is just as good. A solver returns one of them and says nothing.



E3. (shadow prices and kinks) Click ATP LP, choose scan: carbon, and move the carbon limit from 6 to 7, then down to 3 and 2. Note the optimum, the ATP and the carbon shadow price each time. Then click oxygen ≤ 1.5, choose scan: oxygen, and move the oxygen limit from 1.5 to 2 and 3. What happens to the prices at oxygen 2, and why?






Answer E3





Carbon 7: optimum \((1.67, 5.33)\), ATP 26, price 2 (one more unit of carbon gave \(+2\), as predicted). Carbon 3: optimum \((3, 0)\), ATP 18, and the readout says “6 below / 2 above (kink)”: three constraints are active there (\(x_2 \ge 0\), carbon and proteome). Carbon 2: \((2, 0)\), ATP 12, price 6: with little carbon only respiration runs and proteome is slack. The scan is a broken line whose slope is the shadow price, with a kink at carbon 3. With oxygen 1.5: \((1.5, 4.5)\), ATP 22.5, prices carbon 3, proteome 0, oxygen 3 (as in B5). At oxygen 2 the optimum is \((2, 4)\), ATP 24, and every price shows a kink: oxygen “3 below / 0 above”. Oxygen, carbon and proteome all pass through \((2, 4)\): a degenerate corner, where the prices are not unique. At oxygen 3 the oxygen line no longer touches the optimum: price 0, and carbon 2, proteome 1 as without oxygen. A shadow price only holds until the next kink.



E4. (unbounded and infeasible) Click unbounded and walk the simplex path. What does the walk report, and which limit, ticked back on, makes the LP bounded again? Then click infeasible. Lower the demand until the LP becomes feasible. What is the feasible set at that point, and what does the readout give as the price of the demand?






Answer E4





Only one limit is switched on, oxygen \(x_1 \le 3\) (the same as \(4x_1 \le 12\) on the lecture’s failure slide). The walk goes \((0, 0) \to (3, 0)\), then finds the edge up the line \(x_1 = 3\) with rate \(+3\) per unit \(x_2\) and no end: unbounded. Ticking carbon (\(\le 6\)) gives the optimum \((3, 3)\), ATP 27; ticking proteome (\(\le 12\)) gives \((0, 12)\), ATP 36. Either missing limit makes the problem unbounded: in FBA, a forgotten uptake bound. The infeasible case has carbon \(\le 6\) and demand \(\ge 8\); it stays infeasible down to demand 6.5. At demand 6 the feasible set shrinks to the segment of the carbon line from \((0, 6)\) to \((6, 0)\), and the optimum is \((6, 0)\), ATP 36. The demand price reads “0 (infeasible above)”: lowering the demand does not change the best ATP, and raising it makes the LP infeasible, so there is no price from above.



E5. (FBA: knock-outs and oxygen) Open FBA toy network. For the wild type, read the growth, the shadow prices and the fluxes that are not determined. Knock out GLY alone, then GLY and BYP1 together, then RES alone (untick the others between runs). Finally click wild type and lower the oxygen limit from 15 to 10 and 4, and read the prices and the acetate secretion.






Answer E5





Wild type: growth 15, glucose price 1.5, oxygen price 0 (10 of 15 used), and GLY, BYP1, BYP2 each range over \([0, 10]\): the solver’s GLY = 10 is one corner of an optimal edge. KO GLY: growth still 15, and now every flux is determined (the bypass carries all the glucose). KO GLY + BYP1: growth 0, lethal: a synthetic lethal pair. KO RES: growth 6.667, oxygen use 0, acetate 13.333 (fermentation only). Oxygen 10: growth 15, oxygen price “0.833 below / 0 above” and glucose price “1.5 below / 0.667 above”: a kink, exactly where acetate secretion stops in the oxygen scan. Oxygen 4: growth 10, acetate 8, prices glucose 0.667 and oxygen 0.833, the numbers of C7.

title: Exercise: the diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences
text:
Explore
The demo below runs FTCS for the chemotaxis chamber in your browser: source \(c = 1\) at \(x = 0\), empty channel at \(t = 0\), and at \(x = L\) either a sink (\(c = 0\)) or a wall (no flux, ghost point). Panel (a) shows the profile on the grid (dots), the exact series solution (line) and the steady state (dashed), with the time in minutes and seconds. Panel (b) plots the distance from the steady state, \(\max_i |c_i - c_\infty(x_i)|\), against time on log–log axes, with the 5 % level, the time scale \(L^2/D\) (green) and the exact curve (dashed). The animation spends the same number of seconds on every decade of time. When you change a setting the run restarts, and the old curve stays in (b) as a faint trace (the last three). 1 step advances one time step; red dots are values outside \([0, 1]\). The readout gives \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta t\), the step count, \(tD/L^2\), the zigzag factor \(1 - 4r\) and the time at which the profile came within 5 %.



E1. (small molecule and protein) Click ▶ run for the small molecule in the 500 µm chamber and watch both panels. When is the profile within 5 % of the straight line, in seconds, minutes and units of \(L^2/D\)? Then click protein and run again. By what factor does the time change, and how does the new curve in (b) compare with the faint trace of the first run?






Answer E1





Small molecule: within 5 % after 64.4 s = 1.07 min, \(0.2578\,L^2/D\), 1611 steps of \(\Delta t = 0.04\) s. Early on the attractant fills only the first few grid points and the distance stays near 1; it then falls steeply once the profile straightens. Protein (\(D = 100\) µm²/s): 644 s = 10.7 min, again \(0.2578\,L^2/D\) and again 1611 steps, now of \(\Delta t = 0.4\) s. Ten times smaller \(D\), ten times longer. In (b) the new curve has exactly the same shape as the faint one, shifted right by one decade, and the green \(L^2/D\) line (250 s, then 2500 s) moves with it. The 5 % point always sits at about a quarter of \(L^2/D\).



E2. (doubling the length) Back to the small molecule. Move the \(L\) slider from 500 to 1000 µm and run. Read the 5 % time and compare with E1. Then click protein for the 1 mm chamber. Finally: an experimenter wants the protein gradient within 10 minutes. Try \(L = 450\) µm.






Answer E2





\(L = 1000\) µm: 257.8 s = 4.30 min, four times the 64.4 s of the 500 µm chamber. In (b) the curve and the \(L^2/D\) line (now 1000 s) move right by \(\log_{10} 4 \approx 0.6\) decade, without changing shape: time enters only as \(tD/L^2\), and the readout still says 1611 steps and \(0.2578\,L^2/D\). Doubling \(L\) quadruples the wait. Protein in 1 mm: 43.0 min (2578 s). At \(L = 450\) µm the protein needs 8.70 min (522 s), and at 500 µm it needs 10.7 min, so the longest channel is just under 500 µm (\(L \le \sqrt{600 \cdot 100 / 0.258} \approx 480\) µm, as in B2(c)).



E3. (the grid does not change the physics, only the cost) Click reset all. With \(r = 0.4\), set \(N = 20\), then \(N = 100\), and run each to the 5 % point. Then go back to \(N = 50\) and try \(r = 0.25\). Record the 5 % time and the number of steps each time.






Answer E3





\(N = 20\): 64.3 s (257 steps, \(\Delta t = 0.25\) s, \(0.2570\,L^2/D\)). \(N = 50\): 64.4 s (1611 steps). \(N = 100\): 64.4 s (6444 steps, \(\Delta t = 0.01\) s). \(N = 50\), \(r = 0.25\): 64.5 s (2578 steps). The answer agrees to three digits on every grid, and the dots stay on the exact curve; only the cost changes. With \(r\) fixed, doubling \(N\) quarters \(\Delta t = r\,\Delta x^2/D\), so it takes 4× the steps, each with twice the points: 8× the work, as in C3. A smaller \(r\) only adds steps without making the answer better in a useful way.



E4. (breaking the limit) Click reset all, then r = 0.5 and run: the dots stay smooth. Now click r = 0.52 and press 1 step repeatedly. After how many steps does the first red dot (a value outside \([0, 1]\)) appear, and where? Then press ▶ run and watch until the run stops. Repeat with r = 0.6. What does the readout say about the zigzag factor?






Answer E4





At \(r = 0.5\) every value stays in \([0, 1]\) and the run reaches 5 % at about 64 s, like \(r = 0.4\). At \(r = 0.52\) the first value leaves \([0, 1]\) after 27 steps (1.40 s), at the steep front near the source; neighbouring points then alternate up and down, the checkerboard. The readout gives \(1 - 4r = -1.08\): the zigzag flips sign and grows by 8 % per step. Run on, and the zigzag spreads across the channel, the distance in (b) leaves the top of the plot (about \(4\times10^{15}\) near 30 s, as in C4) and the run stops when the values overflow to \(\pm\infty\) at 8.06 min (483.7 s, 9302 steps). At \(r = 0.6\) (\(1 - 4r = -1.4\)) the first red dot comes after 7 steps and the overflow after 125 s (2086 steps). A time step only 4 % above the limit destroys the solution; the maximum-principle check catches it within seconds.



E5. (sink or wall) Click reset all, run once with the sink, then click wall (no flux) and run. What does the profile approach? When is it within 5 % of that steady state, in units of \(L^2/D\)? Compare the two curves in (b).






Answer E5





With a wall the profile fills up and approaches \(c = 1\) everywhere: no gradient at all. It is within 5 % (the wall end at 0.95) after 328.0 s = 5.47 min = 1.312 \(L^2/D\), 8200 steps, five times the 64.4 s of the open chamber, and what is reached is useless for chemotaxis. In (b) the wall curve falls much more slowly at late times: its slowest mode is a quarter sine with rate \(\pi^2 D/(4L^2)\), four times slower than the half sine of the open chamber, as if the channel were twice as long (B7, C5).

title: Exercise: steady state in two dimensions
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write a steady diffusion problem with uptake as a boundary value problem, discretise it in 1D, and solve the tridiagonal system by hand and in code, with fixed-value and no-flux (ghost point) boundaries,
check a BVP solver against an exact solution and by grid refinement (slope 2),
number the points of a 2D grid as one vector, and say where a point’s four neighbours are in that vector,
assemble the five-point Laplacian with Kronecker products (or from triplets), put the boundary values into the right-hand side, and test the matrix with a manufactured field,
recognise the row-major vs column-major ordering bug and the check that exposes it,
solve a problem with Michaelis–Menten uptake by Newton, with Jacobian = Laplacian + a diagonal, and detect a physically impossible root,
judge whether a diffusion model answers the biological question that was asked.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator. The code part uses the same equations at sizes where only code works. Two biological settings: the oxygen chamber of the lecture (2D) and the dead-end trenches of a mother machine (1D).

title: Exercise: steady state in two dimensions
text:
By hand
B1. A 1D oxygen profile. A long chamber, width \(L = 2000\) µm, open on both long sides (\(c = 200\) µM there), cells at half confluence: \(R_0 = 0.25\) µM/s. Use \(N = 4\) (\(h = 500\) µm), so \(D/h^2 = 0.008\) per s. (a) Write the three equations for \(c_1, c_2, c_3\) with the known values moved to the right-hand side, and solve them (use the symmetry \(c_1 = c_3\)). (b) The exact solution is \(c(y) = c_0 - R_0\,y(L - y)/(2D)\). Compare at the grid points. Why is the agreement exact? (c) At which \(R_0\) does the centre reach 0? Which cell density is that? What does the model predict above it, and why is that wrong?
B2. The mother machine trench with constant uptake. A trench of length \(L = 25\) µm, open at \(x = 0\) to the feeding channel (\(c = c_0\)), closed at \(x = L\). Constant uptake \(V_{\max} = 0.6\) mM/s, \(D = 600\) µm²/s. Use \(N = 2\) (\(h = 12.5\) µm, \(D/h^2 = 3.84\) per s): unknowns \(c_1\) (middle) and \(c_2\) (closed end). (a) Write the two equations, using the ghost point \(c_3 = c_1\) for the closed end. (b) Solve them for \(c_1 - c_0\) and \(c_2 - c_0\). (c) Check against the exact solution \(c(x) = c_0 - \frac{V_{\max}}{D}\bigl(Lx - x^2/2\bigr)\). (d) Below which channel concentration \(c_0\) would the closed end run out under this model? Convert to % glucose (180 g/mol) and compare with the 0.2 % of a rich medium. (e) How long could a trench be before its closed end runs out at \(c_0 = 11.1\) mM?
B3. Numbering a grid. A grid with \(n_x = 4\), \(n_y = 3\) interior points, numbered with \(x\) running fastest, \(k = i + (j-1)n_x\) (1-based). (a) Which \(k\) belong to \((i, j) = (2, 3)\) and \((3, 1)\)? (b) Which \((i, j)\) is \(k = 7\)? Give a general formula for \(i\) and \(j\) from \(k\). (c) A Python user keeps the grid in a numpy array of shape \((n_x, n_y)\) and flattens it with the default ravel(). At which (0-based) position does the value of point \((i, j) = (2, 3)\) (1-based) land? Which point does the R-numbered matrix think lives at that position? (d) In each numbering, how far apart in the vector are \(x\)-neighbours, and \(y\)-neighbours?
B4. The matrix of a small grid. Take \(n_x = 3\), \(n_y = 2\), \(D = h = 1\), and \(c = 1\) on all edges. (a) Write the \(6 \times 6\) matrix \(A\), numbering as in B3. (b) Mark the diagonal blocks and the off-diagonal blocks. Which are copies of \(T_3 + 2I\) and which of \(-I\)? (c) Write the right-hand side \(\mathbf b\) (count each point’s neighbours on the edge). (d) Show that \(\mathbf c = (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1)\) solves \(A\mathbf c = \mathbf b\). Why must that be so physically, and why is it a useful test of code?
B5. Kronecker products by hand. \(T_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Write \(I_2 \otimes T_2\) and \(T_2 \otimes I_2\), and their sum. (b) The sum is \(h^2/D\) times the matrix for a \(2\times2\) interior grid. Solve the Poisson problem with \(c_0 = 200\) µM on all edges, \(R_0 = 0.5\) µM/s, \(D = 2000\) µm²/s, \(h = 500\) µm (all four unknowns are equal by symmetry). (c) For a \(2 \times 2\) grid, does the order of the Kronecker factors matter? For a \(3 \times 2\) grid?
B6. Newton with a spurious root. The coarsest possible 1D chamber: \(L = 2000\) µm, \(N = 2\), so one unknown \(c\) at the centre (\(h = 1000\) µm, \(D/h^2 = 0.002\) per s), \(c_0 = 200\) µM, Michaelis–Menten uptake with \(R_0 = 1\) µM/s, \(K_m = 1\) µM. The equation is \[F(c) = 0.002\,(2c - 400) + \frac{c}{1 + c} = 0.004\,(c - 200) + \frac{c}{1 + c} = 0.\] (a) Compute \(F'(c)\). (b) Do two Newton steps from \(c = 200\) (air-saturated start). (c) Do two Newton steps from \(c = 0\). (d) The two runs converge to \(-54.66\) and \(3.66\). Check that both are roots. Which is the oxygen level, and why does the other one exist?
B7. The Jacobian. For the \(2\times2\) grid of B5 with Michaelis–Menten uptake: (a) Write \(J(\mathbf c)\) for a general \(\mathbf c = (c_1, c_2, c_3, c_4)\). (b) Why does uptake add only to the diagonal? Which entries of \(J\) would change if a cell’s uptake also depended on its neighbours’ oxygen? (c) Explain why \(J\) is symmetric positive definite whenever \(A\) is.
B8. Fill-in and cost. In natural order (B3), Cholesky of the 2D matrix fills the whole band between the diagonal and distance \(n_x\). (a) Estimate nnz(\(L\)) \(\approx N n_x\) for the oxygen chamber with \(h = 50\) µm and \(h = 12.5\) µm (\(N\) = number of unknowns), and compare with the lecture table. (b) A banded Cholesky costs about \(N n_x^2\) operations. Estimate it for \(h = 12.5\) µm. (c) A 3D tissue block of \(100 \times 100 \times 100\) points, numbered the same way: what is the bandwidth, nnz(\(L\)) and the memory at 8 bytes per number? What do you conclude?

title: Exercise: steady state in two dimensions
text:
In code
C1. A 1D BVP with an exact solution. Before trusting a solver, test it. Take the trench of B2 (\(L = 25\) µm, \(D = 600\) µm²/s, open end \(c_0 = 1\), closed end by a ghost point) with linear uptake \(r = kc\), \(k = 6\) per s. The exact solution is \(c(x) = c_0\cosh\bigl((L - x)/\lambda\bigr)/\cosh(L/\lambda)\), \(\lambda = \sqrt{D/k} = 10\) µm. (a) Write trench_matrix(N, h, D) that returns the \(N \times N\) matrix of fact 3 (without uptake). (b) For \(N = 10, 20, 40, 80, 160\), add \(k\) to the diagonal, solve, and compute the maximum error. By what factor does it fall per halving of \(h\)? (c) Compare the value at the closed end with the exact one.
C2. Do cells at the closed end starve? Mother-machine trenches are dead ends: nutrient reaches the cells at the closed end only by diffusion through the medium between the cells in front of them [B1, B2]. Use Michaelis–Menten uptake with \(V_{\max} = 0.6\) mM/s and \(K_m = 0.005\) mM, \(D = 600\) µm²/s, \(N = 100\). (a) Write trench_mm(c0, ...) that solves the problem with Newton (the Jacobian is tridiagonal), starting from \(c = c_0\) everywhere, clipping negative values to 0, and checking that no value is negative at the end. (b) Solve for \(c_0 = 11.1\) (0.2 % glucose), \(1\), \(0.3\), \(0.1\) and \(0.02\) mM. For each, report the number of Newton steps, the concentration at the closed end, and the length of trench where \(c < K_m\) (“starved”). (c) Compare with your threshold from B2(d).
The uptake numbers are an order-of-magnitude estimate, not taken from [B1]: an E. coli cell of about 1 µm³ with 0.3 pg dry mass, doubling once per hour on glucose with a yield of 0.5 g dry mass per g glucose, takes up about \(6\times10^{-19}\) mol/s, or 0.6 mM/s per volume of packed cells. \(K_m\) of glucose uptake is a few µM.
C3. Does the model answer the right question? The cells in the trench are packed tightly, so the effective diffusion coefficient is lower than in free medium (by how much is uncertain). (a) With \(c_0 = 11.1\) mM, compute the concentration at the closed end for \(D = 600\), \(60\) and \(6\) µm²/s, and the trench length \(L_{\max} = \sqrt{2Dc_0/V_{\max}}\) at which constant uptake would exhaust the nutrient. (b) Yang et al. [B1] analysed what limits growth in PDMS mother-machine trenches and concluded that it was not nutrient supply along the trench but mechanical constraints on the cells. Is your model consistent with this? What would it take, in \(D\) or in trench length, for nutrients to become limiting? (c) Which question can this model answer, and which can it not? Write three or four sentences.
C4. Assemble the 2D matrix. (a) Write lap2d(nx, ny, h, D) (Kronecker products; in Rust, triplets) and edge_rhs(nx, ny, h, D, c0), which builds \(\mathbf b\) from a grid-shaped array as on the lecture slide. Check B4: print \(\mathbf b\) and solve for the \(3 \times 2\) grid. (b) Build the oxygen chamber matrix for \(h = 50\) µm. Check its size, non-zeros (compare with the count \(5N\) minus the missing edge neighbours) and symmetry. (c) Manufactured field. \(U(x, y) = \sin(\pi x/L_x)\sin(2\pi y/L_y)\) is zero on all edges and \(-D\nabla^2U = D\pi^2(1/L_x^2 + 4/L_y^2)\,U\). Compute the relative error of \(A\mathbf U\) for \(h = 100, 50, 25\) µm. Is it second order?
C5. The ordering bug. Deliberately mix the two orders and see whether your checks catch it. R: build the matrix with the Kronecker factors in the order that belongs to \(y\) running fastest, but keep as.vector for the vectors. Python: keep the \(x\)-fastest matrix but flatten with numpy’s default ravel() (no order="F"). Rust: keep the matrix, but index the vectors with j + ny * i. (a) Run the C4(c) check and solve the constant-uptake problem (\(R_0 = 0.5\) µM/s), with the correct and with the mixed order. Print the check error and the maximum of \(c\). (b) Repeat the mixed version on a square chamber, \(2000 \times 2000\) µm. What do you see, and what is the lesson?
C6. Oxygen under the lid, with Michaelis–Menten uptake. Use \(h = 50\) µm, \(K_m = 1\) µM. (a) Write oxygen_mm(R0, clip) that runs Newton from \(c = 200\) µM everywhere, with or without clipping negative values to zero, and stops when \(\|\mathbf F\| < 10^{-8}\). (b) Without clipping, at \(2\times10^5\) cells/cm² (\(R_0 = 1\)): how many steps, and what is the smallest value? Is it a valid answer? (c) With clipping, for 1, 2 and \(3\times10^5\) cells/cm²: Newton steps, smallest \(c\), and the fraction of the chamber below 10 µM. Plot the last field (R: image; Python: plt.imshow(C.T, origin="lower"), note the transpose).

title: Exercise: steady state in two dimensions
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — 1D equations and boundaries (B1, B2, C1)





Write the stencil at each interior point; any \(c_0\) that appears is a number and goes to the right-hand side with a plus sign. For the closed end, write the ordinary stencil at \(x_N\) and replace \(c_{N+1}\) by \(c_{N-1}\). Divide each equation by \(D/h^2\) first; then the right-hand side contains \(R_0h^2/D\) (B1: \(62.5/2\); B2: \(0.6/3.84 = 0.15625\)). In code: R bandSparse takes the sub-diagonal first in diagonals, so its last entry is the \(-2\) of the ghost-point row; Python scipy.sparse.diags likewise; solve with Matrix::solve or scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve; in Rust use the Thomas algorithm from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse.









Hint 2 — numbering and Kronecker products (B3–B5, C4, C5)





Draw the grid with \(i\) to the right and \(j\) upwards and write \(k\) in each point, as in the lecture figure. From \(k\) (1-based): \(i = (k - 1) \bmod n_x + 1\), \(j = \lfloor (k-1)/n_x \rfloor + 1\). For numpy’s row-major order on shape \((n_x, n_y)\), the 0-based position is \(i\,n_y + j\) with 0-based \(i, j\). In \(A\otimes B\), the factor on the right (\(B\)) acts on the index that runs fastest. Check sizes: \(I_{n_y}\otimes T_{n_x}\) and \(T_{n_y}\otimes I_{n_x}\) are both \(n_xn_y \times n_xn_y\), and so are the swapped versions, so a wrong order never gives a size error.









Hint 3 — Newton with uptake (B6, B7, C2, C6)





\(\frac{d}{dc}\frac{c}{K_m + c} = \frac{K_m}{(K_m + c)^2}\). In B6, \(F'(c) = 0.004 + 1/(1+c)^2\). Each uptake term \(r(c_k)\) depends only on \(c_k\), so its derivative lands on the diagonal of \(J\). In code: R J <- A + Diagonal(x = dr), Python J = A + sparse.diags(dr); in Rust add the diagonal to a copy of the triplets, then solve with Thomas (1D) or CG (2D). Stop on the residual \(\|\mathbf F\|\), and clip with pmax(c, 0) / np.maximum(c, 0) / .max(0.0). After the loop, check min(c) >= 0.









Hint 4 — fill-in estimates (B8)





Unknowns: \(n_x = L_x/h - 1\), \(n_y = L_y/h - 1\), \(N = n_xn_y\). For a 3D block numbered with \(x\) fastest, then \(y\), then \(z\), the neighbour in \(z\) is \(n_xn_y\) away: that is the bandwidth. Memory: nnz × 8 bytes (plus indices).









Hint 5 — manufactured field and ordering (C4, C5)





Evaluate \(U\) at the interior points as a grid-shaped array U[i, j] (R outer(sin(pi * x / Lx), sin(2 * pi * y / Ly)); Python np.outer(...)), flatten it with the same order as \(\mathbf b\), multiply by \(A\), and compare with the exact values flattened the same way. Use \(\max|\cdot|\) relative to \(\max|-D\nabla^2U|\). For C5 also look at \(\max c\): with pure uptake and \(c = 200\) on the edges, no value can exceed 200 (maximum principle).

title: Exercise: steady state in two dimensions
text:
Where this leads

Flow plus diffusion: an advection term makes the matrix non-symmetric; Cholesky and CG no longer apply, and the order of upwind differences matters.
Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation: production and decay terms, the length scale \(\sqrt{D/k}\) of C1, and time-dependent 2D problems, where each implicit time step is a linear solve with the five-point Laplacian of this unit (there done with the FFT on a periodic grid, which diagonalises it).
Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow: real chambers with pillars and curved walls, where a rectangular grid no longer fits.
Iterative linear solvers in depth: conjugate gradient (used in the Rust solutions here), preconditioning, and why 3D problems (B8(c)) need it.
