title: Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Goal
This is an optional further-reading exercise. By the end of it you should be able to:

write a piecewise linear function as a sum of hat functions, and evaluate and integrate it,
compute the 2 × 2 element matrices for \(-(D u')' + k u = f\) and assemble them into the tridiagonal system,
show that on a uniform mesh the finite element matrix is the finite-difference matrix, and on a non-uniform mesh it is the non-uniform difference formula,
solve a 1D finite element problem on a graded mesh and see why putting nodes where the solution changes pays off,
recognise the failure (negative concentrations from elements that are too long) and the checks that detect it.

The by-hand part uses pen, paper and a pocket calculator. The code part runs the same 15-line solver on meshes of up to 200 elements.

title: Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
By hand
B1. Hat functions. Take the nodes \(x = 0, 1, 3, 4\) (a non-uniform mesh). (a) Write \(\varphi_1(x)\) (the hat at \(x_1 = 1\)) as a formula on each element. (b) With nodal values \(u = (1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1)\), evaluate \(u_h(0.5)\) and \(u_h(2)\). (c) What is the slope \(u_h'\) on each element? (d) Compute \(\int_0^4 u_h\,dx\).
B2. Assemble by hand. Take \(D = 1\), \(k = 0\) (pure diffusion, \(-u'' = f\)). (a) Uniform mesh \(0, 1, 2, 3\) (\(h = 1\)). Write the three element matrices and assemble the full 4 × 4 matrix \(K\). Compare its interior rows with the second difference \((-1, 2, -1)/h^2\). (b) Two elements of lengths \(h_1\) and \(h_2\) meeting at node 1, constant \(f\). Write the assembled equation of row 1. Show that dividing it by \((h_1 + h_2)/2\) gives the non-uniform difference formula \[-\frac{2}{h_1 + h_2}\left(\frac{u_2 - u_1}{h_2} - \frac{u_1 - u_0}{h_1}\right) = f.\] (c) Check (b) with \(u = x^2\) (so \(f = -u'' = -2\)) on nodes \(0, 1, 3\).
B3. Elements that are too long. A thinner slab, \(L = 500\) µm, with the same \(D = 100\) µm²/s and \(k = 0.04\) s⁻¹, cut into 2 elements of \(h = 250\) µm. \(u_0 = 1\), no flux at 500 µm. (a) Compute the diagonal entry \(D/h + kh/3\) and the off-diagonal entry \(-D/h + kh/6\) of each element matrix. What sign has the off-diagonal? (b) Assemble the 2 × 2 system for \(u_1, u_2\) (row 1 gets contributions from both elements) and solve it. (c) The exact values are \(u(250) = 0.0067\) and \(u(500) = 0.00009\). What is wrong with your answer? (d) For which \(h\) is the off-diagonal entry negative? Express the limit in terms of \(\lambda\). (e) Repeat (b) with the lumped matrix. Is the answer positive? Is it accurate?

title: Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
In code
C1. The same matrix as finite differences. Use assemble from the Background. (a) For 5 uniform elements on \([0, 500]\) µm with \(D = 100\) and \(k = 0\), print the diagonal and off-diagonal times \(h/D\). Compare with B2(a). (b) Now with \(k = 0.04\): print the diagonal and off-diagonal of the consistent and the lumped matrix, and of the finite-difference matrix \(\frac{D}{h}(-1, 2, -1) + k h\) on the diagonal, with the no-flux last row (from the ghost point) divided by 2 to match. Which one is the finite-difference matrix? (c) Solve the 1 mm slab with 10 uniform elements, consistent and lumped. Which has the smaller maximum nodal error?
C2. Refine where the solution changes. For \(N = 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160\) elements, solve the slab on the uniform mesh and on the graded mesh \(x_i = L(i/N)^2\). Print the maximum nodal error of each and their ratio; plot both against \(N\) on log–log axes and read off the order. Then compute the amount of drug in the gel, \(\int_0^L u_h\,dx\) (in µm × bath concentration), for \(N = 10\) on both meshes, and compare with the exact \(\lambda\tanh(L/\lambda)\).
C3. Failure, and a two-layer gel. (a) For \(N = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10\) uniform elements, print \(h/\lambda\), the smallest \(u_j\) for the consistent and for the lumped matrix. Compare with B3(d). (b) Now the top 100 µm of the gel is a cell-free coating (\(k = 0\) there), cells only below. Give each element the \(k\) of its midpoint. The exact drug level at the interface is \(u(100) = 1/\big(1 + (100/\lambda)\tanh(900/\lambda)\big)\). Compare the FEM value at \(x = 100\) (interpolated if there is no node there) for \(N = 50, 49, 100, 99, 200, 199\) uniform elements. Which meshes have a node at the interface, and what does that do to the error and its order?

title: Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — hats and integrals (B1)





On an element \([x_j, x_{j+1}]\) only \(\varphi_j\) and \(\varphi_{j+1}\) are non-zero, so \(u_h\) is the straight line between \((x_j, u_j)\) and \((x_{j+1}, u_{j+1})\). The integral of a straight line over an element is its length times the mean of the end values (the trapezoid rule of Numerical integration, here exact).









Hint 2 — assembly (B2, B3)





Write each element matrix in its own 2 × 2, then add: node \(i\) gets the bottom-right entry of element \(i\) (on its left) and the top-left entry of element \(i+1\) (on its right). The last node belongs to one element only. In B3, row 1 has \(-\)(off-diagonal)\(\times u_0\) moved to the right-hand side, with \(u_0 = 1\). Useful values: \(D/h = 0.4\), \(kh/3 = 10/3\), \(kh/6 = 5/3\), \(kh/2 = 5\).









Hint 3 — the solver (C1–C3)





The Thomas convention is the one from Implicit schemes and the method of lines: all four vectors of length \(m\), a[1] and c[m] unused. Python’s solve_banded((1, 1), ab, rhs) wants the superdiagonal in row 0 (first entry unused), the diagonal in row 1 and the subdiagonal in row 2 (last entry unused). For the slab use cosh and tanh (Python: np.cosh).









Hint 4 — order and interpolation (C2, C3)





If the error is \(\approx C N^{-p}\), then \(p = \log_2(e_N/e_{2N})\). Plot with matplot(..., log = "xy") (Python: plt.loglog). To read \(u_h\) between nodes use approx (Python: np.interp): linear interpolation is exactly \(u_h\). A per-element vector: the midpoints are head(x, -1) + diff(x) / 2 (Python: x[:-1] + np.diff(x) / 2). Test “is there a node at 100” with a tolerance, not == (How computers store numbers).

title: Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
Exercise: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Where this leads

Steady state in two dimensions (Part 10): the same steady problem on a 2D rectangle with the five-point stencil. A 2D finite element code replaces the loop over intervals by a loop over triangles with 3 × 3 element matrices; the resulting sparse matrix is solved with the same sparse direct solvers.
Iterative linear solvers in depth (Part 11): for 3D meshes with millions of nodes the sparse system is solved iteratively (conjugate gradients works because \(K\) is symmetric positive definite), with preconditioning.
Flow plus diffusion (Part 10) took the Poiseuille profile as given. A Stokes solver (COMSOL, FEniCS, Firedrake, scikit-fem) computes the flow in any geometry; that velocity field can then be fed into the advection–diffusion equation on the same mesh.

title: Quiz: beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow
text:
Further reading: not part of the course.
This material is not included in the course, but it is relevant if you want to learn more about the topic.





Short questions on finite volumes, finite elements and flow. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A culture chamber has round pillars of radius 50 µm. Name two problems a square finite-difference grid has with them.






Hint





Draw the grid cells that lie inside a pillar. Then ask what happens if you want finer resolution only near the pillars.









Answer






The round wall becomes a staircase: its position is wrong by up to \(\Delta x/2\), and a no-flux (or uptake) condition on a slanted wall has no clean stencil, so the flux through the wall, often the quantity of interest, is least accurate. (2) Refinement is global: a finer grid near the pillars is finer along whole grid lines across the chamber, so halving \(\Delta x\) costs 4× the unknowns in 2D and 8× in 3D.





Q2. What equation does a finite-volume method write for each cell, and why does it conserve mass exactly?






Hint





Think of the mass balance used to derive the diffusion equation, before taking a limit.









Answer





One balance per cell: (flux in through all faces) − (flux out) = uptake or accumulation inside. The flux through a face is computed once and used with opposite signs for the two cells sharing it, so what leaves one cell enters its neighbour exactly. Summed over all cells the internal fluxes cancel, and the total changes only by boundary fluxes and sources. This holds for cells of any shape.




Q3. On the nodes \(0, 2, 3\), what are the values of the hat function \(\varphi_1\) (the one at \(x = 2\)) at \(x = 1\), \(x = 2.5\) and \(x = 3\)?






Hint





\(\varphi_1\) is 1 at its own node, 0 at the neighbouring nodes, and a straight line in between.









Answer





\(\varphi_1(1) = 1/2\) (halfway up the left side, from 0 at \(x = 0\) to 1 at \(x = 2\)), \(\varphi_1(2.5) = 1/2\) (halfway down the right side), \(\varphi_1(3) = 0\).




Q4. In the weak form, why do we integrate by parts, and what happens to a no-flux boundary?






Hint





How many derivatives does a piecewise linear function have? What is \(D u'\) at a wall?









Answer





Integration by parts moves one derivative from \(u\) onto the test function, so only first derivatives remain. A piecewise linear \(u_h\) has a first derivative (piecewise constant) but no second derivative at the nodes. The boundary term it produces is \(D u'\varphi_i\), i.e. the flux; at a no-flux wall it is zero, so the condition is satisfied automatically (a natural boundary condition) with no ghost point.




Q5. For \(-D u'' = f\) on a uniform mesh, how does the finite element matrix compare with the finite-difference matrix? And with uptake \(k u\) added?






Hint





Element matrix \(\frac{D}{h}\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\); assemble two neighbours.









Answer





Interior rows are \(\frac{D}{h}(-1, 2, -1)\) with right-hand side \(fh\): the second-difference equation multiplied by \(h\). With uptake, the consistent FEM row has \(\frac{kh}{6}(u_{i-1} + 4u_i + u_{i+1})\) where finite differences have \(kh\,u_i\). Lumping the uptake onto the diagonal makes the two identical.




Q6. The drug penetrates a hydrogel slab with length scale \(\lambda = \sqrt{D/k} = 50\) µm, and the slab is 1 mm thick. With 10 elements, why is a graded mesh \(x_i = L(i/N)^2\) better than a uniform one? Does it change the order of convergence?






Hint





Where does \(u\) change? How many uniform nodes are there?









Answer





All the change is in the top ~150 µm. The uniform mesh (\(h = 100\) µm) has one node in that layer; the graded mesh has nodes at 10, 40 and 90 µm. The maximum error drops from 0.064 to 0.014 for the same 10 unknowns. The order stays 2 (error ∝ \(N^{-2}\) for both); grading changes the constant, about 4.5 times smaller here.




Q7. A finite element solution of the slab with 4 elements of 250 µm returns \(u = -0.17\) at 250 µm. What went wrong, how would you detect it, and how do you fix it?






Hint





Look at the sign of the off-diagonal entry \(-D/h + kh/6\).









Answer





The elements are longer than \(\sqrt6\,\lambda \approx 122\) µm, so the off-diagonal entries become positive and the discrete maximum principle is lost: the solution oscillates and goes negative. Detect it by checking that concentrations stay within physical bounds (here between 0 and the bath value) and by refining the mesh and watching the answer settle. Fix it by refining where the solution changes (elements shorter than about \(\lambda\) in the layer). Lumping keeps the values positive but does not make them accurate.




Q8. Estimate the Reynolds number for water (\(\rho = 1000\) kg/m³, \(\mu = 10^{-3}\) Pa s) flowing at 1 mm/s in a 100 µm channel. What does that mean for the equations?






Hint





\(Re = \rho U \ell / \mu\); convert everything to SI units.









Answer





\(Re = 1000 \cdot 10^{-3} \cdot 10^{-4} / 10^{-3} = 0.1\). Viscous forces dominate inertia, so the nonlinear inertia term of Navier–Stokes can be dropped: Stokes flow, \(\mu\nabla^2\mathbf u = \nabla p\), \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf u = 0\). It is linear, laminar (no turbulence), and one sparse linear solve gives the flow field.




Q9. In a straight channel of width \(w = 100\) µm the mean speed is 1000 µm/s. What is the speed at the centre and at the walls? Where did Flow plus diffusion use this?






Hint





Poiseuille: \(u(y) = \frac{G}{2\mu}\,y\,(w - y)\). Average it over \(0 \le y \le w\).









Answer





The mean of \(y(w-y)\) over the channel is \(w^2/6\) and its maximum (at \(y = w/2\)) is \(w^2/4\), so peak = 1.5 × mean = 1500 µm/s; at the walls the speed is 0 (no slip). Flow plus diffusion took this parabola as the given velocity of the T-sensor; here it is the exact solution of Stokes flow in a straight channel. Around pillars there is no formula and the flow must be computed.




Q10. You are asked to (a) fit a diffusion coefficient to 50 measured profiles across a straight channel, and (b) predict the drug concentration around the pillars of a new chip design drawn in CAD. Which would you do with a finite-difference script, and which with a finite element tool such as COMSOL or FEniCS? What check would you run on the tool?






Hint





Geometry, number of solves, and whether the flow field is known.









Answer






A finite-difference script: the geometry is a rectangle, the flow profile is known (Poiseuille), and fitting needs many fast solves inside an optimiser (Part 9). (b) A finite element (or finite-volume) tool: curved walls from CAD, and the flow field must be computed (Stokes) before the transport. Checks: refine the mesh until the answer settles, check conservation (flux in = uptake + flux out), and reproduce a special case with a known answer, such as Poiseuille flow in a straight section or a 1D slice from your own finite-difference code.

title: Exercise: stiffness and implicit methods
text:
Explore
The demo below puts the stability regions of fact 1 next to a solution. Panel (a) is the complex plane of \(z = h\lambda\): the regions \(|R(z)| \le 1\) of Euler (disc), RK4, backward Euler (everything outside the dashed circle) and the trapezoidal rule \(y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac h2\big(f(y_n) + f(y_{n+1})\big)\), \(R = (1 + z/2)/(1 - z/2)\) (the left half-plane); the selected method is shaded. The two round handles are \(h\lambda\) for the two eigenvalues of the problem; the step slider, or dragging a handle, moves both along their rays from 0. A handle turns red when its \(|R| > 1\). Panel (b) solves the linear system \(\mathbf y' = A\mathbf y\) with those eigenvalues, exact (grey) and by the selected method with the same \(h\). For the first problem, eigenvalues \(-1\) and \(-k\), the solution is \(y_1 = e^{-t} + e^{-kt}\), \(y_2 = e^{-t} - e^{-kt}\): \(y_2\) rises within \(1/k\) and then decays slowly, like the complex \(C\). The second problem uses the enzyme’s eigenvalues at \(t = 0\) (\(-0.0833\) and \(-1201\) per s, over 30 s), the third the 24-hour oscillator (\(\pm i\omega\), over 10 days). The table compares all four methods at the current \(h\), and gives the number of equal steps each needs to bring the error at \(t = T\) below the tolerance.
The numerical solution is computed mode by mode as \(R(h\lambda)^n\), which is exactly what \(n\) steps of each method give on a linear problem.



E1. (the fast point leaves first) Problem \(\lambda = -1, -k\) with \(k = 1000\), method Euler, \(h = 0.001\). Where are the two handles? Click h → stability limit, then drag the slider to \(h \approx 0.0025\). What happens to the fast handle and to panel (b)? Where is the slow handle at that moment, and how large would \(h\) have to be before it reached the edge of the disc?






Answer E1





At \(h = 0.001\): \(h\lambda_\text{slow} = -0.001\), right next to the origin, and \(h\lambda_\text{fast} = -1\), the centre of the disc (\(R = 0\): Euler kills the fast mode in one step). The error at \(T = 4\) is \(3.7\times10^{-5}\). The limit button sets \(h = 0.00198\): the fast handle sits just inside the left edge, \(R = -0.98\), the solution is still fine. At \(h = 0.0025\) the fast handle is at \(-2.51\), outside the disc and red, \(|R| = 1.51\): \(|y|\) passes \(10^6\) after 34 steps, and the error at \(T\) reads “overflow” (it is about \(10^{286}\)). The slow handle is at \(-0.0025\), barely moved; the slow mode alone would allow \(h\) up to \(2\), 1000 times more. The step is set by the fast mode, which decayed after a few milliseconds: that is stiffness.



E2. (step counts at a tolerance) Keep \(k = 1000\) and read the last column of the table at tolerance \(10^{-3}\), then at \(10^{-6}\). Which methods are limited by stability, which by accuracy? Why does RK4 hardly change, while Euler and backward Euler need 1000 times more steps?






Answer E2





At \(10^{-3}\): Euler 2004, RK4 1438, backward Euler 148, trapezoid 84. Euler and RK4 sit at their stability limits (\(4/0.002 = 2000\) and \(4/0.00279 = 1436\) steps): accuracy alone would let them take far fewer. Backward Euler and the trapezoid are set by accuracy. At \(10^{-6}\): Euler 146 524, RK4 1440, backward Euler 146 527, trapezoid 313. Euler and backward Euler are order 1: 1000 times smaller error needs 1000 times more steps, and now accuracy, not stability, sets Euler’s step, so the two are equal. RK4 at its stability-limited step is already far more accurate than \(10^{-6}\), so tightening the tolerance costs nothing. The trapezoid is order 2: a factor 1000 in error costs a factor \(\sqrt{1000} \approx 30\) in steps at most.



E3. (the stiffness ratio) At tolerance \(10^{-3}\), set the ratio \(k\) to 100, 1000 and 10 000 and write down the step counts of Euler, RK4 and backward Euler. How does each scale with \(k\)?






Answer E3





\(k = 100\): Euler 204, RK4 146, backward Euler 148. \(k = 1000\): 2004, 1438, 148. \(k = 10\,000\): 20 004, 14 363, 148. The explicit counts grow in proportion to \(k\) (about \(2k\) and \(1.4k\) steps for \(T = 4\), that is \(T|\lambda_\text{fast}|/2\) and \(T|\lambda_\text{fast}|/2.79\)), although the fast mode contributes nothing after \(t \approx 5/k\). Backward Euler needs 148 steps whatever \(k\) is: its count depends only on the slow solution and the tolerance. At \(k = 100\) all three are about equal: the problem is hardly stiff, and an explicit method is the cheaper choice once you count the Newton solves.



E4. (the enzyme) Click enzyme eigenvalues, method RK4, and click h → stability limit. Read off \(h\) and the step counts for all methods. Then switch on the log time axis, choose backward Euler and set \(h = 0.1\) s, then \(h = 1\) s; compare with the trapezoid at \(h = 1\) s.






Answer E4





RK4’s limit is \(2.32\) ms (\(2.785/1201\)); at \(0.99\) of it, \(h = 2.30\) ms and 13 065 steps, error \(4\times10^{-14}\). The table: Euler 18 017 steps, RK4 12 937, backward Euler 257, trapezoid 250 for an error below \(10^{-3}\), the 18 015 and 12 936 of B1(b) and the 13 000 of the lecture. Backward Euler at \(h = 0.1\) s (300 steps): the fast handle is at \(-120\), far off scale, \(R = 0.008\); on the log axis the first step jumps straight onto the slow curve and the error at 30 s is \(8.6\times10^{-4}\). At \(h = 1\) s (30 steps) the error is \(8.5\times10^{-3}\). The trapezoid at \(h = 1\) s is also stable, but its fast factor is \(R = -0.997\): the fast mode is not damped, it flips sign every step, and the error at 30 s is 0.9. Being stable on the whole left half-plane is not enough for a stiff problem; the method should also damp \(R \to 0\) as \(z \to -\infty\), which backward Euler (and BDF, Radau) do.



E5. (an oscillator is not stiff) Click 24-h clock, \(h = 1\) h. Compare the amplitude after 10 days for all four methods, and the steps each needs for an error below \(10^{-3}\). Where do the two handles lie, and which region boundary matters?






Answer E5





The handles are at \(\pm 0.262i\), on the imaginary axis. Amplitude after 240 steps: Euler 2850 (outside its disc for every \(h\): “stable for \(h \le\) none”), backward Euler \(3.5\times10^{-4}\) (the handles are deep inside its region: it damps a clock that should not decay, as in the lecture), RK4 0.9995, trapezoid exactly 1 (its boundary is the imaginary axis). Steps for error \(\le 10^{-3}\): RK4 300, trapezoid 4547, Euler and backward Euler about 2 million. Both eigenvalues have the same size, so nothing is stiff; a higher-order explicit method (RK4 is stable up to \(h = 10.8\) h here) wins, and an order-1 implicit method is the worst choice.

title: Exercise: nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the lecture’s Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt code on the plasma data in your browser: forward-difference Jacobian, one QR least-squares solve per pass, and for LM Marquardt’s scaling with \(\lambda_0 = 0.01\), divided by 10 after an accepted step and multiplied by 10 after a rejected one. Panel (a) is the RSS landscape of the lecture over \((k_a, k_e)\) on log axes, with \(V\) at its best value for each pair; the stars are the fit (\(V = 20.2\) L) and its flip-flop mirror (\(V = 3.8\) L), the dashed line is \(k_a = k_e\). The paths are the iterates of both methods projected onto \((k_a, k_e)\) (vermillion: Gauss–Newton; green: Levenberg–Marquardt); crosses are rejected LM trial points, and a square on the border marks a point off the map. The methods move all three parameters, so the start \(V\) is a slider, and a path need not follow the landscape exactly. Drag the start point (or click on the map) to choose \(k_a\) and \(k_e\). Step does one pass of each method, Run keeps stepping. Panel (b) shows the data and the current curves; the table gives the pass, the parameters, the RSS, \(\lambda\), whether the last step was accepted, and the status. The buttons (ka, ke, V) and log switch between fitting the parameters and their logarithms.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R, Python and Rust, so the iterates agree with the lecture to the digits shown. In the last passes, where the RSS changes only in the 15th digit, whether a step counts as “down” depends on rounding, so the number of final passes can differ by one or two. The demo also stops when a rejected step is already below the tolerance.



E1. (a good start) Click the good start \((0.5, 0.1, 10)\) and press Step repeatedly. Write down the RSS of both methods after each pass and \(\lambda\) for Levenberg–Marquardt. How many passes does each need? Do the two paths differ much, and why not?






Answer E1





Both start at RSS \(93.53\). Gauss–Newton: \(15.91\), \(0.9775\), \(0.09135\), \(0.06657\), \(0.06646745\), \(0.06646744\), the iterates of the lecture’s gauss_newton and of nls; it stops after 8 passes at \((1.015, 0.1906, 20.22)\). Levenberg–Marquardt: \(12.41\), \(0.8018\), \(0.07744\), \(0.06650\), \(0.06646744\); every step is accepted, so \(\lambda\) falls tenfold per pass from \(0.01\) to \(10^{-9}\), and it stops after 7 passes. With \(\lambda \le 10^{-3}\) the damping rows are tiny and the LM step is almost the Gauss–Newton step: the two paths lie nearly on top of each other along the valley. Near the minimum both gain two to three digits per pass.



E2. (a bad start) Click bad, \((3, 0.05, 50)\), and step. Where does the first Gauss–Newton step go, and what does the table say? Follow Levenberg–Marquardt: which passes are rejected, what happens to \(\lambda\) after each, and how many passes, accepted and rejected steps does it need in total?






Answer E2





Gauss–Newton jumps to \(k_a = -2.225\), \(k_e = 0.1787\), \(V = 0.0443\) with RSS \(6.7\times10^{29}\): off the map (a negative rate cannot be drawn on a log axis), the curve off the scale, status diverged. That is the step that makes nls stop with “singular gradient”. LM rejects pass 1 (trial RSS \(7.0\times10^{21}\), the same wild step slightly damped) and pass 2 (trial RSS \(11.4\)), so \(\lambda\) goes \(0.01 \to 0.1 \to 1\). At \(\lambda = 1\) the step is short and downhill: pass 3 is accepted (RSS \(4.63\), \(\lambda = 0.1\)), pass 4 rejected again (\(\lambda = 1\)), pass 5 accepted (\(3.39\)). Then every step is accepted, \(\lambda\) falls tenfold per pass and the steps become Gauss–Newton steps: \(2.39\), \(0.121\), \(0.0685\), \(0.06647\). The demo stops after 13 passes, 9 accepted and 4 rejected (the last rejection is a step already below the tolerance), at \((1.015, 0.1906, 20.22)\). The lecture’s run needs 15 passes; the difference is only in the last passes, where rounding decides whether the RSS went down.



E3. (log-parameters are not enough) Keep the bad start and switch to log. Step again. Does Gauss–Newton stay positive now? Does it converge? How many passes does Levenberg–Marquardt need now?






Answer E3





In logs every iterate is positive, but Gauss–Newton is still not safe: the first step crosses the diagonal to \((0.526, 0.655, 18.4)\) with RSS \(18.15\), twice the start’s \(9.53\); the second goes to \(k_a = 2.2\times10^{-4}\), \(k_e = 617\), \(V = 0.0031\) (RSS \(63.97\), close to \(\sum y_i^2 = 64.5\): the model predicts almost nothing). There the Jacobian is numerically singular and the method stops (singular gradient), as on the lecture slide. Levenberg–Marquardt rejects only the first step (\(\lambda \to 0.1\)), then goes straight down the valley: RSS \(2.45\), \(0.108\), \(0.0665\), done after 8 passes (6 accepted, 2 rejected) instead of 13. Log-parameters give positivity and better scaling; damping is still needed.



E4. (the mirror) Switch back to (ka, ke, V) and click mirror: the good start with \(k_a\) and \(k_e\) swapped and \(V\) multiplied by \(k_e/k_a\), i.e. \((0.1, 0.5, 2)\). Compare the starting RSS with E1, run both methods, and compare the end point, its RSS and the curve in panel (b) with the fit. Then drag the start point to a few places on each side of the dashed line \(k_a = k_e\) and press Run. Which minimum does each start find?






Answer E4





The starting RSS is \(93.53\), the same as the good start: the swapped parameters give the same curve already at the start. Both methods converge (GN 8 passes, LM 8 passes with one final rejection) to \((0.1906, 1.015, 3.796)\) with RSS \(0.06646744\), equal to the fit’s in all printed digits; the curve in panel (b) is the same curve. This is the flip-flop: the data cannot tell fast absorption and slow elimination from the reverse. Levenberg–Marquardt mostly finds the minimum on the side of the line where it starts: starts with \(k_a > k_e\) mostly end at the fit, starts with \(k_a < k_e\) almost always at the mirror, as in the multistart of C7. Gauss–Newton, started far from either minimum, often diverges instead. Only the RSS cannot decide; prior knowledge (\(V = 3.8\) L is about the plasma volume) or an IV dose can.



E5. (watching \(\lambda\) work) Click far, \((10, 4.5, 10)\), still in (ka, ke, V), and press Run. How does \(\lambda\) behave during passes 4–18, and what does the LM path do on the map? Where does it end, although the start has \(k_a > k_e\)? Then switch to log with the same start: what happens now?






Answer E5





Gauss–Newton jumps to \(k_a = 123\), \(k_e = -27.1\), RSS \(1.8\times10^{282}\): diverged. Levenberg–Marquardt rejects three steps (\(\lambda = 10\)), then alternates: accepted at \(\lambda = 10\) (\(\lambda \to 1\)), rejected at \(\lambda = 1\) (\(\lambda \to 10\)), again and again. It has found the largest step it can trust, and \(\lambda\) hovers between 1 and 10 like a trust-region radius. The path crawls along the flat plateau, \(k_a\) from 10 to 1.9 in short steps, with the RSS falling slowly from \(67.7\) to \(47.1\). At pass 19 a longer step crosses the line \(k_a = k_e\) to \((0.17, 2.39)\), and from there \(\lambda\) falls and the method converges quickly to the mirror \((0.1906, 1.015, 3.796)\) after 30 passes (18 accepted, 12 rejected). The side of the start does not guarantee the side of the end. In log, LM accepts two long steps and runs off to \(k_a = 1.1\times10^{15}\), \(k_e = 1.1\times10^{-5}\) (RSS \(34.3\)) and stops with a singular Jacobian: the run-off of the multistart slide. A fit that ends with a much larger RSS than others has failed; this is why one runs several starts and compares the RSS.

title: Quiz: steady state in two dimensions
text:
Short questions on steady diffusion, the five-point Laplacian, grid ordering and Newton with uptake. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. What is the difference between the diffusion problems of the last two units and the steady-state problem of this unit? What information does a steady-state problem need, and what does it not need?






Hint





Set \(\partial c/\partial t = 0\). What is left of the initial condition?









Answer





The steady state has \(\partial c/\partial t = 0\), so \(D\nabla^2c = r(c)\): a boundary value problem (Poisson; Laplace if \(r = 0\)). It needs boundary conditions (fixed value or no flux on every edge) and the uptake law, but no initial condition and no time step: one (linear or nonlinear) system instead of thousands of time steps.




Q2. A 1D chamber with constant oxygen uptake is solved with only 3 interior points, and the grid values agree with the exact solution to 15 digits. Does that show that the code is second-order accurate?






Hint





What shape is the exact solution, and what is the error term of the second difference?









Answer





No. With constant uptake the exact solution is a parabola, and the second difference is exact for parabolas (its error term contains the fourth derivative, which is zero). Every correct code gets this right on any grid, so it cannot reveal the order. Use a test with a non-polynomial exact solution (linear uptake, cosh) or a manufactured field, and check that the error falls 4× per halving of \(h\).




Q3. On a 2D grid with \(n_x = 79\), \(n_y = 39\) interior points, numbered with \(x\) running fastest, where in the vector are the four neighbours of unknown \(k\)? Why is the matrix not tridiagonal?






Hint





\(k = i + (j - 1)\,n_x\).









Answer





\(x\)-neighbours at \(k \pm 1\), \(y\)-neighbours at \(k \pm n_x = k \pm 79\) (missing where the point is next to an edge). The \(y\)-coupling puts non-zeros 79 places from the diagonal, so the matrix is banded with bandwidth \(n_x\) (block tridiagonal), not tridiagonal.




Q4. Which Kronecker formula gives the five-point Laplacian when \(x\) runs fastest, and which when \(y\) runs fastest? Why does a mix-up never give an error message?






Hint





In \(A \otimes B\), the right factor acts on the index that runs fastest.









Answer





\(x\) fastest: \(I_{n_y}\otimes T_{n_x} + T_{n_y}\otimes I_{n_x}\). \(y\) fastest: \(T_{n_x}\otimes I_{n_y} + I_{n_x}\otimes T_{n_y}\) (times \(D/h^2\)). Both are \(n_xn_y \times n_xn_y\), so all sizes match and every solve runs. The result is simply the solution of a different problem.




Q5. R: as.vector(C). numpy: C.ravel(). For a grid stored as C[i, j] with shape \((n_x, n_y)\), which index runs fastest in each? How do you make numpy behave like R?






Hint





Column-major vs row-major.









Answer





R stores matrices column by column (column-major): as.vector(C) runs over \(i\) (\(x\)) first. numpy is row-major by default: C.ravel() runs over \(j\) (\(y\)) first. Use C.ravel(order="F") and c.reshape((nx, ny), order="F") to get R’s order (or use the other Kronecker formula, consistently). For plotting, matplotlib’s imshow(C) puts rows vertically: use imshow(C.T, origin="lower").




Q6. A student tests the assembly of her 2D matrix on a square \(40 \times 40\) grid with the field \(\sin(\pi x/L)\sin(\pi y/L)\), and everything checks out. Why might an ordering bug still be there? How should she test?






Hint





What happens to the two Kronecker formulas when \(n_x = n_y\)?









Answer





For \(n_x = n_y\) (and equal spacing) the two Kronecker formulas give the same matrix, and a field symmetric in \(x\) and \(y\) looks the same after swapping. The bug is invisible until the grid becomes a rectangle. Test on a grid with \(n_x \ne n_y\), with a field that differs in \(x\) and \(y\) (e.g. \(\sin(\pi x/L_x)\sin(2\pi y/L_y)\)), and check that the error is small and falls 4× per halving of \(h\). Also check bounds: with pure uptake no value may exceed the boundary value.




Q7. Why does solve(A, b) on the chamber matrix become much faster after A <- forceSymmetric(A)? What is fill-in doing here?






Hint





Which factorisation does each call use, and with which ordering?









Answer





On a general sparse matrix, solve uses sparse LU; on a matrix marked symmetric it uses sparse Cholesky (CHOLMOD) with a fill-reducing ordering. In natural order, elimination fills the whole band of width \(n_x\) (16 million non-zeros at \(h = 12.5\) µm); reordered, 1.5 million. Fewer non-zeros means less memory and less work: about 0.16 s instead of seconds. Python’s spsolve also reorders (COLAMD) by default.




Q8. Constant oxygen uptake gives a negative oxygen level in the centre of a dense culture. Is that a numerical error? What is the fix?






Hint





Would a finer grid change the sign?









Answer





No: the grid solution is accurate; the model is wrong. It lets cells consume at full rate even when no oxygen is left. Michaelis–Menten uptake \(R_0c/(K_m + c)\) slows down as \(c \to 0\), keeps \(c \ge 0\), and makes the problem nonlinear (Newton). Check min(c) >= 0 on every concentration you compute.




Q9. For \(\mathbf F(\mathbf c) = A\mathbf c + r(\mathbf c) - \mathbf b\) with Michaelis–Menten uptake, what is the Jacobian, and why does it have the same sparsity pattern as \(A\)?






Hint





On which unknowns does the uptake at point \(k\) depend?









Answer





\(J = A + \operatorname{diag}\bigl(R_0K_m/(K_m + c_k)^2\bigr)\). The uptake at point \(k\) depends only on \(c_k\), so its derivative appears only on the diagonal, which is already non-zero in \(A\). \(J\) is also symmetric positive definite, so each Newton step is a sparse Cholesky solve (or CG) of the same kind as the linear problem.




Q10. Newton converges quadratically to a residual of \(10^{-12}\), but the oxygen field has a minimum of \(-27.6\) µM. What happened, and what two checks would have caught it?






Hint





Is \(c/(K_m + c)\) positive or negative for \(c = -27.6\), \(K_m = 1\)?









Answer





Newton found a spurious root: for \(c < -K_m\), \(c/(K_m + c) > 0\), so the equations are satisfied by a field with negative oxygen that is “consumed”. The first step from an air-saturated start jumps to the (negative) constant-uptake answer and Newton settles there. A small residual only says that a root was found, not which one. Checks: min(c) >= 0 after the solve (and in every step), and the maximum principle (values between 0 and the boundary value). Fix: clip negative values to 0 after each step, or start from \(c = 0\).




Q11. A diffusion model of a mother-machine trench shows that glucose at the closed end stays above 97 % of the channel value in rich medium. Does that prove that cells at the closed end grow as fast as those at the open end?






Hint





What is not in the model?









Answer





No. It shows only that glucose diffusion, with these parameters, does not limit growth. Other factors (mechanical constraints on packed cells, other nutrients, waste products, oxygen) are not in the model, so it can rule out one explanation but cannot confirm growth. Yang et al. concluded that mechanics, not nutrient supply, limits growth in such trenches: the model is consistent with that, but could not have found it.

title: Exercise: stochastic simulation
text:
Explore
The demo below runs Gillespie’s algorithm in your browser for the two genes of this exercise, both with an ODE mean of 10 mRNA (time in hours): the constitutive gene (\(k = 10\), \(\delta = 1\)) and the bursty telegraph gene (\(k_\text{on}\), \(k_\text{off} = 9\,k_\text{on}\), \(k_m = 100\), \(\delta = 1\); the promoter is on 10 % of the time for every \(k_\text{on}\), so the mean stays 10 while the burst size \(k_m/k_\text{off}\) changes). The tab One cell follows a single cell from \(m = 0\): panel (a) shows \(m(t)\) as a step function (promoter-on periods shaded green) with the ODE mean dashed; Step fires one reaction, and panel (b) shows how it was drawn: the waiting time \(\tau = -\ln(u_1)/a_0\) read off the exponential distribution function, and the reaction picked where \(u_2 a_0\) falls on the stacked bar of propensities. Run animates, Reset replays the same cell, New cell draws another one. The tab Many cells simulates \(N\) cells to time \(T\) and compares (c) the histogram of counts with the exact distribution and (d) the Fano factor with the exact curve. The tau-leaping box (constitutive gene only) replaces each reaction by a leap of \(\tau\) hours with Poisson numbers of reactions.
The demo has its own seeded generator, so its numbers differ from those of R, Python and Rust; compare statistics, not single cells.



E1. (one reaction at a time) With the constitutive gene, click Step four times. For each step write down \(a_0\), \(u_1\), \(\tau\), \(u_2 a_0\) and the reaction, and check one \(\tau\) and one choice by hand as in B2. Why is the first reaction certainly make? Then click Run (or keep stepping) to the end of the 20 h window: how many reactions were needed, and how does the cell compare with the ODE?






Answer E1





Step 1: \(a = (10, 0)\), \(a_0 = 10\), \(u_1 = 0.777\), \(\tau = -\ln(0.777)/10 = 0.0252\) h (1.5 min); \(u_2 a_0 = 1.88 < 10\): make, \(m = 1\). Step 2: \(a_0 = 11\), \(u_1 = 0.956\), \(\tau = 0.0041\) h (15 s); \(u_2 a_0 = 10.11 \ge 10\): degrade, \(m = 0\). Step 3: \(a_0 = 10\), \(\tau = 0.0566\) h; \(u_2 a_0 = 9.72\): make. Step 4: \(a_0 = 11\), \(\tau = 0.0518\) h; \(u_2 a_0 = 9.995\), just below 10: make, \(m = 2\). At \(m = 0\) the degradation propensity \(\delta m\) is 0, so its piece of the bar has length 0 and cannot be hit. The 20 h take 447 reactions (about \(a_0 = 20\) per hour once \(m \approx 10\)). The cell rises with the ODE curve and then wanders between 3 and 22 around 10; the steps are random and unequal, with no step size to choose.



E2. (a burst, step by step) Switch to bursty (telegraph) (the default \(k_\text{on} = 0.5\)). Step once: which reaction is possible, and what is the mean waiting time? Keep stepping (about 40 steps) until the promoter switches off. What is \(a_0\) while the promoter is on, how long are the waiting times, how long was the promoter on, and how many mRNA did the burst make? Which reaction fired at the end, and where on the bar did \(u_2 a_0\) fall? Then Run to 20 h and describe the trajectory.






Answer E2





From \(g = 0\), \(m = 0\) only switching on has a non-zero propensity: \(a_0 = k_\text{on} = 0.5\) per hour, mean wait 2 h; here \(\tau = 0.504\) h (30 min). While on, \(a_0 = 4.5 + 100 + m\), from 104.5 up to 136.5 per hour: waiting times of seconds (mean about 30 s), and almost every step is make. On step 40 the promoter switched off at \(t = 0.777\) h, after 0.27 h (16 min) on; the burst made 35 mRNA and \(m = 32\) (3 had decayed). The off piece (4.5 of 136.5) is a thin sliver at the left of the bar, and \(u_2 a_0 = 3.21\) fell into it. After that \(a_0 = 0.5 + m\): only decays, minutes apart, until the next burst. Over 20 h: 11 bursts of very different sizes (2 to 35 mRNA), \(m\) up to 47, and a silent stretch from 4.8 h to 7.4 h with only 0 or 1 molecules. The ODE mean is the same smooth curve to 10 as for the constitutive gene; no single cell looks like it.



E3. (same mean, different distribution) Open Many cells (\(N = 1000\), \(T = 30\) h). Read the mean ± SE, the variance, the Fano factor and the fraction of cells with no mRNA for the bursty gene, then for the constitutive gene, and compare each with the exact value. Then click \(T = 1\) for both: does the mean still match, and against what?






Answer E3





Bursty: mean \(10.36 \pm 0.41\) (exact 10), variance 165.6 (160), Fano 15.98 (16), 17.4 % of cells with 0 mRNA (exact 20.3 %). Constitutive: mean \(9.95 \pm 0.10\), variance 9.63 (10), Fano 0.97 (1), no cell with 0 (exact \(e^{-10} = 4.5\times10^{-5}\)). Both means agree with 10 within 1 SE, but the bursty histogram has a peak at 0 and a tail beyond 60, while the constitutive one is the narrow Poisson(10). Note the SE: with the same \(N\) it is 4 times larger for the bursty gene, since \(\sqrt{160/1000} = 0.40\). At \(T = 1\) h: constitutive \(6.18 \pm 0.08\) against the ODE value \(10(1 - e^{-1}) = 6.32\) (1.7 SE); bursty \(4.85 \pm 0.31\) against 5.42 (1.8 SE), with 65 % of cells still at 0 because many promoters have not fired yet. For linear propensities the ODE gives the exact mean at every time, so both agree within the Monte Carlo error.



E4. (burstiness at a fixed mean) Stay in Many cells with the bursty gene (\(N = 1000\), \(T = 30\)). Click \(k_\text{on} = 1\) and \(5\), and drag \(k_\text{on}\) to 20 and to 0.2. For each, note the burst size \(k_m/k_\text{off}\), the mean and the Fano factor, and watch the dots in panel (d). Which limit is the constitutive gene? Finally, at \(k_\text{on} = 0.5\), set \(N = 100\) and \(N = 5000\): how do the mean’s SE and the Fano factor change?

The more bursty the gene, the more cells it takes to measure the mean: at \(k_\text{on} = 0.5\), \(N = 100\) gives \(11.49 \pm 1.29\) and Fano 14.5, \(N = 5000\) gives \(9.85 \pm 0.18\) and Fano 16.2. E5. (tau-leaping goes wrong) Back on One cell with the constitutive gene, tick tau-leaping and set \(\tau = 1.5\) h. Step through the 20 h, and click New cell until a count goes negative (red). What does panel (b) show for that leap? Then in Many cells set \(N = 2000\) and \(T = 10\), and read the variance and the fraction of runs that went negative for \(\tau = 0.1, 0.5, 1, 1.5\). The trajectory jumps by 10 to 20 molecules from one leap to the next instead of wandering around 10: with \(\delta\tau = 1.5\) a leap removes on average 1.5 times the molecules present, so it overshoots, as Euler’s method does for \(\delta h > 1\). The fifth cell (New cell four times) goes negative twice; at \(t = 7.5\) h: \(m = 22\), make Poisson(15) = 18, degrade Poisson(33) = 41, so \(22 + 18 - 41 = -1\), clipped to 0. title: Exercise: gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Explore
The demo below races four optimisers on a function of two variables, in your browser. Left: the contour map, the start (white square), the minimum (black cross) and the path of each method: steepest descent with Armijo backtracking, Newton with the same line search (if \(H\) is not positive definite it adds \(\mu I\), as in C4(c)), BFGS with \(B_0 = I\), and Nelder–Mead with R optim’s rules (best point dashed, current simplex shaded). All are the algorithms of the lecture slides; the gradient methods stop when \(\|\nabla f\| < 10^{-8}\) (bowl, Rosenbrock) or \(10^{-4}\) (4PL, as in the lecture), Nelder–Mead when the three corner values agree to a relative \(10^{-8}\). Right: \(f - f^*\) on a log scale against the iteration, and the number of calls of \(f\), \(\nabla f\) and \(H\). Click the map to start from somewhere else; ▶ race replays the run iteration by iteration. The 4PL presets are the lecture’s SSE as a function of EC50 and Hill slope only, with bottom and top fixed at the best fit.



E1. (zig-zag and the condition number) On the bowl \(f = \tfrac12(x^2 + \kappa y^2)\), from the default start \((-1.6, 1)\), set \(\kappa = 1\), \(10\), \(100\) and \(1000\) and note the iterations and \(f\) calls of steepest descent each time (use the all button of the iteration axis). What shape does its curve have on the log plot, and how does the number of iterations scale with \(\kappa\)? How many iterations do Newton and BFGS need?






Answer E1





Steepest descent: \(\kappa = 1\): 1 iteration (the gradient points straight at the minimum); \(\kappa = 10\): 76 iterations, 255 \(f\) calls; \(\kappa = 100\): 861 and 5673; \(\kappa = 1000\): 9475 and 94 366. The iterations grow about tenfold per tenfold \(\kappa\), as \((\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)\) predicts (\(\log \varepsilon / \log\frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1} \approx \tfrac{\kappa}{2}\log\frac1\varepsilon\)). On the log plot the curve is a straight line after the first steps: linear convergence, with a slope that flattens as \(\kappa\) grows. On the map the path zig-zags across the valley. The \(f\) calls per iteration also grow (3, 7, 10): the backtracking must halve \(\alpha\) until it is below about \(2/\kappa\). Newton needs 1 iteration for every \(\kappa\) (the quadratic model of a quadratic is exact); BFGS 1, 5, 4, 3, almost independent of \(\kappa\).



E2. (the banana) Choose Rosenbrock (start \((-1.2, 1)\), minimum \((1, 1)\), \(\kappa(H^*) = 2508\)) and press ▶ race. Which method arrives first? Read off the iterations and the \(f\), \(\nabla f\) and \(H\) calls of each method, and describe the tail of the Newton and BFGS curves. If a call of \(f\) took a second (an ODE model), which method would you pick?






Answer E2





Newton: 21 iterations, 29 \(f\) calls, 21 gradients, 21 Hessians. BFGS: 35 iterations, 55 \(f\) calls, 36 gradients. Nelder–Mead: 86 iterations, 163 \(f\) calls (stopping at \(f - f^* = 1.9\times10^{-8}\)). Steepest descent: 19 435 iterations and 193 366 \(f\) calls. Newton and BFGS follow the curved valley slowly at first (\(f - f^*\) is still \(0.02\) after 15 Newton and \(0.015\) after 25 BFGS iterations), then fall off a cliff: Newton’s tail bends ever steeper (quadratic: \(7.8\times10^{-5}\), \(2.8\times10^{-7}\), \(8.5\times10^{-12}\), \(3.7\times10^{-21}\), the exponent roughly doubles), BFGS’s a little less steeply (superlinear: \(5.5\times10^{-7}\), \(8.7\times10^{-10}\), \(1.9\times10^{-13}\), \(2.7\times10^{-17}\)). Steepest descent is linear and very slow along the valley floor. With costly \(f\) and an analytic gradient, BFGS: no second derivatives, and 55 \(f\) calls plus 36 gradients. Newton is fewer iterations, but each Hessian costs as much as \(n\) extra gradients when it is not available analytically. Nelder–Mead needs no gradient at all, but stops at a lower accuracy.



E3. (units) Choose 4PL, EC50 in µM (start EC50 = 1, hill = 1), then 4PL, EC50 in nM (start 1000 nM, hill 1: the same point), then 4PL, log₁₀ EC50. Compare the maps, \(\kappa(H)\) at the minimum, and the iterations of each method. Why is Newton’s path the same in µM and nM, and steepest descent’s not?






Answer E3





The maps in µM and nM look identical: only the numbers on the \(x\) axis change by a factor 1000. But \(\kappa(H)\) goes from \(1.03\) (µM) to \(1.02\times10^{6}\) (nM): \(\partial^2\mathrm{SSE}/\partial\mathrm{EC50}^2\) is divided by \(1000^2\). Steepest descent: 70 iterations in µM; in nM it hits the limit of 20 000 iterations with \(f - f^* = 147\), stuck near EC50 = 1015 nM: the step that is stable for the Hill direction moves EC50 by almost nothing. Newton: 4 iterations in both, along the same path: the Hessian contains the units, so \(H^{-1}\nabla f\) rescales them away. BFGS 8 → 11, Nelder–Mead 27 → 40 (its first simplex has the step \(0.1 \times 1000 = 100\) in both coordinates, so one corner sits at hill = 101). With \(\log_{10}\mathrm{EC50}\): \(\kappa = 8.4\), steepest descent 136 iterations, Newton 4, BFGS 7. (The 4-parameter \(\kappa = 550\) of the lecture comes mostly from bottom and top, fixed here.) The cure in practice is to rescale (parscale) or to fit \(\log\mathrm{EC50}\).



E4. (“converged” is not “found the minimum”) Stay with 4PL, EC50 in µM and click the map near EC50 = 3.5, hill = 0.4 (bottom right). Where do steepest descent and BFGS go, what do they report, and what is \(f - f^*\)? Then try a few starts nearby. Which methods reach the minimum from all of them?






Answer E4





From \((3.5, 0.4)\) steepest descent and BFGS leave the map upwards: the very first step pushes the Hill slope from 0.4 to 36. The model curve is then a step function, and the SSE hardly changes with the parameters. There the gradient is below \(10^{-4}\), so both stop with a ✓ (“converged”), at hill ≈ 36 (EC50 1.0 and 3.1) with \(f - f^* = 1.7\times10^3\) (SD, 21 iterations) and \(3.6\times10^3\) (BFGS, 8 iterations): a flat plateau, not a minimum. Exact numbers depend on where you click: from \((3.5, 0.5)\) steepest descent runs to its iteration limit on the plateau while BFGS finds the minimum; from \((3.8, 0.3)\) both overflow to NaN. Newton (with one \(H + \mu I\) step, because \(H\) is indefinite there) and Nelder–Mead reach the minimum from all these starts. The lesson is the lecture’s: check the SSE and the fitted curve, not the convergence flag, and use multistart (C8).

title: Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton
text:
Try it: an optimiser race




The four methods of this lecture, as on the slides, computed live in the browser on functions of two variables: steepest descent with Armijo backtracking (vermillion), Newton with the same line search and H + mu I when H is not positive definite (blue), BFGS with B0 = I (orange), Nelder-Mead with optim’s rules, simplex shaded (green). Right: f - f* on a log axis against the iteration, and the counts of f, gradient and Hessian calls. Start on the bowl with kappa = 10: press race, steepest descent zig-zags, 76 iterations, a straight line on the log plot; Newton 1 step, BFGS 5. Drag kappa to 100 and 1000: steepest descent 861 and 9475 iterations (switch the iteration axis to “all”), Newton still 1. Then Rosenbrock: Newton 21, BFGS 35, Nelder-Mead 86, steepest descent 19435; point at Newton’s tail, the exponent doubles (quadratic), BFGS slightly slower (superlinear). Then the 4PL with EC50 in µM (bottom and top fixed at the best fit): kappa 1.03, all fast. Switch to nM: the map looks the same, kappa is 1e6, steepest descent is stuck after 20000 iterations, Newton takes exactly the same 4 steps. Finish by clicking near EC50 = 3.5, hill = 0.4: steepest descent and BFGS shoot to hill = 36, a plateau, and report convergence with SSE 1700 too high.

title: Exercise: numerical integration
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the rules of this exercise in your browser. Tab (a) Rules and order draws an integrand with the panels of the chosen rule (for Gauss–Legendre, each bar is as wide as its weight) and plots \(|\text{error}|\) against \(n\) for all five rules on log–log axes, with dashed reference lines of slope \(-2\) and \(-4\); the readout gives the estimate, the error, and the order measured from \(n\) to \(2n\), \(\log_2\big(\text{err}(n)/\text{err}(2n)\big)\). The integrands are the lecture’s PK model on \([0, 6]\) h (exact AUC 32.624), a chromatography peak with \(\sigma = 3\) s, a one-hour constant-rate infusion (500 mg, \(V = 50\) L, \(k_e = 0.2\)/h) whose concentration has a kink at 1 h, \(\sqrt{x}\), and the 10 blood samples of the Background. Tab (b) Adaptive quadrature runs the adaptive Simpson routine of C4 (tolerance \(10^{-6}\)) or a 21-point Gauss–Kronrod routine that follows QUADPACK, the library behind integrate and quad (R’s default tolerances; it reproduces R’s output for dnorm digit for digit). Ticks under the axis are the evaluation points, bars are the pieces; start over and step show the subdivision one step at a time, run animates it.



E1. (orders on the PK curve) With the PK curve and the trapezoid rule, set \(n = 4, 8, 16, 32\) and note the error and the measured order. Repeat with Simpson. Then click Gauss–Legendre and try \(n = 4\) and \(8\). Compare with B3 and C1. How many function values does each rule need for an error below \(10^{-6}\)?






Answer E1





Trapezoid: errors 2.7, 0.72, 0.18, 0.046, measured orders 1.91, 1.98, 1.99, 2.00: order 2, as in B3. Simpson: 0.66, 0.059, 0.0041, 0.00026, orders 3.49, 3.85, 3.96, 3.99: order 4, reached only once \(h\) is small compared with the absorption phase. On the log–log plot the trapezoid points follow the slope-\(-2\) line, the Simpson points the slope-\(-4\) line. Gauss–Legendre: \(n = 4\) gives \(0.030\), \(n = 8\) gives \(3.2\times10^{-8}\), and from \(n = 16\) on the error sits at the rounding level (\(7\times10^{-15}\)): no straight line, the error falls faster than any power of \(n\). For \(10^{-6}\): the trapezoid needs about \(7\,000\) intervals (\(0.046\cdot(32/n)^2 = 10^{-6}\), off the plot), Simpson about 130 (\(n = 128\) gives \(1.04\times10^{-6}\)), Gauss–Legendre 8 points.



E2. (smoothness and order) Choose the infusion integrand and Simpson. Read the measured order at \(n = 16, 32, 64\), and look at how the parabolas cross the kink at \(n = 16\). Then set \(n = 12\) and \(n = 24\). Check Gauss–Legendre at \(n = 8, 16, 32, 64\), and Simpson on \(\sqrt{x}\). Finally pick the peak and compare the trapezoid rule with Simpson at \(n = 16\) and \(n = 20\) (\(h = 3.75\) s and \(3\) s).






Answer E2





Infusion, Simpson: orders 3.06, 2.97, 3.01 (errors \(2.7\times10^{-3}\), \(3.2\times10^{-4}\), \(4.1\times10^{-5}\)): the kink lowers the order from 4 to 3, because the parabola across the kink cannot bend sharply and its error dominates. At \(n = 12\) and \(24\) a grid point sits on the kink (\(h = 0.5\) and \(0.25\) h; the readout says so): errors \(9.3\times10^{-6}\) and \(5.8\times10^{-7}\), order 4.00 again, 300 times smaller than with \(n = 16\). Putting a point at the kink (splitting there) restores the order. Gauss–Legendre: \(0.28\), \(0.046\), \(0.028\), \(0.0049\): erratic, and only about order 2.5 instead of the plunge of E1; a single high-degree polynomial cannot follow a kink. On \(\sqrt{x}\) Simpson measures 1.50, as in C2. The peak goes the other way: the trapezoid errors are \(4.9\times10^{-2}\) and \(4.0\times10^{-5}\) (relative \(5\times10^{-9}\), as in the lecture), Simpson’s \(2.1\times10^2\) and \(36\). Simpson is \((4T(h/2) - T(h))/3\) and so carries the error of the coarse \(T(h)\); for a peak that starts and ends at the baseline the trapezoid error is not \(C h^2\) but falls faster than any power of \(h\), so the extrapolation that assumes \(C h^2\) makes it worse.



E3. (AUC from the 10 samples) Click PK: 10 samples. Compare the linear trapezoid and linear-up / log-down on the left panel, also with log scale on, and read the per-interval errors in panel (b). Which interval causes the 4 % bias? Where are the remaining errors of the log-down rule? Finally read \(\lambda_z\), the extrapolated tail and \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-\infty}\) for each rule, and compare with the model value 50.






Answer E3





Linear: 51.6175 (+4.2 %), log-down: 48.91575 (−1.2 %), true 49.52521. The 12–24 h interval alone contributes \(+2.08\) of the linear rule’s \(+2.09\) total: a straight line over a 12 h gap on an exponential decline. On the log scale the elimination phase is a straight line, and the log-down segments follow it; the bar for 12–24 h drops to \(-0.07\). The log-down rule’s remaining errors are in the first three intervals (\(-0.18\), \(-0.09\), \(-0.21\) mg·h/L), where the curve rises and is concave and both rules use straight lines: more early samples would help, not another rule. \(\lambda_z = 0.2037\)/h, tail \(C_\text{last}/\lambda_z = 0.442\) (under 1 % of the total), \(\mathrm{AUC}_{0-\infty} = 52.06\) (linear) and \(49.36\) (log-down) against \(\text{Dose}/(V k_e) = 50\).



E4. (watching adaptive quadrature) Open tab (b). With the PK model and adaptive Simpson, click start over, then step a few times, then run. Where do the pieces end up? Read the final evaluations and the error. Now choose the chromatogram peak (at 340 s, \(\sigma = 3\) s). What does adaptive Simpson return, after how many evaluations? Move the peak to 300 s; then back to 340 s with initial pieces 60. Finally try Gauss–Kronrod 21 on the peak at 340 s.






Answer E4





The first step compares one Simpson panel on \([0, 24]\) (estimate 17.1) with two, disagrees and splits; the pieces then shrink near the absorption peak (widths down to 0.047 h) and stay wide in the tail (up to 1.5 h): 269 evaluations, 67 pieces, error \(9.0\times10^{-10}\), as in fig05 and C4. On the chromatogram adaptive Simpson stops after 5 evaluations with \(2\times10^{-34}\) and an error estimate of \(5\times10^{-35}\), while the true area is 7519.885: the points 0, 150, 300, 450, 600 s all see baseline, the two Simpson estimates agree, and the piece is accepted. The demo flags it as a silent failure. With the peak at 300 s the middle point hits it and the routine refines (2689 evaluations, error below \(10^{-9}\)). Sixty initial pieces of 10 s fix it at 340 s (2905 evaluations), as in C4(c). Gauss–Kronrod finds the peak at 340 s with 273 evaluations, because one of its 21 points lies at 344.7 s, within 2σ.



E5. (why integrate(dnorm, 0, 20000) is 0) Choose dnorm on [0, L] with Gauss–Kronrod 21. Click the presets \(L = 2000, 2300, 4300, 4400, 5000, 20000\) and record the first-pass result, the final estimate, the error estimate and the number of evaluations. Compare with B5 and C5. Then, at \(L = 20000\), tick split at x = 10; and switch to adaptive Simpson without the split. Why does adaptive Simpson succeed here but fail on the chromatogram?






Answer E5





At \(L = 20000\) the 21 points start at 43.4, all values are exactly 0, the error estimate is 0 and the routine stops at once: 0 with error estimate 0, as in R. At 5000 the first pass gives \(3\times10^{-25}\); its error estimate has hit its upper cap (the spread of the integrand values), which QUADPACK does not trust after the first pass, so it bisects once, but the left half \([0, 2500]\) is missed too: \(2.3\times10^{-6} \pm 4.6\times10^{-6}\) after 63 evaluations, R’s output for C5. At 4400: \(5.7\times10^{-5} \pm 1.1\times10^{-4}\) (the half \([0, 2200]\) just misses). At 4300 the half \([0, 2150]\) has a point at 4.7, the routine sees the peak and returns 0.5 after 399 evaluations. At 2000 and 2300 the first pass is already non-zero (\(3.7\times10^{-4}\) and \(2.1\times10^{-5}\)) and the answer is 0.5 (357 evaluations). So B5’s rule of thumb (closest point within \(5\sigma\), \(L \lesssim 2300\)) predicts the first pass; the one bisection that QUADPACK does on a “saturated” estimate stretches the working range to about 4300. Splitting at 10 gives 0.5 with 42 evaluations. Adaptive Simpson returns 0.5 for every \(L\) (509 evaluations at 20000), because its first three points include the endpoint 0, where the peak is. On the chromatogram the peak sits between its first points. Every rule misses something; plot the integrand and give the routine the scale.

title: Exercise: flow plus diffusion
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the Péclet number of a microfluidic device and estimate a mixing length \(\approx \bar u w^2/D\),
discretise the advection term with central and upwind differences, and predict from the cell Péclet number \(u\Delta x/D\) when central differences wiggle,
show that upwind differences add a numerical diffusion \(u\Delta x/2\), and detect it with grid refinement,
choose a stable explicit time step from the CFL condition \(C + 2r \le 1\),
solve a steady channel problem by marching downstream with a given Poiseuille profile, and check the solver against an exact solution and with flux conservation,
use the solver for an H-filter, a Christmas-tree gradient generator, and to fit a diffusion coefficient to a downstream profile with Brent’s method.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator. All “measurements” on this page are synthetic: generated from the model plus noise. The device parameters are our own round numbers, typical for microfluidics but not taken from a specific paper.

title: Exercise: flow plus diffusion
text:
By hand
B1. Péclet numbers and mixing lengths. A T-sensor has width \(w = 100\) µm and mean speed \(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s. (a) Compute Pe \(= \bar u w/D\) and the mixing length \(\bar u w^2/D\) for a small molecule (\(D = 1000\) µm²/s), a protein (\(D = 100\)) and a cell (\(D \approx 0.05\) µm²/s). (b) The flow is halved. What happens to Pe, to the mixing length, and to the amount of sample processed per minute? (c) A serpentine in a gradient generator is 50 µm wide and carries \(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s. How long must it be to mix two half-streams to 1 % (Fact 1), for a small molecule and for a protein chemokine (\(D = 100\) µm²/s)? What happens to the outlet gradient if the serpentines are only 3 mm long and the molecule is the protein? (d) Back-diffusion: in the test problem (Fact 2), \(c \approx e^{-us/D}\) at a distance \(s\) upstream of the chamber. For \(D = 1000\) µm²/s and perfusion speeds \(u = 10\), 100 and 1000 µm/s, give the layer thickness \(D/u\) and the distance at which the drug is down to 1 %.






Solution B1


















\(D\) (µm²/s)
Pe
mixing length \(\bar u w^2/D\)




small molecule
1000
100
\(10^3\cdot 10^4/10^3 = 10^4\) µm = 10 mm


protein

100 mm

0.05
\(2\times10^6\)
\(2\times10^8\) µm = 200 m




Pe and the mixing length both halve: the streams mix in half the distance, because each parcel spends twice as long in every millimetre. Only \(Dx/\bar u\) matters. But half the volume per minute flows through the device: a shorter device at the old speed would do the same separation with the full throughput.
\(0.42\,\bar u w^2/D = 0.42\cdot 1000\cdot 2500/D\): 1.05 mm for the small molecule, 10.5 mm for the protein. With 3 mm serpentines the protein is far from mixed (3 mm is about \(0.12\,\bar u w^2/D\): the first Fourier mode has decayed only to \(e^{-\pi^2\cdot 0.12} \approx 0.3\) of its start value). Each new channel then carries a stream that is still partly two streams side by side, so the next split does not take the intended shares, and the outlet profile is not the designed staircase. Designers lengthen the serpentines or slow the flow.
\(D/u = 100\), 10 and 1 µm. The drug is down to 1 % where \(us/D = \ln 100 = 4.6\), i.e. \(s = 4.6\,D/u\): 461, 46 and 4.6 µm. Even a slow perfusion protects the upstream channel.




B2. Central and upwind on a tiny grid. Take the test problem with only \(N = 4\) intervals and cell Péclet number \(P = 4\) (so Pe = 16). Unknowns \(c_1, c_2, c_3\); \(c_0 = 0\), \(c_4 = 1\). (a) Write down the three central-difference equations (Fact 3) and solve them. (Hint: express \(c_2\) and \(c_3\) in terms of \(c_1\).) Which values are negative? (b) Do the same for upwind (Fact 4). (c) The exact solution is \(c_i = (e^{4i} - 1)/(e^{16} - 1)\). Compute \(c_3\) (use \(e^{-4} \approx 0.0183\)). Compare with (a) and (b). (d) For each scheme, find \(\rho\) such that \(c_i = \rho^i\) solves the difference equation (besides \(\rho = 1\)). Compare with the exact growth factor per cell, \(e^{P}\).






Solution B2






Central with \(P = 4\): \(3c_{i-1} - 2c_i - c_{i+1} = 0\). \(i = 1\): \(-2c_1 - c_2 = 0\), so \(c_2 = -2c_1\). \(i = 2\): \(3c_1 - 2c_2 - c_3 = 0\), so \(c_3 = 3c_1 + 4c_1 = 7c_1\). \(i = 3\): \(3c_2 - 2c_3 - 1 = 0\), so \(-6c_1 - 14c_1 = 1\), \(c_1 = -0.05\). Hence \(c = (0, -0.05, 0.10, -0.35, 1)\): \(c_1\) and \(c_3\) are negative, and the signs alternate.
Upwind with \(P = 4\): \(5c_{i-1} - 6c_i + c_{i+1} = 0\). \(i = 1\): \(c_2 = 6c_1\). \(i = 2\): \(c_3 = 6c_2 - 5c_1 = 31c_1\). \(i = 3\): \(5c_2 - 6c_3 + 1 = 0\), so \(30c_1 - 186c_1 = -1\), \(c_1 = 1/156\). Hence \(c = (0, 0.0064, 0.0385, 0.1987, 1)\): positive and increasing.
\(c_3 = (e^{12} - 1)/(e^{16} - 1) \approx e^{-4} = 0.0183\) (and \(c_1, c_2\) are tiny: \(6\times10^{-6}\), \(3\times10^{-4}\)). Central is wrong in sign and size; upwind has the right shape but is 11 times too large at \(x_3\): the boundary layer is smeared.
Central: \((1 - P/2)\rho^2 - 2\rho + (1 + P/2) = 0\), i.e. \(-\rho^2 - 2\rho + 3 = 0\), roots 1 and \(\rho = -3\). Check: \(c_i = (\,(-3)^i - 1)/((-3)^4 - 1) = ((-3)^i - 1)/80\) gives \(-0.05\), \(0.1\), \(-0.35\). Upwind: \(\rho^2 - 6\rho + 5 = 0\), roots 1 and \(\rho = 5\); \(c_i = (5^i - 1)/624\). Exact: \(e^4 = 54.6\). Neither comes close, because a grid with \(P = 4\) cannot resolve a layer that is a quarter of a cell thick; but a negative \(\rho\) is qualitatively wrong, while \(\rho = 5\) is only too small.




B3. Numerical diffusion. (a) Verify the identity \(\dfrac{c_i - c_{i-1}}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{c_{i+1} - c_{i-1}}{2\Delta x} - \dfrac{\Delta x}{2}\cdot\dfrac{c_{i+1} - 2c_i + c_{i-1}}{\Delta x^2}\) and conclude that upwind with \(D\) is central with \(D + u\Delta x/2\). (b) Check it with B2: the central scheme with \(D_\text{eff} = D + u\Delta x/2\) has cell Péclet number \(P_\text{eff} = u\Delta x/D_\text{eff}\). Compute \(P_\text{eff}\) for \(P = 4\) and the central \(\rho\) for \(P_\text{eff}\). Show in general that \(P_\text{eff} < 2\) always. (c) In the back-diffusion problem (\(u = 100\) µm/s, \(D = 1000\) µm²/s), what is \(D_\text{num}\) for \(\Delta x = 50\), 10 and 1 µm? From what grid spacing is \(D_\text{num}\) less than 10 % of \(D\)? (d) For the stimulus pulse of the lecture (\(u = 200\) µm/s, \(D = 100\) µm²/s, \(C = 0.5\)) the numerical diffusion is \(u\Delta x(1 - C)/2\). Which \(\Delta x\) keeps it below 10 % of \(D\)? How many grid points and time steps does that need for 3 mm and 16 s? (e) At \(C = 1\) the numerical diffusion vanishes. Why can we not simply run at \(C = 1\) here?






Solution B3






Put the right-hand side over the common denominator \(2\Delta x\): \((c_{i+1} - c_{i-1}) - (c_{i+1} - 2c_i + c_{i-1}) = 2c_i - 2c_{i-1}\), divided by \(2\Delta x\) gives the left-hand side. Multiply by \(u\): \(u\cdot\text{upwind} = u\cdot\text{central} - \tfrac{u\Delta x}{2}\cdot\text{second difference}\). Moving the last term to the diffusion side of \(u c' = D c''\) gives \(u\cdot\text{central} = (D + u\Delta x/2)\cdot\text{second difference}\).
\(P_\text{eff} = P/(1 + P/2) = 4/3\), and \(\rho = (1 + 2/3)/(1 - 2/3) = 5\): exactly the upwind \(\rho\). In general \(P/(1 + P/2) = 2P/(2 + P) < 2\) for every \(P > 0\), so the upwind scheme never wiggles.
\(D_\text{num} = 100\,\Delta x/2 = 50\,\Delta x\): 2500, 500 and 50 µm²/s. Below 100 µm²/s needs \(\Delta x < 2\) µm.
\(200\cdot\Delta x\cdot 0.5/2 = 50\,\Delta x \le 10\) gives \(\Delta x \le 0.2\) µm: 15 001 points, \(\Delta t = C\Delta x/u = 0.0005\) s, 32 000 steps. About 5×10⁸ point updates: feasible, but a coarse upwind grid is clearly not.
With \(D > 0\), \(r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2 > 0\), so \(C = 1\) gives \(C + 2r > 1\): unstable (C2 shows it). Pure advection at \(C = 1\) is the exact shift \(c_i^{n+1} = c_{i-1}^n\), but only without diffusion and only for constant \(u\).




B4. The CFL condition by hand. Pulse problem: \(u = 200\) µm/s, \(D = 100\) µm²/s, \(\Delta x = 10\) µm. (a) Express \(C\) and \(r\) in terms of \(\Delta t\) and find the largest stable \(\Delta t\) from \(C + 2r \le 1\). Which part of the condition dominates? (b) Take \(C = 0.5\), \(r = 0.025\). At step \(n\) the values at \(x = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40\) µm are \((1, 1, 0, 0, 0)\), with \(c_0 = 1\) held by the inlet. Compute \(c_1, c_2, c_3\) at step \(n + 1\). (c) Repeat with \(C = 1.2\), \(r = 0.06\). What goes wrong? (d) T-sensor, explicit marching (Fact 6 with forward Euler in \(x\)): the step must satisfy \(D\Delta x/(u_j\Delta y^2) \le 1/2\) in every row. With \(\Delta y = 2\) µm, \(D = 1000\) µm²/s, \(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s, compute the limit in the middle row (\(u = 1500\) µm/s) and in the first row (\(y = 1\) µm). How many steps for a 20 mm channel?






Solution B4






\(C = 200\,\Delta t/10 = 20\,\Delta t\), \(r = 100\,\Delta t/100 = \Delta t\) (with \(\Delta t\) in s). \(C + 2r = 22\,\Delta t \le 1\): \(\Delta t \le 1/22 = 0.0455\) s, i.e. \(C \le 0.909\). Advection dominates (\(C\) is ten times \(2r\)); the diffusion-only limit \(r \le 1/2\) would allow \(\Delta t = 0.5\) s.
Weights \((C + r, 1 - C - 2r, r) = (0.525, 0.45, 0.025)\). \(c_1 = 0.525\cdot 1 + 0.45\cdot 1 + 0.025\cdot 0 = 0.975\); \(c_2 = 0.525\cdot 1 + 0.45\cdot 0 + 0.025\cdot 0 = 0.525\); \(c_3 = 0\). The front moves half a cell (and spreads).
Weights \((1.26, -0.32, 0.06)\). \(c_1 = 1.26 - 0.32 + 0 = 0.94\); \(c_2 = 1.26\cdot 1 = 1.26\). A value above 1 appears where there was none: a new maximum, which the next steps amplify into a growing zigzag. One negative weight is enough.
\(\Delta x \le u_j\Delta y^2/(2D) = 4u_j/2000\): 3.0 µm in the middle row; in the first row \(u = 6000\cdot 0.01\cdot 0.99 = 59.4\) µm/s and the limit is 0.119 µm. The slowest row decides: \(20\,000/0.119 \approx 168\,000\) steps. Implicit marching with \(\Delta x = 50\) µm needs 400.




B5. The Christmas tree by hand. In stage \(n \to n + 1\), new channel \(k\) (\(k = 0, \dots, n\)) receives a share \(k/n\) of upstream stream \(k - 1\) and \((n - k)/n\) of stream \(k\), fully mixed. (a) Start from the inlets \((0, 1)\) and compute the next two stages. (b) Show that a linear staircase \(c_k = k/(n - 1)\), \(k = 0, \dots, n - 1\), becomes the linear staircase \(k/n\) after one stage. (c) Start from three inlets \((0, 1, 0)\) and compute two stages. What shape is forming? (d) Why does the outlet staircase need a wide channel in which diffusion can act before it reaches the cells, and why should the cells not sit too far downstream?






Solution B5






\(n = 2\): \((0,\ \tfrac12\cdot 0 + \tfrac12\cdot 1,\ 1) = (0, 0.5, 1)\). \(n = 3\): \(k = 1\): \(\tfrac13\cdot 0 + \tfrac23\cdot 0.5 = \tfrac13\); \(k = 2\): \(\tfrac23\cdot 0.5 + \tfrac13\cdot 1 = \tfrac23\). So \((0, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, 1)\).
\(c'_k = \dfrac{k}{n}\cdot\dfrac{k - 1}{n - 1} + \dfrac{n - k}{n}\cdot\dfrac{k}{n - 1} = \dfrac{k(k - 1) + k(n - k)}{n(n - 1)} = \dfrac{k(n - 1)}{n(n - 1)} = \dfrac kn.\)
\(n = 3\): \((0,\ \tfrac23,\ \tfrac23,\ 0)\). \(n = 4\): \(k = 1\): \(\tfrac14\cdot 0 + \tfrac34\cdot\tfrac23 = 0.5\); \(k = 2\): \(\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23 + \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23 = \tfrac23\); \(k = 3\): \(0.5\). So \((0, 0.5, 0.667, 0.5, 0)\): a hump, roughly a parabola.
At the outlet the profile is a staircase with jumps between neighbouring streams; a cell 10 µm wide sitting on a jump sees a sharp step, not a gradient. Diffusion across the 50 µm streams smooths the steps within about a millimetre (C5). But diffusion keeps acting on the whole profile, so far downstream the gradient flattens, fastest near the slow walls. The cells must sit in between.




B6. Marching and what a fit can tell. (a) In the T-sensor (\(w = 100\) µm, \(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s), how long does fluid take to reach \(x = 1\) mm in the middle of the channel and at \(y = 1\) µm? How far does a small molecule (\(D = 1000\) µm²/s) diffuse in each time, using \(\sqrt{2Dt}\)? (b) Write \(u(y) = \bar u f(y)\). Show that the marching equation depends on \(D\), \(\bar u\) and \(x\) only through \(\xi = Dx/\bar u\). (c) A fit with an assumed \(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s gives \(D = 398\) µm²/s. Later you find that the pump delivered only 80 % of the nominal flow. What is the corrected \(D\)? (d) Would measuring the profile at two distances \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) let you determine \(D\) and \(\bar u\) separately? What would?






Solution B6






Middle: \(u = 1500\) µm/s, \(t = 1000/1500 = 0.67\) s, \(\sqrt{2\cdot 1000\cdot 0.67} = 37\) µm. At \(y = 1\) µm: \(u = 59.4\) µm/s, \(t = 16.8\) s, \(\sqrt{2\cdot 1000\cdot 16.8} = 183\) µm, more than the channel width. Near the walls the streams are mixed long before they are mixed in the middle.
\(\bar u f(y)\,\partial c/\partial x = D\,\partial^2 c/\partial y^2\). Divide by \(\bar u\) and write \(\xi = Dx/\bar u\), so \(\partial/\partial x = (D/\bar u)\,\partial/\partial\xi\): \(f(y)\,\partial c/\partial\xi = \partial^2 c/\partial y^2\). No parameter is left except through \(\xi\).
Only \(D/\bar u\) is determined: \(D = 398 \cdot 0.8 = 318.6\) µm²/s (C6 confirms 318.56).
No: both profiles depend on \(D x_1/\bar u\) and \(D x_2/\bar u\), so \((D, \bar u)\) and \((2D, 2\bar u)\) fit equally well; the parameters are not identifiable (Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters). You need \(\bar u\) independently: the flow rate \(Q\) from a calibrated pump or by weighing the outflow, and the cross-section: \(\bar u = Q/(wh)\).

title: Exercise: flow plus diffusion
text:
Where this leads

Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation (unit 35) adds production and degradation terms to the diffusion equation; the explicit/implicit stability rules and grid-refinement checks of this unit carry over.
The flow profile was given. Computing flow fields in real geometries (the Stokes and Navier–Stokes equations) and handling curved walls is the subject of Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow (Part 11).
Better advection schemes (higher-order upwind, flux limiters, semi-Lagrangian methods) reduce numerical diffusion without wiggles; we do not cover them. The fit in C6 had one parameter; fitting several (for example \(D\) and an unknown inlet concentration) uses the methods of Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting, and the identifiability problem of B6 is treated in Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters.

title: Exercise: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the decay length \(\lambda = \sqrt{D/k}\) of a synthesis–diffusion–degradation gradient, and use it to go between \(D\), \(k\), \(\lambda\) and threshold positions,
set up the steady gradient on a grid with ghost-point boundaries, solve it with the Thomas algorithm, and check it against the exact solution and the mass balance,
take IMEX Euler steps (diffusion implicit, reaction explicit) and say when the explicit reaction makes them unstable,
measure the error of Lie and Strang splitting and explain when it vanishes,
compute the dispersion relation of a two-species model from 2 × 2 eigenvalues and find the band of growing wavelengths (Turing instability),
run a 2D pattern simulation and decide, by refining the grid and the time step, whether a pattern is real or an artefact.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator. The code part checks the hand answers and then goes to sizes where only code works. All “data” in this exercise are synthetic: model output plus noise. Literature numbers are approximate.

title: Exercise: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

compute the decay length \(\lambda = \sqrt{D/k}\) of a synthesis–diffusion–degradation gradient, and use it to go between \(D\), \(k\), \(\lambda\) and threshold positions,
set up the steady gradient on a grid with ghost-point boundaries, solve it with the Thomas algorithm, and check it against the exact solution and the mass balance,
take IMEX Euler steps (diffusion implicit, reaction explicit) and say when the explicit reaction makes them unstable,
measure the error of Lie and Strang splitting and explain when it vanishes,
compute the dispersion relation of a two-species model from 2 × 2 eigenvalues and find the band of growing wavelengths (Turing instability),
run a 2D pattern simulation and decide, by refining the grid and the time step, whether a pattern is real or an artefact.

The by-hand part needs pen, paper and a calculator. The code part checks the hand answers and then goes to sizes where only code works. All “data” in this exercise are synthetic: model output plus noise. Literature numbers are approximate.
