title: Exercise: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
By hand
B1. Decay lengths. (a) Our running example has \(D = 100\) µm²/min and \(k = 0.01\) per min. Compute \(\lambda\), and \(D\) in µm²/s. (b) Bicoid (approximate literature values): \(\lambda \approx 100\) µm and a lifetime \(1/k \approx 50\) min. Which \(D\) (in µm²/s) does that require? Which \(\lambda\) would a lifetime of 50 min give with \(D = 0.3\) µm²/s (a FRAP estimate) and with \(D = 7\) µm²/s (an FCS estimate)? (c) Fgf8 [M4] (approximate): \(D \approx 50\) µm²/s and \(\lambda \approx 200\) µm. Infer \(k\) and the lifetime in minutes. (d) In a long embryo, \(c(x) = c_0 e^{-x/\lambda}\) with \(c_0 = j\lambda/D = 1\). Where is \(c = 0.1\)? Now \(k\) doubles everywhere with \(j\) and \(D\) unchanged. What are the new \(\lambda\), \(c_0\) and threshold position? (e) Instead, both \(D\) and \(k\) go up by a factor 1.5 (all rates faster at a higher temperature). What happens to \(\lambda\), to \(c_0\), and to the time the gradient needs to form?
B2. A three-node grid. Take \(L = 200\) µm, \(N = 2\) (\(\Delta x = 100\) µm \(= \lambda\)), \(D = 100\), \(k = 0.01\), \(j = 1\). (a) Write the three equations for the steady state at \(x_0 = 0\), \(x_1 = 100\), \(x_2 = 200\) µm, using the ghost points. (b) Solve them by hand. (c) Compare with the exact values \(c(0) = \coth 2 = 1.0373\), \(c(100) = \cosh 1/\sinh 2 = 0.4255\), \(c(200) = 1/\sinh 2 = 0.2757\). How large is the relative error? (d) Check the mass balance \(k\int c\,dx = j\) with the trapezoid rule on your three values.
B3. IMEX on one mode. Use \(G = (1 - k\Delta t)/(1 + Dq^2\Delta t)\). (a) With \(D = 100\), \(k = 0.01\), a short wave of wavelength 20 µm (\(q = 2\pi/20\)) and \(\Delta t = 10\) min: compute \(G\). What factor would a fully explicit Euler step, \(1 - (Dq^2 + k)\Delta t\), give? (b) For the uniform mode (\(q = 0\)), what is the largest stable \(\Delta t\)? Is \(\Delta t = 150\) min accurate? (Compare \(G\) with \(e^{-k\Delta t}\).) (c) A ligand binds receptors at an effective rate of 1 per s. Which \(\Delta t\) does IMEX need? (d) The Schnakenberg reaction (below) has eigenvalues \(\lambda = -0.1 \pm 0.995i\) at its steady state. For which \(\Delta t\) is \(|1 + \Delta t\lambda| \le 1\)? (Use \(|1 + \Delta t\lambda|^2 = (1 - 0.1\Delta t)^2 + 0.99\,\Delta t^2\).)
B4. When do the parts commute? Two cells exchange morphogen at rate 1 and decay at rates \(k_1\) and \(k_2\): \(\mathbf c' = A\mathbf c - K\mathbf c\) with \(A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}\), \(K = \begin{pmatrix} k_1 & 0 \\ 0 & k_2\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Compute \(AK - KA\). When is it zero? (b) If \(k_1 = k_2 = k\), show that \(e^{(A - kI)t} = e^{At}e^{-kt}\), so Lie splitting with exact sub-steps has no error at all. (c) Which of these have a splitting error: decay with a temperature step; uniform decay with a source in cell 1; uniform decay without a source?
B5. Turing by hand. Schnakenberg with \(a = 0.1\), \(b = 0.9\). (a) Show that \(u^* = a + b\), \(v^* = b/(a+b)^2\) is a steady state, and compute it. (b) Compute the Jacobian \(J\) of \(f = a - u + u^2v\), \(g = b - u^2 v\) at the steady state, its trace and determinant, and its eigenvalues. Is the uniform state stable without diffusion? What kind of fixed point is it (Equilibria, stability and the phase plane)? (c) With \(d = 20\), write \(\det\bigl(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d)\bigr)\) as a polynomial in \(q^2\). For which \(q\) is it negative? Which wavelengths can grow? (d) Show that the trace of \(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d)\) is negative for every \(q\). What does that imply about how instability can arise? (e) Find the smallest \(d\) for which some \(q\) is unstable. Why can there be no pattern with \(d = 1\)?
B6. Artefact or pattern? (a) The 2D simulation has \(d = 20\) and \(\Delta x = 1\). What is the largest stable step for explicit (FTCS) diffusion of \(v\) in 2D, \(\Delta t \le \Delta x^2/(4d)\)? How many steps to \(t = 200\), compared with IMEX at \(\Delta t = 0.1\)? (b) The fastest-growing wavelength is 12.9 (\(q = 0.487\)). The grid sees \(q^2\) as \(\tfrac{4}{\Delta x^2}\sin^2(q\Delta x/2)\). Compute this for \(\Delta x = 2\), \(1\) and \(0.5\), and the relative error against \(q^2 = 0.237\). How many grid points per wavelength does each grid have? (c) A checkerboard pattern has wavelength \(2\Delta x\). With \(\Delta x = 1\), is that wavelength inside the unstable band of B5(c)? What does it tell you if you see one?

title: Exercise: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
In code
C1. Steady state and its order. Write a function that solves the steady gradient for a given \(N\) and returns the maximum error against the exact solution and the mass balance \(k\int c\,dx\) (trapezoid rule). Use \(N = 5, 10, \dots, 320\). (a) Read the order off the errors. Check B2 with \(N = 2\) and \(L = 200\) if you like. (b) Replace the ghost point at \(x = 0\) by the one-sided condition \((c_1 - c_0)/\Delta x = -j/D\) (row 0 becomes \(c_0 - c_1 = j\Delta x/D\)). What happens to the order, and to the mass balance?
C2. How fast does the gradient form? Start from \(c = 0\) and take IMEX steps with \(\Delta t = 0.5\) min up to \(t = 1000\) min. (a) Compute the local accumulation time \(\tau(x) = \int_0^\infty \bigl(1 - c(x,t)/c_s(x)\bigr)\,dt\) (trapezoid rule over the steps) at \(x = 0\), 100 and 200 µm and compare with \((1 + x/\lambda)/(2k)\). (b) Run IMEX to \(t = 5000\) min with \(\Delta t = 1\), 10 and 50 min and compare with the steady state cs. Why does the step size not matter?
C3. Splitting error. Use the exact solution of the grid ODEs, \(\mathbf c(t) = \mathbf c_s + e^{Mt}(\mathbf c_0 - \mathbf c_s)\) with \(M = -K_D - \mathrm{diag}(k_i)\), as reference. Do the diffusion sub-step exactly with the matrix exponential of the augmented matrix \(\begin{pmatrix} -K_D & \mathbf s \\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}\) (it includes the influx), and the decay exactly (\(c_i \to e^{-k_i\Delta t}c_i\)). (a) With the temperature step \(k = 0.01\) for \(x < 250\) µm and \(0.02\) beyond, the influx on and \(\mathbf c_0 = 0\): errors of Lie and Strang at \(t = 60\) min for \(\Delta t = 20, 10, 5, 2.5, 1.25\). Orders? (b) Influx off, uniform \(k\), start from the steady state cs (production has stopped). Error? (c) Influx off, temperature step. Error? Compare with B4.
C4. The temperature step [M1]. Assume that in the warm (27 °C) half of the embryo \(k\) is twice its 20 °C value, with \(D\) and \(j\) unchanged. On a grid with \(\Delta x = 1\) µm, find where the steady gradient crosses \(c = 0.1\) (linear interpolation) for: all cold, all warm, posterior half warm, anterior half warm. Compare with B1(d). Which half sets the threshold position?
C5. Decay lengths from many embryos [M3, M4]. Twenty synthetic Fgf8-like profiles: embryo \(e\) has a true \(\lambda_e = 200\,(1 + 0.2 z_{e})\) µm and measured values \(c(x) = e^{-x/\lambda_e}(1 + 0.2 z_{ie})\) at \(x = 0, 20, \dots, 400\) µm, with \(z\) uniform on \((-0.5, 0.5)\) from the generator lcg below (seed 2; one block of 22 numbers per embryo, the first for \(\lambda_e\)). (a) Fit \(\lambda\) for each embryo by a straight line through \(\log c\) against \(x\). Report the mean and standard deviation of \(\lambda\), and \(k = D/\lambda^2\) with \(D = 50\) µm²/s. (b) Add a constant background 0.05 to every value before fitting. What happens to \(\lambda\) and \(k\)? Why?
C6. Dispersion relation. For \(d = 5, 10, 20\), compute the largest real part of the eigenvalues of \(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d)\) on \(q = 0, 0.001, \dots, 1.5\). Report the unstable band, the fastest-growing \(q\), its wavelength and rate. Then find the threshold \(d_c\) with a root finder on \(\min_q \det\bigl(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d)\bigr)\) and compare with B5(e).
C7. A 2D Turing pattern. Simulate Schnakenberg with \(d = 20\) on a periodic \(80 \times 80\) grid (\(\Delta x = 1\)) from \(u = 1 + 0.02z\), \(v = 0.9 + 0.02z\) (\(z\) from lcg, seed 1: first \(N^2\) numbers for \(u\), next \(N^2\) for \(v\), filled column by column), IMEX with \(\Delta t = 0.1\) to \(t = 200\). Count the spots (grid points above the mean that are larger than all 8 neighbours). Time it.
C8. Is the pattern real? (a) Repeat C7 with \(\Delta x = 2\) and \(0.5\) (same box, \(N = 40\) and \(160\)). (b) Repeat with \(\Delta t = 0.4\), \(0.2\) and \(0.05\). (c) Set \(d = 5\) (no Turing instability, C6) and run to \(t = 150\) with \(\Delta t = 0.1\) and \(0.4\). Explain the difference with the eigenvalues of \(I + \Delta t\,J\) (B3(d)).

title: Exercise: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — decay lengths (B1)





\(\lambda^2 = D/k\), so \(k = D/\lambda^2\) and \(D = \lambda^2 k\). Keep the units together: µm²/s divided by µm² gives 1/s; 1 µm²/s \(= 60\) µm²/min. A threshold \(c_T\) is crossed where \(c_0 e^{-x/\lambda} = c_T\), i.e. \(x = \lambda\ln(c_0/c_T)\). The formation time scales like \(1/k\).









Hint 2 — the grid and the ghost points (B2, C1)





At node 0: \(D(c_{-1} - 2c_0 + c_1)/\Delta x^2 - k c_0 = 0\) with \(c_{-1} = c_1 + 2\Delta x\,j/D\) gives \((2r + k)c_0 - 2r\,c_1 = 2j/\Delta x\). At the last node use \(c_{N+1} = c_{N-1}\). In B2, \(r = D/\Delta x^2 = 0.01\). Solve the last equation for \(c_2\) in terms of \(c_1\) and work upwards. The trapezoid rule gives the end points half weight.









Hint 3 — IMEX and splitting (B3, B4, C2, C3)





For a mode, diffusion is multiplication by \(-Dq^2\); IMEX treats it implicitly (divide by \(1 + Dq^2\Delta t\)) and the reaction explicitly (multiply by \(1 - k\Delta t\)). For B4(b), \(kI\) commutes with every matrix, and \(e^{X+Y} = e^X e^Y\) when \(XY = YX\). Matrix exponential: R Matrix::expm, Python scipy.linalg.expm, Rust nalgebra’s .exp(). The augmented-matrix trick: the last component stays 1, so \(e^{\Delta t\,\text{Aug}}\) applied to \((\mathbf c, 1)\) gives the solution of \(\mathbf c' = -K_D\mathbf c + \mathbf s\).









Hint 4 — dispersion relation (B5, C6)





\(J = \begin{pmatrix} \partial f/\partial u & \partial f/\partial v \\ \partial g/\partial u & \partial g/\partial v\end{pmatrix}\) with \(\partial f/\partial u = -1 + 2uv\), \(\partial f/\partial v = u^2\), \(\partial g/\partial u = -2uv\), \(\partial g/\partial v = -u^2\). For a 2 × 2 matrix, \(\lambda = \tfrac12\bigl(\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}\bigr)\). A quadratic \(d\,Q^2 - \beta Q + \Delta\) in \(Q = q^2\) is negative between its roots, which exist when \(\beta^2 > 4d\Delta\). Code: R eigen and uniroot; Python np.linalg.eigvals and scipy.optimize.brentq.









Hint 5 — the 2D simulation (C7, C8)





R: fft on a matrix is the 2D transform; fft(z, inverse = TRUE) is not normalised, so divide by \(N^2\). outer(s, s, "+") builds \(\kappa_{kl} = s_k + s_l\). Python: np.fft.fft2 and np.fft.ifft2 (normalised), reshape(N, N, order="F") to fill column by column as R does, np.roll for periodic neighbours. Rust: 1D transforms from rustfft along columns, then along rows; build in release mode (cargo run --release).









Hint 6 — fitting the decay length (C5)





\(\log c = \log c_0 - x/\lambda\) is a straight line; its slope is \(-1/\lambda\). R lm(log(c) ~ x), Python np.polyfit(x, np.log(c), 1) (slope first). A constant offset is not a straight line on the log scale: where \(c\) is small, \(\log(c + 0.05)\) flattens out.

title: Exercise: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Where this leads

This is the last core unit. Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow (Part 11, optional) shows how real tissue and chip geometries are meshed, and Iterative linear solvers in depth (Part 11, optional) how the implicit step is done when the grid is too large for a direct or FFT solve.
Fitting a reaction–diffusion model to real gradient data uses the tools of Nonlinear least squares and ODE fitting and Identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters (Part 9): with only a steady profile, \(D\) and \(k\) appear only as the ratio \(\lambda^2 = D/k\) and are not separately identifiable; a time course or an FCS measurement of \(D\) breaks the tie.
We used IMEX Euler (order 1). Production codes use higher-order IMEX schemes, Strang splitting with a stiff ODE solver for the reaction, or adaptive method-of-lines solvers (Implicit schemes and the method of lines).

title: Quiz: flow plus diffusion
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of advection–diffusion and its discretisation. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A channel is 200 µm wide and carries a mean flow of 500 µm/s. A drug has \(D = 500\) µm²/s. Compute the Péclet number across the channel and the distance after which two side-by-side streams are mixed to about 1 % (use the plug-flow estimate \(0.42\,\bar u w^2/D\)).






Hint





\(\text{Pe} = \bar u w/D\). Keep everything in µm and s.









Answer





\(\text{Pe} = 500\cdot 200/500 = 200\). Mixing length \(0.42\cdot 500\cdot 200^2/500 = 0.42\cdot 40\,000 = 16\,800\) µm, about 17 mm: 84 channel widths. With Pe ≫ 1, streams flow side by side a long way.




Q2. You solve the steady problem \(u\,c' = D\,c''\) with central differences, \(u = 100\) µm/s, \(D = 1000\) µm²/s, \(\Delta x = 30\) µm. Do you expect wiggles? What is the largest \(\Delta x\) that avoids them?






Hint





Compute the cell Péclet number \(P = u\Delta x/D\) and look at the sign of the coefficient \(1 - P/2\).









Answer





\(P = 100\cdot 30/1000 = 3 > 2\): the coefficient of \(c_{i+1}\) is \(1 - 1.5 < 0\), the recurrence has a negative root \(\rho = (1 + 1.5)/(1 - 1.5) = -5\), and the solution alternates in sign near the boundary layer. Wiggles disappear for \(P \le 2\), i.e. \(\Delta x \le 2D/u = 20\) µm; for second-order accuracy you want \(P\) well below 2.




Q3. An upwind simulation of a protein (\(D = 100\) µm²/s) in a channel with \(u = 1000\) µm/s on a 2 µm grid looks smooth and plausible. Why should you not trust it yet?






Hint





Upwind = central + something. How large is that something here?









Answer





Upwind adds a numerical diffusion \(u\Delta x/2 = 1000\cdot 2/2 = 1000\) µm²/s, ten times the protein’s real \(D\). The simulation is (nearly) the solution for \(D = 1100\) µm²/s: it spreads the protein like a small molecule. Smoothness is no evidence of accuracy. Check by refining the grid (the answer must stop changing) or by comparing \(D_\text{num}\) with \(D\) before running.




Q4. A simulated dye concentration contains values of \(-0.2\) next to a steep front. Name two different numerical causes, and a quick check that tells them apart.






Hint





One cause is in the steady discrete equations, one in the time stepping.









Answer






Central differences with cell Péclet number \(u\Delta x/D > 2\): the discrete equations have an oscillating solution. The wiggles have a fixed size and do not grow in time (they appear in a steady solve too). (2) An unstable explicit time step, \(C + 2r > 1\) (or \(r > 1/2\), or \(C > 1\)): a zigzag that grows step by step until it overflows. Check: compute \(P\), \(C\) and \(r\), and watch \(\max|c|\) over time: bounded means (1), growing means (2). In both cases the fix is a finer grid or (for 2) a smaller or implicit step.





Q5. Explicit upwind with \(u = 500\) µm/s, \(D = 1000\) µm²/s, \(\Delta x = 5\) µm. What is the largest stable time step? Is it set by advection or by diffusion?






Hint





\(C = u\Delta t/\Delta x\), \(r = D\Delta t/\Delta x^2\), and the condition is \(C + 2r \le 1\).









Answer





\(C = 100\,\Delta t\) and \(r = 40\,\Delta t\), so \(C + 2r = 180\,\Delta t \le 1\): \(\Delta t \le 5.6\) ms. Both matter: advection alone would allow 10 ms (\(C \le 1\)), diffusion alone 12.5 ms (\(r \le 1/2\)). On fine grids diffusion wins, since \(r\) grows like \(1/\Delta x^2\) and \(C\) only like \(1/\Delta x\).




Q6. In the T-sensor we solved a steady 2D problem by “marching” in \(x\) as if \(x\) were time. What assumption makes this possible, and when would it fail?






Hint





Which term did we drop, and what does that do to the direction in which information travels?









Answer





We dropped diffusion along the flow, \(D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2\), which is about \(1/\text{Pe}^2\) times smaller than advection when \(\text{Pe} \gg 1\). Then the concentration at \(x\) depends only on what happened upstream, like a solution at time \(t\) depends only on earlier times. It fails when Pe is not large (diffusion upstream matters, as in the back-diffusion problem), when the flow reverses or recirculates (eddies, dead-end side chambers), or where \(u = 0\) along a whole region. Then one solves the full steady problem as one sparse linear system (Steady state in two dimensions).




Q7. Why is explicit marching impractical for the T-sensor with a Poiseuille profile, even though it works well with plug flow?






Hint





The “time step” in row \(j\) is \(\Delta x/u_j\).









Answer





Explicit marching needs \(D\,\Delta x/(u_j\Delta y^2) \le 1/2\) in every row, so \(\Delta x \le u_j\Delta y^2/(2D)\). Near the walls \(u_j \to 0\), so the step must shrink towards 0: with 2 µm cells it is 0.12 µm in the first row against 3 µm in the middle, 168 000 steps for 20 mm. It is stiffness again (Stiffness and implicit methods): the slowest fluid sets the step for everyone. Backward Euler (one tridiagonal solve per step) has no such limit.




Q8. An H-filter extracts 45 % of a small molecule in a 1.6 mm channel at \(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s. You double the flow rate to process more sample. How long must the channel be for the same extraction?






Hint





The marching equation depends on \(D\), \(\bar u\) and \(x\) only through one combination.









Answer





Only \(Dx/\bar u\) matters, so doubling \(\bar u\) needs twice the length: 3.2 mm. The protein carried along stays the same fraction (17 %), since it obeys the same scaling. The channel length per unit throughput is fixed by \(D\).




Q9. In the simplified Christmas-tree model, new channel \(k\) in stage \(n \to n + 1\) takes \(k/n\) of upstream stream \(k - 1\) and \((n - k)/n\) of stream \(k\). Starting from inlets \((0, 1)\), what are the concentrations after two stages? What does the model assume about each serpentine?






Hint





First stage: \(n = 2\), three channels.









Answer





\((0, 1) \to (0, 0.5, 1) \to (0, \tfrac13, \tfrac23, 1)\): a linear staircase, and it stays linear at every stage. The model assumes each serpentine mixes its two inputs completely, i.e. it is longer than about \(0.4\,\bar u w^2/D\) for the molecule used. For a slowly diffusing protein at high flow that may fail, and the outlet profile then differs from the design.




Q10. You fit a diffusion coefficient to a T-sensor profile with the marching model. On a coarse grid (\(\Delta x = 1\) mm, one step) the fit gives \(D = 505\) µm²/s; on fine grids it settles at 396. Why is the coarse estimate too high, and how do you know when the grid is fine enough?






Hint





What does a coarse backward-Euler step do to the profile, compared with the exact solution?









Answer





Backward Euler damps each Fourier mode (rate \(\lambda\)) by \(1/(1 + \lambda\Delta x)\) per step instead of the exact \(e^{-\lambda\Delta x}\), and \(1/(1 + z) > e^{-z}\). So one coarse step spreads the interface too little; to reproduce the measured spreading the optimiser must raise \(D\). The fitted parameter absorbs the discretisation error, here 27 % upwards. Refit on a sequence of finer grids until the fitted \(D\) stops changing to the precision you need (here \(\Delta x \le 25\) µm): the same grid-refinement check as for any simulation, applied to the estimate.




Q11. The flow rate in your T-sensor experiment is only known to ±10 %. How precisely can you estimate \(D\) from downstream profiles, however many profiles you measure?






Hint





Which parameter combination do the profiles determine?









Answer





To about ±10 %. The profiles depend only on \(D/\bar u\) (times \(x\)), so \(D\) and \(\bar u\) are not separately identifiable: a 10 % error in \(\bar u\) is a 10 % error in \(D\). More profiles or less noise shrink the uncertainty of \(D/\bar u\), not that of \(\bar u\). Measure the flow rate independently (calibrated pump, weighing the outflow, bead tracking).

title: Exercise: identifiability and uncertainty of fitted parameters
text:
Explore
The demo uses the model and data of this exercise. Every sample keeps its own noise value from the course data, so all 12 samples and from 3 h reproduce the fits of the lecture; with noise switched off the data are the true curve and the SEs use \(\sigma = 0.1\), as in se_design (C7). Drag a sample (black dot) along the time axis. Panel (b) shows \(\Delta S/s^2\) over \((k_a, k_e)\) with \(V\) re-fitted (blue, thick at 3.84) and the Wald ellipse from the \((k_a, k_e)\) block of \(s^2(J^TJ)^{-1}\) at the same level (red); (c) the profile of \(k_a\) (\(k_e\) and \(V\) re-fitted for each \(k_a\)) with the Wald parabola (red dotted); (d) the singular values of the log-parameter Jacobian. Grey: the 12-sample design, for comparison.



E1. (the bowl is fine) With all 12 samples, read off the estimates, SEs, correlations and singular values, and compare them with the Background block and C4. Does the red ellipse in (b) match the thick blue contour? Compare the profile and Wald intervals in (c). Where is the second well of the profile, and how deep is it?






Answer E1





\(k_a = 1.015 \pm 0.0624\), \(k_e = 0.1906 \pm 0.0104\), \(V = 20.22 \pm 0.716\); correlations \(-0.82\), \(0.90\), \(-0.91\); singular values \(8.78, 3.48, 1.01\) with \(\kappa = 8.73\), and \(v_3 = (0.69, -0.60, 0.40)\): all as in the Background block and C4. The ellipse lies almost on the 3.84 contour, a tilted valley (corr \(-0.82\)). Profile interval \((0.90, 1.14)\), Wald \((0.89, 1.14)\): the quadratic picture holds. The profile has a second well at \(k_a = 0.19\), the flip-flop solution (\(k_a\) and \(k_e\) swapped), with \(\Delta = 0\): exactly as deep as the first. The hump between them is what keeps a local fit on one side.



E2. (the sparse design) Click from 3 h. Read the SE of \(k_a\), the Wald interval, the profile interval and the level at which the profile levels off on the right. What happens to the 3.84 contour in (b) for large \(k_a\), and what does the ellipse do instead? Which singular value dropped most, and what is \(v_3\)?






Answer E2





\(k_a = 1.122 \pm 0.406\) (36 %), Wald \((0.33, 1.92)\), profile \((0.68, \infty)\): the profile levels off at \(1.07\) on the right, below 3.84, so there is no upper bound (C5). In (b) the 3.84 contour is open to the right: for large \(k_a\) the valley runs horizontally at \(k_e \approx 0.17\)–\(0.23\), every fast absorption fits. The ellipse must close, so it ends at \(k_a = 1.92\), and on the left it reaches \(0.33\), below the true lower bound 0.68: wrong at both ends. \(\sigma_3\) fell from 1.01 to 0.211 (\(\sigma_1\) only from 8.78 to 6.03), \(\kappa = 28.6\), and \(v_3 = (0.98, -0.19, 0.06)\) is almost pure \(\log k_a\) with SE \(0.369\) along it.



E3. (move one sample) Still on from 3 h, drag the 3 h sample to 2 h, then 1 h, then 0.5 h (the times snap to 0.05 h). Each time, note the SE of \(k_a\), \(\sigma_3\) and the profile interval, and watch the ellipse and the profile. How much did moving a single sample buy, at the same cost of six samples?






Answer E3





At 2 h: \(\mathrm{SE}(k_a) = 0.160\) (15 %), \(\sigma_3 = 0.464\), profile \((0.80, 1.49)\): the profile now closes on the right, but it is still clearly asymmetric (Wald \((0.73, 1.36)\)). At 1 h: \(0.093\) (9 %), \(\sigma_3 = 0.682\), profile \((0.87, 1.24)\) against Wald \((0.85, 1.22)\). At 0.5 h: \(0.083\) (8 %), \(\sigma_3 = 0.746\), profile \((0.89, 1.22)\), Wald \((0.88, 1.20)\). The ellipse shrinks from a long cigar to a small, tilted one, and the 3.84 contour closes around it. One sample moved from 3 h to 1 h divides the SE of \(k_a\) by more than 4, and with 6 samples we come close to the 12-sample value 0.062. The profile shows the same as \(\sigma_3\): the weakest direction got stronger, and the quadratic picture became valid again.



E4. (before the experiment) Untick noise: the data are now the true curve and the SEs use \(\sigma = 0.1\). Compare from 3 h with spread: read SE/est. of \(k_a\) (for small values this is the SE of \(\log k_a\)) and compare with the lecture slide “Design in code”. Then click all late, first without and then with noise. What do the SEs, the correlations and (d) say?






Answer E4





From 3 h: SE/est. of \(k_a\) 40 %, of \(k_e\) 11 %, of \(V\) 6.1 %; spread: 10 %, 8.7 %, 5.9 %. These are the lecture’s \(0.398, 0.115, 0.061\) and \(0.101, 0.087, 0.059\): the design can be judged from \(J\) at a guess of \(\theta\), with no data. Without noise the profile of “from 3 h” still levels off (at 0.98), so the problem is the design, not the noise realisation. All late (7–12 h) without noise: \(\mathrm{SE}(k_a) = 10.7\) (1100 %), \(\mathrm{SE}(V) = 41\), \(r(k_e, V) = -1.00\), \(\sigma_3 = 0.0092\), \(\kappa = 496\). With noise the fit wanders off to \(k_a = 2.64\), where \(\sigma_3 \approx 0\): \(J\) is singular and there are no standard errors at all. Only the tail \(A e^{-k_e t}\) is seen, two numbers for three parameters.



E5. (only the rising phase) Click first 3 h (with noise). Which parameters are now badly determined? Look at the correlations and at the profile in (c): what happened to the two flip-flop wells?






Answer E5





Now \(k_e\) (\(0.181 \pm 0.105\), 58 %) and \(V\) (\(20.7 \pm 4.4\), 21 %) are poor, \(k_a\) is at 28 %; the correlations are \(-0.97\), \(0.99\), \(-0.99\), and \(v_3 = (0.40, -0.86, 0.31)\) is mostly \(\log k_e\). Three hours do not show the elimination. In (c) the hump between the two wells is only about 1.7, below 3.84, so the profile interval is \((< 0.05, 1.60)\): it contains the flip-flop branch. With only the rising phase the data cannot even tell which rate is absorption and which is elimination. Early samples fix \(k_a\), late samples fix \(k_e\): a good design has both, as spread does.

title: Quiz: reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Short questions to test your understanding of reaction–diffusion models and how to simulate them. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A morphogen has \(D = 10\) µm²/s and a lifetime of 10 min. Roughly how far does its steady gradient reach (its decay length)? At what distance has it fallen to 1 % of its value at the source, in a long tissue?






Hint





\(\lambda = \sqrt{D/k}\) with \(k = 1/\text{lifetime}\); convert minutes to seconds. \(c = c_0 e^{-x/\lambda}\).









Answer





\(k = 1/600\) per s, \(\lambda = \sqrt{10 \cdot 600} = \sqrt{6000} \approx 77\) µm. 1 % at \(x = \lambda\ln 100 = 4.6\,\lambda \approx 355\) µm.




Q2. Which of these makes a synthesis–diffusion–degradation gradient twice as long: doubling \(D\); halving \(k\); doubling \(D\) and halving \(k\); doubling both \(D\) and \(k\)?






Hint





\(\lambda\) depends on the ratio \(D/k\), under a square root.









Answer





Only doubling \(D\) and halving \(k\) together: \(D/k\) goes up 4×, \(\lambda\) 2×. Doubling \(D\) or halving \(k\) alone gives \(\sqrt2 \approx 1.41\)×. Doubling both leaves \(\lambda\) unchanged (the gradient forms twice as fast, and with a fixed influx its amplitude \(j/\sqrt{Dk}\) halves).




Q3. Two students put the no-flux/influx boundary at \(x = 0\) on the grid in different ways: one with a ghost point, one with the one-sided difference \((c_1 - c_0)/\Delta x = -j/D\). Both get a plausible-looking exponential. Name two checks that tell the versions apart, and what each shows.






Hint





One check needs an exact solution, one does not.









Answer






Grid refinement: halving \(\Delta x\) cuts the error by 4 with the ghost point (order 2) but only by 2 with the one-sided boundary (order 1); without an exact solution, compare successive refinements. (2) Mass balance: at steady state \(k\int c\,dx\) must equal the influx \(j\). The ghost-point scheme satisfies it to rounding on every grid; the one-sided version is off (32 % at \(\Delta x = 50\) µm in the lecture).





Q4. In IMEX Euler for \(\partial c/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2 + f(c)\), which term is treated implicitly and which explicitly? Give one reason for each choice.






Hint





Think about which term is stiff, which is nonlinear, and which couples neighbouring grid points.









Answer





Diffusion implicitly: on a fine grid it is stiff (fastest rate \(4D/\Delta x^2\)), and it is linear, so the implicit step is one tridiagonal (Thomas) or FFT solve. The reaction explicitly: it may be nonlinear, and treating it implicitly would need a Newton solve every step; it is local, so evaluating it at the old values costs one function call per point.




Q5. An IMEX simulation of a ligand that is taken up by receptors at an effective rate \(k = 5\) per min uses \(\Delta t = 0.5\) min. The grid is fine and diffusion is fast. Is the step stable? What would you change?






Hint





Implicit diffusion does not help the reaction. Look at \(1 - k\Delta t\).









Answer





\(k\Delta t = 2.5 > 2\), so \(|1 - k\Delta t| = 1.5\): the explicit reaction is unstable, and the uniform mode (which diffusion does not damp) grows with alternating sign. Either take \(\Delta t < 2/k = 0.4\) min (and smaller still for accuracy, e.g. \(\Delta t \le 0.1\)), or treat the uptake implicitly / exactly (it is local and linear: \(c \to c\,e^{-k\Delta t}\) in a splitting scheme).




Q6. Lie splitting with exact sub-steps (exact diffusion, exact decay) is still only first order. For which of these problems is it exact: (a) uniform decay, no source; (b) uniform decay with a source at one end; (c) decay rate that changes along the embryo?






Hint





The splitting error comes from \(\mathcal{AB} - \mathcal{BA}\).









Answer





Only (a). Uniform decay is \(kI\), which commutes with the diffusion matrix, so \(e^{(A - kI)t} = e^{At}e^{-kt}\). In (b) the source is decayed only in the reaction step, so order matters; in (c) \(\mathrm{diag}(k_i)\) does not commute with diffusion (\(AK \ne KA\) when the \(k_i\) differ).




Q7. An IMEX run with \(\Delta t = 50\) min reaches exactly the same steady gradient as one with \(\Delta t = 1\) min. Does that show that \(\Delta t = 50\) min is a good choice?






Hint





Write down the fixed point of the IMEX step.









Answer





No. At a fixed point \(\mathbf c^{n+1} = \mathbf c^n\), and \(\Delta t\) cancels from \((I + \Delta t K_D)\mathbf c = \mathbf c + \Delta t(\mathbf f(\mathbf c) + \mathbf s)\): the steady state is the same for every stable step. The transient (how fast the gradient forms, the accumulation times) can still be badly wrong. Check the time course by halving \(\Delta t\).




Q8. What is a Turing instability, and how do you compute whether a two-species model has one?






Hint





Two conditions: without diffusion, and with diffusion. One matrix per wavenumber.









Answer





A uniform steady state that is stable without diffusion (all eigenvalues of the reaction Jacobian \(J\) have negative real part) but unstable with diffusion for some wavelengths. For each wavenumber \(q\), compute the eigenvalues of the 2 × 2 matrix \(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(D_u, D_v)\); the largest real part against \(q\) is the dispersion relation. If it is positive for a band of \(q\), perturbations with those wavelengths grow into a pattern, initially at the fastest-growing wavelength.




Q9. For the Schnakenberg model with \(a = 0.1\), \(b = 0.9\), can there be a Turing pattern when both species diffuse equally fast (\(d = 1\))? Why?






Hint





\(J = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 1 \\ -1.8 & -1\end{pmatrix}\). With \(d = 1\), \(J - q^2 I\) has the same eigenvectors as \(J\).









Answer





No. With equal diffusion, \(J - q^2 I\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_J - q^2\): diffusion only shifts every eigenvalue further left, so a stable state stays stable. In general, \(\det(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d)) = d\,q^4 - (0.8d - 1)q^2 + 1\) can only become negative if \(d > 8.57\): the substrate must diffuse much faster than the activator.




Q10. Your 2D simulation shows a fine checkerboard: high and low values alternate from one grid point to the next. Turing pattern or artefact? What do you check?






Hint





What is the wavelength of a checkerboard, in units of \(\Delta x\)?









Answer





An artefact. A checkerboard has wavelength \(2\Delta x\), the shortest the grid can hold, and it is set by the grid, not the model. It is the signature of an unstable explicit diffusion step (\(D\Delta t/\Delta x^2\) above \(1/4\) in 2D). Check: compute \(D\Delta t/\Delta x^2\) for every species; halve \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta x\), and see whether the wavelength follows the grid; compare with the unstable band from the dispersion relation.




Q11. A pattern has 47 spots with \(\Delta x = 1\) and 63 spots with \(\Delta x = 2\). With \(\Delta x = 0.5\) it has 46. Which grid would you trust, and how would you report the result?






Hint





Look for the point where refining stops changing the answer.









Answer





\(\Delta x = 1\) (or 0.5): halving the spacing from 1 to 0.5 changes the count by one, which is within the variation from a different noise layout, while \(\Delta x = 2\) (6 points per wavelength) is clearly under-resolved. Report a grid-independent statistic (spot count or spacing, about 12) together with the refinement test, not the exact positions of the spots, which depend on the initial noise.




Q12. With \(d = 5\) the Schnakenberg model has no Turing instability, yet IMEX with \(\Delta t = 0.4\) produces large moving blobs. Explain.






Hint





The reaction Jacobian has eigenvalues \(-0.1 \pm 0.995i\). Which modes does implicit diffusion fail to damp?









Answer





The reaction part is explicit Euler, which is stable on \(\lambda = -0.1 \pm 0.995i\) only for \(\Delta t < 0.2\) (\(|1 + \Delta t\lambda|^2 = 1 - 0.2\Delta t + \Delta t^2\)). At \(\Delta t = 0.4\) the factor is 1.039, so long waves and the uniform mode, which implicit diffusion hardly damps, grow by about 4 % per step and saturate in nonlinear oscillating blobs. With \(\Delta t = 0.1\) the solution stays uniform, as theory says. The “pattern” is made by the time step.

title: Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Goal
By the end of this exercise you should be able to:

write Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel as splittings \(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + M^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x})\) and run them by hand on a tiny grid,
predict their speed from the spectral radius of the iteration matrix, and explain why they slow down by a factor 4 each time the grid is refined,
count conjugate gradient iterations as the grid grows and relate them to \(\sqrt{\kappa}\),
use a preconditioner (diagonal, incomplete Cholesky) and say when it helps,
recognise a nonsymmetric system, see CG fail on it, and solve it with GMRES.

This is an optional further-reading unit, so the exercise is shorter than usual. The by-hand part needs pen and paper (and a calculator for B2–B4). The code part reuses the jacobi and cg functions you wrote in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse (C8).

title: Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
By hand
B1. Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel on four points. Take \(m = 2\) (four interior points, numbered 1 2 in the bottom row and 3 4 in the top row) and \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 1, 1, 1)\). (a) Write down \(A\). Check that \(\mathbf{x} = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)\) solves \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\). (b) Do three Jacobi steps from \(\mathbf{x}_0 = \mathbf{0}\). By what factor does the error shrink per step? (c) Do two Gauss–Seidel sweeps from \(\mathbf{0}\), in the order 1, 2, 3, 4. Give the error of point 4 after each sweep and their ratio. (d) Compare (b) and (c) with fact 3 (\(h = 1/3\)).
B2. A spectral radius. For a row of three cells, \(A = \begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix}\). (a) Write down the Jacobi iteration matrix \(T_J = I - D^{-1}A\). Show that \((1, \sqrt2, 1)\) is an eigenvector and find all three eigenvalues (the trace and the other two eigenvectors \((1, 0, -1)\) and \((1, -\sqrt2, 1)\) help). (b) What is \(\rho(T_J)\)? Compare with \(\cos(\pi h)\), \(h = 1/4\). How many Jacobi steps per digit? (c) For the chamber with \(m = 63\): \(\rho_J = \cos(\pi/64) = 0.998795\). How many sweeps per digit, and how many for six digits? Gauss–Seidel? (d) Why does Jacobi diverge for \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\) but converge for \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\)?
B3. Cost of refining. On the chamber, CG took 100 iterations and Jacobi 11 302 sweeps at \(m = 63\). (a) Predict both counts for \(m = 127\) and \(m = 255\) (use \(1/h = m + 1\)). (b) One iteration of either costs about \(2\,\text{nnz} \approx 10n\) floating-point operations for the matrix–vector product. Estimate the total work of CG and of Jacobi at \(m = 255\). (c) A 1 mm³ tissue block at 10 µm resolution: \(m = 100\) in 3D, \(n = 10^6\), seven non-zeros per row. CG’s iteration count depends on \(h\), not on the dimension. Estimate the iterations, the work, and the memory for \(A\) (12 bytes per non-zero) plus four vectors. Compare with the Cholesky factor of about \(6\times10^8\) non-zeros.
B4. A small step is not a small error. A Jacobi run on the chamber with \(\rho = 0.9988\) is stopped when the largest change in one step falls below \(10^{-6}\). (a) Assume each later step is \(\rho\) times the previous one. Sum the geometric series to estimate the distance from the true solution. (b) How many more sweeps would it take to make that error 1000 times smaller? (c) Why is a test on the residual safer? Why is it still not a test on the error?
B5. What a diagonal preconditioner can do. (a) \(A = \begin{pmatrix}100&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Compute its eigenvalues and \(\kappa(A)\). Then compute \(\kappa\) of \(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\), \(D = \text{diag}(100, 1)\). (For CG, preconditioning with \(D\) is equivalent to running CG on \(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\).) (b) For the chamber matrix, \(D = 4I\). What does Jacobi preconditioning change?

title: Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
In code
C1. Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel as splittings. Write splitting(A, b, M, tol, maxit) that iterates \(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + M^{-1}\mathbf{r}\) and returns the solution, the number of iterations and the history of relative residuals. Run it with \(M = D\) and \(M\) = lower triangle (R: tril; Python: scipy.sparse.tril and spsolve_triangular) for \(m = 7, 15, 31\). Compare with the predictions \(\ln(10^{-6})/\ln(\cos\pi h)\) and half of that. For \(m = 31\), print the ratio of the last few successive residuals.
C2. The spectral radius. For \(m = 7\), form \(T_J = I - D^{-1}A\) and \(T_{GS} = I - M^{-1}A\) as dense matrices and compute their spectral radii (R: eigen; Python: np.linalg.eigvals). Compare with fact 3 and with B2. Also compute \(\rho(T_J)\) for the \(2\times2\) matrix of B2(d).
C3. CG against grid size. Count CG iterations for \(m = 31, 63, 127, 255\). In R and Rust use your hand-written CG with a relative tolerance; in Python use scipy.sparse.linalg.cg with rtol=1e-6 and a callback that counts. Print \(\kappa = \cot^2(\pi h / 2)\) and \(\sqrt\kappa\) next to the counts, and the oxygen in the centre. Fit the slope of log(iterations) against \(\log(m+1)\).
C4. Preconditioning. The second chamber has a cell aggregate of radius 0.3 mm in the middle, where \(D\) is 10 times lower: \(A = -\nabla\cdot(D\nabla\,\cdot)\) with \(D\) evaluated between grid points. Use the starter code below. For \(m = 63\), on the uniform and the aggregate chamber, count iterations of plain CG, Jacobi-preconditioned CG and IC(0)-preconditioned CG. Print the smallest and largest diagonal entry. Check that \(LL^T \ne A\), and that \(L\) has as many non-zeros as the lower triangle of \(A\). (Python: pass the preconditioner to cg as M=, a LinearOperator whose matvec applies \(M^{-1}\).)






Starter code for C4: the aggregate chamber and IC(0)






RPythonRust


lapD <- function(m, Dfun) {                  # -div(D grad u), D on cell faces
  h <- 1 / (m + 1); I <- Diagonal(m)
  G1 <- bandSparse(m + 1, m, k = c(0, -1), diagonals = list(rep(1, m), rep(-1, m)))
  Gx <- kronecker(I, G1); Gy <- kronecker(G1, I)
  fx <- expand.grid(x = (1:(m + 1) - 0.5) * h, y = (1:m) * h)   # x-faces
  fy <- expand.grid(x = (1:m) * h, y = (1:(m + 1) - 0.5) * h)   # y-faces
  t(Gx) %*% Diagonal(x = Dfun(fx$x, fx$y)) %*% Gx +
    t(Gy) %*% Diagonal(x = Dfun(fy$x, fy$y)) %*% Gy
}
aggregate_D <- function(x, y) ifelse((x - 0.5)^2 + (y - 0.5)^2 < 0.3^2, 0.1, 1)
ic0 <- function(A, m) {                      # incomplete Cholesky, five-point pattern
  n <- nrow(A); d <- lw <- ls <- numeric(n); dA <- diag(A)
  w <- c(0, diag(A[-1, -n])); s <- c(rep(0, m), diag(A[-(1:m), -((n - m + 1):n)]))
  for (k in 1:n) {
    if (k > 1) lw[k] <- w[k] / d[k - 1]
    if (k > m) ls[k] <- s[k] / d[k - m]
    d[k] <- sqrt(dA[k] - lw[k]^2 - ls[k]^2)
  }
  bandSparse(n, k = c(0, -1, -m), diagonals = list(d, lw[-1], ls[-(1:m)]))
}


def lapD(m, Dfun):                            # -div(D grad u), D on cell faces
    h = 1 / (m + 1); I = sparse.identity(m)
    G1 = sparse.diags([np.ones(m), -np.ones(m)], [0, -1], shape=(m + 1, m))
    Gx = sparse.kron(I, G1); Gy = sparse.kron(G1, I)
    faces, nodes = (np.arange(1, m + 2) - 0.5) * h, np.arange(1, m + 1) * h
    Dx = Dfun(*[g.ravel() for g in np.meshgrid(faces, nodes)])          # x-faces
    Dy = Dfun(*[g.ravel() for g in np.meshgrid(nodes, faces)])          # y-faces
    return (Gx.T @ sparse.diags(Dx) @ Gx + Gy.T @ sparse.diags(Dy) @ Gy).tocsr()

def aggregate_D(x, y):
    return np.where((x - 0.5) ** 2 + (y - 0.5) ** 2 < 0.3 ** 2, 0.1, 1.0)

def ic0(A, m):                                # incomplete Cholesky, five-point pattern
    n = A.shape[0]; d = np.zeros(n); lw = np.zeros(n); ls = np.zeros(n)
    dA = A.diagonal(); w = A.diagonal(-1); s = A.diagonal(-m)
    for k in range(n):
        if k > 0: lw[k] = w[k - 1] / d[k - 1]
        if k >= m: ls[k] = s[k - m] / d[k - m]
        d[k] = np.sqrt(dA[k] - lw[k] ** 2 - ls[k] ** 2)
    return sparse.diags([d, lw[1:], ls[m:]], [0, -1, -m], format="csr")


// rust/examples/iterative_solvers_c4.rs  —  cargo run --release --example iterative_solvers_c4
// The starter functions are lap_d, aggregate_d, ic0 and ic_solve in that file
// (shown in full in the C4 solution). ic0 returns the diagonal d and the
// west / south entries lw, ls of L; ic_solve applies (L L^T)^{-1}.



IC(0) for the five-point matrix: row \(k\) of \(L\) has entries only at \(k-1\) (west neighbour), \(k-m\) (south neighbour) and \(k\). Cholesky’s formulas then reduce to \(\ell_{k,k-1} = a_{k,k-1}/d_{k-1}\), \(\ell_{k,k-m} = a_{k,k-m}/d_{k-m}\), \(d_k = \sqrt{a_{kk} - \ell_{k,k-1}^2 - \ell_{k,k-m}^2}\); the products that would create fill-in are never formed.



C5. A nonsymmetric system: the perfused chamber. Medium flows through the chamber from left to right with Péclet number 50. With upwind differences (Flow plus diffusion), the row for point \((i, j)\) becomes \((4 + \text{Pe}\,h)u_{ij} - (1 + \text{Pe}\,h)u_{i-1,j} - u_{i+1,j} - u_{i,j-1} - u_{i,j+1} = \Phi h^2\). For \(m = 63\): (a) Build \(A\) and check whether it is symmetric. (b) Run plain CG for 50, 100 and 300 iterations and print the true relative residual. (c) Solve with GMRES (R: hand-written as on the slide; pracma::gmres exists but needs a dense matrix. Python: scipy.sparse.linalg.gmres with restart=300 and a callback with callback_type="pr_norm"). Report iterations and relative residual. In Python, also run with the default restart=20. (d) Run GMRES on the symmetric chamber and compare the count with C3.

title: Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Hints






Hint 1 — Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel by hand (B1)





Each row of \(A\) for \(m = 2\) has 4 on the diagonal and \(-1\) for the two neighbours inside the grid (point 1 touches 2 and 3, point 4 touches 2 and 3). So one update of point \(i\) is \(x_i = (1 + \text{sum of its two neighbours})/4\). Jacobi uses only old values; Gauss–Seidel overwrites \(x_1\) first and uses the new \(x_1\) when it updates \(x_2\) and \(x_3\).









Hint 2 — eigenvalues (B2, C2)





Multiply \(T_J\) by the vector and see if you get a multiple of it. The eigenvalues of \(T_J\) add up to its trace, 0. A \(2\times2\) matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\a&0\end{pmatrix}\) has eigenvalues \(\pm a\). In code, max(Mod(eigen(T)$values)) (R) or np.max(np.abs(np.linalg.eigvals(T))) (Python); use Mod/abs because a nonsymmetric \(T\) may have complex eigenvalues.









Hint 3 — scaling (B3)





Doubling \(m + 1\) halves \(h\). Jacobi’s count grows like \(1/h^2\), CG’s like \(1/h\). At \(m = 255\), \(n = 65\,025\). For memory, 1 GB \(= 10^9\) bytes, and a vector of \(10^6\) doubles is 8 MB.









Hint 4 — the geometric series (B4)





If the last step was \(s\) and every later step is \(\rho\) times the previous one, the remaining distance is \(s(\rho + \rho^2 + \dots) = s\rho/(1-\rho)\). To shrink the error by a factor \(F\) takes \(\ln F / (-\ln\rho)\) steps.









Hint 5 — splittings in code (C1)





R: solve(M, r) with M <- Diagonal(x = diag(A)) or M <- tril(A) dispatches to a cheap diagonal or triangular solve; wrap it in as.vector. Python: for Jacobi use r / A.diagonal(); for Gauss–Seidel spsolve_triangular(sparse.tril(A, format="csr"), r, lower=True). Pass the solve as a function so one splitting serves both.









Hint 6 — counting iterations (C3, C5)





scipy calls callback(xk) once per CG iteration; keep a counter in a list (count = [0], count[0] += 1) so the inner function can change it. In scipy 1.12 and later the tolerance argument is rtol (formerly tol). info = 0 means converged, info > 0 means the iteration limit was reached. For gmres, callback_type="pr_norm" calls the callback once per inner iteration with the residual norm; maxiter counts restart cycles.









Hint 7 — preconditioners (C4)





Jacobi: Minv = function(r) r / d with d <- diag(A). IC(0): with L <- ic0(A, m) and Lt <- t(L), apply \(M^{-1} = (LL^T)^{-1}\) by two triangular solves, solve(Lt, solve(L, r)). Python: LinearOperator(A.shape, matvec=lambda r: spsolve_triangular(Lt, spsolve_triangular(L, r, lower=True), lower=False)) with Lt = L.T.tocsr().









Hint 8 — the advection matrix (C5)





Add Pe * h times a lower bidiagonal matrix (1 on the diagonal, \(-1\) below it) to the 1D operator in \(x\) only, then combine with the \(y\) operator by kronecker as in lap2. Symmetric? isSymmetric(A) (R), abs(A - A.T).max() == 0 (Python). To see CG fail, compute the residual \(\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|\) from the returned \(\mathbf{x}\), not CG’s internal residual.

title: Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
Exercise: iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Where this leads

Steady state in two dimensions and Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation (Part 10) produce these matrices; with Newton’s method for nonlinear uptake, every Newton step is a linear solve, and inside a large 3D model that solve is a preconditioned Krylov method.
Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow (Part 11): finite-element meshes give sparse matrices without a grid structure; there, algebraic multigrid and ILU replace the hand-written IC(0) for the five-point pattern used here.
How eigen() works, and big problems (Part 5): Lanczos and Arnoldi, the eigenvalue versions of the Krylov recurrences in CG and GMRES.

title: Quiz: iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Further reading: not part of the course.
This material is not included in the course, but it is relevant if you want to learn more about the topic.





Short questions to test your understanding of iterative linear solvers. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. A sparse direct solve of the 2D oxygen chamber with 640 000 unknowns takes 11 s. Why can you not simply do the same for a 3D tissue block with \(10^6\) unknowns?






Hint





What happens to the Cholesky factor, compared with the matrix itself, in 2D and in 3D?









Answer





Fill-in. Even with the best ordering, the Cholesky factor of a 3D grid matrix has far more non-zeros than the matrix (44 times more already at \(50^3\)), growing like \(n^{4/3}\), and the work grows like \(n^2\). For \(100^3\) that is roughly \(6\times10^8\) non-zeros (about 7 GB) and an hour of computing, against 7 million non-zeros (84 MB) for \(A\) itself. An iterative method stores only \(A\) and a few vectors; CG solved the \(100^3\) block in 203 iterations, 6 s in R.




Q2. Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel are both “splittings” \(\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + M^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x})\). What is \(M\) in each, and why must \(M\) be cheap to solve with but close to \(A\)?






Hint





Think of the two extremes \(M = I\) and \(M = A\).









Answer





Jacobi: \(M = D\), the diagonal of \(A\). Gauss–Seidel: \(M\) = the lower triangle of \(A\) including the diagonal (a forward substitution, which is what “use new values as soon as they exist” means). With \(M = A\) one step would give the exact answer but solving with \(M\) would be the original problem; with \(M\) far from \(A\) the iteration matrix \(T = I - M^{-1}A\) has a large spectral radius and the method is slow or diverges.




Q3. The iteration matrix of a splitting has spectral radius \(\rho = 0.99\). Roughly how many iterations does it take to gain one digit? Six digits? What if \(\rho = 1.01\)?






Hint





The error shrinks by about \(\rho\) per step. Solve \(\rho^k = 0.1\).









Answer





\(k = \ln 10/(-\ln 0.99) = 2.303/0.01005 \approx 229\) iterations per digit, about 1375 for six. With \(\rho = 1.01 > 1\) the error component along the corresponding eigenvector grows by 1 % per step: the iteration diverges, whatever the start (unless that component happens to be exactly zero).




Q4. You refine the chamber grid from \(h\) to \(h/2\) in 2D. By what factor do (a) the number of unknowns, (b) the Jacobi sweeps, (c) the CG iterations, and (d) the total work of Jacobi and of CG change?






Hint





\(\rho_J = \cos\pi h \approx 1 - \pi^2h^2/2\), and \(\kappa \approx 4/(\pi^2h^2)\).









Answer






×4 (\(n = m^2\)). (b) ×4: sweeps per digit \(\approx 0.47/h^2\). (c) ×2: CG needs \(\sim\sqrt\kappa \sim 1/h\) iterations. (d) Work per iteration ∝ \(n\), so Jacobi ×16 and CG ×8. Only multigrid keeps the iteration count constant, so its work grows ×4, like the number of unknowns.





Q5. Why does a finer grid make Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel slower, in words a biologist would accept?






Hint





How far does information travel in one sweep? Which kind of error is left after a few sweeps?









Answer





Each sweep only lets a grid point “talk” to its immediate neighbours: it is like diffusion with a time step of one grid spacing. Wiggly, local errors are averaged away within a few sweeps, but a smooth error that spans the whole chamber (e.g. the oxygen level in the centre being too high everywhere) can only be corrected by information that travels from the walls, one grid point per sweep, many times back and forth. A finer grid means more grid points between the walls and the centre.




Q6. A colleague runs Jacobi on a large diffusion problem and stops “when the solution no longer changes”: the largest change in one sweep is below \(10^{-8}\). The spectral radius is \(0.9999\). How far from the solution can the result be? What should they check instead?






Hint





Add up all the remaining steps as a geometric series.









Answer





Remaining error \(\approx 10^{-8} \times 0.9999/0.0001 \approx 10^{-4}\): four orders of magnitude more than the step. Slow methods take small steps without being close. Check the relative residual \(\|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|/\|\mathbf{b}\|\), report whether the iteration limit was reached, and on a small version of the problem compare with a direct solve. (Even the residual bounds the relative error only up to a factor \(\kappa(A)\).)




Q7. What is the Krylov space after \(k\) iterations, and what does CG choose from it?






Hint





Which vectors can you make from \(\mathbf{b}\) using \(k\) products with \(A\)?









Answer





\(\mathcal{K}_k = \text{span}\{\mathbf{b}, A\mathbf{b}, \dots, A^{k-1}\mathbf{b}\}\). For SPD \(A\), CG picks the \(\mathbf{x}_k\) in \(\mathcal{K}_k\) with the smallest error in the \(A\)-norm, equivalently the minimiser of \(\tfrac12\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{x}\) over \(\mathcal{K}_k\), using only a short recurrence (four vectors of storage). That optimal choice is why CG needs about \(\sqrt\kappa\) iterations where Jacobi needs about \(\kappa\).




Q8. You run CG on the perfused chamber (advection–diffusion with upwind differences). It returns after maxit iterations without an error message. What went wrong, how would you have noticed, and what should you use instead?






Hint





What property of \(A\) does CG assume? What does the advection term do to it?









Answer





The advection term couples each point only to its upstream neighbour, so \(A \ne A^T\), and CG’s derivation (minimising a quadratic) no longer holds: in the lecture the true residual grew to 314. Check isSymmetric(A) before using CG, and always compute the true relative residual of the returned \(\mathbf{x}\). Use GMRES (or BiCGSTAB) instead: 116 iterations there, 187 with restarts every 20.




Q9. Jacobi (diagonal) preconditioning did nothing for CG on the uniform chamber but halved the iteration count when a cell aggregate lowered \(D\) tenfold in the middle. Explain both.






Hint





What is \(D\) for the uniform chamber? What does scaling by a constant do to a condition number?









Answer





Uniform chamber: \(D = 4I\), so \(D^{-1}A = A/4\) has the same eigenvectors and the same condition number, and CG takes exactly the same steps (100 at \(m = 63\)). Aggregate: the diagonal varies from 0.4 to 4, so rows are badly scaled relative to each other; part of the large \(\kappa\) is due only to that scaling, and the diagonal preconditioner removes it (197 → 103). It cannot fix the \(1/h^2\) growth that comes from the grid itself.




Q10. What is “incomplete” in incomplete Cholesky, and what is the trade-off when you allow more fill-in?






Hint





Compare with the fill-in of the full Cholesky factor in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse.









Answer





IC(0) runs the Cholesky algorithm but throws away every entry that would fall outside the sparsity pattern of \(A\) (the fill-in). So \(L\) is as sparse as \(A\) and \(LL^T \approx A\), not \(= A\). Allowing more fill-in (IC(\(k\)), threshold dropping) makes \(LL^T\) closer to \(A\) and the iteration count smaller, but costs more memory and more work per iteration (two larger triangular solves), and for very much fill you are back to a direct solver. Count both iterations and time.




Q11. GMRES never lets the residual grow. Why not always use GMRES, even for SPD matrices? And what is the risk of restarting it?






Hint





What does GMRES store after \(k\) iterations?









Answer





GMRES stores an orthonormal basis of the Krylov space, one vector of length \(n\) per iteration, and orthogonalises each new vector against all old ones, so memory and work per step grow with \(k\) (\(n = 10^6\), \(k = 300\): 2.4 GB). For SPD matrices CG reaches the same accuracy in about the same number of iterations (99 vs 100 on the chamber) with four vectors. Restarting after \(k\) steps (GMRES(\(k\))) caps the memory but throws away the subspace; convergence slows (187 instead of 116 in the lecture) and on hard problems can stall completely. The cure is a better preconditioner.




Q12. In one or two sentences: why does multigrid need the same number of iterations on every grid?






Hint





Which error does a smoothing sweep remove well, and how does a smooth error look on a coarser grid?









Answer





A few Gauss–Seidel sweeps remove the wiggly error on any grid in a few steps, independently of \(h\); the smooth error that is left looks wiggly on a coarser grid, where it is again removed quickly, and so on down to a tiny grid solved directly. Every error component is thus handled on the grid where it is wiggly, so a V-cycle reduces the error by a fixed factor regardless of \(h\) (5 cycles to \(10^{-6}\) for every \(m\) from 15 to 511 in the lecture), at a cost proportional to \(n\).

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
About this lecture
Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse ended with a glimpse of Jacobi and conjugate gradient. This optional lecture explains why they behave as they do, and what is used in practice.

On 2D and especially 3D grids, a sparse direct solve fills in: memory and time explode. Iterative methods only need products A\mathbf{x}.
Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel are splittings. Their speed is the spectral radius of an iteration matrix (eigenvalues again), and it gets worse as the grid is refined.
Conjugate gradient (SPD matrices) needs about \sqrt{\kappa} iterations; preconditioning makes \kappa smaller; GMRES handles nonsymmetric matrices; multigrid needs the same number of iterations on every grid.
Biology: oxygen in a cell-laden gel, refined until each grid point is one cell, and then in 3D.


This is further reading: not required for the rest of the course. It assumes the sparse-matrix material of Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse (Part 3), eigenvalues from Part 5, and the 2D Laplacian of Steady state in two dimensions (Part 10), which we rebuild here in one slide so that the lecture can be read on its own. The message to take away is the last bullet: the number of iterations depends on the condition number, and the condition number of a diffusion matrix grows as the grid is refined. Everything else (preconditioning, multigrid) is an attack on that growth.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Recap: the glimpse from Part 3
From Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse, on the morphogen in a row of 1000 cells:

An iterative method improves a guess using only A\mathbf{x}: O(\text{nnz}) work per step, no fill-in, no factor stored.
Jacobi: \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + D^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}), D = diagonal of A. It took about 4160 iterations; CG took about 240.
Jacobi gains digits at a fixed rate (linear convergence) and diverges for \begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}; CG needs A SPD.
Check: monitor the residual \|\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}\|, stop on a tolerance, report when the iteration limit is hit.

Open questions from then: why 4160 and 240? Why does Jacobi diverge for the 2\times2 matrix? And what if A is not symmetric?

One-slide recap; the exercise of that unit (C8) had the students write jacobi() and cg() in about 10 lines each, so we do not repeat the code here. Today’s answers: 4160 comes from the spectral radius of the Jacobi iteration matrix (0.995 there); 240 from the square root of the condition number; the 2 x 2 diverges because its iteration matrix has an eigenvalue -2; and for nonsymmetric matrices we use GMRES.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
section: Biology: oxygen in a culture chamber
text:
Biology: oxygen in a culture chamber


A 1 mm × 1 mm gel with cells, oxygen enters through all four walls (concentration 1 = ambient). Cells consume it: hypoxic core where c < 0.25 (about 5 % O₂).
Steady state: -D\,\Delta c = -q. With u = 1 - c (the oxygen deficit): -\Delta u = \Phi, u = 0 on the walls, \Phi = qL^2/(Dc_0) = 12.
At h = 7.8 µm (about one grid point per cell): 16 129 unknowns. Centre c = 0.116; 14 % of the gel is hypoxic.


The model is the culture-chamber problem of Steady state in two dimensions (Part 10), with uniform zero-order consumption (Michaelis-Menten uptake is the nonlinear version treated there). Numbers, all order-of-magnitude: D = 2000 µm^2/s for oxygen in water, c0 = 0.2 mM (air-saturated medium), about 1e8 cells per mL each consuming about 50 amol O2 per second gives q of about 5 µM/s, and with L = 1 mm that is Phi = q L^2 / (D c0) = 12. The real experiments [O1, O2] use gas-impermeable barriers or a PDMS membrane to shape the gradient on purpose; here we just ask how hypoxic the middle of a thick gel gets. The point for this lecture: a question about cells needs a grid with roughly one point per cell, and in 3D that is a million unknowns per cubic millimetre.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
The matrix: a 2D Laplacian
library(Matrix)
lap1 <- function(m) bandSparse(m, k = -1:1,
  diagonals = list(rep(-1, m - 1), rep(2, m), rep(-1, m - 1)))
lap2 <- function(m) { I <- Diagonal(m); T <- lap1(m); kronecker(I, T) + kronecker(T, I) }
m <- 127; A <- lap2(m); b <- rep(12 / (m + 1)^2, m^2)    # multiplied through by h^2
c(n = nrow(A), nnz = nnzero(A))
#     n   nnz
# 16129 80137
u <- solve(A, b)                     # sparse direct solve (Cholesky, reordered)
1 - u[(m^2 + 1) / 2]                 # oxygen in the centre
# [1] 0.1159863

Each row: 4u_{ij} - u_{i-1,j} - u_{i+1,j} - u_{i,j-1} - u_{i,j+1} = \Phi h^2. SPD, five non-zeros per row.
kronecker builds the 2D operator from the 1D one; the same trick with three factors gives 3D (seven non-zeros per row).


This is the construction of Steady state in two dimensions; we multiply the equation by h^2 so that A has integer entries 4 and -1 and the right-hand side is Phi h^2. The unknowns are numbered row by row (natural ordering): u[i + m (j-1)]. lap2(3)[1:4, 1:4] shows the pattern: 4 on the diagonal, -1 for the left/right neighbour (next to the diagonal) and for the neighbour above/below (m positions away), with a 0 where a row of the grid ends. At this size, the direct solve takes a fraction of a second. The question of the next slide is what happens when we refine or go to 3D.

CG on that block: 6.9 M non-zeros stored (83 MB), 203 iterations, 6 s in R.


Numbers from make-iterative-solvers-figs.R (Cholesky(A, perm = TRUE), timed on one core) and from one CG run on lap3(100). The 3D 100^3 row is an extrapolation from the measured 3D points (nnz(L) ~ n^(4/3), time ~ n^2 for nested dissection), so read it as an order of magnitude. Why 3D is so much worse: with the best ordering (nested dissection), the separators that cut the grid into pieces are lines in 2D (m points) but planes in 3D (m^2 points), and the separator blocks become dense. Memory per non-zero: about 12 bytes in CSC (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse), so 600 M non-zeros is about 7 GB. An iterative method stores A, x and a handful of vectors: memory O(n). The price: the number of iterations, which is the rest of this lecture.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel as splittings
Split A = M - N with M easy to solve. Then A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} becomes the fixed-point iteration \mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{x}_k + M^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}_k).








method
M
one step means




Jacobi
diagonal D
every point: average of its 4 old neighbours (+ source)


Gauss–Seidel
lower triangle of A (incl. diagonal)
sweep through the grid, use new values as soon as they exist



Four interior points, A = lap2(2), \mathbf{b} = (1,1,1,1), exact x_i = 0.5, start at 0:

Jacobi: x_i = 0.25 \to 0.375 \to 0.4375: error 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, halves each step.
Gauss–Seidel, first sweep: 0.25,\ (1 + 0.25)/4 = 0.3125,\ 0.3125,\ (1 + 0.625)/4 = 0.40625.


The general picture: any matrix splitting turns the linear system into a fixed-point iteration x = g(x), exactly as in Bisection and fixed-point iteration (Part 2); there the iteration converged when |g’| < 1 near the root, here the role of g’ is played by the iteration matrix T = I - M^{-1} A (next slide but one). M must be cheap to solve with: a diagonal for Jacobi (one division per point), a triangle for Gauss-Seidel (one forward substitution, also O(nnz)). In the four-point example each point has two neighbours inside the domain; for Jacobi all four values stay equal, x <- (1 + 2x)/4, so the error is multiplied by exactly 1/2 each step. Gauss-Seidel uses the freshly computed value of point 1 when it updates point 2, and so on; after one sweep it is already further along. Exercise B1 completes the second sweep.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Both in ten lines
splitting <- function(A, b, M, tol = 1e-6, maxit = 1e5) {
  x <- numeric(length(b))
  for (it in 0:maxit) {
    r <- b - (A %*% x)[, 1]                     # residual
    if (sqrt(sum(r^2)) < tol * sqrt(sum(b^2))) return(it)
    x <- x + as.vector(solve(M, r))             # x <- x + M^{-1} r
  }
  NA                                            # not converged
}
m <- 63; A <- lap2(m); b <- rep(12 / (m + 1)^2, m^2)
c(jacobi = splitting(A, b, Diagonal(x = diag(A))), gauss_seidel = splitting(A, b, tril(A)))
#       jacobi gauss_seidel
#        11302         5652

Stop on the relative residual \|\mathbf{r}\| / \|\mathbf{b}\| < 10^{-6}. tril keeps the lower triangle; solve with a triangular sparse M is a forward substitution.
3969 unknowns, and still 11 302 Jacobi sweeps. Gauss–Seidel takes exactly half. Why these numbers?


The same function does both methods; only M changes. That is the point of the splitting view. Gauss-Seidel needing exactly half the Jacobi iterations is no accident for this matrix: its spectral radius is the square of Jacobi’s (next slide). In practice Gauss-Seidel is written as a loop that overwrites x in place, point by point; the triangular solve is the same arithmetic. Each run takes a few seconds in R; at m = 127 it takes 45 193 Jacobi sweeps.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
section: The rate is a spectral radius
text:
The rate is a spectral radius
The exact solution is a fixed point, so the error \mathbf{e}_k = \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x} obeys \mathbf{e}_{k+1} = T\,\mathbf{e}_k, \qquad T = I - M^{-1}A. Write \mathbf{e}_0 in eigenvectors of T: each component is multiplied by its eigenvalue every step. The slowest one wins: error \approx \rho(T)^k, spectral radius \rho(T) = \max|\lambda_i(T)|.
A7 <- as.matrix(lap2(7))                       # 49 unknowns, h = 1/8
TJ  <- diag(49) - A7 / 4                       # Jacobi: I - D^{-1} A
TGS <- diag(49) - solve(A7 * lower.tri(A7, diag = TRUE), A7)
rho <- function(T) max(Mod(eigen(T)$values))
c(rho(TJ), rho(TGS), cos(pi / 8), cos(pi / 8)^2)
# [1] 0.9238795 0.8535534 0.9238795 0.8535534

Converges if and only if \rho(T) < 1. Iterations per digit: \ln 10 / (-\ln\rho). For the 2\times2 of Part 3, \rho = 2: divergence.
For this grid \rho_J = \cos \pi h, \rho_{GS} = \cos^2 \pi h. At m = 63: \rho_J = 0.99880, 1910 sweeps per digit, \approx 11\,460 for six digits (measured: 11 302).


This is the power iteration of Power iteration and friends (Part 5) in disguise: repeatedly multiplying by T, the error lines up with the dominant eigenvector, and the residual ratio settles at rho (exercise C1 checks this: 0.99518 for m = 31). Mod() because T_GS is not symmetric and could have complex eigenvalues (here they are real). eigen() is the dense routine of How eigen() works, and big problems; fine for 49 unknowns, and the formula cos(pi h) comes from the sine modes of the Laplacian that we met in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences. The 2 x 2 matrix [1 2; 2 1] from Part 3 has T_J = [0 -2; -2 0], eigenvalues +2 and -2, so the error doubles. Sufficient condition for Jacobi to converge: strict diagonal dominance. The prediction 11 463 slightly overestimates because the start error does not have its full component in the slowest mode.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
section: Why they slow down as the grid is refined
text:
Why they slow down as the grid is refined


 Gauss–Seidel error, m = 31.


Each sweep only talks to neighbours: wiggly error is averaged away fast, smooth error barely moves.
\rho_J = \cos\pi h \approx 1 - \tfrac{\pi^2h^2}{2}, so sweeps per digit \approx 0.47/h^2: halve h, 4× the sweeps (and 4× the unknowns).
The same fact as a condition number: \kappa(A) = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min} \approx 4/(\pi^2h^2) (Pivoting, norms and conditioning): 1659 at m = 63, 26 560 at m = 255.



The left panel is random error; after 10 sweeps the high-frequency part is gone; after 200 only the smoothest mode, a single bump, is left, and it decays by a factor cos^2(pi h) = 0.990 per sweep. Information travels one grid point per sweep: for the centre to learn about the walls takes at least m/2 sweeps, and averaging needs many crossings. Plain Jacobi additionally keeps a checkerboard mode with eigenvalue -cos(pi h), which is why multigrid uses Gauss-Seidel or damped Jacobi as the smoother. The eigenvalues of the 2D Laplacian (h^2-scaled) are 4 sin^2(i pi h / 2) + 4 sin^2(j pi h / 2), from about 2 pi^2 h^2 to about 8; hence kappa = cot^2(pi h / 2), about 4 / (pi^2 h^2). The same eigenvalues set the explicit time-step limit in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences. Total work for Jacobi is then sweeps x unknowns ~ h^-4 in 2D: refining by 2 costs 16 times.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
section: Failure: a small step is not a small error
text:
Failure: a small step is not a small error
A tempting stopping rule: stop when the iterate no longer changes.
u <- as.vector(solve(A, b))                    # reference, m = 63
x <- numeric(m^2); d <- diag(A)
for (it in 1:1e5) {
  step <- (b - (A %*% x)[, 1]) / d             # Jacobi step
  x <- x + step
  if (max(abs(step)) < 1e-6) break             # "nothing changes any more"
}
c(it, max(abs(x - u)))
# [1] 5.875000e+03 8.286336e-04

Steps of 10^{-6}, but the error is 830 times larger: with \rho close to 1 the iteration crawls. Error \approx step \cdot \rho/(1-\rho) = 8.29\times10^{-4}.
Check: stop on the residual relative to \|\mathbf{b}\|; on a test problem, compare with a direct solve; look at the residual curve: a straight line on a log scale with a shallow slope means “still far away”.


This is the classic failure of slowly converging linear iterations: the change per step is small because the method is slow, not because it is done. The estimate: the remaining error is the sum of all future steps, a geometric series step (rho + rho^2 + …) = step rho / (1 - rho); with rho = cos(pi/64) = 0.9988 the factor is 833, and the measured error 8.29e-4 matches it to two digits. The deficit u is about 0.88 at most, so we have three correct digits, not six. A residual test is better but not perfect either: a small residual is not a small error when A is ill-conditioned (Pivoting, norms and conditioning), error <= kappa * residual in relative terms. Exercise B4 does the geometric-series estimate by hand.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Conjugate gradient: the Krylov idea
After k products with A, every method on these slides has \mathbf{x}_k in the Krylov space \mathcal{K}_k = \text{span}\{\mathbf{b}, A\mathbf{b}, A^2\mathbf{b}, \dots, A^{k-1}\mathbf{b}\}. Jacobi uses only the newest direction with a fixed weight. CG picks the best \mathbf{x}_k in all of \mathcal{K}_k:

For SPD A, solving A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} = minimising f(\mathbf{x}) = \tfrac12 \mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}^T\mathbf{x}. CG minimises the error in the “A-norm” over \mathcal{K}_k.
Search directions \mathbf{p}_k are A-conjugate (\mathbf{p}_i^TA\mathbf{p}_j = 0): a step never spoils earlier ones. Each step: one A\mathbf{p}, two dot products, three vector updates. Memory: 4 vectors.
Bound: error \le 2\left(\frac{\sqrt\kappa - 1}{\sqrt\kappa + 1}\right)^k, so iterations \approx \tfrac12\sqrt{\kappa}\,\ln(2/\text{tol}): \sqrt\kappa instead of \kappa.


Krylov space: the only vectors you can make from b with k multiplications by A. Gradient descent on f (Gradient descent, Newton and quasi-Newton, Part 9) also stays in this space but zigzags when kappa is large; CG keeps a memory of the previous direction so that the new direction is conjugate to all old ones, and the minimisation over the growing space is exact without storing it (a three-term recurrence; Lanczos in How eigen() works, and big problems is the same recurrence used for eigenvalues). In exact arithmetic CG finishes in at most n steps; that is irrelevant in practice, where we stop after far fewer. For m = 63: kappa = 1659, sqrt = 41, times ln(2e6)/2 = 7.3 gives about 300 as the bound; the measured 100 is better because the bound is a worst case over right-hand sides. What matters is the scaling: sqrt(kappa) ~ 1/h. Note: Jacobi can also be seen as using K_k, but it picks a fixed polynomial in A, not the optimal one.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
CG against the splittings


Same chamber, m = 63, tolerance 10^{-6}: Jacobi 11 302, Gauss–Seidel 5652, CG 100, CG with an incomplete-Cholesky preconditioner 40.
CG’s residual is not monotone (it minimises the A-norm of the error, not the residual), but the trend is steep.


Log-log axes so that all four fit (the x axis is iteration + 1, so that the start, iteration 0, can be shown); on linear iteration axes the splittings are straight lines (linear convergence, Convergence and cost) with slope log10(rho). CG’s curve bends downwards: it gets faster as the Krylov space captures the extreme eigenvalues. Each CG iteration costs about the same as a Jacobi sweep (one sparse matrix-vector product plus a few vector operations), so the 100 vs 11 302 is a fair comparison of work. The green curve is preconditioned; we come to it in two slides. The non-monotone residual is the reason to stop on a tolerance and not on “the residual went up”.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Iterations against grid size


Doubling m: Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel ×4 (slope 2), CG and preconditioned CG ×2 (slope 1), multigrid constant (5 V-cycles).
Work = iterations × unknowns: in 2D, Jacobi \sim h^{-4}, CG \sim h^{-3}, multigrid \sim h^{-2}, i.e. O(n).


Measured counts (dots); Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel stop at m = 127 (45 193 and 22 598 sweeps; minutes in R), and the dotted line is the prediction log(1e-6)/log(cos(pi h)) from the spectral radius. CG: 24, 50, 100, 203, 409, 827 for m = 15 … 511: exactly a factor 2 per refinement, as sqrt(kappa) ~ 1/h predicts. Incomplete-Cholesky CG lowers the constant (13 … 275) but not the slope. Multigrid needs 5 cycles from m = 15 to 511; each cycle costs a few sweeps on the fine grid. In 3D the picture is the same with n = m^3: CG on 100^3 took 203 iterations, the same as 127^2 in 2D, because the iteration count depends on h, not on the dimension.
