Jacobi: useless on the uniform chamber, halves the count with a jump in D. IC: 2–4× fewer, but still doubling with m.


The failure case for a preconditioner is the left column: on the constant-coefficient Laplacian, D = 4I, so D^-1 A = A/4 has the same condition number and CG takes exactly the same steps. With a 10-fold jump in D, plain CG pays for the jump (kappa grows about 10x, iterations about 2x: sqrt(10) would be 3.2, the bound is pessimistic) and the diagonal scaling removes most of it. IC(0) costs two triangular solves per iteration (about twice the work of a matrix-vector product), so 40 IC iterations are roughly 120 plain CG iterations of work: a real but modest gain, and not every preconditioner pays off in wall-clock time. Check: always report both iteration count and time. Oxygen diffusion in dense tissue is perhaps 2-3 times slower than in water; a 10-fold drop is typical of larger molecules (antibodies, drugs binding to tissue), so treat the aggregate as an illustration.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
section: Flow through the chamber: A is not symmetric
text:
Flow through the chamber: A is not symmetric


Perfused chamber: medium flows left to right, u = 100 µm/s, Péclet number uL/D = 50; upwind differences as in Flow plus diffusion. Now A \ne A^T.
CG fails silently: the true residual grows to 314 after 300 iterations. Check: isSymmetric(A) before using CG.
GMRES converges in 116 iterations; restarted GMRES(20) in 187.


Advection-diffusion with the upwind scheme of Flow plus diffusion: the advection term adds Pe h to the diagonal and -Pe h to the upstream neighbour only, so the matrix is no longer symmetric (Pe h = 0.78 at m = 63). The fixed concentration on the outflow wall is a simplification to keep the matrix small; the matrix structure, not the boundary details, is the point. CG’s derivation needs symmetry (the minimisation of x^T A x / 2 - b^T x only gives Ax = b for symmetric A); here it does not converge and nothing in the algorithm warns you. Nonsymmetric matrices also arise from Newton’s method on reaction-diffusion systems (the Jacobian) and from implicit time steps with flow. The perfused gel is better oxygenated (minimum 0.88) because the flow brings oxygen in.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
GMRES in one slide
Generalised Minimal RESidual: the \mathbf{x}_k \in \mathcal{K}_k with the smallest residual. Arnoldi builds an orthonormal basis Q of \mathcal{K}_k (Gram–Schmidt); a tiny least-squares problem gives the best combination.
gmres <- function(A, b, k = 300, tol = 1e-6) {
  Q <- matrix(0, length(b), k + 1); H <- matrix(0, k + 1, k)
  beta <- sqrt(sum(b^2)); Q[, 1] <- b / beta
  for (j in 1:k) {
    w <- (A %*% Q[, j])[, 1]                           # one product with A
    for (i in 1:j) { H[i, j] <- sum(Q[, i] * w); w <- w - H[i, j] * Q[, i] }
    H[j + 1, j] <- sqrt(sum(w^2)); Q[, j + 1] <- w / H[j + 1, j]
    e1 <- c(beta, rep(0, j)); Hj <- H[1:(j + 1), 1:j, drop = FALSE]
    y <- qr.solve(Hj, e1)                              # (j+1) x j least squares
    if (sqrt(sum((e1 - Hj %*% y)^2)) < tol * beta) break
  }
  list(x = as.vector(Q[, 1:j] %*% y), it = j)
}

Residual never increases. Price: stores all k basis vectors, work per step grows with k. Restart after 20–50 steps (GMRES(k)); restarting can stall. On the symmetric chamber: GMRES 99, CG 100 (CG is the cheap version).


The least-squares problem is the QR approach of Least squares: normal equations vs QR (Part 4), at size (j+1) x j; qr.solve does it. Production codes update a QR of H with Givens rotations instead of re-solving. Memory: k vectors of length n; for n = 1e6 and k = 300 that is 2.4 GB, which is why restarts are used. GMRES(20) needed 187 iterations instead of 116 here; on harder problems restarted GMRES can stall completely (the residual stops decreasing), and the cure is a better preconditioner rather than a longer restart. Alternatives with short recurrences for nonsymmetric matrices: BiCGSTAB, IDR(s). Arnoldi is also what eigs/ARPACK runs for eigenvalues (How eigen() works, and big problems).

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Multigrid in one picture


A few Gauss–Seidel sweeps make the error smooth. Smooth error on a fine grid is wiggly on a coarser grid, where sweeps are cheap and effective again. Recurse down to a tiny grid, solve, interpolate back up.
One V-cycle costs a few fine-grid sweeps; 5 cycles to 10^{-6} for every m from 15 to 511: O(n) work.


The slide on grid refinement showed that relaxation kills high-frequency error and leaves smooth error; multigrid turns that weakness into a method. On the coarse grid (every second point, a quarter of the unknowns in 2D) the remaining error has half as many points per wavelength, so it looks rougher and relaxation works on it. The coarse problem is the residual equation A e = r, restricted. Our 40-line implementation in make-iterative-solvers-figs.R uses Gauss-Seidel V(2,2) cycles with Galerkin coarse operators and needed 5 cycles for m = 15, 31, 63, 127, 255 and 511. Algebraic multigrid (AMG) builds the coarse levels from the matrix alone, so it also works on unstructured finite-element meshes (Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow); used as a preconditioner for CG, it is the default choice for large diffusion problems. Libraries: hypre (BoomerAMG), PETSc, pyamg (Python), AMGCL.

R has no iterative solvers in base or Matrix; the packages listed exist on CRAN but are not needed for this unit and are not on the install page. In Python, scipy’s cg and gmres take a callback (cg: called with the current iterate; gmres: with callback_type=“pr_norm”, called with the residual norm at every inner step), which is the way to count iterations; their info return value is 0 on success and positive when the iteration limit was hit. Large-scale codes (PETSc, Trilinos, hypre) offer all of these with many preconditioners. A practical rule: start with a sparse direct solver; when memory runs out or 3D grids appear, switch to preconditioned CG or GMRES, and keep the direct solver on a small grid as the test.

title: Iterative linear solvers in depth
text:
Summary

Why iterative: in 3D the Cholesky factor fills in (n^{4/3} memory, n^2 time); iterative methods need only A\mathbf{x} and O(n) memory.
Splittings \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + M^{-1}(\mathbf{b} - A\mathbf{x}): Jacobi (M = D), Gauss–Seidel (M = lower triangle). Error \sim\rho(T)^k, T = I - M^{-1}A; converge iff \rho < 1.
On a diffusion grid \rho = \cos\pi h, \kappa \approx 4/(\pi^2h^2): smooth error decays slowly, iterations ×4 per refinement.
CG (SPD): best point in the Krylov space, iterations \sim\sqrt\kappa \sim 1/h. Preconditioning shrinks \kappa (Jacobi: fixes scaling only; incomplete Cholesky: 2–4×). Multigrid: constant.
GMRES for nonsymmetric A (flow); stores its basis, restart with care. CG on a nonsymmetric matrix fails without a warning.
Checks: relative residual, not step size; isSymmetric; maxit reached?; compare with a direct solve on a small grid.


The one-line version: the cost of an iterative solve is (cost per iteration) x (number of iterations), the first is O(nnz), the second is set by the condition number, and the condition number of a diffusion problem grows like 1/h^2. Preconditioners and multigrid exist to break that growth. Where this connects: Steady state in two dimensions and Reaction-diffusion and pattern formation (Part 10) produce the matrices; Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow (Part 11) produces bigger and less regular ones, for which algebraic multigrid and Krylov methods are the standard tools inside COMSOL, FEniCS and friends.

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
About this lecture
So far in Part 10 molecules only moved. In an embryo they are also made and destroyed: \partial c/\partial t = D\,\partial^2 c/\partial x^2 + f(c). The reaction term f changes what the equation can do.

Synthesis–diffusion–degradation: a source and first-order decay give an exponential gradient with decay length \lambda = \sqrt{D/k}. We check the grid against the exact solution.
IMEX (diffusion implicit, reaction explicit) and operator splitting: two ways to treat the two terms differently. Each has its own error and its own failure.
Turing patterns: two species, a uniform state that is stable without diffusion becomes unstable with it. Eigenvalues of a 2 × 2 matrix per wavenumber say which wavelengths grow.
A 2D simulation in a few seconds, and the checks that separate a real pattern from a numerical artefact.
Biology: the Bicoid gradient and the temperature-step experiment [M1]; embryo trap arrays [M3]; Fgf8 in zebrafish [M4].


The last core unit of the course, and the one that uses the most earlier material: the tridiagonal Thomas solver (Part 3), stiffness and implicit steps (Part 8), eigenvalues and the phase plane (Parts 5 and 8), the FFT (Part 6). Time units in this lecture are minutes, to match the morphogen in a row of cells from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse; lengths are µm. All data are synthetic: the model plus noise. Literature values are quoted as approximate orders of magnitude; check them against the papers before using them.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Biology: the Bicoid gradient


bicoid mRNA sits at the anterior pole of the Drosophila egg. The protein spreads and is degraded: high at the head end, low at the tail. Target genes read the concentration as position.
Reported values (approximate): decay length \approx 100 µm, about 1/5 of the 500 µm egg; protein lifetime tens of minutes; D from about 0.3 µm²/s (FRAP) to about 7 µm²/s (FCS).


Bicoid is the textbook morphogen. The decay length of about 100 µm (roughly 20 % of egg length) is widely reported (e.g. Houchmandzadeh et al. 2002; Gregor et al. 2007). Diffusion coefficients disagree by a factor of about 20 depending on the method (FRAP in Gregor et al. 2007, about 0.3 µm^2/s; FCS in Abu-Arish et al. 2010, about 7 µm^2/s), which is part of a long debate about how the gradient forms. These are not on our source list; treat them as approximate and check before quoting. Our running numbers, D = 100 µm^2/min (1.7 µm^2/s) and k = 0.01 per min (lifetime 100 min), are Bicoid-like in spirit: they give the right decay length, not a fitted model.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Recap: what you already have


Morphogen in a row of cells (Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse):

exchange rate 1 per min, decay k = 0.01 per min, source in cell 1,
a tridiagonal system, solved by thomas(a, b, c, d) in O(n),
decay length \sqrt{D/k} = 10 cells.


Diffusion on a grid (The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences, Implicit schemes and the method of lines):

nodes x_i = i\,\Delta x, stencil (1, -2, 1)/\Delta x^2, ghost points for no flux,
FTCS needs D\,\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2,
backward Euler: no step limit, one Thomas solve per step.


Today: the row of cells is a diffusion grid with \Delta x = one cell. With \Delta x = 10 µm, exchange at 1 per min means D = 1 \cdot 10^2 = 100 µm²/min.

One slide only; all of this was taught in its own unit. The link in the last line is worth a moment: the compartment model “each cell passes morphogen to its neighbour at rate D_cell” and the finite-difference grid “D/dx^2 times the second difference” are the same equations with D_cell = D/dx^2. So a cell-based model is a finite-difference (finite-volume) discretisation with the grid fixed by the biology, and the decay length of 10 cells is 100 µm.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Adding a reaction term
Mass balance per slice, now with production and decay:
\frac{\partial c}{\partial t} = \underbrace{D\,\frac{\partial^2 c}{\partial x^2}}_{\text{diffusion}} \; \underbrace{-\,k\,c}_{\text{decay}}, \qquad 0 < x < L

Source: an influx j at the anterior pole, -D\,\partial c/\partial x = j at x = 0. Wall at the posterior pole: \partial c/\partial x = 0 at x = L.
Numbers: D = 100 µm²/min, k = 0.01 per min, L = 500 µm; j is chosen so that c(0) \approx 1.
Steady state: D\,c'' = k\,c. Solutions e^{\pm x/\lambda} with \lambda = \sqrt{D/k} = \sqrt{100/0.01} = 100 \ \text{µm}.


The reaction term is local: it involves only c at the same point. Diffusion couples neighbours; reaction does not. That difference is what IMEX and splitting exploit later. Exact steady state with these boundary conditions: c(x) = (j lambda / D) cosh((L - x)/lambda) / sinh(L/lambda). With j = D/lambda = 1 µm/min (in units of concentration) this gives c(0) = coth(5) = 1.0001. In the infinite embryo it is simply e^{-x/lambda}. Students who did the exercise in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse saw the discrete version: c[11]/c[1] = 0.368, one decay length.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
The decay length \lambda = \sqrt{D/k}
A molecule lives about 1/k and moves about \sqrt{2D/k} in that time: the gradient reaches about \lambda before it is degraded.

c falls by e every \lambda. A threshold c_T is crossed at x_T = \lambda\ln(c_0/c_T): for c_0/c_T = 10, x_T = 230 µm.
\lambda depends on the ratio D/k. Double both: same gradient, formed twice as fast.


Only two of D, k, lambda need to be measured; the third follows. For Bicoid, lambda = 100 µm and a 50 min lifetime would need D = 1e4 / 3000 = 3.3 µm^2/s, between the FRAP and FCS values: this arithmetic is part of the debate. The Fgf8 row is approximate: an FCS diffusion coefficient of order 50 µm^2/s and a decay length of order 200 µm were reported by Yu et al. 2009 [M4]; the lifetime 200^2/50 = 800 s is our inference, not a quoted number. The last bullet matters for the temperature experiment later: if every rate scales by the same factor, the steady gradient does not change.

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Steady state on the grid
D <- 100; k <- 0.01; L <- 500               # µm^2/min, 1/min, µm
lam <- sqrt(D / k); j <- D / lam            # lambda = 100 µm, c(0) close to 1
N <- 50; dx <- L / N; x <- (0:N) * dx; r <- D / dx^2
lo <- c(0, rep(-r, N - 1), -2 * r)          # -D c'' with ghost points:
di <- rep(2 * r, N + 1)                     #   both end rows get a 2
up <- c(-2 * r, rep(-r, N - 1), 0)
src <- c(2 * j / dx, rep(0, N))             # the influx enters via the ghost point
cs <- thomas(lo, di + k, up, src)           # (-D c'' + k c) = src
exact <- j * lam / D * cosh((L - x) / lam) / sinh(L / lam)
max(abs(cs - exact))
# [1] 0.001247396

Ghost point at x = 0: c_{-1} = c_1 + 2\Delta x\, j/D (the slope is -j/D). At x = L: c_{N+1} = c_{N-1}.


The same three-diagonal layout as in Implicit schemes and the method of lines: lo, di, up are the diagonals of minus D times the second difference, so a steady solve adds k to the diagonal and an implicit step uses 1 + dt times the diagonals. The ghost point at the source end: the central difference (c_1 - c_{-1})/(2 dx) = -j/D gives c_{-1}; substituting into the stencil at node 0 doubles the coupling to c_1 and adds 2 j / dx to the right-hand side. thomas() is the function from Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse, unchanged. The matrix is not symmetric (the 2 in the end rows), but it is diagonally dominant, so Thomas without pivoting is safe.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Check against the exact solution


Ghost point: error falls 4× per halving of \Delta x (order 2). With \Delta x = \lambda (orange) the shape is still right to about 10 %.
Failure: the one-sided boundary (c_1 - c_0)/\Delta x = -j/D is only first order, and it breaks the mass balance: k\int c\,dx should equal j; at \Delta x = 50 µm it is 1.32\,j.


Two independent checks, as in Structure: symmetric, banded, sparse. The convergence check needs an exact solution, which we have here and rarely have in practice. The mass balance does not: at steady state everything that comes in must be degraded, k times the integral of c (trapezoid rule) equals j. With the ghost point this holds to rounding error on every grid; with the one-sided boundary it is off by 81 % at dx = 100 and 32 % at dx = 50. The lesson generalises: one sloppy first-order boundary row spoils a second-order scheme everywhere. A grid with dx = lambda is far too coarse for a quantitative answer, but it still gives the shape: the decay length sets the resolution needed, as the wavelength will for Turing patterns.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: How fast does the gradient form?
text:
How fast does the gradient form?


Start from c = 0. Near the source the gradient is ready in about 1/k; further away it takes longer.
Local accumulation time \tau(x) = \int_0^\infty \bigl(1 - c(x,t)/c_s(x)\bigr)\,dt. Numerically: 50.2, 100.0, 150.3 min at x = 0, 100, 200 µm. Formula for a long embryo: (1 + x/\lambda)/(2k) = 50, 100, 150 min.


Profiles from IMEX Euler (next slides) with dt = 1 min. Right: c divided by its steady value at three positions. The accumulation time is the area above the curve: a mean time to reach steady state, defined without choosing a threshold such as 90 %. The formula (1 + x/lambda)/(2k) for a semi-infinite domain with a constant influx is from Berezhkovskii, Sample and Shvartsman (2010); our numbers, computed with dt = 0.5 min and the trapezoid rule (exercise C2), agree to within 0.3 %. Biology: the gradient is not instantaneous. With a lifetime of 100 min the posterior part needs hours; for the real Bicoid gradient the lifetime and so the formation time are thought to be shorter. Whether the gradient is at steady state when it is read is a real question in the field.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Two terms, two time scales
Euler on the method-of-lines system \mathbf c' = -K_D\mathbf c - k\,\mathbf c + \mathbf s must be stable for both parts:









part
fastest rate
Euler needs
here (\Delta x = 10 µm)




diffusion
4D/\Delta x^2
\Delta t \le \Delta x^2/(2D)
0.5 min; at \Delta x = 1 µm: 0.005 min

\Delta t \le 2/k
200 min


fast receptor binding
\approx 1 per s

Diffusion on a fine grid is stiff (Stiffness and implicit methods): treat it implicitly. That is a linear, tridiagonal solve.
Reactions are often nonlinear (Hill functions, u^2v) but local. Fully implicit means a Newton solve with the coupled Jacobian every step.
Idea: implicit where it is cheap and needed, explicit where it is not.


K_D is the positive diffusion matrix (lo, di, up). The table is the stability limit of Euler, h |lambda| <= 2, for each part separately. For the Bicoid model the reaction is slow and linear, so it would be fine to do everything implicitly (backward Euler with k on the diagonal, as in Implicit schemes and the method of lines). The point is the general case: with a nonlinear reaction, backward Euler on the whole system needs Newton for systems of equations at every step, with a Jacobian that couples the diffusion band and the reaction. The receptor-binding row is an order of magnitude only: binding to abundant receptors can be much faster than degradation, and then the reaction is the stiff part.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: IMEX Euler: diffusion implicit, reaction explicit
text:
IMEX Euler: diffusion implicit, reaction explicit
\frac{\mathbf c^{n+1} - \mathbf c^{n}}{\Delta t} = -K_D\,\mathbf c^{n+1} + \mathbf f(\mathbf c^{n}) + \mathbf s \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (I + \Delta t\,K_D)\,\mathbf c^{n+1} = \mathbf c^n + \Delta t\,\bigl(\mathbf f(\mathbf c^n) + \mathbf s\bigr)
imex <- function(c, dt, nsteps, f) {          # f(c): reaction, explicit
  for (n in seq_len(nsteps))
    c <- thomas(dt * lo, 1 + dt * di, dt * up, c + dt * (f(c) + src))
  c
}
f <- function(c) -k * c                       # linear decay
for (dt in c(1, 10, 50))                      # run to t = 5000 min, compare with cs
  print(max(abs(imex(rep(0, N + 1), dt, 5000 / dt, f) - cs)))
# [1] 2.38698e-14
# [1] 1.121325e-14
# [1] 1.076916e-14

One Thomas solve per step, any f, no Newton; order 1. The steady state is exact for every \Delta t (\Delta t cancels at a fixed point).


The left-hand matrix is the same as for backward Euler on pure diffusion, so the Thomas call is the one from Implicit schemes and the method of lines. The reaction only enters the right-hand side, evaluated at the old values, so it can be anything: a Hill function, a two-species reaction, a lookup table. In the loop, the IMEX run to t = 5000 min reaches the steady state of the grid to rounding error, with a step of 1, 10 or even 50 minutes. That is a useful property (the long-time answer does not depend on the step), but it also means a large step can hide a wrong transient. IMEX stands for implicit-explicit; higher-order versions (IMEX Runge–Kutta, SBDF2) exist.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
When IMEX fails
One Fourier mode e^{iqx}, with linear decay f = -kc: each step multiplies it by
G(q) = \frac{1 - k\,\Delta t}{1 + D q^2\,\Delta t}.

The denominator \ge 1: the diffusion part never limits \Delta t.
The numerator is Euler on the reaction: |1 - k\Delta t| \le 1 needs \Delta t \le 2/k, and the uniform mode (q = 0) gets no help from diffusion.
Fast receptor binding at 1 per s: IMEX needs \Delta t \le 2 s, as slow as explicit diffusion on a 30 µm grid.
Check: compute \Delta t\,\lambda for the eigenvalues \lambda of the reaction Jacobian, and stay inside Euler’s stability region (|1 + \Delta t\lambda| \le 1).


A Fourier mode is an eigenvector of the diffusion matrix (with periodic boundaries exactly, otherwise approximately), so the scheme acts on it as on a scalar: the implicit factor 1/(1 + D q^2 dt) times the explicit factor 1 - k dt. Stiff reactions are therefore the weak point of IMEX. Remedies: treat the stiff reaction implicitly too (it is local, so this is a small Newton solve per grid point, not a big coupled one), or split the operators and solve the reaction exactly or with a stiff ODE solver. The same check reappears for the Turing model, where the reaction eigenvalues are complex: -0.1 ± 0.995i.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Operator splitting
Write \mathbf c' = \mathcal A\mathbf c + \mathcal B\mathbf c with \mathcal A = diffusion (with the influx), \mathcal B = reaction. Solve each part on its own, one after the other:

Lie splitting: \Delta t of diffusion, then \Delta t of reaction.
Strang splitting: \Delta t/2 reaction, \Delta t diffusion, \Delta t/2 reaction.

for (s in 1:nsteps) {                     # both parts done exactly here
  lie    <- exp(-kx * dt) * diffuse(lie, dt)
  strang <- exp(-kx * dt / 2) * diffuse(exp(-kx * dt / 2) * strang, dt)
}

Each sub-problem gets its best solver: diffusion by a tridiagonal solve (or FFT), the decay exactly, a stiff reaction by an ODE solver per grid point.


kx is the decay rate at each grid point (it varies along the embryo later). diffuse(c, dt) solves the pure diffusion problem with the influx for time dt. To see the splitting error alone, we do it exactly here with the matrix exponential of the 51 x 51 diffusion matrix (Matrix::expm in R, scipy.linalg.expm, nalgebra’s exp in the exercise); in practice it is a backward Euler or Crank–Nicolson step with Thomas. The reaction step is a set of independent scalar ODEs, one per grid point; for c’ = -k c it is a multiplication by exp(-k dt). Splitting is how many large simulation codes are organised: diffusion, reaction, and in Flow plus diffusion also advection, each by its own method.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
The splitting error





Error at t = 60 min against the exact solution of the grid ODEs. Lie: slope 1. Strang: slope 2 (for small steps). IMEX: slope 1.
Exact sub-steps, still an error: doing \mathcal A then \mathcal B is not doing both at once unless they commute, \mathcal{AB} = \mathcal{BA}.
Here they do not: the influx at x = 0 is decayed only in the reaction step. With no source and uniform k the error is 10^{-15} (exercise).



For matrices, e^{(A+B)h} = e^{Ah} e^{Bh} only if AB = BA; the leading error per step is h^2/2 (AB - BA), so Lie is first order globally. Strang is symmetric and the h^2 term cancels: second order. Here the Strang slope approaches 2 only for small steps (the ratio between the last two points is 3.7): at large steps the stiff diffusion modes and the boundary source reduce the order, a known effect. When do the parts commute? Uniform decay k I commutes with any diffusion matrix, so a pure decay problem has no splitting error at all. A spatially varying k(x) or a localised source breaks it. That includes the temperature step on the next slide. Check in practice: halve dt and compare, exactly as for any time stepper.

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: A temperature step across the embryo [M1]
text:
A temperature step across the embryo [M1]




Lucchetta et al. held a Drosophila embryo between two laminar streams at different temperatures (about 20 and 27 °C), so its halves develop at different speeds [M1].

Model (synthetic, assumed): k doubles in the warm half; D, j unchanged.
Where is c = 0.1? All cold: 230.7 µm. All warm: 138.3 µm. Posterior warm: 220.2 µm. Anterior warm: 138.9 µm.
k(x) varies, so Lie splitting has an error; IMEX and a steady solve do not care.



The experiment is described in Implicit schemes and the method of lines, which computes the temperature inside the embryo: the step is sharp, so modelling k as a step function is reasonable. The factor 2 for k over 7 degrees is an assumption (a Q10 of about 2.7), not a measurement, and we ignore the smaller change of D (about 20 % from the lower viscosity of warm water). In this toy model the threshold position is set almost entirely by the anterior half, where the gradient is high: warming the posterior moves it by 10 µm, warming the anterior by 92 µm. What the real embryo does, and how the patterning network compensates, is the subject of the paper [M1]; our model only shows how to ask the question quantitatively. The steady solve is the same Thomas call with a k vector on the diagonal.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Measuring gradients in many embryos

Embryo trap arrays [M3]: a microfluidic array that holds many Drosophila embryos upright, so the Dorsal gradient around the embryo’s circumference can be imaged in hundreds of embryos at once. Many embryos → a distribution of gradient shapes, not one curve.
Fgf8 in zebrafish [M4]: a source–sink gradient. FCS gave a diffusion coefficient (order 50 µm²/s); the profile gave \lambda (order 200 µm). Then k = D/\lambda^2 \approx 1.3\cdot10^{-3} per s: degradation inferred, not measured. Blocking receptor-mediated uptake (endocytosis) flattens the gradient, as \lambda = \sqrt{D/k} predicts.
Exercise (synthetic): fit \lambda to 20 noisy profiles by a straight line through \log c: 200.3 \pm 12.2 µm. With a background of 0.05 added: 229.9 µm. The log fit is biased by any offset.


Both papers are on our source list but were only read at abstract level; quote the numbers as orders of magnitude. The trap array paper [M3] imaged the Dorsal nuclear gradient, which is formed by a different mechanism (nuclear import downstream of Toll signalling), so the SDD model does not apply directly; the point here is the data: one profile per embryo, many embryos, and the need to fit each one. The circumference is a ring, so a model of it would use periodic boundary conditions, as the 2D Turing simulation below does. For Fgf8, the source-sink picture is: freely diffusing molecules from a local source, removed by receptor-mediated endocytosis in the target cells. The fit in the exercise is linear least squares from Part 4; the bias from a background offset is a classic failure: always subtract the background (or fit it as a parameter, Part 9) before taking logs.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Turing’s idea: diffusion can destabilise
Two species, an activator u and a substrate v (Schnakenberg model, dimensionless):
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = a - u + u^2 v + \nabla^2 u, \qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial t} = b - u^2 v + d\,\nabla^2 v

a = 0.1, b = 0.9: uniform steady state u^* = a + b = 1, v^* = b/(a+b)^2 = 0.9.
Without diffusion it is stable: Jacobian J = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & 1 \\ -1.8 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, trace -0.2, det 1 (Equilibria, stability and the phase plane).
With v diffusing d times faster than u: some wavelengths grow. Spots or stripes appear from noise.


Turing (1952) showed that diffusion, which on its own smooths everything, can make a stable uniform state unstable when two species diffuse at different rates: local activation, long-range inhibition (or depletion). Here u makes more of itself (u^2 v) and uses up v; v diffuses fast, so a local peak of u drains v from a wide surrounding region and suppresses u there. Turing-type mechanisms have been proposed for digit spacing, hair and feather follicles and fish skin stripes; for most, whether the real molecules behave like the model is debated. We use Schnakenberg because its algebra is simple, not as a model of a specific tissue. Length and time are dimensionless: D_u = 1 sets the length unit.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: Linear stability, one wavelength at a time
text:
Linear stability, one wavelength at a time
Perturb the uniform state by \boldsymbol\delta(t)\cos(qx). Then \nabla^2 \to -q^2, and
\frac{d\boldsymbol\delta}{dt} = \bigl(J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d)\bigr)\,\boldsymbol\delta \qquad\text{a 2 × 2 matrix for each } q.
J <- matrix(c(0.8, -1.8, 1, -1), 2)                 # column-wise
growth <- function(q, d) max(Re(eigen(J - q^2 * diag(c(1, d)))$values))
q <- seq(0, 1.5, by = 0.001)
g <- sapply(q, growth, d = 20)
range(q[g > 0]); q[which.max(g)]; 2 * pi / q[which.max(g)]
# [1] 0.272 0.822
# [1] 0.487
# [1] 12.90182

Unstable for 0.272 < q < 0.822; fastest growth at wavelength \approx 12.9, rate 0.263.


cos(qx) is an eigenfunction of the second derivative with eigenvalue -q^2, so each wavelength evolves independently in the linearised problem, the same idea as the Fourier modes of the diffusion equation in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences. For each q we need the eigenvalues of a 2 x 2 matrix: exactly the phase-plane test from Equilibria, stability and the phase plane, now repeated for every wavelength. The curve of the largest real part against q is the dispersion relation. The pattern that emerges from small random noise is dominated, at first, by the fastest-growing wavelength. Python: numpy.linalg.eigvals; in the exercise Rust uses the trace-determinant formula.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
The dispersion relation





d = 1, 5: every q decays. d = 10, 20: a band of unstable wavelengths.
Trace of J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(1, d) is -0.2 - q^2(1 + d) < 0 always, so instability needs \det < 0: a real eigenvalue crossing 0, a pattern that stands still.
\det = d\,q^4 - (0.8d - 1)\,q^2 + 1. Negative for some q only if d > d_c = 8.57.



Trace-determinant classification from Equilibria, stability and the phase plane: with negative trace, the only way to an unstable eigenvalue is a negative determinant, which makes one eigenvalue real and positive: a saddle in the (delta_u, delta_v) plane for that wavelength. The kinks in the curves are where the two eigenvalues change from a complex pair to two real ones. The determinant is a quadratic in q^2; its minimum is negative when (0.8 d - 1)^2 > 4 d, i.e. d > 8.57 (exercise B5). So the substrate must diffuse at least 8.6 times faster than the activator: the classic difficulty of Turing models, since similar-sized proteins diffuse at similar rates.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: A 2D simulation: IMEX with the FFT
text:
A 2D simulation: IMEX with the FFT
N <- 80; dx <- 1; dt <- 0.1; d <- 20; a <- 0.1; b <- 0.9   # periodic 80 x 80
s <- 4 / dx^2 * sin(pi * (0:(N - 1)) / N)^2
kap <- outer(s, s, "+")              # five-point Laplacian in Fourier space
z <- lcg(2 * N^2) - 0.5              # small noise (same numbers in Python, Rust)
u <- matrix(1 + 0.02 * z[1:N^2], N); v <- matrix(0.9 + 0.02 * z[-(1:N^2)], N)
solve_diff <- function(w, Dw)        # solves (I - dt Dw Laplacian) w_new = w
  Re(fft(fft(w) / (1 + dt * Dw * kap), inverse = TRUE)) / N^2
for (n in 1:2000) {                  # to t = 200
  f <- a - u + u^2 * v; g <- b - u^2 * v                   # reaction: explicit
  u <- solve_diff(u + dt * f, 1); v <- solve_diff(v + dt * g, d)   # diffusion: implicit
}

Periodic grid: fft diagonalises the five-point Laplacian, so the implicit solve is a division. 2 s in R.


The same IMEX Euler as in 1D; only the linear solve differs. On a periodic grid the eigenvectors of the five-point Laplacian (Steady state in two dimensions) are the 2D Fourier modes, with eigenvalues -(4/dx2)(sin2(pi k/N) + sin^2(pi l/N)): that is kap. So: transform, divide each coefficient by 1 + dt D kap, transform back. Cost O(N^2 log N) per step, much cheaper than a sparse solve. With walls instead of periodic edges one would use a sparse direct solve (Steady state in two dimensions) or a cosine transform. Explicit FTCS would need dt <= dx^2/(4 d) = 0.0125 for v: 16 000 steps instead of 2000. lcg is a tiny random number generator (Park–Miller) defined in the exercise so that all three languages start from the same noise; R’s runif would do as well. fft in R does the 2D transform of a matrix; Python numpy.fft.fft2.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
The pattern forms


From 1 % noise: a mixture of wavelengths at t = 10, spots by t = 30, a nearly hexagonal array of 47 spots at t = 200.


u on the 80 x 80 periodic domain. At t = 10 the perturbation has grown from 0.01 to about 0.03 in amplitude and already shows the preferred length scale; this is the linear regime, where the dispersion relation applies. By t = 30 the nonlinear terms limit the growth and spots form; between t = 30 and 200 the spots rearrange slowly into a nearly regular array. The final spot spacing (about 12, as 47 spots in a box of side 80 suggest) is close to, but need not equal, the fastest linear wavelength 12.9: the nonlinear dynamics select the final spacing. The exact arrangement of spots depends on the initial noise; the spacing does not.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Pattern or artefact?


\Delta x = 1 and 0.5: 47 and 46 spots. \Delta x = 2: 63 spots, smaller and blocky. Only 6 grid points per wavelength: the grid changed the answer.
Right: d = 5 has no Turing instability, yet \Delta t = 0.4 produces large blobs. With \Delta t = 0.1: uniform, as theory says.


Left and middle: same model, same time step, different grids. Halving dx from 1 to 0.5 changes the spot count by one (the noise is laid out differently on a different grid, so the exact count wanders slightly); going from 1 to 2 changes it by a third. The five-point Laplacian underestimates q^2 for short waves (by 7 % at the fastest wavelength with dx = 2), which shifts the band, and spots only 3-4 points wide are badly resolved. Right: a parameter set that cannot make a Turing pattern, with an IMEX step that is too large for the reaction (next slide). It is not even stationary: it oscillates in time. A student who varied only d would conclude that d = 5 makes patterns.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: Why the time step made a pattern
text:
Why the time step made a pattern
for (dt in c(0.1, 0.2, 0.4))                  # Euler factor of the q = 0 mode
  print(max(Mod(eigen(diag(2) + dt * J)$values)))
# [1] 0.9949874
# [1] 1
# [1] 1.03923

The reaction Jacobian has eigenvalues -0.1 \pm 0.995i: a weakly damped oscillator. Euler is stable on it only for \Delta t < 0.2 (Initial value problems and Euler’s method).
Long waves get almost no damping from implicit diffusion, so they grow by 4 % per step: the “pattern” is the time step.
Check: the pattern must not change when \Delta t is halved, and |1 + \Delta t\lambda| \le 1 for the reaction eigenvalues. (For d = 20: 48, 48, 47, 47 spots at \Delta t = 0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05.)


|1 + dt lambda|^2 = (1 - 0.1 dt)^2 + 0.99 dt^2 = 1 - 0.2 dt + dt^2, below 1 only for dt < 0.2. The table shows the real pattern (d = 20) is robust: from dt = 0.4 to 0.05 the spot count changes by at most one, because the Turing modes grow much faster than the spurious oscillation. So the same too-large step is harmless in one parameter regime and creates a pattern in another. That is why the check is “refine and compare”, applied to every result you report, not just once. The general rule: a pattern whose wavelength or existence depends on dx or dt is a property of the method, not of the model.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
section: Before you trust a reaction–diffusion simulation
text:
Before you trust a reaction–diffusion simulation

Resolution: at least ~10 grid points per decay length or per pattern wavelength. Refine \Delta x; the answer (threshold position, spot spacing, spot count) must not move.
Time step: halve \Delta t; nothing should change. Explicit reaction: |1 + \Delta t\lambda| \le 1 for the reaction eigenvalues; explicit diffusion: D\Delta t/\Delta x^2 \le 1/2 (1D), \le 1/4 (2D).
Exact solutions and invariants: steady state vs \lambda = \sqrt{D/k} formula; mass balance k\int c = j; uniform state unchanged without noise.
Linear theory: the band of growing wavelengths from the 2 × 2 eigenvalues should match the early pattern. A pattern where theory says none: suspect the method.
Boundaries: second-order (ghost points); periodic vs walls changes the pattern near edges.
Splitting: Lie is first order even with exact sub-steps; prefer Strang, or check with a smaller \Delta t.


These are the checks of the unit, collected. Most need no exact solution: mass balance, refinement in dx and dt, and comparison with linear theory. The linear theory check is the reaction-diffusion version of “check against a simpler model”: the dispersion relation is cheap (2 x 2 eigenvalues) and tells you which wavelengths can grow at all. A grid-scale checkerboard (wavelength 2 dx) is the signature of an unstable explicit diffusion step, as in The diffusion (heat) equation by finite differences; the right panel of the artefact slide shows that a too-large reaction step can produce smooth, convincing-looking structures instead.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
Summary

Reaction–diffusion: \partial c/\partial t = D\,\nabla^2 c + f(c). Synthesis–diffusion–degradation gives an exponential gradient with decay length \lambda = \sqrt{D/k}: 100 µm for our Bicoid-like numbers.
On the grid: ghost-point boundaries (order 2), one Thomas solve. Checks: exact cosh solution, mass balance k\int c = j, refinement. A one-sided boundary is order 1 and breaks mass balance.
IMEX Euler: diffusion implicit (no step limit), reaction explicit (any f, no Newton). Limited by Euler on the reaction: \Delta t \le 2/k; the steady state is exact for any \Delta t.
Splitting: Lie (order 1), Strang (order 2); an error even with exact sub-steps, unless the parts commute (they do not with a source or k(x)).
Turing: per wavenumber, eigenvalues of J - q^2\,\mathrm{diag}(D_u, D_v). Here a band of growing wavelengths for d > 8.57.
Artefacts: a too-coarse grid changes the spot count (63 vs 47); a too-large \Delta t makes a “pattern” where there is none. Refine both.


The technical summary of the unit. Every item has a check attached; the artefact slide is the one to remember. The next slide closes the course as a whole.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs

title: Reaction–diffusion and pattern formation
text:
What you can now do

Numbers (Part 1): predict rounding, overflow and cancellation; read the order of a method off a log–log error plot.
Equations (Parts 2–4): solve nonlinear equations and linear systems, use structure (banded, sparse), know when a fit or a solve is ill-conditioned.
Eigenvalues and approximation (Parts 5–7): compute eigenvalues and the SVD, interpolate, differentiate and integrate numerically, use the FFT.
Dynamics (Part 8): integrate ODEs with step-size control, recognise stiffness, classify steady states.
Fitting (Part 9): optimise, fit models to data, and ask whether the parameters are identifiable.
Space (Part 10): turn a PDE into a grid, choose explicit or implicit time stepping, and check the result.
Above all: every method can fail, and you know the check that catches it: an exact case, a refinement, an invariant, a second method.


A one-slide wrap-up of the whole course. The common thread is the last bullet: each unit paired a method with a biological problem, showed it working, showed it failing, and gave the check. That habit transfers to any numerical tool, including ones this course did not cover. Part 11 (Further reading) has two optional decks for those who want to go further: Beyond rectangles: finite elements and flow, and Iterative linear solvers in depth.

title: Implicit schemes and the method of lines
section: Try it: one time step, three schemes
text:
Try it: one time step, three schemes




The chamber (N = 50, dx = 10 µm), computed live with FTCS (orange), backward Euler (blue) and Crank–Nicolson (red), all with the same r = D dt / dx^2. Left: the profiles at time t; right: the error at the reference time against dt for all three, with slope-1 and slope-2 guides and the shaded region where FTCS is unstable. Start on the sharp start at r = 0.4: all three agree with the exact curve, FTCS error 8e-5 with 1500 steps. Click 0.6: FTCS overflows, the other two do not notice. Click 40 and press play: FTCS is gone in a few steps, backward Euler is smooth but lags (error 0.011 at 60 s, 15 steps), Crank–Nicolson overshoots the source at the first grid point (1.1775) and flips back and forth. Click 4 and 10: Crank–Nicolson with 60 to 150 steps beats FTCS with 1200; read the cost line. Then switch to the smooth sine: backward Euler on slope 1, Crank–Nicolson on slope 2 until it hits the space-error floor at 1.2e-4, the same picture as the previous slide, now with a marker you can move. The Embryo tab (later slides) runs the embryo model; the flow-stopped case with dt = 50 ms reproduces the Crank–Nicolson figure.
crumbs: Part 10: Diffusion and heat: finite-difference PDEs
Implicit schemes and the method of lines

title: Exercise: implicit schemes and the method of lines
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the three schemes in your browser. The Race tab solves the chamber (\(L = 500\) µm, \(D = 1000\) µm²/s, \(N = 50\), \(\Delta x = 10\) µm) with FTCS, backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson, all with the same time step, set by \(r = D\,\Delta t/\Delta x^2\) from 0.1 to 100 (\(\Delta t\) from 0.01 to 10 s). Two starts: the sharp start (source \(c = 1\), sink \(c = 0\), empty channel; exact solution: the Fourier series, error measured at \(t = 60\) s) and the smooth sine (both ends 0, \(c = \sin(\pi x/L)\); exact solution \(e^{-D(\pi/L)^2t}\sin(\pi x/L)\), error at \(t = 30\) s). Panel (a) shows the profiles after \(n\) steps; panel (b) the largest error at the reference time against \(\Delta t\) for all three schemes, with slope-1 and slope-2 guide lines (dashed) and a marker at the current \(\Delta t\). The readout gives the growth factor of the zigzag mode for each scheme (fact 5), the errors and the cost: the number of steps (one Thomas solve each for the implicit schemes) and rough operation counts, at 5, 8 and 13 operations per grid point and step for FTCS, backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson. The Embryo tab runs the model of B5 and C5 (\(N = 200\)) with backward Euler or Crank–Nicolson.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R, Python and Rust, so the numbers agree with the code on this page to the digits shown.



E1. (stable or not) On the sharp start, click \(r = 0.4\), \(0.5\) and \(0.6\) and read the FTCS error at \(t = 60\) s and its zigzag factor. Then click \(r = 40\) (\(\Delta t = 4\) s). What happens to each of the three schemes? Press play to watch it happen from \(t = 0\).






Answer E1





FTCS: error \(8.5\times10^{-5}\) at \(r = 0.4\) (zigzag factor \(-0.6\)), \(1.7\times10^{-4}\) at \(r = 0.5\) (factor \(-1\)), and at \(r = 0.6\) the error is \(\infty\): the factor \(-1.4\) applied 1000 times overflows, although \(r\) is only 20 % above the limit. At \(r = 40\) the factor is \(-159\); after 15 steps the FTCS values are of order \(10^{31}\) and the plot shows only vertical lines. Backward Euler (factor 0.006) gives a smooth profile, slightly behind the exact one, with error 0.011, as on the lecture slide (c = 0.7583 at 100 µm). Crank–Nicolson (factor \(-0.975\)) has the right shape in the middle, but near the source it zigzags: \(c(10\text{ µm}) = 1.1775\), above the source value 1, error 0.20. Both implicit schemes are stable at \(r = 40\); neither is as accurate as FTCS at \(r = 0.4\).



E2. (orders) Switch to the smooth sine. Click \(r = 1\), \(10\) and \(100\) (\(\Delta t = 0.1\), 1 and 10 s) and write down the backward Euler and Crank–Nicolson errors at \(t = 30\) s. By what factor does each error change per factor 10 in \(\Delta t\)? Where in panel (b) does the Crank–Nicolson curve stop following slope 2, and at what level?






Answer E2





Backward Euler: \(8.3\times10^{-4}\), \(7.2\times10^{-3}\), \(0.063\): a factor 8.7 per decade, close to 10, so order 1 (parallel to the slope-1 line). Crank–Nicolson: \(1.2\times10^{-4}\), \(7.2\times10^{-5}\), \(4.7\times10^{-3}\). Between \(\Delta t = 5\) and 10 s it follows slope 2 (\(1.1\times10^{-3}\) to \(4.7\times10^{-3}\), factor 4.4 per halving). Below about 1 s it is flat at \(1.2\times10^{-4}\): the space error of the 10 µm grid, which no time step can remove (the floor of fig04 and C2(c)). The dip to \(7\times10^{-5}\) near \(\Delta t = 1\)–2 s is the lucky cancellation of time and space errors. FTCS leaves the chart to the right of the dashed line (at \(r = 1\) its error is \(10^{126}\)); it comes back only for the last few points, \(\Delta t \ge 5\) s, where 3–6 steps are too few for the rounding errors that seed the zigzag to grow.



E3. (sharp data) Back to the sharp start. Compare the two implicit curves in panel (b): for which \(\Delta t\) is Crank–Nicolson better, and for which is backward Euler better? Then click \(r = 4\) and \(r = 10\) and read \(c(10\text{ µm})\) and the errors. Why does the same scheme that wins on the sine lose here at large \(\Delta t\)?






Answer E3





Crank–Nicolson wins clearly up to \(\Delta t = 1\) s (error \(2.7\times10^{-5}\) to \(8.9\times10^{-5}\), against \(1.4\times10^{-4}\) to \(2.8\times10^{-3}\) for backward Euler); the curves cross near \(\Delta t = 1.5\) s, and above that backward Euler is better (\(r = 40\): 0.011 against 0.20; \(r = 100\): 0.027 against 0.56). At \(r = 4\): \(c(10\text{ µm}) = 0.9762\) for both, error \(2.4\times10^{-5}\) (CN) against \(1.1\times10^{-3}\) (BE), the lecture’s fix “CN with \(\Delta t = 0.4\) s”. The sharp start contains strong high modes; Crank–Nicolson multiplies them by nearly \(-1\) when \(r \gg 1\) (\(-0.975\) at \(r = 40\), \(-0.78\) at \(r = 4\)), so they survive and flip. The sine has no high modes, so there is nothing to flip.



E4. (what a step costs) Still on the sharp start at \(t = 60\) s, read the cost line for \(r = 0.4\), \(r = 10\) and \(r = 40\). Which run reaches an error below \(10^{-4}\) with the fewest operations? How does it compare with FTCS at its limit?






Answer E4





FTCS at \(r = 0.5\) needs 1200 steps, about 294 000 operations, for an error of \(1.7\times10^{-4}\) (at \(r = 0.4\): 1500 steps, error \(8.5\times10^{-5}\)). Crank–Nicolson at \(r = 10\) (\(\Delta t = 1\) s): 60 Thomas solves, about 38 000 operations, error \(8.9\times10^{-5}\): about 8 times cheaper than FTCS for a slightly smaller error. At \(r = 40\) Crank–Nicolson costs only 15 solves (about 9 600 operations), but its error is 0.20; backward Euler with 15 steps (about 5 900 operations) gives 0.011. A larger step is only cheaper if the answer is still good enough; for this chamber \(\Delta t \approx 1\) s with Crank–Nicolson is the sweet spot.



E5. (the embryo) Open the Embryo tab (streams on, Crank–Nicolson, \(\Delta t = 1\) ms, \(R = 100\) µm) and press play. When are the two points of panel (d) within a few tenths of a degree of their final values? Read the 10–90 % width. Then set \(R = 50\) and \(R = 150\) µm. Finally choose flow stopped with \(\Delta t = 50\) ms and step through \(t = 50\), 100 and 150 ms, first with Crank–Nicolson, then with backward Euler.






Answer E5





\(\tau = 12.3\) ms. The posterior point (375 µm) is at 24.3 °C after \(\tau\), 26.7 °C after \(4\tau = 49\) ms and 26.8 °C at 100 ms; the anterior point (125 µm) warms by 0.17 °C, by conduction from the warm half. So the profile is steady after about 50–60 ms. Width at \(t = 100\) ms: 133.9 µm against \(2\lambda\ln 5 = 133.8\) µm, with \(\lambda = 41.6\) µm. \(R = 50\) µm: \(\tau = 3.1\) ms, \(\lambda = 20.8\) µm, width 67.0 µm (formula 66.9). \(R = 150\) µm: \(\tau = 27.8\) ms, \(\lambda = 62.4\) µm, width 210 µm against 201 µm: the tips are now only \(4\lambda\) from the middle and the formula, which ignores them, is no longer good to 1 %. Flow stopped, Crank–Nicolson, \(\Delta t = 50\) ms (\(r = 1120\)): after one step the step points the wrong way (26.4 °C at 245 µm, 20.6 °C at 255 µm), after the next the right way again (20.6 and 26.4 °C), then wrong again (26.2 and 20.8 °C), and the readout counts the points that change direction; the error against the exact series stays near 3 °C. Backward Euler with the same step is smooth, error 0.4 °C at 50 ms and 0.2 °C at 100 ms: this is fig03 of the lecture.

title: Exercise: steady state in two dimensions
text:
Explore
The demo below solves the lecture’s oxygen chamber in your browser: \(4000 \times 2000\) µm, \(D = 2000\) µm²/s, \(c_0 = 200\) µM on the open edges, \(R_0 = 0.5\) µM/s per \(10^5\) cells/cm², \(K_m = 1\) µM. Panel (a) is the top view: the colour is the oxygen level (grey where it is negative), the vermillion line the hypoxic contour, the white circle the lowest value, the pink dotted line the outline of the cells when they do not cover the whole floor. Edges drawn in blue are open to medium (\(c = c_0\)), grey ones are sealed (no flux, by a ghost point as in the trench). Drag on the map to move the dashed cross-section, which panel (b) shows, or switch the mouse to paint or erase cells. grid check replaces panel (b) by a table for \(h = 200\) down to \(12.5\) µm.
The demo does not use the lecture’s sparse direct solve and Newton but an iterative method, nonlinear SOR (successive over-relaxation): sweep through the grid in the order \(k\), solve each point’s five-point equation for its own value (for Michaelis–Menten a quadratic, whose non-negative root is taken), and over-relax. It solves the same equations, so the numbers agree with the lecture’s to the digits shown. Every change restarts it from the current field (a warm start); the readout counts the sweeps.



E1. (constant uptake fails) The demo starts with constant uptake at \(10^5\) cells/cm². Read the lowest oxygen level. Move the cell slider to \(2\times10^5\): what happens, and on what fraction of the chamber? Find the density at which the centre first reaches 0. Then, still at \(2\times10^5\), switch to linear kc and to Michaelis–Menten, and compare the lowest value and the hypoxic area of the three models.






Answer E1





At \(10^5\) cells/cm²: min \(c = 86.15\) µM in the centre, as on the lecture slide. At \(2\times10^5\): \(-27.71\) µM, and the field is negative (grey) on 13.7 % of the chamber: impossible, since constant uptake keeps consuming oxygen that is not there. The centre crosses 0 between \(1.75\) (\(+0.76\) µM) and \(1.80\times10^5\) cells/cm² (\(-4.94\) µM). Linear uptake (\(k = R_0/c_0\)) never goes negative, but gives min \(81.96\) µM and no hypoxia at all: it is right at the edge and far too weak inside (18× too low at 10 µM). Michaelis–Menten gives min \(0.564\) µM and 10.0 % of the chamber below 10 µM, as in C6. Only the last one is both possible and realistic.



E2. (a hypoxic threshold) With Michaelis–Menten uptake, move the density through \(1.5\), \(1.7\), \(1.75\), \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\times10^5\) cells/cm² and record the lowest value and the hypoxic area. Where does the core appear, and how fast does it grow? At \(2\times10^5\), move the threshold slider to 5 and 20 µM. How much does the answer depend on that convention?






Answer E2

The core appears at about \(1.75\times10^5\) cells/cm², where constant uptake would just empty the centre (E1). Above that the centre is nearly anoxic (\(c \ll K_m\), so those cells consume almost nothing) and the core grows quickly, then more slowly. At \(2\times10^5\) the threshold matters: 5.7 % below 5 µM, 10.0 % below 10 µM, 16.3 % below 20 µM. “About 10 %” is only meaningful together with the threshold that defines it.



E3. (which edges supply the oxygen?) At \(10^5\) cells/cm² with Michaelis–Menten uptake (fully open: min \(87.19\) µM), untick left and right, so that only the long edges are open. Then open them again and untick top and bottom instead. Finally seal only top. Where is the lowest value in each case, and why do the results differ so much? Use the 1D estimate \(c_0 - R_0L^2/(8D)\) for a gap of width \(L\) between two open edges.






Answer E3





Only top and bottom open: min \(76.34\) µM, near the centre, no hypoxia. The 1D estimate across the 2 mm gap gives \(200 - 0.5\cdot2000^2/16000 = 75\) µM: the short edges were adding only about 11 µM. Only left and right open: the oxygen has to travel up to 2 mm, the 1D estimate across 4 mm is \(200 - 500 < 0\), and indeed 49.4 % of the chamber is hypoxic (min \(0.000\)). Top sealed: the sealed wall acts as a mirror, the chamber behaves like half of one twice as wide, and the lowest value moves onto the sealed wall (\(y = 2000\), min \(0.001\), 17.3 % hypoxic). The supply depends on the distance to the nearest open edge, so the short dimension of the chamber decides.



E4. (cells only in a spheroid) Click spheroid (a disc of cells of radius 700 µm) and use Michaelis–Menten uptake with the slider at 3, then 4 \(\times10^5\) cells/cm². Read the two hypoxic fractions in the readout. Which one would you report for a biological experiment? Use paint to add cells around the disc, and watch the hypoxic core.






Answer E4





At \(3\times10^5\): min \(7.61\) µM, hypoxic 0.7 % of the chamber but 3.4 % of the cells. At \(4\times10^5\): 5.7 % of the chamber but 28.9 % of the cells. For a biological statement you want the fraction of cells that are hypoxic: the empty floor around the disc only passes oxygen on and dilutes the chamber-wide number. A disc of cells is much better supplied than the confluent layer at the same density (at \(2\times10^5\) its centre stays at 68 µM), because the oxygen does not have to pass other consuming cells on its way in. Painting cells around the disc lowers the oxygen arriving at its edge, and the hypoxic core grows although the disc itself is unchanged.



E5. (is the grid fine enough?) Click reset, choose Michaelis–Menten and \(2\times10^5\) cells/cm², and open grid check. Compare the column of min \(c\) and of the hypoxic area with the lecture’s table. How do the differences between successive rows shrink? How do the numbers of sweeps grow, and what does that mean for the work per halving of \(h\)? Then click \(h = 200\) and \(h = 12.5\) and compare the cross-sections.






Answer E5





min \(c\): 0.811, 0.609, 0.564, 0.553, 0.551 µM; hypoxic area: 13.5, 10.4, 10.0, 9.7, 9.5 %, the lecture’s numbers. The differences in min \(c\) fall by about 4 per halving (0.045, 0.011, 0.0027 from \(h = 100\) on): second order. The area changes irregularly and slowly, since it counts grid points below a threshold. The sweeps roughly double per halving (60, 102, 192, 363, 696), and each sweep visits 4 times as many points, so SOR costs about 8 times more per halving: \(h = 12.5\) µm takes on the order of a second. That growth is why large grids need better iterative methods (preconditioned CG, multigrid) or a sparse direct solve. After clicking \(h = 200\) and then \(12.5\), panel (b) shows the fine solution with the \(h = 200\) grid as a dashed grey curve: only 21 points along \(x\), yet nowhere more than 0.6 µM away from the fine curve: the curves lie on top of each other at this scale.

title: Numerical integration
section: Try it: where the points land
text:
Try it: where the points land




Computed live in the browser: a 21-point Gauss-Kronrod routine that follows QUADPACK with R’s default tolerances, so it gives R’s numbers digit for digit. Start at dnorm on [0, 20000]: the ticks under the axis are the 21 points, the zoom on the right shows the first one at 43.4, the readout says 0 with error estimate 0, flagged as a silent failure. Click 2000: the first pass sees the peak, the routine bisects towards 0, 0.5. Click 4400 and 5000: one bisection, still missed, 2.3e-6 with error 4.6e-6, as integrate(dnorm, 0, 5000). Back to 20000 and tick “split at x = 10”: 0.5 with 42 evaluations. Then switch to adaptive Simpson: it returns 0.5 for every L, because its first point is the endpoint 0. Switch the integrand to the chromatogram peak at 340 s: adaptive Simpson now stops after 5 evaluations with 0, and 60 initial pieces fix it. Use start over and step on the PK model to show the bisection piece by piece. If time allows, tab (a): the PK curve with trapezoid and Simpson, n = 4 to 32, the log-log plot with slopes 2 and 4, then the infusion with its kink (Simpson drops to order 3, and n = 12 puts a point on the kink).

title: Exercise: flow plus diffusion
text:
Explore
The demo below runs the lecture’s three problems in your browser, with the lecture’s numbers. Steady layer: the back-diffusion test problem (\(L = 500\) µm, \(u = 100\) µm/s, \(D = 1000\) µm²/s), solved with central (a) and upwind (b) differences on the grid set by the slider, against the exact solution (black) and, for upwind, the exact solution with \(D + u\Delta x/2\) (grey dashed). Moving pulse: the 1 s stimulus pulse (\(u = 200\) µm/s, \(D = 100\) µm²/s, cells at 2000 µm), explicit Euler in time with upwind and (tick central) central differences; (a) shows the profile at the snapshot time, (b) what the cells see; the readout checks \(C + 2r \le 1\) and gives the numerical diffusion and the peaks. T-sensor / H-filter: the channel seen from above (\(w = 100\) µm, Poiseuille flow, sample in the lower half), computed by implicit marching as in C3 and C4 (\(M = 50\) cells across, 800 steps of \(L/800\)); the orange lines are the 10 % and 90 % levels of the interdiffusion zone, the purple line marks where every \(|c - \tfrac12| \le 0.01\), and panel (b) shows the outlet profile and the share of each species’ flux that leaves through the buffer half.
The browser computes in the same IEEE doubles as R, Python and Rust. The tridiagonal solves and the explicit updates are the ones on this page, so the scheme values agree with your C1 and C2 code to the digits shown. The exact pulse uses a 7-digit approximation of erfc, so its last digits can differ a little.



E1. (where the wiggles start) In the Steady layer tab, click the lecture grids \(P = 1\), \(P = 2\) and \(P = 5\), and use the slider for \(P = 2.5\). For each, note \(\rho\) of the central scheme, its minimum value and its maximum error, and compare \(\rho\) with the exact growth factor per cell \(e^P\). Tick whole channel at \(P = 5\): how far upstream do the wiggles reach?






Answer E1





\(P = 1\) (\(\Delta x = 10\) µm): \(\rho = 3\) (\(e^P = 2.72\)), min \(c = 0\), error 0.035, no wiggles. \(P = 2\) (\(\Delta x = 20\) µm): \(\rho = \infty\), min \(c = 0\), error 0.14: every value copies its upstream neighbour, so the solution is 0 up to the last interior point and then jumps to 1 (a kink, but no negative values). \(P = 2.5\) (\(\Delta x = 25\) µm): \(\rho = -9\), min \(c = -0.111\), error 0.19, wiggles. \(P = 5\) (\(\Delta x = 50\) µm): \(\rho = -2.33\) (\(e^P = 148\)), min \(c = -0.429\), error 0.44. The threshold is exactly \(P = 2\), where \(1 - P/2\) changes sign and \(\rho\) jumps from \(+\infty\) to negative values. The whole-channel view at \(P = 5\) shows the sign alternating all the way to the inlet (\(-0.429\), \(0.184\), \(-0.079\), \(0.034\), …), shrinking by a factor \(|\rho| = 2.33\) per cell upstream: the oscillation is a property of the discrete equations everywhere, not only at the layer.



E2. (smooth but smeared) Stay in Steady layer. At \(P = 5\), compare the upwind solution (b) with the black and grey curves and read off \(D_\text{num}\). Then move the slider to the left until \(D_\text{num}\) is below 10 % of \(D\). What are \(P\), \(\Delta x\) and the two maximum errors there? Compare the upwind errors at \(P = 0.25\) and \(P = 0.125\), and the central errors at the same two grids: which orders do you see?






Answer E2





At \(P = 5\) the blue points lie on the grey curve (exact with \(D + u\Delta x/2 = 3500\) µm²/s), not on the black one: \(D_\text{num} = 2500\) µm²/s \(= 2.5\,D\), error 0.16, and no wiggles (\(\rho = 6 > 0\)). \(D_\text{num} = u\Delta x/2 = (P/2)\,D\), so it is below \(0.1\,D\) only for \(P < 0.2\): the slider gives \(P = 0.125\), \(\Delta x = 1.25\) µm (400 cells), \(D_\text{num} = 62.5\) µm²/s \(= 0.063\,D\). There the upwind error is still 0.022, the central error \(4.8\times10^{-4}\). From \(P = 0.25\) to \(0.125\) (halving \(\Delta x\)) the upwind error goes from 0.042 to 0.022 (halves: first order), the central error from 0.0019 to \(4.8\times10^{-4}\) (quarters: second order). Upwind never wiggles, but it needs a much finer grid for the same accuracy.



E3. (numerical diffusion and the CFL limit in time) Open Moving pulse and click lecture: Δx 10, C 0.5. Read the peak the cells see, and compare the blue curve with the black and grey ones. Click Δx 1 and move \(\Delta x\) to 5. Then click C 0.9 and C 0.95 (both at \(\Delta x = 10\) µm, snapshot \(t = 6\) s) and read \(C + 2r\) and the range of \(c\).






Answer E3





Lecture setting: \(\Delta t = 0.025\) s, \(r = 0.025\), \(C + 2r = 0.55\); the cells see a peak of 0.6405 at 10.48 s against the exact 0.975 at 10.50 s. The blue curve lies on the grey one: exact with \(D + D_\text{num} = 100 + 500 = 600\) µm²/s. \(\Delta x = 5\): peak 0.769 (\(D_\text{num} = 250\)); \(\Delta x = 1\): 0.932 (\(D_\text{num} = 50\)). The peak time is right in every case; only the height and width are wrong. C 0.9: \(C + 2r = 0.990\), stable, range 0 … 0.971 at 6 s, peak 0.886 at the cells: a larger time step reduces \(D_\text{num}\) to \(u\Delta x(1 - C)/2 = 100\). C 0.95: \(C + 2r = 1.045 > 1\), and by \(t = 6\) s a zigzag has grown to \(-1750\) … \(1743\) (the lecture’s 1700); at the cells the readout reports a maximum of \(1.3\times10^7\). The limit is \(C + 2r \le 1\), not \(C \le 1\) alone.



E4. (central differences with explicit time steps) Tick central and click lecture: Δx 10, C 0.5 again. What happens, and what does the readout say about the condition \(C \le 2/P\)? (Not derived on this page: for central differences in space with explicit Euler in time, the von Neumann analysis gives stability, for \(r \le 1/2\), only when \(C^2 \le 2r\), i.e. \(u^2\Delta t \le 2D\); with \(r = C/P\) this is \(C \le 2/P\). The answer below explains it as a negative effective diffusion.) Now lower \(C\) to 0.1. Then try \(\Delta x = 2\) with \(C = 0.5\), and finally Δx 1. Note the range of \(c\) at \(t = 10.5\) s and the peak at the cells for the central scheme each time. Why can the central peak be higher than the exact one? Also try \(C = 0.9\) at \(\Delta x = 1\): which scheme fails now?






Answer E4





At \(\Delta x = 10\) µm (\(P = 20\)), \(C = 0.5\) violates \(C \le 2/P = 0.1\): the central solution grows to \(|c| \approx 10^6\) by 6 s and exceeds \(10^{12}\) at 11 s, while upwind with the same \(\Delta t\) is stable. At \(C = 0.1\) (condition met) it no longer explodes but wiggles: range \(-0.339\) … \(1.23\) at 10.5 s, peak 1.236 at the cells, against the exact 0.975. \(\Delta x = 2\), \(C = 0.5\) (\(P = 4\), exactly at \(C = 2/P\)): range \(-0.244\) … \(1.25\), peak 1.245, wiggles again because \(P > 2\). \(\Delta x = 1\), \(C = 0.5\) (\(P = 2\)): range 0 … 0.998, no wiggles, peak 0.998 at 10.51 s, higher than the exact 0.975 (upwind gives 0.932). Explicit Euler adds a negative numerical diffusion \(-u^2\Delta t/2 = -C u\Delta x/2 = -50\) µm²/s, so the central scheme behaves like \(D = 50\): too sharp a peak. The condition \(C \le 2/P\) is the same as \(D - C u\Delta x/2 \ge 0\): the scheme blows up when its effective diffusion coefficient is negative. At \(\Delta x = 1\), \(C = 0.9\) the roles swap: \(r = 0.45\), \(C + 2r = 1.8\), and upwind blows up within 0.2 s, while central stays bounded (peak 1.000, effective \(D = 10\)). On a fine grid the diffusion part \(2r = 2C/P\) of the condition dominates.



E5. (the H-filter) Open T-sensor / H-filter and set \(L = 2\) mm (\(\bar u = 1000\) µm/s). Click the three species and read the fractions in the buffer outlet, the width of the 10–90 % zone at the outlet and where the stream is mixed to 1 %. Compare the small molecule’s mixing point with \(\bar u w^2/D\) and with the plug-flow estimate \(0.42\,\bar u w^2/D\) (Fact 1). Then set \(\bar u = 500\) µm/s and \(L = 1\) mm: what changes and why?






Answer E5





At 2 mm the buffer outlet receives 47.4 % of the small molecule, 19.3 % of the protein and 0.1 % of the cells (the lecture’s 47 %, 19 %, 0.1 %). The 10–90 % zone fills the whole channel for the small molecule, is 45 µm wide for the protein and 1.7 µm for the cells (less than one 2 µm grid cell). The small molecule is mixed to 1 % at about 3.1 mm (3.13 mm with \(L = 2\)), against \(\bar u w^2/D = 10\) mm and \(0.42\,\bar u w^2/D = 4.2\) mm for plug flow: with the Poiseuille profile the slow fluid near the walls mixes early, and here that wins. The protein needs 31 mm, ten times longer (\(D\) is ten times smaller); the cells 62 m. With \(\bar u = 500\) µm/s and \(L = 1\) mm every number is the same (47.4 %, 19.3 %, 0.1 %; \(Dx/\bar u = 2000\) µm² for the small molecule in both cases) and the mixing point halves to 1.56 mm: only \(Dx/\bar u\) matters (B6). A slower flow is a longer channel, at half the throughput.

Try it: wiggles, smearing and the CFL limit




The lecture’s two 1D problems, computed live in the browser. title: Exercise: Fourier series and the FFT
text:
Explore
The demo below samples a clock gene, \(x(t) = 8 + 1.5\cos(2\pi(t-6)/P) + B\cos(2\pi t/P_u)\) plus normal noise, every \(\Delta t\) hours, and computes the DFT of the samples in your browser. The top panel shows the true signal (grey), the samples (blue) and the Fourier curve through the samples (the trigonometric interpolant of fact 4, orange dashed; with the low-pass filter on, the smoothed curve in green). The bottom panel shows the amplitude \(2|X_k|/n\) of each bin against frequency in cycles per day, with the true frequencies (dotted), the Nyquist frequency \(1/(2\Delta t)\) (black line) and, for a rhythm faster than Nyquist, an arrow to where it lands. With the Hann window the amplitude is \(2|X_k|/\sum_j w_j\) of the mean-removed samples (C5). The readout gives the mean, the strongest bin, the amplitude and peak time of the 24-h bin, and warnings. The noise is fixed: at the 2-h times of the first 48 h it is exactly the noise of the dataset in the Background, so course data reproduces those 24 numbers.



E1. (the course data) Click course data. Read off the mean, the amplitude and the peak time of the 24-h bin, and compare with the lecture. What is the Nyquist period, and which periods lie on the frequency grid? Now set sample every to 4 h (every other sample of the same experiment) and to 1 h, and set duration to 96 h with 2-h sampling. What changes on the frequency axis in each case, and what happens to the estimates?






Answer E1





Mean \(8.045\), amplitude \(1.465\), peak at \(6.45\) h, exactly the fft() results of the lecture (true values 1.5 and 6 h). Nyquist period \(2\Delta t = 4\) h (6 cycles per day); the bins are at periods \(48/k\): 48, 24, 16, 12, …, 4 h, spaced \(1/48\) per hour (0.5 per day). With 4-h sampling the bins keep the same spacing but stop at 8 h (Nyquist 3 per day): amplitude \(1.400\), peak \(6.35\) h. With 1-h sampling (new noise between the old times) the axis runs to 12 per day: \(1.433\), \(6.20\) h. With 96 h at 2 h the Nyquist frequency stays at 6 per day but the bins are twice as dense (\(96/k\), the 24-h bin is \(k = 4\)): \(1.529\), \(6.28\) h. \(\Delta t\) sets the highest frequency, the record length sets the spacing; all three designs estimate the 24-h rhythm about equally well, because it is slow and on the grid.



E2. (aliasing) Click + 4.8 h, every 2 h (C4, without noise), then every 4 h. For each, where is the second peak, and what are the amplitude and peak time of the 24-h bin? Follow the purple arrow and explain the 4-h result with the folding rule \(f \mapsto |f - m f_s|\). Then drag sample every to 3 h and to 2.5 h. Where does the 4.8-h rhythm appear now? What is the largest sampling interval on the slider that shows it at its true period?






Answer E2





Every 2 h: a peak of height 1 at 5 per day (\(48/10 = 4.8\) h), below Nyquist (6 per day); the 24-h bin is untouched, \(1.500\) at \(6.00\) h. Every 4 h: Nyquist is 3 per day, the 4.8-h rhythm (5 per day) folds to \(|5 - 6| = 1\) per day, exactly the 24-h bin. The readout says amplitude \(1.803\), peak \(3.75\) h: the alias \(\cos(2\pi t/24)\) adds to the true \(1.5\cos(2\pi(t-6)/24)\), giving \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1.5^2} = 1.80\). The orange curve through the samples is a smooth 24-h wave; nothing in the samples betrays the fast rhythm. Every 3 h (\(f_s = 8\) per day): it appears at \(|5 - 8| = 3\) per day, a false 8-h period. Every 2.5 h: at 5.2 h, close to but not at the truth. Only \(\Delta t \le 2\) h shows 4.8 h (Nyquist needs \(\Delta t < 2.4\) h).



E3. (leakage and the window) Click course data and set duration to 60 h (\(T/P = 2.5\) cycles). Which bin is strongest now, and what happened to the 24-h estimate? Tick Hann window. Then click leakage (a 25.5-h free-running rhythm over 120 h, every 30 min, log scale), compare the spectrum with and without the window around 2 per day (12 h) and at 6–12 per day, and look at the end of the orange curve in the top panel.






Answer E3





At 60 h the bins are at \(60/k\): 60, 30, 20, 15 h, so 24 h is not on the grid. The strongest bin is 30 h (\(1.041\)), the 20-h bin has \(0.837\), and the energy spreads into all other bins: the amplitude 1.5 is nowhere. With the Hann window the peak becomes \(1.252\) (30 h) and \(1.185\) (20 h): closer to 1.5 and much less spread, but still not 24 h; only a 24-h or 48-h record puts the rhythm on a bin. In the leakage preset the strongest bin is 24 h (\(1.288\), not 1.5) and every bin is raised: about \(0.07\) at 12 h and still about \(0.01\) at 10–12 per day. With the window the peak bin reads \(1.418\), the 12-h bin falls to about \(0.003\) and beyond about 6 per day the bins fall below \(10^{-4}\) (off the bottom of the plot). The orange curve jumps back at \(t = 120\) h: the DFT treats the record as one period, and 4.71 cycles do not join up.



E4. (low-pass filtering) Click low-pass (96 h every 30 min, noise sd 1, keep periods \(\ge 8\) h). Read the rms error of the samples and of the smoothed curve. Drag keep periods ≥ to 2, 4, 12, 24 and 48 h and record the rms error each time. Which cut-off is best here, and why would you not choose it for a real gene? What goes wrong at 48 h?






Answer E4





Samples \(0.97\) (the noise), smoothed \(0.41\) with 25 of 192 coefficients. Cut-off 2 h: \(0.75\); 4 h: \(0.55\); 12 h: \(0.37\); 24 h: \(0.24\); 48 h: \(1.07\). The smaller the band you keep, the less noise passes, until the band no longer contains the signal. 24 h is best here only because the truth is a pure 24-h cosine with a whole number of cycles; a real gene has harmonics (12 h, 8 h) and an ultradian component that such a filter would remove (try fast amplitude 1 with cut-off 8 h). At 48 h the cut-off is above the clock frequency: the rhythm itself is filtered out, and the smoothed curve is almost flat, worse than the raw data. The same bias–noise trade-off as in C6.

title: How eigen() works, and big problems
text:
Recap: power iteration and friends


From Power iteration and friends:

Power iteration \mathbf x \leftarrow A\mathbf x/\|A\mathbf x\| finds the eigenvalue of largest |\lambda|; the error shrinks by |\lambda_2/\lambda_1| per step. Fish Leslie matrix: \lambda_1 = 1.177, rate 0.654, 55 steps.
It fails when |\lambda_2| = |\lambda_1| (semelparous fish: the estimate cycles) and crawls when the ratio is near 1 (slow-switching cells: 5406 steps).
Inverse iteration with shift \sigma finds the eigenvalue nearest \sigma; Rayleigh quotient iteration (\sigma = current Rayleigh quotient) converges cubically for symmetric A.
One eigenpair per run.


Our test matrix for this lecture:
A <- matrix(c(4, 1, 0,
              1, 3, 1,
              0, 1, 2), 3)   # symmetric
power_rq(A, c(1, 1, 1))$lambda
# [1] 4.732051              # 51 steps
eigen(A)$values
# [1] 4.732051 3.000000 1.267949
Rate 3/4.73 = 0.63 per step. eigen() returns all three, to the last digit, in microseconds. How?


Recap only; do not re-teach. The numbers are the ones students saw in Power iteration and friends: the fish Leslie matrix (lambda_1 = 1.177, |lambda_2/lambda_1| = 0.654, 55 iterations to a residual of 1e-10), the semelparous variant whose four eigenvalues share one modulus, the slow-switching cell-state chain (5406 iterations and still only 5 digits), and Rayleigh quotient iteration on the trait correlation matrix (exercise C7 there). power_rq is that lecture’s power iteration with 2-norm normalisation and the Rayleigh quotient as the estimate; on A it reaches a residual of 1e-10 after 51 steps. This matrix (eigenvalues 3 + sqrt 3, 3, 3 - sqrt 3) is our small test case throughout the lecture. The questions for the next slides: how to get all eigenvalues at once, and how to make the convergence much faster than 0.63 per step. Both answers reuse the pieces above: power iteration on many vectors at once, and shifts.
